stories.title: Ida May Merry: enrollment and the Golden post office
stories.hook: Ida May Merry was born on 12 June 1898 to a Choctaw mother, and in later life she served the community of Golden as its postmaster.
body: On 27 April 1899, Bessie Merry swore an affidavit for the Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes. She was 19, the wife of Lewis Merry and the mother of a daughter, Ida May Merry, born on 12 June 1898; she was a Choctaw citizen by blood, and Lewis a citizen by marriage. On the same page midwife Eliza Jones swore that she had attended the birth. Only a clerk’s note on census card 5754, in a hand that might be a 17 or a 12, hints at another day. Bessie and the midwife gave 12 June under oath, and when Ida died in 1993 her obituary and her gravestone gave 12 June too.

On 6 October 1902 the Commission wrote to J. L. Merry at Glover about bringing his family and witnesses to support their enrollment application; the case was Choctaw D 128. The next year it wrote to Lewis Merry at the same place, under 7-D 128, about Louis, Bessie and Ida May. The same case, the same address and the same family make this a probable identification: J. L. and Lewis, or Louis, were very likely one man, though nothing yet proves it or tells what the initials stood for.

As the case dragged on, the family asked why their enrollment was still pending. On 24 October 1903 a commissioner answered that the application had not yet been decided; it was not a final enrollment decision. The letter went to Lewis Merry at Glover, Indian Territory, yet spoke of the application of Louis Merry, his wife Bessie and their minor child Ida May, so even the Commission used both spellings for the same man. On 18 January 1908 a letter to Louis returned his and Bessie’s marriage license and certificate after a copy was kept; they had married at Lukfata on 7 September 1896.

When Ida died, the February 1993 Bishinik remembered her as the daughter of J. L. and Bessie Durant Merry, born on 12 June 1898. Her mother had been born a Durant, so the Bessie Merry who swore the affidavit was very probably the Bessie Durant the family recalled in a 2008 notice. Her father was J. L. there rather than Lewis, but the letters of 1902–1903 probably join those names.

Ida was remembered as a former postmaster at Golden. After her husband died in 1941 she went to work as assistant postmaster and then postmaster, and she retired at 72. She was survived by a son, Lewis O. Whitfield. Her husband went by several forms of his name: he was Clinton O. C. Whitfield when Ida died, and Oliver C. Whitfield in 1920, when the household was Oliver C., Ida M. and a son Oliver L.

Ida’s daughter Catherine Ouida Carroll carried on the family’s postal work. She served 22 years at the post office in Golden and retired as postmaster in 1990. When she died in March 2007 she was remembered as the daughter of Oliver Clinton and Ida May Merry Whitfield, and her brothers who had gone before her as Omagene Clinton and Oliver Lewis Whitfield. Those fuller names explain the initials of 1920, though her brother was Lewis Oliver at some times and Oliver Lewis at others.

Another daughter, Elma, was born at Glover in 1918 and spent 30 years teaching and working in education in Oklahoma and New Mexico. When Elma Severn died, the December 2011 Biskinik named her father as Oliver Clinton and her mother as Ida Mae Merry Whitfield, Mae rather than May.

In the end the family was enrolled. On the final rolls Louis Merry, Bessie Merry and Ida May Merry stand together on Choctaw card 5754, Bessie as roll number 15526 and Ida May as 15527. Their enrollment belongs to history; it does not measure anyone’s DNA or settle present-day tribal citizenship.

By then Bessie Merry was 21, three-quarters Choctaw by blood; Ida May was 4, and three-eighths; and Louis Merry, 30, was enrolled as “IW,” an intermarried white citizen, roll 1363. Ida’s three-eighths was exactly half her mother’s fraction, as the Commission reckoned it when one parent was white. When their card was first made out on 26 April 1899 they had been 27, 19 and 1. Of all the families in this branch, only the Merrys were enrolled on the Dawes rolls. No Sandridge, Box, Whitfield, Cash, Logan of this family, Kernell or Nelson of this family was enrolled; the only Sandridges on the Choctaw rolls are a Freedmen family on card 81, with no known connection.

Bessie’s own parents were Peter and Ellen Durant of Bok Tuklo County. Both were dead by 26 April 1899, when card 5754 was made out, and so were Louis’s parents, Calvin and Elizabeth Merry, who were not Choctaw citizens. Durant was a prominent Choctaw name, with more than a hundred Durants on the rolls of 1898–1914, many of them full-blood, so it is Bessie’s own card, not the surname alone, that ties her to Peter and Ellen.

Ida’s childhood was divided. Her parents had separated: “She spent her childhood visiting her parents and attending Indian Boarding Schools.” Bessie married again and lies at Denison Cemetery, Idabel, under her later husband’s name: “Bessie E. Kernell, Nov. 11, 1879 – Mar. 22, 1950.” Ida’s father, it seems, married again too. An undated list of county marriage licenses, from an unnamed newspaper, includes “Joshua L. Merry to Mrs. Mattie Erwin, Glover.” The wedding is said to have been in 1908, and the name is sometimes spelled Ervin. Who Mattie was is uncertain. A Mattie E. Clay, Abner Clay’s wife, was known to the Commission under the name Clay through March 1904, but nothing in the Clay and Gibbs family papers, including the Dawes files for cards 507 and 966, names an Erwin or shows that she was the same woman.

The marriage license and his stone at Glover Cemetery together suggest the answer to the riddle of the initials. The stone reads “In sacred memory of J. L. Louis Merry, Apr. 10, 1872 – July 1, 1932,” with the line “Dear Papa, we miss you.” The J. L. of the 1902 letter and of Ida’s 1993 obituary, and the Lewis or Louis of Bessie’s 1899 affidavit and the rolls, was probably Joshua Louis Merry. He was remembered as the first postmaster at Glover, whose post office opened in 1901, so three generations of the family ran local post offices: J. L. at Glover, Ida at Golden, and Ida’s daughter Catherine at Golden. He is said to have been born in Sevier County, Arkansas, to John Calvin Merry and Eliza Jane McGregor, and the 1880 census household described below makes that very probable, though not yet certain.

Ida’s husband lies at Glover Cemetery under the name “O. C. (Clint) Whitfield, July 27, 1893 – Mar. 21, 1941.” He was Oliver Clinton, and people called him Clint, which is why he was Clinton O. C. when Ida died and Oliver Clinton when their children died. He is said to have been born at Chapel Hill, Sevier County, Arkansas, to William Franklin “Frank” Whitfield and Emma Ward, though those parents are not yet proved. Ida died on Thursday, 28 January 1993; she “passed away Thursday,” her family wrote. Her stone reads “Her children rose up and called her blessed.”

Joshua L. Merry was indeed Glover’s first postmaster, appointed on 26 June 1901. Grant Foreman counted him first among Glover’s postmasters in 1928, George H. Shirk did the same in 1948, and Joshua L. Merry was still postmaster there, under that full name, in 1903, 1905 and 1907.

Lewis came from Arkansas farm country. In June 1880, as Joshua L., eight years old, he was living on his father Calvin Merry's farm in Monroe Township, Sevier County, with his mother Eliza Jane and his brothers Festus Lee, Benjamin, John and George; his parents had married at Mount Ida in 1859, and his mother had been born a McGregor.

When Louis Merry died at Golden on the first of July 1932, the house could not hold the mourners. The service moved to the Golden schoolhouse, and even there scores stood outside while an Indian quartet sang and the Masons of Idabel waited to take him to the grave. Four brothers survived him, scattered from Valliant to California, the boys of Calvin Merry's Arkansas farm, and his daughter Ida, by then Mrs. Clint Whitfield.

stories.note: The 1993 original obituary directly names Bessie Durant Merry as Ida’s mother and Lewis O. Whitfield as her son. Her father is J. L. in that obituary, Lewis in the 1899 affidavit and Louis in the final-roll index; the 1903 letter supports Lewis/Louis as variants for the same applicant, while the 1902 J. L. letter shares the case reference and Glover address with the 1903 response. This supports a probable identification, not proof or a full first-name expansion. Her husband appears as Clinton O. C. in the obituary and Oliver C. in the census. The 1920 son Oliver L. is a probable match to Lewis Oliver. The final-roll index and census card 5754 have been checked, and several original application letters have been reviewed; the card names Bessie’s parents as Peter and Ellen Durant. Her death date, 28 January 1993, comes from her gravestone and agrees with the obituary’s “Thursday.” Catherine’s 2007 obituary supplies Oliver Clinton for her father and Oliver Lewis for her brother; the earlier recorded variants are retained. Elma’s 2011 obituary is another child obituary naming Oliver Clinton; that fuller display name is supported, while the census identification and earlier variant remain qualified.

stories.title: Alfreda Whitfield Sandridge and her Choctaw family
stories.hook: Alfreda Whitfield’s grandmother Ida Merry Whitfield and her great-grandmother Bessie Durant were both original Choctaw enrollees.
body: Alfreda Whitfield was born in 1939 at Wheelock, Oklahoma, to L. O. and Violet Box Whitfield. She married Larry Sandridge in 1958 at First Assembly of God in Broken Bow. Her family remembered her love of gardening, fishing and time with her grandchildren, and her work at the Choctaw Casino in Idabel.

Violet grew up in McCurtain County. In 1930 she was nine, a daughter in the household of Tyro Box and his wife Annie. Her father was T. S. Box, and Violet and her husband ran a grocery in Golden. The initials fit Tyro, though that rests on probability more than proof. Annie’s own family is described further on.

Tyro Box was probably a Texas boy. In 1900 a twelve-year-old Tyro Box was living in Van Zandt County, Texas, as a son of Alonzo and Emma Box. When Tyro Stevens Box registered for the World War I draft in McCurtain County, he gave a birth in May 1888 in Texas, though in 1930 his household gave his birthplace as Oklahoma. His unusual name and the same birth month make it probable, though not proven, that the Van Zandt County boy was Violet’s father and that Alonzo and Emma were her grandparents.

When Alfreda and Larry reached their 50th anniversary, the family’s notice in the Choctaw Nation’s Biskinik remembered Alfreda’s grandmother Ida Merry Whitfield and her great-grandmother Bessie Durant, both original enrollees. In 1899 Bessie Merry had sworn that she was the mother of Ida May Merry and that Lewis Merry was the father, so Bessie Merry was very probably the Bessie Durant the family remembered.

Alfreda’s father, Lewis Oliver Whitfield, was probably the boy called Oliver L. Whitfield in 1920, in the McCurtain County household of Oliver C. and Ida M. Whitfield; his age and family fit, though his names were the other way round. Years later the family’s Biskinik notice remembered the late Lewis Whitfield and Ida Merry Whitfield among this branch’s elders.

In the end the family’s own notices settle most of the Box questions. When Annie F. Box died in 1959 she left a daughter, Mrs. Louis Whitfield of Golden. When Violet died in 1962 her father was T. S. Box of Millerton. And when Tyro Stephen Box died in 1967 he was remembered as born on 22 May 1888 at Pittsburg, Texas, the same month and year as the boy of 1900 and the man who registered for the draft. Annie had been born a Logan. Her brothers were Rob and Walter Logan and her sister was Mrs. Bell Culpepper of Dallas, and at Wheelock Cemetery her parents are remembered as Dudley Logan and Annie Wedgeworth Logan. Dudley Timothy Logan came to Titus County, Texas, from Greene County, Alabama, and died there in 1898, eight years before Annie moved from Mount Pleasant to McCurtain County.

Family tradition gives Tyro’s mother as Emillie Wilkerson, and others have suggested the same Wilkerson maiden name for Emma Box, and Texas birth entries for two of her children, Claude in 1891 and Flossie in 1894, now give their mother as Emily Wilkerson.

stories.title: Audrey Sandridge: wartime work and a community switchboard
stories.hook: From a McCurtain County childhood to wartime work and the telephone office, Audrey Nelson Sandridge’s life connected work and community.
body: Audrey Inez Nelson was born in 1917 in the Redland area of McCurtain County, Oklahoma, the daughter of William Nelson and Julia Robbins, as her family remembered them. In 1920 she was two years old, at home with William and Julia Nelson.

During the 1940s, Audrey and her husband Lemuel Sandridge worked at the Red River Arsenal plant making ammunition. Audrey also worked the switchboard there. After they returned to Broken Bow, she worked as one of the early telephone operators at Pine Telephone Company.

Her community life centred on Broken Bow First Assembly of God, where she worked with the young people, the Sunday school and the fellowship meals. Audrey and Lemuel’s son Larry carried the family story into another generation in McCurtain County.

stories.title: Alice Walker’s Illinois beginnings
stories.hook: Alice Walker grew up in Washington County, Illinois, and died in Houston in 1922, with her mother’s name and even her birth year still uncertain.
body: In 1860 and again in 1870, an Alice M. Walker was living in Washington County, Illinois, in the household of Wm P. and Abigail Walker. In those years no one wrote down how the people in a household were related to one another.

By 1900 Floyd and Alice Livesay were living in Brazoria County, Texas, with children who included Lester W. Livesay. When their son Walter died in 1912, his parents were named as Floyd Livesay and Alice Walker. In 1920 Floyd H. and Alice M. Livesay were living together in Houston.

Alice May Livesay died in Houston on 23 October 1922, a married housewife born in Illinois, and was buried at Pearland the next day. The informant, who signed as F. C. Livesay rather than F. H., gave her father as Wm P. Walker, though the handwritten surname is hard to make out.

Her mother was given as Addie Bruce, born in Illinois, a surname sometimes read as Brace. The mother in the Walker home of 1860 and 1870 was Abigail. Addie Bruce and Abigail Walker are different names, and no record yet establishes whether they identify the same woman, so Alice’s mother remains uncertain.

Even her birthday was in doubt at her death. She was said to have been born on 11 January 1860, yet her age was given as 67 years, 9 months and 12 days, which would mean 11 January 1855. The girl in the Walker household was born about 1859, and Alice’s headstone at Pearland reads 11 January 1859. The census and the stone agree on about 1859, the likeliest of the three, though the other two cannot be ruled out.

Birth field: 11 January 1860; age 67 years, 9 months, 12 days implies 1855; the matching census child suggests about 1859. The identification of Alice across records remains probable. Abigail Walker and any proposed Abigail Schanck identity have not been merged with Addie Bruce or attached as Alice’s mother. This could concern the later census household, but the groom’s middle initial differs from Wm P. and the bride’s surname differs from Addie Bruce. The original marriage record has not been examined; neither this couple’s identity with the census household nor Schanck’s identity with Alice’s recorded mother is established.

stories.title: From Illinois to the Texas Gulf Coast
stories.hook: Floyd and Alice Livesay brought their family from Illinois to Brazoria County, Texas, in the mid-1890s, and later generations put down roots there.
body: By 1900 Floyd and Alice Livesay were living in Brazoria County, Texas, with children born in Illinois and in Texas. Their son Lester W. had been born in Illinois in November 1894, and their daughter Ruth in Texas about 1898, so the family made the move between those births. Why they came is not known.

The household Floyd and Alice kept in 1900 was a full one. Walter, the eldest, was twenty; the next son, seventeen, whose name was taken down as something like Call T., was almost certainly the William Paul who would be buried at Pearland; Melvin was twelve, Lester six, and Ruth, born in Texas, two. Floyd and Alice had been married twenty years. By 1910 the house had emptied and filled again: Lester at fifteen, Ruth at twelve, and a late son, Earl, aged six and born in Texas. In 1920, in Harris County, Floyd was sixty-five and Alice sixty-two, and Earl, sixteen, was the only child left at home.

Floyd ran a grocery in Pearland. When he died in 1932 the Houston Chronicle said he had come from Illinois to Pearland about 37 years before, in the mid-1890s, which fits the birthplaces of his children. Among his survivors was a son, L. W. Livesay.

Lester W. Livesay married Sadah H. McCormick in Harris County on 10 October 1911. By 1920 they were living in Harris County with their young children, among them a son, Lester Jr., who was remembered at his death as the son of Lester W. Sr. and Sadah McCormick. His railroad career and ranches carried the story into Pearland and East Texas.

When Walter Livesay, the eldest son, died, his parents were given as Floyd Livesay and Alice Walker. Floyd himself died a widower and a retired groceryman in Houston on 5 May 1932, and was buried at Pearland the next day. He was said then to have been born in Illinois on 5 February 1857, though in 1900 his birth had been given as February 1856. In 1900 even Lester’s birth month and year did not quite agree with his age.

Floyd’s boyhood was probably spent in Washington County, Illinois. In 1860 a four-year-old Floyd H. Livesay was living there in a household headed by Lydia Livesay, with David Livesay, 28. Ten years later a fourteen-year-old Floyd H. was living with David in the same county. Some have proposed David and Tabitha Flannigan as Floyd’s parents, but no one then wrote down how the people in those households were related, and there was no Tabitha in the house in 1860. Those households are a promising trail, but they do not tell who his parents were.

When Floyd died, the informant, E. W. Livesay, left both parents’ names and birthplaces unknown, so nothing from his death ties him to the Illinois household. Whether David Livesay and Tabitha Flannigan were his parents is still an open question.

Within three years of Floyd and Alice’s move to Pearland, the Handbook of Texas counted 75 residents and twelve businesses there. The 1900 hurricane “destroyed fruit trees and slowed growth for a period of time,” and a 1918 freeze ended a later revival based on oranges and figs.

Floyd and Alice outlived two grown sons. Walter, their eldest, died on 26 January 1912, aged 31. The Houston Post reported that he “died Friday afternoon in a sanitarium in Houston” and was buried from the Sid Westheimer parlors “under the auspices of Magnolia Camp No. 13, Woodmen of the World,” in Evergreen Cemetery. The cause is said to have been renal tuberculosis. William Paul Livesay died in San Antonio on 13 April 1915, aged 32, and was buried at Pearland. Alice died in 1922 and Floyd in 1932. They lie side by side in the Old Settlers Cemetery at Pearland.

Floyd Livesay brought his family down from Illinois to Pearland about 1895 and kept a grocery there. He died in Houston in May 1932, at the home of his son Earl on Pearson Street, and was carried back to Pearland to be buried. Ruth, Lester, Earl and Melvin followed him to the grave, with nine grandchildren and two great-grandchildren.

stories.title: The Sandridge family of Broken Bow
stories.hook: The Sandridges went from a farm near Broken Bow, Oklahoma, to service aboard a Navy helicopter carrier.
body: Larry Lamar Sandridge grew up in Broken Bow, Oklahoma, where he graduated from high school in 1956. He served in the Army and Navy as an aviation electrician, including service aboard the helicopter carrier USS Thetis Bay. His parents were Lemuel Lamar Sandridge and Audrey Inez Nelson.

In 2008 Larry and his wife Alfreda Whitfield Sandridge celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary, and the Choctaw Nation’s Biskinik printed the news with their photograph. Their marriage joined the Sandridge and Whitfield families, and when Alfreda died she was remembered with their daughter and with her own parents.

Larry’s father, Lemuel Sandridge of Broken Bow, was a son of Clinton Lamar Sandridge, who was born in Arkansas and came to McCurtain County in 1919 to farm. When Clinton died in 1961 the McCurtain Gazette counted Lemuel among his sons. Through Clinton the family reaches back into an earlier generation of Sandridges in the region.

Larry and Alfreda had a daughter. In 1930 Lemuel was at home with Clinton and Maggie. Clinton’s age that year does not agree with the birth years given at his death or carved on his gravestone, and Maggie’s maiden name is still uncertain.

stories.title: Railroad and ranch: the Livesays in East Texas
stories.hook: Lester Livesay worked on the Southern Pacific Railroad and ran cattle ranches in Pearland and Carthage.
body: Lester Woodrow Livesay Jr. was born in Houston in 1916, the son of Lester W. Livesay Sr. and Sadah McCormick. He grew up in Pearland and became a Southern Pacific Railroad engineer. He also operated a cattle ranch there, then began another ranch after moving to Carthage in 1961.
When he died in 2001 he was remembered with his wife, Barbara Phillips Livesay, and with family across several generations, an East Texas Livesay family whose story leads on into Oklahoma.
Lester and Barbara were the parents of Wayne Woodrow Livesay, and the family has confirmed the generation that followed; living relatives are named only by their family roles.

Railroading ran on into the next generation. Wayne Woodrow Livesay, born in Houston on 13 February 1940, became a locomotive engineer. He worked, as his family remembered, “for Burlington Northern Santa Fe Railroad for 30 years and retired in 2000.” He died in April 2013 at Cushing, Nacogdoches County, close to his mother’s birthplace, and is buried in McKnight Cemetery there.

stories.title: The air commander behind the Andrews name
stories.hook: From the Stevenson family in Tennessee came Frank Maxwell Andrews, a pioneer of American air power and the namesake of Joint Base Andrews.
body: Frank Maxwell Andrews was born in Nashville on 3 February 1884, the son of James David Andrews and Lula Adaline Maxwell. He graduated from West Point in 1906 and began his Army career in the cavalry. During the First World War he entered aviation and earned his pilot’s wings in 1918.

In 1935 Andrews took command of the newly organized General Headquarters Air Force. He argued for a modern long-range bomber force and supported developing and buying the Boeing B-17. By 1943 he was commanding United States forces in the European theater, where American and Allied forces were preparing for the campaigns ahead.

When his father died in 1937, Frank recalled how the family had traveled to a world’s fair by train under oil lamps when he was a boy. Years later he flew his father to the Chicago fair in an amphibious airplane, landing on Lake Michigan.

On 3 May 1943 Andrews was killed when the B-24 bomber Hot Stuff crashed in Iceland. In 1945 Camp Springs Army Air Field in Maryland was renamed Andrews Field in his honor; it became Andrews Air Force Base in 1948 and is now part of Joint Base Andrews.

The family connection runs through the Stevenson line. Elam and Lydia Stevenson’s sons included Abner Arrington Stevenson, our ancestor, and his brother James Calvin. James’s daughter Eliza Catherine married William Thomas Andrews; their son James David was Frank’s father. Elam and Lydia are the shared ancestors.

stories.title: A minister’s memoir that connected two families
stories.hook: In 1912 William Thomas Andrews set down the names of his wife’s parents and their children, preserving a link between the Stevensons and the Andrews family.
body: William Thomas Andrews grew up in Giles County, Tennessee, after his mother brought the family there from Limestone County, Alabama. He was licensed to preach in 1856. On 30 November of that year he married Eliza Catherine Stevenson, daughter of the Rev. James C. and Margaret C. Stevenson.

In a 1912 autobiography Andrews named their five sons and daughter. The first son named was James David Andrews of Nashville, the future father of Frank Maxwell Andrews. James David’s later memorial also named William Thomas and Eliza as his parents.

Andrews spent his first fourteen years in ministry as a local preacher, then joined the North Alabama Conference. His assignments took him to Limestone, Scottsboro, Florence, Gadsden, Talladega and other communities. His published account lists those appointments across decades of church work.
His portrait was printed as the frontispiece of the book.

stories.title: Junior Thompson, from Jeter to Speer
stories.hook: A childhood in a household of several generations, and a marriage that joined the Thompson and Hulsey families.
body: William “Junior” Thompson Jr. grew up on his parents’ farm at Jeter in Choctaw County, Oklahoma. In 1940 he was six, sharing the household with Simon and Frances Thompson, his brothers and sisters, and his Pisachubbe grandparents.

At sixteen, in 1950, he was still at home in Jeter and still in school, as he had been at Hugo a few years before. His father worked his own farm, and his Pisachubbe grandmother still lived with them; Junior grew up in a house where children and elders lived side by side.
By December 1956 Junior was living out at Speer, and that month he and Mary Ellen Hulsey of Hugo took out their marriage license, joining the Thompson and Hulsey branches of the family.

He stayed close to Hugo all his life. He was living there when his father Simon died in 1990 and when his sister Ethel Hamill died in 2002, the same year he lost Mary Ellen. He died on 17 February 2007.

He and Mary Ellen share one granite marker at Woodlawn Cemetery in Choctaw County, under a scroll lettered THOMPSON: "Mary E. / Aug. 22, 1938 / Nov. 4, 2002" on one side and "William, Jr. / Mar. 14, 1934 / Feb. 17, 2007" on the other.
He died on Saturday, 17 February 2007, at 72, and Miller & Miller of Hugo held his funeral three days later.

stories.title: Lizzie’s road from Alabama to Apache
stories.hook: Married in Alabama in 1889, she made her later home near her children in southwestern Oklahoma.
body: Lizzie Newton was born in Etowah County, Alabama, on 20 February 1873. She married John M. Shackleford there on 1 December 1889. Her father Balas Newton gave written consent to the marriage.

In 1880 seven-year-old Elizabeth was in the Etowah County household of Balus Newton and his wife Mary. The rare name, place and age make this a probable match for Lizzie and her father in the 1889 marriage. Mary Ann Dockery, who married a Bailus Newton in 1867, is a probable mother, though no record says so.

The family’s travels eventually took Lizzie to Texas. In 1933 she moved from Dawson County to the Apache community in Caddo County, Oklahoma. She belonged to the Baptist church, and several of her grown children also made their homes in or around Apache.
She spent her final days at the home of her son Ed, six miles southwest of town, and died there on 8 November 1951, aged seventy-eight. She was buried in Fairview Cemetery at Apache.

Her family had grown across Oklahoma, Texas and California. At her death it included nine surviving children, forty-two grandchildren and sixteen great-grandchildren. Sons Ed and John and daughters Mrs. Joe Haskell and Helen Josey lived at Apache; other children had settled in Lawton, Texas and California.

stories.title: A miner’s household in the Ouachitas
stories.hook: In 1880 B. F. Hulsey worked as a miner and raised a young family in Montgomery County, Arkansas.
body: B. F. Hulsey was thirty-two in Center Township in June 1880. Born in Georgia, he was working as a miner in the Ouachita country of western Arkansas. His wife Sarah G., thirty, had been born in Arkansas.
B. F. was not the only miner on the page: William W. Gleason and C. W. Dyer also gave that occupation. Mining was part of the local community, though nothing shows the men worked together.

Three children were at home: Margaret M., six; George W., four; and Charles F., five months. The household offers a likely childhood home for the later George Washington Hulsey of Story. George’s own 1918 draft registration gives a December 1875 birth, consistent with the four-year-old.

Margaret M. is called a daughter and George W. and Charles F. sons of B. F. Margaret had been born about 1874, George about 1875–76, and Charles early in 1880. Sarah G. appears as B. F.’s wife. Those relationships establish the household, but they do not expressly establish that Sarah was every child’s biological mother.

A later family account connects a Benjamin F. Hulsey with a son George Washington and children named Charles, Mary and Francis. It also gives a wife named Margaret Partain and dates that conflict with other accounts. The overlapping names are useful clues, but it does not resolve the mother’s identity or prove that all the Benjamin Hulsey records concern one man.

Of Sarah G. herself there is little more than her age and her Arkansas birth: her father was born in North Carolina and her mother in Tennessee, which outlines her own family without naming either parent. Her maiden name and full given names are still unknown. She is not Sarah Rebecca Graves, whom George later married, and nothing yet identifies her with Sylvania Susane Partain, the name a descendant's photo caption gives for George's mother.

stories.note: The original 1880 census records B. F. Hulsey, 32, born Georgia, with wife Sarah G., 30, born Arkansas, and son George W., 4, in Center Township, Montgomery County, Arkansas. George’s December 1875 birth in the 1900 Sulphur Springs census and 24 December 1875 birth on his 1918 draft card are consistent with the child’s age. A 1977 family query associates a Benjamin F. Hulsey with a son named George Washington. The connection remains probable: no record yet explicitly connects the adult George, husband of Sarah Rebecca Graves, to the named 1880 parents. This household has not been securely identified with the separate Benjamin Franklin Hulsey biography or with Sylvania Partain. The 1977 query is an unsourced family-research submission with conflicting names and dates; it calls the wife Margaret Partain and gives a 1921 death. It is supporting evidence, not proof of the connection or of a mother’s identity. Sarah G. is recorded as B. F.'s wife, not explicitly as George's mother, so she is a probable mother or stepmother. This story now includes the shorter entry about Sarah G.; its old link opens this page.

stories.title: Moonshine and federal court in Hugo
stories.hook: An October arrest report and later federal court notices preserve a different side of life in Hugo.
body: On a Saturday night in October 1961, two men looking for whisky visited John W. Moffitt in Hugo. They left without a purchase, but Moffitt later caught up with them in town and offered a half-gallon. When he handed it over, the buyers showed their badges: one was a federal alcohol-tax agent and the other worked for the state liquor board.
Moffitt, thirty-six, was arrested and brought before U.S. Commissioner Lon Kile on Monday. His bond was set at $1,000.

Oklahoma had been dry since statehood. Voters repealed prohibition on 7 April 1959 and allowed package sales, but they refused local option, and liquor by the drink stayed illegal until 1984. The "Cannon raids" of the late 1950s had already shut off most of the state's supply. In that Oklahoma a half-gallon sold in town was a crime.

The following spring, federal court news named John Winfred Moffitt of Hugo. In May 1962 he pleaded guilty to two counts of violating the federal liquor stamp law. A June sentencing list recorded John Winfred Moffitt of Choctaw County receiving two years’ probation for operating a still.

stories.title: The consent folded into their marriage book
stories.hook: A father’s permission survived with John and Lizzie’s Alabama marriage papers.
body: John M. Shackleford and Lizzie Newton obtained their marriage license in Etowah County, Alabama, on 30 November 1889. A small note was kept over the page: permission from her father, Balas Newton, for the couple to marry.

The consent is dated 28 November. John certified two days later that he had written and signed it at Balas’s direction. In a separate statement, sworn before the probate judge, he presented the permission and explicitly identified Lizzie as Newton’s daughter. The wedding was on 1 December 1889.

By 1900 John and Elizabeth were raising their family in Gilbert Precinct, Etowah County. Their daughter Mary Tinsley later married Woodford Grady Moffitt, carrying this Alabama branch into the Moffitt family in Oklahoma.

Etowah County had been created only 23 years before the wedding, and for two of those years, 1866 to 1868, it was called Baine County. In 1900 the household at Gilbert held John, 37, Elizabeth, 28, and five living children: “Balous” 8, Myrtle 6, May 5, Robert 3 and Eddie 8 months. Mary, born 4 June 1895, was the “May, 5.” Her brothers and sisters were Balis Anthony (1892-1982, who died in Los Angeles County), Robert Yates (1897-1961), John Newton (1906-2002), Hazel Marzee King (1908-1980), Edward Richard (1910-1988) and Helen Elizabeth Josey (1915-1997). Notices of 1961 and 1981 also name sisters Josephine Haskell, Eulah Tillman and Beulah Hutchins, who do not fit the 1900 household.

Hazel was born at Rattan in Delta County, Texas, so the family was in northeast Texas about 1908 before reaching Martin County. By 1930 John Morgan was there with his wife and children, and Grady and Mary and their six boys were living with them. In 1930 his birth year was given as 1863; his marker says 1862.

John Morgan Shackleford's grave in Evergreen Cemetery at Stanton, Martin County, Texas, lies on the far north side, to the right of the first gate. The flat granite marker is carved with a bird and flowers and reads "John M. Shackleford / Sept. 30, 1862 / May 22, 1930." Lizzie, who outlived him by twenty-one years, is buried in Oklahoma at Apache. His own parents are unknown.

In 1933 Lizzie moved from Dawson County, Texas, to Apache, Caddo County, Oklahoma, where several of her grown children lived. She died at her son Ed’s home southwest of town on 8 November 1951 and is buried at Fairview Cemetery, Apache.

The Shackelfords of Virginia trace to an immigrant, Roger, who received a grant in Gloucester County in 1658. A Shackleford family history of 1940 says the family had no coat of arms, and Mary’s descent from Roger is not proved.

stories.title: A father’s permission, preserved on paper
stories.hook: Named as Lizzie Newton’s father in the original papers for her 1889 marriage.
body: In November 1889 Balas Newton gave written permission for his daughter Lizzie to marry John M. Shackleford in Etowah County, Alabama, and John swore to it.

In 1880 a Balus Newton lived in Etowah County with wife Mary and daughter Elizabeth, aged seven. Their uncommon names, location and Elizabeth’s age make them a probable match for the Balas and Lizzie of the 1889 marriage. Mary is called Balus’s wife, but nothing says she was Elizabeth’s mother.

The 1880 home held nine people. Balus was forty-four and farming; Mary, thirty-six, was recorded as keeping house. The seven children listed as Balus’s sons and daughters ranged from a twelve-year-old son, whose occupation was farm hand, to an eight-month-old daughter born in November. Between them were Ann, ten; Lindsey, nine; Elizabeth, seven; Hezekiah, four; and Amanda, three. Alabama was the birthplace of Mary and all seven children, and was given for Balus too, though the Confederate veteran of that name was born in Pickens District, South Carolina, so the match is probable, not certain.
In March 1901 a Balus Newton made final proof on land before the county clerk, but no age or family names are given, so he may or may not have been Lizzie’s father.

Lizzie's father had fought for the Confederacy twice over: at twenty-five in Company E of the 1st Florida in 1861, and later in Company E of the 51st Alabama Cavalry, until he came home in April 1865. Born in Pickens District, South Carolina, in October 1835, he was still drawing an Alabama pension near Gadsden at seventy-five and signed his papers with a mark.

stories.title: Singing, holidays and a house full of family
stories.hook: From a Jeter farm childhood to a family of children, grandchildren and Christmas gatherings.
body: Faye Smith was the youngest child of Charles Oscar and Artie Pearl Smith, born at Forney, Choctaw County, on 23 March 1929. Her father had been born at Hagansport, Texas, in 1889 and her mother in Butler County, Kentucky, in 1898; they married in 1915 and crossed the Red River into Oklahoma, so Faye's farm childhood sat at the end of two families' moves from Kentucky and Texas. She was "Fay May," 2, at Jeter in 1930, the youngest of four, and "Fay," 12, in 1940, when the family was still on a rented farm on Hugo Route 1 and her father, who had worked every week of 1939, reported an income of $105.

She married John W. Moffitt at Paris, Texas, on 12 June 1947. She was eighteen. John, born at Frogville in 1925, had been discharged from the Navy on 9 May 1946 after service on a floating drydock in the Pacific and the minesweeper USS Chief, a little more than a year before.

She made her home around family life. Singing, shopping, visits with friends and trips to the Nutrition Center filled her days. Holidays were a particular pleasure, and her Christmas portrait catches her smiling beside the tree.

John died on 19 September 1990, and she outlived him by more than twenty-four years. By her death at Paris on 23 December 2014, the family had grown to 20 grandchildren, 38 great-grandchildren and two great-great-grandchildren. Her funeral was held in Hugo, with burial at Grant Cemetery beside John, in the cemetery where her parents also lie.
In April 1950, at 907 South J Street in Hugo, she was “Marylyn F.”

stories.title: Edith, the Thompson daughter who was proud to be Choctaw
stories.hook: Junior's younger sister was the baby of the house in 1940, and she was proud of her Choctaw heritage all her life.
body: Edith Irene Thompson was born at Hugo on 27 December 1939 and was the baby of the household on the Thompson farm at Jeter the following spring. Hugo itself was only thirty-eight years old; it was founded in 1901 where two railroads crossed and became the seat of Choctaw County. Her parents were Simon and Frances (Pisachubbe) Thompson, and she shared the crowded farmhouse with her brothers and sisters, among them William "Junior" Thompson, the grandfather of this family, and with her grandparents Robert and Lizzie Pisachubbe, who lived under the same roof.

Her father had been enrolled as a baby on the Dawes rolls in 1899. When she died in 2012 it was said that she loved her family very much, enjoyed spending time with them, and was "especially proud of her Choctaw Indian Heritage."

She married twice. Her first husband, Bert Jones, died before her; at her death she was married to Cleatus Williams. Her children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren lived around Hugo and Blackwell. Edith died at Durant on 12 April 2012, aged 72. By then she had buried both parents, her brothers Leonard and Junior, and her sisters Ethel Hamill and Norma Homer. Only one brother, Bernie of Grant, was named among her survivors.

stories.title: A Regulator the Governor wouldn't pardon
stories.hook: One of thirteen men left out of Governor Tryon's 1768 pardon.
body: The Regulators were backcountry farmers in North Carolina who rose up (1766–1771) against corrupt officials and illegal fees. William Moffitt of Deep River was in the movement from its start: in August 1766 the inhabitants of Deep River chose "Wm Cox and Wm Masset" (a misreading of Maffet) to attend the Regulators' first general meeting. In 1768 he signed their petitions alongside the movement's leaders, Herman Husband and James Hunter, and on 21 May 1768 he was named first on the committee to carry their grievances to the Governor.

On 3 October 1768, at Hillsborough, Royal Governor William Tryon pardoned the Regulators except thirteen named men, and "William Moffitt" is one of them. He was never outlawed, and a general pardon in 1769 covered "all persons concerned in the said late Insurrection." His name is on the memorial trail at Alamance Battleground, and James Otis listed him among "the patriots of upper Carolina" in his 1901 boys' novel The Boy Spies with the Regulators.

William married Mary Davies at Cane Creek Quaker Meeting on 2 April 1763, when he was 23. He and Hugh Moffitt, probably his brother, married sisters, and Hugh ran the first mill on Richland Creek, which gave the community of Moffitt, North Carolina, its name; the Moffitt's Mills post office lasted from 1823 to 1935.

His will, dated 13 March 1796, begins “I William Moffitt of Randolph County in the province of North Carolina, being weak in body.” He gave his sons Robert, William and David land, and his daughters Naomi (Neomi Macky), Catharine Cox, Hannah Cox, Mary Wilkinson and Margaret £3 each, with Margaret also getting cows, sheep and a bed.

Robert, our ancestor, received the 250 acres William had bought of William Cox, except “the new field that is cleared upon the River,” which his mother kept for life. William got the 225-acre plantation where his father lived, with a share reserved for Mary while she was a widow. David, who was clearly under age, got land on Tibs Run, wagon iron “brought from Pig River,” and a quarter of a lot in Campbelltown in Cumberland County. If David died young, his brothers inherited and each sister would get £15.

“My Loveing Wife Mary Moffitt” received the wagon, the still, the plantation tools and the stock, and was named executrix with “my son Robart Moffitt” as executor. The witnesses were Hugh Moffitt and Charles Moffitt. The Quaker records of Center Meeting show Robert, “son of William & Mary,” marrying Martha Chamness in 1797.

William and Mary had eight children: Naomi (born 11 June 1763), Catharine (1765), Hannah (about 1771), Mary (1773), Margaret (1774), Robert (1778), William (1781) and David (4 February 1785). All five daughters and three sons are named in Mary's will.

Family legend says the Moffitts came from Dumfriesshire, Scotland, descended from a "Robert Bruce Moffitt" born in 1716. No record names such a man. The Alamance Battleground Book of Remembrance instead says William was born about 1740 in Donegal, Ireland, to Robert and Martha Steward Moffitt and came through Philadelphia, which fits Ulster Scots, but gives no source.

His name is also on the Regulators' letter, address and indictment of September 1768. Court records add two earlier items: a deed proved by "Wm. Moffitt" in May 1765 and his witnessing of William Cox's will, proved at Hillsborough in February 1767.

A Moffitt genealogy of 1928 for the descendants of Silas Moffitt of Hamilton County, Indiana, gives that family's own tradition of William's origins: sons of "Robert and Margaret Moffat" who "migrated to Donegal County, Ireland," and whose children included James, Charles, William, Adam, Margaret, Catharine, Robert, Mary, Hugh, Patrick and John. It says that "William married Mary Davis and Hugh married Hannah Davis, both being daughters of Charles Davis," and that Mary Moffitt Wilkinson, "our own foremother," was "said to have been their fifth child," married to William Wilkinson, "an Englishman, on the 26th day of the 3rd month, 1795." This agrees with the "Mary Wilkinson" of William's will, and the two witnesses to that will, Hugh and Charles Moffitt, match two of the brothers in the book's list. The parents differ from the Book of Remembrance's Robert and Martha Steward Moffitt, so the Donegal family is tradition, not record.

The book also repeats a story about "the Davis millions." Hamilton County heirs, it says, raised money to send an agent to the old country to look into an inheritance, but "this supposed wealth, like the fortune at the foot of the rainbow, was always just out of reach."

The Bible record of Abijah Moffitt names William's parents: Robert Moffitt, born in Scotland and later of County Donegal, and Margaret Stuart, with eleven children, six of whom came to America. It adds that William and his brother Hugh both married Davis daughters in North Carolina, which matches William's 1763 marriage to Mary Davies. The Alamance Battleground Book gives the mother as Martha Steward. Both accounts are family-based, not contemporary records.

In an 1853 letter, Hugh's son Joseph Moffitt named his father's brothers, including William, and said their parents were Robert Moffitt and Margaret Stewart. Joseph also named his mother Hannah Davis and said her sister Mary married a Moffitt. This fits the William and Mary Davies of Randolph County, though the letter does not explicitly name Mary's husband as William. The surviving account is a 1924 printed transcription, not the original manuscript. Hugh's 1799 Chatham County will independently names his wife Hannah and son Joseph, strengthening the identification of the letter's family.

stories.title: The baby of the 1899 enrollment
stories.hook: Enrolled as a Choctaw at seven and a half months, a 19-year-old farmer in 1918, and in 1940 the head of a house with three generations under its roof.
body: Simon was born on 4 May 1899, and by autumn he was the youngest person in the family's Choctaw enrollment, only 7½ months old. His mother Betsy and his grandmother Emeline Tims, who had been the midwife at his birth, both swore statements so that he could be enrolled, and he received his own land allotment near his parents'.
When he registered for the World War I draft on 12 September 1918 he was 19, a farmer working for his father at Corinne, of medium height and build, with black hair and brown eyes.

By 1940 he and Frances owned a $400 farm at Jeter, in a county where nearly three of every four farmers were tenants, and were raising five children: Ethel 13, Leonard 10, Junior 6, Bernice 3 and a baby daughter. Frances's parents Robert and Lizzie Pisachubbe lived with them, with Robert and Lizzie's orphaned niece and nephews, Frances's double first cousins. Simon had three years of schooling and had worked all 52 weeks of 1939. When he died in 1990 he was remembered as a retired farmer and a Methodist who had lived in the Hugo area for 64 years, and he left 17 grandchildren and 20 great-grandchildren. He and Frances, who married in 1925, are buried at Long Creek Cemetery near Hugo, also called Choctaw Cemetery.

The timing was close. His mother's family applied for enrollment on 1 May 1899, three days before the 4 May birth date given in the sworn statements, so his own statement was added afterward. His enrollment was recorded on 19 December 1899; the statement was returned for correction and the corrected one filed on 20 February 1900. A later account gives 14 May 1899 as his birthday, but the statements, made much closer to the event, say 4 May. At four he received a 160-acre homestead, the northeast quarter of Section 11, Township 5 South, Range 19 East, and on 6 December 1907 he was issued a citizenship certificate at Hugo.

His wife's parents had been enrolled that same year: her mother Lizzie, a 7-year-old daughter of Legion and Molsey Austin of Fowlerville, and her father Robert Pisachubbe, who was 11 and lived at Goodland. The two families lived forty miles apart in 1899 and joined in 1925 when Simon married their daughter Frances.

stories.title: Neighbors at Hagansport
stories.hook: In 1910 Oscar Smith, 19, and Pearl Satterfield, 11, lived a few doors apart in the same Texas farm community. Four years later they married.
body: Charles Oscar Smith was born on 29 May 1889 at Hagansport, Franklin County, Texas, a farm community that grew up around a Sulphur River crossing called Hagan's Port. In the 1880s it had about 150 people, a gin, a mill, four churches and a one-room school.

In June 1900 "Oscar," 10, was in the Franklin County household of John and Emma Smith, with Vera, Luina, Lona, Allie and baby Jimmie. John owned his farm free of mortgage. Emma died on 15 March 1905, at 37, and her stone at Hagansport reads "Emma / Wife of / J.B. SMITH / Gone but not forgotten."

By April 1910 John B. Smith had remarried, and Oscar, 19, was working on the home farm. On the same day, a few doors away, were the Satterfield family: John C. and Samantha, lately from Kentucky, and their daughter Pearl, 11. Oscar and Artie Pearl Satterfield married in Franklin County, Texas, on 15 November 1915.

They later crossed the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma. Charles died on 17 August 1971 and Artie on 21 July 1983, and they are buried together in Grant Cemetery, south of Hugo. John B. Smith died in 1918 and lies beside Emma at Hagansport, in a grave "marked with a wooden stob."

When he registered for the draft in 1942 he gave his name as Charlie Oscar Smith, 52, of Forney in Choctaw County, with mail at Hugo Route 1, working on a farm. He gave his birthplace as 'Higgensport, Texas,' the Franklin County community more often spelled Hagansport, and named Mrs. Pearl Smith as the person who would always know his address.

Charles and Pearl can be followed from Texas to the Choctaw County farms. Their first daughter, Nellie Mae, was born at Talco, Texas, on 3 April 1917, two years after their marriage; by 1920, "C O Smith," 28, and Pearl were renting a farm at Oakes Township in Choctaw County, Oklahoma. In 1930 they were at Jeter with four children, and in 1940 "Oscar Msith," 50, was a farmer on rented land on Hugo Route 1 who had worked all 52 weeks of 1939 for an income of $105. When Nellie died in 1973 her parents were given as "Charley O. Smith" and "Pearl Satterfield."

stories.title: Judge and Choctaw senator
stories.hook: Spencer Academy, Mount Hermon and Roanoke College, then county clerk, legislator and judge in Cedar County.
body: Joseph was a full-blood Choctaw, born in Cedar County in December 1861, two miles west of High Hill church. His parents were John and Betsy Thompson, both dead by 1899; his son Joel said John died when Joseph was nine.

In 1891, while he was still a young man, it was written of Joseph that he was educated at Spencer Academy and at 'Mount Harmon Institute, Northfield' (D. L. Moody's Mount Hermon School for boys in Massachusetts), and finished at Roanoke College in Salem, Virginia, where he stayed until 1886 (a date hard to square with the 20 acres of his own that he was farming in Cedar County in 1885, so the years in the sketch are loose). Joel remembered it in a different order: three years at Roanoke, then three years at a college in Massachusetts studying law.

In 1885, at 24, he was farming 20 acres of his own in Cedar County, with a horse, six cattle and 30 hogs. He began as a schoolteacher, was appointed county clerk of Cedar County in 1889, and the next year was elected to the lower house of the Choctaw Council, 'one of the youngest members of the legislature.' Joel said he later served as County Judge of Cedar County, holding court at Sulphur Springs near present-day Rattan, and about six years as a Senator.

He married Betsy Tims in 1889. They started in a one-room log house. In 1901 he built a big white house with two front rooms, a wide hall, an L-shaped kitchen and dining room, and lots of porches, 300 yards from High Hill Methodist Church. He sat on the school board, raised an orphan boy named Wister Davis, and had a son named Peter Pitchlyn Thompson.

By 1910 Joseph, 48, was farming his own allotment free of mortgage in Wilson Township, Choctaw County. He named Mississippi as the birthplace of both his parents, which fits a family that came west on the Removal. Living with them was 19-year-old "David Wister," the orphan the family raised, whom Joel remembered as Wister Davis. Their nearest neighbors included Henry W. Thompson and two Tims households, one headed by James Tims, very likely Betsy's brother Jimmie. Henry, despite the shared surname, was the son of Simon and Lucy Thompson, while Joseph's parents were John and Betsy.

Joel said his father was 'second of nine children' and that the 1901 house stood on a farm that raised 'plenty of hogs' and 'lots to eat.' He added that his father 'was always interested in the government of his people.' The county officers Joel named were Robert S. Frazier, High Sheriff, and Noah Frazier, Clerk, with James Brown Tims as a representative in the Council.

After statehood Joseph still had business with Washington over his land. He filed a petition on 27 August 1908 from Fort Towson, and again on 10 September 1915 from Corinne; the Secretary of the Interior approved removal of restrictions on his land on 28 March 1916. In 1903 he had gone to Atoka to pick out the allotments for his wife and children.

The Mount Hermon part of the story fits the school's own history: by 16 October 1883, as the boys moved into the new brick cottages, "four Indians had arrived as pupils from the Indian Territory." They were not named, so no one can say for certain that Joseph was among them.

quotes.t: He could have sentenced criminals to be shot, but I don't know whether he did or not. I do know that he had lots of them whipped at the old whipping post on the Sulphur Springs Court ground.

stories.note: The 1891 sketch heads him 'Joseph B. Thompson,' probably a printer's error; everything else in it fits. It also calls his father 'Rev. John Thompson,' a Presbyterian minister in Cedar County for twenty years, which does not fit Joel's memory that John died about 1870. Roanoke College had about 35 Choctaw students between 1876 and 1896, but Joseph does not appear in the 1881-82 catalog; that fits the sketch, which has him at Mount Hermon first, but the 1882-86 catalogs have not been seen. Joseph's terms as judge and senator have not yet been found in Choctaw Nation records. A Find a Grave memorial gives his birth as 1862 and has him at High Hill, but his burial there is unverified; his death in 1927 comes from family files. The orphan he raised is 'Wister Davis' in Joel's interview.

stories.title: Home from the Navy, lost in the Red River
stories.hook: John's older brother cooked for the Navy through the war, then died two summers after coming home.
body: Dois, "Dais, 19" in 1940, was born 16 February 1921, the third of Grady and Mary's sons. He joined the U.S. Navy on 3 September 1942 and served as a Ship's Cook until 27 January 1946, the same years his younger brother John spent in the Navy in the Pacific.

On Thursday afternoon, 21 August 1947, he dove into shallow water in the Red River at Arthur City and broke his neck. A companion, Mac Davidson, pulled him out, and an ambulance took him to the Sanitarium of Paris. He died days later, at 26.
His funeral was at Grant Baptist Church, and he is buried at Shoat Springs Cemetery near Hugo. In October 1947 his father Grady signed the application for his military headstone.

He died single, 26 years, 6 months and 9 days old, a discharged U.S. Navy man, born in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, and living at Grant. It gives the cause as a fracture of the fifth cervical vertebra with a severed spinal cord, from an accident on 21 August at the Red River bridge north of Paris, and he lived four days. His father Grady Moffitt signed as informant and gives his mother's maiden name as Mary Shackelford, born in Alabama.
His rating was SC1C, Ship's Cook First Class, U.S. Naval Reserve, and the date 25 August 1947 appears on his death record.

stories.title: Killed in France, 1918
stories.hook: A runner in the Choctaw Code Talkers' regiment, awarded the Croix de Guerre.
body: Judge Tims's son by Willie Jane Maxwell, enrolled Choctaw by Blood, and "Edmund, 3" in 1896. He served first in Co. L, 1st Oklahoma Infantry, then as a company runner in Co. D, 142nd Infantry, 36th Division. On 9 October 1918, near St. Étienne, France, a fellow runner spoke with him at 8 a.m. and an hour later found him killed by shrapnel.

He was posthumously awarded the French Croix de Guerre with Palm and lies in the Meuse-Argonne American Cemetery. The 142nd was the regiment of the Choctaw Code Talkers. The regiment's commander wrote how Choctaw speakers were first used to send messages in this same St. Étienne fighting. Edmond is not listed as a code talker, but he served alongside them.

Two books printed in 1920 carry his name. The division's history closes with an honor roll of its dead, and under "142d Infantry" it lists "TIMS, EDMOND, Private, Co. D," with the date October 8, 1918. The War Department's casualty lists, printed that year, include among the Oklahoma privates killed in action "TIMS, Edmond, Hugo."
The honor roll dates his death 8 October 1918; the company runner remembered the morning of the 9th. Both dates fall within the same two days of the 142d Infantry's fighting at St. Étienne.

The morning of 8 October gave Edmond's battalion a hard start. The First Battalion lost its commander, Capt. Charles Kuhlman, and "half of the battalion headquarters group, including several runners," to a single shell before the jump-off, and Company D "wandered into the French sector to the left" and stayed there.

stories.title: In the Navy in the Pacific
stories.hook: Born at Frogville. Enlisted in the Navy at 18 and served on a floating drydock that came under air attack at Leyte.
body: Born 25 October 1925 at Frogville, Oklahoma, a Red River community of about 40 families, to Grady and Mary Moffitt; his older brothers were Alvin, Odis and Dois. In 1930 the family was living with his mother's parents in Martin County, Texas, and in 1940 he was "Johnnie," 14, at 411 North H Street in Hugo. In August 1941, when he was fifteen, a "John Moffitt" was among the twenty members of Hugo's Boy Scout Troop 81, sponsored by the Masonic Lodge, who left for a five-day camp at Paris, Texas, for swimming, life saving, hiking and a round of Scout tests; the name, age and town fit, but nothing else in the notice identifies him.

He enlisted in the U.S. Navy on 17 December 1943, at 18. It has been said that he trained as a corpsman (medic) at the Navy Hospital Corps School in San Diego, but nothing confirms it, and the one rating found for him, aboard USS Chief in November 1945, is F1c, fireman first class, an engineering rating. From the day it was commissioned, 22 March 1944, he served on ARD-19, a floating drydock towed across the Pacific to Manus and then to Leyte in the Philippines. In late November 1944, while ARD-19 held the mine-damaged destroyer USS Ross, a Japanese fighter crashed into the dock and started gasoline fires, and the crews shot down a second attacker. ARD-19 earned a battle star for Leyte, then moved to Subic Bay on Luzon, where it kept repairing ships until after the war. For nearly all his time aboard, its commanding officer had a name much like his: Lieutenant Commander Allan P. Moffat.

Chief had a war behind her before he joined. She was an 890-ton Auk-class minesweeper, commissioned on 9 October 1943. In June 1944 she swept mines ahead of the Saipan and Tinian landings, and she was at Okinawa from late May to late August 1945. In September 1945 she swept minefields at Wakayama, Japan, ahead of the occupation forces and helped salvage the minesweeper YMS-418. He came aboard on 7 November 1945 from Mine Squadron Four, rated F1c; where he joined her, in the Philippines or in Japan, is not known.

From November 1945 he was aboard the minesweeper USS Chief, which had swept mines off Japan and was on occupation duty at Nagoya and Sasebo until March 1946, when she sailed home to San Francisco. He was discharged on 9 May 1946 and married Faye Renee Smith in Paris, Texas, on 12 June 1947. He belonged to Emanuel Baptist Church in Hugo and died at Choctaw Memorial Hospital on 19 September 1990. His funeral followed two days later at Grant Cemetery.

Chief arrived at San Francisco in April 1946. She went out of commission in reserve at San Pedro on 17 March 1947, was recommissioned for the Korean War, and was sold to Mexico in 1973 as ARM Jesus Gonzalez Ortega.
His flat bronze marker at Grant Cemetery names the service first: "John W Moffitt / US Navy / World War II / Oct 25 1925 / Sep 19 1990."
In April 1950 John and Faye were renting at 907 South J Street in Hugo, where he ran a filling station and worked sixty-hour weeks; he had finished the tenth grade before the Navy.

stories.title: The school where 'Swing Low' was written down
stories.hook: Joseph Thompson's boarding school north of Doaksville gave the world a famous spiritual.
body: Spencer Academy was the first school created under the Choctaw Council's school law of 1842. It opened on 1 February 1844, a quarter mile north of present-day Spencerville on the old Fort Smith–Fort Towson military road, and was named for Secretary of War John C. Spencer, who gave it a 250-pound bell. Presbyterian missionaries ran it from 1846. Its three two-story halls had long porches, and the dining room served tanfula, a Choctaw crushed-corn dish.

The school closed in 1861. During the Civil War its buildings served as a Confederate hospital and sheltered homeless Choctaw families. It reopened in 1871 and ran until 1881, when a new Spencer Academy opened at Nelson, about twenty miles west of the old site near present Soper. Joseph Thompson, born in 1861, was of school age during the reopened years. Among Spencer's earlier students was Allen Wright, later Principal Chief, who gave Oklahoma its name.

Before the war, Wallace and Minerva Willis, enslaved people hired out to the academy, sang their songs at their cabin door. Superintendent Alexander Reid wrote them down, and in 1871 he spent a day in Brooklyn teaching them to the Fisk Jubilee Singers: 'Steal Away to Jesus,' 'I'm a Rolling,' and 'Swing Low, Sweet Chariot.' Whether Wallace Willis composed the songs himself is debated.

The school of Joseph Thompson's boyhood was a smaller place than the one Reid had run. When it reopened, the Choctaws placed it with the southern Presbyterians, and the Rev. J. H. Colton of Fayetteville, North Carolina, took charge on 24 May 1871 under a contract for sixty boys. He could find teachers for only thirty-two. There were fifty students in 1874, a third of the antebellum number, and in October 1876 the trustees asked for his dismissal. His successor, John J. Read, a Confederate veteran from Hinds County, Mississippi, came in December 1876 and struggled most with boys who did not understand English. In November 1880 the Council told the school its boys were "to go to school and not to work," and Read left in the summer of 1881.

In late 1877 the Council voted to move the school to Nelson, about twenty miles west of the old site near present Soper, close to the railroad and reachable in high water. Its single two-story wooden building of twenty-eight rooms faced south, and the first term there began in November 1882. The 1889 map of Indian Territory marks both "Spencer Acady" on the old site and "New Spencer Academy" beside Nelson.

stories.title: Henry and Hannah in the Ozarks
stories.hook: From Randolph County to the Stone County hills: a farm owned free and clear, and a widow who kept going for 22 years.
body: Henry was born in August 1855 in Lawrence County, Arkansas, the son of Nathan and Rebecca Moffitt, and appears as "Henry, 4" in their 1860 household. He and Hannah Grimes married about 1876. In June 1880 they were farming in Janes Creek Township, Randolph County, with daughter Josephine, 3, and son Jesse, 1.

By 1889 they were in Stone County, where son Tom was born at St. James, the old Buck Horn settlement. In May 1864 Buck Horn had seen the county's bloodiest Civil War fight, when Jo Shelby's Confederates attacked a band of bushwhackers. Grady was born near Mountain View in 1891, the year after the town incorporated.

In 1900, in Franklin Township, Henry was a farmer who owned his farm free of mortgage, with Hannah and five children at home: Jesse, Gimsa, Bertha, Tom and Woodford (Grady), 8. Henry died at Mountain View the next year, at 46. No grave has been found for him.

Hannah, who could not read or write, kept the family going. In 1910 she was a widow renting a house with Tom, a railroad section hand, and Grady, who worked in the timber. She had borne seven children, six still living. She died at Herpel, a Rocky Bayou settlement east of Mountain View, on 4 April 1923, and her stone in Herpel Cemetery reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt."

stories.title: Quakers and the first Indy 500
stories.hook: A New Jersey Quaker family that moved west, a grandson who fought for the Union, and a cousin whose firm won the first Indianapolis 500.
body: The Nordykes were Quakers from Burlington County, New Jersey. Henry Nordyke married Rebecca Perkins there in 1731/2. Their descendants moved to Guilford County, North Carolina, then on to Ohio and Indiana with the Quaker migration away from slavery.

Aden was the oldest son of Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers, born in Burlington County in 1762. An Ohio county history says that while the family lived in Georgia he was shot in the arm during an Indian attack. He married Martha Johnson at Deep River, Guilford County, in 1787, and later moved on to Indiana, where he died in 1842.

An 1899 biography of Captain Adin Nordyke of the 63rd Indiana calls his father Robert Nordyke "son of Adin and Sarah Nordyke," and his mother Elizabeth Shaw. If this is our Aden, the captain was his grandson. Raised a Quaker, he "still holds to that doctrine," yet he fought at Resaca, Atlanta, Allatoona, Franklin and Nashville. Since our Sicily Nordyke married Noble Shaw, the two Guilford County families were probably linked twice.

Aden's brother Micajah moved to Clinton County, Ohio, in 1805 (one account says 1806) and gave the land for the East Fork Friends burying ground at New Vienna. Micajah's son Ellis, born in 1807, was a Quaker millwright who founded a flour-mill machinery works at Richmond, Indiana, with his son Addison. Daniel W. Marmon joined in 1866, and the firm moved to Indianapolis in 1876 as Nordyke & Marmon. On 30 May 1911 Ray Harroun drove its yellow No. 32 Marmon "Wasp" to victory in the first Indianapolis 500, averaging 74.6 miles per hour.

A Quaker entry dated 12 December 1787 reads: "Martha, dt Robert & Cecilia, Surry Co., m Adin Nordyke." If this is Aden's wife, her parents were Robert and Cecilia of Surry County. The name would also fit Aden's daughter Sicily, a form of Cecilia. The entry gives no surname for Martha, so the link to Martha Johnson is unproved. The same records list Aden's children with Martha beginning "Sicily b. 8-2-1790. Mary 2-15-1792."

The Deep River Quaker meeting recorded the marriage intention of Adin Nordyke and Martha Johnson on 12 December 1787, naming his parents as Abraham and Mary Nordyke, which ties Aden to the Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers household that had come south from Burlington, New Jersey.

stories.title: The blue-and-white coverlets in Mary's will
stories.hook: Mary Moffitt divided a household among eight children: pewter, bedding, a coffee mill, her big Bible, and the work of settling her estate.
body: On 23 September 1820, Mary Moffitt made a will that records her household almost object by object. She was weak in body but declared herself sound in sense and memory. For each of her five daughters she set aside a pewter dish, six plates and two basins. Bedding received the same careful attention: white sheets, checked sheets, blankets, a blue-and-white flowered coverlet and a blue-and-white double-diamond coverlet. These were separate possessions to be passed to particular people, rather than an anonymous lot to sell.

Naomi Mackie was to have Mary's saddle and best cloak. Catharine Cox received the dresser and cupboard. Hannah Cox received the walnut chest and the big Bible. Mary Wilkinson was left the copper kettle and a five- or six-gallon pot. Margaret Moffitt received a feather bed, bedstead and pillows, the case of drawers, pewter teapot, coffee mill, square walnut table, flax and cotton, provisions and forage, and half the cattle, sheep and hogs. Mary was dividing the tools of cooking, sleeping, dressing and keeping a farm household.

Her sons Robert and William each received bedding and fifty dollars; David received the still, livestock, plantation utensils, cider vessels and 150 dollars. Leftover money was to be divided equally among all eight children, or the gifts reduced equally if the estate fell short. Mary directed the remaining household furniture and clothing to her daughters and the jack screw to her three sons. She appointed Margaret executrix alongside David as executor, and William Cox and Stephen Cox witnessed. The daughter who received the coffee mill would also share responsibility for carrying out the whole plan.

Mary had married William Moffitt at Cane Creek Monthly Meeting on 2 April 1763. His 1796 will had left her the wagon, still, household goods, farming tools and livestock, with rights in the home plantation during her widowhood. More than twenty years later, her own choices show how those broad provisions had become a detailed set of gifts to Naomi, Catharine, Hannah, Mary, Margaret, Robert, William and David. She dated the will “the 23rd day of the 9th month, 1820,” in the Quaker style, and her son Robert, our ancestor, was alive when she wrote it. Her death is given as February 1822 in one account, but that may only be when the will was filed.

She was a daughter of Charles and Hannah (Matson) Davies. Her family had followed the Quaker road from Pennsylvania through Virginia to Cane Creek, North Carolina. Her sister Hannah married Hugh Moffitt, joining the Davies sisters to two Moffitt households. Mary's will brings that large family down to a smaller scale: one saddle, one Bible, particular coverlets and the people she wanted to have them.

stories.title: The midwife of Doaksville
stories.hook: Daughter of John Steadman and O-we-na, she was the midwife at the birth of her grandson Simon.
body: Emeline was born on 26 January 1842. She was enrolled as Choctaw by Blood, one-quarter blood, along with her sons Johnny and Calvin. Her father, John Steadman, was not a Choctaw citizen, and her mother, O-we-na, had died in Towson County; nothing states John's race or O-we-na's ancestry.

She and Vinson farmed in the High Hill neighborhood north of Doaksville. Their children included James, Mitchell, Betsy (Mrs. Joseph Thompson), John, Rev. Robert Tims, Willie, Rosie and Calvin, and several of them later lived around Spencerville.

When her grandson Simon was born on 4 May 1899, Emeline attended as the midwife. On 17 October 1899 she swore before a notary at Doaksville that "there was born to her on said date a male child… said to have been named Simon Thompson," the affidavit that put Simon on the rolls. She died on 16 March 1918 and is buried at High Hill Cemetery.

Her grandson Joel did not remember her maiden name ('Grandmother Tims first name was Emmaline'), so the name Steadman comes from her enrollment, not from family memory. Joel placed her home 'about four miles north and a little west of Doaksville,' in Towson County, 'known as the Charley Blankenship place now.' A local history says six or seven miles. Betsy and Joseph were married there in 1889.

Emeline and Vinson are 'buried there at the old place,' Joel said. Her memorial at High Hill Cemetery gives her dates, while a Tims headstone photographed in a local history is captioned Hampton Chapel Cemetery and may belong to a child. Her husband's marker at High Hill is a cenotaph.

Her son, the Rev. Robert James Tims, was remembered in a 1944 Methodist memoir as born six miles north of Fort Towson, "the son of Vincent and Emiline Tims." Another son, James Brown Tims, was born on 25 June 1864 at Doaksville.

Her name appears in the enrollment of nearly all her children: her sons James B., Robert, Mitchell and Willie and her daughters Rosanna and Betsy each named "Emiline Tims" as mother. The men's father is written variously as "Vinson W. Tims," "Vincent Tims" and "Benson Tims," always dead by 1899. In the 1900s she kept being asked to vouch for births.

Her daughter Rosanna was first enrolled with her mother on 24 April 1899 and in October 1900 was moved to the enrollment of her husband James Wilson; the notary who sorted out the name wrote that Rosanna's "mother name is Emaline Times." Emeline swore as midwife to the birth of Rosanna's son (23 March 1903) and, signing as "midwife" on 29 April 1905, of Betsy's son Joseph W. (5 March 1903), swore with Rosanna to the birth of Rosanna's daughter Candace (16 June 1905), and swore with Mildred to the birth of Mitchell's son Vincenta (1904; the Commission acknowledged the affidavits in April 1905).

stories.title: From Butler County to the Red River
stories.hook: A Kentucky farm family that moved to Texas about 1907 and ended up around Soper and Hugo.
body: John C. Satterfield was born in 1864 in Allen County, Kentucky. In 1880, at 16, he was a farm laborer at Renfrow, Butler County, in the household of his father, James H. Satterfield, with his brothers and sisters. His mother, Melissa Gibson, had died in 1877.

A widower with three children, Henry B. (born May 1883), Martha A. (August 1884) and John W. (January 1887), he married Samantha D. "Mantha" Johnson, about 20, in 1892. In 1900 they were farming at Horse Mill, Butler County, with seven children at home. Their son Wavey Lincoln was born near Morgantown on 28 December 1895 by his own draft cards; his headstone gives 9 January 1896. Artie Pearl followed in August 1898. Wavey later served as an Army private in World War I. A family account identifies an early son, Joseph, who died before 1910.

About 1907 the family moved to Franklin County, Texas. In April 1910 John, 46, was renting a farm at Hagansport, with Wavey, Pearl, James, Ira and little Stella. A family account says their last child was born in Texas in 1912. John died in Franklin County a few years later. On 28 July 1917 Samantha married Bird Alexander "Alex" Stephens at Mount Vernon, Texas, and they moved across the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma. Wavey died at Soper in 1952. Their daughter Artie Pearl married Charles Oscar Smith in 1915; both are buried at Grant Cemetery. Samantha died in Choctaw County in 1928 and is buried as Samantha Stephens in Soper Cemetery.
John's father was James Henry Satterfield and his mother Melissa Gibson.

Samantha's husband John C. had a larger family than the two households show. His full brothers and sisters, children of James H. and Melissa, included Sidney Rufus (1865-1949), James Doiser (1867-1929, who went to Clay County, Arkansas) and A. M. (born in Minnesota in 1870, died 1892). His nine half-siblings by Lucinda Phelps lived mostly around Texarkana. He and his brother Sidney both married women of the Clark-Johnson family of Butler County.

The farm John C. Satterfield rented at Hagansport in 1910 was in a county where, by 1908, tenants on the usual share plan gave up half the crop, and farms averaged under 80 acres. The Hagansport soil was heavy clay that stayed sticky after rain and suited cotton better than corn.
