stories.title: A family of Methodist preachers
stories.hook: Elam Stevenson broke with his Presbyterian parents, carried a preacher’s books to Tennessee in his wagon, founded Bee Spring church and preached for more than sixty years.
body: Elam Stevenson was born on 24 September 1787 in what is now Alexander County, North Carolina, the son of James and Jane Stevenson, who were Presbyterians. About 1805 he married Lydia Catherine Payne in Burke County, a daughter of William Payne, who had served six months in the Revolutionary militia, and Catherine Arnold, as her son Rev. John Baxter Stevenson remembered them. In 1806, against his parents’ wishes, Elam joined the Methodists, the first of his family to do so.

In 1813 he was licensed to preach and moved his family to Giles County, Tennessee. Family tradition says they went by pack horse because there were no wagon roads, but Elam remembered it differently: the preacher Philip Bruce asked him to bring a part of his books “in my wagon,” and he did.

Bee Spring Methodist Episcopal Church near Pulaski was his doing. Elam himself dated it to 1814; others put it in 1815, when, as its chief founder, he bought 15 acres for $20 and organized the church with the help of Stephen Loyd, Meshack Boice and James McCowan. He preached for more than sixty years and was ordained an elder in 1859. The frame church built in 1855 was destroyed by the tornado of 29 April 1909, and of the old site only the cemetery remained, ‘sadly neglected.’

Elam and Lydia had eleven children, eight of them sons: Catherine A. (1808–1888), who married William Hamilton and lived in Limestone County, Alabama; William Payne (1810–1892); James Calvin (1813–1899); Abner Arrington (1816–1896); Willis McKendree (1818–1900); Minerva J., born in 1820, an infant who died that December; John Baxter (1821); Thomas Coleman (1825–1906); Lydia Amanda (1827–1901); Elam Augustus (1829–1886), who moved to Arkansas; and Gilbert Worth (b. 1830), a schoolteacher and minister who married Martha J. Tharp. In 1886 a grandson, Coleman L. Stevenson of Giles County, gave the same roll in the family’s own words: “Rev. Elam and Lydia Stevenson, natives of North Carolina, who were married about 1805, and located in Giles County, Tenn., about 1813. To them were born these children: Katherine, William P., James C., Abner A., Willis M., Minerva J., John B., Thomas C., Amanda, Elam A. and Gilbert. The grandfather died in 1875 and the grandmother in 1872.”

How many of the eight sons followed him into the pulpit depends on who is counting, and the answers run from three to five. His grandson Rev. J. B. Stevenson named five in a family letter of 1932: James, Abner, John, Elam Augustus and Gilbert. In 1871 the church historian McFerrin wrote that “four of his sons are preachers of the gospel”; in 1886 Coleman’s father, William P., was said to have “four brothers who are ministers of the gospel, and his father was also a very prominent Methodist Episcopal minister”; and a neighbor in 1884 remembered “James and John and one other.” The family reckoned 292 years of preaching among Elam and his sons.

That neighbor was F. T. M’Laurine, whose family farmed the next place on Little Bradshaw Creek. In an 1884 piece, “Old Times in Giles,” he remembered: “Elam Stevenson and family settled 1½ miles south of us near Bee Spring church in 1815 or 1816; he soon after obtained license to preach and was a Methodist preacher all his life; died a few years since a very old man. He had one daughter, Catharine, who married a Mr. Hamilton. His sons were William, James, Coleman, John and others; James and John and one other were Methodist preachers, all good, industrious citizens. William married a Miss Malinda Rowe, a daughter of Joseph Rowe who lived near by. She was a beautiful young lady. James married a daughter of Mr. Duncan Brown, sister of ex-Gov. N. S. and J. C. Brown. John is a noted Methodist preacher.”

The Browns were the family of Neill S. Brown, governor of Tennessee from 1847 to 1849, and John C. Brown, governor from 1871 to 1875, both Giles County men, so James married into the family of two governors. The unnamed “one other” preacher fits Abner, and the neighbor’s Coleman was the son also known as Thomas C. Seventy years on, M’Laurine’s dates had drifted a little: Elam himself put Bee Spring’s founding in 1814, and the family was in Giles County by about 1813, a little earlier than the 1815 or 1816 he remembered.

Our line runs through Rev. Abner Arrington Stevenson (1816–1896). In 1880 Abner, 63, gave his occupation as “Farming Preacher,” and his household in Giles County included his wife, Martha, and their son Gilbert F., 18: the Frank Stevenson who later brought his family to Hugo. Frank was apparently named for his uncle Gilbert.

Lydia died on 6 March 1872. Elam lived three more years. “Died, at the residence of W. M. Stevenson, near Bethany, on the 13th inst., Rev. Elam Stevenson, in his 88th year,” ran the notice of 18 March 1875, which called him “this venerable minister of God” and said he “had been greatly afflicted, but never complained.” Family tradition says he was buried under the pulpit. The stone over Elam and Lydia at Bee Spring reads, on his side, “Nearly 62 years a minister of the gospel. He was pure in heart and life,” and on hers, “Nearly 70 years a Methodist. She consecrated her household to God and the church.” In May 1878 another writer, describing the Bee Spring graveyard, wrote of “old Father Stevenson and his beloved consort” as among “the founders and upholders of Methodism at Bee Spring.”

Elam is remembered today in an encyclopedia article of his own, which follows his life from his marriage and his turn to the Methodists to his license in 1813, the move to Giles County that year and the founding of Old Bee Spring Methodist Church. It calls his father a captain in the Revolution, but James Stevenson served as a private.

stories.title: James Satterfield's own account of his family
stories.hook: James Satterfield told the story of three generations of his family, and it was printed in 1885.
body: In 1885 a history of Kentucky printed short biographies of farmers and businessmen county by county. One was of James H. Satterfield, then of Butler County, and it reads like his own account of the family.

It says his father, Henry Satterfield, was a native of Maury County, Tennessee, and died in 1861. Henry married Mary, daughter of John M. Garrison of Allen County. Henry was the son of Ephraim Satterfield, "a native of Virginia, who died about 1850."

James married Melissa A. Gibson, "daughter of James and Cynthia (Woodcock) Gibson, of Allen County." They were married in Allen County on 17 September 1859. Their children were Henry W., John C., Sidney R., James D., Martha A. and Mary C. John C., born in February 1864, is our John C. Satterfield, who later farmed at Horse Mill in Butler County. Melissa died in 1877.

After Melissa died in 1877, James married Lucinda Belle Phelps on 2 June 1878 in Butler County. They had nine children between 1879 and 1899. Several of those half-siblings of John C. married in Bowie County, Texas, or nearby Arkansas between 1909 and 1917, and James himself died in Bowie County on 24 November 1922 (the sheet also gives 1924).

His account says more than the family papers do. James "was born April 14, 1838, in Allen County, Ky., where he grew to manhood. In 1867 he removed to Dakota County, Minn., and in 1875 he returned to Kentucky, and located in Warren County. In 1876 he settled in Butler County, where he has since resided." James spent eight years in Minnesota; if the family went with him, John C. was three when they left and eleven when they came back.

He described his war service as brief: "In 1861 he enlisted in the Ninth Kentucky (Federal) Infantry, remaining in the field but three months, after which he was engaged in the recruiting service." He dated his first marriage to "September 15, 1859," two days before the 17 September of the county's marriage register, named his second wife as Lucinda B., "daughter of Solomon and Sarah J. (Deweese) Phelps, of this county," and listed the three children of that marriage, Martha B., Alonzo T. and Minnie E.

He was 23 that year, a young farmer in Allen County, and his father died the same year. The 9th Kentucky Infantry was organized at Camp Boyle, Adair County, and mustered in for three years on 20 November 1861; its first winter was spent in camp at Columbia, Kentucky, until it marched for Bowling Green and Nashville on 15 February 1862. If James joined in the autumn of 1861, his three months fit that camp period. His account does not say whether he was discharged, detailed or transferred, and his service has not been matched to a roster. The regiment went on to Shiloh, Corinth, Perryville (in reserve), Stones River, Chickamauga, Missionary Ridge, the Atlanta campaign and Jonesboro, and mustered out on 15 December 1864. Its dead numbered 357: 8 officers and 96 enlisted men killed or mortally wounded, and 3 officers and 250 enlisted men dead of disease. Butler County, where James settled in 1876, put up a veterans’ monument on the courthouse lawn in 1907 to the soldiers of both armies, described as one of two such Kentucky monuments.
By 1885 he was well off for a farmer: "Mr. Satterfield is a farmer, and owns 1,340 acres of land, where he now resides, and 425 acres in Tennessee."

Melissa died on 2 May 1877. James's birth is given elsewhere as 14 April 1837, and he died on 28 November 1922 at Redwater in Bowie County and was buried at Reed Cemetery. A daughter, A. M., was born in Minnesota in 1870, and a son, James Doiser, in Allen County in February 1867.

No James H. Satterfield appears on the rolls of any Kentucky Union regiment, which does not disprove his account of three months' service. His Minnesota years, on the other hand, are borne out: a James H. Satterfield was the first director of School District No. 95 in Marshan Township, Dakota County, in 1874.

stories.title: Betsy Tims and the Pine Ridge school
stories.hook: A Choctaw woman of Towson County, and the girl from the Pine Ridge school.
body: Betsy and her family applied for Choctaw enrollment on 1 May 1899, and the Secretary of the Interior approved it on 12 December 1902. She was enrolled as Choctaw by Blood and received a land allotment that included a 160-acre homestead north of Doaksville.

She went to school at the old Pine Ridge mission near Doaksville, founded by the missionary Cyrus Kingsbury in the 1830s, where the Choctaw Nation's Chuwahla Female Seminary opened in 1844. Her son Joel said her family was "quite prominent in public affairs." Her brother James Brown "Jimmie" Tims served in the Choctaw Council as a Representative.

She was 'Miss Betsey Ann Tims' before her marriage, and her first child, Alexander, was born in March 1890. Her parents were Vinson and Emeline Tims; her brothers and sisters included James, Mitchell, John, Rev. Robert Tims, Willie, Rosie and Calvin.

Her son Joel added a correction to the family story about her schooling: he believed it 'was after the Mission school had been suspended and that it was very likely neighborhood schools which she attended, schools held at the old Academy site.' Whatever the building, she remembered it. Her father, whose name was written 'Vincent Tims,' was dead by 1899, and her mother, 'Emiline Tims,' was still living in Towson County.

Joel named seven children who lived to be grown: Alex B., Joel J., Peter Pitchlyn, Simon W., Joseph W., Jincy and Marietta. A daughter, Ella, died in May 1899, and Joseph W., born in March 1903, was enrolled under the Act of 3 March 1905. In March 1920 she petitioned from Corinne to lift the restrictions on her land, and the request was approved on 30 April.

quotes.t: She always told us, as we passed that old Pine Ridge school site, "There is where I went to school."

stories.title: A wheelwright on the move
stories.hook: Four censuses follow Nathan from North Carolina to Arkansas to Missouri, and from owning land to owning almost nothing.
body: Nathan was born in 1814 in Randolph County, North Carolina, a son of Robert and Martha (Chamness) Moffitt, and grew up in the Center Quaker Meeting community, which hosted meetings of the North Carolina Manumission Society in those years. He married Rebecca Williams in Randolph County on 13 October 1835. In 1840 he was in the county’s South Division, and a son, Calvin, was born there on 4 December 1841.

The family's route shows in its children's birthplaces: the older children were born in North Carolina up to about 1842, the younger ones in Arkansas from about 1843. In 1850 Nathan, 36, was farming in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas, with Rebecca and eight children.

By 1860 he was working as a wheelwright near Smithville, with land worth $1,200 and personal property worth $1,000, and the family had grown to include twin girls born in 1859. Henry, our ancestor, was 4.

Lawrence County in the 1850s was a mix of small farms around the county seat at Smithville; in 1860 it counted 494 enslaved people among 8,875 white residents. Patrick was born in May 1853 (one source gives 11 May, at Sylamore) and Henry in 1855. The war brought jayhawkers and bushwhackers to the county, though no major battle.

The Civil War brought raiders on both sides to Lawrence County. By June 1870 Nathan and Rebecca had moved to Dent County, Missouri, where he was farming with no land of his own and $300 in personal property.

Oregon County, where they next lived, was largely pro-Southern and suffered raids. Its courthouse at Alton burned in October 1863; the historical marker says Union troops burned it, while a 2024 survey says Southern partisans did, and the marker adds that Lee’s surrender “did not end the Civil War in Oregon County.” Rebecca died there in 1871, and that year Nathan married a widow, Nancy (Rowe) Cole. Nathan died in Oregon County on 23 December 1873. That August his son Patrick had married Alice Ann Cole there. (Patrick’s own death is given as 20 December 1905 at Mountain View in one source and as November 1904, with burial at Sallisaw, in another.)

Nathan’s brothers and sisters spread widely: Sarah and Naomi to Iowa, Robert to Strawberry Township and then Howell County, Missouri, while Hannah, Lydia, Aaron and William C. stayed in Randolph County. Aaron’s son Veno Moffitt died in 1864 as a Confederate prisoner at Elmira.

A Calvin V. Moffitt served as a private in Company L, 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union). The regiment was organized at Little Rock in December 1863, and Company L was made up in Montgomery County, far from Lawrence County. Whether that soldier was Nathan’s son is uncertain, though a Calvin V. Moffitt of Lawrence County is also said to have served in two Confederate units and later claimed a few months in a Union one. Family accounts place Nathan’s son Calvin later at Duncan, Oklahoma, where he died on 13 February 1913.

stories.title: Three wills from Quaker New Jersey
stories.hook: A grandfather's will names Ann Staples, her husband Thomas Rogers, and their daughter Mary, who married into the Nordyke family.
body: Thomas Rogers married Ann Staples on 30 October 1736 at Upper Springfield Meeting in Burlington County, New Jersey. Ann, about twenty-two, was the daughter of Thomas Staples and Mehitable Gaunt, and her mother had grown up on Hananiah Gaunt's farm near Oneanickon in the township that was formed on 6 November 1688. The Old Upper Springfield Friends Burying Ground and meeting house are now on the National Register of Historic Places.

When Ann's father wrote his will on 25 October 1758 he named his daughter "Ann, wife of Thomas Rogers" and his granddaughters "Mehetable and Mary Rogers." That Mary Rogers married Abraham Nordyke on 1 June 1761, which ties the Rogers family directly to the Nordykes and to Aden and Sicily after them.

Thomas Rogers appears again at Burlington in December 1748, when Thomas Staples Jr., an innholder, died without a will and administration went to Thomas Rogers, the husband of Ann Staples, with two Burlington men as bondsmen. If Staples Jr. was Ann's brother, it fits Thomas acting for the estate. Ann died on 23 March 1791.

John Rodgers of Burlington left his son Thomas one-third of the residue in a will dated 23 January 1764 and proved 26 March 1767. That son is probably Ann Staples's husband, but his wife is not named, so the identification is only probable. The Staples and Gaunt wills name the relationships on Ann's side; John Rodgers's will adds a likely connection on Thomas's side.

stories.title: Timberman at Ervin, laborer in the Depression
stories.hook: Tall, stout and gray-eyed in 1917, Grady supported his family as a timberman and faced long periods without work in 1939.
body: Born 6 November 1891 at Mountain View, Arkansas, the youngest of Henry and Hannah Moffitt's children at home in 1900. In 1910, at 18, he was living with his widowed mother in Stone County and working in the timber, apparently making barrel staves.
Grady and Mary married about 1914, and their first son, Alvin, was born in September 1915.

When he registered for the WWI draft on 5 June 1917 he was 25, working as a timberman for C. D. Neese at Ervin, Oklahoma, married and supporting a wife, his mother and a child. He was tall and stout, with gray eyes and dark hair.
Ervin existed as a place only from 1904 to 1922, and which sawmill Grady worked for there is not known. The county’s biggest was the Pine Belt Lumber Company at Fort Towson, begun in 1902.

In February 1920 he was a tenant farmer in Wilson Township, Choctaw County, with Mary, sons Alvin and Odis, and a nephew and niece; his brother Tom farmed next door. In April 1930 the family, now with six boys, was living with Mary’s parents, John Morgan and Lizzie Shackleford, on a farm near Stanton, Martin County, Texas, the county where her father is buried, and Grady, a road-work laborer, was out of work. Martin County had been nearly empty a decade before: its population grew from 1,146 in 1920 to 5,785 in 1930 as cotton farming spread across the plains, and the lean years that followed were hard on its farmers.
Hugo was a young town. It was founded in 1901 where the Frisco’s north-south line crossed the Arkansas & Choctaw, and the Frisco depot went up in 1914.

In 1940 the family was renting at 411 North H Street in Hugo: Grady, 48, a laborer with five years of schooling, had been unemployed 50 weeks, worked 12 weeks in 1939 and earned $100. At home were Mary ("Manile"), 44, and the children Odis 21, Dais 19, Johnnie 14, the twins Alton and Eldon 11, Donald 8, and two little ones not yet identified among the nine children below.

Their children were Alvin B. (1915-1994, U.S. Army Air Corps in World War II), Odas Eugene (1918-1995; “Odis” in 1940, “Ottis” in 1920), Dois L. (1921-1947), Jimmie Gaynell (1923-1926), John Winfred (1925-1990), the twins Alton V. (1928-1975) and Eldon Herman (1928-2014), Donald K. (1931-2014) and Henry Wayne (1934-1937).

One of the twins seems to turn up in September 1953: "Vernon Moffitt, 24, son of Mr. and Mrs. W. E. Moffitt, Box 255, Grant, Okla.," was finishing his Air Force basic airmen's course at Lackland, the "Gateway to the Air Force," near San Antonio. The age fits a twin born in 1928, probably Alton V., but the father's initials are printed as W. E. rather than W. G. and no twin is named.

Grady and Mary lost two children at three years old, Jimmie Gaynell (17 January 1923 to 26 October 1926) and Henry Wayne (13 January 1934 to 12 May 1937), dates confirmed at the cemetery, and their son Dois died in 1947, after breaking his neck in the Red River. Grady died on 21 June 1972 and is buried beside Mary at Shoat Springs Cemetery near Hugo. His brother Tom, who farmed beside him in 1920, later lived in Paris, Texas, where he died in 1953; his stone is marked WW I and WW II. Their brother Jesse is buried at Tahoka, Texas.

When he registered in 1942 for the "old man's" draft, Grady was 50, living on North Broadway in Hugo, unemployed, with his birthplace given as Stone County, Arkansas. The person who would always know his address was "Mrs. Mannie Moffitt," Mary's nickname in 1940 too.

stories.title: Witness to the Treaty of Doaksville
stories.hook: His name is on the 1837 treaty, and his trading firm fed Chickasaw families arriving from Mississippi.
body: On 17 January 1837, "at Doaksville, near Fort Towson, in the Choctaw country," the Choctaw and Chickasaw nations signed the treaty that let the Chickasaws settle inside the Choctaw Nation. The witness list reads: Wm. Armstrong, Henry R. Carter, Josiah S. Doak, Vincent B. Tims, Daniel McCurtain (U.S. Interpreter)… followed by the marks of the three Choctaw district chiefs.

Born in South Carolina (family accounts say Chester County), Vincent was a trader and the partner of Josiah Doak, whose trading post gave Doaksville its name; a missionary later remembered the town's founders as "Josiah Doak and Vinson Brown Tims, an Irishman." Doak & Tims held the army contracts of 1838 and 1839 to feed Chickasaw emigrants arriving at Doaksville, at 13 cents a ration, and handled the annuity payments that drew crowds to Doaksville. The partnership was dissolved by public notice in 1844.

On 29 May 1847 he bought the Dancing Rabbit Creek treaty allotment of Henry Graves, "son of Chief Netachachie," one of the three district chiefs whose marks appear on the 1837 treaty. That December "Jos. R. Berthelet and Vincent B. Tims of the Choctaw Nation" were invited within the bar at the Red River Raft Convention, which pressed Congress to clear the great logjam that blocked steamboats on the Red River.

He and his full-blood Choctaw wife stayed at Doaksville the rest of their lives. Family accounts say Vincent died at Doaksville in June 1864, while Confederate troops held Fort Towson a mile away, but he was still signing letters as the Confederate postmaster there on 9 September and 1 November 1864.

The trader's origins, in the one local history that traces him, are modest: 'Born in South Carolina, V.B. Tims is said to be of Irish descent.' A local history has him coming to the Doaksville area with Josiah Doak in the early 1830s; the earliest record of him there is from 1837. In March 1843 he ran an office there for letters to the Agent for Claims, and in February 1844 the partnership with Doak was dissolved 'by mutual agreement,' after which he kept the business on his own. One of the firm’s unpaid store accounts, for 1840 to 1844, was still being pursued in 1848 and reached the Supreme Court of Texas in 1849.

His South Carolina family now has a name. Joseph Tims signed his will at Chester on 20 November 1841, and he wrote it like a man who did not expect to see his son again. To 'my son Vincent Brown Tims' he left a man named Allen, a woman named Mary, and a piece of land running from a big poplar corner past a house to a post oak at Thomas Wright's line, next to Mrs. Robertson's place. Then he added a condition that fits a son who was living far away: should Vincent die 'and never come to this country' without heirs, the land was to go to his brother Alford. By then Vincent had been trading at Doaksville, five hundred miles to the west, for most of a decade. Joseph died in the autumn of 1844, and his sons Joseph T. and Alford Tims took up the executorship on 4 November.

The will settles less about Vincent's mother than it once seemed to. Joseph's 'beloved wife Winifred' received Lucy, Ned and the fifty-acre Peetree Tract for her life or widowhood, with the right to stay in her house. But the will never calls her the mother of any of his children, and six years later Winifred Tims was keeping house in Chester at thirty-nine, with a six-year-old daughter, Frances. A woman born about 1811 cannot have been the mother of a son born in 1803, so Winifred was Joseph's later wife, and Vincent's own mother is still unnamed.

His middle name has a story behind it. His father's sister Elizabeth Tims married a man named Vincent Brown, and when her widowed mother lay dying in the mid-1820s the old lady feared that 'Vincent Brown would make a fuss' over a twenty-pound legacy. Vincent Brown Tims, born in 1803, was very probably named for that uncle by marriage. It is also why some online trees make a Brown woman his mother: the Brown in the family was his aunt.

Another Tims will from Chester District, which the family transcription calls Joseph's first, names sons Amos, John and Joseph and daughters Sarah Estes, Mary Carter, Frances Boyd and Elizabeth Tims, each with an enslaved man, woman or child. An Amos Timms, whose place in the family is not yet clear, made his own will in 1831, leaving his 112-acre plantation to his sister Johannah. Both originals survive in the Chester probate files.

The question of the two wills now has an answer. Sarah Estes was, by the family's own Bible and the Estes genealogy of Chester County, a daughter of Joseph Tims and Mary Glover, and that Joseph died in August 1801. So the first will was the older Joseph's, and the son Joseph it names was very probably the man whose will of 1844 remembered Vincent. Vincent's grandparents, then, were Joseph and Mary (Glover) Tims, who had come from Lunenburg County, Virginia, to the Chester and Union country by 1770; their story is told in “Before Doaksville.”

Three of his children are known by name: Vinson W. (born 1838), Edward Ward (born 1842) and a daughter, Phoebe, who died before final enrollment. His great-grandson Joel Thompson said that 'Venson Brown Tims' was the first postmaster at Doaksville and that Edward succeeded him on his death. Edward was appointed postmaster on 24 October 1887, and a 'V. B. Tims' had been appointed on 17 May 1871, seven years after the family date of Vincent's death. Local history says that in 1861 he was 'designated' to be Indian Agent for the Choctaws had the Confederacy won, but only one local history says so.

William Gardner, a Choctaw merchant born in 1830, was said in 1891 to have opened his own store at Hamilton, in Blue County, "after he had been to work for E. B. Tims, the sutler at Doaksville." The initials are printed "E. B." rather than "V. B.," but the trade and the town point to the Doaksville trader, so this was probably Vincent.

Two more glimpses show him as a man of business. In December 1845 a New Orleans commission house named "Doak & Tims, Doaksville, C. Nation" among its references in a newspaper advertisement, next to Maj. William Armstrong of the Choctaw Agency. And by June 1854 "V. B. Tims, Choctaw Nation" held 10 shares at $25 each in the Cairo & Fulton Railroad Company of Arkansas, among other Choctaw Nation stockholders; the road was chartered to link Cairo, on the Mississippi, with Fulton on the Red River.
The army contracts behind the thirteen-cents-a-ration figure were signed on 1 January 1838 and 1 January 1839, each naming "Doak & Tims."
In April 1841 a clerk in the Doaksville trading house wrote home that "Mr. Tims one of the men I am living with is now in New York purchasing a stock of goods."

The post office he is remembered for was still in the government's list in 1877: "Doaksville," "Choctaw," "V. B. Tims," with a year's compensation of $37.77. An 1871 list likewise carries a "V. B. Tims" among the postmasters. The initials are the trader's, though whether the postmaster of the 1870s was Vincent himself or his son Vinson, who would have used the same initials, is not known.

His wife was Betsy Tims, a Choctaw of Towson County who, like Vincent, was dead by 1899; their son Edward W. Tims named them as his parents when he enrolled, calling Vincent a non-citizen. Betsy Thompson, born in 1870, was a granddaughter of that Betsy Tims and shared her name.

stories.title: An indentured boy from London
stories.hook: Bound for seven years' service in Maryland at 15, he ended up a landowner and overseer of a Quaker meeting.
body: Anthony Chamness was the son of John and Ann, born about 1713 in East Smithfield, London. The church at St John’s, Wapping, recorded his baptism there in February 1713, the name written “Chamniss,” as son of John Chamness and Ann Weary, who had married at the same church on 4 January 1704. On 9 February 1724/5, giving his age as 15 and his home as Whitechapel, he bound himself to John Cooke, a London victualler, for seven years' service in "Maryland (his Majesty's Plantation in America)." A boy baptized in 1713 would not have been 15 in February 1724/5, and the two dates have not been reconciled. He was out of his time by 1732.
On 24 November 1735 he married Sarah Cole in St. Paul's Parish, Baltimore County, into a Cole family that had been in the county since the 1690s.

The Chamnesses moved with the Quakers from Gunpowder Meeting in Maryland to Monocacy (1741), Carver's Creek in North Carolina (1749), and Cane Creek, where Anthony received a 490-acre grant in June 1751. When Cane Creek Monthly Meeting was organized that year he was named its overseer. As a Quaker historian wrote, “the large settlement of Friends in Alamance, Chatham, Guilford, Randolph and Surry counties was formed by Quaker immigrants,” and Anthony is one of them: an English servant boy who became a landowner and the officer of a meeting. His farm, a mile west of the meetinghouse, had a grist mill. He married three times and died on 20 September 1777.

His son Joseph, born in Baltimore County in 1740, married Margaret Norton at Cane Creek in 1763, became the meeting’s recorder of marriage certificates, and later farmed near Providence in Randolph County. Joseph’s daughter Martha was born on 6 October 1778 at Center, then in Guilford County (Randolph County was not cut from Guilford until 1779). She married Robert Moffitt at Providence, under Center Monthly Meeting, in 1797 and lived until 1865. Her son Nathan Moffitt, born in 1814, left Randolph County for Arkansas in the early 1840s rather than for Indiana.

The Chamness name did also leave by the Quaker road. Dover Monthly Meeting's list of Friends who took certificates to Indiana between 1830 and 1860 includes “Camness,” one more spelling of a name the Wapping clerk had written “Chamniss” a century earlier, though the match is by surname only.

Anthony married three times: Sarah Cole in 1735; then Rachel Haworth, the widow of Stephanus Haworth, who died on 19 March 1775 and is buried at Deep River; and, on 9 May 1776, Margaret Evans Williams, a widow. He made his will on 24 November 1776 in what was then Chatham County and died the next September.

A Hussey family tradition, written down in 1928, differs from the indenture. A letter of 30 April 1917 from Dr. John M. Hussey of Somerville, New Jersey, states "that Martha Chamness, who married Stephen Hussey, was the daughter of Anthony Chamness and his wife, Sarah Cole; that Anthony Chamness had been kidnapped in England as a child and brought to America where he was 'bound out' till he reached a certain age; that he was the heir of an estate in England, which he had to go to England in order to claim but his wife would not consent to his going." The 1928 writer thought the inheritance "somewhat of a myth," since immigrants often told such stories. The kidnapping tale and the indenture of February 1724/5, in which a fifteen-year-old of Whitechapel bound himself to a London victualler for service in Maryland, may be two tellings of one event. The same book dates Martha's marriage to Stephen Hussey to September 1762.
He and his wife Sarah signed as witnesses at their son Joseph's wedding at Cane Creek on 17th of the 3rd month 1763.

The London parents of Anthony's father John Chamness are unknown. One family tree proposes Anthony Chamness and Ann Pitts, who married at St James, Duke's Place, on 23 September 1686, but John's baptism in November 1682 is earlier than that wedding.

A family history of 1922 describes the home Anthony and Sarah kept near Cane Creek, as remembered by a neighbor about a century earlier: "The farm lay a mile west of Cane Creek Friends church, was a good body of land and lay fine. The dwelling was large, perhaps 20x80 feet, consisted of two main rooms, made of hewn oak logs, with two shed rooms with porch the whole length on the front side." A small creek ran through the farm with a grist mill, and in the barn stood "a stationary thrashing machine propelled by horse power," to which neighbors hauled their wheat. It calls the home "one of hospitality, and a kind of social center," and says Sarah taught her daughters to spin and weave. The family register lists the children's births in Baltimore County, Maryland, then in Frederick County, Maryland (1742 to 1746), then in Orange County, North Carolina (1749 to 1761). Sarah was "the mother of thirteen children" and died probably about 1773; a tradition holds that Anthony was drafted for the army but not forced into it because of his conscience, though that is judged "barely credible" given his age.

stories.title: Union soldier, 42nd Indiana
stories.hook: Enlisted in 1861 and marched through a Kentucky winter of mud and measles. How long he served is a family puzzle.
body: Daniel Waters O'Neal was born on 25 October 1838 in Tennessee, the year before his parents settled in Gibson County, Indiana. He married Vashti Pearson on 5 January 1860. On 21 October 1861, at 22, he was mustered in as a private in Company F, 42nd Indiana Infantry, the company raised at Oakland City.

The regiment's first winter was its hardest. At Calhoun, Kentucky, the men camped on ground "fully ankle-deep in mud in its best parts," and within twenty days a third of them were in the hospital, many with measles. At Sacramento, Kentucky, they raided the hen-roosts and were arrested until the chaplain talked them free. When they marched into Nashville on 25 February 1862 they found an unlocked pork-house, and by the time headquarters sent a search party "not an ounce of the meat could be found."

A family biography says Daniel was discharged for disability, blindness, at Nashville on 15 March 1862, but the regiment's roll carries no remark beside his name, which usually meant a man served out his three years. Company F went on to Perryville, Stones River, Chickamauga, Missionary Ridge and the Atlanta campaign.

Daniel farmed in Gibson County, and he and Vashti had ten children, two of whom died as infants, among them Parsis Jane, born in 1868. He is buried in Somerville Cemetery under a family stone, with a side stone reading "DANIEL with Co. F. 42 Reg. Ind. Vol." His father, Archibald O'Neal, died in 1841; his widowed mother, Parses Shaw, later married Hugh Watt.

Daniel's funeral was held by Rev. Wright at the United Presbyterian Church of Somerville. He and Vashti lie in the same plot. A twenty-five-foot limestone monument to Company F was raised in 1893 at Oakland City, and it is said to carry the name 'D. O'Neal,' though that has not been confirmed.

A published roll of Company F reads beside his name: "O'Neal, Daniel W., vet. mustered out July 21, '65." "Vet." marks a man who reenlisted as a veteran when the 42nd did in January 1864, and 21 July 1865 is the day the regiment mustered out. If the roll is right, Daniel stayed in Company F to the end of the war rather than leaving in March 1862, and the regiment's later campaigns at Chickamauga, Atlanta and Bentonville would have included him. His application for an invalid pension in December 1865, five months after the muster-out, fits a man who came home with the regiment.

The Company F monument at Oakland City, dedicated in September 1893, carries, in the words of a 1913 booklet, "the names of all the original members of the company and the recruits, 143 in number," and beneath a scroll "Starved to death at Andersonville" the names of eleven company men who died as prisoners after Chickamauga.

Calhoun left a story the regiment told on itself. Col. James G. Jones kept a canteen of whisky in his quarters against "the bad weather and poisonous miasma" of the Calhoun camp, and one morning found it empty: "That d——d Lieutenant-Colonel Denby has been at my canteen, drank it all." The sentinel before headquarters, "being also a little afraid of malaria," had emptied it himself. The same camp sent a third of the men to the hospital within twenty days, and of the measles cases a few "transferred to Evansville died." In Company F's war its captain, William M. Cockrum, was wounded at Stones River and captured at Chickamauga.

Eight of his ten children lived to adulthood: Mary Elizabeth (1860-1960), William Allen (1863-1933), John Sherman (1866-1940), Parsis Jane (1868-1956), George Johnson (1875-1965), Daniel Clinton (1878-1954), David Commodore (1881-1955) and the youngest daughter, Charity Louisa (1887-1979). William was born in Tennessee, probably in 1863 while Daniel was in the army, though in 1880 the household gave Indiana as his birthplace and Missouri as George's. Three of the five sons died at Somerville, one at Evansville and one in Pike County, all within about thirty miles of the farm. Mary and Parsis went west.

stories.title: A murder trial in early Maryland
stories.hook: Anthony Chamness's wife came from a Baltimore County family whose patriarch was murdered.
body: Sarah Cole never knew her father, Joseph Cole of Baltimore County, Maryland, who made his will before she was three. Nearly fifty years later her uncle William Cole's 1769 will still called her "dau. and heir of testator's bro. Joseph." The Quaker meeting at Cane Creek in North Carolina wrote her down as "daughter of Joseph and Susanna Cole."

On 24 November 1735, at seventeen, she married Anthony Chamness at St. Paul's Parish, Baltimore County. He was a London-born boy who had served out his indenture and was about twenty-two. They moved with the Friends to Monocacy, to Carver's Creek in 1749 and to Cane Creek in 1751, and Sarah bore thirteen children; their son Joseph was born in 1740. A family history describes the farm they kept a mile west of the meetinghouse, a hewn-oak log house with a long porch, a grist mill on a small creek and large meadows, and says she taught her daughters to spin and weave. She died about 1773 and was probably buried in the Friends' graveyard at Cane Creek. Her son Joseph's daughter Martha married Robert Moffitt in 1797.

Her people had stories of their own. Joseph was the son of John Cole and Johanna (Hannah) Garrett, and Johanna's father, Dennis Garrett, was struck with a sword in 1691 and died weeks later. John Cole, then about twenty-two, was among the witnesses against the Baltimore County tailor John Oldton, who was condemned to hang, was reprieved and later served as captain of the county's rangers.

Dennis's widow Barbara remarried, to a Broad (John in most records; Marye calls him Thomas). In August 1712, as Barbara Garrett Broad, she deeded property to "her grandson Dennis Garrett Cole, s. of John and Hannah Cole," a boy named for the grandfather he never knew. The Coles were landholders: John Cole had surveys called Cole's Choice, Cole's Addition and Cole's Adventure north of the Patapsco.

stories.title: Court day at Sulphur Springs
stories.hook: A log courthouse, a whipping post, and a justice system built on keeping your word.
body: Cedar County was created by the Choctaw Nation's Doaksville Constitution of 1860 and lasted until statehood in 1907. Each county elected a judge for a two-year term to oversee county business, a sheriff, who collected taxes and took the census, and a ranger, who sold stray livestock. When an arrest or a sentence had to be carried out, the sheriff called on the district Lighthorsemen.

The Cedar County court met at Sulphur Springs, near present-day Rattan, on the first Monday of each month, in "a large log house, constructed of long, straight logs" that also served as a Choctaw Methodist church. Families camped at the springs on court days. A stump from the tree used as the whipping post is kept by the Pushmataha County Historical Society in Antlers.

Choctaw law punished crimes such as theft with lashes, fifty for a first offense and one hundred for a second. H. B. Cushman, who knew the Nation, described what came after: the whole crowd shook hands with the man who had been whipped, and the matter was never spoken of again.

From 1866 the Nation's death penalty was carried out by rifle. By custom a condemned man went home to plant and harvest his crop and came back on the appointed day, often choosing a friend or relative to fire the shot so no one would seek revenge. Capital cases went to the district court, not the county judge, so when Joel said his father "could have sentenced criminals to be shot," the whippings are the part that fits a county judge.

The court came to Sulphur Springs by an act of council. On 3 December 1891 the General Council removed the Cedar County court ground "from Pine Hill court ground to Sulphur Spring," to be known as Sulphur Spring court ground, and set its first session for the first Monday of January 1892. Joseph Thompson had been elected to the council's lower house the year before, though the printed act does not say who proposed it.

stories.title: Postmaster and judge of Doaksville
stories.hook: Vinson's brother was a Towson County judge and Doaksville's postmaster, and he was considered for Principal Chief.
body: Doaksville was the capital of the Choctaw Nation from 1858 to 1863. By 1850 it was the largest town in Indian Territory, and in 1860 a convention there adopted the constitution that governed the Choctaw Nation until 1906. At the end of the Civil War there were two surrenders at Doaksville: Principal Chief Peter Pitchlynn surrendered the Choctaw forces on 19 June 1865, and General Stand Watie surrendered his Cherokee, Creek, Seminole and Osage troops on 23 June, the last Confederate general to lay down arms.

Edward Ward Tims, Choctaw by Blood, served as District Trustee of Apukshunnubbee District in the early 1880s and for many years as County Judge of Towson County. On 24 October 1887 he was appointed postmaster at Doaksville, succeeding James T. Fleming; the office closed in 1903, when the name changed to Fort Towson.

On 29 April 1888 in Towson County he married Willie Jane Maxwell of Arkansas. After statehood he retired to his allotment southeast of Hugo. He died on 7 February 1923 and is buried in Springs Chapel Cemetery near Hugo.

His second wife, Willie Jane, was born on 27 July 1870 and died on 8 October 1922, four months before him. Their children were Lucy Ann (1889-1970), Minnie (1891-1930), Edmond (1893-1918), Benjamin (1897-1969), Myrtle (1899-1988), Abel (1901-1966) and Nora (1906-1977). By his first wife Polly, a full-blood Choctaw, he had a son, Columbus, born on Christmas Day 1860, who died on 21 October 1918 and is also buried at Springs Chapel.

In January 1940 it was proposed that his old log house, a quarter mile northeast of Fort Towson, become a museum, and Tims was remembered as 'once county judge of Towson County' and 'once considered for the position as principal chief of the Choctaw Nation.' The house was said to have been the setting for talk of the 1860 Council and the 1837 treaty. That detail is local lore, not a record. Joel Thompson remembered him simply as the man 'who was post master and Judge at Doaksville for so many years.'

A newspaper dispatch of the time shows how far that went. Dated Little Rock, Ark., 5 August 1886, and headed “Choctaws Hold an Election,” it read: “The election for principal chief of the Choctaw Nation was held yesterday.” It names four men: Ben Smallwood, Thompson McKinney, J. P. Folsom (printed Fulsom) and Edward Tims, and adds that a large vote was cast and that unofficial returns pointed to the election of McKinney. The dispatch gives no vote totals. Thompson McKinney went on to serve as Principal Chief, so Edward Tims, then in his mid-forties and a county judge, was a losing candidate in a four-man race for the highest office in the Nation.

When Edward applied for enrollment at Doaksville on 8 May 1899, he was "Tims, Edward W.," age 58, one-half blood, with parents "Vincent B. Tims," dead, a non-citizen, and "Betsy Tims," dead, of Towson County. His son Columbus, born in 1860, was enrolled as "Tims, Columbus," 40, three-quarter blood, with parents "E. W. Tims" and "Polly Tims," the latter dead.

His second marriage is documented: the Commission's decision gives the wedding as 29 April 1888, and a copy of the marriage certificate, signed by R. S. Frazier, reads the same; family accounts that give 19 April are a few days off. Their youngest child enrolled, Abel E., was born on 14 December 1901. The enrollment also includes a ward, Adam Nanomantubbe, whom O. W. Seay of Oscar called Edward's orphan grandson in a letter of 1903.

stories.title: The Pisachubbes of Speer and Jeter
stories.hook: A full-blood Choctaw farmer who registered for both world wars and lived with his daughter's family in 1940.
body: Robert was a full-blood Choctaw, enrolled at age 11 along with his widowed mother Eunice. In 1917 he was 28, married with one child, farming for himself at Speer; the registrar wrote "Indian" for race, black eyes and black hair, medium height, slender. In 1942, at 53, he registered again for the WWII draft of older men, still at Speer, naming his wife Lizzie.
In 1940 he and Lizzie were living with their daughter Frances and son-in-law Simon Thompson at Jeter, with their niece Alice and nephews Eli and Edward: twelve people in the house.

The three young relatives were orphans. Robert's older brother, William Harrison Pisachubbe, had married Lizzie's younger sister Adline Austin, so two Pisachubbe brothers had married two Austin sisters, and their children were double first cousins of Frances. Adline died at Speer in 1929 and William Harrison in 1937.

When William Harrison died in 1937, his relative Judge T. W. Hunter gave the Hugo Daily News a family history: the Pisachubbes came from Mississippi with the first group of Choctaw exiles in 1832 and settled at Fort Coffee, near present-day Spiro. His funeral was held at the family home near the Long Creek school house, with Choctaw Presbyterian minister Rev. Logan Harlin officiating.
The name Pisachubbe ends the way many Choctaw war-names do; its exact meaning is not recorded.

His land stayed in the family. In 1979 a court decree of heirship for his daughter Frances Pisachubbe Thompson covered Section 29, Township 5 South, Range 17 East, the same section as his allotment, and an order in his own estate followed in 1982.

His father was the late Joseph Pisachubbe, and Robert was 11 when the family was enrolled in 1899; he was approved as Choctaw by Blood on 12 December 1902. His wife Lizzie came from the Austin family of Fowlerville; her brother James, who died in 1899 before enrollment, was struck from the rolls by the Department on 16 September 1904.

quotes.t: He was a full blood Choctaw Indian, and was well known among the white people as well as among members of his tribe.

stories.title: Working at Camp Pike
stories.hook: In 1918, George Hulsey registered for the draft while working at Camp Pike near Little Rock.
body: George Washington Hulsey was forty-two when he registered for the draft on 12 September 1918. He gave his birth date as 24 December 1875 and his permanent address as Story, in Montgomery County, Arkansas. For work he was away at Camp Pike, the Army’s large training camp near Little Rock, employed as a laborer by the Stewart-McGehee Construction Company. His nearest relative was Sarah Rebecca Hulsey at Story. He was short and slender, with blue eyes and black hair.

He married Sarah Rebecca Graves on 22 December 1901, when she was seventeen. They had ten children, among them Oscar, born in 1910. George died in 1935 and is buried in Breashears Cemetery near Story. Family accounts also place a Benjamin F. Hulsey there, but the shared cemetery does not by itself establish their relationship.

Rebecca and George Washington Hulsey had ten children: William Roy (1904), John Wesley (1906), Noah (1908), Oscar Franklin (1910), Fred (1913), Ruby Ellen (Stipe, 1915), Grady (1918), Louis Daniel (1920), Grace Irene (Dunagan, 1923) and George Paul (1925). Oscar was the fourth. Rebecca was 17 at the wedding and 41 when the last child was born.
Accounts differ on George’s exact death date, 5 August or 21 August, but the year 1935 is sure. A death date of 22 December in one family tree seems to repeat his wedding anniversary.
At Oscar’s death in 1982, two sisters and four brothers survived him. Of his nine siblings, three had therefore died before him.
When he died in 1935, the oldest child, William Roy, was about 30 and the youngest, George Paul, about 9 or 10; his widow, Sarah Rebecca, was 51. She died at Bandon, Oregon in 1972.

Camp Pike was under heavy strain when he signed. Eleven days after the draft card, on 23 September 1918, the camp base hospital admitted 214 influenza cases in a single day, and by the end of October 12,393 men had reported sick with the disease.

In June 1880, B. F. Hulsey, a thirty-two-year-old Georgia-born miner, lived in Center Township with his wife Sarah G., thirty, and children Margaret M., six, George W., four, and infant Charles F. George’s later December 1875 birth date fits the child’s age. These point toward this household as his childhood family, though that is only probable.

His flat granite marker in Breashears Cemetery reads "George / Hulsey / Dec. 24, 1876 / Aug. 5, 1935." The stone settles the day of death as 5 August. Its birth year, though, is a year later than the December 1875 that George himself gave in 1918 and that appears in 1900; the marker was cut after his death, and George's own word carries more weight.

stories.title: Benjamin Hulsey: from Georgia to Arkansas
stories.hook: A Georgia-born Benjamin turns up in a blacksmith’s household, on an Arkansas cavalry roster and in later family accounts, but nobody can yet join them into one life.
body: Hulsey family accounts trace Benjamin Franklin Hulsey to the mountains of Union County, Georgia, and a household headed by the blacksmith Salathiel Hulsey and Elizabeth. In November 1850 that household held a Benjamin, three years old, with a six-year-old girl just above him. Three fits the family birth date of 2 February 1847, but nothing gives an exact birthday or shows that this child grew into the later Arkansas man.

A private Benjamin F. Hulsey served in Company D of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, a Union regiment recruited during the winter of 1863–64, while a grave account instead gives Benjamin Confederate cavalry service. Similar unit names blur the line between the two armies, and without a service or pension file no one can say which, if either, was his.

Family accounts name Sylvania Susane Partin as a wife, while a 1977 family account names Margaret Partain. The 1880 Montgomery County household that probably includes young George Washington Hulsey names the wife as Sarah G. None of those women has been securely identified with another, and Sylvania has not been established as George’s mother.

In September 1893 in Garland County, Benjamin F. Hulsley and Lucy Morgan, fifteen, took out a marriage license dated 25 September, though no one can read when the ceremony itself took place, so the license date should not automatically become their wedding date. Whether this couple belongs with the 1880 household is unresolved.

In June 1900 Benjamin was farming in Mountain Valley township of Garland County with his young wife Lucy, whom he had married in 1893, and six children. The four eldest, Charles, born in January 1879, Martin, Mary and Francis, had an Arkansas-born mother, as Sarah G. had been, and Charles was surely the five-month-old baby of the Center Township house twenty years before. Benjamin still could not write his name, any more than he could the day he enlisted at Cedar Glades, and in July 1888 he had applied for, and won, a Union invalid pension for his service in Company D of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry. Only his age, fifty-nine in 1900, refuses to fit.

In February 1910 a $175 land transfer was reported from B. F. Hulsey and wife to C. Floyd Huff: the west half of the northwest quarter of section 10, township 2 south, range 19 west. With neither his full name nor his home address given, it is only a possible match.

A family account places Benjamin’s death at Story on 16 December 1924 and his burial at Breashears Cemetery; a 1977 family account instead gives 1921. These accounts hold clues worth following, but they do not yet make one continuous life or prove that he was George Washington Hulsey’s father.

stories.title: A WPA laborer in the Ouachitas
stories.hook: Out of work 48 weeks of 1939, on a government job, with five children in a rented house.
body: Oscar Hulsey was born at Hot Springs, Arkansas, on 27 October 1910. In April 1940, at 29, he and Katie, also 29, were renting a house valued at $2 at South Fork in Montgomery County, Arkansas, with Leon 11, Delis 9, Benney 6, Glen 4 and Mary 2. Oscar was a laborer in "Government work" (the Depression-era WPA), had been unemployed 48 weeks, had worked 16 weeks in 1939 and earned $140. He had five years of schooling.

He had married Katie Stevenson on 27 October 1927, his 17th birthday; she had turned 17 twelve days earlier. He registered for the WWII draft at Mount Ida on 16 October 1940. The family later moved to the lumber towns of McCurtain County, Oklahoma. Oscar died at his home at Holly Creek on 17 June 1982, at 71, and was buried at Wheelock Cemetery near Millerton, the old Choctaw mission ground.

Oscar and Katie had seven children: Franklin Leon (1929-2015), Delphia (1931-2005), Bennie George (1933-1947), Glen (1935-2001), Mary Ellen (1938-2002), Charlie (1940-2010) and Willis Delane (1943-2004). Mary Ellen was born at Broken Bow, Oklahoma, and the family was back in Montgomery County by 1940.

At his death in 1982 Oscar was remembered as a Hot Springs native who had 'lived in the area for many years.' He died at his home at Holly Creek, between Broken Bow and Wright City in the old sawmill country. His funeral was held at 2 p.m. on Sunday at Wheelock Cemetery, with Rev. Bob Lewis officiating. He was survived by four sons, two daughters, two sisters, four brothers, ten grandchildren and nine great-grandchildren.

Wheelock was the Presbyterian mission to the Choctaws; its church was organized in December 1832 by Rev. Alfred Wright, whose 1853 gravestone stands in the same graveyard. Oscar was buried among the missionaries' graves in 1982.

A McCurtain County marriage license for "Oscar F. Hulsey" and Katie "Steveson," as the clerk spelled it, was filed on 27 February 1943. It probably belongs to this couple, though it gives no ages or residences. The family's own account puts the marriage on 27 October 1927 and their children began in 1929, so the 1943 license may be a later or second legal marriage, or a re-licensing; the paper license is held by the clerk in Idabel.

Four events mark the middle of his life. In January 1938 he was arrested after a two-day search and charged with assault with intent to kill in the stabbing of Eddie Stevenson, his brother-in-law. He was divorced from Katie in Arkansas on 26 September 1941 and married Hester May Whittington at Mount Ida on 3 November 1941. In 1945 Katie sued for divorce in McCurtain County, and the district court granted it in January 1946; and when his son Bennie was killed on a bicycle near Hugo in 1947, Oscar was living at Wright City.

stories.title: The Choctaw removal
stories.hook: Several ancestors were born in the old Choctaw Nation in Mississippi before the Trail of Tears.
body: Family trees say Pisachubbe "Wilson" (born 1807), Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi (born 1825) and Jackson Gardner (born about 1820) were born in the old Choctaw Nation in Mississippi, though nothing states where any of them was born, and O-we-na is placed only in Towson County. The Choctaw were the first nation removed under the Indian Removal Act, walking and riding west in 1831–1833.
These families settled in the Kiamitia, Blue and Towson counties of the new Choctaw Nation, where their grandchildren were enrolled by the Dawes Commission seventy years later.

A 1937 account of the Pisachubbe family says they came from Mississippi with the first group of exiles in 1832 and settled first at Fort Coffee, near present-day Spiro. At Doaksville, the trading firm of Doak & Tims, Vincent Tims's partnership, held army contracts in 1838 and 1839 to feed arriving Chickasaw emigrants at 13 cents a ration.

Two cautions on the Mississippi-born names. None of them has been found on a removal-era list. The proposed mother-and-son link between Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi and Joseph Pisachubbe is unproved; her age alone does not resolve it.

A full-blood Nancy Pisachubbi, 69, enrolled in 1899, gave her father as Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, dead, and her mother, Malindy, dead and of Mississippi. She appears to be the tree's Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, though nothing says whose mother she was.

The best-documented part of the removal's first winter is the stretch from the Mississippi to the Red River. About 18,880 Choctaws were counted in Major Francis Armstrong's census of 1831; by the first week of November four thousand were on the road, and between 26 November and 8 December about 2,500 were landed at Arkansas Post in a blizzard. A Choctaw letter of February 1833 shows Doaksville already a place where annuities were issued and 'a small town' of white traders stood below the Kiamichi.

stories.title: The Depression, house by house
stories.hook: The 1940 census caught both of Dad's and Mom's families at the bottom of the hard years.
body: In April 1940 each man was asked how many weeks he had worked the year before. Grady Moffitt in Hugo: 12 weeks, $100, unemployed 50 weeks, a crowded rented house. Oscar Hulsey at South Fork, Arkansas: 16 weeks on a government relief job, $140, unemployed 48 weeks, five children in a house worth $2. Simon Thompson at Jeter: 52 weeks on his own farm, worth $400, feeding twelve people, including his in-laws and their nieces and nephews.
Within a few years John Moffitt was in the Navy, the Hulseys had moved to the Oklahoma lumber towns, and the three families' children would meet and marry in Hugo.

The three houses sat in counties moving in opposite directions. Montgomery County, Arkansas, where the Hulseys were living at South Fork, had peaked at 12,455 people in 1910 and was down to 8,876 by 1940. The Caddo River Lumber Company had cut out the virgin pine and, in 1937, took the logging camp at Mauldin away almost overnight, hauling the buildings off by rail and pulling up its track behind it. Many families left to look for work. What public work there was came from the New Deal: the CCC and the WPA put up public buildings and park shelters in the Ouachita hills, and a married man with five children on a relief job in 1940 was most likely working for the WPA.

Choctaw County, across the Red River country to the west, was filling up instead, from 24,142 people in 1930 to 28,358 in 1940. The census taker that April worked from enumeration-district maps that still show the world the three families knew: Hugo outlined with its 1930 count of 5,272, Jeter township to its west, and Speer, Grant, Soper and Spencerville scattered along the section lines.

stories.title: Doaksville: the biggest town in Indian Territory
stories.hook: A trading post by the Kiamichi grew into the busiest town in the Choctaw Nation, then faded within a lifetime.
body: Doaksville took its name from Josiah Stuart Doak, co-owner of a trading post. He and his brother first set up at the mouth of the Kiamichi River, then moved about a mile west after the U.S. Army founded Fort Towson in 1824. Choctaw people relocated from Mississippi settled here, and steamboat access on the Red River made it a principal town of the Nation.

By 1840 it had several stores, a gristmill, a blacksmith and a hotel. In 1842 the Indian agent William Armstrong called it one of the most orderly and quiet towns in the West. A post office opened in 1847, and by 1850 it was the largest town in Indian Territory, with more than thirty buildings and two newspapers, one printed in Choctaw.

The Army left Fort Towson in 1854 and the town's importance began to slip. The Civil War wrecked the plantation economy around it, and when a railroad, the Arkansas and Choctaw, at last came through a short way off early in the 1900s, most businesses moved to the new town of Fort Towson on the line. The post office closed in 1903. (One account dates the railroad to 1870, but no line ran through that corner of the Choctaw Nation so early.) Only the Fort Towson-Doaksville Cemetery remains; the Oklahoma Historical Society acquired the site in 1960 and it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on May 29, 1975.
This is the town and neighborhood of the Cedar, Towson and Kiamitia county families, framed here as the place they lived near, not as a record of any one relative.

stories.title: The 1860 constitution written at Doaksville
stories.hook: A convention at Doaksville set the framework that governed the Choctaw Nation until its government ended in 1906.
body: The Choctaw and Chickasaw nations formally separated in 1855, and in 1860 a convention at Doaksville ratified the Doaksville Constitution, which guided the Choctaw Nation until 1906. Doaksville, a river-and-trading town that had been the largest settlement in Indian Territory since about 1850, served as the capital in this period; sources differ on the exact dates, and the capital later moved to Chahta Tamaha in 1863. Vincent B. Tims, partner of the town's founder, Josiah Doak, had been trading there since the late 1830s.

The constitution organized the Nation into counties inside its districts. Cedar County, for example, took its name from Big Cedar Creek (the Choctaw word for cedar is Chuala), was bounded by the Kiamichi River on the west and the Little River on the east, and had its seat at Sulphur Springs. Each county elected members to the National Council and also a county judge, a sheriff and a ranger to two-year terms. The judge ran county administration, the sheriff collected taxes, watched for intruders and took the census, and the ranger advertised and sold stray livestock.

For families in the Kiamichi country this was everyday government: the people holding these offices were their neighbors. Edward Ward Tims lived under it for decades. He was a district trustee in the early 1880s and a long-serving county judge of Towson County, and in 1887 he was made postmaster of Doaksville itself. The same constitution and the same county offices were still in force when the Dawes Commission came to enroll the Nation. Cedar County and its neighbors ceased to exist on 16 November 1907, when Oklahoma became a state.

stories.title: The last Confederate general lays down arms near Fort Towson
stories.hook: The Civil War ended in Indian Territory in the Choctaw Nation, a few miles from where these families lived.
body: After the Army abandoned Fort Towson in 1854, the post saw a brief resurgence during the Civil War when Gen. Samuel Bell Maxey chose it as headquarters for Confederate forces in Indian Territory.

On June 23, 1865, Cherokee Brig. Gen. Stand Watie surrendered his First Indian Brigade at Doaksville, near the fort, signing with two Union commissioners. He is generally called the last Confederate general officer to surrender. Some sources place the signing at Fort Towson itself; the date is consistent. Some writers call it the Battle of Doaksville, but no fight by that name is documented.
Doaksville was a fitting place for the war to end. A few weeks into the conflict, in June 1861, a Confederate flag was flying over the town, where the family's Vincent B. Tims lived out his life.

The Doaksville site was added to the National Register of Historic Places on May 29, 1975. Archaeologists dug there in 1995, 1996 and 1997, and a walkway and signs went in during 2001. For Choctaw families of the area the surrender was the end of four years in which their homeland was a Confederate district.

stories.title: Fort Towson: the army post built to receive the Choctaw
stories.hook: The Army established Fort Towson in 1824, before the forced removal of the Choctaw from Mississippi.
body: In May 1824 a company of the Seventh Infantry pitched camp on Gates Creek, near where the Kiamichi runs into the Red River. The soldiers called it Cantonment Towson, after Gen. Nathan Towson, the army's paymaster general and a hero of the War of 1812. They had a long list of jobs: watch the boundary with Mexican Texas, keep the peace, and stand between the Plains tribes and the Choctaw who were expected to arrive from Mississippi.

Much of the work was unglamorous and unpopular. The troops enforced the federal law of 1802 against hunting and unlicensed trading on Indian land, moved off Anglo settlers who believed they were living in Miller County, Arkansas, and cut roads to Fort Smith and to Fort Jesup in Louisiana. The post was abandoned in 1829.

After the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek it reopened in 1830 as Camp Phoenix and was soon renamed Fort Towson, this time with solid barracks and officers' quarters. It was meant as a buffer for the Choctaw slated for removal to the area, and for several years it served as a terminal on the Choctaw Trail of Tears. A trader named Josiah Doak, who had first set up at the mouth of the Kiamichi, moved about a mile west to be near the soldiers, and his store grew into Doaksville. Vincent B. Tims, Doak's partner and an ancestor of this family, signed as a witness when the Choctaw and Chickasaw met at Doaksville, near Fort Towson, in January 1837.

The fort was a staging ground for troops headed to the Mexican War in 1846-48. A young Lieutenant Jefferson Davis served there, and Sam Houston is known to have visited. Troops left for good in 1854. During the Civil War General Samuel Bell Maxey made the old post his headquarters for Confederate forces in Indian Territory. The state acquired the property in 1967 and a visitor center and sutler's store are open to the public.

stories.title: Allotment and the persistence of Choctaw government
stories.hook: The Thompson family’s enrollment and land selections unfolded as Choctaw leaders faced federal pressure to divide the Nation’s land.
body: On 23 April 1897, representatives of the Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations and the Dawes Commission signed the Atoka Agreement. It set terms for dividing tribal lands into individual allotments and reserved coal and asphalt lands. The agreement treated Freedmen and their descendants unequally, assigning them smaller allotments.

The agreement scheduled the end of the tribal governments for March 1906. The Choctaw and Chickasaw governments ratified it in November 1897, but Chickasaw voters rejected it in December, as Chickasaw law required a popular vote. The Curtis Act of 1898 required resubmission, and the agreement passed in a joint election on 24 August 1898.

The Dawes Commission had been established in 1893, before the agreement. Its enrollment process later reached the Thompson, Tims and Pisachubbe families. Betsy Tims Thompson applied with her family in 1899, and her son Simon’s birth that May required sworn statements from Betsy and his grandmother Emeline Tims.

In 1902 Choctaw and Chickasaw leaders and the federal government negotiated a supplemental agreement. A Choctaw executive committee circulated information and invited citizens to raise concerns before the vote. That October, Choctaw voters also chose a principal chief in a contested race; Green McCurtain was declared the winner. How any member of the Thompson family voted is not known.

Allotment changed the relationship between families and land. In 1903 Joseph Thompson selected tracts for Betsy and their children, including a homestead for Simon. Tribal land was divided into individual holdings, while federal restrictions governed transactions in many allotments. Allotment made it easier for Choctaw land to pass out of Choctaw hands.

The Nation did not disappear when federal policy reduced the government’s authority. Choctaw community members continued to meet and organize, and an advisory council emerged in the 1930s. In 1971 Harry J. W. Belvin became the first elected principal chief in decades to serve without the required presidential appointment. In 1978 a Choctaw council formed to develop a new constitution and restore representative government. Simon Thompson lived through these changes; his own political activities are not known.

stories.title: A monument for both armies
stories.hook: On the courthouse lawn in Morgantown stands a Civil War monument that honors soldiers from both sides.
body: Butler County, Kentucky, was created by the General Assembly on January 18, 1810, from parts of Logan and Ohio counties, and named for Major General Richard Butler, who died at the Battle of the Wabash in 1791. Its county seat, Morgantown, began in 1791 as a two-acre tract belonging to Christopher Funkhouser, and for a while it was called Funkhouser Hill. Salt-making was the first industry, and from 1833 a lock-and-dam plan made the Green River a way to market, with towns at Lock and Dam 3 (Rochester) and 4 (Woodbury).

The county was strongly Union but sent men to both armies, and it felt the war directly. Fighting broke out near Morgantown on October 29, 1861, and a skirmish followed the next day where Confederate forces were encamped. The war slowed the county's growth.

After the war, veterans of both sides raised money together for a monument on the courthouse lawn. The Confederate-Union Veterans' Monument, dedicated in 1907, is made of zinc, lists county residents who fought on each side, and is described as one of only two Kentucky Civil War monuments honoring soldiers from both sides, a sign of how neighbors and kin had been divided and then lived side by side.

The county reached its largest population, 15,896, in 1900, and about 1907 the Satterfields left Butler County for Franklin County, Texas. The river locks that had once carried the county's goods were washed out or abandoned later, in 1965 and 1980.

stories.title: Allen County and its county seat
stories.hook: Allen County was cut out of Barren and Warren counties in 1815 and named for a colonel killed in the War of 1812.
body: Allen County was established in 1815 from parts of Barren and Warren counties. It honors Colonel John Allen, a state senator and soldier killed at the Battle of Frenchtown in Michigan during the War of 1812. Today it covers 352 square miles on the Tennessee line, adjoining Macon and Sumner counties in Tennessee.

The county seat began as a settlement on Bays Fork in 1797 that grew into a stagecoach station. The town was laid off in 1816, established in 1817 and named for Charles Scott, Kentucky's fourth governor. Early on it was also called Allen Court House and Scottville. It was incorporated in 1860.

A fire at the courthouse in 1902 destroyed some county records, which is why some Allen County families are hard to trace in local papers. The county's population has grown from 14,628 in 1990 to 20,588 in 2020, and it was a dry county until voters approved legal alcohol sales in 2023.

stories.title: A crossing on the Sulphur River
stories.hook: Hagansport began as a river crossing, and its post office came and went over 70 years.
body: Hagansport grew up at a Sulphur River crossing called Hagan's Port, named for an early settler. The spelling Hagansport was in use by 1857, when F. M. Sims was postmaster. The post office closed in 1866, reopened in 1876, and closed for good in 1929. The village sits on a divide between the Sulphur River and White Oak Creek, about eleven miles northwest of Mount Vernon.

By 1884 the community had about 150 people, four churches, a school, a mill and a cotton gin. In 1896 its one-room school had 69 pupils. The U.S. Bureau of Soils, which surveyed the county in 1908, found the cotton land around the village on a clay loam and warned that the river bottoms below were "more or less subject to overflow." John B. Smith farmed land he owned there in 1900; a tenant such as John C. Satterfield, who rented a farm at Hagansport in 1910, usually kept half the crop.

Emma Smith was buried in Hagansport Cemetery in 1905. By the 1930s the center had moved south onto Farm Road 71, with a sawmill, two churches, a school and 125 people, and later it shifted again, to its present spot at the junction of Highway 37 and Farm Road 71. About 40 people lived there in 1985, and the Handbook of Texas says the estimate was still 40 through 2000.

stories.title: Cotton, rails and tenant farms in Franklin County
stories.hook: Between 1879 and 1929 the county's cotton acreage grew more than fourfold while yields fell by more than half.
body: Franklin County was created in March 1875 and named for Benjamin C. Franklin, and Mount Vernon won the county-seat election on 30 April of that year. White settlers had come from the late 1830s, mostly from Tennessee and the upper South, along the old Cherokee Trace. The county is small, 294 square miles of post-oak and blackjack woods, bounded on the north by the Sulphur River, with Big Cypress Creek running through the south.

For its first dozen years the county had no railroad and no navigable water. The East Line and Red River Railroad reached the southeast corner in 1876, and in 1887 the St. Louis, Arkansas and Texas Railway crossed the middle of the county and became the main route to market.

Cotton was the cash crop and corn fed the family; together they made up about three of every four harvested acres in 1880. In 1879, 706 farms planted 8,660 acres of cotton. By 1929, 1,678 farms planted 37,969 acres. Yields fell from about half a bale per acre to about one-fifth. Tenants were 34 percent of farmers in 1880 and 62 percent in 1930. Farm values fell from $4,172 in 1920 to $2,085 in 1930, and the first paved roads came only after voters approved a $200,000 bond issue in 1916.

John C. Satterfield reached the county from Kentucky about 1907 and in 1910 rented a farm at Hagansport, near the high-water mark of the county's population, which peaked at 9,331 in 1910. It fell to 8,494 in 1930 and bottomed at 5,101 in 1960, as the Depression and the shift to livestock took hold. Cotton fell to 16,582 acres by 1940. Oil found near Talco in 1936 reached northeastern Franklin County, but a 1939 local paper judged it not large enough to disturb the way of living.

stories.title: Grant began as a railroad stop in the Choctaw Nation
stories.hook: Grant grew from a store of about 1885 into a station on the Frisco line, when the land was still part of the Choctaw Nation.
body: Grant was founded as a station stop on the St. Louis and San Francisco Railroad, which opened through Indian Territory in June 1887, though the town may trace to a store Basil Gooding opened about 1885. It was named for President Ulysses S. Grant.

A post office opened at Grant, Indian Territory, on January 31, 1889. At its founding the town lay in Kiamitia County, part of the Pushmataha District of the Choctaw Nation (some accounts say Apukshunnubbee).
The town counted 289 people in 2010 and 190 in 2020.

Charles Oscar and Artie Smith are buried at Grant Cemetery. A Red River ferry six miles south connected residents with Texas markets, and when the Arkansas & Choctaw laid its track five miles north, business drifted to Hugo. Grant had 416 people in 1910 and 296 in 1930, with a cotton gin, bank, hotel and a newspaper, the Grant Graphic. By 1930, 73 percent of Choctaw County's farmers were tenants.

stories.title: From Evansville to Perryville and Stones River
stories.hook: Raised in October 1861 from six southwestern Indiana counties, the 42nd was in the field at Perryville within a year and at Stones River by New Year's.
body: The 42nd Indiana Infantry was organized at Evansville and mustered in for three years on October 9, 1861, under Colonel James Garrard Jones. Its men came from six counties of southwestern Indiana.

In the autumn of 1862 the regiment moved into Kentucky, pursued Bragg's army from October 1 to 15, and fought at the Battle of Perryville on October 8. One of its lieutenant colonels, Charles Harvey Denby, left after Perryville to command the 80th Indiana.

The regiment then returned to Nashville and advanced on Murfreesboro on December 30, 1862. At Stones River (December 30, 1862 to January 3, 1863) Lieutenant Colonel James M. Shanklin commanded and was surrounded and captured on 3 January 1863.
From January 1863 the regiment belonged to the XIV Corps, Army of the Cumberland.

The Perryville losses were plain. On the morning of 8 October 1862 the regiment "numbered less than five hundred effective men. The entire loss, officers and men, killed, wounded and missing, was 166, or fully one-third of the entire command." Company G, one of the largest, had 52 rank and file in the fight and lost 22 killed and wounded. The regiment's actual fighting, a veteran wrote, "was not to exceed two hours." It was "the first general engagement the regiment was in, and its loss was by far the greatest of any of the succeeding ones."

At Stones River, on the morning of 31 December 1862, the regiment fought in the cedar woods beside the 15th Kentucky, whose colonel was killed. Company F's captain, William M. Cockrum, was wounded in the right shoulder.
At Chickamauga (September 19-21, 1863) the regiment was commanded by Lieutenant Colonel William T. B. McIntire. In November 1863 it fought at Lookout Mountain and Missionary Ridge.

At Chickamauga the regiment lost "eight killed, fifty-three wounded, and thirty-two missing, making a total of ninety-three," nearly all the missing taken prisoner; Company F's captain was among them. The reenlistment followed: the government "offered inducements to the men to re-enlist, or veteranize, on the first day of January, 1864," and "there were but few in the 42d Indiana who did not re-enlist." The regiment reached Indianapolis on 28 January 1864, where Governor Morton and others addressed a public reception, and the soldiers "became recruiting officers" to fill the ranks.

The 42nd reenlisted on January 1, 1864, and served in the Atlanta Campaign from May 1 to September 8, 1864: Resaca (May 14-15), Kennesaw Mountain, Peachtree Creek (July 19-20), the Siege of Atlanta (July 22 to August 25) and Jonesboro (August 31 to September 1).

Company F paid for the Atlanta campaign in names: David W. Johnson (killed 14 August 1864), John Warick (7 August 1864) and David W. Wallam (31 May 1864, at Altoona or Allatoona). The regiment's losses for the campaign could not be given by name, because "the day's and month's losses were reported in the aggregate, and not in detail." The last of Company F's dead, Lt. John Q. A. Steele, fell at Bentonville on 19 March 1865.

It went on to the March to the Sea, the siege of Savannah and the Carolinas, fighting at Bentonville March 19-21, 1865, and marched in the Grand Review at Washington on May 24, 1865. It mustered out at Louisville on July 21, 1865.
Total losses were 310: 113 killed or mortally wounded, and 197 dead of disease.
