stories.title: A company town built around a sawmill
stories.hook: Wright City began about 1909 as a Dierks lumber company town, with the mill, houses, stores, bank and hotel all owned by the company.
body: The town had two names before it had its present one. When the post office was chartered on March 24, 1910, it was Bismark, after a Nebraska town the Dierks brothers knew. During World War I it became simply Wright, to shed the association with the German chancellor, and on May 18, 1920 it was renamed Wright City for William Wiley Wright, the county's first war casualty. The Choctaw Lumber Company, a subsidiary of Dierks Lumber and Coal, founded the town about 1909 beside a large timber-processing plant. Its first log was cut July 13, 1910.

The company supplied a sawmill, planer, railroad shops, housing, stores, a bank, a hotel, an ice factory and fire and police protection, and donated land for a school and churches. A company railroad ran from Valliant to De Queen, Arkansas.

This was the country the Hulsey family came to. By 1920 George Washington Hulsey, a farmer the family remembers as a preacher, had moved his wife Sarah and their six children from Arkansas to tenant-farm in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County. In 1930 the household of ten was renting near Wright City, with the mill and its company railroad close by.

Together the Wright City and Broken Bow mills could cut nearly 250,000 board feet of pine and 60,000 of hardwood a day. Workers struck for two months in 1947 and won an eight-cent hourly raise. Wright City had fewer than 500 people in the 1920s, 1,121 in 1950 and 1,068 in 1970.

Dierks Forests sold its non-core properties in August 1965, the town incorporated in 1966, and in 1969 Weyerhaeuser bought the mill complex that still anchors the town's economy. Its Little Cheyenne Rodeo, a rodeo, barbecue and dance started by local cowboys in 1933, is still held every July.

stories.title: The Oath, the Burned Fields, and the Road West
stories.hook: For the families who stood at Alamance, the battle lasted an afternoon. What came after lasted years.
body: Governor William Tryon's militia of about 1,000 won the field on May 16, 1771. Casualty figures are disputed: one account has the governor's side losing 9 killed and 61 wounded, others run to 27 government dead, and the Regulators carried off their own casualties, so perhaps 100 or more is only an estimate.

James Few was hanged at the camp the next day without a court. Of fourteen captives tried at a special term of the superior court at Hillsborough, twelve were convicted of treason and sentenced to hang. Six were pardoned at the last minute by King George III on Tryon's recommendation, and six were hanged at Hillsborough on June 19, 1771, among them Benjamin Merrill, Robert Matear, James Pugh and Captain Robert Messer.

Tryon then marched across Regulator country, burning homes and destroying crops. Residents were made to surrender their firearms, and he offered a pardon to nearly everyone who would swear an oath of allegiance to the Crown; within six weeks 6,409 people had done so.

Many Regulators and their families moved west. A few settled on the Mississippi near the site of Memphis and moved on again when some of Tryon's former militiamen turned up. Others went to Tennessee, where the Watauga Association formed in 1772 and the State of Franklin in 1784. Later study found that of 883 known Regulators only 34 became Loyalists, while 289 were Whigs.

quotes.t: Many Regulators and their families migrated westward, beyond North Carolina.
quotes.c: Summary of the aftermath of Alamance

stories.title: A Town Born at a Railroad Crossing
stories.hook: Hugo did not grow from a farm or a fort. It sprang up where two railroad lines crossed in the Choctaw Nation.
body: The Frisco built a north-south line through the area in 1887. In 1901–03 the Arkansas and Choctaw Railroad, later taken over by the Frisco, built an east-west line from Hope, Arkansas, toward Ardmore. The territorial town that sprang up at the crossing became Hugo.

It was founded in late 1901 in Kiamitia County, part of the Pushmataha District of the Choctaw Nation, and named for the French novelist Victor Hugo. The name was suggested by the wife of surveyor W. H. Darrough, a fan of his books.

Hugo grew fast. By 1910 it had 4,582 people, two newspapers, four banks and a creosoting plant, and in 1920 it had 6,368. The Depression closed three of its banks and the 1930 count dropped to 5,272, though by 1940 it was back to 5,909, with 111 retail businesses. The Frisco depot was built in 1914 and is a museum today. Agriculture, timber and ranching have been mainstays of the local economy since the start, which fits the family's timber work in Choctaw County.

The Al G. Kelly and Miller Brothers Circus moved its winter quarters to Hugo from Kansas in the early 1940s (sources give 1941 and 1942), and fifteen different shows have used the town as headquarters, at times about twenty wintering there. Showman's Rest at Mt. Olivet Cemetery was set aside for performers in 1960. In 1974 the Corps of Engineers finished Hugo Dam and made Hugo Lake.

stories.title: The County That Had Two Names
stories.hook: Etowah County was created under one name and renamed two years later, so the same ground carried two names within a few years.
body: Before 1866 the area was split mainly between DeKalb and Cherokee counties.
On December 7, 1866, the first postwar legislature created Baine County, named for David W. Baine, a politician and Confederate officer who died in battle in 1862. Gadsden was made the county seat.
On December 1, 1868, after the 1868 constitutional convention abolished Baine County, the same boundaries became Etowah County, from a Cherokee-language word.
So the same ground was DeKalb or Cherokee before 1866, Baine from 1866 to 1868, and Etowah afterward.
src: Wikipedia, Etowah County, Alabama (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etowah_County,_Alabama)

stories.title: Four documents, one name: William Moffitt in 1768
stories.hook: In a single spring and autumn, William Moffitt's name went onto a petition, a committee list and the Governor's list of men too dangerous to pardon.
body: The Regulators kept their papers, and so did the royal government. William's year can be followed in print. On 30 April 1768 the Regulators issued their eighth Advertisement, and "William Maffet" is among the signers, alongside nearly the whole leadership. The meeting agreed to "send 12 men that we have chosen to meet on the said 11th day of May at Thomas Lindley's," the mill on Cane Creek.

The ninth Advertisement, the petition on public fees, carries roughly 450 names. "Wm Moffit" signs on page 734; a "James Moffitt" signs on page 737, probably a relative. Then on 21 May 1768, at George Sally's house, the Regulators chose a committee to collect their grievances and carry them to the Governor. The list begins "Wm Maffit." His name is first.

In September, while the Governor’s troops were on the march from Salisbury to Hillsborough, James Hunter delivered a letter to Tryon signed for the Regulators by four men: Peter Julian, James Evans, Abraham Teague and William Moffitt. It protests loyalty, saying the Regulators “will when occasion requires fight for and defend him to the last drop of blood” for King George, and that they bear “no ill-will to any but our cruel Oppressors from which number we exclude your Excellency.” It then turns: “But will nothing propitiate but our blood, we are determined at all events to fall like men, and sell our lives at the very dearest rate.” The last line is a plea: “We beseech you Sir not to drive us to despair.”

When the Regulators were assembled at Hillsborough, they sent "The humble Address of the Inhabitants of several Counties called Regulators." They were "desirous to submit ourselves to the clemency of your Excellency, and to lay aside all method of redress of our grievances, but by a due course of Law," and they begged that the Governor "will forgive all our past offences by your gracious Proclamation." It is "Signed in behalf of the said Counties," and the first name in the list of twenty-two signers is William Moffitt's, ahead of Peter Julian, Lewis Lowry, Christopher Nation, Samuel Low, John Marshill and the rest.

The court of the same month showed the other side. At the Hillsborough Superior Court on Thursday the 29th, the clerk wrote: "The indictment preferred against James Hunter, Ninion Hamilton, Isaac Jackson, John Philip Hartso, William Moffitt, John Pile & Francis Dossett, for a Rout, having been returned by the Grand Jury 'a true bill as to all except John Pile,' it is ordered by the Court that the bill be Quashed, by reason of the irregularity of the return, and that the Attorney General prepare a new bill." Two more bills against other Regulators were quashed the same day. No later bill against him is known.

The Governor's answer came on 3 October 1768 at Hillsborough. His proclamation pardoned the insurgents except thirteen men, and "William Moffitt" is on the Council's list between Malachi Fyke and Christopher Nation. A general pardon of 9 September 1769 covered "all persons concerned in the said late Insurrection" and listed no exceptions; the pardon text does not say outright that it reached the thirteen.

His name does not appear in 1771. The reward proclamation outlawed only four men, and the sixteen men excepted from the June 1771 pardon include no Moffitt. Whether he stood on the field at Alamance on 16 May 1771 is not recorded.
In 1901 the boys' novel The Boy Spies with the Regulators printed Tryon's list, with "William Moffat" on it, as the names of "the patriots of upper Carolina in the opinion of William Tryon."

stories.title: What William did after Alamance
stories.hook: The records leave William out of the 1771 outlaw lists, and family accounts say he fed the Patriots rather than fought in the Revolution.
body: After the Regulators were beaten at Alamance in May 1771, the Governor outlawed four leaders and named sixteen more for exception from pardon. William is on neither list. Where he lived afterward is not recorded beyond the Deep River neighborhood of his 1768 papers.

A family history says he took the oath that followed Alamance, never to bear arms against the King, and stayed neutral in the Revolution because of it. No militia service for him has been found. Instead, family accounts and a battleground memorial book say he supplied provisions to the Patriots, and a pay voucher is cited for provisions furnished.

The mill is where the sources disagree. The community of Moffitt, North Carolina, takes its name from the mill on Richland Creek, and a post office called Moffitt's Mills ran from 1823 to 1935. Hugh Moffitt, William's probable brother, is credited with the first mill. Family histories say William and Hugh built it together, and a Patriot record credits a James Moffitt of Brush Creek with "supplied sundries to the militia; ran Moffitt's Mill." That is likely another brother, and which Moffitt the vouchers name is not known.
A Patriot named Robert Moffitt, born 1762 of Brush Creek, is a different man from William's son Robert.

The Randolph County militia's first court met on 16 September 1801. Governor Caswell commissioned John Collier, Richard Owen and Joseph Shepherd as the regiment's officers, and the nine company captains were Shubal York, Joseph Smith, Dobson Burrow, Robert Redding, Samuel Moffitt, Colon Steed, John Brown, Charles Duncan and John Craven. Governor Caswell is credited with the commissions, but he died in 1789, so the commissions and the 1801 date cannot both be right. A Samuel Moffitt among the captains may or may not belong to William and Mary's household or to Hugh Moffitt's.

stories.title: Two weddings at Cane Creek, sixteen days apart
stories.hook: In the spring of 1763 the Cane Creek meetinghouse saw Joseph Chamness marry Margaret Norton and William Moffitt marry Mary Davies. Their children would marry each other in 1797.
body: Cane Creek Monthly Meeting was organized in 1751, with Anthony Chamness named its overseer. By 1763 the Chamnesses had been in North Carolina for fourteen years, since a transfer from Monocacy in Maryland to Carver's Creek Meeting in 1749, followed by a 490-acre grant on Cane Creek dated 24 June 1751.

On 17 March 1763 Anthony's son Joseph, born in Baltimore County, Maryland, married Margaret Norton, daughter of Edward and Elizabeth Norton, who had arrived from Virginia in 1762. Joseph became the meeting's recorder of marriage certificates. Margaret bore eleven children and died in 1784.

Sixteen days later, on 2 April 1763, William Moffitt, 23, married Mary Davies, 22, at the same meeting. Her father Charles Davies had crossed the Atlantic as a bound youth, married Hannah Matson of Merion in Pennsylvania in 1732 or 1733, and followed the Quaker migration south. He was recorded as a minister at Cane Creek in 1761 and was disowned by the meeting five years later, after complaining that the women's minutes were "mixed with an untruth." He bought 187 acres in Orange County on 2 August 1758 and died on 13 May 1801; Hannah died on 25 October 1812.

Margaret's daughter Martha was born in 1778. On 20 September 1797 she married Mary's son Robert at Providence, under Center Monthly Meeting, and the Chamness and Moffitt lines joined. Their son Nathan carried the Moffitt name to Arkansas.

The Chamness-Norton marriage certificate reads: "Whereas, Joseph Chamness, son of Anthony Chamness and Sarah, his wife, of Orange County, in the Province of North Carolina, and Margaret Norton, daughter of Edward Norton and Elizabeth, his wife, of Rowan County; and Province aforesaid; having declared their intentions of Marriage with each other before several Monthly Meetings of the people called Quakers, held at Cane Creek, in Orange County, and Province aforesaid, according to the good order used amongst them, and having consent of parents, or parties concerned, their said proposals of marriage were allowed by said meeting." The day was "the Seventeenth day of the Third Month in the Year of Our Lord One Thousand Seven Hundred and Sixty-three," when the two stood up "in a public meeting of the said people, held at their meeting house at Cane Creek" and each promised "with Divine Assistance" to be a faithful and loving spouse until death.

Beneath the signatures of "Joseph Chamness" and "Margaret Chamness," twelve witnesses signed: "John Marshall, Joseph Pike, William Piggott, John Stout, John Davis, William Marshall," and, in the second column, "Thomas Branson, Anthony Chamness, Edward Norton, Sarah Chamness, Elizabeth Norton, Elizabeth Chamness." A family historian remarked: "We note, also, the parents of Joseph and Margaret and his oldest sister all signed the certificate." So the page carries the names of all four grandparents of Martha Chamness, who would marry Robert Moffitt in 1797: Anthony and Sarah Chamness, and Edward and Elizabeth Norton. It is added that Joseph was made recorder of marriage certificates in 1764 and that the meeting's records from then until 1769, when he moved into Providence Meeting in Randolph County, "must be" in his writing.

stories.note: Charles Davies's wedding is given as 9 Feb 1732 (old style, meaning 1733) and 9 Dec 1732 in different sources. One Find a Grave account places his birth in Luton, England and says he was indentured to a Quaker family in Philadelphia, while the Cane Creek family account says only that he was "sold to pay his passage." A note on that memorial suggests the disownment may be tied to a Deep River marriage dispute; the 1766 minute, since examined (see “The charge against the women's minutes”), says only that he charged the women's minutes with an untruth and does not name the entry, so that remains a possibility.

stories.title: Robert Moffitt's year: a father's will in 1796 and a Chamness wedding in 1797
stories.hook: Robert Moffitt was named executor of his father's will in 1796 and married Joseph Chamness's daughter Martha at Providence meeting on 20 September 1797.
body: On 20 September 1797, Robert Moffitt and Martha Chamness married at a public Quaker meeting at Providence. Their Quaker certificate names Robert as the son of William Moffitt, deceased, and Mary, of Randolph County; Martha was the daughter of Joseph Chamness and Margaret Norton. The witnesses include William Moffitt, Joseph Chamness, Hannah Chamness and Mary Moffitt: the groom's mother Mary, a William Moffitt who was probably his brother, the bride's father, and Hannah, who was Joseph's second wife and Martha's stepmother. Margaret had been dead since 1784, when Martha was five.

Robert had come to the altar with an estate. His father William's will of 1796 named "my son Robart Moffitt" executor and left him 250 acres bought of William Cox, except "the new field that is cleared upon the River," which Mary kept for life. His brother William got the 225-acre plantation, and the youngest, David, land on Tibs Run, wagon iron brought from Pig River and a quarter of a lot in Campbelltown. Mary got the wagon, the still and the stock. Martha, born 6 October 1778, was eighteen when she married him. Her father had served the meeting as its recorder of marriage certificates, and she was a granddaughter of Anthony Chamness.

They raised nine children in Randolph County. Randolph had been cut from Guilford in 1779, and Asheboro, its seat, was incorporated in 1796, the year William Moffitt wrote his will. The children were Naomi (1800), Sarah (1801; 21 April 1800 in her own profile), David (1802), William C. (1803; 17 April 1802 in his), Aaron (1805), Hannah, Lydia (1811), Nathan (1814) and Robert (1815). Robert was alive in 1820 when his mother dated her will "the 23rd day of the 9th month, 1820," naming "my three sons," and he is in the Randolph County census of 1830 and 1840. Martha lived until 1865.

The family that Robert and Martha founded scattered with the century. Sarah and Naomi went to Iowa with their Barker husbands; Sarah died at Lorimor in 1860; Hannah and Lydia stayed in Randolph County; Nathan went to Arkansas in the early 1840s, and the youngest Robert died at Hutton Valley, Howell County, Missouri, in 1872. Their grandson Veno died in 1864 as a Confederate prisoner at Elmira. Both of the families behind that wedding, Moffitt and Chamness, signed the same certificate in 1797.

stories.note: A memorial gives 6 October 1778 for Robert’s birth and 6 October 1844 for his death, but that birth date also appears for Martha; neither date has been verified. As executor in 1796, Robert was probably born by about 1775. Martha’s death is given as 11 October or 11 November 1865. Her parents and the children’s list come from compiled Quaker abstracts. The records do not establish that Robert was the Patriot Robert Moffitt of Brush Creek or Robert son of Hugh; neither married Martha. Robert’s exact birth date is unverified; 6 October 1778 duplicates Martha Chamness’s documented birth date and has been removed from the tree.
stories.place: Married 20 September 1797 at Providence meeting house, under Centre Monthly Meeting, North Carolina. Robert inherited 250 acres his father had bought of William Cox and was still living in 1820. Martha, born 6 October 1778, a daughter of Joseph Chamness, lived until 1865. Their nine children were Naomi, Sarah, David, William C., Aaron, Hannah, Lydia, Nathan and Robert.

stories.title: ARD-19: the drydock that could not sail
stories.hook: John's first ship had no engines, was 488 feet long, and was hit by a Japanese fighter while it held a damaged destroyer.
body: ARD-19 was a floating drydock built by the Pacific Bridge Company at Alameda, California, in 1943-44. It was about 488 feet long, 81 feet wide and 5,200 tons, with two 40 mm and two 20 mm gun mounts. It had no engines, so it was towed. Its work was to lift destroyers, minesweepers and landing ships out of the water at forward bases so their hulls could be repaired close to the fighting.

It was commissioned on 22 March 1944, the day John's muster rolls begin. It was towed across the Pacific in stages to join Service Squadron 10, the Navy's mobile base force, and reached Seeadler Harbor at Manus in the Admiralty Islands at the end of August 1944. In November it moved up to San Pedro Bay, Leyte.

The destroyer USS Ross had hit two Japanese mines off Dinagat and Homonhon on 19 October 1944, killing three men and leaving twenty missing. She was docked in ARD-19 on 24 November. Shortly before noon on 27 or 28 November (the two ship histories differ), a Japanese Army fighter crashed into the dock, starting gasoline fires that spread to Ross. Gunfire from ARD-19, Ross and LST-556 shot down a second fighter that was strafing them. The damage was heavy but kept the dock busy with its own repairs "for only a brief time." ARD-19 earned one battle star for Leyte, for 10-29 November 1944.

ARD-19 then carried on repair work at Subic Bay on Luzon "until after the end of World War II." Later its life was long: it was recommissioned in 1963 as USS Oak Ridge to dock ballistic-missile submarines and served until 2001.

On a crew of about 130 there was usually no doctor, and one or two corpsmen ran sick call. On a repair dock that meant burns, crushed hands and welding-flash eye injuries. That was general practice for such ships. John's rate and duties aboard ARD-19 are not known; on USS Chief in November 1945 he was rated F1c, fireman first class, so he may not have served as a corpsman at all.

stories.title: Joel Thompson tells it in Hugo, 1937
stories.hook: At 45, Joel Thompson sat down with a WPA interviewer and described the log house, the deer, the court and the schools of his boyhood.
body: On 28 August 1937 a Works Progress Administration field worker, Hazel B. Greene, took down Joel Thompson's story at his home on North G Street in Hugo. Joel was born on 29 January 1892, 'about 2 miles west of High Hill Methodist Church,' the son of Joseph P. Thompson and Betsy Tims. He said his father 'was second of nine children.'

He named the brothers and sisters who lived to be grown: Alex B., then himself, Peter Pitchlyn, Simon W., Joseph W., Jincy, who married Wilson Aaron, a full-blood Choctaw, and Marietta, who married Stephen Caldwell, also a full-blood. The family also raised an orphan boy, Wister Davis, from the time he was twelve. Our Simon is the fourth name on that list.

His picture of the place is plain and specific. The family finished school and Sunday school in the High Hill church house, and Joel got through the seventh grade there. The 1901 house had chimneys at each end, made of 'mudcats, or stick and dirt above the fireplaces which were made of native rocks.' Doaksville, where they got their mail and did their trading, was eight miles south by a very sandy road. Corinne was three miles north 'over the mountain,' which was easier once a store opened there.

He also remembered what his people did when someone was sick. Before white doctors came, and sometimes after, the family used Choctaw healers, who boiled tobacco in a pot set in a hole, spread a sheet over it, and laid the patient across the steam with the aching place directly above the pot.

Joel was 45 and said plainly what he could not recall, such as the maiden names of his grandmothers. Where his account can be checked against other records, it mostly holds up. Where it cannot (his father's years as judge and senator, the Massachusetts college), it is still the only account.

stories.title: Choosing the land, 1903
stories.hook: Joseph Thompson went to Atoka in 1903 and picked out the family's homesteads, including a 160-acre quarter for his four-year-old son Simon.
body: The family applied for Choctaw enrollment on 1 May 1899 and the Secretary of the Interior approved it on 12 December 1902. The next step was land. In the fall of 1903 Joseph P. Thompson gave testimony at Atoka, where the Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes took the selections, naming tracts for his wife and children.

For Betsy he selected a homestead of Lots 3 and 4 and the south half of the northwest quarter of Section 4, Township 5 South, Range 19 East, about 160 acres valued at $519.71. In November 1903 he added the northwest quarter of Section 9 in the same township, another 160 acres valued at $520.

Simon, then four years old, received his homestead on 2 October 1903: the northeast quarter of Section 11, Township 5 South, Range 19 East, 160 acres valued at $520. Further tracts were selected for him in November 1903, March 1904 and October 1907, and his citizenship certificate was issued at Hugo on 6 December 1907. A younger child enrolled as a 'new born' under the Act of 3 March 1905 was enrolled separately. Ella, who died in May 1899, was dismissed from the roll and received no land.

Allotments were held under federal restrictions, so the owners had to ask permission to sell or free their land. Joseph's petition was filed on 27 August 1908, when he was at Fort Towson. He filed again from Corinne on 10 September 1915, and the Secretary of the Interior approved removal of restrictions on 28 March 1916. Betsy's report was filed on 29 March 1920 from 'R.F.D. #1, Box 45, Corinne'; it was approved on 30 April and the order removing restrictions was mailed to her on 11 May 1920.

stories.title: Three weeks in the spring of 1899
stories.hook: The family applied for enrollment on 1 May 1899. Simon was born on 4 May and his five-year-old sister Ella died on 22 May.
body: Ella was the third child of Joseph and Betsy Thompson to be listed on the Choctaw rolls. In 1896 she was 'Ella' in Cedar County, and in 1899 'Thompson, Ella N.,' a daughter, age 5, three-quarter blood.

The family made its application on 1 May 1899. Three days later Betsy gave birth to Simon, with her mother Emeline as midwife. On 22 May, Ella died. Ella's own card puts it in plain words: 'Died May 22, 1899.' The proof of her death was not filed until 18 April 1901.

Because she had died before the enrollment was approved, her name was struck. Her name was dismissed from the rolls under an order of 31 March 1905. She received no allotment, but she stands in the family's enrollment with her parents and brothers.

Sworn statements about her death survive. On 13 April 1901 at Doaksville, Joseph P. Thompson, then 39, swore that he was the father of "Ella N. Thompson" and that she "died on 22 day of May 1899." A second affidavit, as an acquaintance, was sworn the same day by Robert Tims, 26, her mother's brother; both were sworn before the notary R. L. Carter of Doaksville. The Commission had written to Joseph on 9 March 1901 that it "has information of the death of your daughter" and sent a blank form, and on 18 April it acknowledged "your affidavit and that of Robert Tims, relative to the death of your daughter, Ella N. Thompson, which occurred May 22, 1899."

stories.title: Betsy's brother on Merchants Row
stories.hook: Betsy's brother sat in the Choctaw Council, and in 1937 he described his grandfather's store at Doaksville, in front of the old rock jail.
body: James Brown Tims, called Jimmie, was a son of Vinson and Emeline Tims and Betsy's elder brother. Joel Thompson remembered that when his father Joseph served as county judge and then senator, 'James Brown Tims was a Representative in the Choctaw Council.' Joel said the Tims family was 'quite prominent in public affairs.'

Jimmie was interviewed in 1937, the same year as his nephew Joel, and is said to have described his parents, Vinson and Emeline, and the stand of V. B. Tims on Merchants Row in Doaksville, in front of the old rock jail, whose foundations can still be seen. (It is not clear whether he meant his grandfather Vincent or his father Vinson.) An article on Cedar County's Choctaw name, Chuala, 'cedar,' from Big Cedar Creek, also cites his interview.

The jail is still there in outline. Visitors to the Doaksville site today walk past capped stone wells, a few foundations and the outlines of three jail cells. His brother Mitchell Tims (1869-1950) is buried at High Hill Cemetery near the old home place. By 1910 a James Tims household, probably his, was among the Thompsons' nearest neighbors in Wilson Township.

After he died, the Methodist Indian Mission of Oklahoma printed his memoir in the minutes of its September 1941 session at Ware's Chapel, near Anadarko: "James Brown Tims was born eight miles north of Ft. Towson, in what was then known as Doaksville, Indian Territory, on June 25, 1864. He was seventy-seven years of age at the time of his departure." That puts his death between 25 June and the conference of 12-14 September 1941. The memoir was signed by the Rev. Johnson W. Bobb, superintendent of the Choctaw District.

"Brother Tims was better known among the Choctaws as J. B. Tims. Of him it can be said: He loved everybody and everybody loved him." He began as a class leader and later became a local deacon in the Methodist Church, "preached to and led his people in the Christian way for about forty-five years," and served the Antlers Circuit for eleven of them. "Very influential among his people, Brother Tims always stood for right living and for Christian Education. At one time he was a member of the Choctaw Council." That last line is the same office his nephew Joel Thompson gave him in 1937.

He was still at work in 1940: James B. Tims was a local deacon of the Choctaw District in 1934, 1935 and 1936, and in 1940 was listed as "Tims, J. B., L.D., Rt. 1, Ft. Towson." A later memorial roll puts his death under 1940, but it warns that it contains errors, and the memoir's age of 77 fits 1941.

In 1899 Jimmie's household was enrolled: "Tims, James B.," age 36, one-half Choctaw, of Towson County, post office Alikchi, whose parents were "Vinson W. Tims," dead, and "Emeline Tims." He had been "Jas. B. Tims" in 1896. His wife, "Mary J.," 31, full-blood, was the daughter of Dixon Willis and Elizabeth Willis, both dead. Their children were Evelyn, Dixon and Rufus (Rufus an infant of five months when they applied on 18 April 1899).

Twins followed. On 27 August 1901 the Commission wrote that it had the application for "Lewie Tims and Lula Tims, twin children of James B. and Mary J. Tims, born July 19, 1901," and sent two forms because each child needed a separate application. Lula died on 19 January 1902 at about six months. On 30 October 1902 the Commission acknowledged "your affidavit and that of Mary J. Tims relative to the death of your minor daughter, Lula Tims," and her enrollment was canceled in 1904. Lowie was enrolled.

In 1919 he was among the Indian pastors the Southern church helped to support. In the Board of Missions' appeal, "J. B. Tims, Bruno Circuit (part support)" appears with a grant of $40 a year, in a list that also includes Wewoka, Chickasaw, Jesse, LeFlore and McCurtain circuits. The memoir of 1941 says he later spent eleven years on the Antlers Circuit.

stories.title: A 45-year-old farmer joins the Union army at Cedar Glades
stories.hook: Born on Toms Creek, North Carolina, he served on Georgia juries, farmed in the Arkansas hills and enlisted in 1864 at 45.
body: Gilliam Graves was born about 1813 in North Carolina, on Toms Creek in Randolph County. On 18 August 1832 he married Mary Tyler there. The county had been cut from Guilford in 1779, and his neighbors on the Deep River side included Friends whose meetings were draining toward Indiana. Gilliam went south instead. He was in Cherokee County, Georgia, by December 1835, when he served on a county jury; he served again on 5 November 1838 and is on the county's 1840 census. By 1853 he was on the tax lists of Montgomery County, Arkansas, at Cedar Glades, and in 1860 he was written down as 'Galem' Graves.

On 14 January 1864 he volunteered at Cedar Glades for the Union army, in Company D, 4th Arkansas, the same company that carried Benjamin F. Hulsey. He gave his age as 45; a farmer, five feet ten inches tall, with black eyes. He deserted on 12 October 1864 and returned on 25 December 1864. His second marriage, on 18 August 1845 in Montgomery County, was to Delila Hawthorne; if that is right, he was in Arkansas well before the 1853 tax list. Both of his first two marriages are dated 18 August, thirteen years apart, which may be a copying error; neither date has been checked. The children Aaron and John, listed in 1860 as born in Alabama about 1847 and 1849, also sit awkwardly with an Arkansas marriage in 1845. His third wife was Mary 'Polly' (Gray) Washburn.

He died, supposedly killed by robbers, in January 1876 in Garland County (another account gives 22 October 1876; the two dates conflict and neither rests on a record), and is buried beside Polly in Mountain Valley Cemetery. His son Jesse is the Graves who stands behind our Sarah Rebecca. Jesse is said to have been born about 1855 in Blount County, Alabama, which does not square with Gilliam’s Arkansas tax roll of 1853 and is unresolved.

Garland County was not yet three years old when he died: a history of the Ozark region says it “was established April 5, 1873,” with Hot Springs the seat, and that “the greater part is mountainous, leaving only a small area worthy of the labor of the husbandman.” Hot Springs is given as the birthplace of G. W. Hulsey, on 24 December 1876 in one account (his 1918 draft card gives 24 December 1875), and of Oscar Hulsey in 1910.
Gilliam's parents are unknown; no sourced father has been found.

His later years are recorded in some detail. He was on the Montgomery County tax lists in 1853-59, 1861, 1865, 1867-68, 1871 and 1872, and in 1860, as "Galem Graves," his household held children Sarah 15 (born Georgia), Aaron 13 and John 11 (Alabama), Julia 9 and Nancy 5 (Arkansas). No trace of his family has been found for 1850 and 1870. A history of the county he came to says it “was organized December 9, 1842,” its settlers “came into the valleys of Montgomery in the thirties,” “in 1845 there were twenty-one slave-owners,” and “the spinning-wheel and loom have not yet disappeared.” Its seat is Mount Ida.

In January 1854 he was made guardian of the children of Samuel and Sarah Graves, and again in April 1861 of the minor heirs. His first wife, Mary Tyler, married him in Randolph County on 18 August 1832; a Charles Tyler, 79, lived in Cherokee County, Georgia, in 1850 with a boy, William D. Graves, 10, born Georgia, who may be Gilliam's son left with his grandfather.

His third wife, Polly Gray Washburn, died about 1879; his second, Delila Hawthorne, died about 1860 at Cedar Glades. His family tradition, recorded twice in the genealogy, makes his father an American Indian , though no record supports it.

The Union 4th Arkansas Cavalry at Cedar Glades was a company of neighbors. A petition of 10 March 1864 from Union men of Montgomery County said "Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down" on 1 March, and the men who enlisted with Gilliam on 14 January included William Haskins, 45, John Stroud, 45, John Tidwell, 32, born in Blount County, Alabama, and others.

The regiment he joined was the 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union), organized at Little Rock in December 1863. Its Company L wrote from Montgomery County on 10 March 1864 that wives and children of Union men at Cedar Glades were being shot, and a battalion of the regiment fought through the county in July. His desertion on 12 October 1864 and return on 25 December 1864 fall in the period of the autumn expedition from Little Rock to Fort Smith, but no record places his company on it.

Who Gilliam's parents were is still unknown. The Graves Family Association, which has worked through the Randolph County Graveses in the old records and by the Y-DNA of their male lines, places him, without proof, among the descendants of John Graves and his wife Margery Harvey, who farmed 312 acres on Bumpers Fork of Little River and whose will of 1811 names their sons Samuel, William, Leonard and John. The association suggests he came through Leonard, and notes that the family already had two other Gilliams, a son and a grandson of John. The Y-DNA of Gilliam's male-line descendants matches the descendants of John Graves, who settled at Concord, Massachusetts, in 1635, and two family accounts make his father an American Indian, a story the association itself calls folklore. When Leonard and Samuel sold their parents' Bumpers Fork land in 1822, the buyer was a Silas Moffitt.

stories.title: From Alabama to the Cedar Glades
stories.hook: A family account traces Jesse Graves from Alabama to Arkansas, where his household grew through several marriages.
body: Jesse S. Graves is placed by the Graves family in Blount County, Alabama, about 1855, a son of Gilliam Graves. He may be the Jesse King Graves of the family tree, but that is not settled. The family traces Gilliam from North Carolina through Georgia and Alabama to Cedar Glades, Arkansas.

Jesse married Sarah Emma Fisher at Jack Phillips's home in Montgomery County on 2 April 1871, at 18 and 15. A family account of 1977 names Margaret Crumpton as his second wife, and a Jesse Graves married Margaret Crumpton in Garland County on 31 January 1884, but the groom's age differs from the age given for Jesse in 1871.

A Jesse Graves married Nancy Cutter in Garland County on 19 September 1889; her story, and the tangle of her names, is told under her own name. The 1977 account names Sarah Rebecca as Jesse's daughter but not her mother.

The ages do not fit together. Jesse was 18 in 1871, yet the grooms in 1884 and 1889 are each 38, five years apart. There may be an error, or they may be different men, and whether they were Sarah Rebecca's father is unsettled.

The 1977 account lists John and Henry Crumpton, Cindy Sutton, and Issas and Prince Cuttler among Jesse's stepchildren. A list of burials made in 2002 names Jesse in McGill Cemetery, Garland County, though the family places his grave in the yard of his old home on Walnut Valley Road.

stories.title: Where the Thompsons got their mail
stories.hook: Joseph and Betsy's addresses on the records move from Doaksville to Fort Towson to Corinne as the post offices changed around them.
body: In 1899 the family's post office was Doaksville, Indian Territory, in Cedar County. Joel Thompson said Doaksville was about eight miles south of the home place, and that the family did 'all of our trading' there. A faint pencil note added in April 1905 changes it to 'Ft. Towson, I.T.' The Doaksville post office had closed in 1903, when the name became Fort Towson.

Corinne, three miles north 'over the mountain,' was more convenient. Its post office opened on 24 August 1904 and ran until 1958; it was named for Corinne Estill Lesueur, the daughter of a Confederate officer who later became Missouri's secretary of state. By September 1915 Joseph was writing from Corinne. In September 1918 Simon, 19, gave his work on his draft card as farmer for his father at Corinne. In 1920 Betsy's address was 'R.F.D. #1, Box 45, Corinne.'

In 1910 the family was in Wilson Township of Choctaw County, which was formed at statehood in 1907 from parts of Cedar, Towson and other old counties. They had not moved far; the county and post office names changed around them.

stories.title: Peter, the brother just older than Simon
stories.hook: Joel's interview lists his brother as 'Peter Pitchlyn,' the same name as a famous Choctaw principal chief.
body: Joel Thompson's list of his brothers includes 'Peter Pitchlyn,' and in 1899 the boy was enrolled as 'Peter P.,' age 2, three-quarter blood; in 1896 he had been 'Peter B.,' probably a clerk's slip. He was the brother just older than Simon.
The name matches Peter Pitchlynn, a principal chief of the Choctaw Nation during Joseph's boyhood. The interview does not say whether the boy was named for him.
Peter P. Thompson (1896-1979) lies in High Hill Cemetery, near the church where the family worshipped and went to school.

A Peter Thompson of Fort Towson appears in Methodist Indian Mission records for nearly thirty years. In 1938 he was among the church school superintendents for the Choctaw District, "Peter Thompson, Ft. Towson, Okla.," and, a line below, "Mitchell Tims, Ft. Towson, Okla.," Peter's uncle. In 1940 Peter Thompson was a lay delegate for the Rufe Circuit, in 1947 and 1948 "High Hill . . . Pete Thompson, Fort Towson," and he was still a lay delegate in 1952, 1955 and 1965.
No middle initial is given, so this is probably, not certainly, Joseph and Betsy's son. The Fort Towson address, the High Hill church and his burial at High Hill all point to him.

stories.title: High Hill: church, school and cemetery
stories.hook: Betsy's parents are remembered at the old place, the Thompsons went to church and school in the High Hill church house, and several of the family are listed in the cemetery.
body: Joel Thompson remembered High Hill as a Methodist church where 'they had school in the church house for many years.' His father sat on the school board and the children went to school and Sunday school there 'all of our lives.' The 1901 house stood within 300 yards, and in camp-meeting weeks the Thompsons had 'lots of company,' with whole deer, hogs and turkeys barbecued for the crowd.

Betsy was married at her parents' home about four miles north and a little west of Doaksville, in Towson County, the place later known as the Charley Blankenship place. Joel said his grandparents Vinson and Emeline Tims were 'buried there at the old place.' High Hill Cemetery, three miles east of the junction of the Spencerville Road and State Highway 147 and half a mile south, holds Peter P. Thompson (1896-1979), Mitchell Tims (1869-1950), and Emeline Steadman Tims (1842-1918). Vinson's marker there is a cenotaph.

The name is a puzzle. Another High Hill, two miles south of Alderson in Pittsburg County, appears in a different interview, and the two should not be confused. For this family, High Hill rests on Joel's memory and on the graves of Emeline, Vinson and Peter.

High Hill was a church of the Methodist Indian Mission of Oklahoma, on the Rufe Circuit. In 1941 the Choctaw District listed the churches "in Choctaw county: High Hill, Hampton Chapel, Honey Spring, Pecan Groves, Kullichito," and from 1942 to 1948 High Hill's church school was led first by Willie S. Tims and then by Pete Thompson, both of Fort Towson. The 1943 minutes call the burying ground the "High Hill Indian Cemetery, north of Fort Towson."

Its neighbor, Hampton's Chapel, which the minutes call "the Church in the Wild Woods," ten miles north of Fort Towson, hosted the whole conference on 13-15 September 1940, with the Rev. Edgar Tims as host pastor. The same book lists Betsy's brother Mitchell Tims of Fort Towson among the Choctaw District's church school superintendents, as the 1938 and 1939 lists do, and puts Betsy's brothers J. B. Tims and Robert J. Tims on the roll of local deacons.

stories.title: The Choctaw names
stories.hook: Ata-sa-ha-bi, Lotima, O-we-na, Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, Brazil and Siney were the parents of our enrolled ancestors.

subject.name: The Choctaw names on the cards

body: The enrollment of 1899 named parents who did not themselves enroll, because they were dead. Legion Austin's father was Ata-sa-ha-bi and his mother Lotima, both dead and both of Towson County; Molsey Austin's parents were Brazil and Siney, both dead, of Red River. Emeline Tims's mother, O-we-na, was Choctaw of Towson County, and Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi is the Mississippi-born name on another line of the family.

The names tell something about the Choctaw naming practice. A linguist, Ovid Vickers, wrote that in old Mississippi names were 'nearly always connotative,' earned by deeds, and that 'a great proportion of those who had earned second names as a result of participation in a war were given names carrying the termination abi signifying killer.' Surnames such as Thompson, Austin and Gardner were adopted after 1830, often from the given name of a respected white man.

Pisachubbe, Te-hol-ba-ta-bi and Ata-sa-ha-bi all look like names of this kind, ending in the war-name element. Their exact meanings are not recorded, and the Choctaw Nation's language staff cautions against reading the ending 'killer.' O-we-na is a Choctaw given name, meaning unknown. Joel Thompson said his father's mother's family 'had some sort of a Choctaw name' and 'never adopted a white man's name,' the same pattern from another line.

quotes.t: a great proportion of those who had earned second names as a result of participation in a war were given names carrying the termination 'abi' signifying 'killer.'

stories.title: The Act nobody could find
stories.hook: In the Regulators' own account of how their movement began, William Moffit is the man who went through the laws and found no such Act as the deputy sheriff claimed.
body: In May 1768 the Regulators' committee wrote out a plain account of their quarrel with the Orange County officers, to carry to the Governor with their petition. It was Regulators' Advertisement No. 11. Midway through comes a scene at a tax meeting on Deep River, William Moffitt's own neighborhood.

The High Sheriff, Mr. Harris, had published an advertisement citing an Act of the Assembly as the authority for the tax, and many paid but disputed the authority of the Act. At the meeting, the committee wrote, Deputy Sheriff John Wood, "being questioned about the Act confidently persisted in the affirmative. Upon which William Moffit on examining the Laws, no such Act could be found, Wood now finding his knavery was detected, no less confidently denied the Advertisement to be Harris's." The sentence is clumsy in print, but its sense is plain: William looked through the laws, the Act was not there, and the deputy then denied that the advertisement was the sheriff's at all.

The committee drew its own moral. "This unprecedented Effrontery, convinced the Spectators that there was Knavery, and Collusion," and, judging the whole business of a piece, they "formed themselves into Bodies under the denomination of Regulators." By the committee's account, it was this scene that led the neighborhood to organize.

William's name is at the foot of the document. It closes "Signed in behalf and by Order of the Regulators by us the Committee," over eight names: John Low, James Hunter, Rednap Howell, Harmon Cox, John Marshel, W. Cox, W. Moffitt and George Hendry. A second paper, dated at Thomas Cox's mill on Monday 30 May 1768, orders the narrative carried to the Governor and Council by James Hunter and Rednap Howell, and William Moffitt signs that one too.

He had known the Cox family on Deep River for years. Court records cited in a Cox family history show William Moffitt proving a deed from Thomas Cox to Jacob Grigg for 179 acres in May 1765, and witnessing the will of William Cox, dated "the 20th Day of the first month 1767," together with John Cox and John Allen. When the Orange County court sat at Hillsborough in February 1767, the clerk recorded that "this Will was Exhibited in Open Court & Duly proved by the Oaths of William Moffitt, & John Allen." Years later two of his daughters, Catharine and Hannah, are named in the family wills as Cox wives, and the 250 acres he left his son Robert were land he had bought of William Cox.
The name is spelled Maffet, Moffit and Moffitt for the same man. The 1765 deed and the 1767 will are known only at second hand, through a Cox family history.

stories.title: A postmaster's letters, August to November 1864
stories.hook: The Confederate Post Office Department's surviving papers include letters signed by V. B. Tims, postmaster at Doaksville, and the last is dated 1 November 1864.
body: Doaksville was the end of two Confederate mail routes, and in 1862 and 1863 its postmaster was J. P. Kingsbury. By 1864 the office was in the hands of V. B. Tims.

On 16 August 1864 he wrote to Dr. James H. Starr, the Post Office Department's agent at Marshall, Texas, that he had advertised for bids to carry the mail on Route 410 from Doaksville to Fort Washita, "the time having expired, I have now to inform you that there was but one bid given in and that was by Thomas M. Arnett." On 9 September, signing himself in full as "Vincent B. Tims, P. M.," he sent back the contract and oath executed by Arnett, with the news that Arnett's application for exemption from army service had been refused by the district headquarters at Fort Towson, so he could not start work. The contract then went to the second-best bidder, and an October letter from Tims reports the new contractor, James M. Nunn, at work on the route.

The last letter is the plainest. "Doaksville C. N., Nov 1st 1864," it begins: "I herewith enclose you my accounts current from January 1st to Sept. 30th 1864 inclusive which shows a balance of Twenty cents due to you. I herewith enclose you Ten Dollars new issue from which please deduct my account and send the balance in postage stamps." It is signed "V. B. Tims P. M." His accounts for the first nine months of 1864 left a balance of twenty cents. The volume of mail handled at Doaksville in 1862 and 1863 "was quite small."

These letters bear on the date of his death. The family accounts give 14 or 17 June 1864, and his great-grandson Joel Thompson remembered him as the first postmaster at Doaksville. But the postmaster who signed in September and November 1864, with the same name and initials he used on the Chickasaw treaty of 1837, was alive and in office months after that date. The June 1864 date cannot stand, and the 1871 postmaster-roll entry for a 'V. B. Tims,' which seemed to conflict with it, may simply be Vincent himself.

One more signature is on a petition of 1 July 1864 from the postmasters along the Washington-to-Doaksville mail route, who complained that since the army courier line had stopped "we are deprived of all means of hearing from our friends and relatives in the army." It was signed by R. D. Wright of Netra Bok, Arkansas, William K. McKean of Ultima Thule, Arkansas, P. P. Pitchlynn at Eagle Town and "V. B. Tims, P. M., Doaksville, C. N." General Maxey forwarded it from Fort Towson on 30 July, and on 8 August Dr. Starr replied that the contractors had been ordered to resume service or the route would be readvertised.

stories.title: In his own words, 1869
stories.hook: At 81, too old and nervous to write, the Rev. Elam Stevenson dictated his memories of early Methodism in Giles County to his son Augustus, and a church historian printed them.
body: In 1869 the Methodist historian John B. McFerrin asked old Elam Stevenson for what he remembered of the first Methodists in Giles and Lincoln counties. The answer is dated "Elkton, Giles county, Tennessee, July 28, 1869." It came through Elam's son John, and was written down by another son, Augustus, "as I am too old and nervous to write now." McFerrin printed it in 1871.

Elam is frank about his health. "My memory is failing me, and I am much afflicted with asthma, and I am not able to be out of my bed more than half my time. I have come down to the edge of the last river, and expect soon to cross over and join those who have gone on before." Of the people who came to the country when he did, "not one is now left; they are all gone, and I am left with only my wife as survivors of a past generation." He lived six more years, and Lydia three.

He remembers the move in 1813. The preacher Philip Bruce, he says, "came to my house and asked me to bring a part of his books in my wagon, as he had no conveyance but a one-horse sulky. I agreed to do so, and accordingly brought the books." Bruce's brother had married a sister of Elam's wife, and Bruce "made our neighborhood his home, after coming to Tennessee." This is Elam's own word on the journey, and it speaks of a wagon, which sits badly with the family story of a pack-horse crossing because there were no wagon roads.

He writes about his church as someone who helped build it. "Our Church at Bee Spring (so named because it was famous as a place for coursing wild bees, in the early settlement of the country) was organized in 1814. The society now numbers about two hundred, and worships in a large frame-church, and is in a prosperous condition. The present is the fourth house of worship we have had." In 1814, he adds, "Brothers Coleman Harwell, Meshach Boyce, and myself, began to preach in Lincoln county, in what is now called the Shiloh neighborhood, in private houses," and in 1815 the first society there was formed at the house of Seaborn Bruce.

McFerrin follows the letter with a short sketch of the writer: "Elam was the third son, and the first of the family to join the Methodist Church. He professed religion in 1804, and joined the Church in 1806. He was much opposed by his parents, who were Presbyterians... He was licensed to preach in 1813, and the same year removed to Tennessee." His house "was a welcome home" to every preacher on the Richland Circuit. "All his children are members of the Church, and four of his sons are preachers of the gospel; one of them, the Rev. J. B. Stephenson, once of the Tennessee, but now of the North Alabama Conference, is an itinerant." The sketch also calls his father James "a Captain in the Revolutionary war," a title the family later repeated and the militia record does not support.

stories.title: News of the Stevenson preachers, 1875-1885
stories.hook: A weekly Giles County newspaper printed Elam Stevenson's death notice in 1875 and kept naming his preaching sons for the next ten years, including one who talked of moving to Texas.

subject.name: Rev. Elam Stevenson and his sons

body: Giles County, Tennessee, had a weekly paper, the Pulaski Citizen, and its neighborhood columns noted who was preaching where, who was sick and who had come home. The Stevenson preachers turn up in it again and again between 1875 and 1885.

On 18 March 1875 the Citizen printed a death notice: "Died, at the residence of W. M. Stevenson, near Bethany, on the 13th inst., Rev. Elam Stevenson, in his 88th year." It called him "this venerable minister of God," who "died as he had lived, with perfect Christian resignation," and said he left "a large line of descendants—children, grand children, and great-grand children, who will ever revere his memory." The 13th of March matches the date on the family's own record of his death. The W. M. Stevenson whose house it was is most likely his son Willis M., who is on the family roll of Elam's eleven children.

Three years later a writer visiting Bee Spring church walked through its graveyard and wrote: "Here repose the sacred dust of old Father Stevenson and his beloved consort, and many others, the founders and upholders of Methodism at Bee Spring." No first name is given, but Bee Spring was the church Elam founded in 1814 or 1815, and Elam and Lydia were its founders.

Elam's son Abner appears as a working circuit preacher. When the Mt. Pisgah circuit preachers published their monthly appointments on 21 November 1878, the list read "Blooming Grove, 4th Sunday, 11 a. m., Abner Stevenson." In February 1878 a neighborhood correspondent, after listing the sick of the community, added: "We are informed that Rev. Abner Stevenson has a cancer cure. If true, come over." In August 1879 the paper's account of a revival at Bee Spring, where 41 people professed faith in seven days, listed him among the ministers who "aided in other services." In May 1884 a column reported: "We had two sermons at Rocky Point last Sunday, one by Abner Stevenson and one by W. H. Dixon," and said the fourth Sunday in June was his.

Texas comes into the story in 1881. On 27 January the Friendship column reported: "Rev. Abner Stevenson has abandoned the idea of going to Texas and will remain where he is now living." On 5 May the Bee Spring column added: "Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week." A George W., the same age as Gilbert, was in Abner's household in 1870, so this is probably that son; why he went or how long he stayed is not said. Abner stayed in Giles County, and it was his son Gilbert, known as Frank, who later took a preacher's family west. Frank's seven children were born in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas.

One more brother is in the paper. On 20 August 1885 the county correspondent wrote of visiting "our old friends, Rev. and Mrs. Jas. C. Stevenson of near Bryson," who "speak of celebrating their golden wedding in October." James C. is the third of Elam's children, and a family letter of 1932 remembers "Uncle Jimmie" as having preached 63 years.

stories.title: A circuit preacher near Idabel
stories.hook: Betsy's brother preached for forty years in the Choctaw country, and a memoir written by his nephew in 1944 names his parents as Vincent and Emiline Tims.
body: Robert James Tims was a brother of Betsy (Tims) Thompson. The Methodist Indian Mission of Oklahoma printed his memoir in the minutes of its September 1944 session at Salt Creek Church, near Holdenville, signed by his nephew, the Rev. Edgar Tims. It begins: "Robert James Tims was born six miles north of Fort Towson, Oklahoma, being the son of Vincent and Emiline Tims."

He stayed in the Fort Towson community until he entered Spencer Academy and finished his schooling there, and "upon leaving school it was his good fortune to meet Fannie Weesley, and they were married." The marriage lasted 48 years, until she died a few months before him. They had no children, "but a mighty host of friends."

In 1904, the memoir says, he was converted and licensed to preach, and he was later ordained a deacon. He was pastor of the Rufe Circuit, whose churches in the 1940s included High Hill and Hampton Chapel, for two years, and then of the Idabel Circuit for six, until failing health made him retire to a home five miles west of Idabel. He was among the clerical members in 1934 and 1935, pastor of the Idabel Circuit in 1936, and in 1940 "Tims, Robert J., L.D., Idabel."

"He preached his last sermon at Thomas Chapel on Sunday just before his triumphant passing on Tuesday." He died on Tuesday, 12 September 1944, and was buried in the Idabel cemetery. The memoir closes: "The name of Robert Tims will always be affectionately mentioned in the churches where he ministered."

Robert was enrolled at Doaksville on 25 April 1899 for Cedar County: "Tims, Robert," age 25, three-quarter blood, with his wife "Fannie," 18. His parents were "Vincent Tims," dead, and "Emiline Tims," and hers "John Wesley," dead, and "Winnie Wesley," both of Cedar County; the memoir spells her family name Weesley. In April 1901, aged 26, he swore a statement as an acquaintance on his niece Ella's death, signing his name "Robert Tims."

stories.title: Six brothers from Donegal and the extra T
stories.hook: A descendant's Bible record says Robert Moffitt of Donegal had eleven children, and that six sons came to America and agreed to end the name in 'itt'.
body: The Bible record of Abijah Moffitt says Robert Moffitt was born in Scotland, went to Ireland when young, and there married Margaret Stuart. It names eleven children: James, Charles, William, Adam, Margaret, Mary, Catheren, Robert, Hugh, John and Patrick.

An earlier account comes from a member of the next generation. On 4 August 1853, Joseph Moffitt wrote from Randolph County, Indiana, naming his parents Hugh Moffitt and Hannah Davis, Hugh's brothers including William, and Hugh's parents Robert Moffitt and Margaret Stewart. Joseph said Hannah's sister Mary married a Moffitt, but did not name her husband. The letter as printed in 1924 fits the William Moffitt who married Mary Davies at Cane Creek; identifying him as Hugh's brother remains an inference rather than an explicit statement in this letter.

A separate 1799 Chatham County will helps anchor Joseph's account: Hugh Moffit named his wife Hannah, his son Joseph and other sons. Joseph's letter names brothers Robert, John, Joshua, Charles, Jeremiah and Nathan, all also named in the will. The letter adds three sisters and says the children were raised in Chatham County. This is first-hand family testimony about Joseph's parents and siblings, though his statements about earlier generations and places still need corroborating records.

In the Bible record, John crossed first and went back to Ireland; liking the country, he returned with five brothers to Philadelphia. From there they went to North Carolina, to what became Chatham and Randolph counties. William, Adam and Charles died in North Carolina. It says Hugh went to Ohio in 1798 or 1799 and died near Chillicothe about 1800. A will made by Hugh Moffit of Chatham County on 1 October 1799 says he had disposed of his affairs in preparation to move his family to the Northwest Territory; this fits a late-1799 move but makes the earlier departure uncertain. Robert started back for Ireland and was never heard of again, and was supposed lost at sea. Patrick never left Ireland. The record adds that 'William and Hugh married Davis daughters of North Carolina,' which matches William Moffitt's marriage to Mary Davies at Cane Creek in 1763.

Family tradition explains the spelling: the brothers agreed to end the name in 'itt' so that kin could recognize each other wherever it turned up. That part is tradition, not record. North Carolina papers of the 1760s write the name Maffet, Moffit and Moffitt.

The Carolina end is on record. At Cane Creek Meeting in 1763 William married Mary Davies and, in the family's account, his brother Hugh married her sister Hannah, which shows the brothers had joined the Quaker neighborhood of Charles Davies rather than a Presbyterian one. The counties give a sense of how little the family needed to move. Orange was formed in 1752 from Johnston, Bladen and Granville; Chatham in 1770 from Orange; Guilford in 1770 from Rowan and Orange; and Randolph in 1779 from Guilford. A household on one stretch of the upper Deep River could have been written into the Orange court records in 1765, the Chatham records in the 1770s and the Randolph records in 1796, the year William made his will, without anyone leaving home, if the family stayed put.

The Alamance Battleground Book of Remembrance gives William's parents as Robert and Martha Steward Moffitt, without citations. The two accounts agree on Robert and Donegal and differ on whether his wife was Margaret or Martha. Neither names Robert's own parents; the Moffat ancestors some trees give for Robert have no sources.

A Moffitt genealogy of 1928 tells the crossing differently from the Bible Record: "William came first, alone, and went back," and then "he and five other brothers afterward came to Philadelphia and remained there for some time." It says Robert and Margaret migrated to Donegal after the marriage, and that all of their children but Catharine and Patrick crossed to America. Eastern Donegal was settled from Ayrshire and Galloway by the Cunninghams and Stewarts, which fits the bride's surname but names no parish.

The claim that Robert was 'Robert Bruce Moffitt,' born in 1716 at Moffat Wells in Dumfriesshire, does not hold up. The 1928 genealogy says Robert Moffat married Margaret Stuart 'at Moffat Wells, Scotland,' which it describes as 'a mineral spring' near the town of Moffat, so the 'Wells' is a spa, not a birthplace, and it gives the date of the wedding as 'supposed to be about 1750,' an impossible date since William, listed third among their children, was born about 1740. The 1928 account places the wedding in Scotland; the Bible account places it in Ireland. The book gives no birth year for Robert and no middle name. One family tree gives about 1705, not 1716, and has no 'Bruce.' No record carries either detail.

Donegal Moffitt researchers report that Robert and Adam Moffitt held the lease of the townland of Doagh Crabbin in Clondavaddog parish in 1743, when Gustavus Hamilton's estate was sold to Nathaniel Clements, and that Robert married a Margaret Stewart. Nothing ties that Robert to William of Randolph County except the family story. An unsourced tree gives Robert's father as an Alexander Moffat born in 1670, and no record supports that.

quotes.t: According to tradition, William came first, alone, and went back. Being pleased with the country, he and five other brothers afterward came to Philadelphia and remained there for some time. Later they went to Chatham or Randolph County, N. C.

stories.title: Stripped of their property for fines
stories.hook: William Brown's memories, written into the Nottingham Quaker minutes in 1786, say his parents lost most of what they owned to fines for their faith.
body: Willyam Browne, son of Richard Browne, was born on the twenty-ninth day of the first month 1658; in the Friends’ calendar then in use, the first month was March. His mother is not named at his birth. Sons James in 1656 and Jeremiah in 1660 are also reported; the mother’s name appears as Mary, Marrey or Margery in later accounts and is unresolved. Richard is described as of Boasworth, usually taken to be Husbands Bosworth in Leicestershire.

Forty years after William Brown died, a great-nephew set down William's stories in the East Nottingham Quaker minutes on the 28th day of the 1st month 1786. They say Richard had leaned toward both the Baptists and the Puritans and was reputed a teacher among both, and that about 1663 William's parents 'had suffered greatly and were much stripped of their property for fines &c.' The memorial miscalls the father 'William senior'; the birth register gives Richard.

James Brown reached Pennsylvania by 1677. William followed between 1682 and 1684, after marrying Dorothy in England, and married three more times in Pennsylvania, the first of them, in 1684, to Ann Mercer, his second wife. He died in West Nottingham in 1746, on 23 August by the 1786 family memorandum or 1 October by another account.

The East Nottingham memorandum tells how the Brownes became Friends when William Dewsbury sat at their table, how Richard's wife asked why he had brought "that madman" into the house, and how his landlord made him pay his rent twice because he would not swear that it was paid.

stories.title: The Settle families’ 1682 crossing
stories.hook: The 1682 Settle certificate names both families; eleven years later John Cowgill married Bridget Croasdale at Neshaminy.
body: In June 1682, Friends at Settle in Yorkshire prepared a certificate for families leaving for Pennsylvania. Among them were Ellen Cowgill, a widow, and her children, and Thomas Croasdale, his wife Agnes and six children. John Cowgill and Bridget Croasdale belonged to those two families. Later accounts differ over whether the party sailed on the Lamb or the Welcome; the certificate does not name a ship.

Bridget was born on the thirtieth day of the sixth month, 1671; in the Quaker calendar then in use, sixth month was August. She was about eleven when the family left England. On 19 October 1693, she married John Cowgill at Neshaminy in Bucks County, Pennsylvania.

Their daughter Elizabeth was born on 24 August 1694. Elizabeth later married William Brown Jr.; their daughter Elizabeth Brown married Edward Norton, and their granddaughter Margaret Norton married Joseph Chamness. That is the path from Bridget’s Yorkshire family to the Moffitts.

Bridget died on 26 April 1701. They had four children: Elizabeth (born the 24th of the 6th month, 1694), Thomas (21st of the 4th month, 1696), John (8th of the 5th month, 1698) and Ellin (14th of the 10th month, 1700); some family trees convert Elizabeth’s birth to June rather than August. In 1703/4 John married Rachel Baker, the widow of Job Bunting of Darby, and had four more children: Rachel, Mary, Ebenezer and Eleazer.

About 1713 or 1714 he moved to the lower part of New Castle County, Delaware. Land records say that on the 26th of the 3rd month 1715 (26 May) a warrant was signed to John Cowgill “for the resurvey of a tract of land in a fork of Appoquinimink Creek,” and on the 1st of the 5th month 1715/6 he “desired the grant of about 100 acres of vacant land, near his other tract in New Castle county, where he had planted a tan-yard.” On the 10th of the 3rd month 1718 (10 May), “having erected a tan-yard on a branch of ‘Black Bird’s Creek,’” he asked for another hundred acres on rent.

His sons Thomas and John followed him and married sisters, daughters of Joshua Clayton of Little Creek Hundred. Thomas had Thomas, Ezekiel and Jane; John married Lydia Clayton “of Kent county” in 1720. The daughters Elizabeth and Ellin married the Nottingham brothers William Brown Jr. and Thomas Brown. John Cowgill died on 2 July 1731. His grandson John Cowgill of Little Creek was hauled through Dover in a cart in the Revolution for refusing Continental money.
His later land records also concern land near Blackbird Creek in New Castle County.

stories.title: Dennis Garrett of Long Island Point, struck with a sword in 1691
stories.hook: Dennis Garrett helped buy the point that became Fell's Point, was struck on the forehead on 31 July 1691, and lingered until 2 September.
body: Dennis Garrett was one of the first settlers on the site of Baltimore. With Thomas Stone he bought "Long Island Point," a tract surveyed for William Poultney on the site of what became Fell's Point, and his descendants are numerous through the Cole, Gorsuch and Ensor families. He and his wife Barbara had a daughter, Johanna, who married John Cole.

Dennis died on 2 September 1691, weeks after being struck on the forehead with a sword. John Oldton, a Baltimore County tailor, was indicted for the assault. The indictment gives the attack as 31 July, yet says Dennis languished from 30 July until his death; the two dates are inconsistent.

The witnesses included Philip Roper, Nicholas Hale, John Cole, Thomas Stone, Abraham Vaughan and Barbara Garrett. Cole was the husband of Dennis’s daughter Johanna; Barbara was his widow. Oldton was condemned to be hanged, but the Governor and Council ordered a stay on 11 April 1692 and a royal pardon followed. He became captain of the county rangers in 1694/5.
A later account describes the death as the result of an affray.

Barbara married again within the year, to John Broad, who had come to Maryland in 1670 or earlier as an indentured servant brought over by Henry Hosier. The only land he ever bought was Broad's Choice, 173 acres along both banks of Herring Run, which he patented on 10 November 1695, in what is now Herring Run Park in Baltimore. After Dennis died, Thomas Stone had given his interest in Long Island Point to Barbara; she left the point and carried her three Garrett children to the farm on the Run, where she raised two more, Thomas and Jane. John Broad was listed in the 1692 tax list with John Cole as a near neighbor. When he died in January 1709 the inventory showed a modest household: two feather beds, pewter and earthenware, a very old horse, twelve cows, five steers, a bull, some ailing pigs and about 4,000 pounds of tobacco hanging in the sheds. The family signed with marks. His will, written about 1702, left Broad's Choice to Thomas and Jane, and Barbara ran the farm for them while they were minors. In August 1712 she signed herself "Barbara Broad of Back River" and gave her property to her children and grandchildren, among them her grandson Dennis Garrett Cole. She died in 1733. The family line runs through Johanna to her son Joseph Cole and his daughter Sarah, who married Anthony Chamness.

stories.title: Thirteen cents a ration: the Doak & Tims contracts, 1838-1839
stories.hook: A House report of 1843 prints the army's signed contracts with Doak & Tims to feed Chickasaw emigrants at Doaksville, at thirteen cents a ration.
body: The Doaksville trading firm of Josiah Doak and Vincent B. Tims shows up in a report to the House of Representatives of 25 February 1843 on "Frauds upon Indians." The report reproduced a run of army subsistence contracts from the removal years, and four of them are with "Doak & Tims." The report charges the firm with nothing; the contracts are printed as exhibits among those of other suppliers.

No. 41 is "an extract from a contract made January 1, 1838, between Captain R. D. C. Collins, United States army, and Doak & Tims." It reads: "That the said Doak & Tims shall furnish complete rations to a party of about two hundred Chickasaw emigrants, and all such of said tribe who may join said party, to be supplied at this place from time to time . . . for the term of twelve months from the date of this contract; the ration to consist of one pound of beef or pork, or three-quarters of a pound of salt pork or bacon, a pint and a half of corn meal, and one gallon of salt to the hundred rations." For each ration "the said Doak & Tims shall receive from the United States the sum of thirteen cents".

No. 42, of the same date, has them feed up to two hundred horses belonging to the emigrants, "one gallon of good sound merchantable corn" a ration, again at thirteen cents. No. 44 renews the arrangement on 1 January 1839: "the said Doak & Tims shall furnish and deliver, to the Chickasaw Indians, at the depot at Doaksville, Choctaw nation, west, all rations of subsistence that shall be required at said depot, be the same more or less, for one year from the date hereof," at "thirteen cents" a full ration.

Elsewhere in the report, the notes to a witness summary say the Fort Towson issues for the twelve months "appear to have been made by David Folsom and Doak & Tims"; the witness, the Chickasaw interpreter Stone Love, "thinks satisfactory" those twelve months' issues. A letter from the officer settling the Chickasaw accounts mentions "a small party subsisting for the year, by Doak & Tims, under a contract with Captain Collins". Another contract, between the removal contractors Glasgow & Harrison and the army, carves out "the party of emigrants now at 'Doaksville,' and being subsisted by Doak & Tims".

These are the contracts behind the thirteen cents a ration that a missionary later remembered for the Doaksville trading establishment of Doak and Tims. They put the firm at Doaksville, feeding Chickasaw families as they arrived from Mississippi, at the start of 1838, before the town had a post office.

stories.title: "Mr. Tims one of the men I am living with": a clerk's letters from Doaksville, 1841 and 1843
stories.hook: A young Connecticut clerk at the Doaksville trading house wrote his mother that Mr. Tims was in New York buying goods; two years later Tims was still making the trip for him.
body: Two letters from Charles Fanning Stewart of Connecticut to his mother, printed in 1931, tell of Doaksville. Stewart, born in 1814, had gone west "after having been engaged to clerk in a trading establishment at Doaksville, a thriving village in the Red River region of the Choctaw Nation." His letter of 17 April 1841 is headed "Doaks Ville, Choctaw Nation West." It describes the place: "Doaks Ville is some sixty miles west of the Boundary line between the United States and the Indian country. It is six miles north of the Red River which forms the line between us and Texas. Fort Towson is only half a mile from us . . . Our trade which is verry extencive is confined to the Red Men of the forrest."

Tims comes in near the end. "Mr. Tims one of the men I am living with is now in New York purchasing a stock of goods," Stewart tells his mother. He had sent fifty dollars with him to leave with her friends in New York, and asked him to collect fifty more that was owed him in New Orleans. Stewart had meant to come home that summer, "but Mr. Tims trip to New York prevented it".

Stewart married Tryphena Wall on 9 May 1842 and opened his own store at Mayhew, on the road between Fort Towson and Fort Washita, with goods bought from his old employer in New Orleans. On 19 April 1843 he wrote that the stock he had brought the previous spring was sold and that he had "sent by my friend Mr. Tims last week for another stock of goods he will be in New York sometime in May." So Tims made the buying trip east in the spring of 1841 and again in 1843, and Stewart, who had clerked in his house, still trusted him to carry his orders and money.

Stewart does not give the firm's name or Tims's first name. The Mr. Tims of the Doaksville trading house in those years is almost certainly Vincent B. Tims of Doak & Tims, whose partnership with Josiah Doak was dissolved in February 1844.

stories.title: Sworn at Tuskahoma: Willie Tims on her marriage, 1902
stories.hook: In December 1902 Willie J. Tims told the Dawes Commission she had lived sixteen years in the Choctaw Nation and had married Edward Tims near Doaksville in 1888.
body: On 8 December 1902 the Dawes Commission took testimony at Tuskahoma from "Willie J. Tims," who gave her age as thirty-two and her post office as Grant, Indian Territory. She was a white woman, born Willie Jane Maxwell, and she was asking to be enrolled as a citizen by intermarriage through her husband, Judge Edward Ward Tims of Doaksville. The Commission asked her the plain questions the law required: how long she had lived in the Nation, whether her husband was enrolled, when and where they married, and who had been married before.

Her answers put the marriage in 1888, "Close to Doaksville," performed by a minister named Frazier, without a license. Edward had been married once before, to a woman whose "given name was Polly," and Polly was dead by then. Willie said the two had lived together continuously, "No" separation, abandonment or divorce, as residents of the Nation.

The Commission's written decision, dated 9 December 1903, gave the date of the wedding as 29 April 1888. A certified copy of the marriage certificate survives, written in the Choctaw Nation's own court style: "Tonson County C. N. April 29th A. D. 1888." It is signed by R. S. Frazier, who wrote that he had that day "Joined the holy Estate of Matrimony, Hon. E. W. Tims and Mifs Wille Maxful all of Tonson County C. N." The clerk copying it in December 1906 kept the old spelling.

She was enrolled as "Willie J.," age 29, an intermarried white citizen; her father, Maxwell, is marked dead and a non-citizen. Her children with Edward were Lucy, Minnie J., Edmond, Benjamin W., Mertle (a baby of two months when the family applied on 8 May 1899) and Abel E., born 14 December 1901 and enrolled on 14 February 1902. Edward also had a ward, Adam Nanomantubbe, a boy whose dead parents are written as Tobias and Susan Nanomantubbe. In July 1903 the Commission answered a neighbor from Oscar, O. W. Seay, who had written that "Mr. Tims has a grandson named Adam Nonomatubi who is an orphan," and told him the boy was already enrolled with the family; the Secretary of the Interior had approved the whole group on 12 December 1902.
Willie Jane Tims was born on 27 July 1870 and died on 8 October 1922, four months before her husband. She is the mother of Private Edmond Tims, killed in France in 1918.
