stories.title: Mitchell and Mildred Tims, and the baby daughter lost in 1900
stories.hook: Betsy's brother Mitchell and his full-blood wife Mildred lost their baby daughter Else before the rolls were made.
body: On 25 April 1899 Mitchell Tims, age 30, one-half Choctaw, of Towson County, post office Doaksville, was enrolled. The clerk wrote his parents as "Benson Tims," dead, of Towson County, and "Emiline Tims," still living in 1896. His father's first name was spelled Vinson, Vincent and, here, Benson, but the family is the same.
His wife Mildred, 19, full-blood, had been "Mildred Billy" in 1896. Her parents were "Nuck-a-masha" and "Me-ley," both dead, of Jacks Fork County.

Their first daughter, Else, was born on 9 November 1899, after the application, and was added to the enrollment on 11 July 1902, though she had already died. On 5 December 1902 the Commission wrote to Mitchell at Doaksville acknowledging "your affidavit and that of James Wilson relative to the death of your daughter, Else Tims," which "occurred November 25, 1900." James Wilson was the husband of Mitchell's sister Rosie. Her enrollment was canceled on 8 July 1904, because she had died before the roll was made.

A second daughter, Agnes E., was born on 21 December 1901 and enrolled on 3 January 1902. A son, Vincenta W. Tims, was born on 28 July 1904. On 25 April 1905 the Commission wrote to Mitchell at Fort Towson that it had received "the affidavits of Mildred and Emeline Tims to the birth of Vincenta W. Tims," so his own mother, Emeline, again vouched for a grandchild's birth, as she did for Betsy's children. Two months later Mitchell wrote to ask whether the birth certificate had arrived, and the Commission confirmed it. The boy was entered on the roll of newborn children.

Mitchell Tims is buried at High Hill Cemetery. In 1938 the Methodist Indian Mission lists Mitchell Tims of Fort Towson, with his nephew Peter Thompson, among the Choctaw District's church school superintendents.
The James Wilson who swore with Mitchell in 1902 is probably his brother-in-law: Mitchell's sister Rosanna married a James Wilson of Cedar County, who was enrolled at Doaksville on 1 May 1899.

stories.title: A letter to the Principal Chief about a baby who had died
stories.hook: Willie Tims, Betsy's brother, was enrolled with his wife Mary and a baby son in 1901; in 1905 he had to correct the rolls for a second baby who had died.
body: On 1 May 1899 "Tims, Willie," age 23, three-quarter Choctaw, of Towson County, post office Doaksville, was enrolled, his parents "Vincent Tims," dead, and "Emiline Tims," living in 1896, the same pair named for Betsy Thompson. His wife Mary, 21, full-blood, had been "Mawey Lewis" in 1896; her parents were "King Lewis" and "Nancy Lewis." Their first son, Roberson, was born on 18 February 1901 and enrolled on 17 May 1901.

The jacket then follows the family for years. A second son, Wilson Tims, was born on 11 May 1904 and was entered when the Secretary of the Interior approved the roll of newborn children on 22 July 1905. But the child had died before the cutoff date of 4 March 1905, though the sworn statement had said he was living. In September 1905 Green McCurtain, Principal Chief of the Choctaw Nation, wrote to the Commission from Kinta that "Willis Tims," of Fort Towson, had told him the child "was at that time deceased" and wanted the name struck from the rolls. The Commission wrote on to the land office to stop any allotment for the dead child.

A daughter, Etline Tims, was born on 6 July 1905. On 19 May 1906 the Commission acknowledged "the affidavits of Mary Tims and Nancy Lewis," her mother and grandmother, to her birth. She was enrolled among the minor children, a girl of seven-eighths Choctaw blood.
A Willie Tims of Fort Towson later appears in Methodist Indian Mission minutes as a church officer at High Hill, but it is not said whether he is this Willie.

stories.title: The man on the card before Joseph's: Henry W. Thompson
stories.hook: Henry W. Thompson was enrolled the same day as Joseph P. Thompson, and his parents were Simon and Lucy Thompson, not John and Betsy.
body: Henry W. Thompson and Joseph P. Thompson both applied for Choctaw enrollment on 1 May 1899. They lived in Cedar County with the same post office, Doaksville. In 1910 a Henry W. Thompson was among the Thompsons' nearest neighbors in Wilson Township.

Henry was written down as "Thompson, Henry W.," age 25, full-blood, with his parents "Simon Thompson" and "Lucy Thompson," both dead, of Cedar County. Joseph's parents, by contrast, were John and Betsy Thompson. On the enrollment Henry is not Joseph's brother.

A note says he was "now the husband of Illie Thompson," with evidence of marriage filed on 16 July 1902. In 1903 the Commission returned to him at Doaksville the "certificate of marriage of Henry Thompson and Mrs. Eli Pesahombi, dated July 11, 1900." Illie, 18, was enrolled with a one-year-old son, Hampton Thompson, born on 12 November 1901, along with a Pisahambe youth and the Aaron family. When the baby's application reached the Commission through a notary at Doaksville in February 1902, it was sent back with a request for the mother's maiden name, since no one of her name had been listed.

stories.title: Joseph W.: a sworn birth in 1905, and Emeline the midwife again
stories.hook: Joseph and Betsy's son Joseph W. was born on 5 March 1903 and enrolled under the 1905 act; his grandmother Emeline Tims swore to his birth, as she had for Simon.
body: Joel Thompson's list of his brothers includes Joseph W. How he got on the roll can be followed. The Act of Congress of 3 March 1905 allowed children born after September 1902 and living on 4 March 1905 to be enrolled, so the family had to swear to his birth and to the fact that he was alive on that date.

In a sworn statement of 29 April 1905 at the Central District, "Betsy Thompson," of Fort Towson, said she was the lawful wife of Joseph P. Thompson, "who is a citizen, by Blood, of the Choctaw Nation," and that a male child "born to me on 5th day of March 1903" had been named "Joseph W. Thompson" and "was living March 4, 1905." On the same page, as "midwife," Emeline Tims swore that she had attended Betsy on the same day and that the child was living on the cutoff date. The notary for both was Thomas Fennell. It is the same arrangement as in 1899, when Emeline attended Simon's birth and swore to it.
He was entered separately among the newborn children enrolled under that act.

The family had very little time. The act of 3 March 1905 authorized the Commission to receive applications for these children "for sixty days after the date of the approval of this Act," and only for children of parents whose own enrollment the Secretary of the Interior had already approved. Joseph P. Thompson had been approved on 12 December 1902, so his son qualified, but the window closed on 2 May 1905. Betsy and Emeline swore their statements on 29 April, with three days to spare.
Joseph W. was one of many. By the middle of 1906 the Department had approved 1,558 Choctaw newborns under the act, beside 15,971 Choctaws by blood on the main roll.

stories.title: One man, two names: William Harrison Pisachubbe enrolled twice
stories.hook: A boys' school list in 1899 put "Harrison Pisachubbe" on the Choctaw rolls, and he was already there as William H. In 1911 the Interior Department sorted it out.
body: When Eunice Pisachubbe's family was enrolled on 10 May 1899 for Kiamitia County, post office Goodland, her son "William H.," 16, full-blood, was among them, noted as "William Harrison" in 1896. His father, Joseph Pisachubbe, is written as dead.

Three months later, on 22 August 1899, a list of students at Armstrong Academy, a Choctaw school, was sent to the Commission, and it included "Harrison Pisachubbe." That name was also put on the final roll, approved on 4 February 1903. In the meantime William H. had received a complete allotment under his first number, and in 1905 the Commission, not knowing about the doubling, made a second, arbitrary allotment in the name of Harrison. The certificates were mailed to Academy, Oklahoma, and came back marked "unclaimed."

On 2 August 1909 William H. testified at Hugo that he had told the postmaster to send the certificates back, as he already had his allotment as William H. Pisachubbe. Eunice, Harrison Nohio and Thomas Hunter also gave testimony. On 1 August 1911 the Commissioner at Muskogee wrote to the Secretary of the Interior that Harrison Pisachubbe was "a duplicate enrollment of William H. Pisachubbe." The Secretary's office approved a notation on the roll on 16 August 1911: "Duplicate enrollment of No. 4466; not entitled to land or money under this number."

William H. had a son, Colbert, born on 26 June 1906 at Hugo, whose mother Mamie signed her application with a mark and whose birth was attended by a midwife, Cassie Davis. His enrollment was refused: the Commissioner decided on 27 November 1906 that, because Colbert "was not living March 4, 1906," the cutoff in the Act of 26 April 1906, he had no authority to consider it, and the Secretary affirmed on 26 February 1907. Mamie is called a non-citizen in the decision.
William Harrison Pisachubbe died in May 1937, and the family's account of the removal from Mississippi in 1832 was given at his death.

stories.title: Edward Pisachubbi's land letter, 1903
stories.hook: Edward, Eunice's ward, wrote to the Commission in January 1903 about land he had picked for himself and his wife Frances.
body: Among Eunice Pisachubbe's household was one who was not her son. "Edward," 17, full-blood, was her ward, and his dead parents were "Simpson Pisachubbe" and "Sallie Pisachubbe," of Jackson County. He was the husband of Frances Byington.

On 31 January 1903 the Commission wrote to him at Hugo, answering his letter of 16 January, "in which you state that you have selected certain lands for the allotments of yourself and your wife, Frances Pisachubbi." He had added that part of the land he described was claimed by another citizen. The Commission told him it had "no means of recording the selections of citizens" and could not settle disputes about possession; the matter would be heard when land offices opened in the Nation, which it expected between the first of March and the first of April. A follow-up letter said admission to the land office would be by tickets handed out on or after 16 April 1903.
His letters show how the land was chosen in the Choctaw Nation in 1903: families walked the ground first and wrote to the Commission, and then had to apply in person at the land office.

The office the Commission promised Edward opened later than it had expected. Because the winter of 1902-03 was unusually wet, the Commission put off the land offices until spring, and on 20 March 1903 it published a notice that they would open on Wednesday, 15 April, at Atoka for the Choctaw Nation and at Tishomingo for the Chickasaw. Choctaw land could be applied for only at Atoka. Crowds were waiting on opening day; the first four days went entirely to handing out tickets of admission, and the first allotments were recorded on 20 April 1903.

Edward's worry about another claimant was common. On 23 April the Commission withheld all the estimated pine-timber land in the two nations from allotment, after learning that lumber speculators planned to take control of it. By 30 June the Atoka office had issued 1,537 tickets, standing for about 6,000 allottees, and taken 1,812 allotment applications covering some 300,418 acres. Disputed tracts went to contest hearings before the Commission.

stories.title: Doak & Tims in the Texas Supreme Court, 1849
stories.hook: A Doaksville store's unpaid account from 1840 to 1844 ended up before the Supreme Court of Texas, in a case titled Love v. Doak & Tims.
body: Doak & Tims, the Doaksville trading firm of Josiah Doak and Vincent B. Tims, appears in the law reports of Texas. (The report gives Doak the middle initial L.; the 1837 treaty he witnessed has Josiah S. Doak.) The case, Love v. Doak & Tims, was decided at the December 1849 term.

The court summarized the suit this way: it "was brought in the names of the appellees as copartners, trading as merchants, for the use and benefit of Josiah L. Doak, one of the said copartners." It was an action on a store account against a man named Love who lived across the Red River in the Choctaw Nation. The first item in the account was dated 1840 and the last 30 July 1844; the suit was begun in Grayson County, Texas, on 24 January 1848. A witness testified that he had sold Love goods up to 28 August 1840, "that at the time said account was made the defendant was a resident of Mississippi," and that Love "did remove in 1841" to the Choctaw Nation. A second witness said that in 1844 he had presented the account for payment and asked Love for an order on a Colonel Upshaw, or his note, and Love said he would settle it himself.

The trial jury found for Doak & Tims. On appeal, Chief Justice Hemphill reversed and dismissed the case on the law of limitations: the debt was more than two years old, and nothing in writing acknowledged it. This is the same partnership that held the army ration contracts of 1838 and 1839 and kept the store described in letters of 1841; the suit of 1848 came four years after the partners dissolved their business by mutual agreement in 1844, and it is brought for the use and benefit of Doak alone.
The account shows the store selling goods on credit over four years, with the bill pursued years later in a Texas court.

stories.title: Nancy Pisachubbi, daughter of Te-hol-ba-ta-bi
stories.hook: Nancy Pisachubbi's parents were written down in 1899, but nothing connects her to Joseph Pisachubbe.
body: In May 1899 "Pisachubbi, Nancy," age 69, a full-blood woman of Eagle County, post office Luk-fa-tah, Indian Territory, was enrolled, alone, and her enrollment was approved on 12 December 1902.

Her parents were two names: her father was "Te-hol-ba-ta-bi," dead, of Eagle County, and her mother was "Malindy," dead, with Mississippi written as her county. Her stated age suggests a birth around 1830, but her birthplace is not given.

One family tree gives Joseph a mother named Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, born about 1825 in Mississippi. The Nancy Pisachubbi whose father was Te-hol-ba-ta-bi has no husband or children listed, and nothing establishes that she was Joseph’s mother or that the two Nancy entries are the same person. A Case Pisachubbi enrolled beside her had a father called Pisachubbi and a mother called Noise; their relationship to Nancy is not established.

Eagle County was one of the nineteen counties the Choctaw General Council created in 1850, the far eastern county of the Apukshunnubbee District, with Arkansas as its eastern line and Little River on the south. Its seat, Eagletown, had had a United States post office since 1 July 1834 and is usually counted the first permanent town the Choctaws built after removal. Nancy, whose mother was remembered as a Mississippi woman and who was born about 1830, was most likely carried west as a small child in the removals of 1831 to 1833.

Her post office, Luk-fah-tah, was older than most in the Nation. It opened on 14 February 1853, with Emilius G. Corder as postmaster, closed on 9 July 1866, the day a long list of Indian Territory offices was discontinued after the war, and reopened on 21 January 1873 under the spelling Lukfata, with John N. Hodges. The 1889 Rand McNally map of Indian Territory places Lukfata just inside Boktuklo County, a few miles west of the Eagle County line, so the office served families on both sides of it. Eagle County's ground went wholly into McCurtain County at statehood in 1907.

stories.title: "Rosey Ann Tims": a notary's letter and a grandmother who delivered the babies
stories.hook: Betsy's sister Rosie married James Wilson. In October 1900 a Doaksville notary wrote to the Dawes Commission to say who she was, and her mother Emeline attended her children's births.
body: Rosie does not appear under the Tims name on the roll. She was enrolled on 24 April 1899 with her mother as "Rosanna Tims," and when she married James Wilson she was moved to his enrollment. On 1 May 1899 at Doaksville (the same day as Henry W. Thompson and Joseph P. Thompson), "Wilson, James," age 24, full-blood, of Cedar County, with parents "Simon Wilson" and "Melissie Wilson," both dead, was enrolled; his wife "Rosanna," 18, three-quarter blood, with her parents written "Benson Tims," dead, and "Emiline Tims," of Towson County; and a baby son. A note says Rosanna was "transferred to this card with her husband, Oct. 26, 1900."

How she was found is on record. In September 1900 the notary R. L. Carter of Doaksville sent in an application for the baby, Islam Wilson, born on 10 August 1900. The Commission sent it back because it could not identify the mother, who gave her age as eighteen and had clearly been married since she was listed. On 19 October 1900 Carter replied: "Rosey Wilson the wife of James Wilson was registered as Rosey Ann Tims and has been married since she was registered. Her mother name is Emaline Times her father died before he was registered." The Commission wrote back on 27 October that it had identified her as "Rosanna Tims the daughter of Emiline Tims, who was listed for enrollment April 24th, 1899." It still wanted the marriage certificate, and on 19 August 1902 acknowledged one between "James Wilson and Rosa Tims."

Two more children are on the jacket. A son was born on 23 March 1903, and Rosanna swore to the birth on 25 March 1905 with her mark, her husband James Wilson and John Aaron as witnesses. The midwife's statement, sworn on 19 April 1905, is signed "Emeline Tims," Rosanna's mother, who swore the same kind of affidavit for her grandson Joseph W. Thompson ten days later. A daughter, Candace, was born on 16 June 1905; in May 1906 the Commission acknowledged "the affidavits of Rosanna Wilson and Emeline Tims to the birth of Candace Wilson."
Rosie's husband is probably the James Wilson who swore with her brother Mitchell Tims in 1902 to the death of Mitchell's baby daughter.

stories.title: The boy who died before the roll was taken
stories.hook: Born 15 November 1898, dead by April 1899, and still on a federal roll until 1904 when the Department struck him off.
body: James Austin was the second child in his parents' household. His father Legion swore at Fowlerville in early May 1899 that the boy was born on 15 November 1898 and was "now living." He was enrolled at age 1, with a note: "died April 1899."

The boy's birth proof is as plain as such papers get. The form's printed "Affidavit of Mother" is crossed out and "Father" written over it, and Legion signed by mark as a 33-year-old citizen by blood. The second statement, normally for a doctor or nurse, was sworn by a neighbor, Leonidas Willis, who "knew" of the birth and also made his mark.

Proof of the death reached the Commission on 2 December 1902. The Secretary of the Interior approved the other four on 12 December 1902, with James marked "Died prior to September 25, 1902." The Department did not cancel his enrollment until 16 September 1904.

The date in the clerk's note was not chosen at random. On 25 September 1902 the Choctaws and Chickasaws voted at a special election to ratify the Supplementary Agreement that Congress had approved on 1 July 1902. That agreement governed the allotments. Its section 22 provided that a citizen on the rolls who died after ratification but before receiving land would still have land allotted in his name, and that it would pass to his heirs. A child who had died before that day had no such claim. "Died prior to September 25, 1902" therefore marked James off from the land his parents and sisters would choose the next year. The same agreement opened the Choctaw land office at Atoka in April 1903.

stories.title: A baby on a card that was nearly closed
stories.hook: Born 5 August 1900, a year after her family applied, and added by a letter and an affidavit signed with two marks.
body: Adline was born on 5 August 1900, a year after her parents' application and two years before the roll was approved. Her father wrote to the Commission from Garvin that October; on 9 October the Commission replied with a blank infant application and the instruction that if the mother or the midwife could not write, two disinterested witnesses must attest each mark.

Her mother, "Mulcy Austin," swore on 19 April 1901 that she was 25, a citizen by blood and "the lawful wife of Leageon Austin," and that a girl was born 5 August 1900 and named Adline Austin. The midwife, Sinie Hall, swore the same. Both signed with a mark before the notary William Swink at Fowlerville, with two witnesses, one of them Sallie Johnson.

The Commission acknowledged it on 5 June 1901, "the same being in proper form," and listed the child as Choctaw by Blood. The roll was approved on 12 December 1902. Adline later married William Harrison Pisachubbe, whose younger brother Robert had married her sister Lizzie, and died at Speer in 1929.

Garvin, where Legion wrote from in October 1900, was not yet the town of that name. Its post office had opened on 19 February 1894 at the trading post of James W. Kirk, about a mile and a half southeast of the later town, and Kirk named it for his late father-in-law, Isaac L. Garvin, Principal Chief of the Choctaw Nation from 1878 to 1880. When the Wheelock post office closed in May 1895 its mail was sent to Garvin, so the little office served the old mission neighborhood too. It stood in Red River County, the county Molsey's parents came from.

The town itself came two years after Adline's birth. In 1902 the Choctaw Townsite Commission laid out 126 acres on the railroad then being built across the south of the Nation, and Garvin grew fast: the Garvin Graphic, the first newspaper in what became McCurtain County, began in 1903, a school opened with fifty pupils in 1904, and the place had about 800 people by 1906. After statehood it lost the county seat to Idabel.

stories.title: Four Choctaw counties
stories.hook: The grandparents' counties were Choctaw counties, not Oklahoma ones.

subject.name: Towson, Red River, Blue and Kiamitia

body: In 1899 the clerks recorded where each person had been counted in 1896, and where their dead parents had lived. For this line the answers are four Choctaw Nation counties: Towson for Legion and Molsey Austin and for Emeline Tims; Kiamitia for Eunice Pisachubbe, her sons and the ward Edward; Blue for her parents Jackson and Viney Gardner; and Red River for Molsey's parents Brazil and Siney.

Under the Choctaw constitution and its acts, Towson belonged to the Apukshunnubbee District, while Blue and Kiamichi were counties of the Pushmataha District, each sending one senator. In 1886 the Council cut Jackson County out of Kiamitia, Blue and Atoka, which is why Edward Pisachubbe's dead parents, Simpson and Sallie, are written as of Jackson County in 1899 while he was counted in Kiamitia.

Each person had both a county and a post office. The Austins were Towson County people with a Fowlerville post office, renamed Valliant in 1902, and Eunice was a Kiamitia County woman at Goodland. The old counties vanished at statehood in 1907, and the families that had been counted in four of them came together in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, where Simon and Frances settled at Jeter.

stories.title: Calvin Moffitt, from North Carolina to Oklahoma
stories.hook: Nathan and Rebecca’s son moved through Arkansas to Oklahoma; a Union soldier of the same name may have been him.
body: Calvin, born 4 December 1841 in Randolph County, North Carolina, was the second of Nathan and Rebecca Moffitt's sons, after Miles H., 9, and was eight years old when the family was counted at Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas, in 1850. He was still in the same township in 1860, a year after his parents' twin daughters were born, and when Henry was a child of four.

A "Calvin V. Moffitt" (also written Moffett) served as a private in Company L of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, a Union regiment, aged 22 in 1864. A Calvin V. Moffitt of Lawrence County is also said to have served in two Confederate units and then tried three times for a Union pension, and a Calvin V. Moffitt served in Company G of the Confederate 25th Arkansas Infantry; with the Lawrence County household that makes the identification probable. By 1870 he was married and living at Lebanon Township, Sharp County, Arkansas. His wife was Matilda Dailey (born 23 January 1849 in Polk County, Missouri).

He had six children. Andrew Webster was born in Sharp County on 17 January 1869 and died 24 December 1899. Sarah A. (born 1874 in Missouri) died 11 September 1883, and John W. (born 1877 in Missouri) died 7 February 1885, both as children. Milburn Green (1880-1956) lived and died in Arkansas. Wilson Cornelius, born at Golden City, Missouri, on 14 January 1889, farmed in Stephens County, Oklahoma, later lived in Johnson County, Arkansas, and died at Norco, California, in 1971.

The last child, Girdy Emalah, is shown as born and dying on 19 July 1891. Matilda died the next day, 20 July 1891, at New Pocahontas, Arkansas. In 1900 Calvin, a widower, was head of a household at Reyno, Randolph County. By 1910 he was at King Township, Stephens County, Oklahoma, near his son Wilson, and he died in nearby Duncan on 13 February 1913. A Civil War pension was claimed from Oklahoma.

stories.title: Patrick: the brother who stayed in Stone County
stories.hook: Patrick married in Missouri the year his father died, then lived on in Mountain View, where Henry settled, and buried his wife four months before Henry died.
body: Patrick Green Moffitt was born on 11 May 1853, at Sylamore in the Ozark hills along the White River, though the family was in Lawrence County in 1850 and 1860. He was two years older than Henry. After the family went north into Dent and Oregon counties, Missouri, he married Alice Ann Cole there in August 1873, four months before Nathan's death on 23 December.

Alice Ann was born on 18 December 1857 in Missouri. Nathan's second wife was a widow, Nancy (Rowe) Cole, whom he married in 1871. It is likely, though unproved, that Alice was a Cole child of that household, which would make Patrick's bride his stepsister.

The couple returned to Arkansas and settled at Mountain View, where Henry's family was by 1889. Their daughter Lillian was born in 1894 and died in 1988. Alice Ann died on 26 May 1901 and is buried at Levisy Flat Cemetery; Henry died that September.
Patrick's death is given two ways: 20 December 1905 at Mountain View, or November 1904 with burial at Sallisaw, Oklahoma. The 1905 date is the more widely repeated.

The Mountain View Patrick and Alice came back to was barely a town. The 1880 census counted 99 people there. A wooden courthouse went up in 1888, the town was incorporated in 1890, and the Stone County Academy opened in 1894, the year Lillian was born. Most families lived on small fields of grain and cotton, timber, trapping and livestock.

A portrait of him in later life survives, its mount inscribed “Patrick Green Moffitt, son of Rebecca Williams and Nathan Moffitt, 1853-1905.” It is kept with a memorial at McCoy Cemetery, Sallisaw, Oklahoma, which gives his dates as May 1853 to November 1904 and joins him to a second wife, Cora Arizona (Gammill) Thomas (1869-1939), and to two children. If those links are right, Patrick married again after Alice's death and ended his days in the Cherokee country around Sallisaw, but nothing else yet confirms the second marriage.

stories.title: Uncle Robert in Strawberry Township
stories.hook: Nathan's youngest brother followed him to Strawberry Township, Arkansas, by 1860, buried most of his early children, and ended up in the Missouri Ozarks.
body: Robert was the youngest of Robert and Martha (Chamness) Moffitt's nine children, born 19 June 1815, a year after Nathan. He married Cynthia Gardner, born in North Carolina on 29 April 1815, and in 1850 they were in District 17 of Henderson County, Tennessee, with seven children: John 17, Mary Ann 12, Malcy 10, Alzia 8, Henry P. 6, James H. 3 and Martha E., a baby.

By 1860 Robert, 45, and Cynthia, 45, were in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas, where his brother Nathan was a wheelwright. The household had shrunk to Alzira 18, Parker 15, James 13, Martha 10, Jane 8 and Franklin 5. John, Mary Ann and Malcy are not found again, and Parker is last seen in 1860.

The family moved on into Missouri. Robert died on 9 November 1872 at Hutton Valley, Howell County, and was buried in what is now called Moffitt Cemetery near Willow Springs. Cynthia lived until 9 October 1895.

Four of the children have traceable lives. Alzira Adelaide (1842-1923) married James Thomas Loving in 1867, bore seven children and is buried at Willow Springs. James Henderson Moffitt (1848-1916) became a physician at Redford, Reynolds County; in January 1916 it was reported, "We were greatly pained to hear of the death of Dr. Moffitt which occurred at Redford the evening of the 7th." Martha Elizabeth (1850-1931) died at Springfield and Margaret Jane (1852-1923) at Montier, Missouri.

stories.title: Nathan's nephew, who died in the Elmira prison camp
stories.hook: From Randolph County, North Carolina, Veno was captured in Virginia and died at Elmira; a soldier with his cousin Calvin’s name served the Union in Arkansas.
body: Nathan's older brother Aaron C. Moffitt (6 December 1805 to 20 June 1877) stayed in Randolph County, North Carolina. He married Mary "Polly" Brady on 7 August 1827 and was with her in 1850 and 1870. Their son Veno, called Zeno in 1860, was born about 1828.

Veno married Charlotte L. "Lottie" Gardner (1824-1904), and they had Mary Jane (1860-1920) and the Rev. James Alfred Moffitt (1864-1926). At 34 he enlisted in the Confederate army on 8 April 1863 and joined Company F, 24th North Carolina Infantry.

He was captured near Drewry's Bluff, Virginia, on 16 May 1864. He was sent to the prison camp at Elmira, New York, where he died of chronic diarrhea on 11 October 1864. He is buried in Woodlawn National Cemetery at Elmira.

The war touched Moffitt families in several places. A Union cavalryman in Arkansas shared the name of Veno's cousin Calvin, though the identification remains unconfirmed. Lydia Moffitt Rains lost two sons in the war in North Carolina.

The road from Randolph County to Elmira can be followed, though the records disagree about how it began. The company muster rolls say he enlisted for the war in Randolph County in July 1862 under Major Mallett, while another roll gives 8 April 1863, age 34, and calls him a volunteer. He was present on every roll through December 1863. Captured near Drewry's Bluff on 16 May 1864, he was taken to Fort Monroe on 17 May and Point Lookout, Maryland, on 19 May, and was received at Elmira on 18 August. He died there on 11 October 1864 of chronic diarrhea, with no effects. Two later accounts disagree: one says he was captured at Petersburg on 17 June 1864 and died at Elmira on a date unknown, and another says he died there in November 1864. His name was also written onto a roll of sick prisoners paroled from Elmira on 11 October 1864, the day he died, and the entry was struck out with the word "Dead."

Company F had begun as the Cumberland Plough Boys, farm boys from Cumberland County, and its own history, written long afterward, remembers the loss of the first men the company ever had captured: twelve or fifteen taken at Petersburg in mid-June 1864 when Lieutenant Gainey's detachment held the line too long. That would fit the later account that has Veno taken at Petersburg on 17 June, but his passage to Fort Monroe on 17 May says May, and the company's memory may be a month off, or it may be telling of a different group. The date of his capture stays unsettled between mid-May and mid-June 1864.

stories.title: William C. and his three Randolph County wives
stories.hook: Nathan's brother stayed in North Carolina, married three times, and lost two sons by 1873; his first wife was a Williams, like Nathan's.
body: William Cornelius Moffitt, born about 1802, married Thalitha (Aletha) Williams on 7 August 1827, the same day Aaron, his brother, married Polly Brady. Thalitha was born 16 September 1804 at Deep River, Randolph County, and died before 1866. In 1850 and 1860 they had children at home.

Their children were Milo (1828-1881, died in Chatham County), Dennis (1830-1886), Reuben Elwood (1833-1915), Mahala Adeline (1835-1903), Marshall (1839-1863), Mary Delphina (1842-1898, died at Decatur, Indiana) and John Tyler (1843-1873). Marshall died in 1863, which fits the Civil War, but his service is not known.

William married Elizabeth Fesmire on 2 September 1866; she appears in the 1870 census and died about 1873. On 7 October 1873 he married Araminta Hicks (1844-1932), and in 1880 they had two young children, Hannah V. (born 1875) and William Dufoe (born 1876). He died in 1884 aged about 82; the birth date on his memorial is doubtful.
Nathan's wife was Rebecca Williams, also from Randolph County. Whether Rebecca and Thalitha were sisters is not known.

stories.title: Two sisters who went to Iowa with their Barker husbands
stories.hook: Nathan went west to Arkansas; his sisters Sarah and Naomi married two Barkers and settled in Iowa, where Sarah died on a sled being hauled home.
body: Sarah and Naomi were the oldest of Robert and Martha Moffitt's children. Naomi married Robert Barker on 5 March 1822, and Sarah married the Rev. Beeson Barker in 1821. Both families left Randolph County for Union County, Iowa.

A family memory of Sarah's death survives: "Mrs. Beeson Barker was born in 1800 and died in 1860 in the early winter. She took sick at the home of her son, Jerry, in Winterset. She wanted to come home so Marion Carey took a yoke of oxen hitched to a pin sled with a wagon box on it and putting a feather bed in it, brought her home. She lived only a few days. This broke up the active home of Rev. Barker." She is buried at Groesbeck Cemetery, Lorimor.

Sarah and Beeson had eight children: Aaron Dennis (1824-1881), Jeremiah Harmon (1826-1885), Robert Moffitt (1830-1834), Martha Jane (1831-1838), David Pearce (1834-1918), Mary Rahab (1838-1891), Sarah Ann (1841-1850) and William Beeson (1842-1926).

Naomi and Robert Barker's daughters Mary D. (1823-1899) and Deborah L. (1824-1907) both married their Moffitt cousins, Solomon C. and Stancil, sons of a Charles Moffitt who is given here a wife Mary Beeson (the 1928 genealogy names the wife of the Charles of that generation as Mary Cox, and the two accounts have not been reconciled), and both died in Union County, Iowa.

stories.title: The sisters who never left: Hannah and Lydia
stories.hook: Nathan's sisters Hannah and Lydia stayed in Randolph County, and Lydia lost two sons, Nathan and Daniel, at Raleigh in 1862.
body: Hannah Moffitt, born 11 December 1806, married Isaiah Craven and in 1850 lived in his household in Randolph County. They had at least Hiram Peter (1835-1900), Peter W. (1837-1861), Molcy, and Lewis Pickett (1846-1924). Hannah died on 24 January 1888 and is buried at Concord Cemetery, Coleridge.

Lydia, born in June 1811, married Alfred Rains on 29 or 30 June 1833 and appears in the censuses of 1850 through 1880. Her seven children were Nathan (25 July 1834), Mary (15 April 1836, who married Simon Pickett), Susanna E. (1 September 1838), William A. (15 October 1840), Daniel (15 May 1842), Alfred E. (4 September 1844) and Robert M. (29 March 1853). Four of the seven died before their parents. Susanna was eight when she died in February 1847, and William A. was nineteen when he died on 22 October 1859, a year and a half before the war began, so the statement that Nathan and William Anderson "died in the Civil War" cannot be right for William. The two sons who died in uniform were Nathan and Daniel. Both enrolled on 5 March 1862 in the Randolph Rangers, later Company G of the 46th North Carolina Infantry, and both died of disease at Raleigh, Nathan on 14 May (18 May in a hospital register) and Daniel on 17 May 1862. Alfred Evans served in Company G of the 38th North Carolina from August 1864 and was paroled at Greensboro on 19 May 1865.
Lydia died on 2 March 1885 and is buried in the Rains-Caveness family cemetery at Ramseur. Her brother Nathan, far away in Missouri, had died twelve years earlier.

stories.title: The Grimes farm on Hardin Creek
stories.hook: A Blackshear daughter from Jones County, North Carolina, married a South Carolina Grimes and raised a family at the Haggard farm near Waynesboro, where David H. Grimes was born.
body: John Grimes was born in South Carolina about 1775. Penelope, called Penny, was the daughter of Jesse and Hannah (Huggins) Blackshear of Jones County, North Carolina, and she was born there on 6 June 1789. Jesse took his family to Williamson County, Tennessee, between 1800 and 1810. John and Penelope's first known child, James B., was born in Williamson County about 1807.

In October 1814 the Williamson County court settled the estate of Jesse Blackshare, deceased: his widow had remarried as Hannah Mairs, and the balance was due to "Penny Blackshare and James Blackshare" and the other heirs. Penelope's first child was born about 1807, so she was already married by then; the court may simply have used her maiden name for the share due to her.

The Grimes family later moved to Wayne County. John died there on 14 June 1844 and was buried on the Haggard farm. Their children were James B. (about 1807), a daughter (1810-1815), Elisha S. (about 1817), a daughter (1820-1825), John Anderson (born October 1823), an unnamed son (1825-1829) and William Jasper (born 1826). David H. Grimes, born in 1829 in Wayne County, fits the unnamed son, and a family tree names a John Grimes as his father.
A Blackshear family history lists "A dau., m. Grimes" as the first child of Jesse Blackshear of Jones County and Williamson County. Penelope is shown still living after 1850.

stories.title: "John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor"
stories.hook: In 1872 William Jasper Grimes made a will leaving his land to his second family and his first wife's children, and named his brother John executor.

subject.name: William Jasper, John Anderson and the other Grimes brothers

body: John Anderson Grimes, born in October 1823 in Wayne County, married Mary C. Arnett about 1852. In 1860 he was a farmer, 37, with $4,000 in land and $3,500 in personal property, with Mary, 27, and children Nancy E., 7, George (Kearney), 5, Sarah F., 3, and John, 1. They were still on the family farm in 1900, run by their son George.

William Jasper Grimes was born in 1826. He married first Malaha Keaton and had twelve children between 1844 and 1868, among them Sarah J., Margaret G., John Q. A., Lucinda, Mary P., William Jasper K., Sevilla, Nancy C., Jasper Wayne, Benjamin Stout (a Blackshear name), Fannie and Mahulda Vista. His second wife was Tennessee Ann McClanahan.

His will was probated on 1 July 1872. It leaves his wife Tennessee Ann the home farm for her life and the land bought from John H. Cole, requires that "each of our children at the age of 21 years or at marriage" receive "one good horse, Bridle and Saddle, one cow and calf, one bed, bedstead and furniture," gives his two sons John A. and W. J. Grimes the tract bought from John B. Rutledge, and ends: "I nominate and appoint John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor to this my will."
James B. (born about 1807) and Elisha S. (born about 1817) both lived in Wayne County, Elisha on the Haggard farm.

stories.title: A militia oath before a Grimes justice of the peace
stories.hook: Penelope's brother Elijah swore never to fight a duel, in front of a Wayne County Grimes.
body: Elijah Blackshear was born on 9 June 1800, the son of Jesse Blackshear. He lived in Waynesboro, Tennessee, and married Dicena McMahon about 1820. Their children were Lucinda (1823), the twins Jesse Marion and James Newton (1826), and Hannah Permelia. James Newton married a Grimes, Elizabeth Anne, daughter of Isaac G. Grimes, on 11 April 1847.

On 29 March 1830 Elijah signed two oaths: "I do solemnly swear that I will support the Constitution of the U. S., and the State of Tenn.," and "I, Elijah Blackshear do solemnly swear that I will not give or accept a challenge either written or verbal to fight a duel, nor will I be the bearer of a challenge for such purpose." Both were sworn before Isaac G. Grimes, J.P., the same man who is the father of his son's later wife.
Isaac G. Grimes's relationship to John Grimes is not known.

stories.title: A Lincoln husband, a Sheffield-side bride and one surviving son
stories.hook: A couple married at Rotherham in 1609 and had a son Peter who may have been the later Sandwich settler.
body: Thomas Gaunt was baptized at Silkstone in the West Riding on 22 July 1571, though the register does not name his parents. On 28 August 1609 he married Susan Bate at Rotherham, about thirteen miles from Silkstone and ten from her home parish of Norton, south of Sheffield. Susan had been baptized at St James, Norton, on 23 September 1571, the daughter of James Bate.

Thomas was almost certainly marrying for the second time. His will of 1621 names children George, James, Anne and 'Dynes' as well as Peter, and Susan's own will says Peter was her only son. A Peter Gaunt was baptized at Lincoln on 29 June 1610, the year after the wedding; whether he was the couple’s son and the later Sandwich settler is not proved. The family lived in Lincoln, where Thomas was buried on 14 April 1621; Susan was buried there in February 1626, leaving a will that also names her brothers and sister, Thomas, Adam and Alice Bate.

This Thomas Gaunt is not the Thomas Gaunt of Pinchbeck, Lincolnshire, who married Isabel Wheelwright in 1602, and the unsourced parents some trees give him (Thomas Gaunt and Elizabeth Wheelwright) are set aside. His own parents are not known.

stories.title: The Bates of Jordanthorpe
stories.hook: Susan Bate's father James is known only from the Norton baptisms of his children; where he came from is not recorded.
body: James Bate and Dorothy Harrison married in 1569, and their children were baptized at St James, Norton, a mile north of the hamlet of Jordanthorpe: William in 1570, Susan in September 1571, Jane in 1576. James is called 'of Jordanthorpe' at the marriage of his daughter Elizabeth and at his own death in March 1608. Dorothy outlived him by four years.

James Bate's origins are not known. A baptism for a James 'Batty', son of Robert, at Kirkburton about twenty-five miles away in January 1547/8 fits his estimated birth year, but the name is too common to claim him.
Susan carried the Bate name to Lincoln when she married Thomas Gaunt in 1609, and she remembered her brothers Thomas and Adam and her sister Alice in her will.

stories.title: Friends of Newhey, and the son who crossed the Atlantic
stories.hook: William and Elizabeth Croasdale were buried side by side at Settle Meeting; a family history calls it 'highly probable' that they were the emigrant Thomas's parents.
body: William Croasdale lived at Newhey in the Forest of Bowland, the hill country of what was then the West Riding of Yorkshire, and died there on the 29th day of the 11th month 1666, the old-style January. He was buried two days later at the Friends' burial ground at Settle Meeting, Newton, in the village now called Newton-in-Bowland, which still keeps a Quaker burial ground. His wife Elizabeth was laid next to him after she died in the 4th month of 1672, about six years after him.

They were Friends in the years when that was dangerous. William was probably born about 1618 and Elizabeth about 1622, and both were buried in a Friends' ground in the 1660s, which shows which meeting they belonged to. Their children included Ezekiel, who died in 1708, William of Bradford, who died in 1691, and Mary.

A son named Thomas is placed at Settle by two reference works on early Pennsylvania settlers, and a family genealogist calls it "highly probable" that William and Elizabeth were the parents of the Thomas who emigrated to Pennsylvania in 1682, while noting that other parentage has been suggested. Henry Croasdale of Newhey is another proposed earlier ancestor, but the generations connecting him to the emigrant are unproven. A William, son of Henry Croasdale of Newhey, was baptized on 24 October 1621, later than the c.1618 birth year used here; whether he is this William is not known.
Elizabeth's surname Hayhurst comes from family compilations and has no original record behind it.

stories.title: Henry Croasdale of Newhey, yeoman
stories.hook: A Bowland yeoman named his son William as administrator in his September 1652 will and was buried at Waddington three weeks later.
body: Henry Croasdale lived at Newhey in the Forest of Bowland, within the parish of Waddington. The register records three of his children between 1616 and 1621: Elizabeth, buried 1 June 1616; Edward, baptized 13 January 1617/8; and William, baptized 24 October 1621.

His burial reads 'Henry Croasdell buried Oct: 10' (1652). He had made his will the month before, on 21 September 1652, as 'Henrie Croasdale, yeoman; Newhay within Bolannd', with his son William as administrator; it was registered in 1654. No wife is named.

This Henry is made the grandfather of the Thomas Croasdale who emigrated in 1682, but that step is an inference: the William baptized in 1621 would have been about 23 if Thomas was born in 1644, and some published lines give a different Henry (died 1595).

stories.title: A father who died the year his daughter was born
stories.hook: Agnes Hawthornthwaite is said to have been born in 1633, the year her father William died at 26.
body: Agnes Hawthornthwaite, later wife of Thomas Croasdale, is said to have been born on 13 July 1633 in Tatham parish. Her father William Hawthornthwaite, born in 1607, is said to have married Elizabeth in Lancashire in 1631 and to have died in 1633, aged 26.
The sources for this are indexes of Lancashire parish registers and burials, not the register entries themselves, and nothing ties Agnes to William beyond the dates, so the link is unconfirmed.

Agnes appears at the other end of her life in the Quaker records. She married Thomas Croasdale, and in June 1682 Settle Monthly Meeting issued a removal certificate to a company of Friends bound for America that included Thomas, Agnes and six children. Thomas had bought land in Pennsylvania from William Penn by an indenture of 21 April 1682, on Neshaminy Creek in Bucks County near what is now Langhorne. Agnes died on 20 October 1686 and was buried at Neshaminy (the Colonial Dames honor gives 1684, which cannot stand).
One account gives a different Agnes: born about 1646, married at Lancaster in 1664, and arriving on the Welcome. If that is the right Agnes, William, who died in 1633, cannot have been her father.

Conflict: the NSCDA Founding Females index (citing Sheppard and McCracken) gives Agnes Hathornthwaite Croasdale as born about 1646, married at Lancaster Monthly Meeting on 20 May 1664, mother of six children born at Lancaster, and sailing on the Welcome (left Deal 31 Aug 1682), buried 20 Oct 1684. That cannot be squared with a daughter born in July 1633 to a father buried in 1633, so the parentage is probably wrong; the other trees' ship (Lamb) and her death year (1686) also differ. The Settle certificate and the 1682 indenture are known only through a blog summary, and an administration of Thomas's estate in December 1684 reported there sits oddly with a burial for Agnes in October 1684.

stories.title: A 1686 marriage in Duke's Place
stories.hook: A London record shows an Anthony Champneys marrying Anne Pitts in 1686, but their son John was baptized four years earlier.
body: John Chamness, who married Ann Wearey at St John's, Wapping, in 1704, is said to be the son of Anthony Chamness and Ann Pitts. The only evidence for the parents is the marriage of Anthony 'Champneys' and Anne Pitts at St James, Duke's Place, on 23 September 1686. St James, Duke's Place, stood just inside the walls at Aldgate on old priory ground that had passed to the Dukes of Norfolk; it was consecrated in 1622, its parish claimed exemption from the Bishop of London, and by the later seventeenth century it had a name as a marriage factory, with several weddings a day.

That date is four years after John's baptism, in November 1682 at St Saviour's in Southwark. Though it is said there is 'no geographical or chronological reason to dispute' the link, the order of dates is a reason to be careful. The church's reputation might explain a wedding after the child, since John could have been baptized before his parents formally married, but nothing shows that was the case here. Or the baptism belongs to another family. John, whoever his parents were, is said to have died in London in 1716.

Anthony 'appears to be' the son of a John Chamness of Stansted Mountfitchet, Essex, and his wife Mary Reffell, but those Essex generations are not added here. Ann Pitts is said to have lived until 1745, in Devon.

stories.title: A Quaker family on the Kent
stories.hook: A Chesterfield Meeting birth record gives a John Rogers born in 1687 to John and Mary; whether he is the John Rogers whose son Thomas married Ann Staples is not settled.

subject.name: John Rogers & Mary (Groom) Rogers of Burlington

body: The Burlington County Quaker John Rogers, born about 1656 at Rotherham, is said to have crossed with Friends on the Kent, which loaded at London in March 1677 and landed at the Delaware in 1678. He married Mary Groom, who died on 13 February 1693, and the couple had at least five children.

This family is tied to a John Rogers born 'the 5th day of the 1st month 1687' at Nottingham, Burlington County, by the Chesterfield Quaker birth record, and that John is given a wife Martha Middleton, whose mother's 1712 will names a 'son-in-law John Rogers'.

Two estates have been attached to John Rogers in family trees. John Rodgers of Burlington made his will on 23 January 1764; it was proved on 26 March 1767 and gave his son Thomas one-third of the residue. John Rogers of Windsor made a different will on 6 January 1769, proved on 10 April 1776, naming seven sons and two daughters but no Thomas. Neither gives the testator’s parents. The identity of the John born in 1687, and his connection to our Thomas Rogers, remain unresolved.

stories.title: From the Isle of Man to Belfast to Iredell
stories.hook: A 1720 marriage at Downpatrick is the only solid piece in the chain behind James Stevenson of Iredell County.
body: Henry Stevenson married Ann Curlett on 2 June 1720 at Saul parish, near Downpatrick, the ground where Saint Patrick is said to have founded his first church. Ann had been baptized on 27 May 1698 at Braddan, a parish on the Isle of Man that now includes part of Douglas, a daughter of William Curlett. Their children, as family trees list them, include a James born about March 1721 at Belfast, though a birth in 1721 does not fit the "nearly 90" of 1820.

That James is identified with the James Stevenson who died on 5 March 1820 in Iredell County, North Carolina, a native of Ireland, nearly 90 years old, married 65 years, with 208 descendants. His estate was probated in Iredell in 1820.

Henry's own birthplace and his parents (given as William Stevenson and Katherine Alison) have no cited source. Whether this James is the father of the James Stevenson (1746-1828) in the Stevenson line here is itself only a possibility. A 1955 note in the Skinner genealogy describes an immigrant James Stevenson who died in 1820 and gives his wife as Sally Kelly of Maryland, and it does not call him Henry's son, so the picture of James's origins is unsettled.

Iredell was crowded with Stevensons. William Stevenson of County Antrim, called Little Gabriel, took up land there in 1762 and grew it to nearly 3,400 acres, and he was an elder of Fourth Creek Presbyterian Church. How James Stevenson was related to him, if at all, is unknown.

stories.title: Cedar Creek Friends move south
stories.hook: Robert Johnson, son of Ashley, married Cisley (Virginia) Elmore at Cedar Creek Meeting in 1758 and was sent south to Deep River with her in 1766.
body: On 19 November, in a public meeting at Cedar Creek, Robert Johnson of Louisa County, son of Ashley, took Cisley Elmore, daughter of Thomas Elmore of Amelia County, as his wife. The wedding falls in 1758 as the minute is transcribed, although a 1988 Johnson genealogy prints 1759. That genealogy names her Virginia C. Elmore and records that 'Robert and Virginia Johnson rec. on cert. from Cedar Creek M.M., Va., dated 1766-3-29'. Cisley is the old form of Cecilia, her mother's name, and the family tree carries her as Cecelia. Both were buried at Springfield Meeting in North Carolina, and Robert's estate was opened in Stokes County in 1808.

Robert was born in February 1737 or 1738 in New Kent County, probably the son of Ashley Johnson and Martha Woody, whose family later farmed Chamberlain's Creek in Louisa County. Cisley, born at Black Creek in 1737, was a daughter of Thomas Elmore and Cecilia Ellyson.

Cedar Creek's Friends had been meeting in Hanover County, near the forks of the Anna rivers, since about 1719, and in about 1744 Johnsons, Moormans and Clarks set up Camp Creek Meeting in neighboring Louisa County; the families on both sides of the line intermarried constantly. The drought of 1754-56, the French and Indian War and stricter regulation of Quakers then sent many Hanover and Louisa families to Bedford County, to southwest Virginia and on into North Carolina, where the Established Church had less hold. The Cane Creek meeting, in the North Carolina Piedmont, had held its first monthly meeting on 7 October 1751 and earned the name Mother of Meetings by starting the others, and thirty Pennsylvania families had already settled around it.
An unsourced family tree lists Martha Johnson, born 28 August 1766 at Deep River, who married Aden Nordyke in 1787, among their children. The Quaker minutes support the couple but do not name Martha.

The 1758 entry calls the groom 'Robert, Louisa Co., s Ashely' and the bride 'Cisley ELMORE, dt Thomas, Amelia Co.', which supports Ashley Johnson as his father and confirms the surname Elmore; her first name is Cisley (Cecilia) there and 'Virginia C.' in the 1988 abstract, and the tree keeps Cecelia. The step to Martha Johnson (b. 1766) as their daughter comes from a compiled family history, so it stays probable. The family tree carries the couple as Robert Valentine Johnson (8 February 1737 to 24 April 1807) and Cecelia Johnson; the dates above follow the Johnson genealogy, which has Robert's estate opened in 1808. Robert's last residence is not settled: his estate was opened in Stokes County, but both were buried at Springfield Meeting. stories.title: A gift of everything for 'love and affection'
stories.hook: In 1794 Ashley Johnson deeded his whole estate to his son Elijah in return for keeping him and Martha for the rest of their lives.
body: Ashley Johnson was born about 1710 in St Peter's Parish, New Kent County, Virginia, and married Martha Woody in Henrico or New Kent County; the sources give 12 December 1734 and 10 or 12 October 1735. Both were Quakers, and the early meeting records of Henrico, Curles and Weyanoke carry the family. They raised at least eight sons and five daughters, including Robert, born February 1738. When Robert married Cisley Elmore at Cedar Creek Meeting in November 1758, the minute called him "Robert, Louisa Co., s Ashely," the line that ties the generations together.

By then the family lived in Louisa County, which had been cut from Hanover County in 1742. Two county deeds fill in the later years. On 9 November 1778 Ashley gave his son Elijah 241 acres on Chamberlain's Creek. On 3 February 1794, an old man of about eighty-four, he gave Elijah all his estate, real and personal, "for love and affection and maintenance of the said Ashley Johnson and Martha his wife during their natural lives," except 210 acres jointly to David and James, with a feather bed and furniture each for Martha, Elizabeth and David. It was an arrangement for the old couple's keep.

Martha died on 6 September 1802 and Ashley about 1803, aged about 93; both are buried at Roundabout Castle Cemetery in Louisa County. Their son Robert took his own family south in 1766 with a certificate to North Carolina, and Robert's daughter Martha, born that year, is the proposed wife of Aden Nordyke. Ashley's own parents are disputed and are not attached here.

stories.title: John Johnson’s land on Black Creek
stories.hook: A 1705 patent traces 252 acres beside Black Creek and credits John Johnson with the importation of five named people.

subject.name: John Johnson of St Peter's Parish

body: John Johnson first appears in St Peter’s Parish on 22 November 1702, when a son John was baptized. A patent dated 2 November 1705 granted John Johnson 252 acres in St Peter’s Parish, New Kent County, on the north side of Black Creek. It credits him with the importation of five people into the colony, without saying they were relatives or what their terms of service were.

The five names written beside the grant appear to read Wm Davies, Saml Mitchel, Joan Hillard, Dan Gibbs and George Abraham. Their spellings are tentative readings of the handwriting. The boundary runs between marked trees and along the creek: a pine, a white oak, a maple at a small branch and Thomas Snead’s line. The tract had first been granted to Thomas Reynolds on 25 October 1695, then deserted and granted again to Johnson under a General Court order of 17 October 1705.

A second patent, dated 9 February 1727/8, granted John Johnson of Hanover County 200 acres in Henrico County on the south side of Chickahominy Swamp, for twenty shillings. Later deeds say John and his wife Elizabeth sold that land on 1 November 1736; he is reported to have died on 5 September 1737, though these details are unconfirmed.

A Quaker abstract names Ashley Johnson's mother as Lucretia Massie, but Friends' records call John's wife Elizabeth, and Lucretia and her Massie parentage rest on uncited histories. John's own parents are also disputed.

The five people’s names are tentative readings; the patent says persons, not servants, and gives no ship, arrival dates, kinship or service terms. These patents document land grants and do not establish Ashley Johnson’s parentage, the identity of John’s first wife, or his earlier ancestry. The 1736 sale and reported 1737 death remain based on the separately cited references. This proposed ancestral connection remains probable.

stories.title: A Spotsylvania will with six sons
stories.hook: John Paine's will names six sons, one of them a William, and the line to the Stevenson wife Lydia Payne runs through that name.
body: John Paine was born in Drysdale Parish, King and Queen County, in 1705, a son of Barnett Paine. He witnessed a Spotsylvania County deed in 1740 and died there between the date of his will, 25 July 1764, and the executors' bond of 20 September 1770. The will names his wife Frances and sons John (eldest), Thomas, Barnett, William, Robert and George.
Frances is thought to be a daughter of Robert and Mary (Clayton) Coleman, but there is 'considerable disagreement' over which Coleman family. A 1750 will reportedly calls her 'Francis Pain'.

The link to the Stevensons is by way of Rev. Elam Stevenson's wife Lydia Payne, whose father William Paine (1754-1807, Burke County, N.C.) is listed as one of John's sons. That William is tied to Lydia only through a memorial, and two men named William Paine have been confused, so the whole link is unproven.

stories.title: The stone house on Sugaw Creek
stories.hook: Hezekiah Alexander, a blacksmith turned planter and revolutionary, finished his stone house on Sugaw Creek in 1774, and his daughter Esther, it seems, went west to Kentucky as Mrs. Samuel Garrison.
body: Hezekiah Alexander was born on 13 January 1728 (or 1722, as one Garrison family history has it) at New Munster in Cecil County, Maryland. He married Mary Sample, a daughter of William Sample Sr. and Esther, said to have been a Garrison, and they settled in the Sugaw Creek congregation in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, where they raised a large family: eleven children by the usual count, though the 1796 will and the biography dictionary account for ten, seven sons and three daughters.

He began as a blacksmith and became a planter. From 1768 he was a justice of the peace for Mecklenburg, and in the first years of the Revolution he sat on the county and Salisbury district committees of safety. In 1776 he was one of the thirteen members of the state’s Council of Safety and a delegate to the congress at Halifax, where he served on the committees that drafted North Carolina’s first bill of rights and constitution. He was also a founder and treasurer of Queens College in Charlotte. Later tradition counted him among the signers of the Mecklenburg Declaration of May 1775, which historians doubt, since no account of it can be traced earlier than 1819; his younger brother, John McKnitt Alexander, is the man tradition names as its clerk. The Daughters of the American Revolution recognize Hezekiah as a patriot.

The stone house he finished in 1774 is the oldest in Mecklenburg County. It has been on the National Register of Historic Places since 1970, and the Charlotte Museum of History keeps it and the homesite.

The plantation was worked by enslaved people: at least seventeen men, women and children, whose names survive in the Alexander wills and in the inventory of Hezekiah’s estate taken in October 1801. His will left a woman named Jean, and her children Siah, Frank and Nancy, to his daughter Esther Garrison. Esther was to hold the children, and any Jean might later have, for eighteen years, after which they were to pass to Esther’s own children as they came of age. Other bequests sent Mary to his son James R. Alexander, Ann to Silas, Jack to William Sample Alexander, and Bet and an older man named Sam to his wife, Mary. He made the will on 8 August 1796, or perhaps in 1797. Whether Jean and her children went with Esther and Samuel Garrison to Kentucky about 1800 is not known.

Their daughter Esther was born on 28 September 1762. In his will Hezekiah remembered his daughter “Esther Garrison,” with her “dau. Caroline Garrison and other ch. of Esther.” That she was the Esther who married Samuel Garrison and was the mother of John Milton Garrison of Allen County, Kentucky, is probable.

Hezekiah's younger brother left the trail of paper that his own household lost. The original records of the Mecklenburg meeting of May 1775 were burned when fire destroyed John McKnitt Alexander's house in 1800, and the rough, torn notes found after his death are all the supporters of the declaration have. A collection of forty-one items gathered by Joseph McKnitt Alexander and others, with copies of witnesses' testimony and the papers behind the state's 1831 report, is held at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

stories.title: Two wills on one day
stories.hook: William and Esther Sample each signed a will on 26 January 1769, and he was dead that month.
body: William Sample Sr. was born about 1690, in either Northern Ireland or Scotland, and lived in Cecil County, Maryland, before the family moved to Mecklenburg County. He signed a will on 26 January 1769 and died that same month; his wife Esther, said to have been a Garrison, signed her own will the same day. The loose estate papers name five children: William, John, Joseph, Mary and Agnes.

Their daughter Mary, born 31 January 1734, married Hezekiah Alexander, a fellow Cecil County man, on 12 June 1752. In January 1769 Hezekiah was a county magistrate, an office he held from 1768, and he and Mary were living on the 600 acres or so on Sugar Creek that he had bought in 1767; their stone house was still five years from completion. Mary outlived Hezekiah, who died in 1801, never remarried, and died in 1805. Her youngest sons, Joel and Oswald, divided the land between them, and Oswald received the house. Esther's parentage is not carried further here.
William and Esther lie at Hopewell Presbyterian Church, whose congregation now worships in a stone building from about 1833.

William Sample made his will in Mecklenburg County on 26 January 1769. He named his wife Esther and “Hez: Alexander my Son in law” as his executors, left ten pounds to his daughter Mary Alexander, and remembered his sons John, Joseph and William and his daughter Esther.

stories.title: A Cecil County elder and two McKnitt sisters
stories.hook: James Alexander of Cecil County, a magistrate and Presbyterian elder, married two McKnitt sisters in turn; the first, Margaret, was the mother of Hezekiah, the Mecklenburg patriot.
body: James Alexander was born about 1690 at Manokin in Somerset County, Maryland, into a Scots-Irish family said to descend from a tanner, Joseph Alexander, one of seven brothers who reached Somerset County before 1670. He moved north to Cecil County, where he became a magistrate and an elder of the Presbyterian church. His first wife was Margaret McKnitt, born 26 December 1693, the daughter of John McKnitt and Jane Wallace, and she bore him twelve children by a Bible list, among them Hezekiah, born in 1722 or 1728 (1728 in one standard account). Margaret died at New Munster on 31 July 1736, and James married her sister Abigail, who gave him five more.

Hezekiah grew up in the Cecil County household, learned the blacksmith's trade, and carried the family's Presbyterian faith south to the Carolina backcountry, where he became one of Mecklenburg's leading men.

Hezekiah went first to Cumberland County, Pennsylvania, and then on to the Carolina Piedmont, where he was buying land near the Catawba River by 1764. In 1752 he had married Mary Sample, whose family would follow the same road south. In 1767 he bought more than 600 acres on Sugar Creek in Mecklenburg County and by 1774 had finished a two-story stone house on it, the oldest house in Mecklenburg County and the centerpiece of the Charlotte Museum of History. A magistrate from 1768, he sat on the Mecklenburg Committee of Safety, helped write the state's first constitution as a member of the Provincial Congress, and was a trustee of Queens College.

His father outlived Margaret by forty-three years. James died in Cecil County on 31 May 1779 and was buried at the Head of Christiana Church cemetery near Newark, Delaware. Three separate compilations give his birth as 1690, and he is recognized as a patriot ancestor.

His own parents were Joseph Alexander and Abigail McKnitt, which made his first wife Margaret his cousin. Joseph died in Cecil County by March 1730, and beyond him the 'Seven Brothers' Alexanders from Donegal are a speculative family tradition. Margaret's parents, John McKnitt and Jane Wallace, are named in print but come with no dates.

stories.title: A Continental private and the road to Kentucky
stories.hook: Samuel Garrison, a Revolutionary soldier, moved from Mecklenburg to Kentucky; his family record names John Milton among his children.
body: Samuel Garrison was born on 24 August 1762 in Halifax County, North Carolina, by one account, served in the Revolution as a private in the Continental Line, and was buried in Old Scottsville Cemetery in Kentucky. His wife Esther Alexander was born in Mecklenburg County in 1762, but her place of death is given as Coles County, Illinois, which does not fit a husband buried in Kentucky. His pension file shows North Carolina militia service rather than the Continental Line, and the family record puts Esther's death in Allen County, Kentucky.

John Milton Garrison is said to have come from Mecklenburg County to Warren, later Allen, County, Kentucky, with his parents before 1809, which matches Samuel's move. Samuel's own family record book lists John Milton, born 4 October 1788, among his nine children; no county record names him as Samuel's son. Samuel's father is given as John Garrison of Salem, New Jersey, with no source.

Samuel wrote verse. At some point in the late eighteenth century he set down a poem called "Choice" about the wife he hoped to find, one "ruled by reason not by passion led," of mild temper and good sense, ideally nearing twenty. Whether Esther met every requirement nobody can say, but they stayed married for life and settled on Bay's Fork Creek in south-central Kentucky. The original manuscript of the poem and a family genealogy are now in the Manuscripts and Folklife Archives at Western Kentucky University, and a monument praising his life and Revolutionary service was dedicated on 12 May 2001 at Old Scottsville Cemetery. A book on his descendants, covering Samuel (1762-1833) and Esther Alexander (1762-1829), draws on that collection.

stories.title: A gunshot near his mother's farm, January 1948
stories.hook: Louis Daniel Hulsey, 27, a World War II veteran and timber worker, was found dead near Mena, Arkansas, on 13 January 1948; his death was ruled a suicide.
body: Louis Daniel Hulsey came into the world at Bethel, Oklahoma, on 11 May 1920, the eighth of ten children of George Washington Hulsey and Sarah Rebecca Graves. His family had come across the Arkansas line to tenant-farm in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, and he was born into that move; by 1930 the household of ten rented a farm near Wright City, in the sawmill country.

He was fifteen when his father died in August 1935 and was buried at Breashears Cemetery near Story, Arkansas. Louis grew into a young man who served in World War II; his Arkansas certificate calls him a veteran. By December 1946 he was single, a timber worker, and living thirteen months on his mother's farm in the Acorn community outside Mena, in Polk County, Arkansas. Mena was a railroad town, incorporated in 1896 as Arthur Stilwell's Kansas City, Pittsburg and Gulf line pushed south.

On the morning of 13 January 1948 he was found dead about a quarter mile from his mother's farmhouse at 6:30. The certificate gives the cause as a gunshot wound to the right temple, "Self inflicted," and rules the death a suicide. Coroner O. R. Wood of Mena signed it the same day. His mother Rebecca, then living at Acorn, gave the information that went into the record, and he was buried on 15 January at Storey, the community near which his father had been buried in 1935.

The next day the Idabel paper carried the headline "Gunshot Wound Is Fatal for Former Wright City Man" over an article naming him; Wright City was where the family had lived when he was growing up. He was twenty-seven. When his brother Oscar died in 1982, three of the ten Hulsey children had already gone before him; Louis was one of them.

stories.title: Margaret Crumpton and the Graves family
stories.hook: Margaret Crumpton married Jesse Graves in Garland County in 1884; how she connects to Sarah Rebecca is not settled.
body: In 1880 a widowed Margarett J. Crumpton, age 25, of Mountain Township, Garland County, lived in a household with Rebecca Cornett, age 69, and John W. and William H. Crumpton, ages four and two. The matching name, age and county make her a possible match for the 1884 bride, not a proven one. A Graves family genealogy identifies Rebecca as Margaret's mother and the boys as Margaret's sons, though nothing in the household itself says so.

A Margaret Cornett, age six, was in Searcy County in 1860 with Edward and Rebecca Cornett. That is promising, but linking her to the woman in the 1880 household needs more evidence: Rebecca's ages differ substantially between the two, and the 1860 household stated no relationships.

On 31 January 1884, a Jesse Graves married Margaret Crumpton in Garland County. The register records Margaret as 28 and Jesse as 38. A family account of 1977 names Margaret as a wife of Jesse Graves and Sarah Rebecca as his daughter, but does not say which wife bore Sarah. That age conflicts with the age given for Jesse in 1871, so whether both concern the same man is unresolved.

The Graves family identifies Margaret as Sarah Rebecca's mother and reports that Margaret died on 5 May 1884, the day Sarah was born. Nothing directly confirms the parentage or the death. The genealogy gives two possible maiden names, Speer and Cornett, without resolving the conflict.

stories.title: Married at fifteen in a neighbor's house
stories.hook: Jesse Graves's first wife was 15 when they married at Jack Phillips's house in 1871.
body: Emma Fisher was fifteen when she married, and she married from a neighbor's house. Her father was Nicholas Fisher, and her mother, probably Sarah L. Garrett, married in turn William Gray, a man named Kirkland, Nicholas Fisher and finally Jack Phillips. It was Phillips's home in Mountain Township, Montgomery County, Arkansas, that stood in for a wedding hall on 2 April 1871, when Emma, born about 1856, took Jesse Graves, then eighteen, as her husband.

Jesse was a son of Gilliam Graves, the farmer whose family had come by way of North Carolina, Georgia and Alabama to Cedar Glades and who put on a Union uniform in January 1864. Emma and Jesse settled into the same rough country. In 1873 the legislature created Garland County on 5 April out of parts of Hot Spring, Montgomery and Saline counties, so the Mountain Township they lived in was by then in a new county, and it was in Garland County that they were counted in June 1880.

Their children came steadily: Abraham Nicholas, whose middle name matches her father's, then Catherine Eunice and Greenbury H., and a son Vestal, whose reported birthday of 21 March 1881 falls just after that 1880 enumeration. An Abe N. Graves who died in 1943 and was mourned by a sister, Mrs. Rebecca Hulsey, may be this eldest son, which would make Emma's children the half-siblings of Sarah Rebecca Graves, the Hulsey family's matriarch; that link is a guess from names and has not been proved.

After Vestal's birth Emma disappears. She may have died young, as many wives did in those years, or the family may have moved on, and nothing found yet settles it. Within three years a Jesse Graves married Margaret Crumpton in Garland County, and in 1889 a Jesse Graves married Nancy Cutter. Whether those grooms are the same Jesse is still unresolved, because their recorded ages do not fit a man born in 1853.

stories.title: Nancy Cutter and the Graves household
stories.hook: Jesse Graves married Nancy Cutter in Garland County in 1889, and family accounts give Nancy different surnames.
body: A Jesse Graves married Nancy Cutter in Garland County on 19 September 1889, the groom 38. A 1977 family account names Nancy Wilborn Sutton as a wife of Jesse Graves, while the Graves family calls her Nancy Wilborn Kyle Cuttler. The different names keep the records from being tied together with confidence.

The Graves family says Nancy had earlier married John B. Kyle and Samuel B. Cuttler, and names children Isaac and Prince. It also lists Lucinda, William Vestal, Pearl Mae and Cora Ellen as children of Nancy and Jesse. These relationships are unconfirmed.

In 1920 Nancy was living in Garland County with her daughter Lucinda and son-in-law Benjamin Hogue, and she was still in the county in 1930. The family says Jesse died in 1910 and says Nancy died on 20 November 1932. The 1977 account names Sarah Rebecca as Jesse's daughter but not which wife was her mother; the relationship between Sarah and Nancy is not established.

stories.title: A possible route from Georgia to Arkansas
stories.hook: Robert in Salathiel’s Georgia household may be the Robert Hulsey recorded in Arkansas in 1860; the connection remains open.
body: In 1850 Robert, 17, was in the Union County, Georgia, household of Salathiel, 43, and Elizabeth, 35. The other young Hulseys include Maryan, 19; Elizabeth, 12; Jesse, 10; Jennings, 8; a girl transcribed Lillean, 6; Benjamin, 3; and Nancy, 1. A published extract gives Robert a middle initial R. and reverses the ages of Benjamin and the girl above him.

In 1860, in Carouse Township, Hempstead County, Arkansas, Robert Hulsey, 27, born Georgia, was a farmer with $240 in real estate and $80 in personal estate. Sarah A., 20, born Mississippi, and a one-year-old male born Arkansas lived in the same dwelling. Robert has no middle initial on this page. The infant’s name is indexed as Selatha G.; its handwritten spelling is uncertain, and the published extract’s reading Salathel G. should not be treated as a secure match to Salathiel. No relationships are recorded, and Benjamin is not listed in this household.

If this is the same Robert, he was in Arkansas by 1860. The shared 1850 household suggests that he and Benjamin may have been brothers, but it does not state their relationship. The identity of the Benjamin F. Hulsey on the 1864 Union roster also remains unconfirmed.

stories.title: Gilliam Graves and the orphans of Samuel and Sarah
stories.hook: In 1854 Gilliam Graves was named guardian of the children of Samuel and Sarah Graves; one of them, William Riley, died without a will in 1861.
body: In January 1854 Gilliam Graves was appointed guardian for the children of Samuel and Sarah Graves of Montgomery County, Arkansas. The parents are thought to be Samuel Graves and Sarah Cole, who were married on 30 March 1837 in Randolph County, North Carolina, by Moore Graves.

Gillum and Moor Graves were both in Cherokee County, Georgia, in 1840, and "it is believed that Moore Graves died in the 1840s." The widow Sarah appears on the Montgomery County tax lists from 1851 and bought a 40-acre tract, the NW SE of section 11.

In 1860 the children were a household of their own: William (Riley), 22, farmer, and Alley, 17, Ursa, 15, Alison, 14 and Madison, 11, all born North Carolina. In April 1861 Gilliam is again named guardian for the minor heirs Alley, Ultha, Alison and Madison. William Riley died intestate on 1 November 1861.
How these children were related to Gilliam, whether nephews and nieces or otherwise, is not established.

The county Gilliam answered to was young. Montgomery County had been organized out of Hot Spring County on 9 December 1842, and its seat, first called Montgomery, was renamed Salem in July 1850 and Mount Ida that October, after the post office Granville Whittington had kept in his house since 1842. Mount Ida was incorporated in 1854, the year Gilliam was made guardian, so the bond and the orders for Samuel and Sarah's children went through a probate court in a town only just chartered.

It was thin country. The county counted 1,958 people in 1850 and 3,633 in 1860, when the Graves orphans were enumerated as a household of their own; 92 of those people were enslaved. Most of the county sided with the South when the war came, which is the background to Gilliam's own Union enlistment at Cedar Glades in 1864.

quotes.t: It is believed that Moore Graves died in the 1840s.
