stories.title: Married at nineteen, then to a man twice her age
stories.hook: Polly Gray was 19 when she married Franklin Washburn in 1859; by 1864 she had a daughter by Gilliam Graves.
body: Polly Gray was the daughter of William Andrew Gray and Sarah L. Garrett, a woman who married four times (Gray, Kirkland, Fisher and Phillips). She was born about 1840 in Hot Spring County and, on 1 February 1859, married Franklin W. Washburn; he was twenty-one and she nineteen.

By 1864 she was Gilliam Graves's wife, and their daughter Mary Elizabeth was born on 13 August 1864, two months before Gilliam deserted from the Union army (12 October 1864) and returned on Christmas Day. In 1880 the Graves children by Polly were living with Andrew Washburn, her son by Franklin, and his wife Amanda.
Polly died about 1879 at Cedar Glades. Gilliam, who is supposed to have been killed by robbers in January 1876, is buried next to Polly in Mountain Valley Cemetery, once called Mt. Pleasant Cemetery.

When Polly married Franklin Washburn in February 1859, Hot Spring County's seat was Rockport, on the Ouachita River, where ledges of novaculite made a natural ford. Travelers on the old Military Road had crossed there since the 1830s, and a toll bridge, said to be the first in Arkansas, had gone up about 1847 and washed out more than once. The town had a grist mill, a wagon shop, stores and two Baptist churches, the newer one founded in 1859, and its new courthouse was dedicated in 1860. The Washburns' license would have come from the clerk there.

Rockport did not keep its importance. Union troops under Frederick Steele skirmished there on 25 March 1864 and laid a pontoon bridge the next day, on the march that became the Camden expedition. In 1873 fire destroyed the courthouse, and the same year Garland County was cut out of Hot Spring, Montgomery and Saline counties. Polly's own Cedar Glades had been a Montgomery County settlement; the changes of 1873 and 1917 moved it and its neighbors into Garland County. The county seat went to Malvern, on the railroad, in October 1879, about the year Polly died.

body: In June 1880, B. F. Hulsey’s wife was Sarah G., thirty, born in Arkansas. Three children, Margaret M., George W. and Charles F., were in the household. She is called the wife of their father, but nothing says she was their biological mother.

A family account of 1977 calls Benjamin’s wife Margaret Partain. Other family accounts use Sylvania Susane Partin. Neither name has been linked securely to Sarah G. Similar surnames and a recurring Benjamin are clues, but they do not establish a mother for George Washington.

A September 1893 Garland County marriage bond and license name Benjamin F. Hulsley and Lucy Morgan. The license, issued on 25 September, calls Lucy fifteen. The century printed on the bond was corrected to 1893 by hand, and no ceremony is readable. This shows the couple's application for marriage, while their relationship to the 1880 family remains open.

stories.title: "Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down": a Union petition, March 1864
stories.hook: Weeks after Gilliam Graves joined the Union cavalry at Cedar Glades, Union men from the same county begged the army for help against murder and plunder.
body: Gilliam Graves, 45, volunteered for the Union 4th Arkansas Cavalry at Cedar Glades on 14 January 1864. Less than two months later, on 10 March 1864, a letter went from Little Rock to Col. C. C. Andrews, who commanded the post. It was signed by Oliver Adair "and others" who called themselves "citizens of Montgomery County, Ark., and members of Company L, Fourth Arkansas Cavalry." The printed letter reads Company L, which may be a misprint for D, the company raised at Cedar Glades; the family's own man is on the roster of Company D.

The men wrote that "Deeds of cruelty and barbarity that would shame Indians are of daily occurrence." They gave three cases from a single day: "On the 1st instant the wife of Mr. James Dosier was shot through the shoulders, and her child (one year old) shot through the arms. On the same day Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down, mortally wounded, and his brains then blown out. William Gray (citizen) was shot in a brutal and cowardly manner on same day."

They added that "the plundering of houses, breaking and burning of cotton cards, wheels, &c., belonging to Union citizens is of common occurrence," and asked that about 100 cavalry be sent into the county, where forage and mills were plentiful. Because "our company is not armed," they suggested that guides be taken from among themselves. A "Skirmish at Cedar Glade, Ark." is listed for 1 March, the same day as the shootings, with no circumstantial reports.

The letter does not name Gilliam Graves, and nothing says he or any Hulsey signed it. What it shows is the neighborhood he enlisted from: Union families in the Ouachita hills in the winter of 1864, with their cavalry company still unarmed while their neighbors were being shot at home. Gilliam's later death, "supposedly killed by robbers" in Garland County in 1876, came in the same kind of country.

stories.title: Scouts "to secure all guerrillas and bushwhackers," 1864
stories.hook: The orders and reports that sent the 4th Arkansas Cavalry back through Montgomery County in 1864, with the wounded and missing it cost.

subject.name: The 4th Arkansas Cavalry in Montgomery and Hot Springs counties

body: A Union company recruited at Cedar Glades had to be used somewhere, and the army's papers show where. On 11 April 1864 Col. A. H. Ryan, commanding the 4th Arkansas Cavalry at Lewisburg, was ordered to send 2nd Lt. John N. Jones with 75 men to Hot Springs County. The general "wishes the detail to start at the earliest practicable moment. He orders that no houses be burnt by them and no property destroyed, but he wishes them to secure all guerrillas and bushwhackers who may fall in their way."

On 11 June 1864 an expedition was organized "to make a scout in Saline, Hot Springs, Montgomery, and Perry Counties," with 100 men of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, four companies of the 3rd U.S. Cavalry and part of Merrill's Horse, under Maj. G. Harker, "to be gone six or eight days." Fifteen days later, on 26 June, Capt. Joel Brown of Company A wrote General Steele about the loyal families crowded into Dardanelle: "mostly soldiers' families," "without medical aid, and not enough of men in town to bury the dead."

The army's monthly summary for August 1864 records the result: "14th, a battalion of the Fourth Arkansas Cavalry returned from scout through Saline, Hot Springs, and Montgomery Counties. Fought with small bands of the enemy daily until arriving at Farr's Mill. Captain Green, with twenty-five men of this battalion, engaged Cook's and Crawford's companies, numbering about 100 men, drove them and killed 4 and wounded 6 of the enemy." The battalion itself lost "1 private killed, Captain Quin and Lieutenant Spiva and 6 privates wounded, and 3 men missing."

Nothing in them names Gilliam Graves or Benjamin Hulsey. They show the war they were in: a cavalry that was short of arms and horses, scouting the hills it came from, with soldiers' wives sheltered in river towns and bushwhackers threatening to burn out Union households. Deserters were a constant trouble for the regiment; in the fall a scout at Helena arrested one Company I man at his home. Gilliam's own absence from 12 October to 25 December 1864 fits that same autumn, but the reason for it is not recorded.

quotes.t: to secure all guerrillas and bushwhackers who may fall in their way
quotes.c: Order for a scout to Hot Springs County, 11 April 1864

stories.title: "Starved to death at Andersonville": the Company F monument, 1893
stories.hook: Daniel O'Neal's company raised its own limestone shaft at Oakland City and carved on it the names of eleven men who died as prisoners.

subject.name: Company F, 42nd Indiana: the eleven who starved at Andersonville

body: The monument stands on a small triangle of ground beside the railroad in Oakland City. A 1913 booklet says it was put up by the surviving members of Company F, 42nd Indiana, "as a loving tribute to the memory of their comrades who gave up their lives in defense of the flag." It was built in the summer of 1893 and dedicated that September, with an address by Capt. A. J. McCutchan of Company A.

A committee of Col. W. M. Cockrum, John W. Corder, James T. Bell, John P. Simpson and Washington Strickland raised the money, and Cockrum deeded the lot to the county. The contract went to William Kelley of Oakland City for nearly $1,000. The shaft is of oolitic limestone, twenty-eight feet tall, with a carved soldier on top. "On the several sides of the dies are the names of all the original members of the company and the recruits, 143 in number." That should include Daniel W. O'Neal, who is on the company roll, though no one has confirmed his name on the stone.

On one side is a scroll reading "Starved to death at Andersonville," and beneath it eleven names: Chesterfield P. Dill, Alford Farmer, J. M. Hunter, H. H. Hunter, John H. Martin, Adam Canon, Wm. A. Reavis, W. W. Oliver, A. H. Mariner, Jacob Strickland and A. C. Coleman. The booklet adds: "These all were taken prisoners at the battle of Chickamauga and died at Andersonville." Most can be matched on the company roll, though spelled a little differently: Christfield P. Dill, Alfred Farmer, Henry H. Hunter, Adam Cannon, William A. Revis, William W. Oliver, Adolphus H. Marriner and Andrew C. Coleman.

The shaft also lists the company's battles: Perryville, Stone's River, Stevenson, Flint River, Chickamauga, Lookout Mountain, Mission Ridge, Ringgold, Buzzard Roost, Big Shanty, Snake Creek Gap, Chattahoochee River and Bentonville. Whether Daniel was present for all of them or left in March 1862 is the open question about his service; the men who built this stone, his neighbors from the same few townships, would have known.

quotes.t: Starved to death at Andersonville.
quotes.c: Inscription on the Company F monument, Oakland City, 1893

stories.title: William Thomas Camp, hanged at Princeton, 22 November 1872
stories.hook: A murder over a $75 note ended with Gibson County's first execution, while Daniel and Vashti O'Neal were raising their young family in the county.

subject.name: The first legal hanging in Gibson County

body: An 1884 county history calls it "the first legal execution in this county." William Thomas Camp and J. R. Bilderback, both of Pike County, walked and rode to Haubstadt on 31 July 1871 and, finding no lodging, lay down to sleep in a piece of woods near the village. Camp had picked up a hickory club to use as a cane. As Bilderback slept "with his head on the roots of a tree," Camp "struck him on the head several times and killed him."

"There had been no grudge or quarrel between them, but the motive for the crime was shown by the larceny of a note for seventy-five dollars which Bilderback held on Camp." Camp threw the body into a fallen treetop, took some of the dead man's clothes and rode his horse to New Harmony, where the dead man's brother William had him arrested. Back at Haubstadt he showed where the body lay; a coroner's jury found it "horribly mangled by hogs," and Camp confessed under oath.

Jailed at Princeton, he escaped before trial and hid near his mother's home, was later picked up in Kentucky for horse-stealing and jailed at Owensboro, and was brought back. He was convicted of first-degree murder in July 1872 and sentenced to hang on 4 October. Gov. Baker gave him a respite until Friday, 22 November 1872, "when, at 2 o'clock p.m. of that day, he was executed by Sheriff F. W. Hauss." His lawyers were Col. Charles Denby, who had left the 42nd Indiana to become colonel of another regiment, and C. A. Buskirk.

Daniel O'Neal's household was then on its farm in Columbia Township, with Parsis (born 1868) a small child; the case was the talk of the county but is a place story, not a family one. No O'Neal is named in the account.

quotes.t: There had been no grudge or quarrel between them, but the motive for the crime was shown by the larceny of a note for seventy-five dollars.
quotes.c: History of Gibson County, 1884

stories.title: A Sunday-evening cyclone, 27 February 1876
stories.hook: The worst storm in Gibson County history took the roof off a church at "church time" and carried a house thirteen feet.
body: An 1884 county history says that "on Sunday evening, Feb. 27, 1876, the most severe cyclone which ever passed over Gibson County struck Princeton." It came from the southwest and "destroyed almost the entire southern part of Princeton, doing damage to the extent of over fifty thousand dollars." It "happened about church time and few of the people were at their homes." The roof and steeple of the C. P. Church were taken off.

The Sutton family's two-story frame house was "large," "comparatively new." "The wind lifted the house and it came down over the fence, distant thirteen feet from the foundation," breaking it "into three parts, one part going north, another east and another west." Ten persons were inside, "Mrs. Sutton and seven children, a son-in-law and his children." A two-year-old was found "hanging by its hands to a rafter on top of the fallen house"; a nine-year-old blown out of an upstairs window walked about four hundred feet to a neighbor's door and knocked, "remarking 'his house was blowed.'" Eight of the family were found huddled in a space about ten feet square, saved by a bureau, and "crawled out" through a hole sixteen inches across.

Parsis O'Neal, Katie Stevenson's mother, had been born at Princeton in 1868, and the family's farm was in Columbia Township a few miles south. No O'Neal is mentioned in connection with the storm; it is told here as the county's worst disaster of the years they lived there.

quotes.t: It happened about church time and few of the people were at their homes.
quotes.c: History of Gibson County, 1884

src: History of Gibson County, Indiana (Chicago, 1884), chapter on climate and natural events ("Cyclones") (archive.org, historyofgibsonc0000jast).
stories.note: The O'Neal link to this storm is by place only. The text says the storm "passed out northeast of Oakland" in the OCR, which may be misread.
stories.place: Princeton, Gibson County, Indiana

stories.title: A Stevenson cousin in the 32nd Tennessee, 1862-1865
stories.hook: While Daniel O'Neal wore Union blue in Indiana, a first cousin of his future son-in-law wore Confederate gray from Giles County.
body: In 1886 Coleman L. Stevenson was described as "a first-class farmer and stock-raiser" of the Ninth Civil District of Giles County, born 26 December 1832. He was the eldest son of William P. Stevenson, a brother of Rev. Abner A. Stevenson, and so a first cousin of Frank Stevenson.

It says: "In 1862 Mr. Stevenson enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers, and served until the close of the war. He participated in most of the principal battles, and was a brave and gallant soldier." The 32nd was a Confederate regiment. His family was large: two wives, who were sisters (Louisa and Dorcas Jackson), his own children, and "three orphan children to raise," Martha V., Nancy M. and Mary J. Jackson, daughters of his wife's dead brother and sister-in-law.

The same sketch gives the family's own roll of Rev. Elam Stevenson's children, and records that William P. "has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel." Coleman held 265 acres at home and 400 more elsewhere in Giles County in 1886, was a Democrat, and belonged, like his uncles, to the Methodist Episcopal Church South.
The Stevensons were Giles County people, and Frank's O'Neal in-laws were Indiana Unionists, so the two sides of the family met only after the war, in Frank's marriage to Parsis O'Neal.

quotes.t: In 1862 Mr. Stevenson enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers, and served until the close of the war.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee, 1886

src: Goodspeed Publishing Co., History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County Biographical Appendix, sketch of Coleman L. Stevenson, p. 871-872 (archive.org, historyoftenness00good).
stories.note: Goodspeed does not say the 32nd was Confederate; that is from the regiment itself. Whether Abner or his own sons served is not known.
stories.place: Ninth District, Giles County, Tennessee

stories.title: "I saw him die, and closed his eyes": Elam Stevenson and Philip Bruce
stories.hook: The old itinerant whose books Elam hauled in his wagon died among the Stevensons' neighbors, and Elam shaved and shrouded him.
body: In 1869 Elam Stevenson, then 81 and housebound, dictated to the Methodist historian John B. McFerrin his memories of the preacher Philip Bruce, who came to Giles County in 1813 and "made our neighborhood his home." Bruce, in Elam's telling, was a Virginia Conference man who never married, who had once been offered a rich young Charleston woman's plantation and declined it ("he thought she had about money enough to send him to ruin"), and who after his health failed lived with his brother Joel and taught a day school for the neighborhood's children, giving to the poor every dollar the Conference sent him.

Elam was at the deathbed. "I saw him die, and closed his eyes, shaved him, and assisted in shrouding him. His death was calm and peaceful; there was not a struggle nor a groan. He did not move a muscle, only a slight quiver of the upper lip when the last breath left the body." A few days earlier the circuit preacher had preached to him: "It was a high day with him. He was very happy, and spoke in raptures of heaven." Bruce died in May 1825.

He was buried in the country graveyard "about two miles distant from our church (Bee Spring), by the side of his sainted mother and two of his brothers." His stone, Elam says, was put up by the Virginia Conference and reads: "To the memory of the Rev. Philip Bruce, an itinerant Methodist preacher nearly fifty years. He was born December 25, 1765, and died May, 1825. He loved God and the souls of mankind, many of whom became seals to his ministry."

The same letter records the cost of the Civil War to Elam's church. The first Methodist church in Giles County, Rehoboth, was replaced "by a large frame-church, which was destroyed by the Federal soldiers during the late war." It also tells of Meshach Boyce's son William, who "went to Arkansas at an early day as a missionary, and was drowned in a small stream, the second year of his labors."

quotes.t: I saw him die, and closed his eyes, shaved him, and assisted in shrouding him.
quotes.c: Rev. Elam Stevenson, 1869

quotes.t: a large frame-church, which was destroyed by the Federal soldiers during the late war
quotes.c: Rev. Elam Stevenson on Rehoboth church, 1869

src: John B. McFerrin, History of Methodism in Tennessee, vol. 2 (Nashville, 1871), pp. 180-190, letter of Rev. Elam Stephenson, Elkton, 28 July 1869 (archive.org, historymethodis00mcfegoog).
stories.note: McFerrin prints the name as Stephenson. Page numbers are approximate from the OCR text (182-183 for the Bruce passage).
stories.place: Bee Spring, Giles County, Tennessee

stories.title: Seventeen Hulsey households in Hall County, 1830
stories.hook: In 1830 Hall County had seventeen Hulsey households; Salathiel’s relationship to the others remains unknown.

subject.name: The Hulsey cluster of Hall County, Georgia

body: In 1830 Hall County, Georgia, a county formed in 1818 from the Cherokee cession, had seventeen households headed by a Hulsey, among them Charles, Adler Jr., Joel, Elija, Demsey, William, Sarah, Pleasant, James, Adler Sr., Armistead, Hiram, Micajah, Jesse, Salathiel, Charles F. and Vincent. The 1832 Cherokee land lottery also carried Hall County names: “Charles Hulsy” and “Alder Halsey, Jr.” of Hamilton’s District, and “Pleasant T. Hulsey” and “James Halsey,” a soldier, of Dobbs’s District. Earlier, on 31 October 1820, Franklin County, Georgia, taxed James Hulsey Sr., Joel Hulsey and Pleasant Hulsey. None of these has been tied to Salathiel.

The senior line runs: Charles Hulsey and his wife Hannah, married about 1752, lived in Pittsylvania County, Virginia, in the 1770s, near the North Carolina line, then in Greenville County, South Carolina. A Greenville deed of 1792 names their sons "James, Charles, Jesse, Adonijah and Adler." The article says the family name was spelled "interchangeably Huddlesy, Hulsey, Huldsey."

A Georgia memoir gives the family’s origin. The sketch of Col. William Hulsey, born in DeKalb County on 1 October 1839, says: “JENNINGS HULSEY, native of Virginia, immigrated to South Carolina with his parents while he was a child. Came to Georgia, married REBECCA PATE” and died in DeKalb County, and adds: “The pioneer Hulsey from England.” So the best account of the surname is Virginia, then the South Carolina upcountry, then north Georgia, a path that matches the Hulseys of Franklin and Hall counties. Salathiel named a son Jennings, which may be a clue to a connection and is no more than that; the memoir’s Jennings is the grandfather of a DeKalb County man, not a proven ancestor.

Where Salathiel fits is unknown. Some family trees give him a father Jesse Hamilton Hulsey and a mother Mary Tharp, but nothing supports it; the Hall County Jesse of 1830, and the Jesse among Charles's sons, are both possible fathers by name alone. Salathiel was born about 1807 in Georgia, which puts a South Carolina-born parent in Hall County at the right time.

In 1850 Hall County still held a Charles Hulsey, 55, farmer, real estate $2,000, born in South Carolina, with Hannah, 52, also born in South Carolina, and a widow, Sally Hulsey, 33, with children. None of this ties to Salathiel, but it is the neighborhood he came from.

Arkansas came next. In 1860 a Georgia-born Robert Hulsey, 27, with no middle initial, lived in Hempstead County, Arkansas, with Sarah A., 20, and an infant son whose name is read as Selatha G.; the handwriting is uncertain. This may be Salathiel’s son Robert, but the link is not proved. Benjamin F. Hulsey, then 16 or 17 though he swore he was eighteen, is on the roster of Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry, a Union regiment raised in Montgomery County in the winter of 1863-64; so was Gilliam Graves, the grandfather of the woman George Washington Hulsey, probably Benjamin’s son, would marry in 1901. Montgomery County had been organized on 9 December 1842, and a history of the Ozark region says its settlers “came into the valleys of Montgomery in the thirties.”

stories.title: The 4th Arkansas Cavalry: Union men from the Ouachita hills
stories.hook: A Union regiment raised in Arkansas included Gilliam Graves and soldiers named Benjamin F. Hulsey and Calvin V. Moffitt.
body: The 4th Regiment Arkansas Volunteer Cavalry (Union) was organized at Little Rock in December 1863 and mustered out on 30 June 1865. Its companies were raised among Arkansas Unionists. Company D was recruited in Montgomery County in the winter of 1863–64, and on 14 January 1864 Gilliam Graves volunteered at Cedar Glades, at 45, a farmer, five feet ten inches tall with black eyes. The roster of the same company has a private "Hulsey, Benjamin F." A Calvin V. Moffitt also served in Company L, but whether he was the son of Nathan Moffitt is uncertain.

The regiment's actions read like a calendar of small, hard marches. A skirmish on the Saline River on 15 February 1864. A move to Cedar Glade on 1 March, which is also listed as a skirmish that day (no report was filed). A scout from Little Rock to Benton on 27–31 March, led by Capt. E. H. Vance, who arrested three women hauling cotton for guerrillas and wrote that "the bushwhackers made a desperate rally to get the captured wagon and their fair friends, but they failed to get either." Mount Elba on 30 March. Then the Camden expedition of April 1864, which took in Jenkins' Ferry. In mid-May the regiment was at Dardanelle, and from 25 September to 13 October it took part in an expedition from Little Rock to Fort Smith.

The regiment's own story had darker edges. Union men in Montgomery County were hunted by neighbors, and the March 1864 petition from Company L names a wife and child shot and a doctor killed at Cedar Glades. In September 1864 a detachment out of Helena went looking for "deserters from the Fourth Arkansas Cavalry" and took one, Benjamin Davis of Company I. Gilliam Graves's own roll entry reads that he "deserted on 12 October 1864 and returned on 25 December 1864." No reason is given, and nothing places Company D on any particular march that month.

In November 1864, Maj. Harris S. Greeno led 130 men of the regiment out of Devall's Bluff, where the regiment had its cavalry depot, toward Batesville and Searcy and reported that Price's army had been "badly whipped at every point." The regiment finished the war at Little Rock, scouting to the Saline River and Bayou Metoe in April and May 1865, and was mustered out on 30 June.

stories.title: Buck Horn, March 1864
stories.hook: Two Union reports name Buck Horn: one orders cavalry to "kill, capture, and destroy" a camp there, the other says the farmers wanted "peace on any terms."
body: Buck Horn, in what is now Stone County, Arkansas, is the old settlement near St. James where Henry and Hannah Moffitt's son Tom was born in 1889. Twenty-five years earlier it appears twice in the Union record of the war. On 12 March 1864 the district headquarters at Batesville wrote to Lt. Col. William Baumer, First Nebraska Cavalry, to take men across White River at Ramsay's Ferry and go to Round Bottom, near Sylamore, for forage, protecting the steam transport Miller. The order goes on: "You will endeavor to hunt up the enemy reported to be in camp at McDermott's, near Buck Horn, and kill, capture, and destroy them."

The order shows the care its writer thought necessary. Baumer was to recapture any mules taken from the Union train that he found with local people, "leaving the women and children of the family undisturbed and in possession of their household goods and such work-cattle as they need to cultivate their farms." He was told to be "kind and courteous in your dealings with the defenseless citizens," to give receipts for everything he took, and to "prevent your men from entering houses, pillaging, or burning any houses or fence rails." "Incendiarism or unnecessary severity," the order says, "you are strictly charged to prevent."

A week later Maj. Lewis C. Pace of the Eleventh Missouri Cavalry reported from Batesville on a seven-day scout of 206 miles (15–21 March 1864) after a Confederate force under Rutherford. On the last day he marched "down the river through Buck Horn. Here I could gain no information of Rutherford." His men were out of rations and many horses barefooted. He added a note on the country that fits the hills the Moffitts later farmed: "a rough, rocky, and mountainous country, destitute of forage excepting in the valleys and coves of the mountains," where "the farmers generally are busily engaged preparing their ground for planting, and express a great desire for peace on any terms."
These are two glimpses, not the story of a battle. The county's bloodiest fight of the war came at Buck Horn in May 1864, when Jo Shelby's Confederates attacked a band of bushwhackers.

stories.title: The runner's morning: Company D at St. Etienne
stories.hook: Edmond Tims's company got lost in the French sector that day, but his battalion lost its commander and half its runners to a single shell.
body: The 36th Division's history, printed in 1920, describes the morning of 8 October 1918 from the front. The 142d Infantry was ordered forward at 5:15 a.m. to take the village of St. Etienne-a-Arnes, in Champagne, after the Marines in the 2d Division had taken the ridge. The Second Battalion jumped off from Hill 140 and went through machine-gun fire. The First Battalion, Companies A through D, followed in support. Companies A and B were in the first wave and C and D in the second.

To reach the jumping-off place, the history says, the men of the First Battalion had to pass "in squad columns, or single file, through the trees down the northern slope of Blanc Mont and through the barrage placed by the enemy's batteries to cut off the supporting troops from the fight." They suffered heavy casualties from shell fire and lost their commanding officer, Capt. Charles Kuhlman: "The burst of a shell wounded half of the battalion headquarters group, including several runners." Edmond Tims was a company runner, and a company runner's job was to carry messages between the company and the battalion.

Company D's morning went wrong in a different way. "In this advance the men of Company D failed to follow the wake of Company B and wandered into the French sector to the left, where they remained through the balance of the day." Captain Kuhlman was so badly hurt that his loss "did not become known to his company commanders until the middle of the afternoon." The high-explosive shells were mixed with gas, and many gas casualties followed later in the day. Company B, whose wake Company D had been told to follow, lost its first lieutenant, Arthur J. Matheny, "killed instantly just after he had crossed the last belt of wire," and the second lieutenant, Thomas F. Collins; "more than thirty men in Company B had been killed and more than fifty wounded."

The honor roll at the back of the book lists "TIMS, EDMOND, Private, Co. D," with the date 8 October 1918. The regiment's own report, written in January 1919, says a fellow runner spoke to him at 8 a.m. on the 9th and found him killed an hour later. The two dates are a day apart and both fall inside the 142d's fighting at St. Etienne. Before the war he had served in Company L of the First Oklahoma Infantry, the National Guard regiment that the history says was assembled at Fort Sill in the spring of 1917, after months of border duty the year before.

stories.title: The camp where George Hulsey was working when the influenza came
stories.hook: George W. Hulsey signed his draft card on 12 September 1918 as a laborer at Camp Pike, and eleven days later the camp's base hospital admitted 214 influenza cases in a day.
body: On 12 September 1918 George Washington Hulsey, 42, filled out his draft card at Story in Montgomery County. It gave his employer as the Stewart-McGehee Construction Company at Camp Pike, the Army training camp near Little Rock. The camp had been established on 18 July 1917 and was the mobilization point for the 87th Division.

The Army's medical commission that studied pneumonia and influenza in the camps reached Camp Pike on 5 September 1918. Its report says the camp's death rate from lobar pneumonia, over its whole history, was third among the 32 camps in the country, and from bronchopneumonia fourth. The report adds that "beginning September 1 there had been a gradual increase of the number of patients admitted with the diagnosis of acute bronchitis." On 23 September, 214 cases of influenza were admitted to the base hospital in a single day, and that is the day the commission dates the epidemic.

"The epidemic was at its height from September 27 to October 3, during which period there were in the neighborhood of 1,000 new cases daily." By 31 October it was over, and a second, milder wave came at the end of November. Counting from 1 September to 31 October, the commission recorded 12,393 men reporting sick with influenza and 1,499 cases of pneumonia, with 466 deaths. These are figures for soldiers; the report says nothing about the civilian construction crews working on the camp.
Nothing says whether George Hulsey was working at Camp Pike during those weeks, or whether he was ill. By 1920 he was a tenant farmer in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma.

quotes.t: The epidemic was at its height from September 27 to October 3, during which period there were in the neighborhood of 1,000 new cases daily.

stories.title: Four registration days and the men who signed
stories.hook: On 5 June 1917, 12 September 1918, 16 October 1940 and 27 April 1942, the family's men lined up to give a clerk their name, age and employer.
body: The first World War registration was on 5 June 1917 for men aged 21 to 30. Grady Moffitt was 25, a timberman at Ervin, Oklahoma, married and supporting his wife, his mother and a child; he was tall and stout, with gray eyes and dark hair. Robert Pisachubbe, 28, farmed for himself at Speer, black eyes, black hair, medium height, slender. By age Joel Thompson (b. 29 January 1892), Peter P. Thompson (b. about 1896), Wavey Lincoln Satterfield (b. 28 December 1895, at Morgantown, Kentucky) and Edmond Tims (b. about 1893) all fell into the same registration. Nothing shows that Joel or Peter was inducted. Wavey served as a private in the Army, and Edmond served first in Company L, First Oklahoma Infantry.

The third and widest registration, on 12 September 1918, took in men aged 18 through 45. Simon Thompson, 19, signed as a farmer working for his father at Corinne. George Washington Hulsey, 42, signed at Story, Arkansas, as a laborer at Camp Pike. Edmond Tims died on the fields of St. Etienne less than a month later.

The World War II draft began on 16 October 1940 with men aged 21 to 35. Oscar Franklin Hulsey, 29, registered that day at Mount Ida, Montgomery County. When the war began, Congress required all men aged 18 through 64 to register. The fourth registration, on 27 April 1942, was for men 45 to 64, and was nicknamed "The Old Man's Draft." Its purpose was an inventory of skills and available labor; those men were not liable for service. Charles Oscar Smith, 52, signed as "Charlie Oscar Smith" of Forney, Choctaw County, working on a farm, with mail at Hugo Route 1, naming "Mrs. Pearl Smith" as the person who would always know his address. Robert Pisachubbe, 53, signed at Speer, naming his wife Lizzie.

Their sons went in different ways. Dois Moffitt enlisted in the U.S. Navy on 3 September 1942, aged 21, and served as a ship's cook until 27 January 1946. John Winfred Moffitt enlisted on 17 December 1943, at 18, and served on the floating drydock ARD-19 and the minesweeper USS Chief. No service dates are known for their older brothers Alvin and Odis, or for the Hulsey brothers of Oscar's generation.

stories.title: James Satterfield's second family
stories.hook: After Melissa died in 1877 James H. Satterfield married a 21-year-old neighbor and had nine more children, most of whom ended up around Texarkana.

subject.name: Lucinda Belle (Phelps) Satterfield and her nine children

body: Lucinda Belle Phelps was born on 30 May 1857 in Butler County, a daughter of Solomon Phelps and Sarah J. (Deweese). She married James H. Satterfield on 2 June 1878, a year after Melissa Gibson's death. They had nine children: Martha Belle (born Nov 1879), Alonzo Thomas (1882), Minnie E. (1884), Joe Griffin (1886), Laura E. (1887), Charles J. (1890), George Franklin (1892), Grover C. (1894) and Effie J. (1899). Lucinda died on 5 June 1917.

By 1909 the grown children were marrying in Bowie County, Texas, or across the Arkansas line: Charles J. to Alma Morgan on 5 December 1909; Alonzo to Zoda Mae Slader Reed in September 1914; Grover to Norah Walker on 28 May 1917 at Maud; Joe Griffin to Lennia Champion on 11 November 1917; George to Eula Viola Martin on 2 September 1917 at Hatfield, Polk County, Arkansas. Laura married a Douglas Henry and died in October 1975.
Minnie E. is said to have married a "(?) Smith." That could be a coincidence of a common name, and nothing links her husband to Charles Oscar Smith's family.

James himself died in Bowie County on 28 November 1922 (another account says 24 November 1922 or 1924) and is buried at Reed Cemetery. His 1885 biography already credits him with 1,340 acres in Butler County and another 425 acres in Tennessee.

Three of Lucinda's sons left fuller records. Alonzo Thomas, born 6 June 1882 in Butler County and one of the three children named in his father's 1885 biography, married Zoda Mae Slader Reed in Bowie County, Texas, in September 1914 and died there on 18 December 1950. George Franklin, born at Brooklyn on 10 May 1892, married Eula Viola Martin at Hatfield, Polk County, Arkansas, on 2 September 1917, served in World War I (his stone reads “ARKANSAS CPL CO E 3 TRAINING REGT WORLD WAR I”), and died at Texarkana on 4 January 1958; he is buried at Odd Fellows Cemetery, Lockesburg, Arkansas. Grover Cleveland, born 5 April 1894, married Norah Walker at Maud, Bowie County, on 28 May 1917 and died at Maud on 13 December 1966.

stories.title: The widower Samantha married in 1917
stories.hook: Samantha Satterfield's second husband was a 59-year-old widower whose first wife was part Choctaw and who went back to Texas after Samantha died.
body: Billy Alexander "Bird" Stephens (Bird Alexander "Alex" Stephens in the family's other records) was born on 16 February 1858 in Tennessee, a son of Calaway "Cal" Stephens (1824-1863) and Sarah Ann Little (1822-1913). He was the youngest of six children.

He is said to have married Martha Adeline Liles (born 1861) in Newton County, Arkansas, on 28 March 1878, and she was said to be one-quarter Choctaw. She died in 1916 and is buried at Old Saltillo Cemetery in Hopkins County, Texas. They had eight children, of whom seven are known: John Harvey, Nancy Ann (Brown), Mary Adeline (Simmons), Joseph Carroll, Wiley Alexander, Francis Henry and Tomie Delmane, who died at 10 in 1907.

On 28 July 1917 at Mount Vernon, Franklin County, the 59-year-old widower married 45-year-old Mrs. M. D. Satterfield. They moved to Oaks Township, Choctaw County, and were there in the 1920 census. After Samantha died in October 1928 he went back to Titus County, Texas, and died at Mount Pleasant on 23 January 1944. He is buried at Bridges Chapel Cemetery.

The Choctaw claim finds no support in the enrollment of the Choctaw Nation: no Martha Adeline, no Bird or Alexander Stephens, and no Liles appears among those enrolled. The one-quarter Choctaw statement stays a family tradition.

stories.title: The Clarks of Brooklyn, Kentucky
stories.hook: Newton’s 1850 household includes Polly; Melvina’s death record names her parents as Newton Clark and Mary Dunn.

subject.name: Newton Jasper Clark & Polly Clark (maiden name unresolved)

body: Newton Jasper Clark was born on 6 August 1817 and died on 3 April 1878 in Butler County. His parents are said to be William Clark (1785-1856), born in Granville County, North Carolina, and Levina Willis (1785-1877). William is credited with service in the War of 1812; that is not checked.

Newton Clark and Polly D. Elms took out a license on 20 January 1839. William Anderson joined them in marriage on 24 January and signed the return on 25 January. These are three different events; the 20 January date repeated in family accounts is the license date.

Polly’s age was proved by Moses Elms and Newton’s age was sworn to; neither age in years is given, and how Moses was related to Polly is not stated. At her death in 1929 Melvina’s parents were given as Newton Clark and Mary Dunn. The marriage gives the bride’s name as Polly D. Elms but does not reconcile Dunn and Elms or establish an earlier marriage. That the bride was the Polly in Newton’s 1850 household and Melvina’s mother remains probable.

Family memorials place Newton’s burial at Newton Clark Cemetery, Brooklyn, and give Polly’s death as 16 February 1888 and burial at Clark Cemetery, Morgantown. They link Martha J., Stanford C., Beverly L. "Belva" and Melvina as children. These family links are not independently proved, since the 1850 household states no relationships; Stanford’s age of 8 in 1850 also conflicts with the later 1844 birth date attributed to him.

Newton's stone at the Newton Clark Cemetery near Brooklyn, in Butler County, reads: "Newton Clark was born August the 6 1817 d[ie]d April the 3 1878." Polly's grave in the Clark Cemetery at Morgantown is marked by an uncut fieldstone with no legible inscription, so her death date of 16 February 1888 rests on family accounts rather than on the stone.

Three of the Clark children left records of their own. Martha J., the eldest, born 1 February 1839, married James P. Johnson; their children included Eliza “Ancie,” who married a Satterfield. James died in 1884 and Martha lived on as a widow for 39 years, dying in Butler County on 13 February 1923; both are buried at Satterfield Cemetery near Jetson. Stanford C., born 6 June 1844, served as a private in Troop A of the 12th Kentucky Cavalry, a Union regiment, as his headstone at Belmont General Baptist Church Cemetery, Morgantown, says, and a Stanford Clark is listed as a Union private in Company A of the 12th Kentucky Cavalry. He married Serenia Hunt in 1867 and died on 12 June 1913. Beverly L. “Belva,” born 2 October 1850, married Margaret Ann Coots in 1877, raised eight children mostly in Kentucky, and went west: he died at Cushing, Payne County, Oklahoma, on 18 February 1939 and is buried at Fairlawn Cemetery there.

stories.title: Samantha's brother who stayed
stories.hook: Samantha went to Texas and Oklahoma; her brother Charlie lived and died within a few miles of where they were born.
body: Charlie Johnson was born on 27 April 1885 at Brooklyn in Butler County, a son of Melvina Clark Johnson, 13 years after his sister Samantha. He died on 14 February 1959 at Welchs Creek, Butler County, and is buried at Clark Cemetery, Morgantown, with his mother's Clark family.

He had two wives. The first was Martha Alice Satterfield (27 August 1886 - 22 July 1918), buried at Clark Cemetery; she died at Riverside, Warren County, aged 31. The second was Pernie Brooks (1905-1944). Eight children included Carlie, Cooper F., James Wallace, Artie Mae Roberts, Cevil, Golda Marie Hunt, Chester and Cova Myrl Felty.
Martha Alice's parents are not named, so whether she belonged to the same Satterfield family as her husband's brother-in-law John C. is unknown.

Martha Alice died at Riverside, Warren County, at four in the afternoon on 22 July 1918, of a cancer she had carried for a year; a Bowling Green doctor had attended her since early June. She was a housewife, born in Butler County, and Charlie, as C. C. Johnson of Butler, gave the particulars for her certificate: her father as Jas. Satterfield, his birthplace first written “Minn.” and then “don't know,” and her mother as Adder Johnson of Butler County. She was buried the next day.

Those particulars and her gravestone disagree in three places. Her age at death puts her birth on 27 August 1884, not 1886. Her burial was at Cedar Grove in Butler County, not Clark Cemetery. And a father called James Satterfield fits the Butler County family of James H. Satterfield, who had lived in Minnesota from 1867 to 1875, yet no Martha Alice is known among his children. Her place in that family is still open.

stories.title: Where Hagansport buried its dead
stories.hook: The cemetery where John B. Smith and Emma Langley lie holds about 250 graves, begun in the 1880s.
body: A county history describes the cemetery: "Hagansport Cemetery is in the Hagansport Community and has around 250 graves. Burials probably started in the 1880's. The people of the community had probably used the Pierces Chapel Cemetery previous to the start of Hagansport Cemetery."

The earliest marked grave is Laura Terry's, born 13 June 1870 and died 13 October 1876. Smaller family burying places nearby, now lost, include the Cannon cemetery two miles south of Hagansport and the Singleton cemetery two miles northeast, where "there were once about ten wooden stakes marking gravesites."

Emma Langley Smith, who died on 15 March 1905, and John B. Smith, who died in 1918 and whose grave was marked with a wooden stob, were buried here. Some of John B. and Emma's children also grew up here: Charles Oscar Smith and his sisters Vera, Luina, Lona and Allie and brother Jimmie are the children recorded in 1900.

stories.title: A Butler County burying ground with the family's name
stories.hook: At least five of the Satterfield and Johnson kin are buried at Satterfield Cemetery near Jetson, Kentucky.
body: Satterfield Cemetery lies at Jetson, Butler County. Among those buried there are Sidney Rufus Satterfield (1865-1949), his wife Eliza "Ancie" Johnson (1871-1951), their infant Walter (1890), Ancie's father James P. Johnson (1840-1884) and her mother Martha J. Clark Johnson (1839-1923).

The cemetery is the burial place of those who stayed. John C. and Samantha moved to Texas about 1907; Sidney and Ancie stayed on the farm country of Butler and Warren counties, and Sidney died at Richardsville, Warren County, in 1949.
The Satterfields buried here are the sons and daughters of James H. Satterfield, who farmed in Butler County from 1876 and, by his own 1885 account, owned 1,340 acres there.

stories.title: Buried among the missionaries at Wheelock
stories.hook: Oscar Hulsey's funeral in 1982 was held at a mission graveyard where stones from the 1850s still stand.
body: Wheelock was a Presbyterian mission to the Choctaws. Its church was organized in December 1832 by Rev. Alfred Wright, who removed to the Choctaws' new land in October 1832, and the buildings stood about two miles northeast of the later town of Millerton. A 1914 book on the neighborhood says what remained: 'the two mission school buildings, a strongly built stone church 30 by 50 feet, a two story parsonage and cemetery.'

The same book copies one stone from the graveyard: 'Sacred to the memory of the Rev. Alfred Wright who entered into his heavenly rest March 31, 1853, age 65 years. Born in Columbia, Connecticut, March 1, 1788. Appointed Missionary to the Choctaws 1820. Removed to this land October, 1832. Organized Wheelock Church December, 1832. Received to its fellowship 570 members.' In 1947 the Oklahoma Historical Society's journal listed Wheelock among the state's 'historic old cemeteries ... that offer much fine material.'

Oscar Franklin Hulsey died at his home at Holly Creek on 17 June 1982, at 71. His funeral was held at 2 p.m. at Wheelock Cemetery with Rev. Bob Lewis officiating. He was laid there in a graveyard where, a teacher at the mission school wrote of a three-year-old's burial there in the 1890s, the child was placed 'beside missionaries who had passed away half a century before.'
His former wife Katie is buried at Mount Olivet in Hugo.

stories.title: Two Stevenson stones in Block 2
stories.hook: Frank and Parsis Stevenson lie side by side at Hugo's Mount Olivet, with one birth year on a stone listing that cannot be right.
body: Mount Olivet is Hugo's old municipal cemetery. It was 'Originally called Burgoyne Cemetery' and dates to 1907, 'very nearly to the town's beginning.' It is better known as the home of Showmen's Rest, the circus performers' section dedicated in 1961, with its granite dancing elephant at the entrance.

A listing of Block 2 made in 2000 reads: 'Stevenson  Frank N.  1860  1950' and 'Stevenson  Parsis Jane  1887  1956.' These are stones for Gilbert Franklin 'Frank' Stevenson, who died at Hugo on 9 May 1950, and for his wife Parsis Jane.

Two points need care. The listing gives Frank's birth as 1860, while his family record and a photograph of his stone have 17 November 1861; his 1870 and 1880 census ages fit 1861 or 1862, and the middle initial N is not in his known name. Parsis Jane's death year, 1956, matches the family record, but a birth in 1887 is impossible for the mother of children born from 1884; a photograph of her stone reads 1868, so the listed 1887 is a misreading or comes from another marker. It gives no inscriptions beyond names and years.
Their daughter Katie Cornelia Hulsey died on 30 January 2009, with burial at Mount Olivet. That is nine years after the listing, so her stone is not in it.

stories.hook: The cemetery list confirms the dates of Grady, Mary and three of the boys they buried.

subject.name: Shoat Springs Cemetery: the Moffitt graves

body: Five Moffitt entries stand in a row at Shoat Springs: 'Moffitt, Dois L. -- Feb 16, 1921 - Aug 25, 1947; OK SC1C USNR WWII', 'Moffitt, Jimmie Gaynell -- Jan 17, 1923 - Oct 26, 1926', 'Moffitt, Henry Wayne -- Jan 13, 1934 - May 12, 1937', and 'Moffitt, Woodford Grady -- Nov 6, 1891 - Jun 21, 1972; Mary Tinsley -- Jun 4, 1895 - Aug 26, 1962.'

These match the dates already in the family record. Dois's date of 25 August 1947 is the date on his Texas death record, four days after the Red River accident of 21 August. The rating on his stone, SC1C, is Ship's Cook First Class in the U.S. Naval Reserve, the job he held through the war.
Jimmie Gaynell and Henry Wayne were each three; their parents joined them in 1962 and 1972. The cemetery lies in the community of Hugo.
Only names and dates are recorded, with no epitaphs.

stories.title: The meeting ground where the Chamness stone stands
stories.hook: Anthony Chamness has a 1975 memorial in the Cane Creek cemetery, placed by descendants, not a stone of his own day.
body: On 14 February 1764 William Marshall transferred 26 acres on Cane Creek, next to Simon Dixon's mill dam, to the trustees Peter Stout, Jeremiah Piggott, Benjamin Piggott and David Vestal 'for the use and benefit of Cane Creek Meeting.' The account adds: 'This is the property where the Meeting House and burial grounds are presently located.' A separate Marshall account says William and Rebecca Marshall gave the 26 acres and the house on it.

Of Anthony Chamness it is said: 'In 1975 friends and family erected a large stone in the Cane Creek Meeting's cemetery to commemorate these early pioneers and their devoted service to the Cane Creek congregation.' It dates him 'circa 1713-1777,' says he and Sarah Cole 'were among the first overseers of the Cane Creek Meeting,' and notes that his will was made on 24 November 1776. 'Chamness descendants still come yearly to stroll between the quiet graves.'
The same book says British troops took over the meeting-house during the Revolution and 'some English soldiers are buried in the cemetery.'

The memorial stone is a modern commemoration. It is not said where Anthony, Sarah, William Moffitt or Mary Davies lie, and Quaker burials of that time were commonly unmarked, so those graves remain unlocated.

stories.title: A small graveyard with four Hulsey stones
stories.hook: Both Benjamin and George Washington Hulsey are said to rest at Breashears, but no list names them.
body: Breashears Cemetery lies east of the Montgomery County town of Story, in a field off a gravel road, 'fenced, with a bench under the shade of an old tree.' It has been transcribed at least three times, most recently with 139 names, and an earlier count recorded 117 names and 106 unmarked graves.

The stones are counted by surname: 'Breashears (15), ... Holmes (7), Hulsey (4), ... Kilby (10), Lamb (12), Lenderman (9) ...,' with the majority belonging to eight families. The Hulsey stones are not itemized.

Rev. George Washington Hulsey (d. 5 August 1935, age 58) and Benjamin Franklin Hulsey (d. 16 December 1924), whom family accounts make his father, are the two Hulseys the family has placed here. The four-stone count is consistent with that, but nothing confirms either name. Other burials listed there show the kind of neighbors who surround them: Rev. H. H. Holmes (July 2, 1863 - May 15, 1935, 'The Lord is my shepherd'), M. R. Lenderman (1858-1935) and Gertrude A. Breashears (1881-1952, 'Mother is Resting').
No church is named for the cemetery.

stories.title: What is left of Bee Spring is the graveyard
stories.hook: The church where Elam Stevenson preached for decades was blown down in 1909; by 1956 only the cemetery survived, neglected.
body: The Methodist history of middle Tennessee says the original Bee Spring church 'was organized in 1815 by Rev. Elam Stevenson,' son of a Revolutionary captain (a rank the militia record does not support), who 'professed religion in 1804,' united with the church in 1806, was licensed to preach in 1813 and 'the same year moved to Tennessee.' The first house was logs; a larger log church followed in 1822 or 1823, and a frame church in 1855 whose building committee included J. G. Stevenson. Its members were 'largely the families of the McClaurines, Loyds, McGuires, Sherrills, Moseleys, Bruces, Rowes, and Stevensons.'

Elam's own 1869 account mentions the church-yard: Rev. Meshach Boyce, who helped build the first house, 'died in the faith, and his dust now sleeps in our church-yard at Bee Spring.' A visitor in 1878 wrote that 'here repose the sacred dust of old Father Stevenson and his beloved consort.' Elam had bought the fifteen acres for the church for $20 in 1815.

'On the night of April 29, 1909, the Bee Springs Memorial Methodist Church was totally destroyed by the memorable and terrible tornado which passed through this section of Giles and Lincoln Counties.' The congregation rebuilt at Bryson, three miles away. Of the old site the 1956 history says: 'All that remains of this today is the cemetery, sadly neglected.'

About seventy-five Stevenson graves are listed for Bee Spring. The tall stone over Elam and Lydia reads, on Elam’s side, “Erected to the memory of Reverend Elam Stevenson, born September 24, 1787, died March 13, 1875. Nearly 62 years a minister of the gospel. He was pure in heart and life.” On the back: “Erected to the memory of Lydia Stevenson, born August 16, 1787, died March 6, 1872. Nearly 70 years a Methodist. She consecrated her household to God and the church.”

Some years were hard. In the summer of 1854 Citty died on 20 June, Elam R. on 2 August and William B. F. on 19 August. In the winter of 1856 Louisa (Coleman’s young wife) died on 1 February, Joseph J. on 15 February, Ann Eliza on 2 March and James Elisha on 3 March. An “infant” is dated 6 October 1831 (the first child of William and Malinda), and several more are listed only as “child” or “infant.” No causes of death are given, and which Stevenson household each child belonged to is not always known.

Elam’s sons and their wives lie near him. Rev. Abner A. Stevenson (d. 1896) is listed with his wife Martha S. (Still Watson, 1823-1887, who died on 12 July 1887); his brother Rev. James C. (23 June 1813 to 23 February 1899) lies beside Margaret Caroline (8 December 1816 to 11 February 1886); Willis McKendree is there (18 January 1818 to 6 February 1900), as are Coleman L. (1832-1908), with Dorcas (1832-1892), and Thomas C. (1825-1906). The congregation buried a Stevenson as late as 1994.

stories.title: Hugh Moffitt plans a move west
stories.hook: In 1799 Hugh prepared to leave North Carolina with his family; a later family account says he died near Chillicothe, Ohio.
body: The Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt says "William and Hugh married Davis daughters of North Carolina," and the 1928 Moffitt Genealogy names the wives as Mary and Hannah. In an 1853 letter, Joseph Moffitt named his father Hugh, mother Hannah Davis, and Hugh's brother William. Joseph also said Hannah's sister Mary married a Moffitt; identifying that man as the William in our Randolph County line remains an inference.

A transcribed will dated 1 October 1799 identifies Hugh Moffit of Chatham County, names his wife Hannah and son Joseph, and says he had disposed of his affairs in order to move with his family to the Northwest Territory. It also names six of the brothers Joseph later listed in his letter. These overlapping details strongly support identifying the will and letter with the same Hugh, though neither the will nor the letter has been seen in the original.

Family tradition, set down later in a Bible, has Hugh going to Ohio in 1798 or 1799 and dying near Chillicothe about 1800. The 1799 will supports an intended move and is consistent with a departure later that year, but makes a definite 1798 departure doubtful. Neither the will nor Joseph's letter establishes that Hugh completed the journey or died in Ohio; those details rest on family tradition.

In 1798 Westfield Monthly Meeting in Guilford County sought advice on members moving to the Scioto River, and Cane Creek certificates to Ohio began in 1804. This is context for movement west, but it does not name Hugh or establish his route.

The 1853 letter and the will identify the same immediate family, but the original documents and an Ohio death or burial record have not been seen. The connection to William Moffitt and Mary Davies is supported by family testimony and later genealogy, but remains a lead.

stories.title: Silas Moffitt's wagon: Randolph County to Hamilton County, October 1823
stories.hook: A first cousin of our Robert Moffitt rode ahead to Indiana in 1822, built a cabin, and brought his wife and two children north in a single wagon in the fall of 1823.
body: Silas Moffitt (1794-1873) was the son of Charles Moffitt, one of William Moffitt's brothers, and Mary Cox; our Robert Moffitt was William's son, so the two were first cousins. Silas married Hannah Wilkinson (1799-1886) in Randolph County, North Carolina, on 4 May 1820. Hannah was the daughter of William Wilkinson, an Englishman, and Mary Moffitt, William Moffitt's daughter, who married on the 26th day of the 3rd month, 1795 by the family's account. That makes Hannah Robert's niece, and Silas her first cousin once removed.

The 1928 genealogy says the son-in-law and father-in-law "both seemed to think the Northwest Territory offered them better opportunities, so two years after the wedding they started for Indiana on horseback in quest of their future homes." The land "was bought direct from the government, and so far as is known, most of it was bought in Wilkinson's name." They built "rude cabins" and went back for the families. Wilkinson, "unable to return the following year," died in Carolina before he could make the trip, and his family left soon after.

Silas and Hannah, "with their two children Mary and Charles, along with another family whose names have been lost, made the trip in the early fall and reached the site of their future home on the 8th day of the golden month of October, 1823." A county history says: "The family made the trip from North Carolina with a four-horse team and all their possessions in one wagon." Their eldest son Charles W. was born in North Carolina only weeks before they started.

They lived in the log cabin for three years. Then Silas built a brick house out of brick he made himself, the second brick house in the township. When he died on 28 August 1873, nearly 79 and a few weeks short of fifty years on the place, he owned several hundred acres and had served as county commissioner and for two terms as treasurer of the township trustees. It was said that he "lived and labored for half a century on the old Moffitt homestead." He and Hannah are buried in Carmel Cemetery. The Wilkinsons owned land, slaves and a tan yard, and the family left a slaveholding county for a free state, the same road hundreds of Carolina Quaker families took.

stories.title: Two Quaker families, one road: Davies and Norton to Cane Creek
stories.hook: A Welsh-named indentured servant and an Irish Quaker's son took the same Pennsylvania-Virginia-Carolina road, twelve years apart.

subject.name: Charles and Hannah (Matson) Davies; Edward and Elizabeth (Brown) Norton

body: Charles Davies and Hannah Matson were married in the twelfth month (February) of 1732/3 under a Radnor Monthly Meeting certificate, which places the wedding at the house of Charles Read, a Philadelphia justice of the peace. Charles Davies was an immigrant to Pennsylvania about 1725, and from there went to North Carolina. Hannah was "daughter of John Matson of Merion"; the family's own note in the back of the Cane Creek minute book says Charles "was brought over the ocean and sold to pay his passage." The Davies surname, with its alternate spelling Davis, is Welsh, and Radnor and Merion were Welsh townships in the Quaker settlement west of Philadelphia.

From Pennsylvania the couple went to Virginia. A certificate "having been made for Charles Davis and Hannah, his wife to Hopewell Monthly Meeting" is minuted, but the early Hopewell minutes were burned, so the exact year of the move is lost. Charles and Hannah were charter members of Cane Creek Monthly Meeting and moved "in or before 1750." Cane Creek was set up in the tenth month of 1751; Orange County, in which the land fell, was cut from Johnston, Bladen and Granville in 1752. Charles bought 187 acres from Henry McCullogh on 2 August 1758 and died in 1801.

Edward Norton's son, also Edward, was the other traveler. His 1739 marriage at West Nottingham Meeting names his father as "Edward Norton, dec., of the County & Parish of Armagh, in the Kingdome of Ireland." The Nortons are said to have moved to Hopewell in Virginia, then to Fairfax, and reached Cane Creek in 1762, the year before their daughter Margaret married Joseph Chamness. A Quaker historian describes exactly this stream: in 1754, the first year of New Garden Monthly Meeting, "we have settlers coming in from Pennsylvania, from Hopewell and Fairfax meetings, Virginia," and concludes that "the large settlement of Friends in Alamance, Chatham, Guilford, Randolph and Surry counties was formed by Quaker immigrants, not by the expansion of the native element."

Those two sentences are the family's story in small. The Davieses reached Cane Creek about 1750, the Chamnesses in 1749-51, and the Nortons in 1762. By 1763 the three families met at the meetinghouse for two weddings, sixteen days apart: Joseph Chamness and Margaret Norton on 17 March, William Moffitt and Mary Davies on 2 April.

stories.title: Those who left and those who stayed: Aden Nordyke, Sicily Shaw and Parses
stories.hook: Aden Nordyke died in Indiana in 1842, while his daughter Sicily and her husband Noble Shaw stayed in Guilford County; Parses Shaw turns up in Gibson County in 1839.

subject.name: Aden Nordyke, Sicily (Nordyke) Shaw and Parses (Shaw) O'Neal

body: Aden Nordyke was born in Burlington County, New Jersey, in 1762, and came south with his parents. In the twelfth month of 1787 Deep River Monthly Meeting recorded the marriage intention of Adin Nordyke and Martha, and their daughter "Sicily b. 8-2-1790" is the first among their children. Aden's brother Micajah went to Ohio in 1805; Aden went on to Indiana, where he is said to have died on 9 May 1842.

Sicily stayed. She married Noble Shaw, a member of Dover Monthly Meeting in Guilford County, and lived there until her death in 1861; their family register, Noble's death in 1855 and the 1857 sale of his farm are told in Noble Shaw's story. Seventy-one Friends took certificates from Dover Monthly Meeting between 1816 and 1860, "nearly all" of them to Indiana; the Shaws were among the Friends who watched neighbors go and stayed behind.

Parses is the loose end. An 1884 county history calls Mrs. Parsis Watt "a native of Lawrenceburg, Ohio," who "came to this county in 1839." Lawrenceburg, on the Ohio River near the mouth of the Great Miami, is in Dearborn County, Indiana, in the heart of the White Water country where the Carolina Quakers headed. Parses was about 28 when she and Archibald O'Neal, a Tennessean, came to Gibson County; their son Daniel had been born in Tennessee in October 1838. Archibald died there on 25 April 1841 and she married the County Down Irishman Hugh Watt.

Whether Parses was a child of Noble and Sicily Shaw is not proven. The Dover register has a Parris who lived a year in 1817-18, and Parses, born about 1811, would have to be an earlier child missing from the page. The simplest reading is that her people belonged to the Shaw families who moved from North Carolina to the Ohio-Indiana line; no record names her parents.

stories.title: Four families, two states and one county line: the Satterfield road
stories.hook: From a Carolina Piedmont county to Warren County, Kentucky, with a detour through Tennessee and a widow of 77 who moved to Missouri.

subject.name: The Satterfields and Garrisons: North Carolina to Kentucky to Texas

body: John Satterfield was born about 1766 in Orange County, North Carolina, a county that had been formed in 1752 and has since been divided until the part he came from is Person County. He lived in South Carolina and settled in Warren County, Kentucky, where his will was proved on 10 November 1847 and names thirteen children, among them Ephraim. His son Ephraim, whom his grandson called "a native of Virginia," married Ruth Knowles in Warren County on 12 November 1809. Ruth was born in Virginia about 1783; her father Joshua Knowles, born about 1747, was in Warren County in 1830, and his will of 11 November 1824 names a son John "of Franklin County, Virginia," and a daughter "Ruth Saterfield."

The second generation shows a Tennessee stop. Ephraim's grandson James said Ephraim's son Henry Satterfield was "a native of Maury County, Tenn.; died in 1861, at the age of fifty years," so, if Henry is Ephraim and Ruth's son, as family accounts have it, they were in Maury County about 1811, two years after their marriage. At the same moment another future ancestor was passing the same way: J. M. Garrison married Patsey Cannon, born in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, at Wilson County, Tennessee, on 6 December 1809, and the couple settled in Warren County, Kentucky. In 1815 Allen County was cut from Warren and Barren, and the Garrisons found themselves in a new county. Their daughter Mary, born 17 October 1811, married Henry Satterfield. The Kentucky General Assembly dissolved the Garrisons' marriage by an act of its 1847-48 session, approved on 29 February 1848.

Ephraim died about 1850. His widow Ruth was in Allen County in 1850 with her daughter Elizabeth and in 1860, at about 77, in Gasconade County, Missouri, with Elizabeth and her husband Jesse Agee. She died there in 1864, a long way from Warren County.

Henry and Mary's son James H. Satterfield was born in Allen County on 14 April 1838 and married Melissa Gibson there on 17 September 1859. In 1867 he moved to Dakota County, Minnesota; in 1875 he returned to Kentucky and settled in Warren County, and in 1876 in Butler County, a county created on 18 January 1810 from Logan and Ohio. By 1885 he held 1,340 acres there and 425 acres in Tennessee. Melissa died in 1877, and in 1878 he married Lucinda Belle Phelps in Butler County. He died in Bowie County, Texas, in November 1922 (the 24th or the 28th in different records). His son John C., born in 1864, farmed at Horse Mill in Butler County in 1900. About 1907 the family left for Franklin County, Texas; John died there between 1912 and 1916, and in 1917 his widow Samantha crossed the Red River into Choctaw County, Oklahoma. Their daughter Artie Pearl, born at Morgantown in Butler County on 13 August 1898, married Charles Oscar Smith in 1915.

stories.title: Three Arkansas counties and a Red River crossing: the Moffitt road west
stories.hook: The Moffitts did not come to Arkansas by way of Alabama; they came straight from the North Carolina Quaker country, and left it by the timber trade.
body: The family's Alabama link is a marriage, not a route. Nathan H. Moffitt, born in 1814 in Randolph County, North Carolina, a son of Robert Moffitt and Martha Chamness, grew up in the Centre meeting community; the North Carolina Manumission Society counted sixty-five members in its Centre branch in April 1819, and a New Garden member recalled that the little anti-slavery band there "continued to meet at New Garden until the majority of the members emigrated to the west, preferring to live in a free state." Nathan's own children's birthplaces tell the route: North Carolina up to about 1842, Arkansas from about 1843. In 1850 he was farming in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County. The mother county of northeast Arkansas, Lawrence was created in 1815.

His son Henry, born there in August 1855, was farming in Janes Creek Township, Randolph County, in June 1880, with his wife Hannah and two small children. By 1889 the family was in Stone County, where Tom was born at St. James. Stone County was brand new: a history of the region says it "is one of the new divisions" organized "April 21, 1873," with Mountain View the county seat, and it counted 5,089 inhabitants in 1880 and 7,043 in 1890. Henry's youngest son Grady was born there on 6 November 1891, and Henry died at Mountain View in 1901 at 46.

Grady left the Ozarks in the timber trade. In June 1917 he was a timberman for C. D. Neese at Ervin, Oklahoma, a sawmill town that existed from 1904 to 1922; in 1920 he was a tenant farmer in Wilson Township, Choctaw County. He had married Mary Tinsley Shackleford about 1914, and her people had themselves moved west, from Gilbert in Etowah County, Alabama, in 1900, to Martin County, Texas, by 1930. So Alabama enters the Moffitt line through Mary, whose parents were at Gilbert in 1900 and at Stanton, Texas, in 1930. In 1930 Grady, Mary and their six sons were living with her parents. By 1940 they rented a house at 411 North H Street in Hugo, in the Choctaw Nation, where Grady had been out of work for 50 weeks.

So a family that left Randolph County, North Carolina, for Arkansas in the early 1840s, and Arkansas for Oklahoma in the 1910s, finished its western moves a few miles from the Red River and the old Doaksville road, a few miles from where the Tims family had traded at Doaksville since the 1830s.

stories.title: With 'the first group of exiles': what the winter of 1831-32 was like
stories.hook: The Pisachubbes told their newspaper that they came west with the first group of exiles in 1832 and settled at Fort Coffee. The official record of that first winter, and of Fort Coffee, sets the story's dates.

subject.name: Joseph Pisachubbe's family and the first Choctaw exiles

body: When William Harrison Pisachubbe died in May 1937, the Hugo Daily News printed a family history from his relative Judge T. W. Hunter: the Pisachubbes "came from Mississippi with the first group of Choctaw exiles in 1832 and settled at Fort Coffee," near present-day Spiro. William Harrison and Robert were the sons of Joseph Pisachubbe, who is known only as a dead father. No roll of the removal names him.

The record of the first removal fills in what that sentence meant. Major Francis W. Armstrong took the Choctaw census in the summer of 1831 and counted about 18,880 Choctaws. By the first week of November, an Oklahoma history says, "four thousand Choctaws, some in wagons, some on horseback, some on foot, were on their way to the Mississippi River": five hundred went north to Memphis and took steamboats for Arkansas Post, the rest to Vicksburg. A "fierce winter storm" followed. Between 26 November and 8 December about 2,500 were landed at Arkansas Post. "Few blankets and moccasins or shoes were seen among them; the women generally were barefoot and the young children naked, especially those from the extreme southern part of the nation in Mississippi." There were only forty government wagons for the 350 miles to the Kiamichi country, and the roads were frozen. More than a thousand others went by the Red and Ouachita rivers to Ecore de Fabre. The last parties of 1831 reached the Red River region "during the first week in March, 1832"; on 30 April 1832 Lieutenant Stephenson recorded 3,749 rations being issued at four stations on the Red River, and 536 near the Choctaw Agency by Fort Smith.

The ration was the one Doak & Tims would later be paid for. It was "one and a half pounds of beef or pork, one pint of corn, or an equivalent of corn-meal or flour, with two quarts of salt to the hundred rations," with the corn raised to a quart a day in the fall of 1831.

A family that came "in 1832" is therefore either from the last of the 1831 parties, the winter exiles, or from the 1832-33 removals that the War Department reorganized in May 1832. Fort Coffee, however, was not there to settle at. The garrison at Fort Smith was moved twelve miles up the Arkansas to a new post called Fort Coffee only in June 1834, and the post was abandoned on 27 July 1838. The family's 1937 words most likely name the neighborhood where they put down roots by the agency and the later fort and Skullyville, not a place that existed in 1832. By 1899 the sons were in Kiamitia County, well over a hundred miles south, where Eunice Gardner Pisachubbe and her boys were enrolled at Goodland.

stories.title: Doaksville before the store: 1833 in the removal papers
stories.hook: A Choctaw district's letter of February 1833 complains of white traders in 'a small town below Kiametia' and names Doaksville as the place where annuities were received.
body: Doak & Tims is usually dated by its contracts of 1838-39. The removal correspondence puts Doaksville on the map five years earlier. A letter dated at Horn Prairie on Red River on 6 February 1833 is signed by the treaty captains of Nittuckachee's district. They write that their people "are entirely satisfied with our new country" and ask that their annuity be delivered at Horn Prairie, because "at Doaksville, where we have generally received our arms and articles mentioned in the treaty, our horses have suffered much, as there is no winter range." There was a complaint too: "We have to inform you that we have too many white traders in our country, we wish you to have them removed. ... They have built a small town below Kiametia, consisting of white traders, with the exception of two." They would not object to "a few traders ... but we do not wish to be crowded."

The same volumes carry a smaller clue to the man the town was named for. In the account of Lieutenant J. R. Stephenson, the officer in charge of the subsistence depot at Fort Towson, a line lists Josiah S. Doak with "28 lbs. bacon and 4 lbs. sugar," for the first and third quarters of 1833. What Doak was paid for is unclear, but it shows a Josiah S. Doak dealing with the removal's quartermasters on the Red River in the year of the letter.

Vincent B. Tims was a witness, with Doak, to the Treaty of Doaksville on 17 January 1837 and was feeding Chickasaw emigrants under contract by 1 January 1838, at thirteen cents a ration. His partnership with Doak was dissolved in 1844. A New Orleans advertisement of 10 December 1845 lists references that begin with "Maj. Wm. Armstrong, Choctaw A[gency]" and include "Doak & Tims, Doaksville, C. Nation." Armstrong was the Choctaw agent, and his brother Francis had taken the 1831 census and run the removal; by 1845 the agent himself stood as a reference for the firm. The Doak & Tims Mercantile Company is counted among the stores of Doaksville, with a blacksmith shop and a hotel.

Nothing puts Tims himself at Doaksville in 1833. Family accounts say he was born in South Carolina in 1803 and had a Choctaw wife; his earliest record at Doaksville is the January 1837 treaty. The 1833 letter shows what he walked into: a Red River town already built by white traders, already resented by the Choctaw districts around it, and already the place the government's goods and annuities were handed out.

stories.title: Peter Gaunt, who knew no visible worship in the world
stories.hook: Called before the Plymouth court in 1655 for staying away from church, Peter Gaunt of Sandwich said he knew no public visible worship in the world, and was fined in cattle for the Quaker meetings that followed.
body: Peter Gaunt settled at Sandwich on Cape Cod, in Plymouth Colony, with his wife Lydia, whose surname is unknown. One proposed identification links him to a Peter baptized at St Peter at Gowts, Lincoln, on 29 June 1610, son of Thomas Gaunt and Susan Bate. That identification remains unproved. Thomas and Susan married at Rotherham on 28 August 1609, and Susan's will calls Peter her only son.

The colony’s court books follow Peter Gaunt for six years. At the court of 6 March 1654/5 he was called in "to answare for neglecting to frequent the publick worship of God." Asked to speak to the charge, "Peter Gaunt affirmed hee knew noc publicke vizable worship now in the world, whereunto the said Ralph Allen assented, but Gorg Allen dissented; the case was left to further consideration." Within three years the same court was fining him for Quaker meetings.

On 2 March 1657/8 Gaunt, Daniel Wing, Ralph Allen Jr. and William Allin were summoned "for a tumultuose carriage att a meeting of the Quakers att Sandwich." The court cleared them of that charge, "notwithstanding, for theire vnreuerent carrying themselues before the Court, coming in before them with theire hatts on," it fined each of them twenty shillings. Thomas Butler, whose daughter Dorothy would marry Peter's son Hananiah in 1678, was summoned for the same disturbance and was "admonished and cleared."

The fines were collected in cattle. In June 1660 a note was entered in the court's record that Marshal George Barlow "tooke from Goodman Gaunt, for his fine of 24li, these particulares: seauen cowes & heifers, two steers, seauen bushells and an halfe of pease; and after, when one of the cowes died, hee tooke another liue one in stead therof, because Barlow had not the hide of the dead cow deliuered to him." Thomas Burgis Jr. owned in open court that he had made the report, and was himself fined thirty shillings for refusing to help the marshal. A Quaker list of goods taken from Plymouth Colony Friends about 1658 includes "Peter Gaunt 43 l. 14 s. 6 d."

The summonses kept coming. In October 1660 a long list of people "fined for being att Quakers meetings," ten shillings each, includes "Peter Gaunt, Dorithy Butler, Obadiah Butler." In February 1660/1 the Sandwich constable was ordered to bring Gaunt and nine others to Plymouth "to answare for theire tumultuouse carriages against the marshall and cunstable of Sandwich in the execution of theire offices in the cecuring of two Strang Quakers." A ten-shilling fine on Gaunt "was leuied vpon a mistake" and was given back. In 1661 a list given into the court of those who had sheltered visiting Friends reads: "Wiliam Allin entertained Christopher Holder. Wiliam Newland entertained one forraigne Quaker. Peter Gaunt entertained two forraigne Quakers."

Peter’s death is dated to 10 May 1678, the day of his son Hananiah’s marriage to Dorothy Butler, but that is unconfirmed. Lydia died in April 1692. Their sons included Israel and Hananiah, who went to New Jersey. A Lydia Gaunt named in a 1661 court case involving Thomas Burgis Jr. may or may not have been Peter’s wife.
