stories.title: The Butlers of Sandwich and the marshal
stories.hook: Thomas and Dorothy Butler were fined in cattle and money for Quaker meetings; their son Daniel was publicly whipped in June 1660.
body: Thomas Butler was at Sandwich, Plymouth Colony, soon after the town was founded in 1637. In March 1657/8 he was summoned with Peter Gaunt and others over a Quaker meeting and "admonished and cleared." In 1658-9 he was fined ten shillings "for refusing to assist the marshall, Barlow, in the execution of his office," and the court assigned another fine, fifty shillings for refusing to serve as constable, to Barlow himself.

In June 1660 the court passed two sentences on the family: "Daniell Butler, for rescuing a Strang Quaker, when apprehended by the marshall, Barlow, and for his breakeing away when taken p'soner, is sentanced to bee publickly whipt, which accordingly was pformed." The next reads: "Thomas Butler, and Dorithy, his wife, for turbulent cariages the same night that theire son Daniell was serched for att theire house, fined forty shillings." In October 1660 Dorothy Butler, almost certainly the mother, was fined ten shillings for being at Quaker meetings.
The court later returned twenty shillings taken from Thomas for his wife and son attending a Quaker meeting. Its October list also names Obadiah Butler among those fined.

Thomas was also a land-hunter. In 1665 the court sent Richard Bourne and William Bassett "to view and purchase some lands desired by Edmond Freeman and Thomas Butler lying towards Saconeesett," and when the Indians would not part with that parcel it gave them leave to buy other land for him. In 1667 the court granted Butler "a necke of land called Tassacausett, lying neare to Edmond Freemans land," which he had "bought ... of an Indian called Charles, alias Pampmumitt, for a yoake of oxen," provided the Indian returned three pounds to Butler.

Dorothy died on 9 August 1675 and was buried the next day. Thomas died on 12 March 1690. Their daughter Dorothy, born 23 January 1649/50, married Hananiah Gaunt at the Quaker meeting at Sandwich in 1678, and they carried the Quaker family to New Jersey. Thomas's origin and Dorothy's maiden name are not known.

stories.title: Thirty-five head of cattle: Sandwich in December 1658
stories.hook: A magistrate's letter to a friend in London, printed by Joseph Besse, describes the town where the Gaunts and Butlers lived as nearly all Quaker and being stripped of its cows.
body: In December 1658 J. Cudworth (James Cudworth of Scituate), a Plymouth Colony magistrate who had lost his seat on the bench and his militia captaincy for "entertaining some of the Quakers at my House," wrote to a friend in London. The letter was printed in a Quaker history of sufferings. Of Sandwich, Cudworth said: "almost the whole Town of Sandwich is adhering towards them: And give me leave a little to acquaint you with their Sufferings, which is grievous unto, and saddens the Hearts of most of the precious Saints of God."

He described the method. The Quakers would not swear, so the old law that every man take the oath of fidelity was revived: refuse it and pay five pounds or leave the colony. "When the Time is come, they are the same as they were; then goes out the Marshal, and fetches their Cows and other Cattle ... On this Account thirty five Head of Cattle, as I have been credibly informed, have been, by the Authority of our Court, taken from them the latter Part of this Summer." Some families had one cow, some two, "and many small Children in their Families, to whom, in Summer-time, a Cow or two was the greatest outward Comfort they had for their Subsistence."

A poor weaver with seven or eight small children, lame himself, had two cows, and both were taken. "The Marshal asked him, What he would do, he must have his Cows? The Man said, That God that gave him them, he doubted not, but would still provide for him." The court then fixed fines for the meetings themselves, ten shillings a meeting, which Cudworth reckoned at one hundred and fifty pounds for Sandwich men, "Newland ... for himself and his Wife" being twenty-four of it and the weaver twenty.

The town was watched. "Sandwich Men may not go to the Bay, lest they be taken up for Quakers," Cudworth wrote, and a man who went on business was put in prison for twenty-four hours while witnesses were sent for. By the colony's newest law, anyone who entertained a Quaker "if but a Quarter of an Hour" forfeited five pounds. The letter is followed by a list of other people whose goods were taken at about the same time, for refusing to swear or for absence from public worship. It includes "Peter Gaunt 43 l. 14 s. 6 d.," and the whole list amounts, it says, to about six hundred and sixty pounds.

Peter Gaunt's goods and the Butler family's fines are in the colony's own court books. Twenty years later Peter's son Hananiah and Thomas Butler's daughter Dorothy were married at the Sandwich Friends meeting, and within a few years they left for New Jersey.

stories.title: A "madman" at the table: William Dewsbury and Richard Browne
stories.hook: The Nottingham Friends' family memorandum says our Browne ancestor became a Quaker when William Dewsbury shared his table, and that his landlord then made him pay his rent twice.
body: In 1786 East Nottingham Monthly Meeting entered into its book of births and burials an account of the English father of William Brown the emigrant, written down from the stories of a great-nephew of William's in his eightieth year. It places the father in "Puddington" near Wellingborough, today's Podington, and says he had been "some time in communion with the Baptists, afterwards joining with the sect called Puritans, and is said to have been a teacher among both, and a seeking, religious man." The memorandum calls him William, but the Wellingborough Quaker registers give the father's name as Richard. Other register transcriptions describe Richard as of Boasworth, so the family's English home is given two ways.

The story is that William Dewsbury, "about the first going forth" of that minister, came to the town, and the man noticed "the solidity of his countenance" and asked him in to "break bread." When they sat down the host said grace. Dewsbury sat in a grave manner and answered, "if thou wilt first partake with me I shall be free to partake with thee." After a short silence he was moved to speak, "beginning with these words, 'O Earth! Earth! hear the word of the Lord,'" and the host was convinced. When he came home with Dewsbury his wife asked why he had brought "that madman" to their house. "Why woman," he answered, "he hath brought the Eternal Truth of God to us." She thought it over and was convinced too.

The cost came quickly. The landlord, "a wild airy man and given to sporting," sent his tenant two young hounds to feed and raise. The tenant would not, and the landlord waited. Rent had been paid every half year to a steward without a receipt, so the landlord demanded it again, and said, "except you will take your oath that it is paid, you shall pay it to me." Browne held that Christ had forbidden swearing, so "this Friend had to pay his rent over again," and was then turned off the farm. It took him a considerable time to find another, where he did well. Dewsbury came back, the memorandum adds, and Browne got him leave to speak in the parish church, where "many people were convinced."

Richard died about 1664 by the memorandum's reckoning (a Quaker burial record in the registers gives 1662), and on his deathbed told his wife, "thou shalt live to bring up all our children, and they shall be blessed and be all favoured to keep their habitations in the Truth." The memorandum makes William, born about 1656 in its reckoning, the youngest of nine, six other sons and two daughters. The original Wellingborough register instead gives his birth as the twenty-ninth day of the first month 1658 and names his father Richard; it does not name his mother. The same pages say that when Penn's province was proposed, some Friends doubted whether to go, and Dewsbury, preaching among the Brownes in Northamptonshire, told them: "The Lord is about to plant the wilderness of America with a choice vine or noble seed which shall grow and flourish."

A Quaker history of sufferings records a meeting at Findon where Daniel Brown and Joane Brown, both "of Puddington in Bedfordshire," were taken with some forty other Friends, held overnight in an alehouse, fined forty shillings each, and sent with the rest to the county gaol for six weeks. Nothing in either source ties them to Richard, and the match rests only on the village name, so it remains a possibility.

stories.title: Lots 23 and 33: William Brown on the Nottingham Lots
stories.hook: William Brown is said to have cut the first tree on the Nottingham Lots in 1701; the plat gives him Lots 23 and 33 and his sons the lots beside them, and the first meeting was held in his house.
body: Before Nottingham there was Marcus Hook. William Brown came over about 1682 or 1683 with a first wife, Dorothy, who “could not give up to it cheerfully.” The Nottingham memorandum says he felt a clear sense of duty and that “the Lord wonderfully made way for and assisted him,” and adds that on the voyage his wife died at sea. (The memorandum dates his landing “about the year 1696,” which is wrong.) Their son Joseph had been born in England on 12 June 1682. William went first to his older brother James, a weaver, who was already at Marcus Hook on the Delaware. James had been in Pennsylvania before Penn’s grant, so it is reckoned. He married Honor Clayton, whose father William Clayton came in 1677, and on the 20th of the 12th month 1683 (February 1683/4 in modern reckoning) he took a patent for 115 acres on Chichester Creek, which he named “Podington” after the home village. He conveyed it to his son William in 1706.

About 1692 George Keith, once a leader among Friends, split the Quakers of the Delaware. At Chichester meeting Keith “spake or preached largely, using some arrogant and lofty expressions, beyond the simplicity of the gospel.” James Brown, “having at first a favourable opinion of Keith,” asked his brother afterwards “what he thought of George Keith now; was not he satisfied?” William, “a deep feeling man,” answered, “I am satisfied, but it is in this, that he is in a wrong spirit.” James took it badly and started to leave. William stepped after him and asked whether he remembered “how they used to feel at their meetings when in England, though they were but as lads,” and went on: “In this country we have come under a different dispensation ... We have been looking out and allowed to provide towards an outward inheritance, and settlements for ourselves and families, free from disturbance or persecution; but let us remember that the truth is still as precious as ever.”

The next day Keith held a meeting at the house of Henry Reynolds and called at James’s door on the way. James hesitated; Keith got down from his horse and went in, saying that if James was growing dissatisfied he would satisfy him, but “though he used many words, all did not avail, for James went not to meeting.” James later settled in the same neighborhood at Nottingham and died about 1715, “a religious man and of a good character, but not favoured with a capacity or talent equal to his brother William.” William’s son Richard married Hannah Reynolds of Chichester in 1717.

The Nottingham Lots were thirty-seven rectangular lots of Penn's land laid out in 1701-02 on the border with Maryland. A 1902 history of the Brick Meeting House at Calvert, Maryland, says "all agree that William Brown was the first Friend to settle on the Nottingham lots." The family memorandum says he moved his family there in 1702, "accounted far back in the wilderness." The bicentennial history adds a tradition that Penn himself rode out in the early spring of 1701 with a party that included William Brown, James Brown, John Churchman, Edward Beeson and Henry Reynolds, and that in the fall the two Brown brothers went to the site on pack horses from New Castle to clear ground for corn.

The plat as the history gives it assigns "No. 23 to William Brown" and "No. 33 to William Brown," with "No. 14 to James Brown" and Nos. 26 and 27 to James, and "No. 28 to Messer Brown." Messer is William's son Mercer, born in February 1685/6, whose first name was his mother Ann Mercer's maiden name; the history prints it as Messer, as it was commonly written. William's lot was beside a spring about a mile east of the present Rising Sun, near the road to the Brick Meeting House.

Tradition, "which is now upon record," says William "was the first to take his axe in hand and strike it into a tree, one of the monarchs of the forest," and said, "In humble trust we commence our labor." The spring is said to have been an Indian camping ground on the trail from Pennington to the mouth of the Susquehanna, which an old resident, Jesse Pugh, remembered tracing as a boy.

The records are firmer about the meeting. At Concord Monthly Meeting in the 2nd month of 1705, "two Friends of Nottingham desires on behalf of the rest a First Day meeting at the house of William Brown, and a Fourth Day meeting once a month," and Concord Quarterly Meeting on 9 April 1705 "approves of until further order." The first brick meetinghouse followed in 1724. Penn's spoken gift of forty acres for a meetinghouse, burial ground and school in 1701 was the only title Friends had until 1765, when his sons Thomas and Richard Penn issued a patent to William Brown, Timothy Kirk, William Churchman and Benjamin Chandlee in trust.

William Brown the emigrant died, by the family memorandum, on the 23rd of the 6th month 1746 (23 August), "in the 91st year of his age," having lived at Nottingham about 44 years "in good repute for his integrity; being an elder in the Church, and a substantial Friend." Ninety-one would put his birth near 1655; the Wellingborough register gives 1658. Another account gives his death as 1 October 1746; the memorandum’s 23 August (Old Style) is the date written down by the family. His great-nephew and namesake William Brown, a minister, traveled in Europe with John Churchman from 1750 to 1754 and was the man in whose eightieth year the memorandum was written down.

stories.title: Three cows, two mares and 500 acres: Thomas and Agnes Croasdale on the Neshaminy
stories.hook: Two inventories preserve a family’s Pennsylvania household: livestock, bedding, tools and a 500-acre holding on Neshaminy Creek.
body: Thomas Croasdale of New Hay, Yorkshire, married Agnes Hawthornthwaite of Wyresdale on 1 May 1664. The marriage was recorded by Lancaster Monthly Meeting. Eighteen years later, the couple prepared to leave England with six children. The certificate issued at Settle on 7 June 1682 names the whole household, placing their move within a group of Quaker families rather than an isolated voyage.

Before leaving, Thomas arranged to buy land in Pennsylvania by deeds dated 21 and 22 April 1682. The family history describes a purchase of a thousand acres, but the estate papers later describe a 500-acre holding; in Pennsylvania 500 acres of the purchase were laid out on Neshaminy Creek near the present Langhorne. The records concern different stages of acquiring and settling land; they should not be treated as two measurements of an unchanged farm.

One of those documents survives: the 21 April 1682 indenture from William Penn to Thomas Croasdale, a vellum document with a red seal, signed by both men, at a yearly rent of one peppercorn. It was made before the family crossed the Atlantic.

Thomas died on 2 November 1684, about two years after the move. Agnes became administrator of his estate. On 8 December, James Dillworth and Thomas Constable valued his belongings: clothing, bedding, pewter and brass, cushions, wooden vessels, chests, linen, ironware and hogs. Two mares were worth £8 10s; three cows, a calf and a yearling were valued at £12. The goods totaled £47 9s. The 500 acres were listed but left unvalued.

The inventory of “Agnes Crossdale of Neshaminah Widdowe” was taken by Nicholas Waln, who signed with his mark, and Robert Heaton. It gives the household another outline: brass and pewter, pots, a bed and bedding, a chest, a saddle, hogs, three cows, two bullocks, a heifer, two mares and a colt. This time the land was valued at £50, nearly half the £106 5s total. Small things also survived into the account: a blanket, nails and the tools used around the house and farm, or in its own words, “one Blankit Some nails all the husbandrie Tooles & hustlement about the House.”

Agnes died on 20 October 1686, according to the family account, and sons William and John received administration on 1 November. An inventory is dated the 10th of the 9th month 1685 but registered on the 1st of the 9th month 1686; neither fits a death in October 1686, so one of the years is off. The children’s list names William (born 7 February 1664/5), John, Elizabeth (who died in 1683), Mary, Bridget (30 August 1671) and Alice. Alice married David Potts, and Mary, William Smith. William, who stayed in Bucks County, made his will on the 30th of the 1st month 1715 (30 March), naming his sisters Mary Smith with eight children and Alice Potts with ten. Bridget’s marriage to John Cowgill carries this branch into the Brown, Norton, Chamness and Moffitt families.

In 2022 the National Society of the Colonial Dames of America honored Agnes as an "historic founder" of Pennsylvania on the strength of the 1682 crossing that carried the family to Penn's colony, recalling that nearly a third of the ship's passengers died of smallpox on the fifty-seven days at sea. The honor names the ship as both the Welcome and the Lamb, buries Agnes on 20 October 1684, which cannot stand against her administering Thomas's estate in December of that year, and puts the marriage on 20 May 1664 rather than 1 May.

A later trace of the family’s land survives. In 1728 John Wildman and his wife Mara, the widow of Thomas and Agnes’s son John Croasdale, transferred land in Middletown to a Thomas Croasdale, John's son. He was Bridget’s nephew. A debt involving a Thomas Croasdale and a sheriff’s sale in 1733 may concern the same nephew.

Agnes’s maiden name may link her to a Friend who was jailed. A “William Hathornthwaite” was among forty-three Friends arrested at Swarthmoor in January 1660 for refusing the oath and committed to Lancaster Castle. Nothing ties him to Agnes.

stories.note: Thomas Maxwell Potts’s 1895 book reproduces the inventories and meeting entries; these are printed transcriptions, not images of the original manuscripts. Thomas’s inventory supports his death in 1684 rather than 1682. Agnes’s printed inventory year conflicts with the reported 1686 death and administration. Their own birth dates and parents remain unverified. The ship name is disputed in later accounts. The Swarthmore finding aid describes the 1682 and 1728 documents; their original text has not been independently examined. The 1733 debtor’s identity is not established. The Colonial Dames roll (July 2022) is a derivative biography; it conflicts with the Potts transcriptions on the marriage day (20 May against 1 May 1664), Agnes's burial (20 October 1684 against 1686) and the ship (Welcome against Lamb).
stories.place: From New Hay, Yorkshire, to Neshaminy Creek, Bucks County, Pennsylvania. The Settle certificate of 1682 names Thomas, Agnes and six children.

stories.title: Ellen Cowgill, widow of Giggleswick, and the sons who came as servants
stories.hook: The 1682 Settle certificate calls her "Ellen Cowgill widow & her children"; two of her sons landed in Pennsylvania in service.
body: On 7 June 1682 Settle Monthly Meeting, in the Yorkshire dales, issued a certificate for a party of Friends bound for Pennsylvania. It lists Cuthbert Hayhurst "his wife & family," Thomas Wrigglesworth and Alice, Thomas Walmsley and Elizabeth, Thomas Croasdale "Agness his wife & six children," Thomas Stackhouse and his wife, Nicholas Waln "his wife & three children," William Hayhurst, and "Ellen Cowgill widow & her children." No child is named. Ellen was born near Giggleswick about 1639, so she was about forty-three. Her children appear to have been Edmund, Jennet, John, Jane and probably Ralph, though the certificate does not name them.

Her husband's name is not documented. Many trees name Ralph Cowgill, said to have been hanged in 1682 as a Quaker, but that has no documentation, and some think Edmund Cowgill, baptized in 1634 at Thornton in Craven, more likely. Her maiden name is also disputed: some books give Stackhurst, and several Stackhouse histories say she was not a Stackhouse, so a Thomas Stackhouse of Giggleswick and Anna Evans are not added as her parents.

John, probably about seventeen, came as a servant to Cuthbert Hayhurst. Hayhurst, born at Easington in Yorkshire about 1633, had been among the Friends imprisoned in the West Riding in the 11th month of 1660 for refusing the oath of allegiance. In 1668 he held a meeting at the house of Richard Betteris in Oxford and was arrested while speaking and held for a month by the vice-chancellor. His neighbor Nicholas Waln wrote that "he went through many great exercises and imprisonments." He died in the first month of 1683, only months after landing in Bucks County.

Ralph Cowgill came by a different ship, landing about 28 September 1682. Under Randolph Blackshaw of Hallingee, Cheshire, a list of Bucks County residents prints: "These servants below came in the ship the 'Friend's Adventure.' The Mr., Thomas Wall. Arrived in this river the 28th 7th M., 1682. Servants to Randulph Blackshaw, William Beasy, Ralph Nuttall, and Ralph Cowgill, each to serve 4 years, and to have 50 acres of land apiece." John and Ralph both appear to have been Ellen's children: John, "servant to Cuthbert Hayhurst" and a probable passenger on the Lamb of Liverpool, and Ralph, who came on the Friend's Adventure.

Which ship carried the Settle families has been told two ways. Older family histories say they sailed in Penn's own Welcome, and add that smallpox killed thirty on that ship. A later study says at least four of the seven Settle families sailed on the Lamb of Liverpool, and a Watson family history lists the Lamb, "John Tench, master, from Liverpool," as arriving on 22 October 1682. The party's own certificate does not name a ship.

Ellen settled at Middletown, Bucks County, and is buried in the Middletown Friends cemetery; she died in 1705. John served his time, married Bridget Croasdale at Neshaminy in 1693, and had four children by her before her death in 1701, among them Elizabeth, born in 1694, who married William Brown Jr. John married Rachel Bunting in 1703/4. Jennet married Bernard Lane at Burlington on 2 February 1688. Elizabeth's daughter Elizabeth Brown married Edward Norton, and the line came down through the Nortons and Chamnesses to the Moffitts.

stories.title: Carted through Dover: John Cowgill of Little Creek, 1776
stories.hook: Elizabeth Cowgill's nephew refused Continental paper money on conscience, was declared an enemy to his country by the Kent County Committee in January 1776, and was driven to Dover in a cart with a paper pinned to his back.
body: John Cowgill of Little Creek Hundred was the son of John Cowgill and Lydia Clayton, and the grandson of the tanner John Cowgill of Black Bird's Creek, which makes him a nephew of Elizabeth (Cowgill) Brown, our ancestor. On 4 January 1776 the Committee of Inspection and Observation for Kent County, Caesar Rodney and Thomas Rodney among its members, resolved "that it appears to this Committee, by the confession of John Cowgill, a residenter of Little Creek Hundred, in this County, that he has refused, and, from conscience, shall refuse, to take said Continental money in discharge of debts, or for other purposes, when tendered to him." The committee decided he was "an enemy to his country, and ought to be treated as such by every friend of American liberty; and that they ought to have no further dealings with him."

His daughter Mary Corbit described the arrest in a letter of 1824 to her brother John, who passed it on to Samuel R. Fisher. It began when he asked a tenant to pay rent in specie. He was taken before the Assembly at Dover and threatened with "a heavy fine," and, when he declined to take any part in encouraging war, was let go. Later "going to Meeting on a fifth day, mother and I being in the chaise, and my father on horseback with one of my little brothers behind him," a man in regimentals rode with him half a mile where armed men were waiting. "The child was taken from behind him, and he was ordered to dismount and get into a cart." Friends coming to meeting followed as far as the meetinghouse, where "my father called out and bid us farewell." "A paper was pinned to his back."

Before they entered the town the officer stopped the cart, and, taking his calm for ignorance, said, "Mr. Cowgill you are not aware of the danger you are in!" He answered: "I fear not them that can kill the body, and after that have no more power that they can do; but I fear Him who after he hath killed the body, hath all power." At the liberty pole in Dover it was proclaimed that he had no protection and that anyone dealing with him did so at their peril; "the miller was threatened with the destruction of his mill if he ground for his family, and the school-master forbid receiving his children at school."

The man was let go, and many Friends rode home with him. His daughter wrote, "When we went to bed at night we did not know what would be the issue before morning, and in this way we lived for several years." She told of one of the party who took him that day. The roads were wet and muddy, and Cowgill, seeing the man walking beside the cart, said, "Thee had better get up and sit with me, as the walking is wet and I am fearful thee will take cold." The man said long afterward that he never regretted any act of his life more than being concerned in the affair against "one of the best of men."

Duck Creek Monthly Meeting, on 27 June 1778, received "an account of the sufferings of John Cowgill for refusing Continental Currency" and sent it to the Quarterly Meeting committee. John married Mary Worrell and had a large family; his daughter Mary married William Corbit of Odessa, Delaware.

stories.title: A cane and a sword
stories.hook: Wills and inventories from 1731–32 trace three generations of a Perkins family and their connection to the Nordykes.
body: In May 1731 administration of the estate of Jacob Perkins of "Wellenborrow," Burlington County, who died without a will, went to his son Jacob Perkins, yeoman. The inventory, made on 20 May by Robert Lucas and Joseph Fenimore, comes to 91 pounds 18 shillings 5 pence and "includes cane and sword, £1.10; debt of 14 shillings from Benja. Perkins; 8 years rent due from Benja. Perkins and Wm. Makintass, £1."

The son, Jacob Perkins Jr., made his own will on 26 October 1731. He left his wife Sarah and his children "Abraham, Rebeckah, David, Mary, Ann, Susannah, Hannah, Sarah, Bethseda and Martha." He disposed of "land in Chester, which I bought of John Ward March 15, 1728," and listed bonds due him "from James Smith, Esq., John Shinn and Henry Nordike." He also left ten pounds to St. Mary's Church, Burlington, the Church of England parish, which points to Church of England ties. His son David was executor and the witnesses were Joseph Fenimore, Eliza Fenimore and Sam. Scattergood. The will was proved on 7 December 1731, and the inventory of 6 December, by Fenimore and Scattergood, was 205 pounds 14 shillings 6 pence.

Henry Nordyke and Rebecca Perkins took out a marriage license on 6 January 1731/2, a month after her father's will was proved. He appears in that will as a man who owed him money. Then David died too. His will, made in January 1731/2 "of Wellingborrow, yeoman," leaves his brother Abraham "plantation in Wellingburrow, which came to me by will of my father, Jacob Perkins, dated Oct. 26, 1731," and names his "Sister, Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike" and "Mother, Sarah Perkins." It was witnessed by Joseph Fenimore, Sam'l Scattergood and Henry Nordike, and was proved on 4 March 1731/2.

So within about a year the Perkins household of Willingboro lost a grandfather, a father and a son, and the new son-in-law Henry Nordyke witnessed the last of the wills. Henry and Rebecca's descendants are the Nordykes of the family tree. Abraham, to whom David left the plantation, was also his executor.

quotes.t: Sister, Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike. Mother, Sarah Perkins.
quotes.c: Will of David Perkins of Wellingborrow, 1731/2, Calendar of New Jersey Wills, Lib. 8, p. 184

stories.title: Soldiers on the road to Huntsville: Giles County, 1862-1863
stories.hook: Abner Stevenson's son Gilbert was five months old when the first Federal troops marched into Pulaski.

subject.name: Giles County in the Civil War

body: Gilbert Franklin Stevenson was born near Pulaski on 17 November 1861, to Rev. Abner Stevenson and Martha. A county history says what the next four years were like around the family farm. "The county was continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers throughout the war, being on the line of march from Nashville to Huntsville, Ala. Pulaski, Lynnville, Elkton and Prospect were each visited by Federal troops in large numbers, and Pulaski and Lynnville were fortified." On Fort Hill above Pulaski "a formidable fort or earth-work was erected."

The first Federals to come in any number arrived in April 1862, when Col. Mark Monday brought a detachment of Gen. Negley's brigade from Columbia to drive off John Morgan's cavalry, who were plundering the Federal wagon trains. Gilbert was then about five months old. Monday camped at Pulaski until September 1862. In August 1863 Col. Hayes raided the county with a regiment of cavalry and camped a day and a night in Pulaski. In the same year, in the history's words, "Lynnville and Elkton were both raided by the Federals, the whole county, in fact, being relieved of horses, cattle and grain."

That October Gen. Wheeler retreated south through the county with Gen. Wilder after him, and in November "Gen. W. T. Sherman and his entire army passed through Giles County, en route to Chattanooga, making a short stop at Elkton." Bee Spring, the Methodist church Elam Stevenson helped found, stood in the Twentieth Civil District with Mount Pisgah and Mount Zion.

The history does not name Abner's household. It gives the setting: a Methodist preacher with a farm, a wife, and a new baby on a road that three armies used. Abner's nephews Coleman and Wilbur Stevenson served the other side from their own farms nearby, in the 32nd Tennessee.

stories.title: John Milton Garrison, a Mecklenburg boy who ended up in the legislature's Acts
stories.hook: Born at Cowans Ford in 1788, married in Wilson County at twenty-one, and divorced by the Kentucky General Assembly at fifty-nine.
body: John Milton Garrison was born on 4 October 1788 at Cowans Ford in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, and came as a boy with his parents to Warren County, Kentucky. On 6 December 1809 he married Martha "Patsey" Cannon in Wilson County, Tennessee. Patsey is said to have been born about 1788 in Mecklenburg County. John’s daughter Mary, born 17 October 1811, married Henry Satterfield; whether Patsey was her mother is not known, since no record names Mary’s mother. In 1815 Allen County was formed from Warren and Barren counties, placing the family in a newly named county.

In 1810 he was in Warren County in a household of five that held one enslaved person, a man of about 21. Allen County households in 1820, 1830 and 1840 (7, 11 and 7 people) held no slaves. In 1850 he was 62, a farmer, with real estate valued at $2,250. Whether he held anyone after 1810 is not known.

The marriage ended in the legislature, by statute. The Kentucky legislature's act of 1847-48 read: "That the marriage contract now existing between John M. Garrison, and his wife, Patsey Garrison, be and the same is hereby dissolved, and they are hereby restored to all the rights and privileges of unmarried persons." The chapter was approved on 29 February 1848. It gives no reason.

One family account gives a reason, without a source. It says that during the marriage he "fathered children by Sarah Stamps who lived nearby," that he "had the KY legislature declare those children legitimate," and that after the divorce he married Sarah. In 1850 J. M. Garrison, 62, lived with an "S" aged 57 and three younger Garrisons aged 21, 19 and 6. The legitimation act has not been found, so that part is unconfirmed. He died in Allen County on 18 September 1860. Patsey is said to have died about 1850 in Allen County, an estimate not independently verified.

Mary Garrison married Henry Satterfield and bore twelve children. Her son James called her father "John M. Garrison, of Allen County, Ky." and adds "(now living at the age of seventy-five years)"; because John died in 1860, the parenthesis most likely describes Mary, who would have been 73 or 74 in 1885. His parents were probably Samuel and Esther (Alexander) Garrison, who came to Warren County from Mecklenburg: Samuel's family record book lists John Milton, born 4 October 1788, among their nine children, though no county record names him as their son.

His grave is in the Mount Pleasant United Methodist Church Cemetery near Scottsville, in Allen County, under a modern flat granite marker: "In memory of John Milton Garrison 1788-1860." His daughter Mary is buried far from him, in Wayne County, Iowa, where she died in 1896.

stories.title: What a rented farm at Hagansport meant in 1910
stories.hook: The government's 1908 soil survey says what tenants paid, what the land near Hagansport grew, and why the north end of the county was held back.
body: In April 1910 John C. Satterfield, 46, was renting a farm at Hagansport, and John B. Smith and Emma Liza Langley Smith had farmed there in 1900. The U.S. Bureau of Soils surveyed Franklin County in 1908 and wrote about farming in just that corner, without naming any family.

On renting, the survey says that "the rental paid is on the usual share plan, by which the tenant furnishes everything but the land and buildings and receives one-half the crops. When the tenant furnishes only the labor he is given one-third of the corn and one-fourth of the cotton." In 1900 only 44.1 percent of the county's farms were run by their owners, and the average farm was 77.9 acres. Most land could be bought for $5 to $10 an acre, more in the Sulphur River bottoms. The authors add that "since that date many of the tenants have acquired title."

On Hagansport itself: the town sits on a divide between the Sulphur River and White Oak Creek, with bodies of Wilson clay loam "in the vicinity of Hagansport and Lavada." The survey calls that soil "somewhat better adapted to cotton than to corn," says it was nearly all in cultivation, and gives the cotton yield as "from one-third to three-fourths bale per acre." The bottoms along the river were "more or less subject to overflow." Of the north end of the county, the survey says: "Other small centers in the northern part of the county are Daphne, Lavada, and Hagansport. In this part of the county development is seriously hindered by the absence of adequate shipping facilities."
This is a general portrait. It does not say whether the Smiths owned or rented, or whether the Satterfields farmed on halves or thirds, but it describes the terms on which families like them worked.

stories.title: Fifteen children at Bee Spring
stories.hook: Frank Stevenson was one of fifteen children of a farming preacher, and a twin; eleven of them were under one roof in 1870.

subject.name: The fifteen children of Abner and Martha Stevenson

body: Rev. Abner A. Stevenson and Martha S. Watson were married on 8 December 1838. Their fifteen children, all born in Giles County, were Lucinda C. (3 May 1840), William Elam Fletcher (9 April 1842), Lydia Mary Eliza (20 December 1843), Catherine M. Frances (10 January 1846), Augustus Summerfield (30 October 1847), Ellen Tillman and James Willis (twins, 30 January 1850), Larkin Henry (12 October 1852), Amanda Elizabeth (21 October 1854), Julia Ann Desdemona (July 1857), John Edward Thomas (16 September 1859), the twins Gilbert Franklin and George Washington (both 17 November 1861), Wilson McAlister (15 August 1864) and Manerva Jane (22 July 1866).

In 1870 the household in District 10 held A. A. Stevenson, 54, Martha, 47, and eleven children: Lucinda 28, James 20, Ellen 20, Larkin 18, Amanda 16, Julia A. 14, John E. 12, George W. 8, Gilbert 8, Mack 5 and Manerva J. 3. The two eight-year-olds are the twins. By 1880 the house was nearly empty: Abner, 63, "Farming Preacher," Martha, 56, Gilbert F., 18, Wilson M., 16 and Jane M., 12, with three hired or fostered Whittaker children and a one-year-old grandchild named Berry Andrew, born in Alabama. The Andrew grandchild was probably the youngest son of Abner's daughter Eliza, who had died in November 1878.

Several of the dates agree with the Bee Spring graveyard. W. Mack Stevenson lies there, born 15 August 1864 and dead 30 June 1940, which matches Wilson McAlister. Nathan A. Stevenson, 12 November 1870 to 21 July 1936, is Abner's grandson Nathaniel, William's son. Werner W. Stevenson, 4 March 1880 to 23 June 1974, is James Willis's son. Abner himself lies there, as does Martha S., 19 February 1823 to 12 July 1887.

The children scattered. Lucinda married Perry Pittman Williams and died in 1920; Eliza Mary married John Newton Andrew on 20 December 1870 and died in 1878; Frances married J. M. Whitaker and died on 18 April 1889; Summerfield went to Arkansas and was buried near Crowley's Ridge; Ellen married James Marion Britton; Julia went to Texas as John Newton Andrew's third Stevenson wife; Edward died in El Paso; George, by family account, became a judge at Lubbock; James Willis became a Methodist minister; Manerva married Andrew R. Merrill and moved to Ardmore, Tennessee. Frank went to Indiana.

stories.title: Two Stevenson brothers go to Texas
stories.hook: One brother, by family tradition a judge at Lubbock and the father of thirteen; another died of smallpox at El Paso in June 1886, working for the railway.
body: Frank Stevenson had a twin. George Washington Stevenson was born on the same day, 17 November 1861, and in 1870 both were 8 years old in the same Giles County household. In May 1881 it was noted that "Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week." It is said that George later lived at Lubbock, Texas, where he was a judge, and that he was the father of thirteen children. It names none of them. Lubbock County's county judges for those years (Shannon, Brown, Crump and Bean, 1891 to 1906) include no Stevenson, so if he held a bench it was not that one.

John Edward Thomas Stevenson, born on 16 September 1859, was "John E," 12, in 1870. It is said that Edward "moved to Texas where he worked for the Texas and Pacific Railway" and "died of smallpox in El Paso, Texas on June 26, 1886." He would have been 26. The Texas and Pacific reached El Paso in 1881, so the job fits the date.

The pull of Texas runs through this family. In January 1881 their father "abandoned the idea of going to Texas." Their sister Julia Ann followed her husband John Newton Andrew there, and by the 1870s their sister Ellen Britton's growing family was moving between Giles County and Texas. When Frank and Parsis lived there in the 1890s and 1900s, three of their children were born in Texas.

quotes.t: Edward Stevenson moved to Texas where he worked for the Texas and Pacific Railway. Edward Stevenson died of smallpox in El Paso, Texas on June 26, 1886.

F. Stevenson appears among the county's precinct commissioners in 1894-95, and nothing ties him to George. A Texas death record or a Lubbock court record would settle both. stories.title: One widower, three Stevenson wives
stories.hook: John Newton Andrew of Giles County married a Stevenson cousin, then a Stevenson sister, then Frank's other sister; the last wife took him to Texas.
body: John Newton Andrew was born in Giles County on 20 February 1841. His first wife was Mary Hamilton, a granddaughter of Rev. Elam Stevenson through Elam's daughter Catherine. His second, on 20 December 1870, was Eliza Mary Stevenson, Frank's sister, who bore him four sons (Baxter, Abner, Truman and Perry) and died on 16 November 1878. His third was Eliza's younger sister Julia Ann Desdemona Stevenson, born in July 1856 or 1857. Julia was thus "John's third marriage to a Stevenson woman."

Julia and John had four children, Ray, George, Tina Tisha and Alice. A son, Roy Jackson Andrew, was at Rockwall, Texas, on 30 July 1893 and died in Wilbarger County, Texas, in 1964. John died on 28 March 1909 and Julia on 3 July 1928 at Vernon, Wilbarger County, though one account gives 1925 as her death year, so the date is not settled.

Rockwall comes up again in this family. The possible first husband of Parsis O'Neal, Frank's wife, is said to have died in Rockwall County in 1901. If Frank and Parsis were among the Giles County Stevensons around Rockwall in the 1890s, the Texas births of their children Willie, Frank and Elisha would be explained, though this is only a guess.
src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm)

stories.note: Julia's death year is given as 1925 and 1928 in different WikiTree fields, and her birth as 1856 and 1857. A Texas death certificate or Vernon cemetery record would settle it.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Rockwall and Wilbarger Counties, Texas

stories.title: Ellen Stevenson and the Brittons
stories.hook: A twin born in 1850 who married a Giles County farmer, went to Texas and back, and raised seven children.
body: Ellen Tillman Stevenson was born on 30 January 1850, the twin of James Willis. On 24 December 1871 she married James Marion Britton, born on 3 March 1840 in Giles County, the son of Wilson Britton and Elizabeth Ragains. His brother John Frank Britton died in Collin County, Texas, in 1890.

Seven children are named: Logan Harwell, Sarah Beulah, Amanda Elizabeth, an infant daughter, Wilson Arrington, James Wilson Lafayette "Fate," and Carlos Erskine. In 1880 at Friendship, Crockett County, James and Ellen's household included son L. H., age seven, and daughters B. V., age five, and M. E., age three. Logan's birth is given as 17 September 1872 and Sarah Beulah's as 24 January 1873; these dates are only four months apart and cannot both be right. By 1900 Ellen and James were back in Giles County.

James died on 18 September 1913 in Giles County and Ellen on 4 March 1927 (another account gives 4 February); both lie at Mount Zion (New Zion) Cemetery near Pulaski. Their daughter Amanda married Eli Bascom Pitts on 2 March 1892 and had eleven children. Sarah Beulah married Samuel McNeese and had eight, including twins who died the day they were born, 10 June 1902.

stories.title: A third-generation preacher with three wives
stories.hook: Frank's brother James Willis, a twin of Ellen, became a Methodist minister, married three times, and lived until 1943.
body: James Willis Stevenson, born on 30 January 1850, was the twin of Ellen. He was a Methodist minister. His first wife was a cousin, Nancy J. Stevenson, and their only son was Werner Wesley, born on 4 March 1880. After Nancy died he married Elizabeth A., and then Beatrice, born in October 1870 in Alabama. In 1900 James and Beatrice were in Giles County, and he later lived at Ardmore, Tennessee.

His second and third marriages gave him another ten children: Bessie (1885), Bertha (1887), Coleman (1893), Cletis Z. (1897), Lydia M. (1898), and Nore, Clower, Elizabeth, Charlie and Talmadge Dewitt. He died on 9 November 1943 and was buried at Bee Spring, the church his grandfather founded.

Werner Wesley (1880-1974) stayed in Giles County and married Lila Mitchell. Their daughter Nannie married Robert Hulsey, born in January 1904. No connection between this Giles County Hulsey and Katie Stevenson's husband Oscar Hulsey has been shown.

stories.title: A preacher with soldier sons and a short-lived brood
stories.hook: Elam's oldest son had nine children on a Giles County farm, buried six of them young, and sent two sons into the Confederate 32nd Tennessee.

subject.name: Rev. William Payne Stevenson and Malinda (Rowe)

body: William Payne Stevenson was born on 27 September 1810 in North Carolina, the oldest son of Rev. Elam Stevenson. On 14 October 1830 he married Malinda Rowe in Giles County. In 1886 it was said that he "has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel," and that he settled on his farm in 1838. He lived to 14 January 1892; Malinda died on 21 January 1888. He is buried at Bee Spring.

His nine children were an infant son who lived and died in 1831; Coleman Lafayette (26 December 1832); Elam R. (1835); Joseph J. (1837); Sarah Ann P. (10 March 1840); Wilbur Marion (20 January 1841); Presley W. (8 September 1847); William F. (19 January 1853); and John Henry (1856). Six of the nine did not reach adulthood. Presley W. died on 30 June 1849 (the cemetery reads 30 July), Elam R. on 2 August 1854, William B. F. on 19 August 1854 and Joseph J. on 15 February 1856. Sarah died on 10 February 1846.

The two grown sons went to war. Coleman "enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers" in 1862 and "served until the close of the war," taking part "in most of the principal battles." The 32nd was organized at Camp Trousdale in the summer of 1861, with four Giles County companies, and went first to East Tennessee and Kentucky. The 32nd served in Brown's Brigade of the division of Gen. C. L. Stevenson (no kin), and was reorganized at Jackson, Mississippi. Wilbur Marion served in the same regiment until the fall of 1864, "when left the service due to ill health."

Coleman raised not only his own sons but three orphaned Jackson nieces of his wife (Martha V., Nancy M. and Mary J.). He died on 24 October 1908. Wilbur married Martha Jane Hampton on 9 November 1865. She died on 28 December 1918 and he died the next day, 29 December 1918, in Giles County. No cause is given, but their dates fall in the winter of the great influenza epidemic.

quotes.t: He has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel, and his father was also a very prominent Methodist Episcopal minister.

stories.title: "They who bear the cross shall bear the crown"
stories.hook: Elam's eldest child moved to Alabama with her husband, raised nine children, and is quoted on her gravestone; her sons went on to Texas and Arkansas.
body: Catherine A. Stevenson was born on 2 October 1808 in North Carolina, the oldest of Elam and Lydia's eleven children. She married William B. Hamilton, born in 1808 or 1809 in South Carolina. Their nine children were Lydia J. (1832), Mary A. (1834), James (1839), Elam Carr (1 February 1842), Clatinda I. (20 January 1844), George Worth (1846), Thomas C. (1848), Gilbert William (1850, in Alabama) and John Baxter (30 April 1853, in Limestone County, Alabama). The family was in Limestone County in 1860, 1870 and 1880.

William died on 8 September 1872 and was buried in the Wallace Cemetery in Limestone County. Catherine died on 2 December 1888, and the same cemetery has her stone: "Mrs. C.A. Hamilton born October 2, 1808 died in great peace December 2, 1888. They who bear the cross shall bear the crown." A grandson, Robert J. Hamilton of Ripley, Alabama, described her as "a short, chubby, and very cheerful little lady."

Her children moved west. Her son George became a Methodist minister. Clatinda never married and died on 4 March 1892. Gilbert William married Martha J. Thorpe and lived in Greene County, Arkansas, where their daughter Bessie was born on 31 March 1880; Martha died on 19 May 1881, Gilbert on 6 June 1896, and both were buried at Pruetts Chapel. John Baxter married Mary Arantha Lynch in Kaufman County, Texas, on 31 January 1884 and had nine children there. Her daughter Mary A. became the first wife of John Newton Andrew, who later married two of Frank's sisters.

quotes.t: Mrs. C.A. Hamilton born October 2, 1808 died in great peace December 2, 1888. They who bear the cross shall bear the crown.

stories.title: A doctor and preacher who moved to Arkansas in 1858
stories.hook: Abner's younger brother carried the family trade to Arkansas, taught his sons the pulpit, and is buried at Booneville, not far from Danville where Frank later lived.
body: Elam Augustus Stevenson was born on 3 February 1829 in Giles County, the son of Rev. Elam and Lydia. He joined the Tennessee Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South. In 1858 the Conference recorded "Elam A. Stevenson, transferred to Wachita Conference" (Ouachita, in Arkansas). A 1930 biography of his son says he "came to Arkansas and became pastor at El Dorado and Princeton" in 1858. His son James Baxter was born at Richmond, Arkansas, on 24 October 1860, and Thomas Elam's birth at Booneville is given as April 1857, a year before the transfer, so he may have been in Arkansas earlier than 1858.

Ten years later he was back in Tennessee, where in 1870 "E A Stephenson," 40, lived with Alabama-born wife H. S., 27, and sons Thomas, James and John. In 1875 he was listed as "readmitted" and then "transferred to White River Conference," and appoint "Wittsburg, E. A. Stevenson," in the White River Conference of northeast Arkansas. In 1880 he was at Addison, Winston County, Alabama, aged 51 and married to Hannah, listed as a "Doctor & Preacher" with seven children at home. Hannah Celia Carolan, born in 1844 at Somerville, Alabama, died on 26 October 1884 at Carolan, Logan County, Arkansas. Elam A. died on 17 April 1886 and is buried at Oak Hill Memorial Cemetery, Booneville.

A 1930 biography says he "was a graduate of the Vanderbilt University" at Nashville. Vanderbilt did not open until 1875, when he was already 46, so the claim must be a family exaggeration. It also names his wife as "Earl (Cook)," which nothing else supports, so the sons by his first marriage and by Hannah are not yet separated.

stories.title: Frank's cousin the Arkansas Methodist
stories.hook: A cousin of the Hulsey ancestor Frank preached in Yell County in 1883, was the first pastor of Oklahoma City's Methodist church, and is the Rev. J. B. Stevenson whose 1932 letter is quoted for the family's years of preaching.
body: James Baxter Stevenson was born on 24 October 1860 at Richmond, Arkansas, the son of Rev. Elam A. Stevenson. His 1930 biography says he "grew up in Tennessee, to which State his father had returned when he was six," and that at nineteen he "returned to Arkansas and settled in Booneville, Logan County" (the 1930 text is hyphenated across a line). He was licensed to preach on 21 September 1881. In 1883 "the Arkansas Conference sent him to Yell County, where he remained for two years" and then to the Mulberry Circuit and to Paris, Logan County.

He became "the first pastor of the Methodist church in Oklahoma City" and later served at Guthrie, Fort Smith, Conway, Batesville, Morrillton, Dardanelle, Fayetteville, Paragould, Russellville and Ozark. The Conference appointments confirm some of this: "Conway Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1892, "Van Buren Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1896, "Morrillton Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1900. From 1927 he was pastor at Atkins. He married Lulu Briggs on 14 May 1885. They had four children, among them Eugene Hendrix, a Rhodes Scholar who studied at Oxford and took a doctorate at the University of Pennsylvania.

This is the J. B. Stevenson who wrote in 1932 that "Uncle Jimmie preached 63 years, Uncle Abner 54 years, Uncle John 48 years, my father E. A. Stevenson 38 years, Uncle Gilbert 25 years." The letter is said to have been to "Eugene Hendricks Stevenson," which fits his son Eugene Hendrix. His Yell County parish of 1883-85 is the county where Frank Stevenson was living at Danville in 1910, and his father's burial place at Booneville is in the next county.

stories.title: Golden-wedding preacher, and a general in the family
stories.hook: James Calvin Stevenson married into the family of two Tennessee governors, preached at Giles County weddings for decades, and was great-grandfather to the general for whom Andrews Field is named.

subject.name: Rev. James Calvin Stevenson and Margaret Caroline (Brown)

body: James Calvin Stevenson was born in North Carolina on 23 June 1813 and was brought to Giles County, Tennessee, as a babe, the son of Rev. Elam Stevenson and a brother of Abner. On 19 November 1835 he married Margaret Caroline Brown, who had been born on 8 December 1816.

Margaret came, it seems, from one of the best-known families in Tennessee. A neighbor, F. T. M’Laurine, remembered in 1884 that James “married a daughter of Mr. Duncan Brown, sister of ex-Gov. N. S. and J. C. Brown,” and her grave at Bee Spring remembers her the same way. Her brother Neill Smith Brown was the twelfth governor of Tennessee, from 1847 to 1849, and later United States minister to Russia; her brother John Calvin Brown was a Confederate major general, the nineteenth governor, from 1871 to 1875, and afterward president of the Texas and Pacific Railway. Both were born in Giles County to Duncan and Margaret Smith Brown. The kinship rests on that memory rather than on any will naming Margaret among Duncan Brown’s children.

James was a preacher. Through the 1850s and 1860s he married couples across Giles County, among them Swinney and Dyer on 19 January 1852, Young and Huff on 3 November 1852, Stovall and Stephenson on 3 September 1860, and Woodard and Barnfield on 25 August 1862.

Fifty years on, the couple were still together near Bryson. On 20 August 1885 a county correspondent called on “our old friends, Rev. and Mrs. Jas. C. Stevenson of near Bryson,” who “speak of celebrating their golden wedding in October.” Margaret died a few months later, on 11 February 1886. James lived until 23 February 1899 and is buried beside her at Bee Spring.

They had ten children, among them Sarah, who married James Hollon, and Catherine Eliza, born in 1838, whom her husband called Eliza Catherine. In 1856 she married the Rev. William Thomas Andrews, who in his autobiography of 1912 remembered her as the daughter of James C. and Margaret C. Stevenson and named their son James David Andrews. James David’s son was Frank Maxwell Andrews, a major general by 1937, who rose to lieutenant general and gave his name to Andrews Field, now Joint Base Andrews.

News of James’s death crossed into Alabama, where one of his daughters had lived. Soon after 23 February 1899 the Scottsboro Citizen told its readers that the Rev. James C. Stevenson had died near Bryson, in Giles County, “at the ripe old age of 86 years.” It called him a Methodist preacher for upwards of fifty years. It named him as the father of Mrs. W. T. Andrews, formerly of Scottsboro and by then of Florence: Catherine Eliza, the wife of the Rev. William Thomas Andrews. And it repeated what Giles County took for granted, that his wife had been a Miss Brown, sister of the two former governors, Neill S. and John C. Brown.
That makes two witnesses who knew the family, M’Laurine in 1884 and an Alabama editor in 1899, who said the same thing. It is still a newspaper’s word and not a will. James was in fact eighty-five.

stories.title: Parsis's brothers stayed home
stories.hook: Five of Daniel and Vashti O'Neal's sons and their youngest daughter lived out their lives in or near Gibson County, Indiana, while Parsis and Mary went west.

subject.name: The O'Neal brothers of Gibson County

body: Daniel Waters O'Neal and Vashti Pearson had ten children, and eight of them reached adulthood: Parsis, her sister Mary and the six told here. William Allen was born on 15 April 1863 in Tennessee (though an 1880 listing says Indiana) and died on 11 September 1933 in Pike County, Indiana, with burial at Blackfoot Cemetery. His wife was Nancy Jane Mason, born in 1865 at Oakland City, who died there on 20 June 1923.

John Sherman was born on 15 January 1866, a few months after the regiment mustered out, and died at Somerville on 19 July 1940. He married Jane Minerva Mitchell. George Johnson was born on 16 August 1875; an 1880 listing says in Missouri, so the family may have spent some time there in the 1870s (another account says Tennessee). He lost his first wife, Adella Douglas (born 1875), on 27 February 1906, married Sarah Eleen Reed, and died at Somerville on 12 June 1965 at 89. Daniel Clinton, born 9 June 1878, married Flora Nellie McGregor and died on 3 March 1954. David Commodore, born at Somerville on 22 March 1881, married Birdie Viola Rembe and died at Evansville on 7 May 1955.

The youngest, Charity Louisa, born on 19 December 1887, was the only daughter besides Parsis and Mary to live to adulthood. She married Fred Skomp, born on 7 May 1884 in Greene County, Indiana. He died at Hobart, Indiana, on 5 August 1949, and she died at Valparaiso on 15 November 1979. Vashti's five living sons in 1919 were William, John, George, Clinton and Commodore, and her daughters were Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma, and Mrs. Fred Skomp of Somerville.

stories.title: A hundred years from Indiana to Oklahoma
stories.hook: Parsis's oldest sister married three times, raised her children in Arkansas, and was feted at 100 in Tuttle.
body: Mary Elizabeth O'Neal was born on 16 November 1860 in Gibson County, Indiana, the first child of Daniel and Vashti, ten months after their marriage. By 1878 she had married David Raliegh Farris, born in 1856 in Indiana. Their son Elmer Cooper Farris was born on 25 September 1878 at Princeton and died in Sequoyah County, Oklahoma, in 1948. A second son, Daniel Riley, born in Arkansas on 23 March 1881 and recorded as Fairce, died at Mead, Oklahoma, in 1968.

On 10 February 1884, in Arkansas, Mary married Joseph McConnell Rinker, 29, born in Iowa. Their children were Lydia Bell (1885, Sunset, Arkansas), Armenda Mae (1888), Cynthia Jane (1890), Joseph Jonathan (1892, Fayetteville), Vasha (1895, died 1897), Oscar Ashel (1897), Letha Agnes (1900) and Alta (1902, died 1906). Joseph was in Roger Mills County, Oklahoma, in 1910 and died on 27 May 1919 at Wapanucka.

When she died in December 1960, Mrs. Mary Elizabeth Wilson, 100, was remembered: she "was born in Gibson County, Indiana, near Evansville, and spent most of her early life in Missouri, and raised her children in Arkansas. She first came to Oklahoma in 1907 and moved to Tuttle, from Faxton, in 1926." She "celebrated her 100th birthday in Nov 16, 1960, and passed away at her home on Wednesday, Dec 14, 1960." Survivors included "3 sons, 3 daughters, 51 grandchildren, 150 great-grandchildren, & 73 great great grandchildren." She was buried in Fairlawn Cemetery. Her third husband was James Calvin Wilson, born in 1867 at Princeton, Indiana.
Katie's brother Eddie was born in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, in July 1907, the same year Mary first came to Oklahoma.

On 16 November 1960 Oklahoma turned fifty-three and Mary Elizabeth Wilson turned a hundred, and the Tuttle Times put her on its front page the next day, and an Oklahoma City paper ran her picture under the headline “Tuttle Woman Hits Century.” It traced her road: born near Evansville in Gibson County, several states after that, and then a home near Foss, in Washita County, in the year Oklahoma became a state. She had come with her second husband, Joe Rinker, from Missouri, after the years near Sunset, Arkansas, where they raised eleven children. Six of them were living. She had been in Tuttle since 1926, when she married her last husband, named there as R. F. Wilson, though other records call him James Calvin Wilson, and she still kept her own house.

An estimated 150 grandchildren and great-grandchildren were counted for the day, and her six children were named: O. A. Rinker, Mrs. Bill Rich and Mrs. Jim Welchel, all near Tuttle; Joe Rinker of Elmore City; Mrs. Mae Jennings of Lubbock, Texas; and Dan Fairce of Durant, the oldest living son. Four weeks later she was gone.

stories.title: Seven children in 1910
stories.hook: At Danville, Arkansas, in 1910, Katie was the baby, with six older brothers and sisters born in Indiana, Texas and Oklahoma.
body: On 18 April 1910 at Danville, Yell County, Frank Stevenson, 51, "Clergyman," and his wife Jane, 41, had these children at home: Delphia, 18, born in Indiana; Willie, 16, Texas; George, 12, Indiana; Frank, 8, Texas; Elisha, 6, Texas; Eddie, 2, Oklahoma; and a baby under one year, Arkansas, entered as Katie (her own birth is dated 15 October 1910, so one of the two dates is off by months). Frank and Jane said they had been married 25 years and that seven children had been born. Those are the seven the household reported.

Delphia was the oldest daughter. When Katie died in 2009 she was preceded in death by "daughters Delphia and Mary," so she named a daughter for her sister. Willie was born in Texas about 1894. George Sherman Stevenson died on 3 June 1978 at Kilgore, Gregg County, Texas, with Parsis Jane (O'Neal) Stevenson named as his mother. Frank, born about 1902 in Texas, is "Frank Lester" in other trees, and one list calls the sixth child "Allen" where the household has Elisha.

The youngest brother, Horace Edward "Eddie," was born on 13 July 1907 in Garvin, McCurtain County, Oklahoma. He married Edith Marie Shunkey (born 29 July 1911 at Muskogee, died 2 April 2003 at King City, Oregon), and he died on 1 February 1998 at Portland, Oregon.

Other trees give a different list for the same parents: Iva Myrtle (1884), Adison Galiton (1886), Nellie Vashti (1889), Frank Lester (1902), Horace Edward (1907) and Katie. Iva Myrtle, Adison and Nellie would have been 26, 24 and 21 in 1910, so they could have been grown and away; and their link to this family is not documented.
src: 1910 U.S. census, Danville, Yell Co., Arkansas, as transcribed on the WikiTree pages for Parsis Jane O'Neal (O'Neal-3514) and Gilbert Franklin Stevenson (Stevenson-12558)
WikiTree Stevenson-5100 (Horace Edward Stevenson)

stories.note: Delphia, Willie, George, Frank, Elisha and Eddie are the names on the 1910 census page; the later given names in other trees are not proven. The census is also the only record yet seen for Willie and Delphia.
stories.place: Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas

stories.title: A sixteen-year-old bride in Pulaski County
stories.hook: A Parsis J. O'Neal, 16, is said to have married a 40-year-old Otho Louderbank on Christmas Day 1884, and her grave memorial still carries the Louderback name.
body: An Arkansas marriage record reads: "Parsis J O Neal and Otho Louderback were married 25 December 1884 in Pulaski County, Arkansas. Otho was 40, Parsis, 16 years old." The groom's name is spelled "Louderbank." Pulaski County is Little Rock. In 1880 Parsis, 11, had been in her father's household in Gibson County, Indiana. Parsis's sister Mary was also in Arkansas by February 1884.

William Ortho Louderback was born about 1836 to 1844 at Princeton, Gibson County, the same county as the O'Neals. He is said to have died in 1901 in Rockwall County, Texas, and a daughter, Henrietta Louderback, born in Illinois and dead in Texas in 1955, is listed as a child of Parsis and him.

Her memorial at Hugo is titled "Parsis Jane O'Neal Louderback (26 Mar 1868-26 Jan 1956)," so she was remembered under the Louderback name to the end, while her marriage to Stevenson has no record behind it. In 1910 Frank and Jane said they had been married 25 years, which would put that wedding in 1885, months after the Louderback record. Either the 1910 answer is loose, or the Stevenson household began without a recorded marriage, or the Louderback marriage ended early. Nothing settles it. Willie, Frank and Elisha Stevenson were born in Texas from about 1894, where Otho Louderback died in 1901.

stories.place: Pulaski County, Arkansas; Illinois; Rockwall County, Texas

stories.title: A juror in Cherokee County, the year of the roundup
stories.hook: In November 1838 Gilliam Graves sat on a county jury a few months after soldiers emptied the Cherokee farms of his county into a stockade.

subject.name: Gilliam Graves in Cherokee County, Georgia

body: Gilliam Graves served on Cherokee County, Georgia, juries twice, in December 1835 and on 5 November 1838. The county had been carved out of the Cherokee Nation's Georgia land, and the state gave that land to white men by lottery in 1832. Its seat, first called Etowah, is Canton today.

In May 1838 the rest of the story arrived. Gen. Winfield Scott set up at the Cherokee capital, New Echota, and on 10 May told the Cherokee that "before another moon had passed every Cherokee man, woman, and child must be in motion" for the West. About 7,000 regulars, militia and volunteers were used. Stockade forts were built to hold the people until they could be moved, and five stood in Georgia: Fort Scudder in Lumpkin County, Fort Gilmer in Gilmer County, Fort Coosawatee in Murray County, Fort Talking Rock in Pickens County and "Fort Buffington, near Canton, in Cherokee county."

A historian who gathered the story from people who had lived it wrote: "Families at dinner were startled by the sudden gleam of bayonets in the doorway and rose up to be driven with blows and oaths along the weary miles of trail that led to the stockade. Men were seized in their fields or going along the road, women were taken from their wheels and children from their play." Looters followed the soldiers, and many families, looking back from a ridge, "saw their homes in flames." A Georgia volunteer later said: "I fought through the civil war and have seen men shot to pieces and slaughtered by thousands, but the Cherokee removal was the cruelest work I ever knew."

When about seventeen thousand people had been gathered into the stockades the removal began. It is said that "hundreds died in the stockades and the waiting camps," mostly from the rations, and that "over 4,000" Cherokee died as a direct result of the removal.

Nothing says what Gilliam saw or did that summer. He was in the county, but not where he lived in it. But when he was called to serve on 5 November 1838, the Cherokee families of his county had been gone from their farms for some months. By 1853 he was on the tax lists of Montgomery County, Arkansas, and in January 1864 he volunteered as a Union private at the age of 45.

quotes.t: I fought through the civil war and have seen men shot to pieces and slaughtered by thousands, but the Cherokee removal was the cruelest work I ever knew.
quotes.c: A Georgia volunteer, quoted in James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900), p. 130

stories.title: "Hung up to the first limb": Doaksville, June 1861
stories.hook: In the first week of June 1861 a Northern missionary learned that a meeting at Doaksville, the town where Vincent Tims kept store, had called for hanging men who would not take the South's side.
body: John Edwards, a Presbyterian missionary from New York, had taught at Spencer Academy and since 1853 ran Wheelock Seminary for Choctaw girls. In 1861, as the Choctaw Nation was pressed toward the Confederacy, he refused to pledge himself to take up arms for the South. His account of what followed was printed by the Oklahoma Historical Society a century later, with the editor's remark that a writer at Goodland had told her of the story, "It just would not do to print!"

A few weeks earlier, riding back from Pine Ridge, Edwards had come through Doaksville and found that "The Confederate flag was flying over the town." On 1 and 2 June the Principal Chief, George Hudson, and Peter Pitchlynn stayed with the Edwardses on their way to a special council at Doaksville. Hudson carried a message recommending neutrality; Edwards later heard "that he was compelled by a vigilance committee to change it recommending the Choctaws to join the South."

Then, he writes, "On Thursday afternoon I learned that on Wednesday a public meeting had been held at Doaksville, the capital, at which Capt. Robert M. Jones, the wealthiest Choctaw, took the ground that 'every man that was not with them must be hung up to the first limb between heaven and hell.'" The next morning a neighbor, Mrs. Dukes, came to say "the committee are to be here today to hang you." He handed his keys to a friend, had his pony Jerry saddled, prayed with his wife and was on the road "probably within 15 minutes of the time the word came." His plan was that Mrs. Edwards would follow with the children, and the editor credits her with managing the family's escape.

Jones, the editor's note says, owned about 500 enslaved people, plantations on the Red River and "a large store at Doaksville." His house, Rose Hill, stood east of present Hugo; the state encyclopedia says it burned in 1912.

Vincent B. Tims had been a trader at Doaksville since the late 1830s, in the firm of Doak & Tims, and in 1864 he signed Confederate mail contracts there as "V. B. Tims, P. M." The Edwards account never names him, and nothing says what Tims said or did that week. It records only the town where he did business and the climate in it.

quotes.c: Capt. Robert M. Jones, as reported by John Edwards, Chronicles of Oklahoma 43 (1965), p. 72

quotes.c: John Edwards, Chronicles of Oklahoma 43 (1965), p. 70

stories.title: The logging train that ran away, 25 June 1915
stories.hook: A log hauler jumped from a runaway train on the Pine Belt Lumber Company's railroad near Fort Towson and broke his leg; the company said he had signed away his right to sue.

subject.name: The Pine Belt logging train, 25 June 1915

body: The Pine Belt Lumber Company ran a mill, dry kilns and planers at Fort Towson and a railroad about 15 miles north into the woods, along which it logged. Clifford Riggs hauled logs by wagon and team and was paid $2 a day. His petition says the company gave its workers passes to ride the train between Fort Towson and the woods.

On 25 June 1915, Riggs says in his petition, he boarded a train near his work and "the train in going down a steep grade got out of the control of the train men operating the same and ran away down the grade." He "believed that the only chance to save his life was by jumping." He landed with a compound fracture of the right leg and ankle, was in bed 32 days, and said his injuries were permanent. He sued in the Choctaw County district court for $6,000, charging that the air brakes and steam brakes were old, worn and insufficient, and had been for a long time.

The company answered that its track was only a tramway for hauling logs and not a common carrier, that Riggs had been careless and had accepted the risk, and that before boarding he had signed a paper releasing it from any claim for injuries on the train. A jury found for Riggs.

On 6 April 1920 the Oklahoma Supreme Court affirmed. A contract, it said, "whereby the servant, in consideration of the employment, or of the wages, agrees to release and discharge his master from liability on account of injuries caused by the negligence of his master" is forbidden by the state constitution and "void as against public policy." The opinion does not state how much the jury awarded.

Two years after Riggs jumped, Grady Moffitt, 25, put "timberman" and "C. D. Neese, Ervin, Oklahoma" on his draft card in the same county. Which sawmill bought his timber is not known, and the county's biggest sawmill was the Pine Belt company's at Fort Towson. Nothing links Riggs to the family. The case shows what a timber hand's day could end in, and what a signed paper did not protect against.

stories.title: A Sunday in August 1898: the Austin murder at Hagansport
stories.hook: In August 1898 a farmer near Hagansport was shot on his way to his field by a man hired at the sawmill; the court cases ran until 1906.

subject.name: J. P. Austin, killed near Hagansport

body: On Sunday, 28 August 1898, J. P. Austin walked from his house toward his field in the bottom, "across the lake," and did not come home. His wife Ella took the children to church at Hagansport, a mile or a mile and a half away. That night he was still gone. On Monday morning she went back to Hagansport and asked a neighbor named Martin to look for him, and told him to try the trail from the lake to the field.

He was found there, killed. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals later said the killing occurred "twelve or thirteen miles north" of Mount Vernon. Ella Austin, by then Mrs. Johnson, told the jury why she knew where to send Martin. She said that H. J. Carbough "wanted me to take the life of my husband so that he and I could marry," and that she refused. Weeks later he said he would not do it himself, "but would get some one that would." In July he told her "there was a man at the sawmill by the name of T. C. Wallace and that he would be all right to do the work," for "seventy-five or a hundred dollars." The week before the killing, she said, Carbough warned her not to let the oldest little boy go with his papa.

On the evening of the killing, she testified, Wallace came to her house on foot, carrying a long bundle wrapped in a sack, and said: "Your man is down yonder; the work is done; the man is down yonder between the fields on the trail. You know me by Carbough."

Wallace was held in jail for months before he was indicted, and was tried in Franklin County five days after the indictment, some five years after the killing. The jury gave him death. On 8 June 1904 the Court of Criminal Appeals reversed, finding that he should have had a continuance to bring in witnesses and that the prosecutor had urged the jury that if he was not at the scene, "in God's name he should have told where he was." The case was moved to Camp County and tried again; on 31 May 1905 the court reversed that verdict too, for errors in instructing the jury about the testimony of accomplices. Carbough was tried in Camp County as an accomplice and given life in the penitentiary, and on 7 March 1906 the court affirmed.

What became of Wallace after the second reversal, or whether the widow was ever charged, is not known. The murder happened in the Hagansport neighborhood during the years the Smiths were farming there: Charles Oscar was nine in the summer of 1898, and by 1900 his father owned the farm. Nothing connects the family to anyone in the case.

quotes.c: T. C. Wallace to Mrs. Austin, as she testified; Wallace v. State, 46 Tex. Crim. 341 (1904)

stories.title: A quarrel over the log count at the Frogville sawmill
stories.hook: In July 1912 a log cutter shot the scaler at the Frogville sawmill five times over a pay settlement, thirteen years before John Moffitt was born there.
body: Frogville, on the Red River in Choctaw County, was a place of about forty families when John Winfred Moffitt was born there in October 1925. Thirteen years earlier it had a sawmill, and the sawmill had a log scale. Sloan Pool kept it; a man named Wyrick was the sawyer. The log count in the scaler's book was what a cutter's settlement was figured from, so what he wrote was money.

On 18 July 1912 Pool went out to scale logs with Jess Allen and the old logger A. F. Buxton. A. F. Buxton's son John joined them. Allen, an eyewitness, said they all sat on a log while Pool showed John the book, with every log set down. John said he did not want it to be "like the last month's pay day," and the two argued about whether Pool had "figured" him out of money. Allen said that Pool replied, "in that way I mean to dispute your word," and "John shot him." Pool was hit five times. Allen swore that John stood over the body and said, "the next log you scale will be in hell," and shot him again. Then, Allen said, John took Pool's knife from his pocket, asked "how are you going to swear about this?", cut his own arm with it and pressed the knife into the dead man's hand.

Witnesses said Buxton had been talking for weeks. On the day, a man heard him say he would have his settlement from "those damned fellows over there." At the start of July another had heard him say that "the company was beating him" and that he meant to kill Pool. Buxton swore the opposite: that Pool had cut him once on the breast and twice on the arm with "a little old pocket knife," that he had been carrying the pistol because he was told two men were waiting in the woods to kill him, and that "I shot him to keep him from killing me." His sister, Mrs. Ruth Holden, said Allen had told her in jail that he had sworn falsely against her father.

The jury in the Choctaw County district court found John Buxton guilty of murder on 21 November 1912 and set his punishment at death; his father was found not guilty. The judge sentenced him on 27 November to be hanged. On 22 September 1914 the Criminal Court of Appeals affirmed. Because a new state law on executions had taken effect while the appeal was pending and the date fixed had passed, it sent the case back to Choctaw County to set another day. The opinion says nothing about what followed.

The Moffitts were not yet in the county in 1912; at the 1910 census Grady, 18 or 19, was in Stone County, Arkansas, making barrel staves. By 1917 he was a timberman at Ervin, in this same timber country. That day showed what work at a mill in Choctaw County could come to when the scale and the pay disagreed.

quotes.t: the next log you scale will be in hell
quotes.c: John Buxton, as testified by Jess Allen; Buxton v. State, 11 Okla. Crim. 85 (1914)
