stories.title: Jesse and Hannah: a license, a grant and a widow who remarried
stories.hook: Jesse Blackshear bought a marriage license in Jones County about 1788, took up 77 acres in 1796, and vanishes from North Carolina; his widow Hannah is the one who shows up in Tennessee court in 1814.
body: Jesse's North Carolina paper trail is short. He was a chain-bearer on a Jones County survey in 1782 and again in 1789. Between 1787 and 1789 he paid ten shillings for a marriage license in Jones County, with no bride named. The 1790 census for Jones County counts him as one man over sixteen with two females in the house. In 1794 he entered a plea for land, and in 1796 he was granted 77 acres on the south side of the Trent River. After 1796 he is 'not found in N.C.'

The Tennessee record picks him up. In October 1814 the Williamson County court settled the estate of 'Jesse Blackshare, Dec'd.' His widow and administrator, by then 'Hannah Mairs, wife of Isaac Mairs,' showed a balance of $227.30 'subject to a division between Penny Blackshare and James Blackshare and the above named Legatees,' who are named as Ezekiel, Elisha, Luke, David, Elijah, Jacob and Jesse. So Jesse had at least nine living children in 1814, and one of them is called Penny, the name Penelope Blackshear Grimes went by.

Jesse moved to Williamson County between 1800 and 1810; two of his sons stayed in North Carolina until after 1810. Some of the sons named in the settlement can be traced. Ezekiel (born 13 July 1792) lived in Williamson County in 1820, in Haywood County in 1830, and died at Brownsville on 23 April 1837; his widow, Isabella Dobson, was “bur. in the Ozarks” in 1882. Elisha (about 1794) farmed in Marshall County in 1840. Jacob (born 26 January 1802) moved to McNairy and Obion counties. The first child in the book’s list is “A dau., m. Grimes.”

Hannah was a Huggins, born on 20 May 1771 in Jones County; she died on 4 June 1829 in Wayne County, Tennessee, and was buried in Brown Cemetery, with a second husband, Isaac Mairs or Marrs, and a child by him born about 1807. Her youngest Blackshear child is given as born in March 1804, so Jesse's death and her second marriage fall between 1804 and about 1807. Her father is very probably the Luke Huggins whose Jones County will of 1784 names a daughter Hannah.

The two families were tied twice. Jesse’s father, Elisha Stout Blackshear, whose wife was Susannah, named 'James Huggins' as a son-in-law and his granddaughter 'Susanna Huggins' in his will, so a Huggins had already married a Blackshear daughter; Hannah, a Huggins, married a Blackshear son. Both families lived in Jones County.

stories.note: Jesse's father is stated in a printed genealogy, not in his father's will: Elisha Stout Blackshear's will names only sons Moses and Jacob, and the book says the other sons had already had their share and left. The book names no wife for Jesse; Hannah Huggins rests on WikiTree and a Texas family website. WikiTree's date of 26 July 1803 for Jesse's death sits oddly beside an estate settled in 1814, and WikiTree's 1814 death for Penelope is wrong if she was alive in 1850. Penny as the wife of John Grimes is probable, not proved; the next link down (that David H. Grimes of Wayne County was their son) is only a lead.
stories.place: Jesse was born in Jones (or Craven) County, North Carolina, about 1767, married there about 1788, and took his family to Williamson County, Tennessee, between 1800 and 1810. Hannah Huggins, born in Jones County in 1771, outlived him, remarried, and died in Wayne County, Tennessee, in 1829. Their daughter Penny is the probable wife of John Grimes.

stories.title: Luke Huggins and his 1784 will
stories.hook: A Jones County planter's will leaves a shilling each to his older children and the rest to the youngest, and one of the youngest is Hannah.
body: Luke Huggins was born about 1715, probably in North Carolina, and was a planter in Jones County, which was cut off from Craven County in 1779. He made his will on 8 March 1784 and it was proved in December of that year.

His will provided: to his wife Nelly, the plantation where he lived 'as long as she is a widow or as long as she lives'; to daughters Phebe Shelfer, Sarah Standley and Nelly Littleton, and sons James, Luke and Isaac, one shilling each; to his son Jacob, the land where he lived 'with all the rest of my lands'; and the remainder of the estate to 'my youngest children, namely: Esther, Hannah, Thomas, Charles, and Temperance Huggins,' at his wife's death. Simon Spight and John Parry were executors, and Nathan Bryan, Waxel Parry and Adonijah Parry witnessed.

Hannah was about thirteen. She married Jesse Blackshear a few years later, and the Jones County papers show other ties between the two families: Jesse's father named a James Huggins as son-in-law. A James is also among Luke's sons, so the two families may have married in both directions.

stories.title: Elisha Stout Blackshear's will: a black horse named Pal
stories.hook: Elisha's 1808 will leaves a granddaughter a black horse called Pal and a bed, and gives two grown sons nothing but their clothes because they had already had their share.
body: Elisha Stout Blackshear was born near Little Creek in Kent County, Delaware, about 1736, the son of Alexander and Agnes Blackshear, who left Delaware for Craven County, North Carolina, in the 1740s. His wife was Susanna. She was 'probably Ward': Enoch Ward of neighboring Carteret County named a daughter Susannah in his will, and Elisha's youngest son Jacob later named a son Enoch and lived beside an Enoch Ward in Georgia. No marriage bond has been found for either of them.

He was his father's executor. When Alexander's will was proved in Jones County in September 1786, 'Elisha Blackshear one of the Executors herein named qualified.' His mother's will of 1793 left him 'one Stone Jug for the service he hath done,' and her granddaughter Agnes, 'Elisha Blackshear's Daughter,' eight barrels of corn and her pockets and silver clasps.

His own will, dated 11 December 1808 and proved in November 1810, starts: 'I lend to my wife Susanna Blackshier (during her life or widowhood) my black Horse called Jack and all my household & kitchen furniture.' His sons Moses and Jacob get 'all my wearing clothes only, they having had their proportionable part of my Estate'; the daughters Rebecca, Susanna and Agnes 'have received their proportionable' share; Nancy gets an enslaved man and a young horse called Ball, Elizabeth gets the sheep, and Temperance gets the cattle, the hogs and the rest. To granddaughter Susanna Huggins he leaves 'my black horse called Pal, and one bed & furniture,' and to a granddaughter Koonce a bed. His sons-in-law James Huggins, Samuel Westbrook and Elijah Koonce share his carpenter's and plantation tools.

Jesse, our line, is not named in the will. Jesse was among the eleven children and 'moved to Tenn., and had Ezekiel'; the sons not named in the will, Alexander, James and Jesse, were presumed to have gotten their share earlier and 'struck out to find their fortunes in other parts.' Jesse's birth about 1767 fits Elisha, who would have been about thirty-one.

stories.title: Alexander and Agnes: from Delaware to the Trent
stories.hook: A Delaware clerk took Agnes aside in 1741 to ask whether she really agreed to sell the family farm; her own will of 1793, made with her mark, remembers a stone jug and some silver clasps.
body: In 1735 Robert Blackshaw deeded 100 acres at Little Creek Hundred in Kent County, Delaware, to 'My Son Alexander Blacksliare,' for 'the natural love I bear him.' The land was part of a tract called Blackshier Range, and Alexander already held a proprietary grant to survey it. Robert had been born in New Jersey and had come down the Delaware.

On 12 February 1740 (old style) Alexander and 'Agnis his wife, of Little Creek Hundred,' confirmed the sale of the 100 acres to the executors of Robert Carter of Dover Hundred, who had bought it in his lifetime for fifty pounds. The deed was acknowledged in the Court of Common Pleas on 14 May 1741, when, the clerk wrote, Agnes 'being secretly examined out of the hearing of the said husband did declare that she freely & voluntarily became a party.' Alexander signed with his mark. By 1747 Alexander was witnessing a will in Craven County, North Carolina; in 1748 he petitioned the council at New Bern for a grant.

Over forty years he built up a farm on the south side of the Trent. In 1779 he was taxed in Jones County on 517 acres and five enslaved people. He also turns up in the North Carolina Revolutionary army accounts of 1777 and 1786, in small amounts. His will, dated 3 October 1785, leaves his wife all his estate for her life, 'one Large Bible and one pair of Brass-headed Hand Irons' to his son James, a small house and one acre to his daughter Eleanor Bailey, 100 acres on the south side of the Trent to his son Abraham and then to Abraham's son Alexander, and 82 acres to Elisha until 'my Grandson Jacob Blackshear son of my son Elisha' reached twenty-one. Elisha and Nathan Bryan were executors, and it was proved in September 1786.

Agnes outlived him by seven years. Her will of 6 July 1793 gives 'Elisha Blackshear, my son, one Stone Jug for the service he hath done,' Abraham 'one barrel of Vinegar and my Garden,' and her granddaughter Agnes, 'Elisha Blackshear's Daughter,' eight barrels of corn due from a neighbor and 'my pockits and Silver Clasps.' She signed it 'Agnes B. Blackshear, her mark.' Her maiden name is not recorded.

stories.title: Robert Blackshaw, yeoman of Little Creek
stories.hook: The Blackshear name in this family began as Blackshaw and drifted to Blackshare, Blackshier and Blackshear through the spelling of clerks writing down what they heard.
body: Robert Blackshaw is the earliest of the line that can be followed through records. He was born at Piscataway, New Jersey, on 24 August 1677, 'son of Ellenor and Thomas Blackshaw.' By 1708 he had bought a lot on Second Street in Lewes, Delaware , and in 1712 that purchase came up at the Court of Quarter Sessions. In 1716 the Proprietaries' commissioners at Philadelphia issued warrants for 200 acres and 200 more in Kent County, and a survey of 207 acres near the head of Dover River.

He is listed as a yeoman and a farmer. In 1725 he deeded 200 acres, the grant of 1716, to 'Son Randall,' and in 1735 100 acres of 'Blackshares Range' to 'Son Alexander.' His surname 'began one of its many changes with this Robert, who started out with Blackshaw and ended with Blackshare; his sons went to Blackshere, Blackshier and Blackshear.'

Robert's wife is not named in any record. Robert's son Randall, who married Eve, stayed in Kent County, and Eve's will of 1762 is in the Kent County probate records; Alexander left for North Carolina after selling the land his father gave him.

stories.title: Thomas and Ellenor Blackshaw at Piscataway
stories.hook: Six babies in eleven years, four of them dead by 1688: all that is left of the first Blackshaw couple in the Delaware Valley.
body: Most American Blackshears descend from 'Robert Blackshaw, first documented as son of Thomas and Ellenor of Piscataway, N.J., 1677.' Thomas appears on a 1 January 1677-78 promissory note to Thomas Bloomfield of Woodbridge, for 'Good Merchantable Tobacco,' and as a freeholder in 1683 and again in a later list. He paid quit rents on 37 acres and is listed as an early patentee. He is not in the probate records of Middlesex or Monmouth counties.

The births were: Robert on 24 August 1677; a Thomas on 5 January 1679-80, dead two days later; Joseph on 13 April 1681, dead in October 1687; Timothy on 22 December 1682, 'd. soon'; a second Thomas on 3 September 1685, dead 24 October 1687; and a second Joseph on 15 May 1688. Only Robert and the second Joseph outlived their father.

It has been guessed that Thomas was the son of John Blackshaw and Maude Barlowe of the parish of Prestbury, Cheshire, whose son Thomas was baptised on 25 September 1631 and 'could very well be the first Blackshaw to establish a family in America.' That Thomas's marriage or death in Cheshire could not be found.

stories.title: William and Viney Clark: a bond with Henry Willis
stories.hook: In 1808 a Pulaski County marriage bond was signed by the groom and by Henry Willis; a veteran named Henry Willis said in his pension application that he had lived with William Clark during the War of 1812.
body: William Clark was born on 13 October 1785 in Granville County, North Carolina, and died on 6 January 1856 in Butler County. His wife was 'Vina Clarke' in his household in 1850 and 'Luvina Clark' in 1860.

They married in 1808 in Pulaski County, Kentucky. The county marriage book has the couple's names in the wrong places: 'William Willis & Livina Clark.' Another listing files the same record under 'Viny Willis' and 'William Clark,' 1808. William Clark and Henry Willis stood as bondsmen.

Their first child, Lewis, was born in Pulaski County on 16 April 1809. The family moved to what became Butler County, where Mary (1815), Newton Jasper (6 August 1817), and Emeline (1820) were born, and then to what became Edmonson County, where Harvey was born in 1826. Lewis and Emeline died in Edmonson County and Mary and Harvey in Butler.

Newton Clark and Polly D. Elms married in Butler County on 24 January 1839, after a 20 January license; the return was signed on 25 January. At her death Melvina’s parents were given as Newton Clark and Mary Dunn; that her mother was Polly Elms is probable and the surname difference is unresolved. Melvina married a Johnson, and her daughter Samantha married John C. Satterfield, who is our line.

William Clark's gravestone, in the Clark-Whobrey Cemetery at Roundhill in Edmonson County, records the hour of his death: "In memory of William Clark consort of Vina Clark born Oct. the 13 1785 And departed this life Jan. 6 1856 on sunday morning 8 oo & 55 minutes." The sixth of January 1856 was a Sunday. The stone agrees with the dates given from the Kentucky death register and names his wife as Vina, the form the 1850 census uses.

The War of 1812 service credited to him is still unchecked. A roster lists several privates named William Clark or Clarke, all in companies from other counties. Captain Samuel Tate's Pulaski County company, the one in which a Henry Willis served in 1813, includes an Elisha Clarke but no William.

stories.place: William Clark was born in Granville County, North Carolina, on 13 October 1785. He married Lavina, called Viney, Willis in Pulaski County, Kentucky, in 1808, farmed in Butler County, and died there on 6 January 1856. Lavina, born in South Carolina about 1785, died in Butler County in 1877.

stories.title: Henry Willis: bondsman, levy-exempt, dead by 1818
stories.hook: The documents agree that a Henry Willis stood bond for Lavina Willis in 1808; they do not say whether he was her father.
body: A Henry Willis and his wife Mary sold land on the waters of Clifty Creek and Fishing Creek in Pulaski County, Kentucky, before 14 October 1800. In November 1807 the Pulaski County court excused Henry from the county levy because of old age and infirmity. The next year he is the Henry Willis who stood bond with William Clark for the marriage of Lavina Willis. By 1818 Mary appears alone on the Pulaski County tax list, which is the basis for his death date. In the spring court of 1820 a suit named John, George and Daniel Willis as his heirs.

A Henry Willis can be traced through Washington County, Virginia, where he took title to 400 acres in Rich Valley in 1781-82 and was presented by a grand jury in 1773 for living with Mary Cochran, then to Greene County, Tennessee, and then to Kentucky. That these are one man is 'most likely', but he disappears from each place just as a man of the same name shows up in the next.

Lavina is listed among his children only as a presumption: 'Lavina (aka Viney) Willis married William Clark in 1808. William Clark and Henry Willis stood as bondsmen. The presumption is that Viney is Henry's daughter.' Another Henry Willis, born about 1793, lived later in Edmonson County, drew a War of 1812 pension, and said he lived with William Clark in Pulaski County; that suggests William Clark lived in the household of Henry and Mary, which is how he would have met Viney.

A Henry Willis served in the War of 1812, listed among the privates of Captain Samuel Tate's company, Kentucky Mounted Volunteer Militia, "commanded by Colonel Michael Taul," with service from 23 August to 14 November 1813. The regiment was raised under Governor Isaac Shelby's address of 31 July 1813 and rendezvoused at Newport, Kentucky, on 31 August. Bennett H. Young's history of the campaign names the company's county: Taul's seventh regiment was made up of companies from Wayne, Cumberland and Knox, "and Captain Samuel Tate, of Pulaski."

Shelby's volunteers crossed into Upper Canada that autumn. At the Battle of the Thames on 5 October 1813, Young places General George E. King's brigade, the fifth and seventh regiments, "four hundred and fifty feet behind Trotter," in the second line. Where each private was that day is not recorded, and some men in Tate's company are marked "left behind," one of them "with lame horse."

The soldier was probably not the Henry Willis who stood bond in 1808. That man had been excused from the Pulaski County levy in November 1807 for old age and infirmity. The private of 1813 fits the younger Henry Willis, born about 1793, who later lived in Edmonson County, drew a War of 1812 pension and said he had lived with William Clark in Pulaski County. Nothing states how he was related to Lavina.

stories.title: A family quarrel ends in a stabbing, January 1938
stories.hook: Oscar Hulsey, 27, was arrested after a two-day search in the mountains north of Millerton for stabbing his wife's brother.
body: In the last week of January 1938, Oscar Hulsey and Eddie Stevenson of Millerton, named as his brother-in-law, had a family quarrel that ended with Stevenson stabbed. A local paper put it in six sentences under the headline "Oscar Hulsey Arrested on Assault Count."

It read: "Oscar Hulsey faces a charge of assault with attempt to kill after his arrest Monday night by Deputies James Houston and Bud Butler. He was charged in connection with the stabbing Saturday night of his brother-in-law Eddie Stevenson of Millerton. Stevenson is in the Sanitarium of Paris, where his condition was reported as satisfactory Monday afternoon. The stabbing followed a family quarrel, officers said. Hulsey was arrested in a remote mountain area 30 miles north of Millerton after a two-day search." By its dates the stabbing was Saturday night, 29 January, and the arrest Monday night, 31 January.

The charge did not go away quickly. The district court dockets of September and October 1938 list "the State of Oklahoma vs. Oscar Hulsey" as assault and battery with intent to kill for the October 1938 term, and the dockets of September 1939 list it again, set for Saturday, 14 October 1939. No sentence, plea or dismissal is known. By April 1940 Oscar was back in Arkansas at South Fork in Montgomery County, working on a government job, and in 1941 his marriage to Katie ended in divorce.

stories.title: Killed on his bicycle, July 1947
stories.hook: Bennie George Hulsey, 13, turned in front of a pickup truck west of Hugo and died within the hour.

subject.name: Bennie George Hulsey and the pickup truck

body: The report read: "Choctaw County's second highway fatality was suffered Tuesday night when Bennie George Hulsey, 13, died of injuries received when he turned in front of a pickup truck on his bicycle, the local highway patrol unit reported." Three eyewitnesses told the patrolmen that the boy turned directly into the path of a truck driven by Mack Flinn, 29, of Grant, on U.S. 70 two miles west of Hugo in front of Leon Griffin's store, about 7:30 p.m.

"The boy, son of Mrs. Katie Hulsey, Hugo Route One, was rushed to the Hugo hospital but he succumbed 45 minutes later from a compound fracture of the skull and internal injuries." The patrol said he was knocked 75 feet; Flinn's truck swerved off the road, jumped a four-foot fill and turned over once and a half. Flinn had only a few bruises and two other men in the truck were slightly hurt. The boy's death "marked the second road fatality in Choctaw County during 1947."

Services were set for 11 a.m. Thursday at the Coffey Funeral Home chapel, with burial at Mount Olivet. He was a member of the Assembly of God church and had been born in Danville, Arkansas, the paper says, and had moved with his mother and family to a place on Hugo Route One. The survivors named in the continuation are his mother, his father Oscar Hulsey of Wright City, two sisters, Mrs. Delphia Murphy of Oregon and Mary of Hugo, and four brothers, Leon, Glen, Charles and Willis, all of Hugo. Mary was his sister Mary Ellen, then eight years old.

The Idabel paper, where the Hulseys had lived, ran the story on its front page on Saturday, 26 July, under the headline “Former County Youth Dies in Bicycle Mishap.” It adds what the boys were doing. Pulling a home-made wooden sled and a toy wagon behind their bicycles, Bennie and the son of Leon Griffin had been riding back and forth between the Griffin home and the Griffin store. Bennie and the truck were both headed east when he turned north toward the store's driveway. Highway patrolman Cecil Snapp and Sheriff Bird Collins investigated. It names him as the son of Oscar Hulsey of Wright City and Mrs. Katie Hulsey of Hugo Route 1, and lists his injuries as internal injuries, a compound fracture of the skull and broken ribs.

stories.title: Two courthouses and a second wife
stories.hook: Oscar and Katie were divorced in Arkansas in 1941 and he remarried five weeks later; Katie then sued in Oklahoma, and in January 1946 her divorce was one of a record 26 granted in a single day.
body: Oscar and Katie Hulsey were divorced on 26 September 1941 in Montgomery County, Arkansas. On 3 November 1941, five weeks later, Oscar Hulsey, 31, of Mount Ida, married Hester May Whittington; his birth date was given as 27 October 1910.

The two may have married again afterward. A marriage license was filed in McCurtain County on 27 February 1943 for "HULSEY, OSCAR F" and "STEVESON, KATIE," both named as applicants. It gives no ages or residences, and the paper license is held by the court clerk at Idabel, so whether it records a second marriage of the couple after the Arkansas divorce is not known. If it does, it would explain why Katie needed a divorce in Oklahoma as well.

Katie went back to Oklahoma and appears to have brought a second action there. The court docket of 10 October 1945 reads "Katie Hulsey vs. Os[car Hulsey], divorce," and from 24 November to 15 December 1945 a notice by publication was run in the district court with Katie Hulsey as plaintiff and Oscar Hulsey as defendant, addressed "To: Oscar Hulsey."

The suit ended in January 1946. On Saturday, 12 January 1946, the Idabel paper reported on its front page that a county record had been broken that Wednesday: District Judge George R. Childers had granted 26 divorces in a single day, one more than the previous record of 25, the court clerk, Buel Grinage, said. The paper printed every one of them, the first name of the spouse who filed followed by the other's full name: Addie from C. L. Mahon, Lorene from Jesse Ramage, Floyd from Mary Dimmitt, and so on down a column of twenty-six names. Near the bottom, between Rosa Bell from Lonnie Lewis and John from Dorothy Keiss, is "Katie from Oscar Hulsey." The same front page, a column over, carried the homecoming notices of local men just out of the Army and Navy, which may explain why the judge had so much to do.

By 1950, with both the Arkansas divorce of 1941 and the Oklahoma divorce of 1946 behind them, Katie, 40, was head of a household at Jeter in Choctaw County with her children Glen, Mary, Charley and Willis, "Separated" and "Keeping house." An Oscar Hulsey, "Divorced," lived alone as a farmer on the road between Wright City and Gloster in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, the township where his parents had farmed; he was 38, born in Oklahoma, so the match is probable, not certain.
No reason is given for either divorce.

stories.title: Lydia Payne's parents, in her son's words
stories.hook: The only direct statement of who Lydia Payne's parents were comes from her preacher son: William Payne, a six-month Revolutionary militiaman, and Catherine Arnold.
body: Rev. Elam Stevenson's wife Lydia is the mother of Abner and the grandmother of Frank Stevenson, but her own people were not named in anything the family kept. The answer comes from her son, Rev. John Baxter Stevenson, who wrote a short note about his mother: "My mother was born in Burke Co., N.C., Aug. 16. Her father was William Payne. Her mother was Catherine Arnold. Her ancestry were of English extraction. Her father belonged to the militia during the Revolutionary War, and was in the service six months." He adds that she joined the Methodist church in August 1802 and that "her parents were both of the Methodist Church."

That is a son's own written statement about his mother's parents, as direct as a family record gets, though it is a recollection and not a birth or marriage record, and no will or deed names Lydia as William's daughter. The place fits the Stevenson story: Elam is said to have married Lydia Paine in North Carolina in 1805, and Burke County lies in the same western North Carolina country as Elam's birthplace in what is now Alexander County.

A William Paine household, spelled "Wm Pain" in 1790, was in Burke County in 1790 (twelve people) and 1800 (thirteen), and a widow of the name was there in 1810. William is said to have died on 15 October 1807 and to have a gravestone at Rocky Mount Cemetery, Granite Falls. His children are given as Thomas; Abner Burgess Payne (1777-1845); Sarah, who married a Boyce; and Lydia C. Sarah is placed at Bee Spring, Giles County, in 1830 and 1840, with a grave in the Bee Spring Cemetery, so Lydia seems to have had a sister in the same church neighborhood. A history of the Bee Spring society names a Rev. Meshach Boyce among its first members and says he is buried in the churchyard there; that he was Sarah's husband is a guess.

William is made a son of John Paine of Spotsylvania County, Virginia, whose 1764 will names a son William. Two different men named William Paine have been attached to Catherine Arnold's family, and more research is needed to rule one out, so the step back from William Paine of Burke County to John Paine is unproven.

stories.title: A Spotsylvania will with a daughter 'Catey'
stories.hook: A 1774 Spotsylvania will names a daughter Catey, and a tree makes her Catherine Arnold, wife of William Payne of Burke County.
body: Catherine Arnold is said to have been born about 1751 in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, a daughter of William Arnold (about 1714 to after 1774) and Lydia Bell. The one record behind this is the will of William Arnold, who died there on 17 September 1774 and "names a daughter Catey." Her marriage to William Payne is unsupported.

William Paine's own family is also placed in Spotsylvania, and he and his wife are said to have sold his share of his father's estate there on 20 November 1777 before the family moved to Burke County, North Carolina. A daughter named Lydia may echo Catherine's mother Lydia. None of this has been checked against the will, the deed or a record that gives Catherine's age or origin, so Catherine Arnold's parents are carried here only as a possibility.

stories.title: A family note on the Stevenson immigrant
stories.hook: A family compiler's 1955 notes say James Stevenson of Iredell County was the son of an Irish immigrant James, not of the William some trees give him.

subject.name: James Stevenson, immigrant from Ireland, & Sally Kelly

body: A family book on the Skinner ancestry covers the Stevensons because Rev. Elam Stevenson's descendants married into that line. Its Stevenson chapter first follows a chart that starts with William Stevenson, born in County Antrim, Ireland, who came to Pennsylvania in 1748 and to Iredell County, North Carolina in 1762. Then it adds a correction from "data received May 11, 1955": "The father of James Stevenson was not William Stevenson, immigrant, but was James Stevenson, immigrant from Ireland, who died in 1820. James I married Sally Kelly of Md., who died about 1820 or 1821. James Stevenson II, who m. Jane Stevenson, died in 1828. She died 1814."

James II is the James Stevenson whose 1828 will in Iredell County names his son Elam; his wife Jane is the Jane Stevenson of the next generation. The chapter also quotes McFerrin that Elam was the son of James Stephenson of Iredell, now Alexander County, "who was a Captain in the Revolutionary War." Another passage in the same book says James Stevenson "was born in Ireland. Settled in North Carolina about 1775" and had two other sons besides Elam, which does not agree with the 1955 note (James II would then be the immigrant).

The dates do not fit well: if James II was born about 1746, an immigrant father who died in 1820 and a mother who died about 1820 or 1821 would both have been very old. The 1955 note is therefore a family compiler's statement, not a record, and the parents of James Stevenson stay uncertain until a will, deed or church record names them.

quotes.t: The father of James Stevenson was not William Stevenson, immigrant, but was James Stevenson, immigrant from Ireland, who died in 1820.

stories.title: Jane Stevenson's parents: John, and a Thompson
stories.hook: The same 1955 notes say Elam Stevenson's mother Jane was a Stevenson by birth, daughter of John Stevenson, who died in 1794, and a woman named Thompson.
body: Elam Stevenson's mother is only ever called Jane Stevenson, and the compiler of the Skinner book's Stevenson chapter noted that the wives' maiden names show "Stephenson was Jane's maiden name, and not a variation" of her husband's. In the same note: "James Stevenson II, who m. Jane Stevenson, died in 1828. She died 1814. Jane was the daughter of John Stevenson (d. 1794), and a Thompson."

Nothing more is given: no first name or dates for Jane's mother, no place, no will. This is the only place that names Jane's parents, and it is a compiler's statement from 1955 with no source given, so it stays unproven. Another passage of the book puts the marriage of James and Jane about 1765 and calls James a soldier of the Revolution.

Jane's household was Scots-Irish and Presbyterian, and it did not welcome her son Elam's turn to the Methodists. He joined that church in 1806, the third son and the first of the family to do so, and by his own memory his parents honestly believed he was being deceived by false teachers. He was licensed to preach in 1813. That year, as he got ready to move to Tennessee, a neighbor named Philip Bruce asked him to carry part of his books in the wagon. Jane died the next year. Elam settled near Bunker Hill in Giles County, founded the church at Bee Spring, and died on 13 March 1875, "nearly 62 years a minister," three years after his wife Lydia.

stories.title: Jesse Hulsey, the wounded soldier of Hall County
stories.hook: A Revolutionary veteran with an Indian wound and a North Carolina pension lived in Hall County, Georgia, when Salathiel Hulsey did; whether he was Salathiel's father is open.
body: Jesse Hulsey, "a veteran of the American Revolution," was still living in Greenville District, South Carolina, in 1800, one of only two of the family left in the state, was in Hall County, Georgia, in 1820, and drew a Revolutionary land lottery lot in Troup County in 1827 (granted 12 January 1829). In 1840, at 81, he was a Revolutionary soldier in Hall County.

Then there is his North Carolina pension: on 25 November 1822 Jesse, "of Hawl Co. Ga.," named Samuel Carson his attorney to collect the pension the North Carolina legislature allowed him "in consideration of a wound which I received by the Indians in the Revolutionary War"; he appointed another agent in 1826, and a man swore in Wake County in December 1835 that he had seen him alive in September in Hall County. Family trees call him Jesse Hamilton Hulsey, born 1760 in Goochland County, Virginia, and list the blacksmith Salathiel Hulsey (born about 1807, Franklin County, Georgia) among his many children by Mary Tharp.

A North Carolina resolution of the 1834–35 session directs the treasurer to pay all pension arrears to Jesse Hulsey, then living in Georgia, or his agent N. Edmonson, and to continue payments for Jesse's lifetime. The resolution says his pension had been allowed by an act passed in 1824. It names no wife, children or Georgia county, so it supports the pension account without proving that Jesse was Salathiel's father. Its 1824 date also leaves a question about the 1822 power of attorney, which has not been checked against its original.

The link to our Salathiel is a family-tree assertion. The pieces that fit are place and names: Salathiel is on the 1840 census of Hall County, and his 1850 household in Union County has a Jesse, 10, and a Jennings, 8, while the Georgia history names a Jennings Hulsey who stayed in South Carolina with Jesse in 1800. The pieces that do not fit: the same family tree says a son Jesse Jr. married Mary Tharp in "1779" in Franklin County, Alabama, which cannot be right; the Georgia history treats Jesse as possibly a brother of James Hulsey Sr. of Hall County; and no will, deed or census that lists Salathiel as Jesse's son has been found.

stories.title: A widower in Hopkins County
stories.hook: In 1880 George W. Langley, 38, was alone with two small daughters and his wife's brother and sisters in the house.
body: In 1880, in Precinct 5 of Hopkins County, Texas, George W. Langley, 38, born in Georgia, headed a household. His daughters were Emma J., 12, and Eliza J., 8, both born in Texas. No wife is listed. His own parents were born in Georgia too.

Hopkins County was a young place. The Texas legislature had created it in 1846, its seat had been Sulphur Springs only since 1870, and southerners settled most of it. A rail line, the East Line and Red River Railroad, reached the county in 1876, four years before the count. Emma was born in Texas about 1867, so George had made the move from Georgia by then.

Living with him are Jacob Black, 29, called brother-in-law, and Sarah J. Quinton, 32, and Elizabeth Black, 23, called sisters-in-law. Two Black siblings under his roof and no wife make it likely that Mrs. Langley, born a Black, had died before the count. Other family trees name her Mary F. Black, but that is only a suggestion and is not entered here. What became of George after 1880 is not known.

Emma Elizabeth Langley, wife of John B. Smith, was born on 11 December 1867 in Texas, which makes her 12 in June 1880. The daughter is Emma J., so the identification rests on age, birthplace and neighborhood (Hopkins County lies beside Franklin County, where Emma died in 1905), not on anything naming Emma Elizabeth. If it holds, George stands behind Emma's son Charles Oscar Smith, born in 1889, whose youngest daughter Faye married into the Moffitts.

stories.title: Frances Thompson and the family at Jeter
stories.hook: Frances and Simon built a household at Jeter that included three generations of the family.
body: Frances Pisachubbe was born in 1907 to Robert Pisachubbe and Lizzie Austin. Her parents came from Choctaw families who had been enrolled together in 1899: Robert with his mother Eunice, and Lizzie with her parents Legion and Molsey.

Enrollment in the Choctaw Nation was bound by dates set in law. An act approved on 26 April 1906 allowed a limited application period for children who were minors living on 4 March 1906. Frances was born the following year, which helps explain why she was never enrolled herself.

Frances married Simon Thompson in 1925. In 1930 the couple shared a household at Jeter, Oklahoma, with her parents. Ten years later Simon and Frances were on a farm they owned, valued at $400, with five children in the household.

In 1950 the family was still at Jeter. Frances, then about 42, lived with Simon, five children and her mother Lizzie Pisachubbe, so that the household still held the older generation of the Austin and Pisachubbe families. Frances is buried at Long Creek Cemetery; her marker gives 1979, though a family tree dates her death to April 1978.

stories.title: Lizzie Austin and the two sisters who married two brothers
stories.hook: A seven-year-old of Fowlerville in 1899 became the grandmother who kept a twelve-person house at Jeter.
body: Lizzie Austin was enrolled as a Choctaw on 21 May 1899, when her father Legion applied for the family at Fowlerville in Towson County. She was written down as 7 years old, full-blood, the daughter of Legion and Molsey; by the time the enrollment was approved on 12 December 1902 she was put at 10. Her age moved around in later years too: 42 in 1940, 58 in 1950. The earlier ages point to a birth about 1892, and the 1950 age agrees.

Her small family was already losing members. Her brother James, born 15 November 1898, was enrolled with a note that he died in April 1899, and a younger sister arrived the next year: Adline, born 5 August 1900 and enrolled in June 1901. The two girls grew up to marry brothers. Adline married William Harrison Pisachubbe, and Lizzie married his younger brother Robert, the son of the widow Eunice Pisachubbe of Goodland. The children of the two marriages were double first cousins.

In the summer of 1915 Lizzie, listed as "Lizzie Pisachubbee, nee Austin," applied to have federal restrictions lifted from her land. By 1917 Robert was 28, married with a child, and farming for himself at Speer. In 1920 Lizzie and Robert owned their farm in Jeter Township with their daughter Frances, Robert's widowed mother Eunice, and a young cousin.

The house grew crowded as the old generation died. Her mother Molsey died in 1924 and Eunice in 1927. Adline died at Speer in 1929 and her husband William Harrison in 1937, leaving their children, and by 1940 Lizzie and Robert shared one household at Jeter with Frances, her husband Simon Thompson and their five children, and Alice, Eli and Edward, the orphaned niece and nephews: twelve people. Frances had married Simon in 1925, and so the Austin and Pisachubbe families were joined with Joseph and Betsy Thompson's line. Lizzie was still in that household in 1950 and died in 1964. She is buried at Long Creek Cemetery near Hugo, the cemetery where Simon and Frances lie.

stories.title: The old place north of Doaksville
stories.hook: Vinson Tims farmed north of Doaksville, where his daughter Betsy married Joseph Thompson in 1889 and where he is said to be buried.
body: Vinson W. Tims was born in 1838, the elder son of the Doaksville trader Vincent B. Tims. He and Emeline farmed in the High Hill neighborhood of Towson County, 'about four miles north and a little west of Doaksville,' on land later called the Charley Blankenship place. Their children included James, Mitchell, Betsy (Mrs. Joseph Thompson), John, Rev. Robert Tims, Willie, Rosie (Mrs. James Wilson) and Calvin.

Betsy married Joseph Thompson at that house in 1889. Joel remembered his grandparents as 'buried there at the old place,' which fits the marker at High Hill, a cenotaph that carries only his name and no dates.

The memorial at High Hill Cemetery gives his years as 1838 to 25 October 1891, but a Choctaw census of 1896 seems to show Vinson still living with Emeline and their family in Towson County, and in 1899 Betsy's father, written 'Vincent Tims,' was said to be dead. So when he died is unsettled: 1891 on the memorial, or after 1896 if the 1896 entry is his.

A memoir of his son Robert, printed in 1944 in the minutes of the Methodist Indian Mission, calls Robert "the son of Vincent and Emiline Tims." So the family's own church used "Vincent" for him where the High Hill marker says "Vinson."

Vinson never enrolled, because he was gone by 1899, but his name survives in his children's enrollments. In 1899 clerks wrote it as "Vinson W. Tims" for James B., "Vincent Tims" for Betsy, Robert and Willie, and "Benson Tims" for Mitchell. In every case he was marked dead and placed in Towson County, where the family lived.

stories.title: Eunice Pisachubbe’s family and allotment
stories.hook: A Choctaw widow of Goodland, her sons, and the land they asked leave to sell after her death in 1927.
body: After Eunice died on 19 May 1927, her sons Robert and William H. Pisachubbe, "the lawful issue of the marriage between Joseph Pisachubbe and Eunice Pisachubbe," petitioned the Choctaw County court to approve the sale of her allotment of about 159 acres for $1,200. As full-blood Choctaw land, it could not be sold without a judge's approval. Joseph, their father, had died long before her, and she never remarried.

When Eunice was enrolled at Goodland in Kiamitia County on 10 May 1899, she was 49, full-blood, the daughter of Jackson and Viney Gardner, both dead, of Blue County. Her sons William H., 16 (on the 1896 roll as "William Harrison"), and Robert, 11, were enrolled with her, their father, "Joseph Pisachubbe," dead. Also with them was not a son but Edward Pisachubbe, 17, her ward, whose own dead parents were Simpson and Sallie Pisachubbe of Jackson County, and who was already the husband of Frances Byington.

In 1896 Eunice, Robert and Edward had been counted together as one household in Kiamitia County. William was not with them; he was away at school, and an August 1899 student list from Armstrong Academy put him down again as "Harrison"; a finding in 1911 held that he had been enrolled twice. All four were approved by the Secretary of the Interior on 12 December 1902.

William's son Colbert, born on 26 June 1906, was refused enrollment because he came after the 4 March 1906 cutoff. To settle the question of William's double enrollment, testimony was taken in 1909 from four witnesses, and the Commissioner's letter of 1 August 1911 lists them: William H. Pisachubbe, Eunice Pisachubbe, Harrison Nohio and Thomas Hunter.

Eunice’s land lay in Section 29 of Township 5 South, Range 17 East, less two strips for the St. Louis and San Francisco Railway’s right of way: 10.80 acres from one tract and .01 acre from another, leaving 159.19 acres. Robert and William asked the court to approve a $1,200 deed to L. C. Hudgens; whether the court approved it is not known.

William H. went to school at Armstrong Academy in 1899 under the name Harrison, and for twelve years the Dawes rolls carried him twice, once as William H. and once as Harrison, until the Indian Office struck the duplicate in 1911. In the summer of 1927, a few weeks after their mother's death, Robert and Lizzie and William and Adeline sold forty acres of land to L. C. Hudgens.

stories.title: Joseph Pisachubbe, the father who left little but his name
stories.hook: Dead by 1899, he left two sons, William Harrison and Robert, and a name his descendants still carry.
body: Joseph Pisachubbe is hard to find. When his widow Eunice enrolled the family at Goodland in Kiamitia County on 10 May 1899, the clerk entered his name as the father of her sons William H., 16, and Robert, 11, with the single word "Dead" beside it. He left no enrollment of his own. His sons were born about 1883 and 1888, so he was alive into the late 1880s. Eunice, Robert and their ward Edward Pisachubbe were counted together in 1896, and he was not with them; that alone does not say when he died.

Eunice's widowhood is nearly all that remains of him. When she died on 19 May 1927, her sons Robert and William H. petitioned the Choctaw County court as "the lawful issue of the marriage between Joseph Pisachubbe and Eunice Pisachubbe," and said that he died long before her and that she never remarried. The 159-acre allotment she asked to sell lay in Section 29, Township 5 South, Range 17 East, the same section where Robert's own allotment lies.

The only account of where the family came from was given at William Harrison's death in 1937 by his relative Judge T. W. Hunter: the Pisachubbes came from Mississippi in 1832 with the first group of Choctaw exiles and settled at Fort Coffee, near present-day Spiro. The date has to be read with care. Fort Coffee was established on the Arkansas River only in June 1834, so the family's "in 1832" and "at Fort Coffee" describe the neighborhood by the later landmark; by 1899 they were in Kiamitia County, where a Presbyterian mission had worked at Goodland since 1848. No one says whether Joseph himself was born in Mississippi or among the first children born in the new Nation.

His own parents are unknown. Some family trees give them as a man called Pisachubbe or Wilson and Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, but the Nancy of that name enrolled in 1899 was 69, born about 1830, and her age alone neither establishes nor rules out a mother-and-son relationship; nothing links her to Joseph. A "Case Pisachubbi" and a Sarah Pisachubbi also appear among the Choctaw enrolled, but nothing connects either to Joseph. What his descendants can be certain of is the name, which they carry through Robert and Lizzie to Frances Thompson, and which the clerks spelled Pisachubbe, Pisachubbee and Pisachubbi from one document to the next.

stories.title: John and Betsy Thompson, Joseph's parents
stories.hook: Two names, and a grandson's memory of a burial, are all that survive of the parents of Judge Joseph Thompson.
body: When Joseph P. Thompson was enrolled at Doaksville in Cedar County on 1 May 1899, he gave his parents as "John Thompson" and "Betsy Thompson," both dead, both of Cedar County. Joseph's wife shared his mother's first name, and both women were Betsy. Joseph was born in December 1861, the year the Choctaw Nation sided with the Confederacy, and in 1910 he named Mississippi as the birthplace of both his parents.

His son Joel, interviewed in Hugo in 1937, remembered the rest. Joseph was the second of nine children. John died when Joseph was nine, about 1870, and was buried near the family home toward Spencer Academy. Spencer, which had closed in 1861, reopened in 1871, and Joseph, who had lost his father the year before, was of school age during its reopened years; he was educated at Spencer, and from there he went east to Roanoke College in Virginia.

Betsy's side was a harder subject. Joel said his father's mother's people "had some sort of a Choctaw name" and never took a white man's name, which fits a pattern seen elsewhere in this family: surnames such as Thompson, Austin and Gardner came into use among the Choctaw after the 1830s, often borrowed from the given name of a respected white man, while others, like Pisachubbe and Ata-sa-ha-bi, kept their Choctaw names to the end.

The neighborhood that marked their lives was High Hill, where the Methodist church stood two miles east of their son's birthplace; Joseph later built his white house 300 yards from it, and Emeline Tims, his mother-in-law, is buried in its cemetery. Henry W. Thompson, who was enrolled the same day, was not their son: his parents were Simon and Lucy. The names of Joseph's eight brothers and sisters are unknown.

stories.title: Legion Austin, who swore to his baby son's birth
stories.hook: A Choctaw father, a neighbor and a baby boy whose short life is told in two different ways.
body: Legion Austin, 33, a full-blood Choctaw of Towson County, lived near Fowlerville. His father was Ata-sa-ha-bi and his mother Lotima, both dead and both of Towson County. His wife Molsey's parents, Brazil and Siney of Red River, were also dead.
Fowlerville's post office was established on 7 July 1894 and renamed Valliant on 23 June 1902.

Legion applied for enrollment on 21 May 1899 for his household at Fowlerville. In the end it counted five people: Legion, Molsey, their daughter Lizzie, a son James, whose date of death is told two ways, and a baby daughter Adline, born on 5 August 1900. Legion himself wrote to the Commission from Garvin in October 1900 asking for a blank application for an infant child; the Commission sent it on 9 October. The baby was enrolled on 4 June 1901, as a Commission letter of 5 June 1901 to William Swink at Fowlerville records: "Adline Austin, the infant daughter of Leageon and Muley Austin, born August 5, 1900," the clerk's spellings of Legion and Molsey.

James was recorded as having died in April 1899, with proof of death filed, and his enrollment was canceled in 1904. Yet the birth statement signed by Legion and his neighbor Leonidas Willis on 2 May 1899 still carries the printed words that the child was then living. Which date is right, no one can say.

In 1896 the family had been counted in Towson County, where the clerk wrote his name as "Legend Austin." The Commission approved Legion, Molsey, Lizzie and Adline on 12 December 1902. By then Legion's age was put at 36, three years more than the 33 given in 1899, and neither agrees with his own testimony in November 1902 that he was "about fifty."

He signed by mark. For the statement about his infant son James, sworn at Fowlerville in early May 1899, the clerk crossed out the form's printed "Affidavit of Mother" and wrote "Father" above it, and Legion, "33 years of age and a citizen by blood," swore as the husband of Molsey that the boy was born 15 November 1898. The man who vouched for the birth was a neighbor, Leonidas Willis, who also signed with a mark and is written in as "a Neighbor," not a physician. Nobody named a doctor or midwife for that birth.

stories.title: Molsey Austin and the midwife at Adline's birth
stories.hook: In 1901 Molsey and the midwife who helped her each made their mark to attest her daughter’s birth.
body: On 19 April 1901, Molsey Austin gave a sworn statement about the birth of her daughter Adline, who was born on 5 August 1900 to Molsey and her husband Legion Austin. The family's post office was Fowlerville, Indian Territory, and both parents were citizens of the Choctaw Nation.

Below Molsey's statement stands a second one, made by Sinie Hall, the midwife who attended the birth. Both women signed by mark. J. R. Moore and Sallie Johnson witnessed the marks, and William Swink signed as notary. Together they preserve a mother's account and the name of the woman who helped at the birth.

Molsey's parents were Brazil and Siney of Red River County, and her children were Lizzie, James, said to have died in April 1899, and Adline. The name Siney belonged both to Molsey's mother and, in a similar form, to the midwife, but no one can say whether the two women were related.

The clerks spelled the family's names in several ways, including “Mulcy” for Molsey and “Leageon” for Legion. A later land list gives her as “Molsey Pisachubbi, Austin,” which suggests she later carried the name Pisachubbi.

stories.title: John Steadman, the father of the midwife
stories.hook: A man marked as no citizen of the Choctaw Nation: the father of the Doaksville midwife.
body: When Emeline was enrolled in 1899, the clerk wrote her father as "John Steadman," dead and "Non Citz."; she herself was enrolled as a Choctaw citizen by blood, and her mother was O-we-na. The noncitizen label does not say John's race or birthplace. Emeline was put down as one-quarter Choctaw, but no fraction was written for either parent, so O-we-na's ancestry cannot be worked out from it.

Emeline was born on 26 January 1842, while Fort Towson was still an army post and Doaksville a trading town. Her grandson Joel Thompson could not recall her maiden name when he was interviewed in 1937, so the name Steadman comes from her enrollment and not from family memory. In 1896 she was counted in Towson County as Emeline Tims, aged 57; by the time the final roll was made she was put at 60.

He may have been Irish; family says so. Nothing gives his birthplace, residence or death year, only that he was dead by 1899. But his line traveled far from him. His daughter married Vinson W. Tims, a son of the Doaksville trader Vincent B. Tims, and bore eight children, among them Betsy, who married Judge Joseph P. Thompson in 1889. Emeline herself lived to see her grandson Simon born on 4 May 1899, attended his birth as midwife and swore the statement that put him on the roll.

The law John Steadman married under was strict on paper. An act of October 1840 barred any white man from marrying in the Choctaw Nation until he had been a citizen for two years and required a license from a judge or the district clerk and a ceremony by a minister "before he shall be entitled and admitted to the privilege of citizenship." It forbade a white husband to dispose of his Choctaw wife's property without her consent. Emeline was born in January 1842, so her parents' marriage falls close to the passing of that act. No license or marriage for John and O-we-na has been found, and the "Non Citz." of 1899 records only how the Commission classed him, not whether he ever held Choctaw citizenship.

stories.title: O-we-na, the mother who is a name and a county
stories.hook: Emeline Tims’s mother is known only by her name and her county, Towson.
body: O-we-na is the only parent of Emeline whom the clerks placed in a Choctaw county. In 1899, when her daughter sat before the Dawes Commission, O-we-na was written down as dead and of Towson County, the same county in which Emeline Tims was counted in the 1896 census and lived north of Doaksville. Emeline's father, John Steadman, was marked "Non Citz." O-we-na herself never had an enrollment of her own, because she was gone before any roll was made.

She is a woman we see only by what her daughter carried forward. Emeline was born on 26 January 1842, so O-we-na was a mother in the years just after the Choctaw removal, when Fort Towson was still an army post and Doaksville a trading town. The Choctaw law of October 1840 required a white man to be licensed by a judge and married by a minister before he could claim citizenship through marriage, and Emeline's birth falls very near that law. No license or marriage for John and O-we-na has been found, so how they lived together is unrecorded.

The hyphens in her name are the clerk's. Clerks wrote Choctaw names by ear and broke them into syllables, and O-we-na may have been spelled quite differently by the person who said it. Its meaning is not recorded, and neither is any year of birth or death for her. Emeline was recorded as one-quarter Choctaw, but nothing was written of O-we-na's ancestry, so the fraction cannot be divided between her parents.

What she left behind was a daughter who became the midwife of Doaksville. Emeline married Vinson Tims, raised eight children, and in October 1899 swore that she had attended her grandson Simon's birth. Through Emeline, O-we-na is an ancestor of the Tims and Thompson families of High Hill and of Simon's descendants around Hugo. Her place of burial is unknown.

stories.title: Jackson and Viney Gardner of Blue County
stories.hook: Eunice Pisachubbe's parents, both dead by 1899, lived in the county that held Armstrong Academy.
body: When their daughter Eunice was enrolled at Goodland in Kiamitia County on 10 May 1899, she gave her parents as "Jackson Gardner" and "Viney Gardner," both dead, both of Blue County. Eunice was 49, which puts her birth about 1850. She was counted in Kiamitia, her husband's county, not her parents'.

Blue County in the Choctaw Nation lay in the Pushmataha District, and Armstrong Academy, the Choctaw boys' school where Eunice's son William Harrison's name turned up on a student list in August 1899, stood in it. By 1894 Blue sent one senator, like Kiamichi, Atoka and Jack's Fork. In 1886 the Council cut a new Jackson County from Kiamitia, Blue and Atoka. Samuel G. Gardner of Blue County was a probate judge, but nothing connects Jackson and Viney to him.

Family trees suggest that Jackson was born in Mississippi around 1820, but nothing establishes his birthplace or birth year. A Carney maiden name and other given names for Viney also appear in trees without support. Their daughter Eunice married Joseph Pisachubbe and lived at Goodland, where she raised two sons and a ward. After her death on 19 May 1927, her sons petitioned to sell her 159-acre allotment in Section 29, Township 5 South, Range 17 East.

The Choctaw Nation counted its own people decades before the federal commission made its rolls. A surviving 1860 census of Towson County, for example, lists households, ages, occupations and places of birth, and counts like it may one day carry Jackson and Viney back a generation. A matching name alone would not prove that a person was this Jackson or this Viney, and for now they remain two names beside the word "dead."

stories.title: Brazil and Siney of Red River County
stories.hook: Molsey Austin's parents, Brazil and Siney, lived in the Choctaw Nation's Red River County.
body: When their daughter Molsey Austin was enrolled in 1899, the clerk wrote her parents down as "Brazil," dead, of Red River, and "Siney," dead, of Red River, setting the mother's name in quotation marks. The quotation marks may mean the clerk was unsure of the spelling or that it was a nickname. Brazil was given no surname.

Red River County was one of the Choctaw Nation's counties along the Red River on the Texas border. Molsey was counted in Towson County in 1896 , after her husband Legion Austin, so she had moved from Red River County to Towson. Molsey was 22 in 1899 and swore she was 25 in April 1901, which puts her birth about 1876 or 1877.

A midwife named Sinie Hall attended the birth of Molsey's daughter Adline on 5 August 1900, and signed her statement with her mark at Fowlerville. The two spellings may be the same name; nothing says the two women were kin. What Brazil and Siney left is Molsey, who signed with her mark as "Mulcy Austin" and was later listed as "Molsey Pisachubbi, Austin," and the children of her household: Lizzie, James and Adline.

Red River County was one of the nineteen counties the General Council laid out in 1850, in the southeast corner of the Nation. The Red River was its southern line, Little River its northern, Arkansas its eastern, and a line between the two rivers divided it from Towson County. On the 1889 Rand McNally map of Indian Territory it is almost empty: Kuli Inla, renamed Shawneetown in 1892, and Harris Ferry on the Red River are about the only names in it. Garvin, Idabel and Kullituklo came later, and at statehood in 1907 the whole county went into McCurtain County.
Molsey's move was a short one. Towson County began just across the line to the west, and the Garvin post office her husband was writing from in 1900 stood in her parents' old county.

stories.title: Ata-sa-ha-bi and Lotima of Towson County
stories.hook: Legion Austin's parents survive only as two Choctaw names.
body: Legion Austin's parents were written down in 1899 as "Ata-sa-ha-bi," dead, of Towson County, and "Lotima," dead, of Towson County, with "Ded" beside both and no year of death. Because Legion had already been counted in 1896 as "Legend Austin," the clerk had the parents' names from that earlier count and not from fresh testimony in 1899.

The first name ends in abi, which the Choctaw linguist Ovid Vickers calls a war-name element; "a great proportion of those who had earned second names as a result of participation in a war were given names carrying the termination abi signifying killer." The Choctaw Nation's language staff cautions against reading the ending simply as "killer," and the meaning of Ata-sa-ha-bi is not recorded.

Legion himself bore an English surname, Austin, and signed by mark. In 1899 he gave his age as 33, but in November 1902 he testified he was "about fifty," so his birth falls somewhere between about 1852 and 1866. He had a grown daughter, Viny, born about 1879 to an earlier wife named Betsy, and he raised his nephew Nicholas Greenwood, so the household was wider than the enrollment shows. His daughters Lizzie and Adline married the Pisachubbe brothers Robert and William Harrison, and the line runs through Frances Pisachubbe Thompson.

stories.title: The fifth child, who was eight the summer her brother died
stories.hook: Born at Broken Bow in 1938, Mary Ellen Hulsey grew up between two courthouses and married into the Thompson family of Choctaw County.
body: Mary Ellen Hulsey was born on 22 August 1938 at Broken Bow, Oklahoma, the fifth child of Oscar and Katie Hulsey. Broken Bow had grown up around the Dierks lumber company and was incorporated in 1911, a mill town in the pine hills of McCurtain County. In the spring of 1940, at two, she was living with her parents and four older brothers and sisters at South Fork in Montgomery County, Arkansas.

The family kept pictures of her from those years. At three, at Fort Towson in Choctaw County, she is a smiling little girl with a straight fringe cut across her forehead. In 1942, at four, she sits beside her little brother Charlie, who is two and has his arm around her shoulders; that picture was mounted next to one of the two eldest, Delphia and Leon, with Leon holding a guitar.

Her parents' marriage came apart in her childhood. An Arkansas divorce was entered in Montgomery County on 26 September 1941, when she was 3, and Katie filed again in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, in 1945; that divorce was granted in January 1946, when she was 7. In July 1947 her brother Bennie George, 13, was killed on his bicycle west of Hugo; she was 8. By April 1950 she was 12, living at Jeter in Choctaw County with her mother, who now ran the household on her own, and three of her brothers, Glen, Charley and Willis.

She went to school in Hugo from the age of seven until she was nearly eighteen. Her school picture for 1955–56, printed “School Days,” shows her at seventeen with her dark hair set in soft curls, a high-necked sweater and a level, steady look.

The day after her grandmother Jane died, in January 1956, seventeen-year-old Mary was riding through Hugo with her mother and her aunt from Grand Prairie when their car was struck at Second and Kirk streets. She and her aunt bumped heads, shaken but not badly hurt.

In the first days of December 1956, at eighteen, she and William “Junior” Thompson Jr., four years older and living out at Speer, took out their marriage license at Hugo, and The Hugo Daily News printed their names among the week’s licenses on 5 December. The marriage joined the Hulsey line, from Arkansas and Georgia, to the Thompson family of Choctaw County.

A photograph from her later years shows her in a red top, her hair still dark and cut short, smiling down at something beside her. She died at Hugo on 4 November 2002, aged 64, and is buried at Woodlawn Cemetery in Choctaw County beside her husband. Her mother Katie outlived her by more than six years, and when Katie died in 2009, Mary was among the children she had already buried.

For a time around 1990 she went by Mary Christian, and in December 1991, with that name, she stood on a porch with her mother and her brothers Charlie, Leon and Willis for a family picture. After she died at Hugo on 4 November 2002, her funeral was held two days later through Prater-Lampton-Mills & Coffey.

stories.title: Katie, who lived to ninety-eight
stories.hook: Born at Danville, Arkansas, in 1910 and married at 17, Katie Stevenson Hulsey raised her children alone at Jeter and Hugo and outlived five of her seven children.
body: Katie Cornelia Stevenson, born 15 October 1910, was the youngest of Gilbert Franklin 'Frank' and Parsis Jane (O'Neal) Stevenson. When the family was counted in Frank's rented house at Danville, Arkansas, in April 1910, the last of the seven children was "Katie, a baby," so one of the two dates is off by months; at nine, in 1920, she was still 'Kate.' Danville was a Yell County seat laid out in 1841 and named for a steamboat on the Petit Jean River; her father was a Methodist clergyman there and had children born in Indiana, Texas and Oklahoma before her.

By 1920 the family was farming a rented place on the South Millerton Road in Kirk Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma, near Valliant, a railroad town founded in 1902 in the Choctaw Nation. On 27 October 1927, twelve days after her seventeenth birthday, Katie married Oscar Hulsey, the son of the Rev. George Washington Hulsey and Sarah Rebecca Graves. Two preachers' families, one from Tennessee and Indiana, the other from Georgia and Arkansas, were joined, and their children grew up in the Ouachita hills at places like South Fork, Montgomery County, where they were living in 1940.

The 1930s were hard on the marriage. Oscar was charged after a stabbing in January 1938 that involved Katie's brother Eddie Stevenson ("A family quarrel ends in a stabbing"). An Arkansas divorce was entered on 26 September 1941, and Katie filed in McCurtain County in 1945; the district court granted her divorce from Oscar in January 1946. In July 1947 her 13-year-old son Bennie George died after turning his bicycle in front of a pickup truck west of Hugo, and she moved to Hugo that year. In April 1950 "Kattie," 40, "Separated," was head of a household at Jeter, Choctaw County, with Glen, 14, Mary, 12, Charley, 9, and Willis, 6.

She died at Hugo on 30 January 2009, aged 98, with services on 2 February and burial at Mount Olivet Cemetery, where her parents lie in Block 2. She left 16 grandchildren, 32 great-grandchildren and 26 great-great-grandchildren, and had outlived her daughters Delphia and Mary and her sons Willis, Bennie and Glen. Her daughter Mary Ellen's marriage into the Thompson family connects this line to the Choctaw County side of the tree.

stories.title: From Arkansas to the Oregon coast
stories.hook: Sarah Rebecca Graves arrived on 5 May 1884, married a Hulsey at 17, bore ten children, and ended her life on the Oregon coast.
body: Sarah Rebecca Graves was born on 5 May 1884. A family genealogy names Margaret Crumpton as her mother and says Margaret died the same day, but this is unconfirmed. A 1977 family account names Jesse Graves as Sarah's father and lists Margaret as one of his wives, without saying which wife was her mother. A Jesse Graves and a Margaret Crumpton married in Garland County in 1884, though the groom's age differs from other accounts of Jesse, so it is not certain they are the same people.

On 22 December 1901, at 17, she married George Washington Hulsey in Arkansas. They farmed, first in Arkansas and by 1920 in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma, and between 1904 and 1925 had ten children, from Roy, the eldest, to George Paul, the youngest, with Oscar, the fourth, among them. By 1920 the family was in McCurtain County, Oklahoma. In September 1918 George Washington was a laborer at Camp Pike near Little Rock while she was at Story, Montgomery County; he died in 1935 and she was a widow at 51.

When Abe N. Graves died in 1943, the Arkansas Gazette listed Mrs. Rebecca Hulsey as his sister, which fits the family's account of her Graves relatives. A Graves family genealogy says Jesse was the son of Gilliam Graves, who came from North Carolina by way of Georgia and Alabama to Cedar Glades in Arkansas and volunteered for the Union army in January 1864.

She died on 23 December 1972 at Bandon, on the Oregon coast, at 88, and is buried at Hawthorne Memorial Gardens, Grants Pass. Her grandson Glen, Oscar and Katie's son, died at Veneta, Oregon, in 2001, so more than one branch of the Hulsey family ended up in Oregon.

Her bronze marker at Hawthorne Memorial Gardens in Grants Pass, Oregon, reads "In Loving Memory / S. Rebecca Hulsey / Mother / May 5, 1884 Dec. 23, 1972." She went by her middle name, as in the 1943 notice of her brother Abe's death: Mrs. Rebecca Hulsey.

stories.title: The preacher's son who followed the road west
stories.hook: Born in 1861 at Pulaski, Tennessee, Frank Stevenson was one of fifteen children of a Methodist preacher and went on to preach and farm in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas.
body: In April 1910 Frank Stevenson was a "Clergyman" at Danville, Arkansas. He gave his age as 51, renting, married for 25 years, and his seven children had been born in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas. He had begun life in a Tennessee circuit preacher's household: Gilbert Franklin Stevenson was born on 17 November 1861 near Pulaski, Giles County, one of fifteen children of Rev. Abner Arrington Stevenson and Martha Still Watson, and the twin of George Washington Stevenson.

He was five months old when Federal troops first reached Pulaski in April 1862. Giles County was "continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers," and in 1863 the Federals relieved the county of "horses, cattle and grain." His first cousins Coleman and Wilbur Stevenson served in the Confederate 32nd Tennessee. Giles County itself had been formed only in 1809, from Maury County, four years before his grandfather Elam came. In 1870 he and George, both 8, were in their father's household with younger children; in 1880 he was 18 and a farmer. In January 1881 his father "abandoned the idea of going to Texas," and that May "Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week." Texas was in the family's talk before Frank himself lived there.

He went north to Gibson County, Indiana, where the family of his wife, Parsis Jane O’Neal, lived; her grandparents Archibald and Parses O’Neal had come to the county from Tennessee in 1839. Their children Delphia and George were born in Indiana. Other family trees give them three older children, Iva Myrtle (1884), Adison Galiton (1886) and Nellie Vashti (1889), whose link to this family is not documented. Exactly when the Texas and Oklahoma births fell between about 1892 and 1907 is not known.

He married Parsis Jane O'Neal of Gibson County, Indiana, whose father Daniel had served in the 42nd Indiana. Their older children were probably born in Indiana; later ones were born in Texas (Willie, Frank and Elisha) and Oklahoma (Eddie), and the youngest, Katie, at Danville in 1910. By January 1919 his wife was "Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma," and in 1920 he farmed a rented place on the South Millerton Road in Kirk Township, McCurtain County. Yell County, where he was preaching in 1910, had been organized on 5 December 1840, and had two county seats, Danville and Dardanelle. Katie Cornelia’s birth is given as 15 October 1910 at Danville, which does not fit the baby Katie counted there that April; the two dates have not been reconciled.

He died at Hugo on 9 May 1950, aged 88, and lies in Block 2 of Mount Olivet Cemetery next to Parsis. A cemetery listing made in 2000 reads 'Stevenson, Frank N., 1860-1950,' a year off the family record, and his ages over the years range from 1859 to 1862. His youngest daughter Katie married Oscar Hulsey, a Hot Springs native, in 1927, and she outlived her father by almost sixty years; their daughter Mary Ellen (1938-2002) is buried in Choctaw County beside William Thompson Jr. A photograph of the grave shows a stone reading 'Gilbert Franklin Stevenson, November 17, 1861 – May 9, 1950', which agrees with the family record; the 2000 listing may come from an older marker or a misreading.

In his last years Frank Stevenson was a retired Nazarene minister, living at 506 East Lowery Street in Hugo, where he and Jane had moved from McCurtain County about 1942. He died at home just after midnight on 9 May 1950, at 88, and was buried at Mount Olivet after rites at the Coffey Chapel. His children had scattered from Tacoma to Edinburg; his daughter Katie was the one still in Hugo.
When George, Gilbert's twin, died at Lubbock in December 1946, his certificate gave his mother's family name as Watson, of Tennessee.

stories.title: The farming preacher of Bee Spring
stories.hook: For 54 years Rev. Abner Stevenson rode the Giles County circuits, and in 1880 he gave the census taker his trade as "Farming Preacher."
body: In 1880, at 63, Abner Arrington Stevenson of District 10, Giles County, Tennessee, called himself a "Farming Preacher." He had been born on 16 March 1816, the fourth of eleven children of the Rev. Elam Stevenson and Lydia Payne, in a family that produced five Methodist-preaching brothers; Elam had organized the Bee Spring church in 1814 or 1815 and moved to Tennessee in 1813. A nephew wrote in 1932 that the family counted its years in the pulpit, and set down "Uncle Abner 54 years." A Methodist history of middle Tennessee calls him "a Godly man" who "lived to be very old."

On 8 December 1838 he married Martha Still Watson, born 19 February 1823, and between 1840 and 1866 they had fifteen children. The twins Gilbert Franklin and George Washington were the twelfth and thirteenth; one son, James Willis, became a minister and lived to 1943. A son-in-law, John Newton Andrew, married three Stevenson women in turn. The household was a farm first and a pulpit second: In November 1878 he was down to preach at "Blooming Grove, 4th Sunday, 11 a. m." on the Mt. Pisgah circuit, and in May 1884 two sermons were preached at Rocky Point, "one by Abner Stevenson."

The war came to his farm. His twins were infants when Federal troops reached Pulaski in April 1862, and the county was "continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers." His nephews Coleman L. and Wilbur M., sons of his brother William P., served in the Confederate 32nd Tennessee. His own sympathies are not recorded. In January 1881 he had "abandoned the idea of going to Texas and will remain where he is now living," and that May his son "Judge Geo. Stevenson" had "returned from Texas last week." Another son, Frank, lived in Texas himself in the 1890s.

Martha died on 12 July 1887, and her stone at Bee Spring gives her name and dates and an epitaph. Abner died on 30 July 1896 and was buried at Bee Spring, the church his father founded. The church was destroyed by a tornado on 29 April 1909 and the congregation rebuilt at Bryson; a Methodist history says "All that remains of this today is the cemetery." His son Frank carried the preaching and the road west to Arkansas and Oklahoma, where Frank's youngest daughter Katie married a Hulsey.

stories.title: A blacksmith in the old Cherokee gold country
stories.hook: A Georgia blacksmith and a household that may connect to the Hulseys later found in Arkansas.
body: In November 1850 Salathiel, 43, a Georgia-born blacksmith with $50 in real estate, lived in Union County, Georgia. His household held Elizabeth, 35; Maryan, 19; Robert, 17; Elizabeth, 12; Jesse, 10; Jennings, 8; a girl read as Lillean, 6; Benjamin, 3; and Nancy, 1. Arminda Burnett and J. C. Bell were living there too. Nothing states the relationships, so who was wife and who were children is inferred. In 1840 Salathiel was counted in Hall County, and in 1830 he was one of seventeen men named Hulsey in Hall County, living among the Hulseys of Charles and Adler.

Benjamin was three, and the girl just above him six; a published extract once reversed those ages. Three is consistent with the family’s 1847 birth year for Benjamin, although no exact birthday is given. A compiler of that extract suggested that Robert in this household was the Robert Hulsey found in Hempstead County, Arkansas, in 1860.

Union County, in the northern mountains, was formed in 1832 from the country the Cherokee had held until their removal in 1836-39, once a gold-rush district; settlers there were hardscrabble farmers, mostly from Virginia and North Carolina, and few kept slaves. A blacksmith in such a place shod horses and mended plows. Salathiel was born about 1807 and Elizabeth about 1815, but how Elizabeth and Maryan were related is not known. He is gone by the early 1850s.

In 1860 a Georgia-born Robert Hulsey, 27, lived in Hempstead County, Arkansas, with Sarah A., 20, and an infant son. His age and birthplace fit a possible continuation of Robert in the Georgia household, but neither record gives him a middle initial. The infant’s name, read as Selatha G., is uncertain in the handwriting; the published reading Salathel G. cannot securely link him to Salathiel. Family accounts also place Benjamin in Story, Arkansas, with a son named Martin Salatheil. The age of three in 1850 removes the apparent conflict with Benjamin’s reported 1847 birth, but neither his identity with the Arkansas man nor his relationship to George Washington Hulsey is established.

Salathiel's father may be Jesse Hulsey, the wounded Revolutionary pensioner of Hall County; some family trees say so, but they also name Jesse Hamilton Hulsey and Mary Tharp, and nothing supports either.

stories.title: Eleven in the census, a bride at sixteen
stories.hook: Parsis O'Neal was 11 and "works at home" in Gibson County in 1880; by 1884 she may already have been a bride in Arkansas, and she died at Hugo in 1956.
body: In 1880, in Columbia Township, Gibson County, Indiana, Parsis J. O'Neal, 11, "Works At Home" in her father's house. She was the fourth of the ten children of Daniel Waters O'Neal, a veteran of Company F, 42nd Indiana, and Vashti Pearson. Her grandmother Parses (Shaw) Watt, widow of Archibald O'Neal, was on the old home farm near Oakland City, and her brothers in the household were William (16), John (13), George J. (4, born in Missouri) and Daniel G. (2). She was born on 26 March 1868, three years after her father came home from the war.

At 16 she may already have left. A "Parsis J O Neal" is said to have married Otho Louderback, 40, on 25 December 1884 in Pulaski County, Arkansas, and the memorial for her grave at Hugo carries the name Louderback, though the link is unproven. Her sister Mary was in Arkansas by February 1884. By 1910 she and Frank Stevenson had been married 25 years, which puts the Stevenson household in 1885, and the oldest children, Delphia and George, were born in Indiana.

The Stevensons then followed the work. Willie, Frank and Elisha were born in Texas between about 1894 and 1904, Eddie in Oklahoma about 1907, and Katie at Danville, Arkansas, on 15 October 1910, when Parsis was 42. When her mother died in January 1919, Parsis was "Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma," and in 1920 the family farmed a rented place in Kirk Township, McCurtain County. Her son George Sherman died at Kilgore, Texas, in 1978, with Parsis Jane (O'Neal) Stevenson given as his mother.

She died at Hugo on 26 January 1956, aged 87, and lies in Block 2 of Mount Olivet Cemetery beside Frank. The cemetery canvass of 2000 wrote 1887-1956, but everything from her own lifetime, from 1880 to her children's births, puts her birth in 1868, and a photograph of the stone shows 1868, so the 1887 is a misreading or comes from another marker. Her brothers stayed in Gibson County and her sister Mary lived to 100 at Tuttle, Oklahoma.

Jane outlived Frank by six years. She was living at 204 East Duke Street when she died at noon on Thursday, 26 January 1956, at 87, and the Rev. Wesley Meek of the Church of the Nazarene preached her funeral. She had come from Somerville in Gibson County, Indiana, where her brother George still lived; her sister Louisa Skomp was in Gary. Thirty-eight grandchildren survived her.
