stories.title: Vashti O'Neal's six hours of apoplexy
stories.hook: Married at 15 in 1860, Vashti Pearson O'Neal raised ten children in Gibson County, Indiana, sent a husband to the Union army, and died there in 1919.
body: Vashti Elizabeth Pearson was born on 18 May 1844 and married Daniel Waters O'Neal on 5 January 1860, when she was 15 and he 21. Daniel's father Archibald had come to Gibson County, Indiana, from Tennessee in 1839 and died in 1841, leaving his widow Parses on the farm. In October 1861, with Vashti 17 and their first child, Mary Elizabeth, a year old, Daniel enlisted in Company F of the 42nd Indiana, the company raised at Oakland City, and the war carried much of the regiment from Perryville to Atlanta. A family biography has him discharged for disability at Nashville in March 1862.

Between 1860 and 1887 she bore ten children: Mary Elizabeth (1860, who lived to 100), William Allen (1863), John Sherman (1866, born the year after the war), Parsis Jane (1868), J. A. (1871, an infant death), George Johnson (1875), Daniel Clinton (1878), David Commodore (1881), Nora (1884, an infant death) and Charity Louisa (1887). In 1880 the family was in Columbia Township, and George, the child born in 1875, was listed as born in Missouri. Her five surviving sons lived into their fifties or later, and three of them died at Somerville.

She died at Somerville on 16 January 1919, of "apoplexy, 6 hrs." She professed faith early in life and was a faithful member of Somerville's United Brethren Church. She left her husband, her five sons William, John, George, Clinton and Commodore, two daughters, "Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma," and Mrs. Fred Skomp of Somerville, and a brother, James Pearson of Elberfeld. Her eldest daughter Mary Elizabeth was in Oklahoma in 1919 but went unnamed in the notice of her death, and Parsis's marriage to Frank Stevenson tied the O'Neals to the Stevenson family of Arkansas and McCurtain County.

A Pearson family had been in Columbia Township long before she was born: in 1827 "Solomon Brown and William Pearson had charge of the poor." Nothing ties that William to her father John. Her restored family stone stands with Daniel's at Somerville, and her own marker reads "Vashti, 1844-1919."

stories.title: Martha Still Watson, fifteen children and a preacher's stone
stories.hook: Married at 15 in 1838, Martha Watson Stevenson bore fifteen children in Giles County; her stone at Bee Spring speaks of a better world and the Resurrection morn.
body: On 8 December 1838 Abner Stevenson "married Martha S. Watson," born 19 February 1823 in Tennessee, "the daughter of Mary Watson." She was 15. Between 1840 and 1866 she had fifteen children, the last of them about the time she turned 43, among them the twins Gilbert Franklin and George Washington in November 1861, five months before Federal troops reached Pulaski.

For a Methodist circuit preacher's wife that meant a farm and a houseful of children during the years her husband was riding to Blooming Grove, Rocky Point and the Mt. Pisgah circuit. She died on 12 July 1887, and the Nashville Christian Advocate noted her death in August 1887.

Her mother is given only as Mary Watson. Some trees name William Watson and Mary Brown as her parents, but without support, and the middle name Still is unexplained, so her ancestry stops at Mary. Her son Frank carried the line to Arkansas, where Frank's youngest daughter Katie married Oscar Hulsey.

Her stone in the Bee Spring churchyard is a plain round-topped tablet. It reads "Martha S. Stevenson / Born / Feb. 19, 1823 / Died / July 12, 1887," and below a carved rule: "She started in early life for a better world & has stopped at this Inn until the Resurrection morn, where we will meet again." The cutter's letters read "stated" and "sopped," with the r and t evidently left out. Her stone gives 1887, in agreement with the family dates, though a published notice had 1886.

In June 1880, in the 10th Civil District of Giles County, Martha S., 56, was keeping house for her husband A. A. Stevenson, a farmer and preacher, with Gilbert F., 18, Wilson M., 16, and Jane M., 12, at home. She had been born in Tennessee, and both her father and her mother were Virginians.

One online family tree makes her a daughter of David Milton Watson (1791-1843) and Mary Ann Gary of Mountain Creek, Anderson County, South Carolina, and lists her among their eight children, but cites nothing for it. That couple were born, lived and died in South Carolina, whereas Martha was born in Tennessee to parents who, by her own household's 1880 account, were Virginians. The link does not fit. Her mother remains the "Mary Watson" of the Stevenson family history.

stories.title: The Pearsons behind Vashti
stories.hook: John and Elizabeth Pearson are known only through their daughter Vashti and a son in Elberfeld.
body: John and Elizabeth Pearson were the parents of Vashti Elizabeth, born 18 May 1844, who married Daniel Waters O'Neal in Gibson County, Indiana, on 5 January 1860. Both were dead by January 1919, when Vashti died. The only brother named at her death was James Pearson of Elberfeld, Indiana, a Warrick County town a few miles from Gibson County. Elizabeth's maiden name, Carman, comes from a memorial for her grave.

A Pearson family had been in Columbia Township since at least 1827, when "Solomon Brown and William Pearson had charge of the poor." Nothing names that William as John's father or brother. Decades later several Pearsons, among them a Charles, a Samuel and an L. S., worked as carpenters in Oakland City, though nothing ties them to this family.

Vashti's husband, Daniel Waters O'Neal, served in Company F of the 42nd Indiana. The regiment was organized at Evansville on 9 October 1861, fought at Perryville, Stones River, Chickamauga and Lookout Mountain, took part in the Atlanta campaign and the march through Georgia and the Carolinas, and was mustered out at Louisville on 21 July 1865. Vashti and Daniel had ten children.

stories.title: A Tennessean who lived two years on the Gibson County farm
stories.hook: Archibald O'Neal came to Gibson County, Indiana, in 1839 and was dead by April 1841, leaving a widow, a small son, and a farm that stayed in the family for decades.
body: An 1884 county history sets him down in one plain paragraph: "Archibald O'Neal was an early settler. He came here in 1839. He was a Tennesseean by birth. He died April 25, 1841." He farmed in Columbia Township with his wife Parses, whom the book calls "a native of Lawrenceburg, Ohio." Their son Daniel Waters had been born in Tennessee in October 1838, the year before the move.

His death date appears twice, and the two differ: 25 April 1841 in one place and "Died Ap'l 22,'41," "First Husband of Mrs. P. W." in another. The year is certain, the day is not. His widow Parses then married Hugh Watt, an Irishman from County Down, who died in September 1871. In 1884 she was still on the old home farm, and she died in 1901.

Some family trees give Archibald a birth in Virginia in 1796 and parents named Charles and Martha, without support; the county history says Tennessee. His son Daniel enlisted in Company F, 42nd Indiana Infantry, in October 1861, married Vashti Pearson, and had ten children, among them Parsis Jane, who married Frank Stevenson.

Archibald left almost nothing. A man named Harvey O'Neal, very likely a brother or other close kinsman, had been keeping him in flour and coffee, and had sold him a cow, in 1840, and it was Harvey who settled the estate. The household goods brought $56 at the sale, and when the doctor, the Hargroves' store and the court had been paid the estate was twenty dollars short.

In 1850 Parses, forty and Ohio-born, kept house for Hugh Watt in Columbia Township with their two small children, her son Daniel, twelve, and an Elisabeth O'Neal of eighteen. Elisabeth married William Hartin the next summer.

stories.title: Parses Watt and the old home farm
stories.hook: A widow farmed the old home place near Oakland City, Indiana, with the names of both her husbands written beneath hers.
body: In 1884 “Mrs. Parsis Watt” was a farmer in Section 32 near Oakland City, Indiana, a native of Lawrenceburg, Ohio, who had come to the county in 1839. Listed beneath her name were two others: Archibald O’Neal, her first husband, and Hugh Watt, her second. Lawrenceburg is a town on the Ohio River in Dearborn County, Indiana, so the book's "Ohio" may be a slip.

Archibald O’Neal, a Tennessean, came to Gibson County in 1839 and farmed there. Parses was about twenty-eight, and their son Daniel Waters, born in Tennessee in October 1838, was an infant. Archibald died in April 1841, leaving Parses a widow with their son, then two. She later married Hugh Watt, an Irishman from County Down. Decades after Archibald’s death, she was still living on the old home farm.

Hugh died in September 1871. Thirteen years later Parses was farming in her own name, a widow twice over, and the household had changed over more than forty years. Her son Daniel enlisted in Company F of the 42nd Indiana in October 1861 and he and his wife Vashti Pearson had ten children. Their daughter Parsis Jane, who carried her grandmother's name in a different spelling, married Frank Stevenson, and Parsis Jane's daughter Katie married into the Hulsey family, so Parses is Katie's great-grandmother and stands behind the Hulsey line of Arkansas and Oklahoma.

Archibald’s death is given as April 25, 1841 in one place and April 22 in another; both agree on the year. A family-tree entry gives 12 December 1901 for her death in Gibson County. Her parents are not known. Some trees link her to Noble and Sicily (Nordyke) Shaw of Guilford County, North Carolina, but the Quaker register at Dover shows only a Parris who died in infancy, so that link remains a lead.

stories.title: The Iredell Presbyterians who raised a Methodist preacher
stories.hook: James and Jane Stevenson lived out their lives in Rowan and Iredell counties, North Carolina, and their son Elam took the family into Methodism and Tennessee.
body: James Stevenson was born, it is said, in Bladen County, North Carolina, on 27 May 1746, or perhaps in 1747. His father took up 640 acres at Vashti, in what is now Alexander County, and James made his life in Rowan, later Iredell, County. He and his wife, Jane, were Presbyterians. They were married in 1781, or perhaps as early as about 1765, and their children included James, William, Elam and Phineas. Phineas, Elam’s brother, is otherwise unknown to the family story.

In 1781 James served in the Rowan County militia as a private, under Captain Joseph Sharpe and Colonel Francis Locke, and the Sons of the American Revolution count him among their patriots. Later family accounts made more of his service: a compiler called him a soldier of the Revolution, and a descendant credited him with Ramsour’s Mill and later battles, though nothing confirms it. He should not be confused with Captain James Stevenson of Rowan and Cabarrus counties, an elder at Poplar Tent, who died in 1832.

Jane is said to have died in 1814, though James left a living wife in 1828, and James outlived her by fourteen years. In June 1828 he made his will in Iredell County, naming his son Elam among his heirs, and he died on 3 September 1828. He is said to lie in the Stevenson, or Lackey-Stevenson, Cemetery at Vashti, on the land his father had taken up.

Their son Elam was born on 24 September 1787 in what is now Alexander County. He was the first of the family to join the Methodists. He married Lydia Payne in Burke County, was licensed to preach in 1813, and that year moved his family to Giles County, Tennessee, by pack horse in family tradition, though in his own account he mentions a wagon. He told the story of those years himself in 1869, and the Christian Advocate marked his death in April 1875. Three to five of his sons, depending on who was counting, became preachers; Abner, whose farm and pulpit were near Pulaski, carries this line on.

Who James’s own parents were is uncertain. A family book of 1955 names his father as another James, an Irish immigrant who died in 1820, and his mother as Sally Kelly of Maryland, and gives Jane’s parents as John Stevenson (d. 1794) and a Thompson. The dates are strained: a father who died in 1820 and a mother who died in 1820 or 1821 would both have been very old.

James made his will on 21 June 1828, weak in body but, he said, of perfect mind, and signed it with his mark. He left his beloved wife the house and plantation for her lifetime, and then everything was to be sold and shared among John, James, Jean Elder, Elam, Phinehas and Amos, and the children of his daughter Sarah Templeton, who had died before him. William was to keep the land he already lived on, and two Wallis girls, Nancy and Japhia, were to share equally "with the rest of my children." He named his sons James and Amos his executors.

stories.title: Noble Shaw's 268 acres at Oak Ridge
stories.hook: A Quaker farmer of Guilford County, North Carolina, Noble Shaw died on Christmas Day 1855, and his widow sold his land in the spring of 1857.
body: In March 1857 J. H. Leak and Sicily Shaw, having qualified as administrators of the estate of Noble Shaw, with a will annexed, gave notice that on 16 April they would sell "a tract of land, consisting of 268 acres, well timbered and well watered, convenient to the Oak Ridge Institute, and on the direct road from Danville, Va., to Salisbury," on credit. They signed at Oak Ridge on 24 March 1857, and the notice ran in a Greensboro paper that week.

The sale was to be held “at the dwelling of said deceased,” and the notice ran again on 2 April 1857. “With a will annexed” is the old legal phrase for administrators who carry out a written will when the executor it names cannot or does not act. So Noble left a will, and Sicily, then 66, was one of the two people the court trusted to settle his estate and sell his land.

The farm lay near the Oak Ridge Institute, the academy in northwestern Guilford County, on the road that runs from Danville, Virginia, down to Salisbury. Sicily was born on 2 August 1790, the first of the children of Aden and Martha Nordyke in the Quaker records. Her father Aden had been born in Burlington County, New Jersey, in 1762, was shot in the arm in an attack in Georgia, and married Martha Johnson in 1787 at Deep River Meeting in Guilford County; he later went on to Indiana, while Sicily lived out her years in Guilford County. She died on 16 May 1861, four years after the sale.

Noble was born on 22 April 1787 and was a member of Dover Monthly Meeting, whose register lists his wife Sicily and children Aaron (16 December 1809), Parris (7 July 1817, died 30 May 1818) and Mary (17 November 1820). He died on 25 December 1855. It was a time when Friends were leaving for Ohio and Indiana: seventy-one took certificates from Dover between 1816 and 1860, nearly all of them to Indiana. The Shaws stayed.

Parses Watt of Gibson County, Indiana, who was born about 1811 and died in 1901, is thought to be the Shaws' daughter, but the Quaker register shows only a Parris who lived a year, so she would have to be an earlier child missing from it. If she is theirs, her son Daniel O'Neal's Union service and her great-granddaughter Katie Stevenson's marriage to a Hulsey tie the Guilford County Quakers to the Ouachita hills of Arkansas and Oklahoma.

His small stone stands among the leaves in the Dover Friends Meeting burying ground near Colfax, Guilford County. Lichen covers most of the face; "Noble Shaw," "Died," "25 Dec. 1855" and an age beginning "68" can still be read, matching a birth date of 22 April 1787.

stories.title: The Quaker bride at Deep River, 1787
stories.hook: Martha Johnson was born at Deep River in the Quaker country of Guilford County and married Aden Nordyke there in December 1787.
body: Martha Johnson's name is carried by a single line of Quaker handwriting. The Deep River Monthly Meeting minute of 12 December 1787 reads: "Martha, dt Robert & Cecilia, Surry Co., m Adin Nordyke." She was born in 1766 and was twenty-one at the wedding. If she belonged to the Johnson family of Cedar Creek Meeting in Louisa County, Virginia, her birth falls in the very year, 1766, that a certificate dated 29 March carried Robert and Virginia Johnson south to North Carolina.

Her family tree reaches back into Virginia Quaker country. One genealogy gives her parents as Robert Johnson, born in New Kent County in February 1738, and Virginia C. Elmore, the daughter of Thomas Elmore and Cecilia Ellyson. Robert was a son of Ashley Johnson, and Louisa County, where Ashley farmed Chamberlain's Creek, had been cut from Hanover County in 1742. Cedar Creek recorded Robert and his bride Cisley Elmore marrying in public meeting on 19 November 1758. The marriage entry gives Martha's mother as Cecilia, while the Cedar Creek minutes name Robert's wife as Virginia and do not name Martha at all, so her parentage remains a lead.

Her husband Aden was born in 1762 in Burlington County, New Jersey, the oldest son of Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers, and had come with his parents by way of Virginia and Georgia to Deep River. At Deep River Martha and Aden began a family: Sicily, born 2 August 1790, and Mary, born 15 February 1792. Sicily married Noble Shaw and stayed in Guilford County, where she lived to 1861; she is the link, if Parses Shaw was her daughter, that carries the line on toward Indiana and Arkansas.

Martha died in 1844, two years after Aden, who is said to have died in Indiana in 1842. The Quaker minutes support the Robert and Cecilia of her marriage entry and the Johnson couple of Cedar Creek, but the step between them is a compiled family history, not a record.

stories.title: Six homes in forty-four years
stories.hook: Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers married in a New Jersey Quaker meeting in 1761 and kept moving, through Virginia, Georgia, North Carolina and Tennessee, until they reached Ohio in 1805.
body: Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers were married on 1 June 1761 in Burlington County, New Jersey, and were members of Chesterfield Monthly Meeting. Mary was the granddaughter named in her grandfather Thomas Staples's will of 1758, where he left bequests to "Mehetable and Mary Rogers", the daughters of his daughter Ann and her husband Thomas Rogers. Abraham was probably the son of Henry Nordyke and Rebecca Perkins, who married at Willingboro in 1731/2.

Their moves can be followed in order. In 1771 they transferred to Hopewell Monthly Meeting near Winchester, Virginia. They then lived for eight years in Georgia, where their son Aden was shot in the arm in an Indian attack, and where their son Micajah, born in 1771 in Stafford County, Virginia, hid through a night in the woods at the age of four when an invasion was feared. In 1788 they joined Deep River Meeting in North Carolina, where their son Aden had married Martha Johnson the December before. In 1798 they moved to Lost Creek Meeting near Knoxville, a settlement whose Friends had been refused leave to meet in 1787 because the land title was still disputed with the Indians, and in 1805 to a farm near New Vienna in Clinton County, Ohio, where they helped start East Fork Meeting.

Lost Creek, near New Market a few miles north of Knoxville, was already a settlement with a history of trouble. In 1787 Friends there, near the Holston River, asked New Garden Monthly Meeting for the right to hold meetings and were refused, because they had “settled on lands the title to which was still in dispute with the Indians,” and were told to move off. The Western Quarterly Meeting added in 1792 that no Friend should “remove and settle out of the limits of a Monthly Meeting without first applying to and having consent.” A meetinghouse went up at Lost Creek in 1796. The Nordykes reached it two years later, and it was from there that, as a Quaker historian wrote, many Tennessee Friends “drifted on, like Charles Osborn and William Williams, to the Northwest.”

The last move put Micajah, then 34, his wife Charity, 26, with an infant in her arms and children of three, five and seven, and the “aging grandparents” on the road north. They bought land near what became New Vienna and “helped start a Friends Meeting which was called East Fork,” on a lot that was part of the Nordyke farm. “Micajah had to go to Chillicothe, forty miles distant, to get flour and sugar,” and Charity kept wolves off with brimstone on the fire. One account dates this move to 1805, another to 1806.

Their children included Aden, Israel, Benajah, Beulah, Micajah, Daniel, Phebe and Hiram, and the Quaker habit of recording the hour of birth survives: "Aden was born at 7:00 P.M.; Israel at 3:00 P.M.; Benajah at 9:00 P.M." Mary died in 1814 and Abraham’s burial at East Fork was recorded in 1825, at 89, though another account gives 1822, so the year of his death is unsettled. Aden's daughter Sicily, born in 1790, married Noble Shaw in Guilford County, North Carolina; if Parses Shaw of Gibson County, Indiana, was their daughter, the line runs on to the O'Neals, the Stevensons and the Hulseys of Arkansas.

Abraham came to the Friends by choice, not by birth: Burlington Meeting took him in as a member in April 1758, three years before he married Mary Rogers, whose parents stood up in the meeting to give their consent. Over the next twenty-five years the family's certificates carried them from Burlington to Chesterfield and back, to Bush River in South Carolina, to Wrightsborough in the Georgia backcountry, and in 1783 to Deep River in North Carolina.

stories.title: The man who owed Jacob Perkins money
stories.hook: Henry Nordyke and Rebecca Perkins took out a New Jersey marriage license on 6 January 1731/2, as the Perkins estates were being settled around them.
body: Henry Nordyke of Burlington County and Rebecca Perkins of Wellingborough were granted a New Jersey marriage license on 6 January 1731/2. A license gives permission to marry, not the ceremony or its date. Her father’s will of 26 October 1731 names his daughter Rebeckah without a husband; her brother David’s will, dated January 1731/2, calls her Henry’s wife. A family page places Henry’s birth on 2 January 1710 in the Netherlands, but no ship or church record has been found, so his Dutch origin is only a possibility.

Henry's name appears again in the estates of his wife's family. Her father, Jacob Perkins Jr., made his will on 26 October 1731, naming his wife Sarah and ten children, among them Rebeckah, and listing bonds due him "from James Smith, Esq., John Shinn and Henry Nordike." He left ten pounds to St. Mary's Church, Burlington. The will was proved on 7 December. Rebecca's brother David then died too; his will of January 1731/2 names "Sister, Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike" and was witnessed by Henry himself, and it was proved on 4 March 1731/2.

Their son Abraham, who died at 89 in 1825 by one account (1822 by another), was born about 1736; he was a member of Chesterfield Meeting when he married Mary Rogers in 1761. From there the line goes to Guilford County, North Carolina, to Ohio and Indiana.

Henry was not a Quaker. His son Abraham asked to join the Burlington Friends in March 1758 and was received a month later, and when Abraham and Mary Rogers passed meeting in May 1761, Henry did not come; he sent his consent in writing.

stories.title: Mamie: from Gadsden to the Red River, with eleven children
stories.hook: Born in Alabama, raised in Texas, married into the Moffitts, and called Mamie by the people who knew her.
body: Mary Tinsley Shackleford was born on 4 June 1895 in Alabama, a daughter of John Morgan and Lizzie (Newton) Shackleford. She would later be called a native of Gadsden, Etowah County. In June 1900 she was “May, 5” in her parents' household at Gilbert, Etowah County (an age that points to a year earlier, though her stone and her death notice both say 1895). Where the name Tinsley came from is still unknown.

The family did not stay in Alabama long. Her brother Robert was born at Gadsden in 1897, but her sister Hazel was born in 1908 at Rattan in Delta County, Texas, so the family had crossed to northeast Texas by then. About 1914 Mary married Woodford Grady Moffitt, and by June 1917 Grady was working as a timberman at Ervin in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, supporting a wife, his mother and a child. Their first son, Alvin, had been born in September 1915.

She had at least eleven children, and two died as toddlers. The family moved where the work was. In 1920 they were tenant farmers in Wilson Township, Choctaw County. In April 1930, with six boys, they were living with her parents on a farm near Stanton in Martin County, West Texas, where Grady was an out-of-work road laborer. By 1940 they were renting in Hugo, and in 1950 she was “Mamie,” 54, at Grant in Choctaw County, with Grady and three of the children still at home.

“Mamie” was the name her family used too. When her brother Robert died in California in 1961, “Mamie Moffett” of Oklahoma was named among his six sisters. Mary died the next year, on 26 August 1962, at Paris, Texas, still living at Grant. She was remembered as 67, the wife of Grady and the mother of John Moffitt. She is buried beside Grady at Shoat Springs Cemetery near Hugo, on a stone that reads “Mary Tinsley — Jun 4, 1895 – Aug 26, 1962.”

She died at St. Joseph Hospital in Paris, Texas, on 26 August 1962 after three weeks in a doctor's care, and Grady, giving the details for her death certificate, named her parents as John Shackelford and Lizzie Newton.

stories.title: Twenty-two years a widow at Herpel: Hannah Grimes Moffitt
stories.hook: Her birthplace is a Mississippi River landing or Illinois, depending on the tree, but her stone is in the Rocky Bayou hills and reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt."
body: In 1910 Hannah Moffitt, a widow of 53, was renting a house in Franklin Township, Stone County, Arkansas. Two sons lived with her: Thomas, who worked as a railroad section hand, and Grady, who made barrel staves. Asked how many children she had borne and how many were living, Hannah answered seven and six. She was already nine years into her widowhood: her husband Henry H. Moffitt had died at Mountain View in 1901, and she lived on without him until 1923.

Henry, a farmer who owned his land free and clear in 1900, died at Mountain View in 1901 at 46. Family accounts give the date as 9 September. No grave has been found and he has no memorial of his own; Arkansas did not register deaths in Stone County until 1914. That May, on 26 May 1901, Henry’s brother Patrick had lost his wife, Alice Ann (Cole) Moffitt, who is buried at Levisy Flat Cemetery in Stone County. Hannah could not read or write, but she kept the family together for another two decades.

Henry and Hannah were the same age. Henry was born in 1855, when his father Nathan Moffitt, the wheelwright, and Rebecca Williams were farming in Lawrence County; Hannah was born in July 1855, the daughter of David H. Grimes of Wayne County, Tennessee. Their children were Josephine, Jesse Gee (1879-1957), Gimsa, Bertha, Thomas Berry (1889-1953) and Grady (1891-1972). Jesse Gee went to Texas and died in Amarillo in 1957; Tom died in Paris, Texas, in 1953. In June 1900 she gave her birth as July 1855 in Arkansas, with both of her parents born in Tennessee; her 1910 age of 53 would put it nearer 1857. Where in Arkansas is in dispute: one family tree gives Arkansas City, Desha County, and another gives Illinois instead. The Desha County name cannot be right as written. In 1855 the Mississippi River landing that became Arkansas City lay in Chicot County and had seen little growth; the town was not incorporated until 1873 and was not in Desha County until the boundary moved in 1879.

What the records do show is where she ended up. By 1910 she was among the Moffitts of Stone County, a county only 37 years old. It was created in 1873; its seat, Mountain View, had 99 residents in 1880, got its first wooden courthouse in 1888 and was incorporated on 14 August 1890. Her brother-in-law Patrick Moffitt also lived in Stone County. After Henry's death Hannah kept a household of grown sons going on rented ground, and the two sons at home worked for wages, Tom on the railroad and Grady making barrel staves.

She spent her last years at Herpel, a Rocky Bayou community about six miles east of Mountain View, with a grist mill, a cotton gin, a stave mill and a sawmill. Its post office ran from 1907 to 1957. The Herpel Missionary Baptist Church laid its cornerstone on 5 March 1923, and Hannah died on 4 April 1923, about a month later. She is buried in Herpel Cemetery. Bertha May Moffitt Barham (1888-1930), also buried at Herpel, may be her daughter Bertha, whose birth was given in 1900 as March 1886, but that is not proved. Her stone reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt," the only memorial the couple have, since Henry's own grave has not been located.

Hannah’s marriage connected the Grimes and Moffitt families. Through her husband she was the daughter-in-law of Nathan and Rebecca, whose road led from Randolph County, North Carolina, to Arkansas and Missouri; through her father David she belonged to the Grimes family of Hardin Creek in Wayne County. Her youngest son Grady carried both lines to Hugo, Oklahoma, where he raised his family.

stories.title: Rebecca's bond: a £500 promise in Randolph County, 1835
stories.hook: On 13 October 1835 two Moffitt brothers put up £500 to the Governor of North Carolina so that Nathan could marry Rebecca Williams.
body: The marriage began with a printed form from the North Carolina Governor's office, filled in by hand. "KNOW all men by these presents, that we Nathan Moffitt & David Moffitt are held and firmly bound unto David L. Swain Esquire, Governor, &c.... in the full sum of five hundred pounds current money," and it is dated the 13th of October 1835. The condition reads that Nathan "hath made application for license for marriage to be celebrated between him and Rebecca Williams of the County aforesaid." The bond would be void if no lawful impediment appeared. Both men signed with seals. David Moffitt was almost certainly Nathan's older brother, born in 1802, one of Robert and Martha's nine children.

The form names her "Rebecca," and so does every later record. She is Rebecca Moffet in Nathan's household in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas, in 1850 and Rebecca Moffit in 1870. The county lists the marriage as Rebecca Williams to Nathan Moffitt, 13 October 1835. Some family trees add "Mary," but every record calls her Rebecca. Her birth is given as 1814 above and as about 1816 elsewhere, in Randolph County. Nothing names her parents. Some trees suggest James S. Williams and Polly Garner, but the Williams families of Randolph County were numerous and none can be tied to her.

Her husband's family surrounded her. Nathan's mother Martha Chamness, who was born in 1778 and lived until 1865, was in the same county when Rebecca married, and Rebecca's sister-in-law Thalitha Williams (born 1804 at Deep River) had married Nathan's brother William C. on 7 August 1827. Whether the two Williams women were sisters is not shown. A son, Calvin Vestal, was born in Randolph County on 4 December 1841. By 1850 the couple were in Arkansas, where Patrick Green was born in May 1853, and in 1860 Nathan was a wheelwright with 1,200 dollars in land. Nathan's sister Sarah went to Iowa with her husband, Rev. Beeson Barker, and his brother Robert followed him to Strawberry Township by 1860.

Her last move was to Missouri. In 1870 she and Nathan were farming in Dent County, Missouri, with no land of their own, and she was still living in June of that year. She is said to have died in Oregon County, Missouri, in 1871, and Nathan married the widow Nancy (Rowe) Cole that same year. Her sons were Calvin Vestal (1841-1913) and Patrick Green (1853-1905), among others, and one of the others, Henry, married Hannah Grimes and raised the Moffitts of Stone County.

stories.title: David Grimes of Wayne County, and the daughter born on the river
stories.hook: Born in 1829 into a Tennessee farm family on the Highland Rim, David H. Grimes is known to us mainly through the daughter who married a Moffitt.
body: David H. Grimes was born in 1829 in Wayne County, Tennessee, a young county on the western edge of the Highland Rim. The legislature created Wayne County in 1817 and had to pass the act again in 1819 because the clerk never signed it; its first county court met at the home of Benjamin Hardin on Factor's Fork, where the old Natchez Trace crosses Shoal Creek. It was wooded country of ridges and hollows with iron deposits, and Clifton, on the Tennessee River, became its main commercial town and shipped cotton, livestock, lumber and cross ties downriver. David's world was the Hardin Creek farm of John Grimes and Penelope Blackshear, his probable parents, whose children were James B., Elisha S., John Anderson and William Jasper.

His father John died on 14 June 1844 and was buried on the Haggard farm, when David was about fifteen. His brothers stayed. John Anderson was farming on the home place in 1860 and 1900, and in 1872 William Jasper left a will naming "John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor." David is not named in that will. His birth in 1829 fits an unnamed son placed in the Grimes family after William Jasper (1826), and a family tree names John Grimes as his father, but the link is unproved.

The rest of his life is known mostly through his daughter. A family tree has Hannah born in July 1855 at Arkansas City, Desha County, and David dying there in 1876. The place name is a later label: in 1855 the Mississippi landing now called Arkansas City was in Chicot County, and Desha County took in the area only in 1879. Hannah's 1910 age of 53 would put her birth nearer 1857, and a second profile gives Illinois. Whatever the town, the tree puts David in the lower Mississippi country of Arkansas by the mid-1850s, a long way from Hardin Creek, and has him dying in 1876. Hannah herself gave both of her parents' birthplace as Tennessee in 1900, which fits a father from Wayne County. His daughter's stone in Herpel Cemetery reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt."

stories.title: The recorder of Cane Creek, and eleven children in twenty years
stories.hook: Joseph Chamness wrote the Cane Creek marriage certificates from 1764, lost his wife the year the youngest was born, and lived to see every child married.
body: Joseph Chamness was in his twenty-third year when he married Margaret Norton at Cane Creek Meeting on 17 March 1763. All four parents signed their certificate as witnesses. The next year, in 1764, the meeting made him its Recorder of Marriage Certificates, and the certificate book in his handwriting was kept in the vault at Guilford College when the family's history was written in 1922. He was born in Baltimore County, Maryland, in 1740, and had come south with his father at the age of nine.

Eleven children were born to Joseph and Margaret between 1764 and 1784, the first three in Orange County and the rest in what became Randolph. The children were Sarah (1764), William (1766), Elizabeth (1768), Mary (1770), Joseph (1771), Anthony (1773), Margaret (1776), Martha (1778), Lydia (1780), Edward (1782) and Mourning (1784). Joseph later took a certificate of removal from Cane Creek to Providence meeting in Randolph County, where he owned a farm. Martha, the eighth child, married Robert Moffitt at Providence in 1797, joining the Chamness and Moffitt families.

On the 12th of Fourth month 1784 Margaret died, with the youngest of her eleven, Mourning, a newborn. The family history says that the eldest daughter, Sarah, then in her twentieth year, took charge of the infant and was the guiding star of the household until a stepmother appeared; some three years after her mother's death she married Obadiah Elliott in Randolph County and took the little sister into her own home. Joseph's second wife was Hannah Beeson, daughter of William and Mary Beeson, and they were married at Deep River meeting on 6 March 1786. Their daughter Susanna, born in 1788, was the twelfth child. Twelve Beesons are counted among the relatives of the bride when Joseph's son William married Isabel Beeson in Providence meeting, and records that William's stepmother signed that certificate too.

Joseph died on 17 May 1818 in Randolph County and is buried at Providence Cemetery. He lived to see all his children married and settled, the youngest, Susanna, then about thirty. His own wedding certificate ties the Chamness line to the Nortons, and his daughter's marriage to Robert Moffitt in 1797 tied both to the Moffitts.

stories.title: Pearl's family across the Red River
stories.hook: A Kentucky-born girl became a Texas farm neighbor, married Oscar Smith, and raised four children in southeastern Oklahoma.
body: Artie Pearl Satterfield was born in Butler County, Kentucky, in 1898, into the household of John C. and Samantha Johnson Satterfield. By 1910 the family had moved to Hagansport in Franklin County, Texas. Eleven-year-old Pearl and nineteen-year-old Oscar Smith lived a few households apart. They married in Franklin County, Texas, on 15 November 1915. Their first daughter, Nellie Mae, was born at Talco, Texas, on 3 April 1917.

The Smiths crossed the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma. In 1920, Pearl, Oscar and little Nellie were living on a rented farm in Oakes Township. By 1930 they were at Jeter with four children: Nellie, Robert Lee, Virgil and Faye. Faye had been born at Forney on 23 March 1929. In 1940 the household was still on rented farmland along Hugo Route 1. Pearl's family had gone from Kentucky to Texas to Oklahoma in one generation; the children's birthplaces mark the different stops.

Pearl outlived Oscar and her eldest daughter. Nellie Mae Choat died in Paris, Texas, on 7 July 1973, aged 56, after breast cancer; her parents were given as Charley O. Smith and Pearl Satterfield. She was brought home to Hugo for burial at Mount Olivet Cemetery. Pearl lived until 1983 and was buried beside Oscar at Grant Cemetery. Her youngest daughter Faye lived until 2014, carrying the Smith and Satterfield connection into the Moffitt family.
She was a member of Immanuel Baptist Church in Hugo, and she died at Choctaw Memorial Hospital on 21 July 1983.

stories.title: John B. Smith, who owned his Hagansport farm free and clear
stories.hook: A farmer on the Sulphur River divide who buried his wife at thirty-seven and lay beside her under a wooden stob.
body: In June 1900 John B. Smith, 44, was farming land he owned free of mortgage in Justice Precinct 2 of Franklin County, Texas. With him were his wife Emma, their son Oscar, 10, daughters Vera, Luina, Lona and Allie, and a baby, Jimmie. The family lived around Hagansport, a community that grew up at a Sulphur River crossing called Hagan's Port and that by 1884 had about 150 people, four churches, a one-room school, a mill and a gin. Oscar, later Charles Oscar Smith, had been born there on 29 May 1889.

Emma Elizabeth Langley, called Emma Liza on her memorial, was born on 11 December 1867 in Texas. She was probably one of the two daughters, Emma J., 12, and Eliza J., 8, of George W. Langley, a Georgia-born widower of Precinct 5 in neighboring Hopkins County in 1880. She died on 15 March 1905, aged 37, and her stone in Hagansport Cemetery reads "Emma / Wife of / J.B. SMITH / Gone but not forgotten." Six children were in the house in 1900, the youngest a baby.

John did not stay a widower. By April 1910 he had remarried, and Oscar, 19, was working on the home farm. A few doors away lived John C. Satterfield, lately of Kentucky, with his wife Samantha and their daughter Pearl, 11. Oscar and Artie Pearl Satterfield married in 1915. Owning rather than renting set John apart in the county: in 1900 only 44.1 percent of Franklin County farms were run by their owners, and the usual tenant gave up half the crop.

John B. Smith died in 1918 and was buried at Hagansport beside Emma; his grave is marked with a wooden stob. His father was very probably Noah Smith, a Kentucky-born farmer and justice of the peace whose 1880 household in the same Franklin County precinct included “John B. Smith, 20, son.” His mother is still unknown. His son Charles carried the farm tradition across the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma, where he is buried at Grant.

Emma's marble stone at Hagansport gives her dates beneath "Emma / wife of / J. B. Smith" as "Born Dec 11 1869[?]" and "Died Mar 15 1905." The last digit of the birth year looks like a 9, two years later than the 1867 used here; her age of 12 in 1880 fits 1867 or 1868 better, so 1867 is kept.

stories.title: Thomas Staples and Hananiah Gaunt's daughter
stories.hook: Thomas Staples's will of 1758 names a daughter Ann and two granddaughters, and through one of them the line passes to the Nordykes.
body: Thomas Staples lived in and around Burlington, New Jersey, a river town on the Delaware. He wrote his will on 25 October 1758, naming his daughter "Ann, wife of Thomas Rogers" and his granddaughters "Mehetable and Mary Rogers." His wife Mehitable was the daughter of Hananiah Gaunt, the Cape Cod Quaker who had bought 500 acres near Oneanickon in 1685. Gaunt's 1720 will names "Mahitable Staples" and "son-in-law Thomas Staples," so the two were married by then, and Mehitable, born about 1685, grew up on the Gaunt farm in what became Springfield Township, formed 6 November 1688.

Her mother was Dorothy Butler, born at Sandwich on Cape Cod in 1649/50 and buried at Jobstown in 1714, so Mehitable carried both the Gaunt and the Butler Quaker inheritance south from Massachusetts. Thomas and Mehitable's daughter Ann was born about 1714 and married Thomas Rogers at Upper Springfield Meeting on 30 October 1736; the Old Upper Springfield Friends Burying Ground in the township is now on the National Register of Historic Places.

An estate settled on 6 December 1748 may belong to the next generation: "Staples, Thomas, Jun'r, of Burlington Co., innholder" died without a will, and administration went to Thomas Rogers, the husband of Ann Staples, with John Deacon and John Antram of the City of Burlington as bondsmen. The inventory was only 30 pounds 7 shillings. If this Thomas Jr. was Ann's brother, it fits Thomas Rogers acting for the estate.

Granddaughter Mary Rogers married Abraham Nordyke on 1 June 1761, and from Abraham and Mary the line runs through their son Aden Nordyke and his daughter Sicily Shaw to the Stevensons and Hulseys of Arkansas. The label stays proposed because it all hangs on one link, the one that names Parses Shaw as Sicily's daughter.

stories.title: John Rodgers and a third of the residue
stories.hook: John Rodgers of Burlington left his son Thomas one-third of the residue in a will proved in March 1767.
body: John Rodgers of Burlington, New Jersey, made his will on 23 January 1764. He gave his son Thomas one-third of the residue. An inventory was made on 7 March 1767 and the will was proved on 26 March. The other thirds went to his daughter-in-law Elizabeth, then wife of William Lyndon, with her three daughters, and to the children of his daughter Martha, wife of Robert Hosier.

The son Thomas is taken in this family to be Thomas Rogers, who married Ann Staples at Upper Springfield Meeting on 30 October 1736; their daughter Mary married Abraham Nordyke in 1761. The will names Thomas but not his wife, and gives no name for John’s own wife or parents.

A proposed connection to Martha Middleton and to the John Rogers born in 1687 to John and Mary Groom is unproven. A different John Rogers of Windsor, Middlesex County, made a will on 6 January 1769 that was proved on 10 April 1776, naming sons Isaac, Abraham, Joseph, John, Robert, Amos and Mathew, and daughters Mary and Martha, but no Thomas. Those dates and beneficiaries distinguish the Windsor estate from the Burlington estate proved in 1767, though they do not show which family belongs to the 1687 birth.

One line of the will deserves more than it has had. John Rodgers left fifteen pounds each to “Martha, the wife of John Jones, and Hetteble Staples, daughters of my late daughter Mary Staples.” So a Rodgers daughter, Mary, had married into the Staples family before 1764 and died. That is the same Burlington County family Thomas Rogers married into when he took Ann Staples at Upper Springfield in 1736.

It also explains something nobody had asked about. When Thomas Staples Jr., an innkeeper, died in Burlington in December 1748 without a will, it was Thomas Rogers who took out administration, with John Deacon and John Antram as bondsmen. A brother-in-law could do that. If Thomas Jr. was Mary Rodgers’s husband, which nothing states, Thomas Rogers was his brother-in-law twice over, through Ann on one side and through his own sister Mary on the other. Either way, a Rodgers married a Staples within the same circle, which is what a Rodgers son marrying Ann Staples would look like.

stories.title: Hananiah Gaunt: from a Quaker wedding at Sandwich to 500 acres at Hananicon
stories.hook: Hananiah Gaunt married a Quaker neighbor's daughter at Sandwich in May 1678, traded his Cape Cod land for New Jersey land the next day, and died on his own acres in Springfield Township.
body: On 3 May 1678 Hananiah Gaunt posted his intention to marry Dorothy Butler, daughter of Thomas Butler of Sandwich, at the Sandwich Friends Meeting on Cape Cod. Dorothy had been born at Sandwich on 23 January 1649/50. The next day he and his brother Israel exchanged their Sandwich land for land in New Jersey. On 10 May they were married. His father Peter Gaunt, who had been fined in cattle by the Plymouth Colony court for Quaker meetings, is recorded as dying on 10 May 1678, the same day; one of the two dates is probably wrong. Dorothy's brother Daniel had been whipped for helping a Quaker in 1660.

The couple lived at Dartmouth, Massachusetts, until about 1685. On 11 May 1685 George Hutcheson of Burlington conveyed "to Hananiah Gaunt of Rhode Island, yeoman, for 500 acres in the First Tenth," and the proprietors' survey of July 1685 enters "500 a. near Honeonickon" (later Oneanickon, then Springfield Township). On 18 May 1687 "Hananiah Gaunt of near Oneanickon, yeoman," sold 100 acres to William Bustill, a carpenter of Shrewsbury, and in 1690 Hutcheson deeded him one twenty-fourth of a share of West Jersey, a proprietary right to land.

The 1685 deed calls him “of Rhode Island,” but a list of Dartmouth land owners for 1684-1694 carries his name, and a family history notes undivided Dartmouth land he deeded to William Ricketson on 13 January 1684. Both are later accounts, so this is probable.

He added to the farm. A later survey is entered for him “of 220 a. adjoining Samuel Houghton and Tho. Clark; incl. 9 a. of meadow on a brook near Mount Pisgah; 20 a. of the whole being an allowance for highways for other land.” A neighbor’s survey for Daniel Leeds of 188 acres at Oneanickon is described as lying beside “said Gaunts 9 a. lot,” the meadow ground on the brook.

The 1687 deed to Bustill describes the hundred acres as “N. grantor, E. Ralph Trenoweth, part of 500 a., bought of George Hutchinson May 11, 1685”: Hananiah’s own land lay on the north side and Ralph Trenoweth’s on the east. The West Jersey deed is dated 3 November 1690. It calls Hutcheson a distiller and Hananiah “of Burlington Co., yeoman,” and the share was one Hutcheson had bought of Godfrey Newbold of Handsworth, Yorkshire, on 22 August 1684, “excepting 200 acres.” A West Jersey share was a proprietary right to a portion of the province’s unsurveyed land, and such rights were bought and sold in England and Burlington before the land was laid out.

Surveys of his neighbors' land show him as a settled neighbor. Land "surveyed for William Biddle, at Oneanickon, 8th month, 1686, two hundred and seventy acres of land, and in 4th month, 1689, one tract of two hundred and thirty acres, and two other tracts, containing together three hundred and twenty-three acres" adjoined "lands of Hannaniah Gauntt, John Days, Peter Harvey, Charles Read, Samuel Barker, Daniel Leeds, Michael Buffin, John Browne, and John Shinn."

Dorothy died there on 26 April 1714 and is buried at Jobstown. Hananiah made his will on 17 July 1720, naming his children Daniel, Zebulon, Mahitable Staples and Mary Webb, and his son-in-law Thomas Staples; it was proved on 17 November 1721. His daughter Mehitable, born about 1685, married Thomas Staples, and her daughter Ann Staples, born in 1714, married Thomas Rogers in 1736, and Ann's daughter Mary married Abraham Nordyke in 1761, so the farm at Hananicon is where this line's New Jersey roots begin.
Dorothy's birth date, her father's name and the Sandwich marriage are known only through later family accounts and not from the meeting record itself, so those points are probable.

stories.title: The charge against the women's minutes
stories.hook: In December 1766, Cane Creek Friends expelled Charles Davies after a dispute over the truth of the women's meeting record.
body: At Cane Creek Monthly Meeting on 6 December 1766, Charles Davies came before Friends as a disciplinary matter. His complaint concerned the women's minutes: he had charged them with being mixed with an untruth. What passage he disputed, and his side of the argument, were not written down; only what the meeting decided to do about it was.

Friends had already made repeated efforts to change his mind. The meeting found that the labor had been to no purpose, and it disowned him. The same day, ordinary business went on around the dispute: certificates of membership, a marriage report and appointments to attend the quarterly meeting. The break with Charles was set down in the same practical way as those routine decisions.

Charles and Hannah Matson Davies had raised the family from which Mary Davies married William Moffitt in 1763. Charles owned 187 acres purchased in 1758 and was recorded as a minister in 1761. The 1766 decision was a rupture within that Quaker community, though it does not mean that he left North Carolina or ceased to believe. He lived until 1801. His daughter Mary's own will, written more than fifty years after the dispute, still used the numbered-month date familiar in Quaker records.

stories.title: Married as an orphan at West Nottingham: Elizabeth Brown and Edward Norton
stories.hook: Elizabeth Brown was about eight when her father died. At twenty she married a Quaker born in Ireland, and their road ended at Cane Creek.
body: Their marriage on 16 October 1739 was recorded by the Nottingham Quakers in a few lines. The bridegroom was Edward Norton of West Nottingham, Chester County, son of the late Edward Norton of the Parish of Armagh in the Kingdom of Ireland. The bride was Elizabeth Brown, "dt William & Elizabeth (Cowgill), both dec." She had been born in the twelfth month of 1718, early 1719 by modern reckoning. Her mother died before her father married again in March 1721/2, and her father, William Brown Jr., died about 1727; her stepmother, Margaret Davis, then married William Kirk. Her grandfather, the emigrant William Brown, was an elder of the meeting.

Edward's own connections were tangled with hers from the start. His sister Mary Norton had married Elizabeth's uncle Richard Brown in November 1733, a tangle told under the elder Edward Norton's name, and both couples took certificates to Hopewell Monthly Meeting in Virginia, Edward and Elizabeth on 19 January 1739/40.

From Hopewell the Nortons went on to Fairfax and then south. They reached Cane Creek in 1762, and the next March their daughter Margaret, born about 1740, married Joseph Chamness. The certificate calls the bride's parents "Edward Norton and Elizabeth, his wife, of Rowan County," and both signed as witnesses. Edward died in 1776 and is buried at Providence, Randolph County. Their granddaughter Martha married Robert Moffitt in 1797, which is how an orphan from West Nottingham and a family from Armagh come into the Moffitt story.

stories.title: John Matson of Merion, and the daughter who married at a justice's house
stories.hook: John Matson gave his consent in February 1733 for his daughter Hannah to marry Charles Davis; their daughter Mary married William Moffitt at Cane Creek.
body: John Matson comes into view through his daughter's marriage. In the twelfth month of 1732, by the Friends' count, Charles Davis of Blockley (Davies in the Cane Creek records) and Hannah Matson, "daughter of John Matson of Merion in the same county and province aforesaid with consent of her father," published their intentions under a Pennsylvania law against clandestine marriages and met at the house of Charles Read, Esq., a justice of the peace for Philadelphia. The witnesses were John Matson Jr. and Daniel Matson, probably Hannah's brothers, along with Evan and Jane George, Richard and Thomas George, Ellin Jones and Mary Andrew. Hannah was born about 1715.

John was a Quaker farmer of Merion, in the Welsh settlement west of Philadelphia. By the usual reckoning he was born about 1686 at Upper Merion and married a woman named Margaret before 1709. Their children were Daniel, Hannah, Morris, Catherine, John, Peter and Joseph. Matson is a Swedish name, and Swedes had farmed along the Schuylkill and the Delaware before Penn's grant, but nothing makes him a son of the Swede Johann Mattson; his parentage is undocumented. In 1742 he and his wife took a certificate from Chester Monthly Meeting to Goshen.

John Matson was buried on 3 May 1748, and his will was proved in Chester County on 16 July 1748. By then his daughter Hannah and Charles Davis had left Pennsylvania for Virginia and then Cane Creek, North Carolina, where Charles was disowned by the meeting in 1766 and died in 1801; Hannah lived until 25 October 1812. Their daughter Mary married William Moffitt there on 2 April 1763, sixteen days after the Chamness-Norton wedding, and her son Robert married Martha Chamness in 1797. John Matson of Merion is Robert Moffitt's great-grandfather on his mother's side.

stories.title: Joseph Cole's will, and the two-year-old who became Sarah Chamness
stories.hook: Joseph Cole made his will on 22 January 1720/1, leaving a widow and a daughter, Sarah, not yet three, who later married Anthony Chamness.
body: Joseph Cole of Baltimore County, Maryland, was the son of John Cole and Johanna Garrett. In November 1712 his father conveyed him part of a tract called "Daniel's Whimsey." His mother's father was Dennis Garrett, the early settler killed in 1691.

He made his will on 22 January 1720/1, and it names his wife Susanna and his daughter Sarah. Sarah was born on the 1st day of the 5th month 1718 in the Friends' register, so when her father wrote the will she was not yet three. The Cane Creek register later wrote her down as the "daughter of Joseph and Susanna Cole, of Baltimore Co., Md., now married to Anthony Chainness."

Sarah grew up to marry Anthony Chamness in 1735 and to raise thirteen children at Cane Creek, and her story is told under her own name. Her son Joseph Chamness married Margaret Norton, and their daughter Martha was Robert Moffitt's wife.

stories.title: John Cole of Cole's Adventure: a witness at his father-in-law's trial
stories.hook: John Cole was about twenty-two when he was named as a witness in the Garrett case, and about sixty-seven when he gave evidence on the bounds of his own land in 1738.
body: John Cole was a witness when his wife's father was killed. The court's 1692 indictment of John Oldton for the sword blow that killed Dennis Garrett listed these witnesses: Philip Roper, Nicholas Hale, "John Cole (son-in-law of the deceased)," Thomas Stone, Abraham Vaughan and Barbara Garrett, the widow. John had married Dennis's daughter Johanna. Oldton was condemned to hang and was pardoned; he later served as captain of the county's rangers. John Cole was then about twenty-two.

The records that follow are surveys. Surveys list "Cole's Choice," surveyed for him on 28 July 1694 and never patented; "Cole's Addition," 67 acres surveyed on 29 May 1698 "on the north side of Patapsco River in the woods"; and "Cole's Adventure," surveyed in 1706 on a run called Gwin's Run. In March 1737/8, when a land commission sat on Cole's Adventure, "John Cole, Senior, aged about 67 years," testified that the beginning tree stood about a hundred yards east of Gwinn's Run.

Cole’s Choice was later taken up again under the name “Orange,” and the same survey appears as “Cole’s Chance,” with a deed from John Cole to Robert Green dated 1702. Cole’s Addition lay beside the path called Darley Path, where Chase Street and the Bel Air Road now cross in Baltimore. The 1737/8 commission on Cole’s Adventure was held by Thomas Demmett.

In August 1750 another commission took depositions about Cole's Addition from men who had known him. John Ensor, Sr., aged 55, called him his father-in-law and said that about eighteen years earlier, around 1732, Cole had come with him to the spot and shown him where the boundary oak stood. William Green, aged 58, told the same story: “the aforesaid John Cole said there should have been a bounded tree of Coles Addition.” Ensor was born about 1695, and the Ensor family is counted among the descendants of Dennis Garrett. By then Cole had died, in 1746, at about seventy-six. His land lay in and around the site of Baltimore, which was laid out as a town in 1729.

The family is easy to follow. His son Joseph made a will in 1720/1 and left a daughter, Sarah, who married Anthony Chamness in 1735; a son named Dennis Garrett Cole received land from his grandmother Barbara Garrett Broad in 1712. Sarah's son Joseph Chamness was the father of Martha, who married Robert Moffitt in 1797.

stories.title: Ann Mercer’s six children and her Quaker ministry
stories.hook: Ann Mercer bore six children with William Brown and was remembered among the Friends who spoke in meeting.
body: Ann Mercer, daughter of Thomas and Ann Mercer of Ringwood, was born on the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month 1666: 24 February 1666/7, or 1667 in modern year numbering. That she was the Ann Mercer who became William Brown’s second wife in Pennsylvania is probable. Later accounts place Thomas at Andover before he and his daughter crossed to Pennsylvania about 1682–83 and settled in Aston Township, Chester County. William was born on the twenty-ninth day of the first month 1658 (29 March, Old Style), the son of Richard Browne; his mother is not named. William had married Dorothy in England, and their son Joseph was born there on 12 June 1682. Dorothy died at sea on the voyage to the Delaware. William went first to his brother James, a weaver at Marcus Hook, and in 1684, when Ann was seventeen, he married her.

The Nottingham Quaker registers give the children Ann bore him: Mercer, born the 27th of the 12th month 1685; Ann, 1st of the 10th month 1687; William, 21st of the 7th month 1689; John, 3rd of the 5th month 1691; Richard, 31st of the 1st month 1693; and Thomas, 17th of the 11th month 1694. Mercer, named for her family and often written "Messer," was the first. Ann Mercer died in 1696; a 1709 Quaker list of deceased Friends names her as "Ann Browne daughtr of said Thoms Mercer." Her father Thomas had died on 22 November 1694, eight weeks before her youngest, Thomas Brown, was born in January 1695.

In 1709 the Yearly Meeting remembered Anne Browne among the deceased Public Friends, the people who spoke in meeting. She was named as Thomas Mercer’s daughter, had crossed with her father, received a Testimony for Truth after arriving, and was buried in 1696. This preserves a part of her life beyond the names and dates of her children.

William married Catharine Williams of Philadelphia in 1699, and in 1702 he moved to the Nottingham Lots on the Pennsylvania-Maryland line, where Lots 23 and 33 were assigned to him. A history of the Brick Meeting House says that he "was the first Friend to settle on the Nottingham lots" and that the first meeting was held at his house in 1704. The meeting records put it a little later: Concord Monthly Meeting received the request for a meeting at his house in the 2nd month of 1705, and Concord Quarterly Meeting approved it on 9 April 1705, so meetings were held there by 1705. His fourth wife, whom he married in 1711, was Mary Matthews. A family memorandum of 1786 calls him an elder and a substantial Friend, and puts his death on the 23rd of the 6th month 1746 (23 August, Old Style) in his ninety-first year (another account gives 1 October 1746); the Wellingborough register, which gives his birth in 1658, would make him about eighty-eight.

Ann Mercer’s descendants connect several branches of the family. Her sons William and Thomas married the Cowgill sisters Elizabeth and Ellin; her son Richard married three times and ended with Mary Norton of Armagh in 1733; and William's daughter Elizabeth Brown married Mary's brother Edward Norton in 1739. Their daughter Margaret Norton married Joseph Chamness, and Margaret's daughter Martha married Robert Moffitt. Ann Mercer is Martha Chamness's great-great-grandmother, and so the ancestor of every child Martha bore Robert Moffitt.

stories.title: Chamniss of Wapping: the London parents of a boy bound for Maryland
stories.hook: John Chamness married Ann Weary at St John's, Wapping, in January 1704; twenty years later their son Anthony was bound as a servant for seven years in Maryland.
body: John Chamness and Ann Weary were married on 4 January 1704 at St John's Church, Wapping, the riverside parish beside the Thames, east of the Tower. The parish clerk spelled the name "Chamniss," and Ann's surname Weary or Wearey. Trees that call her Ann Jones have nothing behind them. Their children came steadily: at least eight between 1705 and 1717, baptized in the same parish. Anthony, the one who matters here, was baptized in February 1713 when he was eighteen days old. Cane Creek Meeting later wrote him down as "Anthony Chamness, s. John & Ann, b. about 2 mo. 1713, Est. Smithfield, London," so the family lived at East Smithfield, close to Wapping.

Anthony was bound as a servant on 9 February 1724/5. The indenture, which describes him as of Whitechapel, bound him for seven years to John Cooke, a London victualler, for service in "Maryland (his Majesty's Plantation in America)." It gives his age as fifteen; counted from his baptism he was about eleven. Either way he was out of his time by 1732 and was in Baltimore County, where on 24 November 1735 he married Sarah Cole, the great-granddaughter of the murdered Dennis Garrett.

John and Ann are the founders of the American Chamness line, and they leave only the parish registers: no will, no trade and no death date. Their son, the boy sent to Maryland at the age of eleven or fifteen, became overseer of the Cane Creek meeting and in 1751 took up 490 acres there.

stories.title: Henry Satterfield, who died in 1861 with twelve children
stories.hook: A Tennessee-born farmer in Allen County, Kentucky, and the Garrison daughter who outlived him by thirty-five years.
body: His son James described him in one sentence: "a native of Maury County, Tenn.; died in 1861, at the age of fifty years." He died on 24 December 1861, his parents named as Ephraim and "Rutha" Satterfield. He was born about 1811, two years after Ephraim Satterfield married Ruth Knowles in Warren County, and Maury County is where the sketch places the young couple. His son James was born in Allen County on 14 April 1838.

Henry married Mary Garrison, born 17 October 1811, the daughter of John M. Garrison of Allen County and, it is said, of Martha "Patsey" Cannon. Their twelve children were Louisa J. (Roy), David E., Samuel A., James H., Ruth M. (Massey), John E., Euphema P. (Liles), Hettie C. (Jones), Martha C. (deceased), Sarah E. (Hues), Joseph W. H. and Abraham W. Of the twelve, James H., born in 1838, married Melissa Gibson in 1859 and is the line to the Smiths. In 1861, the year his father died, James enlisted in the Ninth Kentucky, and an S. A. Satterfield, perhaps their son Samuel A., was sued with A. W. Garrison in 1871 in Warren Circuit Court over a lot in Bowling Green, though the court gave only initials.

Mary's parents' marriage ended in the legislature. By an act approved on 29 February 1848 the Kentucky General Assembly dissolved the marriage of her father John M. Garrison and Patsey; Mary was then 36. She outlived Henry by thirty-five years and died on 2 March 1896.

Mary did not die in Kentucky. Her stone stands in Big Springs Cemetery at Lineville, in Wayne County, Iowa, just north of the Missouri line, and reads: "M. C. Satterfield / Died / Mar 2, 1896 / Age 84 Ys 4 Ms 16 Ds." Counting back from the age gives a birth in mid-October 1811, which matches the 17 October 1811 birth given for Mary Garrison, and the initials fit Mary Cannon. Her memorial names John Milton Garrison as her father. No one knows when or why she went to Iowa.

Her children's graves show how far the family spread. Her children lie far afield: Samuel Addison (1835-1913) at Strawn in Palo Pinto County, Texas; James Henry (1838-1922; the cemetery listing has 1837) at Reed Cemetery in Bowie County, Texas; Ruth Melissa Massey (1840-1935) at Llano Cemetery in Amarillo; Euphema Lyles (1845-1922) near Stephenville in Erath County, Texas; Hettie Caroline Jones (1847-1907) at LeGrande in Hart County, Kentucky; and Abraham W. (1860-1933), the youngest, at Eldora in Hardin County, Iowa.

A studio portrait of her, captioned "Age 78," would date to about 1889 or 1890 if the caption is right. It shows an elderly woman in a dark dress and a ruffled, lace-trimmed cap. Who identified the sitter is not known, so the identification rests on the caption.

stories.title: James and Cynthia Gibson of Allen County, Melissa's parents
stories.hook: Two names from a county history, and the daughter who married a Satterfield in 1859.
body: James and Cynthia (Woodcock) Gibson are named once, in the account James H. Satterfield of Butler County gave of himself in 1885: Melissa A., his first wife, was the "daughter of James and Cynthia (Woodcock) Gibson, of Allen County." Melissa married James Satterfield in Allen County on 17 September 1859.

Allen County, created in 1815 from Warren and Barren, was where both families lived. Melissa and James had children together; their children were Henry W., John C., Sidney R., James D., Martha A. and Mary C., among them John C., born in February 1864. In 1867 the Satterfields left for Dakota County, Minnesota, and returned in 1875 to Warren County and then, in 1876, Butler County. Melissa died on 2 May 1877, the year after the move. A fire at the Allen County courthouse in 1902 destroyed some county records.

Melissa's son John C. Satterfield farmed at Horse Mill in Butler County and moved to Hagansport, Texas, about 1907. His daughter Artie Pearl Satterfield married Charles Oscar Smith in 1915, and their daughter Faye (Smith) Moffitt is the link to this family.

stories.title: Ephraim Satterfield, a Virginian by his grandson's account
stories.hook: One of thirteen children named in a Warren County will, he married a Knowles in 1809 and is gone by 1850.
body: His grandson James mentioned Ephraim only in passing, as the father of Henry Satterfield and "a native of Virginia, who died about 1850." The Warren County, Kentucky, records say more. John Satterfield's will, proved on 10 November 1847, names Ephraim among thirteen children: Uriah, Ephraim, Rebecca, Mary, Jeremiah, Phoebe, Nancy, Moses, Sarah, Jesse, Leah, Reuben and John. On 12 November 1809 Ephraim married Ruth Knowles in Warren County, and Ruth's father Joshua Knowles named "Ruth Saterfield" among his daughters in a will of 1824.

Their son Henry was born about 1811, in Maury County, Tennessee, by his grandson's account. Henry's death in 1861 was entered with his parents as Ephraim and "Rutha" Satterfield, which ties Henry to this Ephraim and Ruth. The accounts disagree about Ephraim himself. One family tree has him born in South Carolina in 1787 and dead in 1848, with Henry born in Warren County, while his grandson gave Virginia and Tennessee. A birth in South Carolina fits the will of his father John, who had lived in South Carolina before Kentucky.

By 1850 Ruth was a widow in Allen County, living with her daughter Elizabeth. Ephraim's death falls between his father's will of 1847 and that census, and his grandson dated it about 1850. James H. Satterfield was twelve in 1850.

stories.title: Melvina Clark: a birth date and age that disagree
stories.hook: She died in 1929 with both parents named, but her birth date and recorded age disagree.
body: Melvina died, as Melvina Johnston, at Big Reedy in Edmonson County on 17 January 1929, a widow; her father was given as Newton Clark, born in Kentucky, and her mother as Mary Dunn. Polly Nash of Big Reedy supplied the information. Her husband’s name was left blank.

The certificate’s birth date is read and indexed as 10 November 1851, although the final year digits are not perfectly clear. It also records an age of 78 years, 2 months, 6 days. That age is inconsistent with the written birth and death dates. Both fields are preserved here without choosing a corrected birth year.

In 1850 Newton Clark’s Butler County household held Newton, 32; Polly, 32; Martha, 10; Granville, 9; Stanford, 8; Hester, 6; William, 5; a girl aged 3 indexed as Vina; and Mary, 11 months. The handwriting of the age-three girl’s name does not unambiguously identify her as Melvina. The former claim that this census establishes Melvina’s birth about 1847 is therefore withdrawn. The census has no relationship column, and the identification of Vina with Melvina remains open.

Newton Clark and Polly D. Elms were married in Butler County: license issued 20 January 1839, ceremony 24 January, return signed 25 January. Melvina’s death certificate instead gives her mother’s name as Mary Dunn. Nothing reconciles Dunn and Elms or proves that the same woman bore both names. The identification of the mother named in 1929 with Polly in Newton’s 1850 household and with the 1839 bride remains probable. Some family trees link Newton to William and Lavina (Willis) Clark; that parental link is a separate question.

Her married name was Johnson; her husband's first name is not recorded on the memorials. Samantha D. was born on 28 March 1872 and Charlie in 1885. Samantha married John C. Satterfield in 1892, moved with him to Hagansport, Texas, about 1907, and crossed the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma, after marrying Bird Alexander Stephens in 1917. She died on 1 October 1928 and is buried at Soper Cemetery.

She was buried at Mount Pleasant, the cemetery at Big Reedy, on 18 January 1929. Samantha had died on 1 October 1928; nothing shows that Melvina attended her Oklahoma burial. Charlie remained in Butler County and died in 1959.

stories.title: The Norton from Armagh who left a son and a daughter in Pennsylvania
stories.hook: Edward Norton of Armagh is known only from what his children's marriage certificates say of him, but it is enough to place his family in Ireland.
body: At his son's wedding on 16 October 1739 the bridegroom was described as "Edward Norton of West Nottingham, Chester County, son of Edward Norton of 'ye City and Parish of Armagh,' Ireland, deceased." That is all it says. His wife's name is not given, nor is his trade or the year of his death. He was dead by October 1739.

The other marriage is his daughter's. On 24 November 1733 , "Mary Norton, daughter of Edward Norton, 'of ye County of Armagh,' Ireland," married Richard Brown, son of William Brown of West Nottingham. Another account gives the same marriage as the 24th of the 5th month and calls her "dau. of Edward Norton of Co. Armagh, Irel'd." She was Richard's third wife. Together the two marriages put two adult children of the same Armagh Quaker in Chester County, near the Maryland line, within six years, part of the Irish Friends' emigration.

Richard, born in 1693, was the son of William Brown the emigrant and his second wife Ann Mercer; he had married Hannah Reynolds in 1717 and Rachel Beeson in 1730/1 before Mary Norton. The bridegroom of 1739, Edward Norton the younger, married Elizabeth Brown, daughter of William Brown Jr. and Elizabeth Cowgill, so he married his sister Mary’s husband’s niece.

Both Norton marriages were into the Brown family, and both couples went on to Virginia. Edward Norton the younger and Elizabeth Brown are the Moffitt ancestors; their daughter Margaret married Joseph Chamness at Cane Creek in 1763, and Margaret's daughter Martha married Robert Moffitt. Mary and Richard Brown had three sons, Richard, Joseph and Mercer; Richard died before 1747, and in April 1747 Mary married William Kirk. The elder Edward, who stayed in Armagh as far as the certificates show, is the earliest Norton on this line.

Edward and Elizabeth Norton took a certificate to Hopewell Monthly Meeting in Virginia on 19 January 1739/40, and Richard and Mary Brown with their family took one to Hopewell too. Mary and Richard’s three children were Richard (born 18 September 1734, died 4 September 1738), Joseph (1 April 1736, died 19 May 1751) and Mercer (7 May 1740). Richard left a will. Fairfax Monthly Meeting appointed a committee on the 28th of the 12th month 1746/7 (28 February) to inquire into its settlement, to protect the children, and found it satisfactorily settled. On the 21st of the 1st month 1746/7 (21 March) Nottingham gave William Kirk, the widower of Margaret Davis, a certificate to Fairfax, clear to marry Mary Brown. Margaret Davis, who had died in February 1744/5, had been the second wife of Elizabeth’s father, so Mary Norton’s new husband was Elizabeth’s stepmother’s widower.

Edward and Elizabeth Norton later lived in Rowan County, North Carolina, as their daughter Margaret’s marriage in 1763 shows. That they are the couple of 1739 is probable, not proven, though the names and the Hopewell and Fairfax trail suggest it. If so, Margaret’s grandmother was Elizabeth Cowgill of Neshaminy, and the line from the Settle certificate of 1682 runs through Brown and Norton to the Chamness wedding that put the family into Robert Moffitt’s household.

stories.title: Two Cowgill sisters, two Brown brothers, and a daughter left behind
stories.hook: William Brown Jr. married a Cowgill in 1715, lost her within about six years, died himself about 1727, and left a daughter who married at West Nottingham as an orphan.
body: William Brown Jr. was born on the 21st day of the 7th month 1689, the third child of the Nottingham pioneer William Brown and Ann Mercer. In 1715 he married Elizabeth Cowgill, born on the 24th of the 6th month 1694 at Middletown, Bucks County, to John Cowgill and Bridget Croasdale. Her father had come from Yorkshire in 1682; accounts differ on which ship carried the Settle families. He was a tanner who moved about 1713 or 1714 to the Delaware shore, where on 10 May 1718 he asked for another hundred acres, "having erected a tan-yard on a branch of Black Bird's Creek." The marriage was recorded in Duck Creek Monthly Meeting, on 1 December 1715 by the Quaker count, as that of Elizabeth Cowgill, "daughter of John Cowgill, of Duck Creek in New Castle," and William Brown, "son of William Brown, of Nottingham."

The couple had two children. John was born on the 27th of the 2nd month 1717 and died on the 12th of the 7th month 1723, aged six. Elizabeth was born in the twelfth month of 1718, which in modern dating is early 1719. Her mother died within about three years of that birth, before March 1721/2, when William married Margaret Davis. That marriage produced William (1722) and Jacob (1724), and William Jr. himself died about 1727. His widow married William Kirk on the 6th of the 3rd month 1730. Her stepdaughter Elizabeth was eight or nine when her father died. In 1739 the Nottingham book called her "dt William & Elizabeth (Cowgill), both dec."

The Cowgill sisters had already made two marriages with the Browns. Elizabeth's sister Ellin, born on the 14th of the 10th month 1700, married William's brother Thomas Brown in 1718/9; Thomas died on 19 February 1746/7, and Ellin married again on 13 November 1768, to Lewis Clothier of Kent County, Maryland, and lived to 5 January 1772, aged 71. Two immigrant families, one from Yorkshire and one from Northamptonshire and Hampshire, had become a single network of cousins at Nottingham.

The child they left carried the line. Elizabeth Brown married Edward Norton at West Nottingham on 16 October 1739, her uncle Richard Brown having married Edward's sister Mary six years before, and their daughter Margaret married Joseph Chamness at Cane Creek in 1763. Through Elizabeth Brown, the Cowgill and Brown families became part of the Norton and Chamness lines.

stories.title: John Satterfield's will, with thirteen children in a single line
stories.hook: Born in Orange County, North Carolina, and dead in Warren County, Kentucky, at about eighty-one.
body: John Satterfield was born about 1766 in Orange County, North Carolina, a county formed in 1752 and since divided so that his birthplace lies in Person County. He lived in South Carolina and later settled in Warren County, Kentucky, where he made a will proved on 10 November 1847. It lists thirteen children: Uriah, Ephraim, Rebecca, Mary, Jeremiah, Phoebe, Nancy, Moses, Sarah, Jesse, Leah, Reuben and John.

His wife Mary, born about 1768, is named in the will. Her maiden name is not settled: one memorial gives Jones, and a 1786 marriage in Surry County, North Carolina, gives Haga. John's own father is disputed and is not shown here. Ephraim's place in the list is the link to this family. Ephraim's son Henry died on 24 December 1861, and Henry's death was entered with his father as Ephraim, which matches the Ephraim of the will.

Where John came from is the open question. A Person County family tradition holds that a John Satterfield who died there in 1802 had five sons, Isaac, Jesse, John, William and James, and that John and William "migrated to Tennessee and Kentucky as young men." No document supports the story, though its detail deserves some credit. The 1802 will itself names only a wife Sarah and sons James and Isaac. If the tradition holds, our John, born in Orange County when it still covered Person, would be one of those sons; so far it is a hypothesis and no record joins them.
The sources differ on where Ephraim was born: one family tree has South Carolina in 1787, where John had lived, while his grandson called him a Virginian.
