stories.title: Ruth Knowles Satterfield, who died in Missouri at eighty-one
stories.hook: Born in Virginia, married in Warren County in 1809, widowed by 1850, and buried a long way from either.
body: Ruth Knowles was born about 1783 in Virginia, the daughter of Joshua Knowles, whose 1824 will names "Ruth Saterfield" among his five daughters. On 12 November 1809 she married Ephraim Satterfield in Warren County, Kentucky, a county that dated only from December 1796. Her son Henry was born about 1811, in Maury County, Tennessee, by a grandson's account, and his death in 1861 was entered with his parents as Ephraim and "Rutha" Satterfield.

Where the couple lived in the years between is not recorded. Ephraim's father John named him among thirteen children in a will proved in November 1847, and a grandson put Ephraim's death about 1850. By 1850 Ruth was a widow in Allen County, Kentucky, a county cut from Warren and Barren in 1815, living with her daughter Elizabeth. Her father had died in 1832, and her son Henry would die in 1861.

In 1860 "Rutha Satterfield," about 77, lived in the household of Elizabeth and her husband Jesse Agee in Gasconade County, Missouri. She had been in her daughter's house in 1850 as well, so she probably went west with Elizabeth and Jesse rather than alone. Gasconade County, created in 1820, had filled with settlers from Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee and the Carolinas, and from 1837 with Germans of the Hermann colony. She died there in 1864, having outlived her husband by about fourteen years and her son Henry by three.
Why she went to Missouri is not known. That she was our Ephraim's wife rests on Henry's death entry and her father's will, and is probable.

stories.title: Joshua Knowles's will: a wife named Jemima and five daughters
stories.hook: A Warren County man, counted between 80 and 90 in 1830, who wrote his will in 1824 and lived about eight more years.
body: Joshua Knowles was born about 1747, and the 1830 census counted him in Warren County, Kentucky, between 80 and 90. He wrote his will on 11 November 1824, and it was proved in October 1832. It names his wife Jemima, his son Matthew as executor, his son John of Franklin County, Virginia, and five daughters: Sarah Hays, Polly Stephens, Leaner Jones, Ruth Saterfield and Elizabeth Bailey. Ruth was born in Virginia.

Warren County had been created only in December 1796, when Joshua was about forty-nine, and in 1830, at about eighty-three, he was still living there. His will hints at where he started: his son John was "of Franklin County, Virginia," and his daughter Ruth was born in Virginia, so Joshua probably came to Kentucky from Virginia, though no record of his own birthplace has been found.

Ruth is the daughter that matters here. She had married Ephraim Satterfield in Warren County on 12 November 1809, and her father's will, written fifteen years later, calls her "Ruth Saterfield" in the clerk's spelling. The will does not say whether Jemima was Ruth's mother or a later wife.

By 1824 his five daughters carried five married surnames, Hays, Stephens, Jones, Saterfield and Bailey, and a son was still in Virginia, so the family was already spread across two states. Ruth's husband Ephraim came of a family that had moved from the Carolinas to Warren County, and Ruth later followed a daughter to Missouri, where she died in 1864.
He is buried in Knowles Cemetery at Motley in Warren County. The will comes from a family account and has not been read in the original.

stories.title: Thomas Mercer of Andover, who crossed with his daughter Ann
stories.hook: A Hampshire Quaker widower brought his teenage daughter to Pennsylvania in 1682-83; she married at seventeen, and he died there in 1694.
body: Thomas Mercer and his wife Ann lived at Ringwood in Hampshire when their daughter Ann was born. The Quaker register names both parents and dates the birth to the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month 1666. In the Friends’ calendar then in use, this means 24 February 1666/7, or 1667 in modern year numbering. The entry gives the mother’s first name but no maiden surname. Later family accounts place Thomas at Andover before crossing to Pennsylvania with his daughter about 1682–83; identification with the Ringwood family remains probable.

He took up land in Aston Township, Chester County, and his daughter was married there in 1684 to William Brown, born in Northamptonshire, who had landed a year or two earlier. Ann was seventeen. Her first child, born in February 1685/6, was named Mercer for her family. Thomas Mercer lived long enough to see five grandchildren born, and died on 22 November 1694. A 1709 Quaker list of public Friends who died in Pennsylvania names him and "Ann Browne daughtr of said Thoms Mercer," who died in 1696.

Thomas Mercer's own parents are unknown. Through Ann his line runs to her son William Brown Jr., his daughter Elizabeth Brown, her daughter Margaret Norton and her daughter Martha Chamness, who married Robert Moffitt.

The two Anns belong to different generations: Ann, wife of Thomas, was the mother; Ann Mercer, who married William Brown, was the daughter. The elder Ann’s maiden surname and life dates remain unknown.

The 1709 list remembers the immigrant father and daughter: Thomas Mercer of Andover, who arrived about 1682 or 1683 and died in 1694, and Anne Browne, his daughter, who came with him and was buried in 1696. It also remembers Anne’s public testimony after her arrival. It places Andover in Wiltshire rather than Hampshire, and gives no further parents for Thomas or maiden surname for his wife.

stories.title: Mary Dockery and the Newton household
stories.hook: An 1867 marriage and an 1880 census offer a possible name for Lizzie Newton’s mother.
body: A license was issued in St. Clair County, Alabama, on 11 February 1867 for Bailus Newton and Mary Ann Dockery, and the ceremony took place at a Gibson residence; the day is not clear enough to settle the differing dates.

In 1880 Balus Newton and his wife Mary lived in Etowah County with children including Elizabeth, seven. The surname is Newton, though an index reads Keaton. Balus’s name, the county and Elizabeth’s age fit the father and daughter named as Balas and Lizzie in Lizzie’s 1889 marriage consent.

Mary’s work was entered as keeping house in a household of nine. The eldest boy, twelve, was already listed as a farm hand; the youngest child was an infant of eight months. Elizabeth stood between older children Ann and Lindsey and younger children Hezekiah, Amanda and the baby.

Mary was Balus’s wife in 1880, but nothing says she was Elizabeth’s mother. The earlier marriage to Mary Ann Dockery and the household make her a probable mother, but nothing directly names Lizzie’s mother. When Oda Verbena Newton died, her parents were given as Balous Newton and Mary Marzee Dockery; a similarly named young daughter appears in the 1880 home.

stories.title: A family name on the Armstrong school list
stories.hook: A school list preserves William Harrison Pisachubbe's name and points to a Choctaw education system built and funded by the Nation.
body: On 22 August 1899, a list of Armstrong Academy students was sent to the enrolling Commission. It included Harrison Pisachubbe. Twelve years later, a federal official identified him as William H. Pisachubbe, son of Eunice and brother of Robert, the family's direct ancestor. The school list had given him a second enrollment under his middle name, and in 1911 the correction was made. Nothing says what he studied or how long he attended.

Armstrong Academy had opened in 1845 as part of the Choctaw Nation's school system. The Choctaw Council funded schools, often contracting with religious mission boards to operate them. The Civil War interrupted instruction, and the academy building later served as a Choctaw government meeting place before the Nation's capital moved to Tuskahoma.

In 1883 the Choctaw General Council passed an act establishing a school for orphan boys at Armstrong and appropriated money for its reopening. A separate act set a planned enrollment of fifty boys there and fifty girls at the Choctaw orphan school. The acts show the Nation making educational policy; a place on a later student list does not by itself explain a child's family circumstances or whether a parent was living.

The Oklahoma Historical Society dates the reopened orphan boys' academy to 1884. In 1898 the federal Curtis Act placed Choctaw Nation schools under United States government control. William's 1899 listing therefore belongs to a period when control over an institution begun by the Choctaw Nation was being transferred to the federal government. His own experience at the school is not known.

stories.title: Clinton Sandridge: an Arkansas farmer in Broken Bow
stories.hook: Clinton Sandridge came from Arkansas to McCurtain County in 1919 to farm, and by his death in 1961 his children and brothers were scattered from Oklahoma and Arkansas to Texas and California.
body: Clinton Lamar Sandridge moved from Arkansas to McCurtain County in 1919. He farmed, belonged to the Assembly of God church and made his home in Broken Bow. He died at home early on the morning of 20 December 1961, and the McCurtain Gazette carried the news that same day.

He left two sons, Lemuel Sandridge of Broken Bow and Jack, in Lake Jackson, Texas, and two daughters, in California and Houston. Two brothers survived him, Lon in Little Rock and L. P. in California, but no one then named Clinton’s parents.

Even his birth date was uncertain. The newspaper gave 25 September 1892, but in 1930 he had been 43, which would mean a birth around 1886–1887. His widow went unnamed in the notice. She was Maggie, at home with Clinton and Lemuel in 1930, and her maiden name is still uncertain.

Clinton and Maggie share a double marker at Broken Bow Cemetery: “Clinton L., Sept. 24, 1882 – Dec. 20, 1961” and “Maggie A., May 2, 1891 – July 15, 1982.” Carved between the two names is “Married June 19, 1910.” So he was probably born in 1882, not the 1892 the newspaper printed. Maggie outlived Clinton by more than twenty years.

He was born, the newspaper said, at “Burn, Arkansas,” probably Beirne, a small community in southern Clark County. Near Beirne, in an unmarked grave at Browns Cemetery, lies a Mary E. “Molly” Cole Sandridge, born on 17 May 1861, who died in 1897. She is remembered as the wife of William D. Sandridge, married on 8 October 1877, and the mother of sons Clinton (1882), Lon P. (1889), Joseph Burton (1892) and Lawrence Lafayette (1897). Clinton’s own surviving brothers in 1961 were Lon, of Little Rock, and L. P., in California. William D. and Molly Cole Sandridge were probably Clinton’s parents, though nothing from their own time yet says so.

Clinton’s 1910 marriage to Maggie was his second. His first wife, Esther Margaret Bolls Sandridge, died in 1909 at about 26 and lies at Midway Cemetery near Prescott, in Nevada County, Arkansas. She left three children: Clinton Everett, called Chat, born in 1902; Nobie Jewel, born in 1904; and Mildred Marie, born in 1908. In June of the following year Clinton married Maggie. Lemuel, their only child together, was born on 4 December 1911, at Prescott, it is said.

Chat did not live long. His government headstone at Midway Cemetery reads “Everett Chat Sandridge, Arkansas, Pvt. 1 Cl., U.S. Marine Corps.” He died on 18 April 1932 in Kerr County, Texas, three days before his thirtieth birthday. How he died is not known.

Maggie is remembered by some as Margaret Ann “Maggie” Cash, born at Prescott, a daughter of James L. Cash (1863–1946) and Maxie Ann McClure Cash (1865–1941), who both lie at Midway. In 1930, though, her birthplace was given as Texas, and whether she was born a Cash is still unproved.
Lemuel Lamar Sandridge died on 13 March 1979, it seems in Dallas. He is buried at Hochatown Cemetery beside Audrey, under a stone that names them “Mother” and “Father.”

stories.title: Barbara Phillips Livesay and the Pearland family
stories.hook: Barbara Phillips married Lester Livesay at seventeen, and the date is still carved in a heart between their names on their stone in Carthage.
body: Barbara Phillips was born on 7 April 1918 in Nacogdoches, Texas, “the daughter of Carl C. and Beulah Turner Phillips,” as The Panola Watchman put it on 6 September 1995, after her death. On 21 April 1935, aged seventeen, she married Lester Woodrow Livesay Jr. The date is carved in a heart between their names on the stone they share at Restland Memorial Park, Carthage.

Barbara came from a large family. Three of her brothers, R. Jay, Randall and Samuel Phillips, died before her, as did a sister, Glendale Baits. A brother and a sister outlived her, and were still living when Lester died in 2001. Her parents, Carl and Beulah, and their Houston years have a story of their own.

Barbara and Lester’s family had ties to Houston, Pearland and Carthage. Their children included a son, Wayne Woodrow Livesay, and a daughter, Carylon, who married Jimmy Bardwell. When Carylon died in Carthage on 18 June 2014, the Pearland Historical Society remembered her in its July newsletter as the daughter of Lester and Barbara Livesay and the sister of Wayne; by then both her brother and her husband had died. The Lester and Barbara of that notice were very probably this couple.

Barbara spent her last years in Panola County. She had lived there for three years, “moving here from Mt. Enterprise,” when she died at Panola Nursing Home on 2 September 1995, aged 77. Lester lived until 2001, and when he died he was remembered as the husband of Barbara Phillips, who had gone before him.

stories.title: Julia’s changing names: the family behind Audrey
stories.hook: Julia married at Idabel in 1916 as Julia Myers, and over the next forty years she was also Mrs. Nelson, Mrs. Stevens and Mrs. Ratcliff.
body: Julia went by several surnames in McCurtain County and neighboring Arkansas. On 1 July 1916, at Idabel, Julia Myers, forty, married William A. Nelson, forty-six. Their names, place and ages make them very probably Audrey Nelson’s parents, though Myers may not have been the name Julia was born with.

In 1920, William and Julia Nelson were living in McCurtain County with two-year-old Audrey. William was forty-nine and born in Arkansas, Julia forty-seven and born in Texas. With them were Homer, Willie and Edith Nelson, and Hattie Myres, William’s stepdaughter. It was a blended family, made from more than one marriage, though who Hattie’s father was, and who Julia’s own parents were, is still unknown.

Ten years later, in Broken Bow, twelve-year-old Audry Nelson was living with a divorced, Texas-born parent, fifty-four, whose name was taken down as Julian A. Stevens: very probably Julia herself, given the daughter’s name, age and birthplace. A year earlier, when Audrey’s older sister Hattie Myers Kilgore died, The Broken Bow News of 10 October 1929 had named Hattie’s mother as Mrs. Stevens and her sister as Miss Audrey Nelson.

On 19 August 1950, in Arkansas, Julia Ann Stevens, seventy-six, married Charles M. Ratcliff. She died as Mrs. C. M. Ratcliff on 26 September 1956, and the McCurtain Gazette of 29 September counted Mrs. Lemuel Sandridge and Homer E. Nelson among her children, so she was very probably Julia. She had been born, the paper said, in Bowie County, Texas, on 17 November 1873, though it gave her age as seventy-two, which does not fit that date. She had come to Broken Bow in 1921, after the family’s 1920 home elsewhere in McCurtain County.

Julia’s exact birth date, and how each change of surname came about, are still uncertain; her ages in 1916, 1920 and 1930 point to different birth years. Audrey’s family remembered her mother’s maiden name as Robbins, though none of Julia’s marriages gives it. Who her parents were is unknown.

Part of the answer to why Julia’s name changed again lies in Redland Cemetery. A flat granite marker there reads “William A. Nelson, May 12, 1870 – Aug. 10, 1922.” The name and birth year fit the William A. Nelson, 46, who married Julia Myers at Idabel in 1916, and the 49-year-old Arkansas-born William of 1920. Audrey was five when he died. Julia married again, and by 1930 she was divorced and going by the name Stevens.

William had two older children, Audrey’s half-siblings: Rosa Isabel Nelson Flowers (1894–1985) and Homer E. Nelson (1902–1999). Homer was remembered among Julia’s children when she died in 1956. William is said to have been the son of Aaron Burr Nelson (1815–1888) and Mary Elizabeth Anthony Nelson (1836–1916), though nothing from their lifetimes yet confirms it.

stories.title: Hattie Myers Kilgore: Audrey’s older sister
stories.hook: Hattie Myers Kilgore died at twenty in a Paris, Texas, sanitarium in 1929, leaving a four-year-old son and three sisters, one of them Audrey Nelson.
body: In 1920 Hattie Myres was eleven, William Nelson’s stepdaughter, living in his household in Frisco Township, McCurtain County, with his wife Julia and two-year-old Audrey Nelson. Her different surname is a reminder of Julia’s life before she married William Nelson.

Nine years later Hattie was Mrs. Gordon Kilgore. When she died, The Broken Bow News of 10 October 1929 remembered her as the former Hattie Myers, the daughter of Mrs. Stevens of Broken Bow and a sister of Miss Audrey Nelson. The same mother and sister make her almost surely the girl in the Nelson household. Whether the sisters shared both parents is not known, and Hattie’s father is unknown.

The news ran on the front page under the heading “Mrs. Gordon Kilgore died Oct. 8th.” She died on Tuesday afternoon at the Sanitarium of Paris, Texas, after an illness of several weeks. Her body was taken to Idabel, to the home of a Mr. and Mrs. W. S. Green, whose relation to her is not known; the pastor of the First Baptist Church of Idabel conducted the funeral, and she was buried in the Denison cemetery there. She left her husband; a son, four years old, who goes unnamed; her mother, Mrs. Stevens, of Broken Bow; and “three sisters, Mrs. Alfred and Miss Audry Nelson, Broken Bow, and Mrs. Joe Harrison, Chickasha.” Mrs. Alfred was probably Nona Myers Alford, whose married name the same paper spelled Alford in 1940, when Nona came visiting from Camden; the 1929 spelling looks like a slip.

She was twenty when she died at the Sanitarium of Paris on 8 October 1929, a married woman whose home was Idabel, Oklahoma, where she had fallen ill and where she was buried. Her death was registered under the name Mrs. Gordon Kilgor, with a birth in 1909, the month and day not known, and no parents named. A birth date of 23 September 1906 is sometimes given for her, but it fits neither her age at death nor her age in 1920.

Two people in Hattie’s life are still shadows. Her sister Mrs. Joe Harrison, of Chickasha, is otherwise unknown, and so is whether she shared both of Hattie’s parents. Hattie’s husband, Gordon Kilgore, is known only by name, and at her death only as “Mrs. Gordon Kilgor,” with no dates, birthplace or parents; when and where he married Hattie Myers is not known.

stories.title: A Camden visit brought three generations together
stories.hook: In 1940, Nona Alford’s visit to Broken Bow ended with her sister Audrey, Audrey’s young son Larry and the sisters’ mother Julia joining her in Arkansas.
body: Nona Alford and her married daughter traveled from Camden, Arkansas, to visit friends and relatives in Broken Bow. When they went home, the visiting party grew: Nona’s sister Mrs. L. L. Sandridge, her son Larry, and their mother Julia Stevens accompanied them for several days. The Broken Bow News reported the trip on 7 March 1940. Mrs. L. L. Sandridge was Audrey, and the little boy was her son Larry, of the direct maternal line.

Nona already had a family of her own. She had married Wesley E. Alford in Bowie County, Texas, on 20 June 1919, and by 1930 they were living in Broken Bow with their daughters, Mabel and Geraldine, whose names were taken down that year as Mable and Gerldene. When the daughters applied for Social Security, both named their parents as Nona A. Myers and Wesley E. Alford, keeping the Myers name behind their mother’s married one.

The married daughter on the trip was Mrs. Edwin Chidester: Mabel, who was living in Camden in 1940 as Edwin Chidester’s wife and went by Mabel Alford Chidester. She later became Mabel Crowl, and when her sister Geraldine Forkner died, Mabel Crowl was remembered as her sister.

Julia was the older generation traveling with her daughters and grandchildren between Broken Bow and Camden. That spring she was Julia Stevens, travelling with Audrey Sandridge and Nona Alford: three surnames in one family party, and two sisters side by side.

stories.title: Sadah’s Indiana beginnings
stories.hook: Sadah McCormick was born in Indiana in August 1893, and she may have been the little Sadie of a Madison County household, though who her parents were is still uncertain.
body: Miss Sadah H. McCormick married Lester W. Livesay in Harris County on 10 October 1911, the same day their license was issued: license 22072, its number written in by hand over the printed 21072, on page 402 of volume 4. By 1920 Sadah and Lester were living in Harris County with their children, and in 2001 their son Lester was remembered as the son of Sadah McCormick.

Sadah lived to be 84. As Sadah Livesay Vaughan she died in Houston on 29 April 1978, and the informant, Alice Livesay Kauitzsch, gave her birth as 13 August 1893 in Anderson, Indiana. The unusual name, the Livesay surname and Alice herself make her very probably Lester’s wife. Alice, for her part, gave her parents to Social Security as Lester W. Livesay and Sarah H. McCormack, so Sadah was sometimes Sarah.

At her death her father was named only as J. T. McCormack, his initials never spelled out, and her mother’s maiden name was given as Unknown. Her birth date, too, was set down only at the end of her life, many decades after the event.

A year before the wedding there was a Sadie in Brazoria County. On 18 April 1910, in Justice Precinct 5, Jay T. McCormick, 41, and his wife Frances, 40, had a daughter Sadie, 17, born in Indiana. Her father’s initials, her age and her birthplace all fit, but nothing yet proves that Sadie and Sadah were the same young woman. Until something does, Jay T. and Frances remain unattached research leads, and Frances has no maiden surname.

Ten years earlier the same family was probably in Indiana. On 5 June 1900, in Stony Creek Township, Madison County, James McCormack and his wife Frances had at home Cleveland, Hazel, Sadie, Pernell and Dewey. Sadie, their daughter, was six, born in Indiana in August 1893, the same month, year and state given for Sadah at her death. Several of the names, in the same order of ages, turn up again in the Texas household of 1910, so it seems one family had moved from Indiana to Texas.

Not everything agrees. The father in 1900 was James, born in June 1863, not the Jay T., 41, of 1910; Frances was born in January 1862 and was 38 in 1900, yet only 40 ten years later. Nothing yet ties the girl Sadie directly to Lester Livesay’s wife, so James, Jay T. and J. T. may or may not be one man, and Frances’s birth surname is unknown. When Sadah married in 1911, a note in the margin read “Consent of Mother on file,” but it did not name her mother; the affidavit beneath was left blank and crossed out, and whether that mother was Frances is not known.

stories.title: Wm. P. Walker of the Beaucoup settlement
stories.hook: A government marker remembers him as a private of the Illinois militia, and a family stone a few feet away carries the name of the wife who outlived him by four years.
body: Two stones stand for William P. Walker in Beaucoup Cemetery, Washington County, Illinois. A bronze veteran’s plaque reads “W P Walker, Pvt, Ill Militia, Civil War, 1831–1919.” A granite family stone carries “Wm. P. Walker 1831–1919” and, below it, “Abigail, his wife, 1833–1923.” He is said to have been born at Beaucoup on 15 March 1831 and to have died there on 19 May 1919, and his middle name is given as Pattison, though neither those dates nor that name is carved on either stone.

Beaucoup was one of the oldest settlements in the county. Pioneers from Tennessee settled “where the old Mud Prairie road enters the Beaucoup timber” from 1818, followed by the Whittenbergs, Whites, “Livisays” and others, among them “Rev. James Walker,” until the settlement was “numerically the strongest in the county,” as its historians wrote in 1879. James Walker was remembered among the pioneer Methodist ministers who “moulded” the area’s religious life and among the teachers who kept school there before 1824.

William was probably the son of Rev. James Walker (1800–1857) and Etheldra (often given as Etheldra Jane Ballard, a name that may blend two women), as their household of 1850 suggests. One detail fits: William and Abigail named their eldest daughter Mary Ellen Etheldra.

A William P. Walker served as a private in Company C of the 60th Illinois Infantry, the same company as Jackson L. and John W. Livesay, among men from the Richview and Mount Vernon area. The 60th was raised in southern Illinois early in 1862. William’s plaque, though, says “Ill Militia,” and when he enlisted is not known. Whether the private of Company C was this William, and which service the plaque means, are questions with a story of their own.

The Walker and Livesay families lived side by side at Beaucoup. David P. Livesay, who may well have been Floyd Livesay’s father, is buried in the same cemetery, and Alice Walker married Floyd about 1880. Alice’s headstone at Pearland reads “Jan. 11, 1859,” the same year as her age in 1860. At her death in 1922 her birth was given as 1860, and her age then would mean 1855, but the stone and the census agree on 1859.

In 1860 and 1870 Alice lived with Wm P. and Abigail Walker, and the family stone shows that Abigail was William’s wife. At Alice’s death, though, her mother was given as Addie Bruce. “Addie” was a common nickname for Abigail, but Bruce is not Schanck, and in 1852 a William F. Walker had married an Abigail Schanck in Washington County. Whether Abigail was Alice’s mother is therefore not yet certain.

stories.title: Nine days: Tabitha Livesay’s stone
stories.hook: Floyd Livesay’s birth date is carved in Pearland; nine days later, by an Illinois stone, a young wife named Tabitha died.
body: In Gilead Cemetery, Grand Prairie Township, Jefferson County, Illinois, a lichen-covered marble stone under a carved weeping willow reads: “In memory of Tabitha J., wife of David P. Livesay, died Feb. 14, 1856, aged 27 yrs. 2 ms. 4 ds.” Floyd H. Livesay’s headstone at Pearland, Texas, gives his birth as “Feb. 5, 1856”, the same month and year given for him in 1900, though at his death in Texas the year was given as 1857. If the stone is right, he was born nine days before Tabitha died.

Everything else points the same way. In 1860 four-year-old Floyd H. Livesay was living in Washington County in the household of Lydia Livesay, with David Livesay, 28. In 1870 Floyd H., 14, was living in David’s own household. In 1856 David P. Livesay had been named in a Washington County court case as an heir at law of Robert Livesay, who had died in 1855. By one family account Robert’s widow was Lydia (Fitzgerald) Livesay, and David Pinkney was born on 1 January 1831, just after the family reached Illinois. If so, the motherless boy of 1860 was living with his widowed grandmother and his father.

The pieces fit, but nothing names Floyd’s parents. No one in 1860 or 1870 wrote down how the household was related, Tabitha’s stone does not mention a child, and when Floyd died in 1932 the informant said that both his parents were unknown. So David P. Livesay and Tabitha J. were probably, but not certainly, Floyd’s father and mother. His own wedding in Illinois in 1880, or David’s estate, may one day say.

The Livesays were among the oldest families in the county. The “Livisays” were among the first families at Beaucoup, William B. Livesay laid out Old Richview in 1839, and Livesays helped found the Richview Methodist society. By family tradition Robert and Lydia came from Maury County, Tennessee, about 1830, in a move that brought grandparents, parents, aunts and cousins together, from a family that had earlier come from Franklin County, Virginia. Beyond the 1856 court case, that tradition is unproved.

David P. Livesay remarried. His stone at Beaucoup Cemetery reads “D. P. Livesay 1831–1904” and “Elizabeth, his wife, 1846–1933.” Their children, Floyd’s younger half-siblings if David was his father, included Charles, Mary Ines, Clara and Ella. Floyd married Alice Walker, a Beaucoup neighbor, about 1880 and took his family to Texas in the mid-1890s.

stories.title: Lester W. Livesay Sr.: married at sixteen, buried at ninety-four
stories.hook: Lester Livesay married Sadah McCormick a month before his seventeenth birthday; each later married again, and they were buried apart, Sadah under her second husband’s name.
body: On 10 October 1911, a Harris County clerk issued a marriage license to Lester W. Livesay and Miss Sadah H. McCormick, and the marriage took place the same day. In the margin someone wrote “Consent of Mother on file.” Lester was born on 8 November 1894, by his headstone, so he was a month short of seventeen; Sadah, born on 13 August 1893, was eighteen. Whose mother gave consent is not said, and, given Lester’s age, it may well have been his.

Lester had come to Texas as a small child, and in 1900 he was living with his parents, Floyd and Alice Livesay, in Brazoria County, while Pearland was still a young railroad town. It had been named in 1893, or when the townsite was platted in 1894, “because of the abundance of pear trees.” It had 75 residents in 1898, and the 1900 hurricane “destroyed fruit trees and slowed growth for a period of time.” By 1920 Lester, 24, and Sadah, 26, were in Houston with their daughter Alice, 5, and son Lester Jr., 3.

The marriage did not last. Sadah is buried in South Park Cemetery, Pearland, under a flat stone reading “In loving memory, Sadah M. Vaughan, Aug. 13, 1893 – Apr. 29, 1978.” Her second husband, Jesse Pickard Vaughan, lies in the same cemetery. His government marker reads “Louisiana, Sgt, 155 Ambulance Co., World War I,” and he died at Jacinto City in 1954. When the Livesays divorced, and when Sadah remarried, is not known.

Lester married Esther Voris, born in 1910 and said to be from Alvin, in 1942, it is said. They share a double stone in the Confederate Cemetery at Alvin, Brazoria County, headed LIVESAY. His side reads “Lester W., Nov. 8, 1894 – Aug. 8, 1989.” When he registered for the World War I draft his birth year was given as 1895 instead, and which year is right is still uncertain. He outlived his father by 57 years and his son’s mother by eleven.

His daughter Alice A. “Nonnie” Livesay Kauitzsch (1914–1988) reported her mother’s death in 1978. His son Lester Jr. became a Southern Pacific engineer and cattleman, and when Lester Jr. died in 2001 he was still remembered as the son of “Lester W. Sr. and Sadah McCormick Livesay.”

stories.title: Violet Box Whitfield and the Oak Hill road
stories.hook: In July 1962 a pickup loaded with watermelons left 400 feet of tire marks west of Golden, and Alfreda lost her mother.
body: At two o’clock on a Monday afternoon in late July 1962, Violet Whitfield was driving west on the Oak Hill road, two and a half miles outside Golden, in a 1960 GMC pickup loaded with watermelons. The McCurtain Gazette reported that she lost control coming down a hill. The truck left about 400 feet of tire marks, ran off the right side of the road and overturned once before landing back on its wheels. Violet was thrown out and landed about ten feet beyond it. Two Broken Bow boys riding bicycles watched it happen; they told the trooper they saw the pickup start weaving from side to side as it came down the hill.

Two doctors pronounced her dead at the scene of head and neck injuries. She was 41, and the paper counted her as the county’s second traffic death of the year. Her husband, Louis O. Whitfield, 46 by the paper’s count (45 by the birth date on his gravestone), had been riding as a passenger. He came out of it with a deep cut on his right cheek, bruises and scrapes. The paper put the damage to the truck at $500, and noted that the Whitfields had been in the grocery business at Golden for several years.

Violet had been born at Wheelock on 22 September 1920, as the state’s birth register and the gravestone she shares with Lewis at Wheelock Cemetery have it, though her obituary gave 21 September, and she had lived in McCurtain County all her life; the stone reads 22 September 1920 to 30 July 1962. She left a married daughter, Mrs. Larry Sandridge of Broken Bow, who was Alfreda, then 23; her father, T. S. Box of Millerton; and two sisters and two brothers, two of whom lived at Baytown, Texas.

Violet’s parents were Texans. Annie F. Box was born on 2 June 1886 at Collins, Texas, and came to McCurtain County in 1906 from Mount Pleasant. She died at Hugo Memorial Hospital on 28 December 1959, mourned by her daughter, Mrs. Louis Whitfield of Golden, and by her Logan brothers and sisters. Tyro Stephen Box was born on 22 May 1888 at Pittsburg, Texas, and lived in the county for sixty years. He was a retired engineer and a member of the Valliant Masonic Lodge when he died at the same hospital on 5 October 1967. Pittsburg is in Camp County, next to Titus County, where Mount Pleasant stands; the young couple came north from the same corner of northeast Texas.

Wheelock, where Violet was born and buried, is one of the oldest settled places in the Choctaw Nation. It dates to 1832, when the missionaries Alfred and Harriet Wright followed the removed Choctaw from Mississippi and set up a mission station, school and church northeast of present-day Millerton. Their congregation built a stone church in 1844–46. From 1884 to 1955 Wheelock Academy, beside the old mission, was a boarding school for American Indian girls, most of them Choctaw. Annie Box’s funeral was held in the Wheelock Presbyterian church. The Boxes themselves were Texas-born whites, and none of them was enrolled on the Dawes rolls. The Choctaw ancestry in this branch came through Lewis’s mother, Ida May Merry, not through Violet.

Lewis Oliver Whitfield outlived his wife by 42 years. The bronze plaque at their grave remembers him as a private in the U.S. Army Air Forces in World War II, born on 24 August 1916 and died on 9 August 2004.

stories.title: Omagene Whitfield: a Golden boy on the Tablets of the Missing
stories.hook: Ida Merry Whitfield’s younger son has no grave; his name is carved on a curved wall on the bluff above Omaha Beach.
body: Omagene Clinton Whitfield was born on 1 January 1922, by the family’s account at Golden, McCurtain County, Oklahoma, though the state’s birth index lists him in Beaver County, the younger son of Ida May Merry Whitfield and O. C. “Clint” Whitfield. His middle name was his father’s. Clint died in March 1941, when Omagene was nineteen, and Ida went to work at the Golden post office.

Omagene entered the Army from Oklahoma and was with the engineers from February 1942, serving as a Technician Fifth Grade in the 300th Engineer Combat Battalion, service number 38466149. His older brother, Lewis Oliver Whitfield, Alfreda’s father, also served in the war, as a private in the U.S. Army Air Forces.

Omagene died on 19 June 1944, thirteen days after D-Day. The date and his unit point to a single event. That day the tank landing ship LST-523 struck a mine off the Normandy beaches and sank, “sunk by an enemy mine,” in the Navy’s own brief words. The 300th Engineers were aboard, and by one account the explosion split the ship in two, killing 94 men of the 300th and 41 of the crew. Several of the battalion’s dead from that day are counted among the missing. Omagene was very probably on LST-523, though nothing yet places him aboard by name.

He has no grave. His name is on the Tablets of the Missing at the Normandy American Cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer, the curved wall of the Garden of the Missing on the bluff above Omaha Beach: TEC 5, 300 ENGR COMBAT BN, OKLAHOMA. A photograph of a model of LST-523 has been added to his memorial.

At home the news came slowly and out of order. For months the family knew only that he had been reported missing in France that June. Then, on 28 March 1945, the McCurtain Gazette ran a short front-page item headed “County Man Listed As Dead, Relatives Are Not Notified.” Omagene’s name had been in a War Department list, released to newspapers the previous Saturday, of men killed in action in Europe, but his mother, Mrs. Ida M. Whitfield of Golden, had received no such notice. Three weeks later, on 18 April, the paper printed his photograph in uniform and a fuller notice. He had been killed in action on 19 June 1944, according to a report his mother had received in March, and had been with the Army engineers since February 1942. He was survived by his mother; his brother, Louis O. Whitfield of Tulsa; his sisters, Mrs. Elma Mae Henry and Miss Oudia Whitfield of Golden; his grandmothers, Mrs. W. F. Whitfield of Golden and Mrs. Bessie Kernell of Glover; and an aunt, Mrs. J. B. Greenfield of Idabel. His mother had received his Purple Heart.

In the end the Army counted him as killed in action. On the War Department’s Honor List of Dead and Missing for Oklahoma, closed on 31 January 1946, he stands under McCurtain County as “Whitfield Omagene C, 38466149, TEC5, KIA”: KIA, killed in action, rather than FOD, the finding of death given to men declared dead after being missing. So the man whose name is on the Tablets of the Missing was, by early 1946, killed in action in the Army’s reckoning.

Lewis came home to Golden and lived until 2004. When Ida May Merry Whitfield died in 1993, her obituary gave her younger son a single sentence: “Her younger son, Omagene Whitfield, was killed during World War II.” When his sister Catherine died in 2007, he was remembered by his full name, Omagene Clinton Whitfield, among the brothers who had gone before her.

From Camp White, Oregon, where his engineer battalion trained, Omagene wrote home to his grandmother Bessie and her husband Frank. He told them not to sell out and move to California, where prices were too high, mentioned a medal he had won, and asked whether Grandma's goats were doing all right.

stories.title: Betsy Tims, the Choctaw wife of the Doaksville trader
stories.hook: Her son gave her name in one line: "Betsy Tims," dead, of Towson County.
body: On 8 May 1899, at Doaksville, Edward W. Tims, 58, was enrolled. The clerk wrote his father as "Vincent B. Tims," dead, "Non Citz," and his mother as "Betsy Tims," dead, of Towson County. That line is the only record that names the Choctaw wife of the Doaksville trader.

Edward was entered as one-half Choctaw. Since his father was a noncitizen, that implies that Betsy was counted a full-blood Choctaw, though she was given no fraction, no age and no number. A history of Doaksville written from the Tims family's papers calls her Vincent's "full-blood Choctaw wife" and says the two stayed at Doaksville for the rest of their lives.

Three of her children are known: Vinson W., born in 1838, Edward Ward, born in 1842 by family accounts (58 in 1899), and a daughter, Phoebe, who died before the final rolls were made. Vinson's children were enrolled as Choctaws through him and through his wife Emeline Steadman, and his daughter Betsy, born in 1870, who married Joseph P. Thompson, carried her grandmother's name.

She married in the years when the Choctaw Nation was rewriting its marriage law. On 6 October 1836 the General Council abolished "the custom of not intermarrying with their own Iksa," the matrilineal clans, so that "all persons, without any distinction of Iksa, are left to make their own choice as to whom they shall marry." In October 1840 it ruled that no white man could marry in the Nation until he had been a citizen for two years, that he must take a license from a judge or the district clerk and be married by a minister, and that "no white man who shall marry a Choctaw woman, shall have the disposal of her property without her consent." A white man who left his wife "without just provocation" could be ordered to pay her damages and lose his citizenship. No marriage record for Betsy and Vincent has been found, so it is not known which of these rules applied to them.

Her husband's business ran through the removal years: Doak & Tims held the army contracts of 1838 and 1839 to feed arriving Chickasaw emigrants at thirteen cents a ration, and in January 1837 Vincent witnessed the Treaty of Doaksville. Family files give Betsy's birth as about 1800 in the old Choctaw Nation in Mississippi and her death as about 1860 at Doaksville. Nothing supports either date, and nothing gives her Choctaw name or her parents.

stories.title: Samuel Garrison's two tours: Stono, 1779, and Frederick, 1782
stories.hook: Samuel Garrison was at Stono Ferry at sixteen, served again as the war wound down, and was granted a pension in Kentucky only months before he died.
body: Samuel Garrison was born on 24 August 1762, on the Pennsylvania-Maryland line by his family’s record, though perhaps in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina. He was still a boy when the Revolution reached the Carolinas.

In 1779, at sixteen, he served four months as a private in Captain James Barr’s company of Colonel Charles McDowell’s regiment, in General John Butler’s brigade of North Carolina militia. In old age he remembered that “he was at the Battle of Stono,” the fight at Stono Ferry near Charleston on 20 June 1779, “in which Major Anderson was killed,” and that Colonel Roberts of the artillery was killed too. Stono Ferry was a British victory: General Lincoln’s attack on the British rear guard cost the Americans about 34 killed and more than a hundred wounded, and Colonel Owen Roberts of the South Carolina artillery was mortally wounded. Samuel kept his discharge, signed “Jas. Barr, Capt.” (a name sometimes read as Bass), which certified his service “from the 20th of March till ye 20th of July” and was dated “2nd July 1779 Near Stono”; the date, he said, should have read the 20th.

He served again as the war was ending: five months in Captain Thomas Beatty’s company of Select Militia, raised under a state act, until Lieutenant Conrad Doll discharged him at Frederick County, Maryland, on 14 January 1782. A family genealogist wondered whether Samuel helped guard the British prisoners marched to Frederick after Yorktown, and repeated a claim that he was at Yorktown itself. Samuel claimed nine months of service in all and said nothing of Yorktown.

By his family’s record, on 14 March 1786, in Mecklenburg County, he married Esther Alexander, a daughter of Hezekiah Alexander. He became a church elder there, ordained on 10 September 1793, and they had nine children. Their sixth child was born in Mecklenburg in September 1797 and the seventh at Bays Fork Creek in Warren County, Kentucky, on 1 April 1800, so the family moved west between those dates. Samuel is said to have been Allen County’s first member in the Kentucky legislature, in 1816.

In old age, living at Hickory Grove in Warren County, Samuel went before the court on 6 September 1832, giving his age as 69, to ask for a pension. On the strength of his two original discharges, his certificate was issued on 6 November 1832, counting four months in 1779 and five in 1781–82, at $30 a year from 4 March 1831. He had little time to draw it. Samuel died on 27 March 1833, in Warren County by one account and in Allen County, at a daughter’s home near Scottsville, by another; Allen County was formed partly from Warren, so the two may describe one place. One family correspondent placed his grave on his old home place south of Scottsville; another did not know where it was.

Two questions remain open. The first is Samuel’s father. The family genealogist first named John Garrison (born 1744), a son of a Baptist minister of Monmouth County, New Jersey; later he preferred a different John Garrison, said to be a son of David Garrison Sr., who came to Mecklenburg from Salem County, New Jersey. He admitted that positive proof of that John’s relationship to David had never been found, and the link to Samuel is only “claimed,” so the family’s line stops, for now, at Samuel. The second is his service and Esther’s death. Some have made him a private in the Continental Line and placed Esther’s death in Coles County, Illinois, but his own discharges were from the militia, and the family record puts Esther’s death in Allen County, Kentucky.

Samuel's father is unresolved.

stories.title: Hezekiah Alexander's will names a daughter, Esther Garrison
stories.hook: A 1796 Mecklenburg will ties an Alexander daughter to a Garrison household and to a granddaughter named Caroline.
body: On 8 August 1796 Hezekiah Alexander of Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, made his will, and a codicil followed on 28 January 1797. It names his wife Mary; sons William Semple, James R., Silas, Hezekiah, Amos, Joel and Ozwald; and two daughters, Kezia Alexander and "Esther Garrison," with "her husband" and "dau. Caroline Garrison and other ch. of Esther." William Semple and James R. were to serve as executors with their mother. It does not name Esther's husband, and a later genealogy says only that she married "Unknown Garrison." So no printed account of the will names her husband. That name, Samuel Garrison, comes from the Garrison family record.

The Esther passage matters because it is a record made in Hezekiah's lifetime that ties an Alexander daughter to a Garrison household and to a child, Caroline, who matches the eldest child in Samuel and Esther Garrison's family record (born 9 January 1787). A family genealogist who had a copy of the will quotes the clause for Esther. It leaves a chest of drawers in trust for Caroline, and an enslaved woman named Jean with her children, whom the transcription lists as Siah, Frank and Nancy, for Esther's use for eighteen years, after which they were to be divided between Esther and her children, or, if she died first, among her children as her husband saw fit. His copy is partly garbled, so the names are as he read them. The same will gave four sons Hezekiah's tracts on the French Broad River, each to pay Esther 25 pounds as he reads it. The codicil gave Charles Polk the property that Hezekiah's "late beloved dau. Mary" took with her when she married him.

Hezekiah himself is well documented. He lived from 1728 to 16 July 1801, the son of James Alexander, a Cecil County, Maryland, magistrate and Presbyterian elder, and Margaret McKnitt. He married Mary Sample on 12 June 1752, settled in Mecklenburg, and was appointed a county magistrate in 1768. He sat on the Committee of Safety, was one of thirteen members of the provincial council of 1776, and as a delegate to the Halifax congress that year was placed on the committees that drafted North Carolina's bill of rights and constitution. The entry counts seven sons and three daughters and notes that he enslaved people. In June 1776 Richard Caswell, treasurer of the Southern District, paid Hezekiah Alexander 1,200 pounds for supplies furnished to the militia, and the family's stone house in Charlotte was built in 1774.

Hezekiah did not farm, forge and legislate alone. The 1790 census counts thirteen enslaved people in his household, and the tax lists of 1797 and 1798 show six "black polls," working-age men and women. In April 1791 he bought four more, a girl for 90 pounds 8 shillings, a man for 150, a girl for 136 and a woman for 163, along with livestock and household goods, at the estate sale of a neighbor, Agnes Allen. His will names eleven. Sam, Abram and Bett went to his wife Mary, with the land and the household goods; Jack went to his eldest son, William Sample; Anne to Silas; Hannah to Keziah; and Jean, with her children Siah, Frank and Nancy, to Esther Garrison. A girl named Mary had already been sold to John Parks Jr. through his son James R., and Hezekiah left James the value still owed. The codicil of January 1797 sent "Negro Nance," who had apparently lived with his daughter Mary since her marriage, to Mary's widower, Charles Polk.

Two more children, Nance and Rachel, turn up in the inventory of his estate on 16 October 1801, valued at 150 and 130 dollars, though neither is in the will. Mary Sample Alexander's will of 30 September 1803 left Bett to her son Joel and Bett's daughter, born on 5 September 1799, to Keziah; the faded handwriting has been read as Fanny and as Jenny. The 1800 census, which lists the household under his son Ozwald with Hezekiah and Mary apparently living in it, counts nine enslaved people. Nothing more is recorded of any of them: no surnames, no birthplaces, and no word of what became of them. Hezekiah's grandson S. P. Alexander remembered, in a letter to the historian Lyman Draper in 1874, how the children around 1825 used to gather around an old Black man who told of the wonders he and "Mas. Hezekiah" had seen during the war, so at least one of them was with Hezekiah through the Revolution.

The sources disagree on small points. One account gives Hezekiah's birth as 13 January 1722 and his death as 10 January 1801, against 1728 and 16 July 1801 in another. For Mary Sample it gives death on 17 May 1806 at 71, while another has 17 May 1805. It names three daughters, Esther, Mary and Keziah, and repeats the family account that Mary was killed by a gun accident while her husband cleaned his rifle; the will says only "late beloved dau. Mary." The 1796 will is the one contemporary record here, and it proves only that Hezekiah had a daughter Esther Garrison with a daughter Caroline. Identifying her with Samuel Garrison's wife, and John Milton Garrison as her son, rests on the family record.

stories.note: Evidence: probable. The will abstract is a 1913 editor's summary, not the will itself, and Stuart's quotation is partly garbled; all three agree that Esther Garrison and her daughter Caroline are named. The earlier notes on this site ("Hezekiah & Mary (Sample) Alexander" and "James & Margaret (McKnitt) Alexander") treat Esther's place in this family as a lead; the will and Stuart's copy of it support the daughter, while the tie to Samuel Garrison and John Milton Garrison stays probable. His parents, James Alexander and Margaret McKnitt, are linked in the tree as probable on the biography dictionary's statement. The names and bequests of the enslaved people come from the Charlotte Museum's 2021 addendum, which cites the 1796 will, the 1801 inventory and Mary Sample Alexander's 1803 will (Will Book A, pp. 47-48); the 1790 census entry ("Ezekiah Alexander, Esq.") is identified with this Hezekiah by the museum's historian on the household's makeup.

stories.title: Nine children from a family record: the Garrisons of Bays Fork Creek
stories.hook: John Milton Garrison's brothers and sisters, from Mecklenburg County to Warren County, Kentucky, and on to Alabama.

subject.name: Children of Samuel and Esther (Alexander) Garrison

body: Samuel Garrison kept a record book of births, marriages and deaths, and a family genealogy drawn from it lists nine children. The first six were born in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina: Caroline (9 January 1787), John Milton (4 October 1788), Hezekiah Alexander (February 1791), Mary (31 January 1793, who died on 26 October that year), Hannah (15 September 1794, born at her grandfather Hezekiah Alexander's home) and Samuel Young (September 1797). The last three were born at Bays Fork Creek in Warren County, Kentucky: Calvin Alexander (1 April 1800), Esther (22 February 1802) and Cynthia (19 April 1804). Caroline is the only one also named in a will: her grandfather's will of 1796 leaves a chest of drawers in trust for her.

The record follows several of them into adult life. Caroline married William Ray in 1814. On 10 June 1813 in Warren County, Hezekiah Alexander Garrison married Rebecca Lyle, a native of Loudoun County, Virginia. Nine of their children were born in Kentucky before the family moved to Morgan County, Alabama, where he died on 15 August 1846; she died near Moulton on 5 August 1873. Samuel Young Garrison married Eliza Pogue on 23 June 1829 and, in a second marriage, Chalia S. (Mitchell) Jones on 10 December 1840. Calvin married Mariah Neal and later Nancy Margaret Hawkins. Esther married Samuel Alfred Stubbins on 4 August 1825 and died on 13 December 1831, ten days after the infant son she had borne that November. Cynthia married John C. McPheeters on 22 June 1825.

John Milton Garrison was the first son, and Family informants place him on Trammell Fork Creek in Allen County. They also speak of his burial alone in a field by an old cemetery there, which may not agree with the flat marker at Mount Pleasant cemetery, so the grave is unsettled. Later corrections change an earlier date of 1814 for his marriage to Patsey Cannon to 1808 or 1809, in line with the 6 December 1809 Wilson County marriage, and date the legislature's divorce to 29 February 1848 (the approval date printed with the act) and his marriage to Sarah Stamps to 30 March 1848. The same pages show how unsettled his own children are. One descendant counted ten children, five by Sarah Stamps, and named Nancy, Sidney, John, Charles and William Thurston as hers; another says all of them were born before the divorce; a third list gives Patsey children called John Jr., Samuel Jr., Calvin, Abram and Mary C. The genealogist can neither prove nor disprove any of it.

Only that last list has a Mary, and nothing shows she is our Mary Cannon Garrison, born 17 October 1811; the list is unsourced and reached him through a chain of correspondents. The record that names John Milton as her father is her son James's own account of 1885. A lineage printed in 1952 gives a second compiled list of Esther Alexander Garrison's children: Caroline, Milton, Hezekiah, Hannah, Esther, John and Samuel. It matches the family record for six of the nine names, omits Calvin, Mary and Cynthia, and adds a John who is not in the family record. The two compilations may share a source, so they count as one line of evidence, not two.

The nine children, their dates and spouses come from a family record book as copied by a twentieth-century compiler and from correspondents' letters; neither the record book nor a county marriage or birth record for these children was seen. stories.title: Two uniforms, two pension claims: Calvin Moffitt and David Grimes
stories.hook: A Lawrence County man made three failed tries at a Union pension, and a Confederate lieutenant's widow made a claim of her own.

subject.name: Calvin V. Moffitt and David H. Grimes

body: Two cases of men who served the Confederacy and later sought Union pensions matter here. "Calvin V. Moffitt of Lawrence County served in two Arkansas Confederate units," but when he applied for a pension he "claimed a few months' service in a Union unit and tried three times unsuccessfully to qualify for a Union pension." The files made by that process were far more rewarding for descendants than for Calvin. The second case is "David H. Grimes," a third lieutenant in the 27th Arkansas Confederate Infantry whose widow applied for a Union pension, claiming he had briefly served in 1864 in a Union unit. No dates, wives or place are given for Grimes, and Calvin's father's name is not given either.

Calvin V. Moffitt is probably Nathan Moffitt's son, born in 1841 and raised in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County. A Calvin V. Moffitt was a private in Company G of the Confederate 25th Arkansas Infantry, and a Calvin V. Moffitt (also entered as Moffett and Moffat) a private in Company L of the Union 4th Arkansas Cavalry. That pairing fits the account of two uniforms. Union pensions turned on the unit, not the man's residence, which bears on a puzzle: Company L was made up in Montgomery County, far from Lawrence County. Company G of the 25th was enrolled at Pocahontas, in Randolph County, on 13 March 1862, and the 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union) was organized at Little Rock in December 1863. A C. V. Moffatt, private, Company K, 1st Arkansas Volunteers (30 days, 1861), could be the second Confederate unit, but nothing in that entry names Calvin; the later file described below is the likelier match.

David H. Grimes is harder. A D. H. Grimes rose from corporal to third lieutenant in Company I of the Confederate 27th Arkansas Infantry. That company was organized on 6 July 1862 at Richwoods, Izard County, one of the four parent counties of Stone County, where Henry Moffitt and Hannah Grimes later lived. That fits the rank and regiment, but a family tree has David Grimes living and dying in the Mississippi lowlands of southern Arkansas by 1876, and nothing puts a David Grimes in Izard County. Whether Hannah Moffitt's father is this lieutenant is unsettled.

A Union pension file is built from sworn statements, and a widow's claim has to prove a marriage and a death. If these two men are ours, such files could name Hannah's mother, and the children of both families, and could show where each man lived in the 1890s and 1900s. Calvin's three attempts may have left several sets of papers.

The service files settle much of this. The Confederate file for "Calvin V. Moffitt" shows him enrolled at Pocahontas on 13 March 1862 by Captain Turnbull for twelve months, in a company first carried as Company E of Turnbull's Battalion and then Captain Sloan's company of the 30th Arkansas before it became Company G of the 25th. A roll dated 30 June 1862 gives his age as 21. He is marked present on the rolls from late 1862 through October 1863, and the roll for January and February 1864 ends his Confederate service in four words: "Deserted his company Feb 8, 1864." A separate file for "C. V. Moffatt" puts him in Captain L. W. Robertson's company of 30-day volunteers, mustered on 17 November 1861 and discharged on 17 December, with transportation due "from Pocahontas to Smithville," the Lawrence County seat. That is very likely the second Confederate unit.

Ten weeks after leaving the 25th, on 20 April 1864, he enlisted in the Union army at DeValls Bluff for three years, signing the enlistment paper with his mark. The papers say he was born in Randolph County, North Carolina, was 22, and worked as a "Wagon Maker" ("Waggonmaker" on the enlistment), the trade of his father Nathan, the Strawberry Township wheelwright. He stood 5 feet 11 inches, with light eyes, dark hair and a light complexion. He was mustered in at Little Rock on 12 May 1864, paid a $25 bounty and $13 advance pay, assigned to Company L, and credited to the 1st Congressional District, Lawrence County, Strawberry. Every roll from the summer of 1864 onward repeats the same remark: deserted 20 August 1864 at Camp Fishback near Little Rock. In May 1909 the War Department pulled his records, which fits the later pension attempts.
The D. H. Grimes file adds a little to the lieutenant's side. He was 33 in 1862, born in Tennessee and living in Izard County, and he enlisted at Richwoods on 6 July 1862.

stories.title: A brother and sister, a sister and brother: Dr. James R. Alexander and Dorcas Garrison
stories.hook: Hezekiah Alexander’s son James, a Princeton student turned army surgeon, married Dorcas Garrison in York District, South Carolina, and went west to Kentucky a few years before his sister Esther.

subject.name: Dr. James R. Alexander and Dorcas Garrison

body: James R. Alexander was born on 23 November 1756, on the line between Pennsylvania and Maryland, a son of Hezekiah Alexander, and he was living in Cecil County, Maryland, when the Revolution began; one family history has him born about 1761 instead. In 1776 he was a student at Princeton College.

When the alarm reached Nassau Hall that year, he went home to Cecil County and enlisted as a private in Captain Walter Alexander’s company of the Maryland “Flying Camp,” and he was soon made a sergeant. He fell sick at Elkton, then followed his company north by way of Philadelphia, Trenton, Princeton and Newark, and reached Fort Lee after dark on the eve of 16 November, so that, in his own words, he “saw the battle from Fort Lee but was not in it” when Fort Washington fell across the Hudson. He retreated with the army through New Jersey and was discharged on 1 December 1776.

He went back to medicine and joined his father in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina. On 25 May 1780 Dr. Alexander volunteered again, this time as a surgeon. Four days later, on 29 May, Tarleton’s men cut down Buford’s regiment at the Waxhaws, and James nursed the wounded in a Presbyterian meeting house near the battlefield and then at Charlotte, until the British reached the town that autumn. He became surgeon to Colonel William Lee Davidson’s Mecklenburg regiment and stayed with it until Davidson was killed at Cowan’s Ford on the Catawba on 1 February 1781.

James and Dorcas Garrison were married on 26 November 1789, though where is disputed: Dorcas herself, in her widow's application, said Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, while Mark Garrison, testifying from Parke County, Indiana, in 1839, and the published marriage records say York District, South Carolina. A family record gives the day as the 6th. She had been born on 23 January 1766, perhaps a daughter of John Garrison. That page lists their ten children: Silas (10 May 1791), Amanda (6 February 1793), Charles Grandison (27 August 1794), Mary Sample (April 1796), Mark (29 December 1797), Abigail (8 November 1799), Hannah (19 August 1801), James Rankin (5 July 1803), John G. (March 1806) and Dorcas Reese (28 December 1807). When Hezekiah made his will in 1796, he named James twice, first with "his children," then as co-executor with his brother William Semple.

About 1795 or 1796 James and Dorcas moved to Kentucky, a few years ahead of Esther and Samuel Garrison. In old age James asked for a pension. He applied on 14 May 1833, giving his age as 76, and was allowed $103.33 a year from 1831 for four months as a private and four and a half as a surgeon. He died in Allen County on 11 March 1836, and on 9 May 1839, giving her age as seventy-two, Dorcas applied as his widow. She was still a widow in Allen County in 1850, and is said to have died in 1852. In 1856 their son Mark, writing for himself and for Silas, Charles G., Mary S., Abigail, James R., John G. and Dorcas R., called them the only surviving children, so Amanda and Hannah had died by then. Dorcas's widow's pension, allowed in the same amount as his, was granted under the act of 1838.

The Garrison family’s historian had a phrase for it: a brother and sister Garrison who married a sister and brother Alexander. He admitted that some doubt Dorcas was John Garrison’s daughter, but reasoned from dates and places that she was, and another family history names John Garrison as her father too; York District, where she married, is where Stuart placed John Garrison’s family in the years before about 1795. Whether Dorcas and Samuel were really brother and sister, and which John Garrison was their father, remain unsettled. What is clear is that the Alexander and Garrison families were joined twice, and that both couples ended their days in the same part of Kentucky.

Dorcas's parentage is not established: Stuart reasons that John Garrison was her father but says some doubt it, and the identity of Samuel Garrison's father is a separate open question. The pension file disagrees with itself on the wedding: Dorcas's application gives 26 November 1789 in Mecklenburg County, the family record page gives 6 November, and Mark Garrison's 1839 testimony says York County, South Carolina. stories.title: Elma Whitfield Severn: teacher, coach and principal
stories.hook: Ida Merry Whitfield’s daughter was born at Glover in 1918 and spent thirty years in Oklahoma and New Mexico schools.
body: Elma Mae Whitfield was born at Glover on 12 January 1918, the daughter of Oliver Clinton Whitfield and Ida Mae Merry Whitfield, an original Choctaw enrollee. When her sister Ouida Carroll died in March 2007, “Elma Mae Severn of Valliant” was among the survivors, and when Elma herself died, the Choctaw Nation’s Biskinik of December 2011 remembered her parents by those names. She belonged to the Whitfield household that went from Glover to the Golden post office. She was the younger sister of Lewis Oliver Whitfield, Alfreda’s father, and the older sister of Omagene and Ouida.

Elma was a graduate of Southeastern State Teachers College, in Durant, and spent thirty years in education in Oklahoma and New Mexico as a teacher, basketball coach, 4-H leader and principal; in which schools, and in which years, is not known. The college went by that name from 1921 to 1939, before it became Southeastern State College, so she probably studied there before 1939.

One spring in that career can be glimpsed. At the end of March 1950, in McCurtain County, Mark Severn Jr., 30, born in Oklahoma and working in pipeline construction, was living with his wife Elma, 32, born in Oklahoma, an elementary school teacher who had worked 35 hours the week before, and with a son, who may be living and is not named. This was very probably Elma Whitfield: her age fits her January 1918 birth, and the names, the county, her work and her husband’s Oklahoma birth all agree, though nothing then said she had been born a Whitfield. That spring her brother Lewis kept a general store near Golden and her mother was the Golden postmistress. Where in the county Elma taught is not known.

Her second career was with the Department of Human Services, for seven years. For five of them she worked with older people. The last two were spent “working through the court” with delinquent children, foster homes and adoptions. She trained for that work at the Hissom School for the Impaired and at Oklahoma University. She belonged to the National Retired Teachers Association and the Oklahoma Education Association.

Church was the other thread. She was a longtime member of Southern Baptist churches, where she taught Sunday school, directed Training Union and the Woman’s Missionary Union, and served as Sunday School superintendent, and she belonged to the National Association of Baptist Senior Adults. She left a farewell that begins “Love one another.”

Her husband, Mark Severn Jr., died before her. Some of her surviving children bore other surnames, so she may have married earlier, though no earlier marriage is known beyond the “Mrs. Elma Mae Henry” of her brother Omagene’s death notice in 1945. Elma died on 31 October 2011, aged 93; she lived at Valliant, though where she died is not said. She had outlived her parents, her brothers Lewis and Omagene, her sister, printed as “Oulda” Whitfield Carroll, a variant of Ouida, and an aunt, “May Gimlim.”

Aunt “May Gimlim” is a mystery. She was an aunt on Ida’s side or on Oliver’s, perhaps a sister of one of them, but who she was is not known. And the two sisters were remembered with the same two brothers who had died before them, once as Omagene Clinton and Oliver Lewis and once as Lewis and Omagene, so Lewis Oliver and Oliver Lewis were very probably one man.

Her husband was probably the Mark Severn Jr. of McCurtain County, born in Oklahoma in 1918, who enlisted on 5 December 1941 as a private in the Air Corps, Army serial number 20842194, coming from the National Guard in federal service. He was then single, with a grammar-school education, and working as a general farm hand. He is the only Mark Severn Jr. among the Army’s wartime enlistments, and he came from Elma’s county, though nothing proves he was her husband, and his age of 30 in 1950 is two years short of a 1918 birth.

Whitfield of the 1920 census remains probable, as Ida’s story explains. That story mentions only a son, Oliver L., in the 1920 household; Elma, born in January 1918, would have been two, so the census page is worth rechecking. The obituary prints her sister’s name as Oulda and her aunt’s as Gimlim; both are kept as printed. Living relatives named in the notices are not listed here. The 1950 census entry is probable: the names, county, Elma’s age and trade and Mark’s Oklahoma birth agree, but Mark’s age (30) does not fit the 1918 birth on his enlistment card, and the township name and the child’s age are hard to read. The census page is not reproduced because it names other households, some possibly living.

stories.title: Ouida Carroll and the Golden post office
stories.hook: Ida Whitfield’s younger daughter spent twenty-two years at the Golden post office and retired as a postmaster in 1990.
body: Catherine Ouida Whitfield was born on 15 January 1924, the youngest of the Whitfield children known, and went by Ouida. She was the daughter of Oliver Clinton and Ida May Merry Whitfield, and she married Eugene Carroll Sr., who died before her. She served 22 years at the post office in Golden and retired as postmaster, and she belonged to NAPUS and the National League of Postmasters. She died on 16 March 2007, and the Choctaw Nation’s Biskinik remembered her that May.

The office she worked in was old by then. Golden's post office opened in 1911 and took its name from its first postmaster, James M. Golden; its run of postmasters, her mother Ida among them, is told in “Golden’s postmasters: a father, a daughter and a granddaughter.”

The years suggest that mother and daughter overlapped, though the appointment dates of the Golden postmasters leave little room for it. Twenty-two years ending in 1990 mean a start about 1968. Ida was remembered as retiring at 72, which for a woman born in June 1898 means between June 1970 and June 1971. So Ida and Ouida may have worked at the same office for a few years, or Ouida’s twenty-two years may include time as a clerk or assistant before she became postmaster, or the years may have been rounded. When each woman became postmaster, and when each stepped down, is not known.

Church and community filled the rest of her life. She was a nursery worker and a teacher of children and of senior women at Southwest Friendship Baptist Church in Oklahoma City and at Golden Baptist Church, and she belonged to the Woman’s Missionary Union at both for more than 57 years. After she retired in 1990 she volunteered at the Golden Community Center, the Golden Senior Citizens Center and Golden Baptist Church.
When her sister Elma died in December 2011, Ouida’s name was printed as “Oulda,” and the family’s notices gave her brothers’ names in two different orders.
src: Choctaw Nation, Biskinik, May 2007, p. 11, Catherine Ouida Carroll obituary (22 years at the Golden post office; church and volunteer work; husband and brothers who died before her); PDF page examined 2 Nov 2026: https://www.choctawnation.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/may-2007-biskinik.pdf#page=11

stories.title: The ordnance plants west of Texarkana
stories.hook: In the 1940s Audrey and Lemuel Sandridge made ammunition at what the family called the “Red River Arsenal,” most likely one of the two Army sites that rose west of Texarkana in the war.
body: In the 1940s, as Audrey Sandridge’s family remembered it, Audrey and her husband Lemuel worked at the Red River Arsenal plant making ammunition, and Audrey also worked its switchboard. Just when, and exactly where, is not remembered. What was the “Red River Arsenal”? West of Texarkana, the war brought two great Army sites into being.

The Red River Army Depot, also known as the Red River Ordnance Depot, was activated in August 1941 after the government bought 116 farms and ranches just west of Texarkana. Its mission was to receive, store and issue gun-motor carriages, ammunition, explosives, and supplies and equipment for combat vehicles and demolition work. Construction was at first held back by a housing shortage and a lack of equipment. The depot lay in Bowie County, Texas, 18 miles west of Texarkana.

Next to it stood the Lone Star Ordnance Plant, also called the Lone Star Army Ammunition Plant, on a tract nine miles west of Texarkana. It was an ammunition-loading plant for artillery shells, bombs, fuses, boosters and other items, run for the Army by the Lone Star Defense Corporation, a subsidiary of the B. F. Goodrich Rubber Corporation. Its contract was let on 23 July 1941 and its first small-caliber ammunition was sent out on 27 May 1942. In April 1943 the plant and the depot were consolidated as the Texarkana Ordnance Center.

Neither place was officially called the Red River Arsenal, so the family’s name may be shorthand for either site or for the combined center. Making ammunition sounds most like the loading plant, but that is a guess; who employed the Sandridges, at what jobs and in which years, is not known.

There is one coincidence, though nothing more should be made of it. The depot is in Bowie County, Texas, and Audrey’s mother, Julia Stevens Ratcliff, was born in Bowie County, by the notice of her death in 1956. Nothing ties the Sandridges’ wartime work to that.

stories.title: Glover and De Queen: a thread to Sevier County, Arkansas
stories.hook: Two Glover families, and one later marriage, all point across the line to Sevier County, Arkansas, though none of it is proven.
body: Glover, where the Dawes Commission wrote to the Merry family in 1902 and 1903, lay close to Arkansas. In 1902–1903 it was a country post office in the Choctaw Nation about 40 miles from De Queen, Arkansas, too small for R. L. Polk’s gazetteer to name a postmaster or a single business. De Queen is the seat of Sevier County, and McCurtain County, Oklahoma, lies along Sevier County’s western border.

Three threads run to that county. J. L. Louis Merry, who lies at Glover Cemetery, is said to have been born in Sevier County, and the 1880 census does put a Joshua L. Merry, eight, on his parents’ farm there; Clint Whitfield is said to have been born at Chapel Hill in the same county, though that birthplace is not proved. And in 1950 Julia Ann Stevens and Charles M. Ratcliff, both of Broken Bow, were married in Sevier County.

Even together, these do not prove that either family came from Sevier County, or that they knew one another before they reached McCurtain County. Two remembered birthplaces could match by chance, and a wedding in a nearby Arkansas county seat in 1950 may have little to do with births in the 1870s and 1890s. But if Louis Merry and Clint Whitfield were Arkansas boys, Sevier County is the likeliest place their parents lived, where Louis would have been a boy in 1880 and Clint in 1900.

Louis’s parents were very probably Calvin Merry and Eliza Jane McGregor, whom the 1880 census and an 1859 marriage place in Sevier County and Montgomery County, Arkansas; Clint’s are said to have been William Franklin Whitfield and Emma Ward, but until something from their own day says so, the Whitfield line stops where it is. The Sandridges’ Arkansas roots lay in other counties, so this thread belongs to the Merry, Whitfield and Stevens families.

Two of those threads run to one township. Chapel Hill, where Clint Whitfield is said to have been born in 1893, was in 1890 "a prosperous little village" about the center of Monroe Township, named for an old Union church a mile east of the town site. It had two general stores, a grocery and drugstore, a blacksmith's and a wagon-maker's shop and three physicians; its post office, opened about 1874 a mile and a half east, had moved into the village in 1885, and a private school, Chapel Hill High School, had opened in 1889. Its nearest railroad shipping point was Nashville, thirty-seven miles east. Farther west in the same township, very near the Indian Territory line, stood the post office and trading post of Ultima Thule.

Monroe Township is where the census found Calvin Merry's farm, with eight-year-old Joshua L., in 1880, and where W. F. Whitfield's household was counted in 1900. So the Merrys and the Whitfields came out of the same western corner of Sevier County, the side nearest the Choctaw Nation, though thirteen years apart. That makes it a little more likely that the two families knew each other's country before they crossed the line, but it does not show that they ever met there.
