stories.title: Private Walker of Company C
stories.hook: William P. Walker of Richview enlisted in Company C of the 60th Illinois in March 1864 and served until the regiment mustered out at Louisville in July 1865.
body: William P. Walker’s government marker calls him “Ill Militia,” but he was a volunteer. On 20 March 1864 “Walker, William P.,” of Richview, enlisted in Company C of the 60th Illinois Infantry. He was mustered in at Centralia on 17 April 1864 and “Mustered out July 31, 1865” at Louisville, Kentucky. He was a farmer from Richview, born in 1831 in Washington County, 5 feet 10 inches tall, with black hair, gray eyes and a dark complexion. He died in 1919 and is buried at Beaucoup Cemetery.

At Beaucoup his grave is remembered as “PVT ILL MILITIA CIVIL WAR Co. C, 60th Ill. Inf.,” and in 1879 the county counted William P. Walker among its men of Company C. The same words, “PVT ILL MILITIA,” mark the grave of Simeon Walker, a captain in Company C, and those of two Mexican War veterans who were second lieutenants, so the phrase seems to have been a general marker label for Illinois volunteer soldiers, not a separate militia service.

Company C was raised in Jefferson and Washington counties, and William was one of a group of 1864 recruits. Jackson L. Livesay, also of Richview, a farmer born about 1846 in Jefferson County, joined with him: enlisted 20 March 1864, mustered 17 April 1864, mustered out 31 July 1865. John W. Livesay, of Washington County, a mechanic born about 1834, had joined earlier, on 29 August 1862, and was discharged for disability on 16 February 1865. When William joined, the company’s captain was Simeon Walker, captain from 19 December 1862 until he was mustered out on 14 March 1865. How either Livesay was related to Floyd Livesay’s family, who also came from the Richview area, is not known; the name was common there.

The months he served were eventful ones for the regiment. The 60th was at Rossville, Georgia, until May 1864, then took part in the Atlanta campaign (1 May to 8 September), the March to the Sea (15 November to 10 December) and the siege of Savannah. It went through the Carolinas campaign from January to April 1865, marched in the Grand Review at Washington on 24 May, and moved to Louisville on 12 June, where it served as provost guard at 14th Corps headquarters until it was mustered out on 31 July 1865. William was mustered out with it, at Louisville, on its last day. When he reached the regiment, and which of its fights he shared, is not known.

In old age he was still remembered as a soldier. By 1 January 1883 a Wm. P. Walker of Richview was drawing a federal pension of six dollars a month for chronic diarrhea and disease of the abdominal viscera; no regiment is named, so it is his name and post office that make him probably this William. And on 1 January 1913, at about 81, “Walker, W. P., Pr. C, 60 Ill. Inf.” was still on the rolls of the Grand Army of the Republic’s Simon Walker Post, No. 629, at Richview.

Three Walkers of Washington County served in the regiment: Simon Walker, a sergeant in Company C; William P., a private in the same company; and Levi S. Walker, the regiment’s chaplain. Which Simeon Walker the Richview post honoured is not known; it was already the “Simeon Walker Post, No. 629, Richview” by March 1890, when the Department of Illinois held its Twenty-fourth Annual Encampment at Quincy. Captain Simeon Walker, born on 3 March 1831, may have been the man, though even his death date is uncertain: 11 October 1909 by one account, 29 April 1905 by another. The 29 April is also the day and month on which Etheldra J. Walker died in 1903, which may be a coincidence or a copying slip. Whether these men were kin to William is not known, and his own parents are still unproved.

stories.title: The Walker graves at Beaucoup
stories.hook: Two Methodist Walker families lie in the old Beaucoup cemetery, and among them lie two women named Etheldra.
body: Beaucoup Cemetery, in section 23 of Township 2 South, Range 2 West, dates from 1820. Among its Walker graves, two couples matter most. Rev. James Walker lies there, 1800 to 26 April 1857, aged 57 years, 1 month, 16 days, which puts his birth about 10 March 1800. On the same stone is Etheldra, “wife of Rev. James,” 1805 to 6 June 1878, aged 73 years, 8 months, 8 days. That age would mean a birth about September 1804, a year off the 1805, so her birth year is only approximate.

Something of Rev. James Walker’s life is remembered. He was among the Methodist ministers who came to Beaucoup soon after 1820 and among the pioneer teachers who kept school before 1824, as the county’s historians wrote in 1879. The “Rock Chimney” farm, first settled by John Dees, was sold in 1827 to Captain James Burns, who afterwards sold it to Rev. James Walker. In 1845 a “James Walker, LE,” apparently a local elder, married Andrew White and Polly Ann Tate, whose license was dated 18 February. But no one then wrote down the names of his children.

A second Methodist Walker family is easy to confuse with his. Rev. Simeon Walker Sr. was born in Jackson County, Georgia, on 13 April 1802, was converted at Shiloh, St. Clair County, Illinois, in 1819, and died on 22 February 1880 at his son’s home in Carbondale, as the Southern Illinois Conference remembered him that year. On 15 September 1852 a Simeon Walker “Jr.” married Etheldra Jane Walker. At Beaucoup lie a Simeon Walker (3 March 1831 to 11 October 1909, a captain in Company C, 60th Illinois) and an Etheldra J. (31 July 1833 to 29 April 1903), with several small children who died between 1854 and 1869, three of them marked “son of S. & E.” They were probably the couple married in 1852. How the two Walker families were related, if at all, is not known.

The younger Etheldra matters for the question of William P. Walker’s parents. They are often given as Rev. James Walker and “Etheldra Jane Ballard.” But there were two Etheldras at Beaucoup: the older, wife of Rev. James, and the younger, Etheldra J., wife of Simeon. The “Jane” belongs to the younger woman, who married as a Walker, not a Ballard, and nothing else connects either woman with a Ballard, so the name may blend the two. The families echo each other: William named his eldest daughter Mary Ellen Etheldra, and Simeon and Etheldra J. named a son James H. (12 June 1855 to 21 August 1856). If Etheldra J. was a daughter of Rev. James and Etheldra, she was William’s sister and Captain Simeon his brother-in-law. In 1850 William P. and Etheldra J. were both living in Rev. James and Etheldra’s house, which makes them probably, though not certainly, their children.

William’s wife Abigail is certain, though her maiden name is not. The family stone reads “Abigail, his wife, 1833–1923.” On 25 February 1852 a William F. Walker took out a license to marry Abigail Schanck, and at Beaucoup lies a little George W., 12 September 1853 to 24 October 1854, “son of Wm. R. & A.” The initials differ, F at the wedding, R at the child’s grave, P on the stones, but the dates fit a couple married in 1852 with a first child in 1853, so the wedding may well be theirs. Still, at Alice’s death her mother was named as Addie Bruce, and nothing in the Walker family calls Abigail a Schanck.

The Walkers and Livesays of Beaucoup were already tied by marriage before Alice Walker married Floyd Livesay. Frances C. E. Walker (19 September 1849 to 18 February 1874), daughter of Rev. G. W. Walker and Elizabeth, lies there as the “wife of Chas. M. Livesay.” Her father, Rev. G. W. Walker (1826 to 20 October 1902), had been a Mexican War lieutenant of the 2nd Illinois Foot Volunteers. Three years after Frances died, on 17 May 1877, Charles M. Livesay married Theresa E. Tate.

stories.title: Robert and Lydia Livesay’s ten children
stories.hook: Robert and Lydia Livesay came from Maury County, Tennessee, to Washington County about 1830 and raised ten children there; whether their son David Pinkney, born on New Year’s Day 1831, was Floyd’s father is still unknown.
body: Robert and Lydia (Fitzgerald) Livesay came from Maury County, Tennessee, to Washington County, Illinois, about 1830. A descendant, writing of Jackson Monroe Livesay from the family Bible, remembered them with ten children, among them David Pinkney Livesay, born on 1 January 1831. It is a family memory, set down long afterward, but the county’s own weddings and graves bear much of it out.

The children married and settled around them. Jackson Monroe Livesay married Lucinda Ann Thompson on 15 November 1849. Lorenzo M. Livesay married another Thompson, Margaret Jane, on 22 October 1845. Unity Jane married James L. Logan, sometimes written James I., on 16 November 1849, as the family’s 1856 heirs’ paper also has it, and the eldest son, William E., married Emily Goodner on 1 August 1844. One child did not grow up: at Beaucoup Cemetery a stone for Jasper L. Livesay, “son of Robert & Lydia,” marks his death on 16 August 1841; he had been born on 15 February that year. All of this fits Robert and Lydia’s family as the descendant remembered it, though none of it touches David P. himself.

David P. lies at Beaucoup under a stone that reads “D. P. Livesay 1831–1904” and, below, “Elizabeth, his wife, 1846–1933.” On 28 July 1857, seventeen months after Tabitha J. Livesay died on 14 February 1856, a David B. Livesay took out a license to marry Elizabeth D. Jack. If that was David P., it was his second marriage. But a bride born in 1846 would have been eleven, so either the Elizabeth of the stone was a later wife, her year is wrong, or David B. was another man. Which is true is not known.

The Livesays and Walkers were already tied by marriage. Frances C. E. Walker (19 September 1849 to 18 February 1874) lies at Beaucoup as the “wife of Chas. M. Livesay,” and on 17 May 1877 Charles M. Livesay married Theresa E. Tate. David P. had a younger son named Charles, it is said, but a man widowed in 1874 and remarried in 1877 could have been a child of David’s 1857 marriage only if he had married as a teenager, which seems unlikely, so Charles M. was probably another Livesay.

Floyd’s parents may yet be named at his 1880 marriage to Alice Walker in Illinois, in David’s estate or a notice of his death in 1904, or in the family Bible itself. Until then David P. and Tabitha J. may have been his parents, but no one can yet say so, and none of Robert and Lydia’s other children can be tied to Floyd.

stories.title: Three Pearland glimpses: 1914, 1950 and 1957
stories.hook: In 1914 a Livesay kept a grocery in Pearland; in 1950 two Livesay children were in its school; and in 1957 a Deputy Lester Livesay helped bring a saddle thief to justice.
body: In 1914 “Livesay F H” was among the retail grocers of Pearland, between Peacock and Pearsall. The initials, the town and the trade fit Floyd H. Livesay, who died a retired groceryman in 1932 and who had lived in Pearland since the mid-1890s, so he was very probably that grocer. Pearland then had twenty-three businesses and a population of 400.

In the spring of 1950 the Pearland High School annual, The Gusher, showed a later generation. A Wayne Livesay was in the fourth grade and a Carolyn Livesay in the seventh, and she was in the junior volleyball team’s photograph too. Lester Livesay Jr., who was reared in Pearland, had a son Wayne and a daughter Carolyn Jo, whose name was also spelled Carylon. Wayne Woodrow Livesay, born on 13 February 1940, would have been ten. The children were very probably Floyd’s great-grandchildren, though no parents are named beside them.

Seven years later a Lester Livesay was wearing a badge. In May 1957 The Cattleman, the magazine of the Texas and Southwestern Cattle Raisers Association, reported under the heading “Saddle Thief Sentenced” that a man had been sentenced on 16 April to five years in the penitentiary, on a guilty plea, for stealing two saddles belonging to a man of Brazoria. The case had been investigated by Deputy Sheriffs Lester Livesay and a colleague, with an association inspector. Long afterward, in 2006, Tales from the Brazos remembered a Lester Livesay as “a former sheriff’s deputy who patrolled the Pearland area.”

Which Lester it was is not known. Two Lester Livesays had ties to the county: Lester Jr., who bought a cattle ranch at Pearland in 1953, and Lester Sr., who lies at Alvin (he died in 1989). Lester Jr. was not remembered for any work in law enforcement, so the deputy could have been either man, or another Lester Livesay altogether.
Lester Sr. lies at Alvin on a double stone with his later wife, whose side reads “Esther Voris, Aug. 9, 1910,” with no death year carved.

stories.title: Which Gardner was Eunice's brother? Five sketches from 1891
stories.hook: An 1891 book prints sketches of five Choctaw men named Gardner. Only one names his father as Jackson Gardner, the name on Eunice Pisachubbe's Dawes card, and the book never connects him to her.

subject.name: Gardner men of Blue County in the 1891 sketches

body: When Eunice Pisachubbe was enrolled at Goodland on 10 May 1899, she named her parents as Jackson and Viney Gardner, both dead, of Blue County. Nothing else has turned up about them. One place to look is an 1891 book of biographical sketches, the same book that prints Joseph P. Thompson's. It has sketches of five Choctaw men named Gardner, and they do not share a father.

Josiah Gardner was born at Wheelock in 1851, went to neighborhood schools until he was fifteen and lived with his parents until 1871, when he began farming for himself. At twenty-one he married Elizabeth Beajis, who was part Cherokee and lived three years. In 1877 he married Sallie Thunley, a Choctaw, and had no family by her. The sketch calls him "a fourth son of Jackson Gardner, of the Oklafalaya clan" and says he was a lawyer who practiced in the Choctaw courts. Eunice's card puts her birth about 1850, a year before Josiah's. If the two Jacksons are one man, Josiah would be her brother or half-brother.

James W. Gardner was born in Blue County, Choctaw Nation, in 1849, if the printed "18i9" is read that way, which fits his 1870 marriage. His father died while James was a child, so he stayed home to look after his widowed mother and never had schooling. In 1870 he married Emily Cornwell, the widow of Wm. Lawson, and by 1891 he had a four-hundred-acre farm near Wynne Wood (now Wynnewood), about thirteen hundred head of cattle, part of the town site and four children. His father is not named. A Blue County birth, a father dead early and a widowed mother are all consistent with a Gardner household whose parents were both dead by 1899, but they are consistent with many households.

The other three can be set aside as sons of Jackson. William Gardner, born in 1830 on the Tombigbee River in Mississippi (printed "Tom Bigby"), names his father as Jeremiah Gardner and his mother as Clarissa La Flore, and says the family reached Towson County in 1833. Judge G. W. (Green) Gardner, born at Little River in January 1844 (printed "18-14"), was also a son of Jeremiah, "who came to the Indian Territory in 1833." Judge Jeff. Gardner, born near Wheelock, was the eldest son of "Noll Gardner," at one time an interpreter for the missionaries; a 1941 life of him, as Principal Chief from October 1894, names his parents as Noel and Hannah Gardner, mixed-blood Choctaws from Mississippi, and gives his birth near Wheelock on 12 July 1847 from his tombstone. Wheelock thus had at least two Gardner households in these years, Noel's and Jackson's. William's sketch also mentions a Tims: before he opened his own store at Hamilton, in Blue County, he worked for "E. B. Tims, the sutler at Doaksville," probably Vincent B. Tims.

What this does not show matters as much. Every sketch is the man's own account, and none links Jackson Gardner to Viney, to Blue County or to a daughter Eunice. Wheelock was a mission and academy, and the sketch does not say which county it lay in. A history of the Tobucksy County courthouse at McAlester also names a Josiah Gardner, a full-blood Choctaw lawyer who could neither read nor write; whether he is the Wheelock-born Josiah is not known. Whether Josiah was Eunice's brother stays unsettled.

A Choctaw family researcher’s transcription of the 1855 census adds one candidate. In the Chickasaw District, a Jackson Gardner kept house with Mary Gardner, Simeon, Abiline, Alfred, Jesse, Josiah and Harriet. The Dawes cards, forty-odd years later, fill in some of the grown children. Jesse J. Gardner, 50, Alfred W., 51, and Josiah, 50, a full-blood, all named Jackson and Mary Gardner as their parents. Lon Gardner, 25, full-blood, named Simeon and Harriet. The 1891 sketch of the Wheelock-born lawyer Josiah Gardner calls him “a fourth son of Jackson Gardner” of the Oklafalaya clan; if Abiline was a daughter, Josiah is the fourth son in that census list, and the sketch fits.

The same transcriber also pointed to a Jackson, twelve, in the household of William Gardner, 34, on the removal-era lists of 1831, which would make a Jackson born about 1819, though the match is her own guess. A trees-only tradition puts Eunice’s father at about 1820 in Mississippi. They fit, and that is all they do.

The trouble is Eunice herself. She was about five in 1855 and is not among the children, and her card gives the mother as Viney, not Mary. Either she belonged to a different Jackson Gardner, or Jackson had had an earlier wife, Viney, and Eunice grew up under another roof, or the clerks wrote the names down differently in 1899. Until the cards themselves are opened, Jackson of the Chickasaw District is a candidate and not an ancestor.

Four of Josiah's brothers and sisters, Jesse, Alfred, Harriet and Josiah himself, enrolled in 1899 and every one named the same father: Jackson Gardner, dead, of Blue County, the very words on Eunice's card. Their mother was Mary; Eunice's was Viney. Born about 1850, Eunice sits in the middle of Mary's children, so if she was Jackson's daughter she was probably a half-sister, the child of another wife.

stories.title: Spencer Academy to Salem, Virginia: Joseph Thompson in company
stories.hook: Joseph Thompson's 1891 sketch has him at Roanoke College until 1886. Five other Choctaw men in the same book name the same college, and three of the six went there from Spencer Academy.

subject.name: Joseph Thompson and the Choctaw men who went to Roanoke

body: Joseph Thompson's 1891 sketch says he was educated at Spencer Academy and at "Mount Harmon Institute, Northfield," and completed his education at Roanoke College in Salem, Virginia, "where he remained until 1886." He then taught school, was appointed county clerk of Cedar County in 1889 and was elected to the lower house of the Choctaw Council the next year. The only other account of his college years is his son Joel's memory, which gives a different order; a college catalog of 1881-82 does not list him.

The same volume shows he was not alone in making the trip. Jacob Jackson was born about 1845, went to Fort Coffee Academy and, after the Civil War, to an academy at Little Rock and King's College in Tennessee, and in 1870 to Roanoke College, "where he spent four years." He began practicing law in 1874, served as senator for Skullyville County and was National Secretary of the Choctaw Nation by 1889. Napoleon B. Ainsworth, born at Skullyville in 1856, entered Roanoke at fifteen, "graduated after four years, in June, 1880," and won the orator's medal that year; the dates do not quite agree with each other, since four years from fifteen would be 1875. He went on to law school at the University of Virginia, served the Nation as auditor and in 1883 married Miss Emily K. Thompson at Roanoke, Virginia. Nothing in the sketch ties her to this Thompson family.

Three more followed the Spencer-to-Salem route Joseph took. Solomon E. Hotema, born near Grant in 1854, went to Spencer Academy and had his education "completed at Roanoke College"; he was elected Kiamichi County clerk in 1881, county judge in 1884, 1885 and 1886, representative in 1887 and senator in 1890. The Rev. William H. McKinney, born in January 1861, was at Spencer until 1877, then spent five years at Roanoke, took his A.B. in 1883, went on to a divinity degree at Yale in 1886 and became a district school trustee and a Presbyterian minister. Don Juan Folsom, born in August 1866 in Atoka County, spent three years at Roanoke after Denison High School, returned to Atoka in 1884, and was elected Clerk of the House that year. His mother's maiden name was Thompson; no link to this family is known.

The pattern is the point. By 1891 a Spencer Academy education followed by college in Virginia was a recognized road to Choctaw office, and county clerk and then the House was a common first step; Hotema and Joseph both followed it. That makes Joseph's own sketch more believable. It does not confirm his years at Roanoke, which still rest on a sketch that Joseph supplied himself and on his son's memory, and the sketches of the other five are the same kind of source.

stories.title: A Hulsey pastor at Mount Ida
stories.hook: A Baptist minister named Hulsey served the Mount Ida church for twenty-two years while George Washington Hulsey lived and worked in the same county. Nothing ties the two families together.
body: A short life of the Rev. John Washington Hulsey was printed in 1952. He was born on 17 March 1864 at Arkadelphia, Arkansas, the son of Lucretia Overall Hulsey and Dr. James Carroll Hulsey, a country doctor who practiced around Cameron, Williams, Spiro, Hartshorne and Wilburton in what became Oklahoma. John had little schooling. He was converted in the summer of 1889, at twenty-five, near Bengal in Latimer County, and was ordained by the Harlan's Chapel Baptist Church on 1 September 1889. The article says he could hardly read when he began to preach.

His pastorates run through two states. In Indian Territory and Oklahoma he served Bengal, Cameron and Poteau, organized the First Baptist Church of Wilburton in 1898 and was moderator of the Short Mountain Baptist Association in 1895, 1896 and 1898. In Arkansas he served Waldron, Parks, West Hartford and Mansfield from 1908 to 1913, then Norman, Caddo Gap and Mount Ida in 1914-1917. From 1922 to 1944 he was pastor at Big Fork, Cherry Hill, Antioch and Mount Ida, and his second term at Mount Ida lasted twenty-two years, "until his death." In 1919 he directed the $75 Million Campaign in Montgomery and Polk counties. He died at Little Rock on 17 November 1944, where he had gone to attend the state Baptist convention.

The geography is the reason for interest. George Washington Hulsey, a boy of four in 1880 in Montgomery County, lived at Story in that county in 1918 and dying at Washita, in Montgomery County, in 1935, with his burial at Breashears Cemetery near Story. His son Louis Daniel died near Mena, in Polk County, in 1948. Mount Ida, Caddo Gap and Norman, where the Rev. John Hulsey was pastor, all lie in Montgomery County, and Big Fork, another of his churches, is in Polk County. Family usage calls George "Rev.," although his records name him a laborer and farmer. A family memory of a Hulsey preacher at Mount Ida may belong to this man and not to George, but nothing supports that.

A shared surname, a shared county and the middle name Washington are not evidence of kinship. Nothing connects Dr. James Carroll Hulsey of Arkadelphia to Benjamin F. Hulsey, born about 1848 in Georgia, or to the Salathiel Hulsey household in Union County, Georgia, in 1850.

He had married Mary Lee Oller on 28 February 1886, three years before he began to preach, and from 1922 to 1928 he was a state missionary for the Baptist State Convention. He had not missed one of its meetings since 1900. In November 1944 he came to Little Rock for his forty-fifth, but a heart attack kept him from the sessions, and he died at his son John C. Hulsey’s house on Peyton Street. He was buried at Mount Ida, where he had been pastor, by one count, for thirty of his fifty-five years in the ministry.

Arkansas papers called him the oldest full-time pastor in the state; for twenty-two years he had also preached on Sunday afternoons at Antioch church near Hot Springs. He left his wife, a daughter at Springdale and six sons scattered from Coffeyville to Mobile, one of them in uniform at Camp Fannin, Texas.

In Oklahoma they remembered him as their own. The Wilburton paper recalled that he had been the first pastor of the First Baptist Church there when it was organized in the spring of 1898, and was called back from 1905 to 1907. The McAlester paper added his family: two sisters and two brothers living in McAlester, Mrs. Arizona Smith, Mrs. Media Emery, H. C. Hulsey and W. J. Hulsey.

stories.title: Five post offices and their dates
stories.hook: Each household had a post office. The dates show when Doaksville, Fowlerville and Alikchi opened and changed their names around the family.

subject.name: The post offices on the Thompson, Tims, Austin and Pisachubbe cards

body: In 1899 each household had a post office: Doaksville for Joseph and Betsy Thompson and for Mitchell and Willie Tims, Alikchi for James B. Tims, Fowlerville for Legion and Molsey Austin and Goodland for Eunice Pisachubbe. The Postmaster General's records give the dates for most of them, though they show the offices "on paper" and not always as they ran on the ground.

Doaksville's office opened on 11 November 1847, when the Fort Towson office, which dated from 7 September 1832 with George C. Gooding as its first postmaster, took the Doaksville name. Joseph R. Bertholet (the Berthelet of the Doaksville store) was the first postmaster of Doaksville, appointed in 1847. That bears on a family memory. Joel Thompson said that "Venson Brown Tims" was the first postmaster at Doaksville, but the list gives that place to Berthelet. The two men are linked in the same year: at the Red River Raft Convention held at Clarksville, Texas, in the winter of 1847, two Doaksville citizens, Berthelet and Vincent B. Tims, "took a prominent part."

The office was not always open. It did not operate from 2 July 1866 to 28 May 1867 or from 15 September 1867 to 29 June 1869. A "V. B. Tims" was named its postmaster on 17 May 1871, after the second reopening, and Edward Tims was appointed in 1887. On 12 June 1903 the name was changed back to Fort Towson, which explains why in 1905 the family's address was changed from Doaksville to "Ft. Towson, I.T." Corinne's office, the one the Thompsons were using by 1915, opened on 24 August 1904 with Pearl Wynn as its first postmaster.

Fowlerville was the Austin family's office. It opened on 7 July 1894 with Nathaniel M. Fowler as postmaster and was renamed Valliant on 23 June 1902, with Hosea L. Fowler as the first postmaster under the new name. Legion Austin swore to his son James's birth at Fowlerville in May 1899, his wife's 1901 statement for their daughter Adline was sworn there too, and he is said to have died at Valliant on 8 April 1903, less than a year after the change. Alikchi, James Tims's address, opened on 13 July 1888 with John Wooley as postmaster, almost eleven years before he applied. Spencerville opened on 17 May 1902, and Joseph Thompson is said to have died there in 1927.
Goodland, Eunice Pisachubbe's address, is the one gap: no Goodland office is listed, so which office served her household in 1899 is not known.
src: George H. Shirk, 'First Post Offices Within the Boundaries of Oklahoma,' Chronicles of Oklahoma 26 (1948), pp. 179-237, entries for Alikchi, Corinne, Doaksville, Fort Towson, Fowlerville, Spencerville and Valliant: https://archive.org/details/chroniclesofokla2619okla (opened 2 Nov 2026)

stories.title: A farm near Pearland, May 1950
stories.hook: In May 1950 Lester and Barbara Livesay were living with their two children on a farm in Brazoria County, three years before Lester bought his Pearland ranch.
body: On 3 May 1950 the census taker, Mrs. L. M. Jones, reached the Livesay home in Brazoria County, Texas. There she counted Lester W., head, white, male, 33, married, born in Texas; Barbara, his wife, 32, married, born in Texas; their daughter Carolyn Joe, 14; and their son Wayne W., 10, both born in Texas. The family was living on a farm or ranch.

The ages fit. Lester Jr. was born on 8 May 1916, so he was five days short of his thirty-fourth birthday and still 33. Barbara was born on 7 April 1918 and had just turned 32. Wayne Woodrow was born on 13 February 1940. Carolyn, at 14, was born between May 1935 and May 1936, in the year after her parents’ April 1935 marriage; she was Carolyn Jo to her father’s family, and her name was sometimes spelled Carylon. That same spring a Wayne and a Carolyn Livesay were in the fourth and seventh grades at Pearland.

Mrs. Jones made one small slip. She left Lester’s work blank and wrote it on Barbara’s line instead: at work, 40 hours, an “Engineer” for a private “Railroad” employer. Elsewhere on her page the wives were keeping house and their husbands’ jobs were on their own lines, and Lester was a Southern Pacific Railroad engineer, so the job was almost certainly his, written one line too low.

The farm fits too. Lester was reared in Pearland, and “in 1953, he purchased and operated” a cattle ranch there, as he was remembered in 2001. Three years before that purchase the family was already living on a farm, though whether they owned it, how large it was, and what they raised is not known.

stories.title: D. P. Livesay and his household, 1855 to 1933
stories.hook: A year before Floyd Livesay was born, D. P. Livesay was keeping house with a young woman and an older one; in later years he borrowed sixty dollars at Hoyleton, and his widow lived on until 1933.
body: In 1855, when Illinois took its own census, D. P. Livesay headed a household of three in Washington County: a man aged 20 to 30, a woman aged 20 to 30 and a woman aged 50 to 60, with one man of militia age and fifty dollars’ worth of livestock. Only the head was named. David Pinkney Livesay, born on 1 January 1831 by family tradition, would have been 24, and Tabitha J., who died on 14 February 1856 aged 27 years, 2 months and 4 days, about 26. There was no child yet, which fits a son born in February 1856.

Who the older woman was is not known. Robert Livesay had died on 15 February 1855, and his widow, Lydia, was very probably the Lydia Livesay with whom Floyd was living in 1860. But Lydia was born on 16 October 1807, by family tradition, which would have put her in her forties in 1855, not her fifties. The woman may have been Lydia with her age misreported, Tabitha’s mother, or someone else, and the faint old return is hard to read.

Tabitha lies at Gilead Cemetery in Grand Prairie Township, Jefferson County, as the wife of David P. Her maiden name is said to have been Flannigen, and Flannigans lie near her: a Thomas H. Flannigan who died on 28 January 1853 aged 58 years and 11 days, a Martha Flennigen, “w/o Thomas,” who died on 9 July 1862, and a Mary L. Flanigan with a single date, 22 July 1846. They may have been her family, but nothing yet ties them to her.

Gilead also holds Charles P. Livesay (4 October 1865 to 9 January 1915) and his wife, Mary Delona (21 September 1867 to 3 January 1948). David P. is said to have had a younger son named Charles, and a Charles born in 1865, buried where David’s first wife lies, fits a child of David’s second marriage far better than the Charles M. Livesay who was widowed in 1874. Charles P. was a different man from Charles M., but who his parents were is not known.

A few glimpses of David’s later life survive. On 7 March 1879 he borrowed sixty dollars for one year at ten percent on a personal note at Hoyleton, probably from the Hoyleton Bank. His estate, like Robert Livesay’s before him, went through the county court, with a bond for D. P. Livesay alongside it. And Elizabeth Livesay, very probably his widow, died in Beaucoup Township on 15 October 1933, the year carved for “Elizabeth, his wife” on David’s stone.

Estate papers often name a dead man’s heirs, and if Floyd was David’s son by Tabitha, he may be named among David’s. Until he is, David P. and Tabitha J. may have been Floyd’s parents, but no one can yet say so.

stories.title: The Beaucoup Walkers, 1855 to 1923
stories.hook: In 1855 four Walker households at Beaucoup matched the families on the old stones; William P. Walker died in May 1919, and Abigail in January 1923.

subject.name: William P. and Abigail Walker and their Beaucoup neighbors

body: In 1855 there were several Walker households in Washington County. Only the head of each was named, and everyone else was counted by sex and age group, so each household is a shape rather than a list of names. James Walker’s held a man aged 50 to 60, a woman aged 40 to 50 and two girls aged 10 to 20. Rev. James Walker was born about March 1800, and the older Etheldra, his wife, about 1804 or 1805, so both fit. Simeon Walker Sen.’s held a man and a woman in their fifties and a boy and a girl in their teens; Rev. Simeon Walker Sr. was born in 1802, as his conference remembered in 1880.

Simeon Walker Jun. headed a household of a man and a woman in their twenties and a boy under ten. Simeon Walker Jr. had married Etheldra Jane Walker in September 1852, and a son of “S. & E.” who died young lies at Beaucoup, so the shape fits that couple. G. W. Walker headed a household of a man in his twenties with three females, one under ten, one aged 10 to 20 and one in her twenties. Rev. G. W. Walker was born in 1826 and his wife Elizabeth in 1829, and their daughter Eudora B. A. was born on 7 July 1852, though she died in November 1854 and so was not in the household of 1855, where Frances, five, fits the girl under ten. No relationships were written down, so the ages only show that the families fit.

No household was headed by a William P. Walker. The nearest was a William H. Walker with seven people, including a man and a woman in their twenties and five younger people, which does not look like a couple married about 1852 whose first child, George W., had died in October 1854. William P. may have been counted under other initials, been living in someone else’s household, or simply been lost on the faint old page.

William P. Walker died in Beaucoup Township in May 1919, on the 20th by the state’s register of deaths, though the 19th is the date usually given; one of the two is a slip. Abigail Walker died at Richview on 28 January 1923, the year carved on the family stone: “Abigail, his wife, 1833–1923.”

Levi S. Walker died at Richview on 6 April 1921; a Levi S. Walker had been chaplain of the 60th Illinois, William P.’s regiment, in 1879 reckoning. And a James Walker left an estate in the county court, perhaps Rev. James, who died in 1857. William’s and Abigail’s own death papers, or that estate, may one day say whether Rev. James and Etheldra were William’s parents, and whether Abigail was the “Addie Bruce” named as Alice’s mother in Texas.

stories.title: Joshua L. Merry, first postmaster at Glover
stories.hook: Ida Merry’s father, Joshua L. Merry, became Glover’s first postmaster on 26 June 1901, and he was still serving there in 1907, on the eve of statehood.
body: Ida Merry Whitfield’s father, J. L. Louis Merry, was remembered as the first postmaster at Glover, and so he was. Joshua L. Merry was appointed on 26 June 1901 as the first postmaster of Glover, in the Choctaw Nation, as Grant Foreman set down in his “Early Post Offices of Oklahoma” in the Chronicles of Oklahoma in September 1928, and as George H. Shirk did again in 1948.

An office was formally established when its postmaster was appointed, and six weeks or more usually passed before he was set up and ready to open. So on 1 July 1901, five days after his appointment, Glover was not yet among the government’s post offices of the Indian Territory, which ran straight from Globe to Golconda. By 1 July 1903 it was: Glover, Choctaw, Joshua L. Merry, paid $24.94. In 1905 he earned $56.93, in District 24, and in 1907, the last year before statehood, “Merry, Joshua L, PM $90.”

His full name helps with the family puzzle. To the Dawes Commission he was Lewis or Louis, and its 1902 letter went to J. L. Merry at Glover. In Washington he was Joshua L. in 1903, 1905 and 1907, like the Joshua L. Merry of Glover who took out a marriage license and the “J. L. Louis Merry” of his Glover gravestone. So the Commission’s 1902 letter went to the town’s own postmaster. That Joshua L. Merry was the Louis Merry of card 5754 still rests on the shared place, the initials and later family memory, but no other Merry is known at Glover.

By 1911, after statehood, Glover was in McCurtain County and its postmaster was G. W. Grigsby, born in Texas. When Merry gave up the office is not known. The family’s postal work did run through three generations: Joshua at Glover, Ida later at Golden, and Ida’s daughter Ouida, who retired from the Golden office in 1990.

There may be one more glimpse of him. On 19 June 1905 a J. L. Merry signed as notary public on an affidavit for a Choctaw newborn’s enrollment under the Act of 1905, though where it was sworn, and whether this was Joshua, is not known.

stories.title: Bessie Durant, in her granddaughter’s words
stories.hook: In 1997 Elma Whitfield Severn sent a short sketch of her grandmother to a book of Choctaw original enrollees. It adds a birthplace and a different birth year.
body: In 1997 Wesley and Charleen Samuels published Life and Times of the Choctaw Original Enrollees, a book of family stories sent in by enrollees and their descendants. The book says the stories were printed so that families could tell them “in their own words without substantive change,” and the staff of the Bishinik helped gather them. One short entry, on page 71, is headed “Bessie Durant” and was submitted by Elma M. Severn, granddaughter.

Elma wrote that Bessie Durant, roll number 15526, was born on 11 November 1878 in Choctaw County, Indian Territory, and died on 22 March 1950 at Golden, Oklahoma. Bessie married Louis (J.L.) Merry, roll IW 1363, who was born on 10 April 1872 and died on 1 July 1932 at Golden. They had one child, Ida May Merry Whitfield, roll 15527. In 1997, Elma wrote, Ida had three living children, Lewis O. Whitfield, Elma M. Severn and Catherine O. Carroll, and had lost a son, Omagene Clinton Whitfield, in the Second World War.

Elma had the roll numbers right, and Louis’s dates are the ones on his Glover gravestone; Bessie’s death date is the one on her Denison Cemetery stone. Her birth year is another matter: the stone reads Nov. 11, 1879, while Elma gave 1878. In April 1899, when the family’s card, number 5754, was made out on the 26th and Bessie swore her affidavit as Ida’s mother on the 27th, she was 19. That fits a birth on 11 November 1879, as on the stone; in 1878 she would have been 20. Ages then were often approximate, so 1879 is the likelier year, though Elma’s 1878 cannot be ruled out.

Elma also gave Bessie a birthplace, Choctaw County, Indian Territory. There was no Choctaw County then: it was created at statehood in 1907 from parts of the Choctaw Nation’s Jackson, Kiamichi, Cedar and Towson counties. Elma was probably naming the place by its later Oklahoma county, and her words are a granddaughter’s memory rather than an official record.

Elma left a good deal unsaid. She did not name Bessie’s parents, brothers or sisters, or mention her later surname, Kernell, or the parting from Louis that Ida’s childhood suggests. Bessie’s own parents were Peter and Ellen Durant.

stories.title: Lewis Whitfield goes into the Army, July 1945
stories.hook: A year after his younger brother died off Normandy, Lewis O. Whitfield of McCurtain County was inducted at Oklahoma City.
body: The bronze plaque on Lewis Whitfield’s grave at Wheelock remembers him as a private in the U.S. Army Air Forces in World War II. He went into the Army late in the war. Lewis O. Whitfield of McCurtain County, born in Oklahoma in 1916, enlisted at Oklahoma City on 11 July 1945 as a private, Army serial number 38782151.

He came in through the draft, a selectee enlisting for the duration of the war plus six months, with no branch assignment yet on the day he enlisted. He was married, had finished three years of high school, and gave his civilian trade as plumber, gas fitter or steam fitter. That trade is not heard of again; by 1950 he was keeping a general store near Golden.

The name, county and birth year all fit Lewis Oliver Whitfield, born in August 1916, and he was indeed married, to Violet Box. He was probably assigned to the Air Forces after he was inducted, as his plaque says, but when, and when he came home, is not known.

His number had the same shape as his brother’s. Men inducted through Selective Service received eight-digit numbers beginning with 3 or 4, the second digit standing for the service command; Omagene’s was 38466149 and Lewis’s 38782151. When Lewis went in, Omagene had been dead for more than a year, and their widowed mother, Ida, was working at the Golden post office.

stories.title: Martha Logan's will, 1852
stories.hook: Martha Logan, born in South Carolina about 1779, made her will in Greene County in July 1852 and left the rest of what she had to her son Clemens, the father of Dudley Logan.
body: In 1850 Martha Logan was seventy-one, a South Carolina woman living by herself in Greene County, Alabama. Her family surrounded her. Next door was a Presbyterian minister, James P. McMullin, and a few doors on lived her son Clemens, her daughter Priscilla with her husband Willis Logan, and Leroy Logan, who was probably the widower of her daughter Eliza. Her daughter Mary A. D. Scott was two doors away.

On 14 July 1852 she made her will and signed it "M. Logan." She had outlived two of her children. To the children of her daughter Eliza, and to the children of her son William C., she left a dollar each, the old way of showing that they had not been forgotten. To Priscilla and to Clemens she left enslaved people, a mother named Harriet and her three children Drayton, Clarissa and Sam among them, on condition that each pay $250 to their sister Mary A. D. Scott, whose money was to be hers alone and not her husband's. The rest she left to Clemens, and she made him her executor.

She died that summer. In September 1852 Clemens brought the will into court, and the guardians who stood for the grandchildren were the family itself: Willis Logan for his own children, and Leroy Logan for his children and for the orphans of William C. Logan. Two years later Clemens was dead too.

Her husband is not named in the will. A gravestone in the old Greene County country, which became Hale County in 1867, remembers James C. Logan, born in 1773 and died in November 1840, “a kind husband and affectionate father.” A family history gives his wife as Martha Calhoun and his children by the very names Martha's will gives, so he was very probably her husband and Clemens's father.

quotes.t: a kind husband and affectionate father

Her maiden name Calhoun is a LEAD. 'Leroy Logan' as Eliza's husband is an inference from his serving as guardian for his minor children at the probate; Eliza is not named as his wife. The Find a Grave index links Dudley as James's 'child', which is an error (James died before Dudley's birth). Enslaved people named: Ellen 17, Laura 15, Gale 7 (to Priscilla; Ancestry's index wrongly calls them grandchildren) and Harriet with Drayton, Clarissa(?) and Sam (to Clemens); readings of some names uncertain. 'Calhoun' would tie to the SC Calhouns; do not claim kinship to John C. Calhoun.

stories.title: Clemens Logan's will and his three children, 1854
stories.hook: In the spring of 1854 Clemens Logan made his will in Greene County, Alabama, and by autumn the court was naming a guardian for Elizabeth, Dudley and Martha, his only surviving children.
body: Clemens Logan was born in South Carolina and made his life on Alabama cotton land. In 1850 he was thirty-three, farming in Greene County with land worth $1,600, his wife Mary A. beside him and three children in the house: Elizabeth, eight, Dudley, three, and a baby, Martha, six months old. His brother-in-law Willis Logan lived on one side and another Logan household, Leroy's, on the other, and his widowed mother, Martha, lived alone a few doors up the road.

On 17 April 1854 Clemens sat down to make his will, a man of sound mind "in view of the uncertainty of life and the certainty of death." He left everything to his children. His friend Noah Harris was to sell or keep the land as he saw fit, raise and school the children, and divide the estate among them as each came of age or married. Willis Logan, Alvis L. Logan and John C. McIntyre signed as witnesses. Mary is not mentioned, and she had probably died already.

Clemens did not live out the year. On 9 October 1854 the probate court of Greene County heard his will, and a guardian was named for "Elizabeth Logan, Dudley T. Logan and Martha Logan, minor heirs of the deceased and the only surviving children." Dudley was eight. The boy who would one day take the family to Texas had lost both parents before he was ten.

Noah Harris kept the accounts for the next fourteen years. Elizabeth married first, and in December 1858 the court set apart her third of the estate to "Elizabeth H., wife of Jo. H. Tarkenton." By 1860 Dudley, fourteen, and Martha, nine, were living with the family of William R. Pool, a wagon maker at Havana. The estate's wealth lay in the people it held in slavery, who were divided among the heirs like the land. The court's order of December 1858 setting apart Elizabeth's third names nineteen of them: Abram, Harriet, Jack, Emeline, Jackson, Jo, Betsy, Aley, Bob, Sarah, Sintha, Nancy, William, Eland, Sam, Rachel, Caroline, Morning and John, though some of the names are hard to read. Harriet and Sam were probably the mother and son whom Clemens's own mother had left him six years before. When the war was over Dudley came home of age, and between 1866 and 1868 Harris paid him his share, $813.24, as he and his sister Martha, by then the wife of Edward Hunter, closed their father's estate.

stories.title: Annie Logan in her own words, 1914
stories.hook: At sixty-seven, crippled with rheumatism and unable to find two of her husband's old comrades, Annie Logan wrote to the Secretary of War herself.
body: Annie Logan was born on 15 September 1846 in Alabama, and she married Dudley Logan on 18 April 1866 at the Mount Zion church in Greene County, a year after the war ended. In the autumn of 1914 she was a widow of sixty-eight, living on a rural route outside Mount Pleasant, Texas, and she needed the pension Texas paid to the widows of Confederate soldiers. Texas had begun paying cash pensions to its Confederate veterans and their widows in 1899, the year after Dudley died.

The county judge told her she must have sworn statements from two men of Dudley's company. She knew of none still living. So on 4 November 1914 she wrote to the Secretary of War in Washington in her own careful hand. "He and I were raised in Ala., moved here in 1883, and he died here in 1898." She was sixty-seven, she wrote, afflicted with rheumatism and sadly in need. Dudley had left Alabama with Captain Dave Scarborough's company of cavalry, and sometime during the war he had been transferred to a Missouri brigade of infantry under General Cockrell, to be with his brother-in-law.

She had one more piece of evidence, a letter from her husband's niece. "Dear Aunt Annie," it began, and it passed on what an old neighbor, Sam Wilson, remembered: that he and Uncle Dudley had gone off to the war together in Company B of the Seventh Alabama Cavalry. Judge Sam Porter had said it was not enough, but the lawyer Seb Caldwell, standing by, told her to send it anyway, and so she did. In January Caldwell wrote to Austin on her behalf. He had known her husband, he said, and knew her as a woman respectable, truthful and worthy.

It worked. By 1918 she was signing her affidavit every quarter and drawing her pension, and when she went to visit in Oklahoma, where her daughter Annie Box was living, the pension office wrote to make sure she had not moved away from Texas for good.

quotes.t: He and I were raised in Ala., moved here in 1883, and he died here in 1898

stories.title: Three McCurtain County households, April 1950
stories.hook: In April 1950 the census taker found Larry Sandridge in Broken Bow and Alfreda Whitfield near Golden, eight years before they married.
body: In April 1950 the census takers came through McCurtain County, and three of the homes they visited belonged to the family. On 1 April, in Broken Bow, the first household reached was Lemuel L. Sandridge’s: Lemuel, 38, born in Arkansas; his wife, “Audry I.,” 32, born in Oklahoma; their son Larry L., 11; and a younger son, 8. Lemuel was working 40 hours a week as an electric service man for an electric company, and Audrey was keeping house.

Clinton and Maggie Sandridge lived elsewhere in Broken Bow, where the census taker called on or after 10 April. Clinton, written “Clenton L.,” was 66 and Maggie A., his wife, 58, both married and both born in Arkansas. Their house was on a farm, and Clinton was not working that week. His age adds to the puzzle of his birth: sixty-six in April 1950 means about 1883 or 1884, against 1882 on his gravestone and 1892 in his death notice. Maggie’s 58 fits her May 1891 birth, and her Arkansas birthplace, unlike the Texas of 1930, fits the Prescott birth of a Maggie Cash, though it does not prove she was born a Cash.

From 14 April the census taker worked Sulphur Township, heading west from Golden one mile and south half a mile. There “Louis O.” Whitfield, 33, born in Oklahoma, was keeping his own general store, working 72 hours a week. Violet B., 29, worked the same 72 hours as a clerk in the store, unpaid, as family. Their daughter Alfreda was 11, and two younger daughters, 7 and 4, were at home; the older of the two had been born in California, so the family perhaps spent part of the 1940s there. When Violet died in 1962 the Whitfields had been in the grocery business at Golden for several years; in 1950 the store was already running.

Next door lived a widow of 51, born in Oklahoma, the head of her own household, working 54 hours a week as postmistress at the Golden post office, a government job. Her name was written “James C. Whitfield,” probably a slip of the census taker’s pen, for everything else fits Ida Merry Whitfield: she was 51 that spring, a widow since 1941, and she became postmaster at Golden. If it was Ida, as it very probably was, she was already postmistress, not assistant, by April 1950.
The younger children of these households, who may still be living, go unnamed. Larry and Alfreda, the eleven-year-olds of Broken Bow and Golden, married at Broken Bow in 1958.

stories.title: From Bays Fork to Cotaco Creek: the Garrisons who went to Alabama
stories.hook: John Milton Garrison's younger brother took his family south to Morgan County, and the family Bible he left kept their story.
body: Hezekiah Alexander Garrison was born at Cowan's Ford on the Catawba River in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, in February 1791, and went with his parents, Samuel and Esther (Alexander) Garrison, to Warren County, Kentucky, about 1798 or 1799. On 10 June 1813 he married Rebecca Lyle there. The family list gives her birth as 25 October 1796 in Loudoun County, Virginia, and names her parents as Manasseh Lyle and Sarah Chaney (also written Chemey), who were first cousins; the Lyles had moved from Loudoun to Bedford County, Virginia, and then to Warren County. Another date, 18 August 1796, was printed at her death.

Their first nine children were born in Kentucky, in the part of Warren County that became Allen County: Esther Lyle, Samuel Newton (1816), Hillery Y. (1818), Simon Peter (1820), William Calvin, Hannah A., Nancy B., Sarah H. (1828, who died the next year) and Andrew Jackson (April 1830). Then the family went south. Morgan County, Alabama, was opened to settlement in 1830 and Cynthia C., the tenth child, was born there on 3 April 1832, so the move fell between those dates, and a county history shows a Garrison among the settlers who filed land claims in 1830. The obituaries date the move about 1831 (Hillery's) and 1832 (Simon Peter's, and Rebecca's, which adds "I think"). An old section plat puts the family on a half-section of land straddling Cotaco Creek, about six miles east of Somerville, the county seat, near the Old Center Springs camp ground. The last child, Mary Rebecca, was born in Morgan County on 23 June 1835.

Samuel Newton, the eldest son, died in Morgan County on 27 July 1837, at twenty-one, and E. Welch wrote a long poem on his death "in his Mother's stead" that was kept with the family papers. Hezekiah died on 15 August 1846, the date set down in the family Bible; when Rebecca died, she was remembered only as having lost him "about the year" 1846. In 1850 Rebecca, 55 and born in Virginia, headed a Morgan County household with Andrew Jackson, Cynthia and Mary R., and her married sons Simon Peter and William Calvin lived beside her with their families. Cynthia married W. S. McClanahan on 4 January 1854 and died on 11 November 1856.

Rebecca outlived her husband by twenty-seven years. She was a Methodist for fifty years; until she gave up keeping house, "her house was the preacher's home," and two of her sons became preachers. During the Civil War she saw at least one son side with the Union while her youngest son was killed fighting for the Confederacy; the Union son is not named. She died on 5 August 1873, after nine days in bed, at the home of her son-in-law S. W. Shackelford near Moulton, Alabama.

Nearly all of this comes from one book, Hezekiah's Bible, with handwritten births, marriages, deaths and burials and with newspaper obituaries pasted into its record pages. It passed to his youngest daughter, Mary Rebecca, and then to her daughter Minnie, who gave it before her death to a great-granddaughter of Hezekiah's living in Decatur, and its pages were copied for a Garrison genealogy in 1979.

stories.title: Two preachers from Center Springs: Hillery and Simon Peter Garrison
stories.hook: Two of Hezekiah Garrison's sons became Methodist preachers: one rode Arkansas circuits through the Civil War, the other never left the neighborhood of the old camp ground.

subject.name: Rev. Hillery Y. Garrison & Rev. Simon Peter Garrison

body: Hillery Y. Garrison was born in Allen County, Kentucky, on 22 January 1818 and came with his father to Morgan County, Alabama, about 1831. He professed religion at Barret's Camp-ground in the fall of 1837 under the Rev. William H. Johnston, was licensed to preach in 1842, joined the Tennessee Conference that fall, was transferred to the Alabama Conference and placed on the Coosa Circuit, and "located" (left the traveling ministry) when the year was out. He also studied and practiced medicine. In 1848 he married Jane Alexander, daughter of the Rev. Aaron Alexander of Lincoln County, Tennessee. Jane died at her father's home on 10 October 1850, in her twenty-third year, a few weeks after her sister Martha, her father and her baby of about five months. Hillery's obituary prints her death year as 1830, an evident slip.

He married again, to Eliza C. Beale of Madison County, Alabama, and moved to Arkansas. The family dates that marriage 28 December 1852; the notice printed at his death puts it in 1854, with the move soon after. In the Arkansas Conference, Hilary Y. Garrison (so spelled) was a preacher on trial in 1862 and 1863 and was received into full connection at Jacksonport in October 1864. He worked in the Helena District each year: at Prairie after the conference of November 1862, on the Helena Circuit after October 1863, on the Prairie Circuit after October 1864 and at Clarendon after the conference of 1865. The church kept its minutes through the war in the Confederacy, and they place him at work in the same district through all four years.

He died in Phillips County, Arkansas, on 8 December 1868, after about twenty-four hours of quinsy. He left a wife and one child in Arkansas, "an aged, widowed mother in Alabama," and several brothers and sisters.

Simon Peter Garrison, born in Allen County on 10 January 1820, moved with his parents to Morgan County in 1832 and, as his son Simon R. Garrison wrote, "settled near Old Center Springs' Camp ground." He joined the church at seventeen. On 18 December 1844 he married Louisa Glover, born in Northampton County, North Carolina, on 9 July 1828, whose widowed mother had moved to Morgan County near the same camp ground. They had seven children. Louisa died near Somerville of consumption in February 1874; two of her sons had just entered the ministry. In 1875 Simon Peter married Annie E. Orme, and they had three children, two of whom died as infants.

Simon Peter was an exhorter and class leader for years before he was licensed to preach in 1862. He was ordained deacon at Florence and elder at Decatur, the latter in 1876, and his preaching stayed mostly in his own neighborhood and county; his son called him one of the "old-time" Methodist local preachers. He was a wealthy farmer. He died at Somerville on 13 May 1896 after a long illness and lived to see his two oldest sons preach. He and Louisa are buried in a family cemetery near Center Springs Methodist Church.

quotes.t: He leaves a wife and one child in Arkansas; an aged, widowed mother in Alabama.

stories.title: The youngest child, a carriage shop at Hartselle, and the Bible she kept
stories.hook: Mary Rebecca Garrison married a Morgan County wagon maker, lost a brother in the last weeks of the war, and handed her father's Bible down to her daughter.

subject.name: Mary Rebecca (Garrison) Shackelford & S. W. Shackelford

body: Mary Rebecca Garrison, the youngest of Hezekiah and Rebecca Garrison's eleven children, was born in Morgan County, Alabama, on 23 June 1835. She was still at home with her widowed mother in 1850, in 1850. On 29 September 1858 she married S. W. Shackelford. Her mother died in August 1873 at the Shackelfords' home near Moulton; S. W. Shackelford also lived at Moulton, but the couple's longer home was Hartselle, in Morgan County, where both were buried.

In March 1887 a trade paper noted that "S. W. Shackelford is building a wagon and carriage shop at Hartselle, Ala." The notice says nothing more about him, but the name, the initials and the town agree with the family record.

The family list in the Bible names four Shackelford children. Fannie Laura, born on 10 March 1863, died on 1 April. Robert James, born on 28 August 1864, married Sallie C. Bennet at Zion, Kentucky, on 12 July 1886 and made his home in Nashville. Hillery Sather, born on 12 May 1873, was living at Wynnewood in the Indian Territory when his mother died. Minnie Ann Emma, born on 6 August 1876, married R. L. Cox of Hartselle and lived to be 102; she died in 1978 in a nursing home at Athens, Limestone County, and was buried beside her husband in the Shackelford lot at Hartselle.

Mary Rebecca's brother Andrew Jackson Garrison, born in Allen County, Kentucky, in April 1830, married Sarah Sanders in Morgan County on 30 January 1862. The Bible records in longhand that he "was killed by our Federal Enemys, April 1865, near Crutchers shop, Madison Cty., Ala.," and that he was "a member of Col. Meads Confederate Guerillers." No service record for him was found. An Andrew J. Garrison served as a sergeant in the 1st Alabama Reserves, but nothing ties that man to this one.

Mary Rebecca died at Robert's home in Nashville. Her death notice, clipped from a Hartselle paper and kept in the Bible, says her body was brought home on a Sunday, her funeral was held at the Methodist church, and she was buried in Hartselle cemetery beside her husband. The date of the notice is not given. She had inherited her father's Bible, with its handwritten records and pasted obituaries, and it passed to Minnie, who gave it to a Garrison cousin in Decatur.

stories.title: School District No. 95, Marshan Township, 1874
stories.hook: A James H. Satterfield sat on a new school board in Marshan Township in 1874, bearing out his own account of the family's years in Dakota County.

subject.name: James H. Satterfield in Marshan Township, Minnesota

body: James H. Satterfield's 1885 biography says he moved from Allen County, Kentucky, to Dakota County, Minnesota, in 1867 and went back to Kentucky in 1875. His daughter A. M. was born in Minnesota in 1870.

A county history of 1881 tells how School District No. 95 of Marshan Township began. The district was organized on 31 March 1874 at a school meeting at the house of W. B. Mather, which voted to raise $400 for a schoolhouse; the building went up on the northeast quarter of section 8, on land owned by Peter Huneicker. "The first trustees of the district were elected at this meeting, and were as follows: James H. Satterfield, director; L. D. Massey, clerk; William R. Mather, treasurer." Ella Gilkey taught the first term, four months in the winter of 1875-76, to about twenty-seven pupils. A later history repeats it with the same names.

Marshan was bounded on the north by Nininger, Hastings and Ravenna, on the east by Ravenna, on the south by Douglass and on the west by Vermillion. Its soil was mostly sandy, and the Vermillion River crossed its western sections.

The name, the county and the years agree with his own account, and the school meeting falls a year before he says he left. The clerk's name is a second point of contact. James's sister Ruth M. Satterfield married a Massey and is buried, as Ruth Melissa Massey (1840-1935), at Amarillo. Whether L. D. Massey was her husband is not known. If the director was James, he did not stay to see the first term taught: by his own account he was in Warren County, Kentucky, in 1875.

stories.title: Proposed by J. P. Thompson: Joseph in the council records, 1890–1904
stories.hook: Joel remembered his father as a lawmaker for years, and one line in the printed acts of the October 1904 session may be his: 'Proposed by J. P. Thompson.'

subject.name: Joseph Perry Thompson in the Choctaw General Council

body: In 1891, while he was still under thirty, it was written of Joseph that he began as a schoolteacher, was appointed county clerk of Cedar County in 1889, and "the year following he was elected representative to the lower House," where he was "one of the youngest members of the legislature." His son Joel later added that he served as county judge and about six years as a senator. None of this has been matched to a record of the General Council itself.

The council Joseph joined in 1890 passed several laws for his own county. Among them were an act approved 31 October 1890 that redrew the line between Cedar and Nashoba counties along Ward's Creek, an act approved 15 October 1891 that set up an election precinct "at or near the Gilbert Cooper place" in Cedar County, to be called Lick precinct, and an act approved 3 December 1891 that moved the Cedar County court ground from Pine Hill to Sulphur Spring, the court ground Joel later remembered his father presiding over. It is not printed who proposed these acts or how anyone voted, so they show what Joseph's council did, not what he did in it.

The clearest entry comes at the end. The acts of the General Council for the October 1904 session open with a run of resolutions giving each committee a clerk. One authorized the chairman of the Committee on Petitions to appoint a clerk "to make and keep a full record of the work of said committee," at four dollars a day, paid by warrant of the National Auditor. It closes: "Proposed by J. P. Thompson." Like the bills around it, it took effect "by statute of limitation" on 13 October 1904 (the printer set the year as 1604), over the name of Principal Chief Green McCurtain, attested by J. W. Conser, recording secretary.

Only initials are given. The only adult Choctaw citizen named Thompson whose given names begin with J. P. is Joseph P. Thompson, who was 40 on the final roll. That makes the identification probable rather than proven. It is not said whether J. P. Thompson sat in the House or the Senate, or which county sent him.

It is a small bill, but it places Joseph in the council when the Nation's land had already been divided: the year before, he had gone to Atoka to select the family's allotments. The acts of the 1902 and 1903 sessions contain no bill proposed by a Thompson, so the dates of his House term, his years as county judge and his time in the Senate are not known.

stories.title: Goodland court ground: Kiamitia County's seat in the Pisachubbes' years, 1889–1902
stories.hook: Eunice Pisachubbe's post office in 1899 was Goodland. For thirteen years Goodland was also where Kiamitia County held court, until the council moved it three miles south to the new railroad town of Hugo in December 1902.
body: Goodland began as a Presbyterian mission station. George Ainslie, a missionary who had served there, wrote about it in a letter printed in 1939. He put it about twelve miles southwest of Goodwater and eighteen miles from Doaksville, and said its church was "a colony from Goodwater." When he first saw it in 1852 it was "a pretty and pleasant station" of a mission house and a church that also served as the school, "surrounded by forest with no prairie near." In the same letter he notes that Goodland had only a day school.

The railroad changed its place in the county. On 28 October 1889 the General Council passed two acts for Kiamichi County, as the laws spell it. One moved the Clear Springs election precinct to "Good Land station" and set the first election there for the first Wednesday in August 1890. The other removed the county court ground from Clear Springs to "Good Land station on the St. Louis & San Francisco railway," with court to sit on the first Monday of every month beginning in January 1890. The county judge was to sell the old courthouse at Clear Springs and set the money aside for a new one at Good Land.

That is the Goodland of the family's records. On 10 May 1899 Eunice Pisachubbe, 49, her sons William H. and Robert, and her ward Edward were enrolled for Kiamitia County, post office "Goodland, I.T." The Secretary of the Interior approved their enrollment on 12 December 1902.

A week later the court ground left. In an extra session in December 1902 the council moved the Goodland election precinct to Hugo, "about three miles south of the present site," with the first vote there in August 1903 (approved 18 December). An act approved 19 December removed the county court ground "from its present site, at Goodland" to Hugo, told the county judge to choose a house in the town, and set the first term for the first Monday in February 1903. Another act, approved the same day, let the judge sell "the building formerly used as a court house at Goodland" and buy a building in Hugo "at the junction of the Arkansas & Choctaw Railroad and the St. Louis & San Francisco Railroad." All three were proposed by Jeff Fulton.

Hugo became the family's town. William Harrison Pisachubbe's funeral in 1937 was held near the Long Creek school house, Robert and Lizzie lived at Speer and then with Simon and Frances at Jeter, and Simon and Frances are buried at Long Creek Cemetery near Hugo, . Where on the Goodland road Eunice's own house stood is not known.

stories.title: A corporal named Edward Tims, 1862
stories.hook: An Edward Tims was third corporal in a Choctaw company in 1862, with no age or home given, so whether he was Betsy's uncle Edward is an open question.

subject.name: Edward Tims, Company G, 1st Choctaw Mounted Rifles

body: Whether any relative served in the Civil War is open. A small Confederate file survives for "Tims, Edward" of Company G, 1st Choctaw Mounted Rifles, "also known as Cavalry." It gives his rank as corporal and holds a single card.

The card copies one line of a pay roll. "Edward Tims," "3d Corpl," of Capt. Coleman E. Nelson's Company, 1st Regiment Choctaw Mounted Rifles, appears on a roll of enlisted men for commutation of clothing "for the last six months of the year ending November 23, 1862." The sum is twenty-five dollars. The roll date is written "Aug 13, 1862," which falls before the end of the period it covers; that is not explained. A printed note says Nelson's company was also known as Company G.

Nelson's own file sets the regiment's scene. As captain of Company G of the 1st Choctaw Regiment he signed a petition dated at Fort McCulloch in June 1862, from officers of the Indian regiments in Confederate service, asking that their colonel, Sampson Folsom, be made a brigadier general in the Provisional Army. On the clothing roll his name appears only as the signature to the certificate.

The obvious candidate is Edward Ward Tims of Towson County. In 1899 he gave his age as 58, so he would have been about twenty in 1862, and he is the only Edward Tims among the Choctaw by blood. But the war record names no county, father or age, nothing ties Nelson's company to Towson County, and nothing in his own life mentions service. So it stays a possibility.

Confederate pension applications turn up no help: the only Tims is Mary Amanda, widow of Francis Marion Tims of a Texas regiment, and there is none from Edward or from his wife Willie Jane, who died four months before him in 1922.

stories.title: Born in Fannin County: Benjamin F. Hulsey signs on at Cedar Glades, 1864
stories.hook: His own enlistment paper, signed with his mark, names the north Georgia county where he was born.

subject.name: Benjamin F. Hulsey, Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union)

body: When Benjamin F. Hulsey, private, Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry, joined the Union army, he made two papers. On his volunteer enlistment, sworn at Cedar Glades, Arkansas, on 14 January 1864 before Lt. J. B. Spiva of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, he stated that he was "born in Fannin Co in the State of Georgia," aged eighteen, a farmer, and volunteered for three years. On the declaration of recruit he signed "Benjamin F Hulsey, his mark." The form for a parent's consent in the case of a minor was left blank.

The papers describe him as having black eyes, black hair and a dark complexion. They do not agree on his height: the enlistment gives five feet nine inches, while the descriptive roll and the company descriptive book both give five feet three. He was mustered into service at Little Rock on 17 February 1864. The detachment roll assigns him to Company L, but every company muster roll carries him in Company D. He brought his own mount: the rolls credit him with pay "for use and risk of horse and equipments" from enlistment to 20 June 1864.

He was present on every muster roll from enlistment through April 1865. In November 1864 he was on daily duty "at work on stables," and in February and March 1865 he was on detached service in the quartermaster's department as a teamster. He was mustered out with the company at Little Rock on 30 June 1865, still recorded as eighteen. The regiment had been ordered disbanded on 2 June 1864, "the War Dept not sanctioning the raising of a one year Regt"; his rolls nonetheless run on to June 1865.

Fannin County was created in 1854 from parts of Gilmer and Union counties. A boy of eighteen in January 1864 was born about 1845 or 1846, before the county existed, so the name he gave is most likely the county his birthplace lay in by the time he enlisted. In 1850 a Benjamin, three, was in the Union County household of the blacksmith Salathiel Hulsey, and in 1880 the B. F. Hulsey of Center Township, Montgomery County, gave his age as 32 and his birthplace as Georgia. The three ages differ by a year or two. The Fannin County birthplace fits the Union County household and is the first time Benjamin himself names where he was born, but it names no parent.

He was not the only family name on that day's list. On the same 14 January 1864, at Cedar Glades and before the same Lieutenant Spiva, Gillam Graves, 45, born in Randolph County, North Carolina, signed his own enlistment into the same company. Gilliam Graves was the grandfather of Sarah Rebecca Graves, who in 1901 married George Washington Hulsey.

stories.title: A horse lost near Harrold and two months' pay: Gilliam Graves's service record
stories.hook: On the day Dr. Brown of Cedar Glades was shot, the enemy took Gilliam Graves's horse in a fight in his own county.

subject.name: Gilliam Graves, Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union)

body: Gillam Graves, private, Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry, swore his volunteer enlistment at Cedar Glades on 14 January 1864 before Lt. J. B. Spiva. It says he was born in Randolph County, North Carolina, was 45 years old and a farmer, with black eyes, black hair and a dark complexion, five feet ten inches tall. He was mustered into the service at Little Rock on 17 February 1864. The company descriptive book repeats Randolph, N.C., as his birthplace. The family genealogy gave that birthplace too, but the enlistment is his own statement. His name also appears as Gillman Graves.

Like most of the company he rode his own horse, and the rolls pay him for its use from enlistment. A notation of 1869 explains a gap in that pay: "Horse and equipments captured by the enemy while engaged in action near Harrold Montgomery Co. Ark. March 1st, 1864," so that he was "not entitled to pay for use of horse from March 1st, 1864 to April 10th, 1864." The first of March 1864 is the day the Union men of Montgomery County said Dr. Brown of Cedar Glades was shot down, and the day the army lists a skirmish at Cedar Glade . Harrold is spelled as written; the place has not been identified.

The rest can be told. The return for September 1864 has him absent without leave, and in October he "Deserted Oct. 12/64 at Little Rock," with $18 stopped for arms and accoutrements. He returned on 25 December 1864, "in arrest" on one roll and "restored to duty without loss of pay" on the next. He was then tried by a general court-martial for absence without leave and sentenced to forfeit two months' pay and allowances, under orders of 28 December 1864. He was present on the rolls for early 1865 and was mustered out at Little Rock on 30 June 1865, last paid to 30 June 1864.

He did not serve alone. Benjamin F. Hulsey enlisted the same day before the same officer, and Alson Graves, eighteen, who is probably the Alison Graves of the orphaned household Gilliam had in his guardianship, was in Company D as well.

stories.title: Alson Graves, the ward who enlisted at eighteen
stories.hook: One of the orphans in Gilliam Graves's guardianship turns up beside him in the same Union company.
body: Alison was one of the orphans of Samuel and Sarah Graves of Montgomery County, Arkansas, whose guardian from 1854 was Gilliam Graves, and in 1860 he was fourteen, living with his brothers and sisters in a household of their own.

The story carries forward in a Union record filed as "Graves, Allison," the name being given as Alson Graves. Alson Graves, eighteen and a farmer, volunteered at Little Rock on 21 November 1863 for three years, enlisted by William Brown, recruiting officer of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, before Capt. Geo. H. Hand. He signed by his mark. He was six feet tall. He first appears on a detachment muster-in roll of Lieut. Vance's company, 3rd Arkansas Cavalry, dated at Benton, Arkansas, on 6 December 1863, whose card notes that the organization afterward became part of the 4th. He was mustered into Company L of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry at Little Rock on 21 April 1864, and from then on the company rolls carry him in Company D.

The papers disagree about where he was born and what he looked like. The enlistment and the detachment roll say New Hanover County, North Carolina, with black eyes, black hair and a dark complexion. The company descriptive book says Randolph County, North Carolina, with grey eyes, dark hair and a fair complexion. Randolph County is where the Graves genealogy places the 1837 marriage of Samuel Graves and Sarah Cole.

He was present on every roll from enlistment to April 1865. His first roll notes "No horse," and later rolls pay him for the use of a horse. He was mustered out with the company at Little Rock on 30 June 1865, his age still given as eighteen. His guardian Gilliam Graves served in the same company, which he had joined at Cedar Glades on 14 January 1864.

The name, the age (fourteen in 1860, eighteen in late 1863), the North Carolina birth and his service in his guardian's company all fit the Alison of the 1860 household and the 1861 guardianship, and nothing seen contradicts them. How Samuel and Sarah's children were related to Gilliam remains unknown.

stories.title: W. E. F. Stevenson of the Third Tennessee: Fort Donelson, Camp Douglas and back
stories.hook: Abner Stevenson's eldest son went to war at nineteen with a Giles County company and spent the summer of 1862 in a prison camp in Chicago.
body: William Elam Fletcher Stevenson was the eldest son of Rev. Abner A. Stevenson and Martha S. Watson, born on 9 April 1842. His initials, W. E. F., are unusual enough to follow: W. E. F. Stevenson, private in the 3rd (Clack's) Tennessee Infantry, enlisted on 17 May 1861 at Nashville, mustered by Inspector Scudder for twelve months. One record describes the regiment as first organized at Lynnville, Tennessee, on 16 May 1861.

The Third Tennessee was organized at Lynnville, "this county," on 16 May 1861, and that five of its ten companies came from Giles County. Among them was Company K under Capt. F. C. Barber, which at the reorganization in September 1862 became Company A. Stevenson was carried first in Company K and then in Company A, exactly as that company was renumbered.

The regiment went to Fort Donelson in February 1862. W. E. F. Stevenson was captured there on 16 February and appears on a roll of prisoners of war at Camp Douglas, Illinois, of 1 August 1862. A roll dated at Camp Douglas on 7 September 1862 lists him among the prisoners sent to Vicksburg to be exchanged; its endorsement records that 824 prisoners were received on board the steamer Jno. H. Done near Vicksburg on 23 September 1862. The regiment was reorganized at Jackson, Mississippi, three days later.

He was present on every muster roll from August 1862 through February 1864, once noted as absent from Chickasaw Bayou on detached duty, and by early 1864 his term was entered as "war." He drew clothing on 30 April 1864, signing "E F Stevenson," and again on 7 June 1864, when the receipt has only a mark. He was admitted to the 1st Mississippi C.S.A. Hospital at Jackson, Mississippi, on 28 October 1864 with intermittent fever, and returned to duty on 22 November. The record stops there. The regiment was merged into the 4th Consolidated Tennessee Infantry about 9 April 1865 and paroled at Greensboro, North Carolina, on 1 May 1865, but no parole is recorded for him.
His younger brother Frank, the family's 2nd great-grandfather, was born in Giles County in November 1861, six months after William enlisted. So, as his nephews did, one of Abner's own sons served.
