stories.title: A Georgia-born Robert Hulsey loses an eye: a Confederate discharge, December 1862
stories.hook: Two years before Benjamin F. Hulsey rode for the Union, a Robert Hulsey of the right age was sent home from a Confederate hospital half blind.

subject.name: Robert Hulsey, Company B, 8th Battalion Arkansas Infantry (Confederate)

body: Robert Hulsey, private, Company B, 8th Battalion Arkansas Infantry, left a short record, chiefly his certificate of discharge. The certificate, written at the General Hospital "Okolona" at Meridian, Mississippi, on 15 December 1862, says he was enlisted by Capt. Imboden on 5 March 1862 to serve three years, at a place in Arkansas that reads like "Cordova." It gives his birthplace as Habersham County, Georgia, his age as 30 and his height as five feet six inches, with a dark complexion, blue eyes and dark hair, a farmer.

The examining board of three surgeons found him unable to serve "because of chronic ophthalmia & loss of one eye and serious injury of the other," and recommended his discharge under General Order No. 72. He was honorably discharged at Marion, Mississippi, on 21 December 1862.

Why this Robert matters is his age and birthplace. Thirty in 1862 places his birth about 1831 or 1832. The Robert in Salathiel Hulsey's Union County, Georgia, household was 17 in November 1850, and the Georgia-born Robert Hulsey of Hempstead County, Arkansas, was 27 in 1860; both point to about 1833.

Nothing names his parents, his wife or his home county in Arkansas. He may be Salathiel's son Robert and the Hempstead County farmer, and so a possible older brother of the Benjamin F. Hulsey who joined the Union 4th Arkansas Cavalry in 1864, but none of those links is proven.

stories.title: Elected at Richwoods, dismissed at court-martial: D. H. Grimes, 1862–1863
stories.hook: A 33-year-old Tennessean in Izard County was elected lieutenant within six weeks of enlisting and was dismissed by court-martial eight months later.
body: D. H. Grimes of Company I, 27th Arkansas Infantry, left a short Confederate record, but it is the only description of him yet found. He enrolled on 6 July 1862 at Richwoods, in Izard County, under Captain Riggs, "for the war." The muster-in roll, made at Camp Bragg, Arkansas, on 31 July 1862, lists him as second corporal of Company I in what was then the 1st Regiment of McBride's Brigade, and gives his age as 33. The regiment was also known by its colonel's name, as Shaler's Regiment.

Six weeks later his company chose him as an officer. He was promoted to junior second lieutenant on 18 August 1862, and in April 1863 he was recorded as elected on 18 August 1862, aged 33, from Izard County, Arkansas, and born in Tennessee. Rosters of Hindman's Division for February 1863 list him as third and second lieutenant, and the second of them marks him "Absent sick." A company roll dated 28 February 1863 says instead "Absent without leave."

By March and April 1863 he was present but "In arrest," and his record closes: "Dismissed Court Martial Apr. 4, 1863." The charge is not given. It may be connected with the absence without leave noted a few weeks earlier.

Whether this lieutenant is Hannah Moffitt's father is still open. David H. Grimes of the family tree was born in 1829 in Wayne County, Tennessee, which fits a man of 33 in 1862 who was born in Tennessee, and Hannah herself gave Tennessee for both her parents in 1900. Against that, the same tree places David in the lower Mississippi country of Arkansas in the 1850s and has him dying there in 1876, far from Izard County, and nothing names a wife or child. A widow of a David H. Grimes of this regiment later sought a Union pension; that file, if it can be found, would be the record most likely to settle the question.

stories.title: The Turtle Paws: Marshall Moffitt, who died at Greenville in 1863
stories.hook: William C. Moffitt's son Marshall, whose 1863 death the family tree recorded without a cause, was a private in a Chatham County company of the 44th North Carolina.
body: William C. Moffitt's son Marshall died in 1863, and his service can now be told. A Confederate record for "Marshall D. Moffitt" places him in Company E of the 44th North Carolina Infantry, a company raised in neighboring Chatham County and known as "The Turtle Paws."

The company's muster-in and descriptive roll, made at Camp Mangum near Raleigh on 3 April 1862, says he was born in Randolph County, was 23 years old and stood 5 feet 10 inches. He had enrolled in March, at Lows Store according to that roll and at Pittsboro according to the muster rolls, for three years or the war, and he signed the oath of allegiance to the State of North Carolina himself, as "M. D. Moffitt." He was present on the company's rolls from March through August 1862 and again on the roll for January and February 1863, last paid to 31 December 1862.

A register of Confederate soldiers who died of wounds or disease records his death on 28 March 1863 at Greenville, North Carolina. The state's Roll of Honor gives his county as Randolph, his entry into service as 4 March 1862 and his age as 21, and says simply that he "Died April 1863 of Disease."

His age of 23 in 1862 fits the birth year of 1839 given for William C.'s son Marshall, and the Randolph birthplace and the 1863 death agree, so the identification is probable. Nothing names his parents. His file also holds a stray card for a "W. D. Moffitt," captain of Company H of the same regiment, who resigned on 16 July 1862, and the regiment had another Randolph-born private, Milo M. Moffitt, 18, in the same company; neither is identified here, and Milo is too young to be William C.'s son of that name, born in 1828.

stories.title: Three days apart at Raleigh: the Rains brothers of the Randolph Rangers, 1862
stories.hook: Two of Lydia Moffitt Rains's sons enrolled on the same day in March 1862 and died of disease at Raleigh within three days of each other that May.

subject.name: Nathan, Daniel and Alfred E. Rains

body: A family tree says that two of Lydia Moffitt Rains's sons, Nathan and William Anderson, "died in the Civil War." The Confederate service records tell a somewhat different story: a Nathan Rains and a Daniel Rains, both born in Randolph County, enrolled together and died within days of each other in the spring of 1862.

Both men enrolled for active service on 5 March 1862 at Holts, in Randolph County, in Captain O. W. Carr's company, the "Randolph Rangers," which became Company G of the 46th North Carolina Infantry. The company's muster-in and descriptive roll, dated at Camp Mangum near Raleigh on 16 April 1862, lists each as a farmer born in Randolph County; Nathan stood 5 feet 11 1/2 inches and Daniel 5 feet 9 3/4. Each signed the state oath of allegiance, "N. Rains" and "D. Rains." No ages are given.

Neither left Raleigh. The North Carolina Roll of Honor says Nathan "Died May 14 1862 of Disease at Raleigh" and Daniel died there of disease on 17 May. The Confederate register of deaths agrees on both dates, and a Raleigh hospital register puts the death of N. Rains on 18 May 1862. The illness is not named.

A third brother came later and came home. Alfred E. Rains (also carded as A. Rains and A. C. Rains) was enlisted for the war at Camp Holmes on 19 August 1864 by Colonel Mallett, and served as a private in Company G of the 38th North Carolina Infantry. He drew clothing in November and December 1864, signing by mark, and he was paroled at Greensboro on 19 May 1865 as one of the men surrendered with the Army of Northern Virginia. No service for a William Anderson Rains was found, and none is needed: a brother William A. died on 22 October 1859, before the war.

stories.title: Robert Livesay’s land at Beaucoup
stories.hook: Three federal patents put Robert Livesay on 320 acres in the Beaucoup timber, in the same section as the cemetery where his infant son Jasper was buried in 1841.
body: Robert Livesay came onto the land at Beaucoup in the late 1830s. Buying for cash through the land office at Kaskaskia, he received three federal patents for land in Washington County, Illinois. The first, dated 1 August 1838, covered 200 acres: the southeast quarter of the southeast quarter of Section 11 and the east halves of the northeast quarters of Sections 14 and 23, all in Township 2 South, Range 2 West of the Third Principal Meridian. The second, dated 10 October 1840, added 80 acres in Section 24, and the third, dated 10 March 1843, another 40 acres in Section 11.

Those are the dates the patents were signed, not necessarily the dates Robert chose the land or paid for it; cash entries were often patented a year or more after the sale. Together the three gave him 320 acres, half a square mile, in one block of adjoining sections.

The township is Beaucoup. Beaucoup Cemetery lies in Section 23 of Township 2 South, Range 2 West, the same section as part of Robert’s first purchase. There a stone marks Jasper L. Livesay, who died on 16 August 1841, “son of Robert & Lydia.” He had been born on 15 February 1841, by family tradition, so he lived six months. David P. Livesay, who may have been Floyd Livesay’s father, was buried in the same cemetery in 1904.

The sons followed. On the same day as Robert’s third patent, 10 March 1843, William E. Livesay, named first among Robert’s heirs in 1856, received 40 acres in Section 13 of the same township, next to his father’s land in Sections 14 and 24, and in 1848 he and Demsy Kennedy took 80 acres in Section 12. Jackson M. Livesay’s land, patented on 1 February 1850, lay a few miles east, in Section 8 of Township 2 South, Range 1 West, the Richview township. David P. Livesay, so far as is known, took no land of his own from the government.

Robert died on 15 February 1855, by family tradition, and his estate went through the county court. His patents are the earliest known trace of him on the ground, and they make the Beaucoup neighborhood the home place of the family Floyd Livesay grew up among.

stories.title: Robert and Lydia’s heirs
stories.hook: In 1856 eight living heirs of Robert Livesay set aside their claims until the three youngest had their share, and one son the family remembered is missing from the list.

subject.name: The children of Robert and Lydia Livesay

body: After Robert Livesay died in February 1855, his older children signed a release in favor of the younger ones. William E., Lorenzo M., Jackson M. and David P. Livesay, and Unity Jane with her husband, gave up their claims on the personal estate until the three minors, Nancy P., Daniel M. and Elbert T. Livesay, had each received $125. All eight were “heirs at law” of Robert. The release survives only as a descendant copied it, though Robert’s estate itself went through the county court.

The grown children had married in the county. William E. Livesay married Emily Goodner on a license of 1 August 1844. Lorenzo M. Livesay married Margaret Jane Thompson on 22 October 1845. Jackson M. Livesay married Lucinda A. Thompson on 15 November 1849, and James L. Logan married Unity J. Livesay the next day. The Thompson brides were, by family tradition, daughters of Isaiah and Hannah (Phillips) Thompson. William E. and Jackson M. also took land from the government, William beside his father’s land at Beaucoup in 1843 and Jackson near Richview in 1850.

The minors are harder to follow. Nancy Paulina was born on 19 June 1838, Daniel Marion on 25 July 1842 and Elbert Trumbell on 7 February 1845, by family tradition, and they are seen together only at home, in 1850 and 1860. One small trace may be Daniel’s. On 7 March 1879, at Hoyleton, probably at the bank there, two personal notes were written one after the other: no. 17, $60 for D. P. Livesay, and no. 18, $50 for D. M. Livesay, the second marked paid on 14 May 1880. Nothing says how the two were related, so the D. M. who borrowed beside D. P. was only probably his brother Daniel.

In 1850 Robert Livesay (written “Livesy”) was living in Washington County with Lydia, 43, and David P., 20, Thomas N., 15, Nancy P., 13, Daniel M., 8 and Elbert T., 6. In June 1860, five years after Robert’s death, Lydia Livesay, 52, born in Tennessee, headed a household in the same township with David, 28, Thomas, 24, “Palina,” 20, Daniel, 17 and “Trumbull,” 15: the middle names of Nancy Paulina and Elbert Trumbell. Their ages run seven to nine years above those of 1850, less than the ten years that had passed, so it is the order of the names and the middle names that match, not the exact ages. No relationships were written down in either year, and a four-year-old, Floyd H. Livesay, was in the 1860 household too.

The list also has a gap. Robert and Lydia had ten children, by family tradition, and nine survived Robert, yet the release names only eight. Jasper died in 1841, which accounts for one. The other missing child is Thomas Newton Livesay, born on 22 February 1836. He was probably the Thomas still at home in 1860, so he may have received his share another way, or been left off the copy; no one now knows.

None of this names Floyd Livesay. But wherever the family’s memory of Robert and Lydia can be tested, it holds, which makes it likelier, though not certain, that David Pinkney was their son. Several Livesays of the county served in the 49th and 60th Illinois Infantry in the Civil War, as the county remembered in 1879, but none of the sons named in the release.

stories.title: Lorenzo M. Livesay across the county line
stories.hook: In 1860 and 1870 the census taker found David P. Livesay’s older brother farming in Jefferson County, the county where Tabitha Livesay is buried.
body: Lorenzo Mastin Livesay was the second of Robert and Lydia’s sons in the family sketch, about five when the family left Maury County, Tennessee. He married Margaret Jane Thompson in Washington County on 22 October 1845, and in 1856 he signed the release as one of his father’s heirs at law.

By 1860 he had crossed into Jefferson County, the next county east. On 12 June 1860 the census taker for Township 2 South, Range 4 East, with a Mount Vernon post office, listed Lorenzo M. Livesay, 34, a farmer born in Tennessee, with real estate worth $2,000. With him were Margaret J., 32, also born in Tennessee, and three children born in Illinois: Ephraim J., 11, Mary C., 4, and Elizabeth P., 1. The ages fit the sketch’s account of a boy born in Tennessee about 1825.

Ten years later, on 29 July 1870, he was in Webber Township, in the same township and range, with a Lynchburg post office. Lorenzo M., 44, farmer, born in Tennessee, now held real estate worth $2,400. His wife was Sarah S., 36, born in Kentucky, so Margaret had probably died, though when is not known. Mary C., 14, Elisabeth P., 11, Wilburn W., 9, Elva M., 6, and Lafaetta S., 5, were at home. In the house next to his lived a Jasper Livesay, 21, and his wife Belle; how they were related to Lorenzo is not known.

Lorenzo’s move matters for Floyd’s story because it puts a Livesay household in Jefferson County in the 1850s, the county where Tabitha J., “wife of David P. Livesay,” was buried at Gilead in 1856. Gilead lies in Grand Prairie Township, while Lorenzo’s 1870 home was in Webber Township, so the two were not in the same township. The households show that Robert’s sons moved freely across the county line; they do not explain how David P. came to marry a Jefferson County woman.
Names and ages copied from those old Jefferson County pages may have slipped here and there, but the family is plain to see.

stories.title: Carters and Livesays: from Tennessee to the Beaucoup timber
stories.hook: Robert Livesay came to Illinois, the family remembered, with his parents, aunts, uncles and cousins, more than fifty Carters and Livesays in all; who his own parents were is still not certain.

subject.name: Robert and Lydia Livesay’s parents and kin

body: Family tradition gives Robert Livesay’s parents as John and Rebecca (Carter) Livesay. John’s sister Alice, it says, married Rebecca’s brother Robert Carter, both couples in Franklin County, Virginia, in the 1780s; the families moved to Maury County, Tennessee, some time after 1809; and about 1830 more than fifty of them moved on to Washington County, Illinois, with the Carters going first. Lydia, by the same tradition, was the daughter of Edmund Fitzgerald and Sarah “Sally” Dodson, born on 16 October 1807 in Williamson County, Tennessee. None of the Virginia or Tennessee story is yet proved. A small family burial ground called the Edmund Fitzgerald Cemetery lies in Maury County, about nine miles north of Columbia, but who that Edmund was is not known.

The Illinois end of the story is clearer. On 10 December 1823 Livesay Carter and Robert Carter jointly received a federal patent for 160 acres in what is now Clinton County, through the Edwardsville land office, the earliest known for the family in the state. Livesay Carter, a native of Virginia, went to Tennessee in 1807, came to Illinois in 1818, lived about four years in what became Clinton County and then settled near Nashville, as the county’s historians wrote in 1879. Livesay Carter took his first Washington County patent in 1826, and a Carter Livesay his first in 1831. A Lorenza D. Livesay was patented 80 acres in Section 21 of Township 2 South, Range 2 West on 11 November 1831, and John W. Livesay land in Section 31 in 1834. All of it lay in the same township where Robert bought in 1838.

The Livisays and Carters were among the families of the Beaucoup settlement. Livesay Carter and L. D. Livesay were among the first settlers of Nashville precinct, and John Livesay was among the Methodists meeting at Alexander Anderson’s house in 1832. William B. Livesay laid out the town of Richmond, later Richview, on Section 10 in 1839, and J. M. Livesay and L. D. Livesay later laid out an addition to it. Lorenzo D. Livesay served as a private in J. Burns’s company in the Black Hawk War of 1832.

Lorenzo Dow Livesay is remembered among the county’s veterans as a son of “John C. & Rebecca (nee Carter) Livesay.” If that is right, and if Robert too was a son of John and Rebecca, then Lorenzo Dow was Robert’s brother, and William B., remembered as John’s eleventh child, another. But where that parentage came from is not known, and the birth given for Lorenzo, about 1815, is hard to square with a land patent in his name in 1831. In 1855, too, L. D. Livesay’s household held a man aged 50 to 60, which would place his birth between about 1795 and 1805, close to Robert’s own.

For now Robert’s parents, his possible brother Lorenzo Dow and Lydia’s parents are all uncertain. A Rebecca Livesay left estate papers in Washington County, and Robert’s own marriage to Lydia probably took place in Maury County in the early 1820s, since their eldest son was born about 1823 and Lydia in 1807.

stories.title: Old Settlers Cemetery and the 1890s settlers
stories.hook: Floyd Livesay reached Pearland in the town’s first years, when a land campaign was drawing families from the North. The cemetery begun in 1894 is where he and Alice were buried.

subject.name: Floyd and Alice Livesay at Pearland

body: Pearland’s beginnings are told in a few lines on the Texas Historical Commission’s marker at Old Settlers Cemetery, placed in 1988 on Halik Road. Settlement followed the railroad through northern Brazoria County in 1882. The townsite, first known as Mark Belt, was platted in 1894 and named Pearland for its pear orchards, and an advertising campaign praising the farm conditions “brought many settlers to the area in the 1890s.” Storms and freezes discouraged some of them, but many stayed.

Floyd Livesay was one of those 1890s settlers. When he died in 1932 a Houston paper said he had come from Illinois to Pearland about 37 years before, and by 1900 he was in Brazoria County with children born in Illinois and a daughter born in Texas about 1898. He came, then, within a year or two of the townsite’s platting.

The cemetery began with the burial of Echolean C. Ackerly on 11 August 1894, and four years later her plot and the land around it were dedicated as a community burial ground. The first graves were marked in many ways, from earth scraped over the grave to cement paving, gravel and brick, and with stones ranging from plain markers to carved tombstones. It remained Pearland’s main cemetery until 1936.

Three of the Livesays belong to that period. William Paul Livesay, Floyd and Alice’s son, died in San Antonio in 1915 and was brought back to Pearland for burial. Alice died in 1922 and Floyd in 1932, and they lie side by side in Old Settlers Cemetery; Floyd was buried at Pearland on 6 May 1932. When Floyd was buried, the graveyard had four years left as the town’s principal cemetery, and the family’s later burials are elsewhere, at Alvin and in East Texas.
The marker names none of the Livesays, but they were among the settlers it remembers.

stories.title: The James Walker household in 1850
stories.hook: In the summer of 1850 nineteen-year-old William P. Walker was living at Beaucoup in the home of James and Etheldra Walker, a Tennessee-born farmer and his Virginia-born wife.
body: In August 1850 the assistant marshal Gabriel Jones came through District No. 20 of Washington County taking the census, and by 23 August he had reached the Walkers. The head of the house was James Walker, 50, a farmer with real estate worth $1,000, born in Tennessee. With him were Etheldra, 45, born in Virginia; William P., 19, a farmer; Etheldra J., 17; a boy of 10, most likely James H.; a girl of 8 whose name has faded beyond reading; and Sarah E., 5. All five children were born in Illinois.

The ages match the Beaucoup stones closely. Rev. James Walker died in April 1857 aged 57, so he was born in March 1800; the older Etheldra was born in 1804 or 1805; William P. Walker was born on 15 March 1831; and the younger Etheldra J., wife of Simeon Walker, was born on 31 July 1833. No one then wrote down how a household was related, so nothing here proves that William was James and Etheldra’s son. But a William P. of exactly the right age, living in their house the year before his marriage, who later named his eldest daughter Mary Ellen Etheldra, was very probably their son. That daughter, as Mary E. E. Walker, married Andrew J. Scott on 22 November 1871.

So James came from Tennessee and Etheldra from Virginia, which fits the old memory that the first Beaucoup settlers came from Tennessee. Etheldra’s maiden name is still unknown. William’s mother is often called Etheldra Jane Ballard, a name that may blend the two Etheldras. Yet next door, in 1850, lived John Ballard, 36, a farmer whose birthplace the marshal wrote as “unknown,” with Henry, 21, born in Tennessee. Living next door proves nothing about kinship, and the Ballard name is still only a possibility.

Several other Walker households were counted in the same district in 1850. Simeon Walker, 48, headed one with Sally and a son Simeon, 19. George W. Walker, 23, lived with Elizabeth and the baby Frances C. E.; Levi S. Walker, 20, and William H. Walker, 22, lived close by; and John W. Walker, 25, lived with Lavina E. and an infant son. John W. and George W. were born about 1825 and 1827, old enough to have been older sons of James and Etheldra who had already married and left home, but nothing says so. The only brothers and sisters William can be given with confidence are the children still at home: Etheldra J., the boy of 10, the girl of 8 and Sarah E.

Rev. James died in 1857 and Etheldra in 1878, and estates for a James Walker and an “Ethaldra” Walker passed through the county court, very likely theirs. Either may name their heirs, and settle what the census only implies.

stories.title: Was Rev. James Walker a circuit rider?
stories.hook: Family memory made Etheldra Walker’s father a circuit rider, and a James Walker did ride the southern Illinois circuits in the 1830s, but whether he was the Beaucoup preacher is still an open question.
body: Rev. James Walker of Beaucoup was a Methodist preacher and teacher from the early 1820s. In time he owned the “Rock Chimney” farm, ministered to the Richview church and, as a local elder, performed a marriage in 1845. He died in April 1857.

His family remembered more. In 1894 his son-in-law, Captain Simeon Walker, said that his wife, “Miss E. J. Walker,” born in Washington County on 28 July 1834, “was a daughter of Rev. James Walker, who was also a circuit rider of this state.” That birth date is a year and three days later than the 31 July 1833 usually given for Etheldra, but the words are a family’s own memory that her father rode circuit, though they do not say which circuits.

A James Walker did ride the circuits of southern Illinois. At the Illinois Conference of 1831, held at Indianapolis, a James Walker was among eleven men received on trial as traveling preachers, and a James Walker was also among the local preachers elected to deacon’s orders. That year’s appointments in the Kaskaskia District read “Mt. Vernon, James Walker.” He spent the next two years on the Brownsville Mission and 1834 on the Wabash Circuit, and was then elected to elder’s orders and allowed to locate at his own request. Readmitted the next year, he was sent to Fairfield Circuit, and he located again in 1837. Simeon Walker, the other Methodist Walker of the Richview area, followed him on the Mt. Vernon Circuit in 1832.

James B. Leaton, the historian of early Illinois Methodism, remembered this James Walker in 1883 as a man who “was a native of Georgia” and who “for about thirty years labored quite extensively as a local preacher” until his death, “a good Christian man, enjoying the confidence of all.”

Much of this fits Beaucoup. A local preacher and elder named James Walker was active in Washington County in the 1840s, and Mt. Vernon, in Jefferson County, lies just east of Washington County. But two details do not fit. In 1850 the Beaucoup James Walker’s birthplace was given as Tennessee, not Georgia. And thirty years of local preaching after 1837 would run to about 1867, ten years after Rev. James of Beaucoup died. Leaton’s round number may be loose, or the circuit rider may have been another James Walker; it was a common name.

So whether Rev. James of Beaucoup was the circuit rider is still unknown. Family memory says he rode circuit; the Georgia birth and the long years of local preaching say it may have been another man of the same name.

stories.title: The camp ground at Beaucoup
stories.hook: Before there was a church building in most of the county, the Methodists of Beaucoup had a log meeting house and a camp ground. The Walkers preached there and the Livesays sat in the congregations.
body: In 1879 the Rev. L. F. Cullom, then the pastor at Nashville, set down the story of early Methodism in Washington County. About 1819, he wrote, Daniel and Joseph Whittenburg, John Phillips, George Lowe and their families came from East Tennessee and settled near Beaucoup. Daniel Whittenburg, a local minister of the Methodist Episcopal Church, organized the first society of that church in the county, and the settlers set apart the ground where the Beaucoup church still stood in 1879 for both a church and a camp ground. The first building was of logs. Cullom called Beaucoup the “headquarters of Methodism in this part of Illinois,” and said its yearly camp meetings drew people from forty and fifty miles away.

Whittenberg and Rhodum Allen served the Methodists at Beaucoup as early as 1820, and Revs. Horatio Burns, Lewis Pate and James Walker came soon afterwards. Among the men who served the Richview church as pastors or local preachers were Rev. Simeon Walker, Rev. James Walker and Rev. Levi S. Walker. That church began in Samuel White’s home and built its first church house in old Richview in 1842; among its first members were the families of Thomas Livesay and William Livesay. George Lowe told Cullom that in 1832 there was a society at Alex Anderson’s home whose members included John Livesay. Until 1852 these societies belonged to the Illinois Conference; from that year they were under the new Southern Illinois Conference.

Later memories agree. Dr. John Thomas Foster (1841–1927) recalled camp meetings at Mt. Zion, Beaucoup, Liberty and Locust Creek, where families brought food for themselves and for strangers, and named Simeon Walker as a well-known local preacher who was “frequently at our home”. In 1968, at the county’s sesquicentennial, it was remembered that at Beaucoup “the Methodists predominated,” while the Baptists led at Elkton, and Walker and Livesay were counted among the old Beaucoup family names.

For this family, the camp ground was the center of the neighborhood. Rev. James Walker preached and taught there, the cemetery beside it holds his stone and those of his wife, his probable son William P. and his probable daughter Etheldra J., and the Livesays who later married into the Walker family worshiped in the same circuit. Cullom admitted that he had come to the county only a few months earlier and had gathered his facts by “careful gleaning,” so his dates are best taken as approximate.

stories.title: Etheldra J. Walker and Captain Simeon
stories.hook: William P. Walker’s probable sister married a son of the other Methodist Walker family. Her husband was the captain of William’s company in the Civil War, and the stones at Beaucoup keep the names of their small sons.
body: In August 1850 Etheldra J. Walker, 17, was living with James and Etheldra Walker and William P., 19. Three weeks later the census taker reached the home of Simeon Walker, 48, with Sally, 54, and children including Simeon, 19. A Simeon Walker had married Sally Whittenburg on 11 August 1846, and on 15 September 1852 Simeon Walker Jr. married Etheldra Jane Walker. Etheldra J. Walker lies at Beaucoup, born 31 July 1833, died 29 April 1903, wife of Simeon, and with her Simeon Walker, born 3 March 1831, died 11 October 1909, though he is also said to have died on 29 April 1905. That 29 April is the day and month of Etheldra J.’s own death, in 1903, which may be a coincidence or a copying slip.

The couple buried several young children at Beaucoup: James H. (12 June 1855 to 21 August 1856), Simon G. (28 July 1857 to 1 January 1858) and Elmer D. (4 January 1861 to July 1862), each “son of S. & E.,” and on the same stone Wilbert F. (6 October 1853 to 9 August 1854) and Harry E. (11 February to 11 March 1869). The name James H. repeats the name of Etheldra’s father, and probably of the brother aged 10 in the 1850 household.

Simeon and Etheldra’s family was bound up with William P. Walker’s. Simeon was captain of Company C, 60th Illinois Infantry, from December 1862, so he commanded the company that William joined in March 1864. If Etheldra was William’s sister, as the 1850 household suggests, the captain was also his brother-in-law. On 12 January 1860, at Hoyleton, Simeon Walker of Richview borrowed $56, with J. W. Walker and G. W. Walker as his securities.

Simeon came from the other Methodist Walker family. Levi Sharpe Walker was born in Clinton County on 14 September 1829, the son of Simeon and Elizabeth Sharpe Walker, and his father was an itinerant Methodist preacher, as the Southern Illinois Conference remembered when Levi died. Levi was licensed to preach at Richview in 1856, served three years as chaplain of the 60th Illinois, William’s regiment, and died on 6 April 1921; he was buried at Richview. The father, Simeon Walker Sr., was born in Jackson County, Georgia, in 1802, as the historian Leaton wrote in 1883. That Captain Simeon was his son rests on the “Jr.” at his wedding and on the 1850 household, which does not say how its members were related, so his father is not certain. Simeon and Simeon Jr. each left an estate in the county.

stories.title: Lieutenant George W. Walker of Beaucoup
stories.hook: The Beaucoup Walker who led men to Mexico in 1847 lived beside the Livesays in 1850, and his daughter later married one. Whether he was Rev. James Walker’s son is the open question.
body: In July 1847 a company raised in Washington County left Nashville, marched to Alton and was mustered in on 18 July as Company H, 2nd Regiment of Illinois Foot Volunteers, for the war with Mexico. Its officers included Captain James Burns and Second Lieutenant George W. Walker, as the county remembered them in 1879. Its privates included three Livesays, Carter A., Alfred and John C., and four Walkers, Thomas, John Sen., John Jun. and Ezekiel. The company landed at Vera Cruz on 31 August 1847, skirmished at San Juan on 18 September, wintered at Jalapa, moved to Puebla and was discharged at Alton on 22 July 1848. Ezekiel Walker died at Vera Cruz on 10 September 1847.

George W. Walker married Elizabeth Walker on 21 December 1848. In early September 1850 he was 23, a farmer with land worth $400, living with Elizabeth, 21, and Frances C. E., aged 8 months, all born in Illinois. Frances was born on 19 September 1849, which fits a December 1848 marriage though not quite her age of 8 months in early September 1850. In the next two houses lived Lorenzo M. Livesay, 25, and William C. Livesay, 26, both born in Tennessee; William’s household included Jackson L., 4, the same name as the Jackson L. Livesay who later served with William P. Walker in Company C.

Frances C. E. Walker married Charles M. Livesay and died on 18 February 1874; her sister Eudora B. A. died as a child in 1854. Rev. George Walker died at his home near Beaucoup on 20 October 1902, the Nashville Journal reported that October, having lived on the farm for fifty-four years. He was a Mexican War veteran, and three children survived him: Mrs. A. B. Stephens, D. A. Walker and J. E. Walker. The paper gave his marriage to Elizabeth Walker as December 1828, which cannot be right for a man born about 1826 and is probably a garbled date. Elizabeth Walker died in Beaucoup Township on 11 February 1920, which fits his widow’s stone (1829–1920). His estate, with an administrator’s bond for G. W. Walker, went through the county court.

George W. Walker was born about 1826 or 1827 in Illinois, close to the Beaucoup settlement, and in 1860 he stood security for Simeon Walker together with J. W. Walker. He may have been an older son of Rev. James and Etheldra who had married and left home by 1850, but who his parents were is not known. For now he belongs to the Walker and Livesay story as a neighbor and in-law rather than a proven kinsman.

stories.title: James T. McCormack, teamster, Anderson, 1893
stories.hook: In the year Sadah was born, a James T. McCormack was driving a team in Anderson, Indiana, and he was probably her father.

subject.name: James T. McCormack
subject.rel: Probable father of Sadah McCormick Livesay

body: In 1893 and 1894 James T. McCormack was a teamster in Anderson, Indiana, driving for a firm known only as the A S P Co, and his house stood at the corner of Vine and First streets: “McCormack James T, teamster, A S P Co, h. cor Vine and 1st,” as Knight & Co.’s city directory for Anderson and Madison County put it. What his employer’s initials stood for is not known.

His time and place matter. Sadah Livesay Vaughan was born on 13 August 1893 in Anderson, Indiana, the daughter of J. T. McCormack, as was said at her death in 1978. Seven years later, in 1900, a James McCormack had a daughter Sadie born in August 1893, and in 1910 the head of the same household was Jay T. James T. McCormack of Anderson joins the “James” and the “J. T.” in one man, in the very years of Sadah’s birth. Why he was “Jay T.” in 1910, and what the T stood for, is not known.

Two families of the name lived in Anderson then, and they are easy to confuse. Edward McCormack, a file worker, and Louise A. McCormack both lived at 53 East Lynne, and a McCormick household at 237 South Central Avenue held Elizabeth, a widow, with James and Susan. That Central Avenue family was already in Anderson in 1891, with a James McCormick working at Kilgore’s factory and Mrs. Lizzie McCormick, widow of John, but there was no James T. McCormack in town then, so the teamster arrived between 1891 and 1893–4. Whether Edward or Louise were his relatives is not known.

By June 1900 James and Frances McCormack were farming in Stony Creek Township, on the western edge of Madison County. The teamster of Anderson was probably Sadah’s father, for name, initial, town and date all agree, but it is not proven, and nothing from 1893 names a wife or children, so who her parents were is still not certain.

stories.title: From a Stony Creek farm to a Brazoria fruit farm
stories.hook: Between 1900 and 1910 the McCormacks left a mortgaged Indiana farm for a fruit farm of their own in Brazoria County, Texas, the county next to the one where Sadah married.

subject.name: The McCormack family
subject.rel: Probable family of Sadah McCormick Livesay

body: In June 1900 the McCormacks were farming in Stony Creek Township, Madison County, Indiana. James McCormack was a farmer born in June 1863 in Indiana; his father was born in West Virginia and his mother in Indiana. His wife Frances was born in January 1862 in Indiana, as were both her parents. They had been married seventeen years, and Frances had borne seven children, five of whom were living. The farm was their own but mortgaged. Cleveland, fifteen, was working as a farm hand; Hazel, Sadie, Pernell and Dewey were at home.

Stony Creek Township lies on the western edge of Madison County, along the Hamilton County line. It covered twenty-eight square miles, part of them once a heavily timbered tract called the “Dismal,” which by 1914 had long since been cleared and drained into some of the most productive farms in the county. Lapel and Fishersburg were its only towns, and the Central Indiana railroad ran through it.

Ten years later the family was in Texas. In April 1910, in Justice Precinct 5, Brazoria County, Jay T. McCormick, 41, and Frances, 40, were living with Clevand, 25, Hazel, 20, Sadie, 17, Purnell, 14, Dewey, 9, and William, 7. Everyone was born in Indiana. Jay T. was a fruit farmer working on his own account, and the farm was owned free of mortgage. Cleveland worked on the home farm. Hazel and Sadie were both out at work as housekeepers for private families. The neighbors were fruit farmers too, among them a family whose parents were Holland Dutch.

William, born in Indiana and seven years old in April 1910, was the new child since 1900. Frances now counted eight children, six living, which agrees with one more birth. His Indiana birth means the family was still in Indiana in about 1902 or 1903, so the move to Texas came between then and 1910. The two counts also disagree. James aged five years in the decade, Frances only two. The marriage had lasted seventeen years in 1900 but twenty-five in 1910. Dewey, born in November 1898 by the first count, was only nine in the second. And the father’s birthplace, West Virginia in 1900, became Indiana in 1910. None of these differences can yet be explained.

Sadie was seventeen and working in a Brazoria County household in April 1910. Eighteen months later, on 10 October 1911, Lester W. Livesay and Sadah H. McCormick married in neighboring Harris County, with a note that a mother’s consent was on file. Sadah was born in Anderson in August 1893, the daughter of J. T. McCormack, as was said at her death: the month and year of Sadie’s birth in both censuses. Everything fits closely, so James T. and Frances McCormack were probably Sadah’s parents. But apart from that “J. T. McCormack” at her death, no one is known to have named her parents, and Frances’s maiden name is still unknown.

Their link to Sadah is not entered in the tree; it remains a strong but unproven identification of Sadie with Sadah. James McCormack was not found in the pages of the 1880 Stony Creek Township census that were read; his parents and Frances’s maiden name are still unknown.

stories.title: Clinton Whitfield in Sevier County, Arkansas, 1900
stories.hook: A six-year-old named Clinton, born in July 1893, turns up in a Sevier County household headed by W. F. and Emma Whitfield.

subject.name: W. F. and Emma Whitfield
subject.rel: Probable parents of Oliver Clinton Whitfield

body: Clint Whitfield’s parents are remembered as William Franklin “Frank” Whitfield and Emma Ward Whitfield, and his birthplace as Chapel Hill, Sevier County, Arkansas. In 1900, in Monroe Township, Sevier County, a W. F. Whitfield was living with his wife Emma and four children, the first of them a son named Clinton.

W. F. Whitfield, white, was born in January 1868 in Mississippi and was 32. He had been married eight years. His mother was born in Mississippi; his father’s birthplace was set down as “unknown.” Emma, his wife, was born in November 1874 in Arkansas and was 25. She was the mother of four children, and all four were living. Her parents’ birthplaces were also unknown.

The children were Clinton, a son, born in July 1893 and six years old; Willie G., a daughter, born in March 1895; Robbie W., a son, born in February 1897; and Fannie I., a daughter, born in October 1898. All four were born in Arkansas. The last line of the household is a boarder surnamed Ward, a farm laborer born in August 1871 in Arkansas to parents born in Texas. His given name is hard to read.

Clint Whitfield’s gravestone at Glover gives his birth as 27 July 1893, and the Clinton of 1900 was born in July 1893. The man went by Clint, and the boy was simply Clinton. The parents’ initials and Emma’s name and birth year fit what the family remembered, and a Ward living in the house fits Emma’s being born a Ward, though he is called only a boarder. Taken together these make it probable that this was Oliver Clinton Whitfield’s family, and that Willie, Robbie and Fannie were his younger brother and sisters.

It is not yet proof. Nothing gives the boy the first name Oliver, and nothing from his 1915 marriage or his death in 1941 yet names his parents outright. So W. F. and Emma were probably, but not certainly, Clint’s parents. No community was named that year, so the Chapel Hill birthplace, too, is still unproved.

Emma outlived Frank by more than ten years. She spent thirty-seven or thirty-eight years at Golden and Idabel, and about 1948 she moved to Longview, Washington, where she died at home at the end of March 1955, aged eighty. She had been born at Chapel Hill, Arkansas, on 8 November 1874, and she belonged to the Church of Christ. She was buried in Longview Memorial Park, and one son, Jeff, and six daughters survived her.

stories.title: Alonzo and Emma Box in Van Zandt County, June 1900
stories.hook: In June 1900 Alonzo and Emma Box were farming in Van Zandt County, Texas, with five children at home; Emma had borne eight, and the family’s roots ran back to four different states.
body: On 8 June 1900 the census taker for Justice Precinct No. 6 of Van Zandt County, Texas, reached the household of Alonzo Box, where twelve-year-old Tyro was living with his parents.

Alonzo was born in December 1850 in Arkansas and was 49. His father was born in Alabama and his mother in Mississippi. He was a farmer and owned his farm, which carried a mortgage. Emma, his wife, was born in July 1860 in Mississippi and was 39. Her father was born in Virginia and her mother in Mississippi. They had been married 23 years, which places the wedding about 1877, when Emma was about sixteen or seventeen. She was the mother of eight children, six of them living.

Five children were at home, all born in Texas: Walter, born March 1885, and Tyro, born May 1888, both working as farm laborers; Claudy J., born August 1891; Flossie B., born August 1894; and Archie W., born November 1896. A boarder, Charlie, a married farm laborer of 25, completed the household; his surname is hard to read. Archie’s birth year has sometimes been copied as 1894, but it was written 1896. With six living children and five at home, one living child was elsewhere, and two had died.

Alonzo’s parents came from Alabama and Mississippi, and Emma’s father from Virginia. Emma’s maiden name is not known; a family note calls her Emillie Wilkerson, and Texas birth entries for two of her children, Claude in 1891 and Flossie in 1894, give their mother as Emily Wilkerson. Where Alonzo and Emma were in 1880 is not known either; they may have been counted under another form of his name.

Van Zandt County was growing fast. Its population reached 25,000 by 1900, and the number of farms rose from 2,345 in 1890 to 4,208 in 1900. Canton was the county seat. Within a few years Annie Logan came north from Mount Pleasant to McCurtain County, and by 1942 Tyro, Claude and Archie were all living around Millerton and Valliant. Flossie is buried at Wheelock.

stories.title: Tyro Box registers at Millerton, April 1942
stories.hook: At 53, Violet’s father filled in a draft card, giving yet another birthplace for himself and a clear picture of the man.
body: In April 1942 the Selective Service held its fourth registration, for men born between 28 April 1877 and 16 February 1897, too old for the earlier calls. Tyro Box registered with McCurtain County’s Local Board No. 1 on 25 April 1942, before the registrar Howard Pratt at Valliant.

He gave his name as Tyro Steven Box, his home and mailing address as Millerton, McCurtain County, and his age as 53. He was born on 22 May 1888, the same day remembered at his death in 1967. For his birthplace he wrote Rockwall County, Texas. The person who would always know his address was Mrs. T. S. Box of Millerton, and he named no employer. He signed it Tyro S. Box. The registrar described him as a white man about 5 feet 9 inches tall and 182 pounds, with gray eyes, gray hair and a light complexion.

That was yet another birthplace. At his death he was said to have been born at Pittsburg, Texas; in 1930 his birthplace was given as Oklahoma, and in 1900 only as Texas. Rockwall County was formed in 1873 from part of Kaufman County, where his brother Claude said he was born. Tyro’s own word carries the most weight, but which birthplace is right is still uncertain.

Eight years later the census taker found him at home. In April 1950 Tyro S. Box, 61, and Annie F. Box, 63, both born in Texas, were living in Kirk Township, McCurtain County, along the Wheelock Community school bus route. Their daughter Violet and her husband kept a store near Golden at the same time.

stories.title: Claude and Archie Box: two brothers at Valliant
stories.hook: Two of Tyro’s younger brothers farmed around Valliant, and their own 1942 cards tie them back to the Van Zandt County household.

subject.name: Claude Joel and Archie W. Box

body: In 1900 two younger sons of Alonzo and Emma Box were at home in Van Zandt County: Claudy J., born in August 1891, and Archie W., born in November 1896. Forty-two years later, in the same Oklahoma registration that caught their brother Tyro, two Box men at Valliant filled in draft cards that fit them.

Claude Joel Box, 50, of Valliant gave his birth as 26 August 1892 at Kaufman, Texas, which the registrar spelled Coffman. He worked for himself, and his contact was Mrs. C. J. Box of Valliant. Archie W. Box, 45, also of Valliant, gave 11 April 1896 and Van Zandt County, Texas, written Vanzant. He farmed for himself, and his contact was Mrs. Erma Box. Each man fits one of the boys of 1900 in name, middle initial and county of origin, though each gave a different year or month of birth. When Tyro died in 1967 he left a brother, Arch Box, which fits Archie.

In 1950 Archie W. Box, 53, born in Texas, and his wife Erma L., 45, born in Oklahoma, were living in Kirk Township, McCurtain County, near Tyro and Annie. The younger members of their household, who may be living, go unnamed.

Valliant itself was a young town. Its townsite was surveyed in 1902 for the Arkansas and Choctaw Railroad and named for the railroad official Frank W. Valliant. Its economy rested on farming, with cotton first, and by the early 1920s it had two banks and nineteen other businesses.

Other Box men registered in McCurtain County that April: Terrell Inge Box of Valliant, born 20 December 1896 at Canton, Texas, the Van Zandt county seat; Andrew Clarence Box of Broken Bow; and Ernest Box of Goodwater. Terrell came from the same county, but he cannot have been a full brother of Archie if both men’s birth dates are right, and he is not in Alonzo’s 1900 household. How, or whether, these men were related to Tyro is not known.

stories.title: Birdie Box James of Wheelock
stories.hook: Tyro’s little sister Flossie Belle was widowed at 33 and lived another half century; she lies at Wheelock, where Violet and Annie are buried.
body: In 1900, in Van Zandt County, Flossie B. Box was five, the only daughter at home with Alonzo and Emma Box. She was born in August 1894 in Texas, between her brothers Claudy and Archie.

At Wheelock Cemetery she lies as Flossie Belle “Birdie” Box James, born 4 August 1894 and died 14 November 1979. Beside her is her husband, Raphael B. “Rafe” James, born 20 February 1893 and died 5 January 1928. When he died, Birdie was 33. She outlived him by nearly 52 years.

When Tyro Box died in 1967, his sister Mrs. Byrd James survived him. Byrd was probably her nickname Birdie, and with the girl of 1900 and the birth day on her stone, she was very probably Tyro’s sister. She is buried in the same Wheelock Cemetery as her sister-in-law Annie and her niece Violet.

One family account puts Birdie's birth not in Van Zandt County but at Mount Pleasant, in Titus County, Texas, the town where Dudley Logan's family had settled, and says she died at Idabel. The same account has Rafe born in the Indian Territory on 20 February 1893 and dying at Millerton, near Wheelock, on 5 January 1928, at thirty-four. Their daughter, Florence Madeline James, later Fowler, was born in 1914 and lived until 1996, so Birdie had married Rafe by about 1913 and was left a widow with a girl of thirteen. Where the Boxes were living in 1894, and whether the Mount Pleasant birthplace is right, the 1900 Van Zandt County household alone cannot settle.

stories.title: Other Whitfields in McCurtain County
stories.hook: A Sevier County-born Whitfield farmed at Valliant in 1942, and an Arkansas-born J. D. Whitfield lived in the county in 1950. Neither is yet tied to Clint.
body: Clint Whitfield’s family probably came from Sevier County, Arkansas, and other Whitfields lived near him in Oklahoma who may have been his kin. Two Whitfield men of McCurtain County, born between 1877 and February 1897, registered for the draft in 1942.

John Grover Whitfield, 53, farmed for himself at Valliant. He gave his birth as 6 July 1888 in Sevier County, Arkansas, written “Sever Co.,” and his contact as Ida Whitfield of Valliant. He was born in the same county as Clint, but four years before W. F. and Emma Whitfield married, when Emma was thirteen, so he was not her son. Whether he belonged to W. F.’s family some other way is unknown. The other man, William McKinley Whitfield, gave McCurtain County with a Route 2, Arkinda, Arkansas, mailing address; he was born in 1897 at New Boston, Texas, and shows no tie to Sevier County.
Clint’s probable brother Robbie, born in February 1897, right at the edge of the age range, is missing from that registration; he may have been born too late, or lived elsewhere.

In 1950 a J. D. Whitfield, 46, born in Arkansas, was living in McCurtain County with his wife Bessie, born in Texas, and two daughters. He was born about 1903 or 1904, after 1900, so he could have been a younger child of W. F. and Emma, but nothing yet connects them.

stories.title: Peter and Ellen Durant of Bok Tuklo
stories.hook: When the Merrys applied to the Dawes Commission in April 1899, they named Bessie’s parents, Peter and Ellen Durant of Bok Tuklo, both by then dead.
body: On 26 April 1899 the Merry family applied to the Dawes Commission, giving their residence as the Choctaw Nation and their post office as Glover, I.T., and their case was entered on the Choctaw Roll as field number 5754. The card made out that day lists three people: Louis Merry, 27, an intermarried white man; Bessie, his wife, 19, three-quarters Choctaw; and Ida May, their daughter, one year old, three-eighths. By the final rolls Louis was 30. Bessie and Ida May were enrolled as Choctaws by blood, on rolls 15526 and 15527, and Louis as an intermarried white citizen on roll 1363. Their enrollment belongs to history and says nothing about anyone’s present status. Behind the card lay a forty-page application, with sworn statements from the family and their neighbors.

The card answers the question of Bessie’s family. Her father was Peter Durant and her mother Ellen Durant. Both were dead, and both were of Bok Tuklo, one of the Choctaw Nation’s counties. Louis’s parents were Calvin Merry and Elizabeth Merry, both dead and both “non-citiz,” that is, not Choctaw citizens. For Ida May the clerk simply wrote “No 1” and “No 2,” pointing back to her parents on the lines above.

Clerks’ notes down the middle of the card tell more of the family’s story. Louis had been on the 1896 Choctaw roll as Lewis Merry and Bessie as “Betsy,” both in Eagle County, numbers 14822 and 8644. Ida’s proof of birth was filed on 9 May 1899; the day of birth in the clerk’s note may be June 12 or June 17, 1898, while the family’s affidavits give the twelfth. The family’s case had first been carried as D 128, and was transferred to card 5754 on 21 March 1904. The Secretary of the Interior approved Bessie’s and Ida’s enrollment on 9 May 1904 and Louis’s on 14 March 1905. On 2 April 1904 letters from Principal Chief Green McCurtain and the Choctaw auditor Peter J. Hudson about 1893 leased district money for Bessie were filed with her case.

Without the card, the name alone could never have told who Bessie’s parents were. Ida remembered her mother as a Durant, but Durant was a large Choctaw family name, with many on the rolls. The Commission took applications from 1898 through 1907, with a handful in 1914, and the final rolls were approved on or before 4 March 1907.

Louis’s parents, Calvin and Elizabeth Merry, were very probably the Calvin Merry and Eliza Jane McGregor who married at Mount Ida in 1859 and in 1880 had a boy named Joshua L., eight years old, on their farm in Monroe Township, Sevier County, Arkansas; the card gives no middle name, maiden name or place, so the link is probable, not proved. Bessie’s parents are certain: Peter and Ellen Durant. She had a brother, Ben, and the family belonged to the Bok Tuklo household of a woman named Wilsey Clay.

stories.title: A wedding at Lukfata, 7 September 1896
stories.hook: Louis Merry paid the Choctaw Nation one hundred dollars for the right to marry Bessie Durant. The license burned, but the certificate survived in the Commission’s files.
body: Louis Merry of Lukfata, I.T., and Bessie Durant of Lukfata were joined in marriage at Lukfata on 7 September 1896, “according to the ordinances of God and the laws of the Choctaw Nation.” Rev. J. H. Sleeper married them, with J. W. Costelow and Chas. J. Gaffney as witnesses. A handwritten copy of their certificate was kept in the family’s Dawes file, the Commission’s decision of 10 January 1905 gives the same date, and a letter of 18 January 1908 returned the license and certificate to them.

A white man who wished to marry a Choctaw woman and gain rights in the Nation had to do it under Choctaw law, and the Merry case shows what that meant in practice. R. W. Thomas, a Choctaw by blood living at Lukfata, swore in August 1904 that he was clerk of Bok Tuklo County until 1 October 1896, that Louis Merry applied to him in September 1896 with a petition in proper form signed by ten Choctaws by blood, that he gave Louis the oath of allegiance to the Choctaw Nation, and that he took the regular fee of one hundred dollars and issued him a license to marry Bessie Durant. Louis himself testified in 1902 that he paid one hundred dollars and that Sleeper was a missionary.

The license did not last. At Atoka on 7 December 1900, Louis, giving his name as Lewis and his age as 28, told the Commission that he lived at Lukfata and had lived in that country about eight years, that the license had been shown to Commissioner Ben Watkins when he was put on the 1896 roll, and that it burned in December 1897 when “the house and all its contents were burned.” Ben Watkins, seventy years old, confirmed in a separate statement that he had seen the license and enrolled Louis in 1896.

The two clerks did not agree on one point. Joe A. James, who succeeded Thomas as county clerk on 1 October 1896, testified in November 1902 that he had recorded the license and certificate and handed them back to Louis. In his own affidavit of August 1904 he said he could not now be certain but did not think he had recorded them. Thomas swore that it was not the custom in that county to record marriage licenses at that time. Either way, the Commission accepted the marriage, and the copied certificate is the surest witness to the day.

stories.title: Louis Merry against the Choctaw Nation, 1900–1905
stories.hook: The Choctaw Nation contested Louis Merry’s claim. It took five years, three hearings and a threatened farm before he was enrolled.
body: In August 1900 the Commission wrote to Louis Merry at Lukfata that the Choctaw Nation, through its attorneys, had filed a protest against the enrollment of Louis, Bessie and Ida May Merry. The case was heard at Atoka in December 1900 as Choctaw D 128, with Melvin Cornish appearing for the Nation and J. G. Ralls for the family. Louis testified about the marriage and the burned license, and John M. Hodges testified about Bessie’s father, Peter Durant. The family’s lawyer asked for a copy of the evidence in January 1901.

The case moved slowly. Notices of February and March 1902 called it for final consideration at Muskogee on 4 April 1902, when it was submitted on the record. That year the Commission wrote to J. L. Merry at Glover, and its letter of 27 March 1902 spoke of “yourself and your wife, Bessie Merry and your child, Ida May Merry,” so J. L. Merry of Glover and Louis Merry of card 5754 were very probably one and the same. In November 1902 Louis, now 30 and living at Glover, testified again at Garvin. He said he had lived in the Nation ten years and claimed rights through his wife Bessie Durant, a “full blood Choctaw” in his words, though the Commission enrolled her as three-quarters Choctaw. He admitted that they had separated on 18 June 1902 and that she came back about a month later.

By 1904 the delay was costing him. On 30 September 1904 the Commission acknowledged his letter reporting that on 5 April 1904 a man named Hopper Watkins had filed on his farm in Section 4, Township 6 South, Range 23 East, and that he did not want to lose it. Affidavits from the two Bok Tuklo clerks were filed that August. On 10 January 1905 the Commission ruled in his favor: he had married Bessie under Choctaw law on 7 September 1896, both were residents in good faith, they had lived together except for about a month in 1902, and he was on the 1896 roll in Eagle County as number 14822. The Secretary of the Interior approved his enrollment on 14 March 1905.

Of the later parting, and of his later marriages, nothing was said. But for five years he wrote persistently, by letter and through lawyers, for the citizenship that would let him keep his land, and from 1901 serving as Glover’s postmaster under the name Joshua L. Merry.

stories.title: Ben Durant, Bessie’s brother
stories.hook: Ben Durant, like his sister Bessie, was a child of Peter and Ellen Durant of Bok Tuklo, and he died at twenty.
body: Bessie had a brother. On 21 April 1899, five days before the Merrys applied, Wilsey Clay applied for her household at Red River post office in Bok Tuklo County, and on her card, number 655, the third name is Ben Durant, her grandson, 18, three-quarters Choctaw. His father was Peter Durant and his mother Ellen Durant, both dead, both of Bok Tuklo, exactly like Bessie’s parents on card 5754.

Ben had been on the 1896 roll twice, in Blue County as number 3569 and, as Benj. Durant, in Bok Tuklo County as number 3404. He did not live to be enrolled. He died on 28 September 1901, proof of his death was filed on 25 March 1902, and in 1905 his name was struck from the card with the stamp “DEAD.” His blood degree was Bessie’s three-quarters, and his age, a year younger than hers in 1899, fits a brother.

At Atoka on 7 December 1900, during the Merry case, an old neighbor remembered these two children. John M. Hodges, aged fifty and a Choctaw by blood, said that he knew Peter Durant, that Peter “had two little kids” when he left that part of the country in 1877 or 1878, a girl and a boy, not yet named that he recalled, and that the children “showed the Choctaw blood.” The county he named was taken down as “Matoon County,” a name that matches no known Choctaw county. He thought Peter was “about a quarteroon” and his wife about half Choctaw.

Hodges’ guesses at their blood do not fit neatly, and his dates would put the girl’s birth by about 1877, a little earlier than Bessie’s own ages suggest. Still, a girl and a boy, with parents named Peter and Ellen, sounds like Bessie and Ben. No one in those years called them brother and sister in so many words, but with the same parents on two cards, they very probably were.

stories.title: Wilsey Clay’s household at Bok Tuklo
stories.hook: Bessie’s grandmother was a full-blood Choctaw woman whose children carried three surnames: Clay, Gavner and Durant. The Dawes cards and one witness’s answers let her family be put together.
body: Wilsey Clay applied for enrollment on 21 April 1899, when she was 58. On card 655 she was entered as full blood, of Bok Tuklo County, with Red River as her post office, on the 1896 roll as number 2573. Her parents are given as Joe Cahn and Patsey Cahn, both dead, of Eagle County, the county along the Arkansas line where Louis Merry was enrolled in 1896. With her on the card were her daughter Ida, 18, whose father was Charles Gavner, a non-citizen, and two grandchildren, Ben Durant, son of Peter and Ellen Durant, and Licey Durant, 14, daughter of Thomas and Melinda Durant.

Two neighboring cards fill in the family. Card 656, made the same day, is the household of William A. Durant, whose wife Laura, 19, had been on the 1896 roll as Laura Clay; her parents are Charles Gavener and Wilsey Clay. Card 507, made on 18 April 1899, belongs to Abner H. Clay, 27, of Lukfata, three-quarters Choctaw, son of Henry Clay, dead, and Wilsey Clay. Lukfata is where Louis and Bessie were married in 1896.

What tied Wilsey to Bessie came out at the Merry hearing. At Atoka in December 1900, after John M. Hodges described Peter Durant, the Choctaw commissioner Judge Lewis asked whether that woman was the mother of Abner Clay. Hodges answered that “Peter Durant was the son of Woolsey Clay,” and agreed that Abner was a half brother to Peter. His words came out a little tangled, but with Abner’s card, 507, they make Wilsey the mother of both men, and with her own card, 655, they explain why Peter’s son Ben was living in her household as her grandson.

So Wilsey Clay was very probably Bessie Merry’s paternal grandmother, and Joe and Patsey Cahn her great-grandparents, as far back as the line now reaches. That rests on one witness’s sworn answers, borne out by the cards. Peter’s own father is never named. Wilsey was alive when her enrollment was approved on 12 December 1902, and still living in May 1906, when she gave sworn testimony at Lukfata. Her ages do not quite agree: 58 in April 1899 means a birth about 1841, and 67 in May 1906 about 1839.

stories.title: The 1893 money: Bessie and her cousin Lizzie
stories.hook: In 1902 J. L. Merry wrote to the Choctaw chief about money still owed to two young Durants. The answer came as two warrants of $143.16.
body: Two letters about the 1893 leased district money, from Green McCurtain and Peter J. Hudson, found their way into the family’s case. On 17 December 1902 Green McCurtain, Principal Chief of the Choctaw Nation, wrote from Tushkahomma to “Mr J. S. Merry,” Glover, that he had passed on Merry’s letter about the amount due “Ben and Lizzie Durant, in the money paid in 1893,” to the national treasurer, George W. Scott, at Sans Bois. Ben Durant had died fourteen months earlier.

On 27 March 1903 Peter J. Hudson, auditor of the Choctaw Nation, wrote from Tushkahomma to “Mr. J. L. Merry, Glover, I.T.,” as “Dear Friend,” enclosing two warrants: number 44 for Bessie Merry and number 45 for Liza Durant, each for $143.16 from the leased district fund, $286.32 in all. Each was a pro rata share of $103.00 with four percent interest from 10 June 1893 to 10 March 1903. Merry sent both letters to the Commission, which filed them on 2 April 1904 with his own application.

Who was Liza or Lizzie? She was probably the Licey Durant of Wilsey Clay’s household, daughter of Thomas and Melinda Durant, who was also enrolled as Lizzie Durant on card 966. On 27 April 1899, the same day Bessie swore to Ida’s birth, Lizzie was at Wheelock Seminary, full blood, the daughter of Thomas Durant of Bok Tuklo, and by 8 December 1902 her post office was Glover. By then she was the wife of Fred Gibbs, a non-citizen, with a son born on 30 August 1902.

So in the winter of 1902 a granddaughter of Wilsey Clay was getting her mail at Glover, and her share of the 1893 money was collected through J. L. Merry alongside Bessie’s. That makes Lizzie close kin, probably Bessie’s first cousin. Wilsey Clay herself, sworn at Lukfata on 9 May 1906, answered “Yes” when asked whether she was the mother of Thomas Durant, Lizzie’s father. Lizzie was Bessie’s cousin only if Peter Durant was Wilsey’s son too, as John M. Hodges said in 1900. And to the Choctaw officials who knew him personally, the man the Commission called Louis was J. L.

Lizzie, her husband and son are not added to the tree.

stories.title: A Logan and a Wedgeworth in Greene County, 1850
stories.hook: In 1850, in Greene County, Alabama, three-year-old Dudley Logan lived among his Logan kin, nine doors from a nine-year-old Sarah A. E. Wedgeworth who, it now seems, was not the girl he married.
body: Dudley Timothy Logan came to Titus County, Texas, from Greene County, Alabama, it is said, and his wife’s full name is remembered as Sarah Anne Elizabeth Wedgeworth. In 1850 both names turn up on the same stretch of road in Greene County. Stephen Wedgeworth, 41, a farmer born in North Carolina, lived with Nancy M., 31, and Sarah A. E., 9, both born in Alabama. Nine doors along lived Clement Logan, 33, a farmer born in South Carolina, with Mary A., 28, Elizabeth H., 8, Dudley, 3, and Martha, six months.

Other Logans live in between. Martha Logan, 71, born in South Carolina, heads dwelling 1120, two doors before the Wedgeworths, and Elizabeth Logan, 30, with four children, dwelling 1124. Leroy Logan, 49, and Willis Logan, 44, both born in South Carolina, are on either side of Clement. It looks like a cluster of related Logan households, and a Wedgeworth family among them.

The fit is not perfect. No one then wrote down how a household was related, so Clement and Mary A. are not proved to be Dudley’s parents, and his parents are also remembered as James Clement Logan and Martha Calhoun. A child born in January 1846 should have been four in June 1850, not three. The initials Sarah A. E. match Annie’s full name exactly, but at nine in 1850 she was born about 1841, five years before the 1846 usually given for her. Until something ties these children to the couple who went to Texas, they may or may not be Dudley and Annie.

Dudley’s war was long a mystery, and the Texas stone that names Company B of the 7th Alabama Cavalry answers it only in part. Several Logans from Greene County and the Black Belt served Alabama in the Civil War, among them an A. Logan in the Greene County militia, but no Dudley or D. T. Logan is known among them in Alabama’s own records, so his widow’s claim of Confederate service for him rests on the Texas stone. In 1877 a Dudley Logan, with a John Logan and a T. M. Logan, took the voter registration oath in Tuscaloosa County, Precinct 24, alongside a J. T. Weaghworth who had registered in 1875. Tuscaloosa County borders Greene, so this may be the family on its way west, but no age or residence was written down to prove it.

The Logan household at dwelling 1131 is no longer a guess. When Clement Logan's will was proved in October 1854, the court named Elizabeth, Dudley T. and Martha as his only surviving children, and two years before that the widow of seventy-one at dwelling 1120, Martha Logan, had named him as her son in her own will. The three-year-old Dudley of 1850 was the Dudley Logan who took his family to Texas. The Wedgeworth girl nine doors away is another matter: Annie's own birthday, which she gave in 1914, points instead to Larkin Wedgworth's daughter, who was four that year. Leroy Logan's son, whose name is hard to make out on the census page, was Alvis L. Logan, a witness to Clement's will, and the Elizabeth Logan, thirty, at dwelling 1124 with William C., James C. and Matilda, was probably the widow of Martha's son William C. Logan.

stories.title: Alfred Livesay: Tennessee boy, Mexican War private, Marion County farmer
stories.hook: Alfred Livesay came from Tennessee to the Beaucoup settlement as a boy of seven, went to the Mexican War, preached and farmed, and died in Marion County with six hundred acres to leave his family.
body: Alfred Livesay was born in Tennessee on 15 February 1822 and came to Washington County, Illinois, at seven, so about 1829, the time when the Livesays moved from Maury County, Tennessee, to the Beaucoup country. His parents were John Wesley and Margaret (Lyons) Livesay, both natives of Tennessee, who later settled in Marion County, Illinois, and spent the rest of their lives on one place. He was a cousin of Dr. Thomas Livesay, a leading physician of Marion County. So his family remembered in 1909, in the Biographical and Reminiscent History of Richland, Clay and Marion Counties.

He married twice, it seems. On a license of 6 December 1842 Alfred Livesay married Nancy A. Darter, and on 26 February 1846 he married Hannah Logan, who was born in Washington County on 30 September 1830. What became of Nancy is not known. Probably one Alfred made both marriages, since no other Alfred Livesay is known in the county, but nothing says so.

In 1847 Alfred enrolled at Nashville in Company H of the 2nd Illinois Volunteers, a Washington County company, and served about thirteen months in the Mexican War. He contracted a sickness there from which he never fully recovered. In 1855 an “Alford Livesay” in Washington County had a household of a man aged 30 to 40, a woman aged 20 to 30 and five children under ten, which fits Alfred (aged 33), Hannah (24) and a young family, though the count of eight people does not match the seven listed, and no relationships were written down.

He was a Democrat who never sought office, a farmer and stock raiser, and for some years a Methodist preacher. About 1866 he moved to Patoka Township, Marion County, where he improved his farm. He died on 22 April 1883 and left his family about six hundred acres. Hannah was still living in 1909, managing 134 acres and drawing a pension of twelve dollars a month; they had thirteen children.

Whether Alfred belongs to Robert Livesay’s generation of the family is the open question. John and Rebecca (Carter) Livesay are said to have had a second son named John Wesley Livesay. If Alfred’s father was that John Wesley, Alfred was a nephew of Robert Livesay and a first cousin of Jackson Monroe, David Pinkney and their brothers. But who Alfred’s father’s own parents were is not known, so the connection is unproved, and John Wesley and Margaret stand apart from the John Livesay of the Carter kin.

stories.title: Captain Burns’s companies: Livesays in the Black Hawk and Mexican wars
stories.hook: In 1832 Lorenzo D. Livesay went to the Black Hawk War under Captain James Burns, and in 1847 three more Livesays followed a Captain James Burns to Mexico, where John C. Livesay died at Jalapa.
body: On 25 May 1832 Washington County, Illinois, raised a company for the Black Hawk War under Captain James Burns. Long afterward two old veterans recalled its members, and the first private they named was Lorenzo D. Livesay, the only Livesay in the company. He is remembered as a son of John C. and Rebecca (Carter) Livesay, born about 1815, though that birth is hard to square with the land patent he took out in 1831.

Fifteen years later the county sent men to Mexico. Company H of the 2nd Regiment Illinois Volunteers, under Colonel James Collins, was mustered into service on 18 July 1847 (its officers had been enrolled at Nashville on 10 July, and the regiment was organized at Alton on 3 August) and gathered at Alton. Its captain was a James Burns. Among the privates were Carter A. Livesay, Alfred Livesay and John C. Livesay, whose name was sometimes spelled Livesey, along with a Nicholas H. Darter, the name of the man who had married Mariah Livesay on 16 September 1841.

The three Livesays were not one tidy branch of the family. Alfred was a Tennessee-born farmer and later a preacher, whose story is told separately. Carter was probably the Carter H. Livesay who took out a license to marry Frances Eliz. Anderson on 1 October 1841; he was otherwise known as Carter H., and the A on the roll may be a misprint. A different and older Carter Livesay, born in Virginia, had married Mabel Perkins in 1836; he was the father of A. C. Livesay of Kansas.

John C. Livesay did not come home. He was one of the company’s men who died at Vera Cruz, Puebla and Jalapa, at San Juan, and on shipboard, and the roll of the dead gives him a single line: “John C. Livesay died at Jalapa, May 1848.”

The Captain James Burns of 1847 was probably the Captain James Burns of 1832: the name and county are the same, and in 1855 a James Burnes was living near Livesay Carter. Whether the John C. who died at Jalapa was related to the John C. said to be Lorenzo Dow’s father is unknown; that John C. would have been well over sixty in 1848. What the two companies do show is the Livesays and their in-laws answering the county’s call to arms from the first decade of settlement.

stories.title: Livesay Carter: a surname used as a first name
stories.hook: Livesay Carter, a Virginia-born settler of Nashville, Illinois, carried the Livesay name as his first name, just as a family story of two cousins tells.
body: John Livesay and his sister Alice, the family remembered, married Rebecca Carter and her brother Robert Carter in Franklin County, Virginia, and “both couples named their first sons after their families,” so that Carter Livesay and Livesay Carter were first cousins. The Carters took land in Illinois from 1823 on, beside the Livesays.

Livesay Carter was born on 15 November 1799 and died on 17 October 1875, and he lies in the Masonic Cemetery at Nashville with Mary Carter, 4 February 1800 to 24 October 1873, and Dr. William D. Carter beside them; his name has sometimes been written the other way round, as “Livesay, Carter.” He was a native of Virginia who went to Tennessee in 1807, came to Illinois in 1818, lived four years in what is now Clinton County, and then settled at Nashville, where he lived until his death in 1875, farming and raising stock, as the county remembered him in 1879 in its sketch of his son, Dr. William D. Carter. He built a tread sawmill in 1830 two miles east of the site of Nashville, and was among the commissioners who chose Nashville as county seat.

His wife was a widow when he married her. George T. Hoke, born in Harrison County, Indiana, in 1819, remembered that his widowed mother, a Moore from Jefferson County, Kentucky, came to the county with her people in 1822, met Livesay Carter near Covington and married him in July 1823. They lived together more than fifty years, “when she died,” and Mr. Carter followed in about two years. The dates on their stones fit exactly: Mary died in October 1873 and Livesay Carter in October 1875. Dr. Carter’s mother was remembered as Mrs. Mary Hoke, native of Jefferson County, Kentucky; she and Livesay had eight children, five boys and three girls, the doctor the seventh. The doctor was born on 12 January 1838, or the 2nd by the cemetery’s list.

Two details do not fit neatly. In 1855 a household headed by “Livesay(?) Carter” held nine people, six men of militia age and property valued at $3,670, the highest of any Livesay or Carter household that year. But it counted a woman aged 60 to 70, while Mary, born in 1800, would have been fifty-five. And a man born in 1799 cannot have been the first son of a marriage of the 1780s, as the family story says. Either its dates are loose, or Livesay Carter was not Robert Carter’s first son, or the stone’s year is wrong.

So Livesay Carter was a prosperous Virginia-born settler whose given name makes a Livesay-Carter kinship plausible, and whose arrival, in 1818 and 1823, fits the memory of Carters going first. Who his parents were is not known, and nothing yet ties him to John and Rebecca (Carter) Livesay, so the Carters stand beside the Livesay line rather than in it.
