stories.title: Three more Livesays of the 1830 generation
stories.hook: Three more Livesays of Robert Livesay’s generation, born in the 1820s, two of them in Tennessee, lived and died around Nashville and Richview; none can yet be tied to his house.

subject.name: Robert B., John W. and Lydia Jane Livesay

body: Robert Livesay of Beaucoup and his sons were not the only Livesays who came from Tennessee. Robert B. Livesay died on 7 June 1891 at his daughter’s home at Locust Creek and lies in the Bethel (Darter) Cemetery in Beaucoup Township. He and his wife Nancy were born in Tennessee about 1825, married in Perry County, Illinois, on 26 May 1842, and had children including Sarah J., Charlotte Ann and Delila. Charlotte Ann died on 23 January 1852 aged 6 years, 6 months and 11 days, and her stone survives. Robert B. was a carpenter at Nashville, born in Maury County, Tennessee, who enlisted on 4 February 1865 in Co. I of the 154th Illinois Infantry and was mustered out at Nashville, Tennessee, on 18 September 1865. He was too young to have been the Robert who bought land in 1838.

John W. Livesay was born in Tennessee on 19 September 1826 and “settled SE of Nashville in 1830.” He married Mrs. Elizabeth M. Logan Sanders on 21 December 1848, had eight sons and a daughter, and died at the home of a son in Nashville aged 79 years, 11 months and 10 days, as the Nashville Journal remembered him. That age works out to late August 1906, though his death is also given as September, so the exact day is uncertain. He is easily confused: Alfred Livesay’s father was also John Wesley, and a John Wesley Livesay born about 1834 served in the 60th Illinois.

The third is a woman. Lilly Jane (Livesay) Thompson, 14 July 1824 to 4 December 1887, lies in the Richview Township Cemetery beside William Thompson, 24 October 1819 to 27 February 1879. She was Lydia Jane Livesay when she and William Thompson took out a license on 28 January 1841, at sixteen. Their son Thomas Benton Thompson was born near Richview on 24 January 1842, by his family’s account the first son and second child of eleven; he served in the 49th Illinois from August 1862 and died on 3 February 1890. A first child, then a son within twelve months of the license, is a squeeze, so either his birth year is wrong or the first child was born before the marriage. Thomas was a recruit from Richview in Company F, mustered on 12 September 1862 and discharged on 1 July 1865 as a corporal. He joined five months after Shiloh, where the same company had lost a Richview private, John B. Walker, on 6 April 1862.

None of the three is known to have named a parent. They belong to the same years and townships as Robert’s children, and John W. settled in 1830, but nothing yet ties them to Robert’s house or to John and Rebecca’s. Rebecca Livesay’s estate papers, or a Maury County marriage book or tax list, may one day place them.

stories.title: Ten Livesay households and one Carter, 1855
stories.hook: In 1855 there were ten Livesay households in Washington County, and one Carter; several fit men known from their weddings, and one man is missing altogether.
body: In 1855, when Illinois took its own census, ten Livesays headed households in Washington County, with a Livesay Carter a few lines on: George W., “Jesse(?),” A. C., L. D., J. W., Alford, D. P., James M., I.(?) M., L. M. and Livesay(?) Carter. Only the head was named; everyone else was counted by sex and age group, with the number of militia men and the value of property and livestock. The old script is faint, the initials are hard to read, and several totals do not equal the sum of the age groups.

Some of the heads fit men known otherwise. “Alford Livesay” had a man aged 30 to 40, a woman aged 20 to 30 and five children under ten, which suits Alfred (born 1822) and Hannah Logan (born 1830), married in 1846, with property valued at $375. “D. P.” was David Pinkney. “L. D.” had one man aged 50 to 60, with no property, which suits Lorenzo Dow. “I.(?) M.” had a man aged 20 to 30, a woman aged 20 to 30 and three children under ten, which suits Jackson Monroe (aged 27) and Lucinda, whose Bible, as the family remembered it, recorded Lydia Laura in 1850, Harvey in 1853 and Effie in May 1855. “L. M.” had a man and a woman aged 20 to 30 and three children under ten; Lorenzo M.’s three children of 1860 were of different ages, so that match rests on the initials alone. “J. W.” had a man and a woman aged 20 to 30, four children under ten and property valued at $325, which fits John W. Livesay (born 1826), who married in December 1848.

Others cannot be placed. George W. was aged 30 to 40, which suits the George Washington Livesay of Richview, a mechanic born about 1824, though a George Washington Livesay is also said to have been a son of Carter Livesay. “Jesse(?),” “A. C.” and James M., aged 20 to 30 with two men of militia age, are unknown, though James M. may have been the carpenter of Nashville who became a lieutenant of the 49th Illinois. Livesay Carter’s household was far larger, with nine people, six men of militia age and $3,670 in property.

Two absences stand out. No household was headed by a W. E. or a William E. Livesay, although William Edmund, the eldest of Robert’s sons, had taken land and married in the county; “A. C.” may be a misreading, but nothing shows it. And no household was headed by Lydia Livesay, Robert’s widow by family tradition after his death in February 1855; if she was living, she was counted within a son’s household or missed. Nor can this count help with Floyd’s parentage, because it names no one but the head.

stories.title: Twenty-five Livesay weddings in Washington County, 1831–1877
stories.hook: From a December wedding in 1831 to one in 1877, at least twenty-five Livesay brides and grooms married in Washington County, Illinois, tying the clan to the Andersons, Darters, Thompsons, Whittenburgs and Logans.
body: In the half-century after they reached Washington County, Illinois, the Livesays married often and married close to home. At least twenty-five weddings in the county between 1831 and 1877 had a Livesay as bride or groom, and nineteen of them fell between 1841 and 1853, the years when the children who had arrived around 1830 came of age. Again and again the same families appear beside them: Andersons, Darters, Thompsons, Whittenburgs and Logans.

The first was Sally Livesay’s. She and Alex Anderson took out a license on 28 December 1831, and the marriage was returned on 15 February 1832. In 1832 a society of Methodists met at the home of an Alex. Anderson, with John Livesay among its principal members; if he was the same Anderson, John Livesay may have been a relative of the bride, though that is no more than a possibility.

Licenses followed through the late 1830s and early 1840s: Carter Livesay and Mabel Perkins (21 November 1836), William Thompson and Lydia Jane Livesay (28 January 1841), Thomas W. Livesay and Elizabeth Thompson (22 February 1841), Nicholas H. Darter and Mariah Livesay (16 September 1841), Carter H. Livesay and Frances Eliz. Anderson (1 October 1841), Alfred Livesay and Nancy A. Darter (6 December 1842), Henry Whittenburg and Margaret Rebecca Livesay (31 July 1844) and William E. Livesay and Emily Goodner (1 August 1844).

Then came a run of weddings: Lorenzo M. Livesay and Margaret Jane Thompson (22 October 1845), Alfred Livesay and Hannah Logan (26 February 1846), Daniel Whittenburg and Mary Livesay (16 March 1846), David A. White and Elizabeth Livesay (29 October 1848), John W. Livesay and Elizabeth M. Sanders (21 December 1848), Jackson M. Livesay and Lucinda A. Thompson (15 November 1849), James L. Logan and Unity J. Livesay (16 November 1849) and Terry W. Nichols and Nancy Livesay (18 December 1849). The 1850s brought Ambrose H. Smith and Rebecca E. Livesay (1851), James M. Livesay and Margaret E. Johnson (1851), Parker Dillinger and Frances E. Livesay (1852), William Livesay and Margaret McKelvy (1853), David B. Livesay and Elizabeth D. Jack (1857), Cornelius R. Rhine and Martha R. Livesay (1857) and James R. Breeze and Sarah A. Livesay (1858). The last, long after, was Charles M. Livesay’s marriage to Theresa E. Tate in 1877.

A few of these couples have more to tell. David A. White gave the date of his third marriage, to “Mrs. Elizabeth Livesay,” as 20 October 1848, nine days before the date in the county’s book, and did not say whose widow, if anyone’s, she was. The Thompsons kept coming back: Lorenzo M. and Jackson M. married Thompson brides, Thomas W. Livesay married an Elizabeth Thompson, and a William Thompson married Lydia Jane Livesay. The marriage books do not name parents, so it is not known which of these brides and grooms were Robert’s children, which were John and Rebecca’s, and which came from other branches. The Nancy Livesay who married in 1849 was not Nancy Paulina, who is said to have been born in 1838.

One of the early weddings can be placed in a family. A. C. Livesay was born in Maury County, Tennessee, in 1825 and came with his parents to Washington County, Illinois, in 1832. He married Delinda Finch of Jefferson County, moved to Kansas in 1873 and farmed in Montana Township, Labette County. When his life was written up there in 1901, he named his father as Carter Livesay, born in Virginia, who “was married three times”: first to Elizabeth Wright, a native of Tennessee, the mother of Charlotte, Polly, Thomas, Jesse, William, Caroline, George, Jane, A. C., Robert, Martha and John; then to Rachel Phillips, the mother of a daughter, Rachel; and last to Mabel Perkins, the mother of James, Nelson and Louis. So the Carter Livesay who married Mabel Perkins in November 1836 was the Virginia-born father of a large Tennessee family, and probably not the Carter H. Livesay who married Frances Anderson in 1841, who may have been one of the next generation. How Carter’s family was related to the other Livesays of the county is not yet known.
Floyd Livesay’s own wedding came later. He married Alice Walker in 1880, and the details of that wedding are still unknown.

stories.title: Two Beaucoup-born Livesays in Texas, 1917–1918
stories.hook: When the First World War draft came, two of Floyd and Alice’s Beaucoup-born sons were in Texas: Lester William farming at Pearland, and Melvin working in the oil fields.

subject.name: Lester W. Livesay and Melvin Livesay

body: When Lester William Livesay registered for the World War I draft, he was 22, married, a farmer residing at Pearland, Texas, born on 8 November 1895 at Beaucoup. He was Lester W. Livesay Sr.: Beaucoup, the November birthday and Pearland all fit, and his marriage to Sadah McCormick in 1911 explains the “married.”

The birth year does not match the stone. Lester’s headstone at Alvin gives 8 November 1894, and in 1900 his birth was given as November 1894; the draft says 1895. If the age of 22 is right, he registered after his birthday in 1917, which fits the registration of September 1918 better than the first call of June 1917, though the day he registered is not known.

A second Beaucoup-born Livesay in Texas registered too: Melvin Livesay, born on 15 October 1891 at Beaucoup, aged 26, single, an oil field worker, residing in Texas. Floyd and Alice lived in Illinois until the mid-1890s and then left for Brazoria County with their children, and in 1900 a Melvin T., twelve, was among them. That age points to about 1888 and the draft to 1891, a three-year gap of the sort such records often hold, so the two were probably the same man, Lester’s brother.

The other sons are missing, as they should be. Walter, born about 1880, died in January 1912, and William Paul, born about 1883, died in April 1915, so neither could have registered. Earl, born in Texas about 1904, was too young. Several other Livesays born in the county also registered, among them men at Ashley and Richview, who belong to other families.

stories.title: Walkers in a row: Richview, July 1860
stories.hook: On 3 July 1860 the census taker at Richview wrote down five Walker households within a few dwellings of one another, and gave William P. Walker's wife Abigail a birthplace of New York.

subject.name: William P. Walker and his Walker neighbors

body: On 3 July 1860 the assistant marshal, whose surname reads Blankenship, took the census at the Richview post office, Township 2 South, Range 1 West, Washington County, and on two pages he wrote down five Walker households within a few doors of one another.

Wm P. Walker, 29, a farmer born in Illinois, was at home with Abigail, 27, Mary E E, 5, Alice May, 1, and Carrie Ida, 1, every child born in Illinois. For Abigail the marshal wrote something quite different: “N York.” Her age fits the Beaucoup stone, which gives her birth year as 1833, and it fits the Abigail Shank, 16, born in New York, who was living in a neighboring household in 1850. Alice May at 1 agrees with the headstone date of 11 January 1859.

Three households stood close by. Next door, directly above William’s on the page, was John W. Walker, 35, a farmer, with Lavina E., 30, and four children aged 10, 6, 5 and 2 whose first names are hard to read; a John W. Walker, 25, with Lavina E. and an infant son had been counted in 1850. A few doors on was G. W. Walker, 33, a farmer, with Elizabeth, 31, and Frances C. E., 10, plus younger children, the family of Lieutenant George W. Walker, whose daughter had been eight months old in 1850. Just before, on the previous page, came Simeon Walker, 28, a farmer, and next to him Alex Walker, 24, a farmer, with Sarah A., 21, Wm H., 3, and Edwin F., 8 months, and a 20-year-old schoolteacher, Ellen Barns, in the house.

Simeon Walker’s household is the one the cemetery stones lead one to expect, with one difference. Simeon, 28, was there with E. J., 26, who matches Etheldra Jane, born July 1833. But there were also a girl of 1, whose name reads Clara, and a Caroline, 12, born in Illinois. The Beaucoup stones remember only sons for Simeon and Etheldra J. (Wilbert, James H., Simon G. and Elmer D.), and a daughter of 12 could not be Etheldra’s, since Etheldra was herself 26. So the household held a baby girl who may have been a daughter who died young, or a relative, and an older girl whose connection is unknown.

Five Walker households in eight dwellings fits the picture: Rev. James Walker’s probable sons and daughters had settled together near the old home place. George W. and John W. Walker had already stood security for Simeon Walker’s Hoyleton bank loan in January 1860. No one wrote down how the households were related, and how Alex Walker, who was not in James Walker’s house in 1850, belonged to the others is not known. Rev. James had died in 1857, and his widow Etheldra, then about 55, was not among these Walkers; where she lived in 1860 is not known.

stories.title: William P. Walker's household, Richview, 1870
stories.hook: By June 1870 William and Abigail Walker had six children at home near Richview, among them twelve-year-old twins, and that year Abigail was said to have been born in Illinois rather than New York.

subject.name: William P. and Abigail Walker's household

body: On 20 June 1870 the assistant marshal, John H. Barber, reached the Walker farm near Richview, in Township 2 South, Range 1 West. Wm P. Walker, 39, was a farmer with real estate worth $3,000 and personal estate of $1,500, born in Illinois. With him were Abigail, 37, keeping house; Mary E., 14; Alice M., 12; Carrie, 12, and Ellen A., 12, joined by a bracket and the word “twins”; Wm S., 6; and Charles, 3. Every one of them, Abigail included, was said to have been born in Illinois.

Compared with 1860, the household grew by three children and lost none. Mary E E, 5 in 1860, is now Mary E., 14, and Alice May, 1, is 12, a year older than the headstone's 1859 birth would make her, which is an ordinary census drift. Carrie Ida, 1 in 1860, is Carrie, 12. Ellen A. is new, with no counterpart in 1860, and the twin bracket links her to Carrie, even though the 1860 page already showed two girls aged 1, Alice and Carrie. Either Ellen was missed or misplaced in 1860, or one of the 1870 ages or brackets is a slip. The two later children, Wm S. and Charles, were born in the 1860s; William was serving with the 60th Illinois from the spring of 1864 to July 1865, so William S., aged 6 in June 1870, may have been born while his father was away or just before he left.

By 1870 William was a man of some property. What he owned in 1860 is too faintly written to read with confidence, but now he had $3,000 in real estate and $1,500 in personal property. His post office was still Richview, and his neighbors were farm households, not the railroad workers and merchants of the village.

On 22 November 1871, a year and a half later, Andrew J. Scott married Mary E. E. Walker, who would have been about 16. The initials E. E. match her name in 1860, Mary Ellen Etheldra. These were very probably William P. Walker’s children. Whether Abigail was their mother, and Alice’s, is still uncertain, because at Alice’s death her mother was named as Addie Bruce.
One detail of that summer stands out. Abigail was Illinois-born in 1870, but in 1860 her birthplace had been New York, and the Abigail Shank of 1850 was born in New York too.

stories.title: Abigail Walker: born in New York, or in Illinois?
stories.hook: Abigail Walker, William P. Walker’s wife, was born in New York, or in Illinois: twice she was said to be one and twice the other, and who her parents were is still unknown.
body: In July 1860, at Richview, Abigail Walker, 27, was said to have been born in “N York,” while her husband and children were all born in Illinois. Ten years earlier, on 9 September 1850, in the same Washington County district as the James Walker household, David S. Jack, 32, a farmer born in South Carolina with real estate worth $600, had been living a few doors from John W. Walker with Ruth D., 25, born in New York; Elizabeth A., 1, born in Illinois; and Abigail Shank, 16, female, born in New York. Abigail Walker’s family stone at Beaucoup gives her birth year as 1833, which fits a girl of 16 in the summer of 1850 and a woman of 27 in 1860.

In 1870 Abigail, 37, was given the same Illinois birthplace as everyone else in the house, and when Alice Walker Livesay died in Texas in 1922, her mother was named as Addie Bruce, born in Illinois. So twice she was New York-born (1850 and 1860) and twice Illinois-born (1870 and 1922). Either the census taker of 1870 carried the children’s Illinois down onto the mother’s line, or the 1860 entry is the slip, or two different women are in view; no one can yet say which. If Alice’s mother was the New York-born Abigail, the informant, who signed as F. C. Livesay, gave the wrong maiden name and birthplace decades later and far away. That often happened, but it cannot be assumed.

Her name is the other half of the puzzle. The Abigail Shank of 1850 and the Abigail Schanck licensed to marry a William F. Walker on 25 February 1852 bore the same surname spelled two ways, and Shank and Schanck are ordinary spellings of the same name. So there was an Abigail Schanck or Shank of the right age in the right neighborhood. A William H. Walker stood bond for the groom, so a Walker stood behind him, but the groom’s initial F does not match William P., and no one is known to have called William P. Walker’s wife a Schanck. Bruce, the name given at Alice’s death, is a different name entirely. Only one Bruce lies at Beaucoup, Mary Ann, wife of Samuel, who died in 1846 at 19, and a James Bruce left an estate in the county; neither is known to be connected to Abigail. A married daughter’s death would normally bring out her mother’s maiden name, so her children’s deaths may tell more than any census.

Why Abigail lived with the Jacks in 1850 is not known. Ruth D. Jack was also born in New York, so she may have been a relative. The Jacks were among the early Beaucoup settlers, remembered in the county’s history of 1879, and they were already tied to the Walkers: Isaac Berry Jack had married Elizabeth C. Walker on 3 April 1845.

Abigail’s story is still unfinished. Where she was born, what her maiden name was, and whether she was Alice’s mother are all uncertain, and the answers may lie in the family’s later years: in where her parents were said to have been born in 1880, in the deaths of daughters such as Mary E. E. Scott who lived past 1916, or in the 1852 marriage itself, which would show whether the groom was William P. or William F.

stories.title: Sergeant, lieutenant, captain: Simeon Walker of the 60th Illinois
stories.hook: Simeon Walker rose from sergeant to captain of Company C, 60th Illinois, in ten months, and left the regiment two days before Averysboro.

subject.name: Captain Simeon Walker, Company C, 60th Illinois Infantry

body: Simeon Walker enlisted at Nashville as a sergeant on 10 February 1862 and was mustered in on 21 February 1862. He was “Promoted 2d Lieutenant,” with rank from 20 July 1862, and then captain from 19 December 1862, the day the company’s first captain, John R. Moss of Mt. Vernon, resigned. He was mustered in as captain on 16 April 1863 and mustered out on 14 March 1865. As captain his home was given as Mt. Vernon.

The regiment’s own history gives the setting. The 60th was organized at Camp Dubois, Anna, on 17 February 1862 by Colonel Silas C. Toler. It went to Cairo, then to Island No. 10, the siege of Corinth, and by September 1862 to Nashville, where it was cut off from supplies until November. Toler died on 2 March 1863. The regiment fought at Chattanooga, wintered at Rossville and in February 1864 saw three-fourths of its men re-enlist as veterans; on 26 February it lost 42 killed and wounded at Buzzard Roost. It went through the Atlanta campaign, the March to the Sea and Savannah, then fought at Averysboro on 16 March 1865 and at Bentonville from 19 to 21 March, marched in the Grand Review on 24 May, and was mustered out on 31 July 1865 after provost duty at Louisville.

Simeon Walker’s discharge of 14 March 1865 came two days before Averysboro. Several privates of the company were “Mustered out Mar. 14, 1865” with him, while many of their comrades had “Re-enlisted as Veteran,” so the men of 14 March were probably original enlistees who did not re-enlist. William P. Walker, by contrast, joined as a recruit in March 1864 and stayed to the end in July 1865, so he was probably in the ranks at Averysboro and Bentonville, though no one recorded his engagements.

The regiment’s chaplain was Levi S. Walker of Richview, a Methodist preacher of the other Walker family. One caution remains. As sergeant Simeon’s home was given as Nashville, and as captain Mt. Vernon, neither of them Richview, where a Simeon Walker, 28, was living with E. J., 26, in 1860. That Captain Simeon was Etheldra J. Walker’s husband rests on his Beaucoup grave, where he is remembered as a captain of Company C, 60th Illinois, and on the county’s memory in 1879 of a Simon Walker of that company.

stories.title: The lieutenant who resigned at Jalapa
stories.hook: George W. Walker went to Mexico in 1847 as second lieutenant of the Washington County company, and he resigned at Jalapa on 17 December 1847, five months after the company left Nashville.

subject.name: George W. Walker, Company H, 2nd Illinois Volunteers

body: On 10 July 1847 Captain James Burns, First Lieutenant Malachi Jenkins and Second Lieutenant George W. Walker were all enrolled at Nashville, Illinois, as officers of Company H of the Second Regiment. Beside Walker’s name on the War Department’s rolls is the remark: “Resigned at Jalapa, Mexico, Dec. 17, 1847.”

The regiment was then in winter quarters at Jalapa, and the company’s Mexican service ran until July 1848. So Walker served about five months, through the voyage to Vera Cruz in August, the fight at San Juan on 18 September and the first months at Jalapa, and did not come home with the company. When Rev. George Walker died in 1902 he was remembered as a Mexican War veteran, and by 1850 he was farming at Beaucoup, so he came home to the settlement after all.

Two privates named Walker, John and Thomas, were enrolled at Nashville on 10 July 1847, and one man did not return: Ezekiah Walker, who “Died at Vera Cruz, Mex., Sept. 10, 1847,” and was remembered in the county as Ezekiel. Whether any of these men was kin to George W. Walker or to Rev. James Walker’s family is not known; there was no Ezekiel among the Walker households of 1850.

Two small puzzles remain. The county remembered James K. Finch as third lieutenant, dying at Vera Cruz on 12 September 1847; the War Department listed a second lieutenant James R. Lynch with the same death date and place, so either the same man went by two names or two men died there that day. And an Isaac B. Jack was promoted second lieutenant on 28 February 1848, though the county remembered him only as a private; an Isaac Berry Jack had married Elizabeth C. Walker on 3 April 1845, but whether he was the same man is not known.

stories.title: Abner Clay and Mattie Denson, 20 May 1897
stories.hook: Wilsey Clay’s son Abner took a second wife under Choctaw law. The license, written in Choctaw, survives in the Dawes jacket with an English translation made six years later.

subject.name: Abner H. Clay
subject.rel: Half-brother of Peter Durant and half great-uncle of Ida May Merry

body: Abner H. Clay, 27, three-quarters Choctaw, the son of Henry Clay (dead) and Wilsey Clay, applied for his household at Lukfata on 18 April 1899 and was entered on Choctaw card 507. With him were Mattie, 26, an intermarried white woman, and their children, Abner Henry, Mattie Lorena and Myrtle Eugenia, the last two added after their births in 1899 and 1902. The family’s Dawes file tells how the household came to be.

Abner and Mattie married on 20 May 1897 at Lukfata. The license was issued that day by J. A. James, county clerk of Bok Tuklo County, to “Mattie Denson a United States citizen” and “A. H. Clay a Choctaw citizen.” It was written in Choctaw, and in August 1903 the Commission’s interpreter L. G. Battiest swore at Atoka that his English translation was true. A handwritten certificate in English, signed by R. W. Thomas as judge of Bok Tuklo County, says the same couple were united “according to Regulation and Laws of the Choctaw Nation.” This is the same Thomas who, as county clerk until October 1896, had taken the oath and the hundred-dollar fee from Louis Merry eight months earlier.

Mattie testified at Wister on 16 December 1902 that she was then 32, that she had lived at Lukfata seven years, that she had never been married before, and that Abner had a first wife, Mabel Clay, who had been dead about four years when they married. Her parents, Joseph H. and Mattie E. Denson, are named on the card as non-citizens. Abner and Mattie’s children were born at Lukfata: Abner Henry on 29 March 1898 and Mattie Lorena on 25 September 1899, and Myrtle Eugenia on 8 March 1902, the last of them sworn to at Shawneetown in October 1902, after Mattie had left. The midwives were Amanda Butler in 1898 and Jane Butler in 1899 and 1902.

For the Merry and Durant line the household matters in two ways. Abner was the half-brother of Peter Durant, Bessie’s father, so his three children were probably half first cousins of Bessie. And his marriage was made by the same county officers, at the same place and under the same law that made Louis Merry’s marriage valid, so the two weddings, in 1896 and 1897, show what a white spouse had to do to marry into the Nation. The Clays’ marriage did not last.

stories.title: Abner Clay, Mattie and the allotment letters, 1902–1904
stories.hook: A marriage that ended in October 1902 left the Commission a year of letters about who could choose land for three small children.
body: The Clay family was dividing just as the Nation’s land was being surveyed for allotment, and for more than a year letters went back and forth between the Commission, Choctaw Nation officers and Abner and Mattie Clay. Mattie told the Commission on 16 December 1902 that she had lived with Abner until 9 October, that he had shot her through the arm and beaten her, and that he was living with another woman. She had gone to Lockesburg, Arkansas, in October, and the Commission wrote to her there until February 1904. Abner wrote on 10 December denying the charges, and on 12 January 1903 the Commission wrote that it would take any evidence he offered within thirty days.

The questions put to Mattie show what was at stake. As an intermarried white woman she could be enrolled only if she and her Choctaw husband had lived together as husband and wife in the Nation up to 25 September 1902, and the Commission wanted to know whether they had been divorced. She answered that neither of them had obtained a divorce and that she meant to return to the Nation “some day.” In January and again on 23 February 1903 Abner asked to give further evidence against her application; on 5 March the Commission told him he could appear at Atoka on 13 March, he did not, and on 21 March it acknowledged his letter of excuse. On 2 March 1904 the Commission decided in her favor, finding that they had married lawfully on 20 May 1897 and had lived together to the cutoff date. On 7 April 1904, answering her letter of 31 March from Garvin, Indian Territory, the Commission told her no protest had been filed by the Nations’ attorneys, and she was approved as an intermarried citizen on 7 May 1904.

Meanwhile the children’s land was in dispute. On 29 January 1903 Claude Denson of Shawneetown, who said he was Mattie’s brother, asked who had the right to select allotments for her three children. The Commission quoted the act of Congress that gave minors’ selections to “the father or mother, if members.” Mattie wrote on 9 February that Abner should not be allowed to choose for them, and in February 1904 the Commission passed her protest to the land offices at Atoka and Tishomingo. On 14 March 1903 the Commission also answered a letter in which Abner and other citizens proposed an organization to elect a committee of reliable men to select allotments at Atoka for members too poor or too ill to travel.

The story has no clear ending. By March 1904 Mattie was back at Garvin, in the Choctaw Nation. Who chose the children’s land, whether the couple ever divorced, and what became of Abner after 1904 are not known. But in 1903 Abner Clay, Peter Durant’s half-brother, was an active citizen at Lukfata, writing to the Commission about the way the Nation’s land would be shared out.

stories.title: Wilsey Clay swears, May 1906
stories.hook: At sixty-seven Wilsey Clay stood before a Commission clerk at Lukfata and named another of her sons, Thomas Durant.

subject.name: Wilsey Clay
subject.rel: Great-grandmother of Ida May Merry Whitfield

body: Wilsey Clay’s granddaughter had been enrolled twice. On Wilsey’s own household card, 655, she was Licey, the daughter of Thomas and Melinda Durant; on card 966 she was Lizzie Durant. Whether Thomas was Wilsey’s son or Melinda her daughter was not said, until Wilsey herself was asked.

In 1906 the Commission looked into the duplicate enrollment. Wilsey Clay was sworn at Lukfata on 9 May, with Jacob Homer as interpreter. She gave her age as 67 and said she was a Choctaw by blood. Asked if she was the mother of Thomas Durant, she said yes; he had died several years earlier; his wife was Melinda Durant; and he had two daughters, Jane and Lizzie or Licey, both living. She said Lizzie was one girl enrolled twice: the girl had enrolled herself, and when Wilsey went to Alikchi she enrolled her again under the other spelling. Lizzie, sworn five days later at C. W. Westbrook’s store five miles north of Glover, said the same.

The Department cancelled the Licey Durant entry on card 655 as an error. It recommended the cancellation in August 1906 and the Assistant Secretary of the Interior concurred on 19 September, leaving her enrolled once, as Lizzie, with an allotment already chosen.

Her testimony makes Wilsey Clay the mother of three families: Abner Clay by Henry Clay, Ida and Laura by Charles Gavner, and Thomas Durant. The Durant surname of Thomas and of Peter Durant, whom John M. Hodges called Wilsey’s son in 1900, fits one household, but whether the two men had the same father, or were brothers by the same marriage, is not known. So Peter’s own link to Wilsey is probable, while Thomas’s rests on her own sworn word. It also makes Lizzie, whose 1893 money was collected with Bessie’s through J. L. Merry, a probable first cousin of Bessie Durant Merry.

Fourteen years after her granddaughter Lizzie McGee died, Wilsey Clay went to the county court at Idabel to settle who should inherit Lizzie's allotment. The list of heirs reads like a family tree: Lizzie's father Austin McGee; Wilsey herself; two living daughters, Laura and Ida; and the children of four who were gone, Abner Clay, Emma Costilow, Thomas Durant and Peter Durant, whose only surviving child was Bessie Merry.

Her age (67 in 1906) is a little higher than the 58 of 1899, a difference that is kept as written. The Department’s letter calls the witness “Wilson Clay” and dates the testimony 10 July 1906, which is the date of the typed transcript; the transcript itself dates the testimony at Lukfata to 9 May. Thomas’s relationship to Peter Durant is not stated in any record read and is not linked.

stories.title: Lizzie Durant: Wheelock, a wedding and a baby at Glover
stories.hook: A Wheelock schoolgirl on a Dawes card in 1899 was a wife and mother at Glover three years later, and her mail went through J. L. Merry.

subject.name: Lizzie Durant Gibbs
subject.rel: Probable first cousin of Bessie Durant Merry

body: Lizzie Durant was 13 when she was enrolled on 27 April 1899 at Wheelock Seminary, a Choctaw Nation boarding school, as a full-blood Choctaw whose father was Thomas Durant of Bok Tuklo County (card 966, roll 2580). She said under oath in 1906 that she had been a student there that April. Her grandmother Wilsey Clay had meanwhile enrolled her again as Licey on card 655.

On 24 March 1902 the clerk of the United States court in Indian Territory issued a license for Fred Gibbs of Lukfata, 21, and Miss Lizzie Durant of Lukfata, 18. Milton A. Clark, a minister of the gospel, certified that he married them on 31 March 1902 and returned the paper on 2 April. Fred was not a Choctaw citizen, and the Commission later wrote to Lizzie asking for the license and certificate as authority for the change of her name on its records.

Their son Isaam was born on 30 August 1902. On 1 December 1902 Lizzie swore to his birth before J. L. Merry, notary public, with the midwife Susion Franklin’s affidavit taken the same day. The boy was approved as an infant citizen on 8 December, and the Commission’s letter of that date is addressed to Lizzie Gibbs at Glover. Later that month Principal Chief Green McCurtain wrote to Merry about the 1893 money of “Ben and Lizzie Durant.”

The allotment she mentioned in 1906 had already been selected under the name Lizzie Durant. After that year she drops from view, and when she and Fred Gibbs died is not known. If Peter Durant was Wilsey’s son, as John M. Hodges said in 1900, Lizzie and Bessie were first cousins, though how Thomas and Peter were related is not known.

stories.note: The cousin relationship to Bessie is probable because it needs Peter to be a son of Wilsey Clay (probable) and Thomas a son of Wilsey (proven). Lizzie’s age ranges from 13 to 23 across records dated 1899 to 1906. The boy’s name is spelled Isaam, Isaan and Isom on the documents. Several other records were not found: a marriage record from Fred’s side, and any later census.

stories.title: The notaries at Lukfata and Glover, 1899–1902
stories.hook: Gaffney, Sleeper and Merry each swore Choctaw families’ affidavits at Lukfata or Glover. The last signature is Louis Merry’s own.
body: Choctaw families had to prove births with sworn affidavits, and each one needed a notary public. In the Lukfata neighborhood a handful of men held that job. On 1 May 1899 Mattie Clay and the midwife Amanda Butler swore to the birth of Abner Henry Clay before Chas. J. Gaffney, notary public. A Chas. J. Gaffney was also a witness on the certificate of Louis Merry and Bessie Durant’s wedding at Lukfata in 1896.

On 20 October 1899 Mattie Clay swore to Mattie Lorena’s birth before John H. Sleeper, notary public, at Lukfata. The same J. H. Sleeper, signing as Rev. J. H. Sleeper, performed the Merry wedding in 1896, and Louis Merry later described him as a missionary. So the man who married Louis to Bessie also witnessed oaths for neighbors three years afterward. In October 1902 the notaries were different again: Mattie Clay’s affidavit for Myrtle was sworn on 24 October before W. F. Nichols at Shawneetown, and the midwife’s on 29 October before a notary whose signature reads J. W. Costelow, the name of the other witness to the 1896 Merry wedding.

Then, on 1 December 1902, the notary was Louis himself. The birth affidavits for Lizzie Durant Gibbs’s son Isaam, her own and the midwife Susion Franklin’s, are both signed “J. L. Merry, Notary Public.” He was at Glover then, as postmaster and as an applicant whose own enrollment the Commission was still examining; he had been appointed Glover’s first postmaster in 1901. He signed, in his own hand, with the initials J. L. that the Commission used for him, which fits everything else that makes J. L. Merry of Glover and Louis Merry of card 5754 one man.

It also shows him doing a public job. A Choctaw woman whose husband was a United States citizen brought her sworn statement to Merry, who was himself still an applicant. The affidavit was filed with the Commission and the child was approved a week later.

Gaffney; Dawes Enrollment Jacket for Choctaw by Blood, Card #5754, image 2194; as cited in the story “A wedding at Lukfata”: https://catalog.archives.gov/id/44362518
stories.note: The identity of the 1896 witnesses Chas. J. Gaffney and J. W. Costelow with the notaries of those names in 1899 and 1902 rests on name and place only, and the 1902 signature is hard to read. The identity of the notary J. L. Merry with Louis Merry is probable on the Glover address, the initials and the other J. L. Merry letters. Sleeper’s given name, John H., appears only in the 1899 signature; his church or mission has not been found in any source read, and the jackets do not say whether the notary commission was for a church or for the Nation.

stories.title: Laura Clay and William A. Durant at Red River
stories.hook: Laura, Wilsey Clay’s daughter, married into a household of three motherless boys on the Red River side of the Nation.

subject.name: Laura Clay Durant
subject.rel: Half great-aunt of Ida May Merry Whitfield

body: On 21 April 1899, the same day as her mother Wilsey Clay, Laura was enrolled with her husband’s household on card 656: William A. Durant, 29, and Laura, 19, his wife, both one-half Choctaw, and three sons aged eight, six and five. Their residence was Red River County and their post office Garvin, while Wilsey gave Red River as her post office in Bok Tuklo County, so the family was spread across the Nation’s counties.

William’s parents were Allington Durant and Mary Durant, both dead and both of Red River. Laura’s were Charles Gavener, a non-citizen, and Wilsey Clay, enrolled in 1896 in Bok Tuklo. The boys, Gibby, Eddie and Louie, were William’s sons by Sarah Durant, also dead and of Red River, not by Laura, who at 19 was too young to be mother to an eight-year-old. William and Laura had been on the 1896 roll as Wm. A. Durant and Laura Clay, he in Nashoba County and she in Bok Tuklo. The Secretary of the Interior approved all five on 12 December 1902.

Nothing links William to Peter or Thomas Durant, whose mother was also Wilsey Clay; Durant was a very common Choctaw family name, with several lines. But his household fills out Laura Clay’s life. Laura had the same parents as Ida Clay, so they were sisters, and she was a half-sister of Abner Clay and, probably, of Peter Durant.

Laura’s husband shared a name with the best-known Durant of his generation, and the two are easy to run together. William A. Durant the chief was born at Bennington on 18 March 1866. He was a son of the Rev. Sylvester Durant, a Presbyterian minister, and Martha Robinson. He sat on the Choctaw council from 1890 and was its speaker at twenty-five. He was speaker of the Oklahoma House from 1911 to 1913, and from 1937 until his death at Tuskahoma in 1948 he was the President’s appointee as Principal Chief. In 1892 he married Ida May Corber.

Laura’s William was about four years younger, a son of Allington and Mary Durant of Red River County, both dead by 1899. That April his wife was Laura Clay, nineteen, and his boys were Sarah Durant’s sons. So two men, born four years apart to two Durant households, carried the same name in the same Nation. A Sylvester Durant was major of the First Choctaw Regiment in the war, but whether he was the chief’s father is not shown here, and nothing yet joins Allington’s family to Sylvester’s.

stories.title: Lukfata, the White Clay settlement
stories.hook: Louis Merry’s wedding place was a Choctaw settlement older than the Nation’s Oklahoma counties, and a mission field before it was a county seat.

subject.name: Lukfata
subject.rel: Place of the Merry and Durant wedding, 1896

body: Muriel H. Wright, writing in the Chronicles of Oklahoma in 1950, gave the history of the name. Lukfata, also spelled Lukfahta and Lukfoata, means “White Clay.” It was the name of an old tribal village in what is now Kemper County, Mississippi, and the Choctaws who were removed to the West in 1832 to 1834 gave it to a new settlement in what is now McCurtain County, Oklahoma, about two and a half miles west of Broken Bow. A mission school of the American Board was opened there in 1835. Her notes name the Rev. Henry R. Wilson as the missionary who established the nearby Bok Tuklo mission in 1834, and place the mission about nine miles southwest of Broken Bow, on a creek forking in two. Bok Tuklo is Choctaw for “two creeks.”

The Nation later borrowed that name for a county. Bok Tuklo County lay in the Apukshunnubbee District, with Eagle County on the east, Red River County to the south and Towson County to the west, and its seat was Oak Hill. A county judge, sheriff and ranger were elected for two-year terms, and the county clerk kept the records of the county court. These were the officers the family dealt with: R. W. Thomas as clerk until 1 October 1896 and county judge by May 1897, Joe A. James as clerk, and the licenses they issued for Louis Merry in 1896 and for Abner Clay in 1897.

By the 1890s Lukfata was a post office and a place where Wilsey Clay’s children and grandchildren lived. Abner Clay’s post office was Lukfata in 1899, Thomas Durant lived there, and Louis Merry gave it as his home in 1900, when he had been there about eight years. They lived there just before the Nation’s land was divided into allotments. In 1905 the Sequoyah convention proposed that Bok Tuklo County become part of a new McCurtain County, and the Choctaw Nation’s counties disappeared when Oklahoma became a state in 1907.
Where Bessie Durant was born or raised is not known, but Lukfata is where she married, and where her grandmother’s family clustered.

stories.note: A context story. The place-name history and the mission dates are Wright’s; the county organization is from Wikipedia, which gives no sources of its own for it. The Sequoyah proposal and 1907 statehood are from the Wikipedia article and were not checked against another source. The family facts are from the Dawes jackets cited. Wright’s mission site (Section 2, T7S R23E) and Louis Merry’s farm described in 1904 (Section 4, T6S R23E) are different townships and are not claimed to be near each other.

stories.title: Dudley Logan, private, 7th Alabama Cavalry
stories.hook: Dudley Logan’s grave at Mount Pleasant remembers him as a private of the 7th Alabama Cavalry, and he served in a company raised in his home county of Greene, Alabama.
body: His widow had claimed Confederate service for Dudley Logan, and his grave says where he served. At the Masonic Cemetery in Mount Pleasant, Texas, Dudley Logan lies with the dates January 8, 1846, to November 21, 1898, and the words “Pvt 7th Ala Cav CSA.” Those are Dudley Timothy Logan’s dates, so this is the same man, and his stone, or the funeral record behind it, names his regiment.

He was a private in Company B, 7th Alabama Cavalry, the “Broadfoots of Greene County,” and two other Logans served with him, L. Logan and Zach M. Logan. When, and at what age, he enlisted is not known. A Zachary M. Logan of Company B, 7th Alabama Cavalry, was remembered among Greene County’s Confederate veterans, though Dudley was left off that list.

That goes some way toward answering an old puzzle. Alabama’s own records of Civil War service have no Dudley Logan, yet his widow, Mrs. A. E. Logan of Titus County, filed Texas Confederate pension application 30414 in his name. A man said to have been born in Greene County, Alabama, in January 1846, who served in a company raised in Greene County, whose tombstone names that regiment and whose widow later claimed his service, makes a consistent picture, and the company roll and the Texas stone were set down far apart, one in Alabama and the other in Texas.

Zachary and L. Logan stood beside him on the roll, and there were many Logan households in Greene County in 1850, but whether they were Dudley’s kin, neighbors, cousins or uncles, or no relation at all, is not known. Whether Dudley was a boy of seventeen when he enlisted, or joined later, is not known either; his service file and his widow’s pension file may one day tell.

Annie herself remembered, in 1914, that Dudley had left Alabama with Captain Dave Scarborough's company of cavalry and had later been transferred into General Cockrell's Missouri brigade of infantry, to serve beside a brother-in-law. A niece's letter, passing on what an old neighbor recalled, placed him in Company B of the Seventh Alabama Cavalry, the regiment his stone names. No service record has yet been found to settle it.

stories.title: The Logan stones at the Masonic Cemetery, Mount Pleasant
stories.hook: Dudley’s grave is not the only Logan one in Mount Pleasant. Two boys who died a year apart, in 1888 and 1889, are marked as sons of “D. & Annie Logan.”
body: The Masonic Cemetery lies in the northwest part of Mount Pleasant. It has served the town and county since 1888, when a couple gave five acres to the Masonic Lodge, after the earlier Old Mount Pleasant cemetery was judged too crowded and irregular to keep up. People buried in the old Christian cemetery were reburied in the Masonic one, so some of its dates are older than the cemetery itself.

Several Logans lie there. Dudley Logan, 8 January 1846 to 21 November 1898, is the soldier. Ernest C. A. Logan, 20 April 1876 to 15 August 1889, and Evan A. C. Logan, 23 February 1880 to 15 November 1888, are each remembered as “Son of D. & Annie Logan.” Ernest’s stone carries a short verse about a loss deeply felt, and Evan’s monument is broken and unreadable. They were thirteen and eight when they died, sons of Dudley and of the woman the family calls Annie Wedgeworth Logan.

Three more Logans lie nearby, and a fourth name is linked by marriage. Edd H. Logan, 25 October 1872 to 6 December 1947, is marked “Papa,” and Sallie G. Logan, 23 July 1879 to 9 May 1958, “Mama.” Dudley Edward “Dud” Logan, 25 February 1899 to 15 March 1981, was born three months after Dudley died. A Charles Homer Stewart, 1895 to 1980, was the husband of Eva G. Logan Stewart. None of these stones names a parent, so their place in Dudley’s family is only a guess. Edd was born in 1872, when Dudley was twenty-six, and when Annie Box died in 1959 her surviving brothers were Rob and Walter, not Edd, who had died in 1947. The infant Dud was probably a grandson, and Edd and Sallie were most likely his parents, but none of this is proved.

Annie Wedgeworth Logan herself is not there. No stone for her stands among the Logans, and no Wedgeworth, and no other Annie or Sarah Logan, and no Sallie Logan besides Edd’s wife, is known in any of the cemeteries of Titus County. Either she is buried outside Titus County, or she remarried and lies under another surname. Her death in 1923 is still unproved.

stories.title: Which Wedgworth girl was Annie?
stories.hook: In 1850 there were two Wedgworth girls in Greene County who might have grown up to be Annie Wedgeworth Logan: Sarah A. E., aged 9, and Ann E., aged 4. The younger fits an 1846 birth much better.
body: Sarah A. E. Wedgeworth, 9, was living in Stephen Wedgeworth’s household in Greene County in 1850, but nine years old does not fit a birth in 1846. There was another girl. In the household of Larkin Wedgworth, 39, born in South Carolina, a farmer with real estate worth $2,400, were Sarah J., 36, born in Tennessee, Ann E., 4, and Julia J. T., six months, both born in Alabama. A girl of four in 1850 was born about 1846, exactly the year usually given for Annie, and Ann E. could be Anne Elizabeth.

Next door lived Elizabeth Wedgworth, 48, with property worth $4,800, and Stephen B., 26, a teacher, Middleton, 22, John M., 19, and Martha J., 17. Stephen Wedgeworth, 41, with real estate of $3,200, lived some way off. How any of these Wedgworths were related is not known, and the name was spelled both Wedgeworth and Wedgworth, even side by side.

By 1860 Larkin had moved to Tuscaloosa County. In the Western Division, near the North Port post office, Larkin Wedgworth, 49, a farmer with real estate of $2,100 and personal property of $17,721, was living with Sarah J., 43, and three children: Amanda E. J., 13, Julia J. T., 10, and John T. L., 8. Julia’s age and the parents’ ages and birthplaces fit 1850, so this was Larkin’s family, and the 13-year-old was probably the 4-year-old Ann E. under another reading. Four doors away were Thomas Harkee, 23, and Sarah A. E. Harkee, 20, born in Alabama.

That Sarah A. E. Harkee is a warning. A girl of nine in 1850 would be twenty in 1860, and a young wife of that age with her three initials is a natural fit for Stephen Wedgeworth’s daughter, now married. If so, she was not Dudley Logan’s wife. Two other Tuscaloosa County girls named Sarah A. E. were living there in 1860, aged 19 and 14, so the name was common. Nothing proves that either girl was Annie. But the Larkin Wedgworth family went from Greene County to Tuscaloosa County, where Dudley Logan took the voter’s oath in 1877, and its elder daughter was the right age. Dudley’s marriage, probably before 1880 in Tuscaloosa or Hale County, would tell which girl she was.

Annie settled part of the question herself. When she applied for a Texas widow's pension in 1914 she gave her birthday as 15 September 1846. Larkin's Ann E. was four in the summer of 1850 and Amanda thirteen in August 1860, exactly right for that birthday, while Stephen's Sarah A. E. was already nine in 1850. And when Dudley Logan took out his licence in April 1866, his bride was Miss Sarah A. E. Wedgworth, a single woman, not the young Mrs. Harkee. What still does not fit is the name: the girl in Larkin's house was written down as Amanda, and the woman who married Dudley was Sarah Anne Elizabeth. So Larkin was very probably, but not certainly, Annie's father.

Larkin's own father is no longer a guess. In January 1844, a few months after James Wedgworth Sr. died, his widow Rachel made her mark on a will at Greene County. She owned nothing, she said, but what came to her as James's widow, and she wanted it to go to his descendants. She left two hundred dollars each to his daughters Rachel Carter, the wife of John Carter, and Sally McGee, the wife of Jonathan McGee, and to 'Larkin Wedgworth a son of my said late husband'. She left the same in trust for another daughter, Lucinda Lewis, and for a granddaughter, Sally Ann James Conner, so that their husbands could not touch it. The rest went to James's son Stephen and to his son-in-law Thomas B. Edmiston, whom she made her executors. A Wm. C. Logan was one of the three men who witnessed it. The family fought the will, and in December 1844 a Greene County jury upheld it.

So Larkin and Stephen, who came into Greene County as boys in 1820, were brothers, sons of the James Wedgworth buried in the Wedgeworth Cemetery. In 1830 James's household held two young men in their twenties and one in his late teens, just the ages of Stephen and Larkin. Rachel always wrote of 'my said late husband's' children, never her own, and she was probably his second wife. Larkin's mother is not yet known.

stories.title: New Prospect: Logans and Wedgworths on the same roads
stories.hook: Planters named Logan and Wedgworth both appear at New Prospect in a directory of Greene County, and the 1875 voter register at New Prospect, by then in Hale County, still has both names.

subject.name: Logan and Wedgworth families of Greene County

body: Greene County’s early settlers included planters named Logan and Wedgworth at New Prospect. An Isaac Logan, with the date 1818 beside his name, was a planter there, and Stephen Wedgworth and Larkin Wedgworth were planters at New Prospect in 1855 and 1856, in section 1 of township 21 north, range 3 east. These are the two Wedgworths of 1850, and the Isaac Logan may be the Isaac Logan, 70, born in South Carolina, who headed a large household in the county that year.

The Wedgeworth family was in Greene County long before 1850. Two James Wedgeworths, senior and junior, entered land at Old St. Stephens in December 1823, and Caroline married in 1824, Daniel in 1825, Jane in 1825 and Mary in 1826. Among the Logans, Zachary and James entered land in December 1823 and January 1824, and Isaac married Matilda McGehee in 1824. None of them can yet be tied to Dudley or Annie.

Alabama created Hale County in 1867 from parts of Greene and neighboring counties, and New Prospect became a precinct in it. Among those who took the voter registration oath there in 1875 were a John Logan, a farmer, on 5 June, and Diggs Wedgeworth, who worked for Mrs. Haley, on 29 June. Neither is known to be related to the Texas couple, but both surnames were still there a generation later.

New Prospect was probably home ground for both families, and Clement Logan’s land and the Wedgworths’ farms may have lain there. A Wedgeworth Cemetery lies near Mount Zion in Hale County, apparently not the one near Cook’s Store in Greene County, and who is buried in it is not known.

Snedecor wrote down how the county filled. In 1818 settlers came so fast that he gave up trying to name them all, but among those he did name were the Meriwethers near Springfield and the Logans near New Prospect. His directory adds a date for the Wedgworths: Stephen and Larkin both came in 1820, when Stephen was about eleven and Larkin about nine, so they came as boys in an older Wedgworth household. Who headed it is still unknown.

His map of 1856 shows the neighborhood. New Prospect sits where two roads cross, with Mount Zion Church and a Masonic hall at the crossing and Isaac Logan's name printed beside the village. North of it, toward the Black Warrior, lie the estate of Clem Logan, the land Clemens had left at his death two years before, Willis Logan's land, and the estate of W. C. Logan, Martha's son who had died before 1852. South, across Big Creek, Stephen Wedgworth and Larkin Wedgworth hold neighboring sections. When Dudley Logan and Sarah A. E. Wedgworth were married at Mount Zion Church in April 1866, it was very probably this church, between the two families' fields.

stories.title: An Alabama Logan family at Mount Pleasant in 1860
stories.hook: Titus County had Alabama-born Logans before the war: in 1860 a J. H. Logan, 32, and his family, all born in Alabama, were living at Mount Pleasant.
body: Dudley Timothy Logan came to Titus County, it is said, from Greene County, Alabama. But an Alabama Logan family was already at Mount Pleasant before the war. Between 10 July and 15 September 1860, in Precinct 3, post office Mount Pleasant, the census taker W. S. Stephens counted J. H. Logan, 32, a farmer born in Alabama; N. A. Logan, 26, born in Alabama; M. J., 10, a girl; and P. H., 8, a boy. All four were born in Alabama, and the eldest child was born about 1850, so the parents may have come to Texas only in the last decade.

There was no Dudley Logan in Titus County in 1860, and none, aged 14, in Tuscaloosa County, though other Logans lived there, among them a Ben Logan household. In 1870 a William Logan, 45, born in South Carolina, was living in Titus County, and some of the Logans there in 1900 were Arkansas-born families.

That makes J. H. Logan a possible forerunner for Dudley, though nothing says so. He may have been an older brother or a cousin. He was born about 1828, eleven years after Clement Logan, 33 in 1850, of the Greene County household with a three-year-old Dudley. But nothing links them beyond their surname and state of birth, and the families may have been entirely separate.

Ten years earlier he is not among the Logans of Greene County. The households counted there in 1850, Isaac's, Zachry's, Martha's, Leroy's with Clement's family, Willis's, Lewis's, John L.'s and the widow Elizabeth's, hold no J. H. of about twenty-two, and neighboring Pickens and Sumter counties have none either. The nearest fit is a James D. Logan, twenty-two and born in Alabama, at home in the household of Isaac Logan, seventy, of South Carolina: the right age and the right first initial, but not the right middle one. Zachry Logan's household had a Nancy A., nineteen, but she was a Logan by birth, and the N. A. Logan of 1860 was the wife. Whether James D. was the J. H. of Mount Pleasant, misread by one census taker or the other, is only a possibility.

stories.title: Another Whitfield household, a few doors from W. F.
stories.hook: In 1900 a Mississippi-born Whitfield with eight children lived a few doors from W. F. Whitfield in Monroe Township, Sevier County, and how the two men were related is not known.
body: A few doors from W. F. and Emma Whitfield in Monroe Township, Sevier County, Arkansas, the census taker Rufus J. Nelson wrote down a second Whitfield household in 1900. The head was a farmer born in May 1844 in Mississippi, aged 56, whose father and mother were both born in North Carolina; his initials are hard to read, and look like R. H. He owned his farm. His wife Rachel was born in June of about 1849 and was 50; she and both of her parents were born in Georgia.

Eight children follow, all single and at home. The oldest, Luther, was born in July 1870 in Mississippi and worked as a cattleman. Minnie, born October 1874, is the first child entered as born in Arkansas, and she taught school. After her come a son whose name is only initials, born March 1877 and entered as a mill owner; Daisy, born February 1879; a son whose name looks like Roth, born March 1881; Ollie, born April 1883; Manda, born January 1886; and John, born July 1888. Every child gives a Mississippi father and a Georgia mother. The birth places place the family’s move from Mississippi to Sevier County in the years between Luther’s birth in 1870 and Minnie’s in 1874.

W. F. Whitfield, four households earlier, was also born in Mississippi, in January 1868; his mother was Mississippi-born and his father’s birthplace was unknown. The two men were both Mississippi-born Whitfields living in the same township, and that is all that is certain. The older man’s own parents were born in North Carolina, so he could have been W. F.’s father only through a first marriage to a Mississippi-born woman of whom nothing is known, and that is a guess. He could as easily have been an uncle, a cousin or an unrelated neighbor.

Who W. F.’s parents were is still unknown. He was born somewhere in Mississippi about 1868, in a county that is not known; a marriage, an estate or the census of his Mississippi boyhood may one day name them.
So the neighborhood held another Whitfield family, but it brings Oliver Clinton Whitfield no nearer to proven parents; W. F. and Emma are still only probably his.
src: 1900 U.S. census, Sevier County, Arkansas, Monroe Township, ED 151, sheet 5A (W. F. Whitfield, lines 33–39) and sheet 5B (second Whitfield household, dwelling and family 87, lines 55–64); NARA T623 roll 76; Allen County Public Library microfilm scan, Internet Archive, images n385 and n386, examined 4 Nov 2026: https://archive.org/details/12thcensusofpopu0076unit/page/n386/

stories.title: Alonzo Box’s people
stories.hook: Alonzo Box was born in Arkansas in 1850 to an Alabama-born father and a Mississippi-born mother; who they were is still unknown, though other Box families lived in Van Zandt County.
body: Alonzo Box was born in December 1850 in Arkansas. His father was born in Alabama and his mother in Mississippi. His five children at home in 1900, all born in Texas, had an Arkansas-born father and a Mississippi-born mother. Emma’s father was born in Virginia and her mother in Mississippi, and Emma herself in Mississippi in July 1860. A family born in Arkansas in 1850 to an Alabama father and a Mississippi mother fits a move west along the usual route from Mississippi into Arkansas and then Texas, but who Alonzo’s parents were is not known.

His neighbors in Justice Precinct No. 6 were no kin that can be seen. The households around Alonzo’s were named Vance, Hanks, Hill, Reeves, Carter, Wright, Cade, Jackson, Malone, Maxfield and Tunnell. The only name nearby that looks like Box belonged to a merchant, a Texas-born man of 33 with Georgia-born parents, whose surname reads as Boon or Bonn. No relative of Alonzo’s lived among them.
Where Alonzo and Emma were living in 1880, with their first young children, is not known; Alonzo may have been counted under another form of his name.

Other Box families lived in the county. A Thomas Box was among the jurors summoned for the district court around Buffalo on 12 November 1849, in the court that served Henderson County, from which Van Zandt was cut, as Wentworth Manning recalled in 1919. In 1880 James R. Box, born in Alabama, was living at Colfax, a community in the county, with his wife Sarah M. and six children: Charlie O., Mattie E., Mary E., Lou M., William B. and Ada T. Colfax remembered its Box families as John, Booster, Bill, Cranfil, Elliot, Dr. John, Jim and Terrell Box, with a W. J. Box among its Masonic officers, and Miss A. M. Box married H. D. Fountain there in 1895, as Jack Geddie wrote in his 1963 history of the community.

None of this ties Alonzo to anyone. James R. Box was born in Alabama, like Alonzo’s father, but when is not known, and Alonzo was born in Arkansas. The Terrell Box of Colfax may have been the Terrell Inge Box of Canton who registered for the draft in 1942, a man not in Alonzo’s household who may have belonged to this Colfax family. Alonzo himself is not remembered in either history, and when the Colfax Boxes lived there is not said. For now Alonzo and Emma are the end of the line.
src: 1900 U.S. census, Van Zandt County, Texas, Justice Precinct No. 6, ED 134, sheets 4A, 4B and 5A, enumerated 8 and 9 June 1900 by Wm. B. Tunnell, Alonzo Box household at lines 54–61 of sheet 4B; NARA T623 roll 1675; Internet Archive, images n724 to n726, examined 4 Nov 2026: https://archive.org/details/12thcensusofpopu1675unit/page/n725/

stories.title: Esther Voris and one Brazoria household in 1950
stories.hook: Esther Voris is known only from her half of a headstone at Alvin; in 1950 a Voris household lived in Brazoria County, and whether it was her family is unknown.

subject.name: Esther Voris Livesay
subject.rel: Lester W. Livesay Sr.’s second wife

body: Almost all that is known of Esther Voris Livesay is carved on one stone. The double marker for Lester W. Livesay Sr. in the Confederate Cemetery at Alvin reads “Esther Voris, Aug. 9, 1910,” with no death year. Her surname, her birth date and a place within a few miles of Alvin are all there is. Her parents, brothers and sisters are unknown, and Voris is taken as her maiden name only because the stone gives it that way.

In 1950 at least one Voris household was living in Brazoria County. On or after 7 April 1950 Lester E. Voris, head, white, male, 38, married, born in Texas, working as a body mechanic in a garage, was counted with his wife, Ruby J., 30, also born in Texas, somewhere near an airport road and a highway; the town is not named.

Lester E. Voris was the right age to be a brother, cousin or other relative of a woman born in 1910, and he lived in the county where she is buried. That is all. His age means a birth about 1911 or 1912, so he could not have been an older brother, and nothing links him to Esther or to the Livesays. Other Voris families lived in Harris County.

When Esther died, the details of her marriage, said to have been in 1942, and the family she grew up in are all unknown; she is said to have been born in Alvin, but that too is unproved. Until more is known, her parents are unknown.

stories.title: Beaucoup in 1879: a post office, a store and Logan Livesay’s sawmill
stories.hook: By 1879 Beaucoup was also a little railroad village, laid out only in 1870, with one store, a post office and a sawmill run by a Logan Livesay, a man otherwise unknown.

subject.name: The village of Beaucoup
subject.rel: Home settlement of the Livesay and Walker families

body: The Beaucoup of the 1820s was a timber settlement, with its Methodist camp ground, its cemetery, Robert Livesay’s land and Rev. James Walker’s farm at the Rock Chimney. Fifty years later there was a second Beaucoup, the railroad village. It lay on the St. Louis and South-eastern railroad, four miles east of Nashville in Ashley precinct, and had been laid out in 1870 by James Garvin and Daniel Hay as proprietors. By 1879 it had a post office, one store, kept by E. Patterson, and a sawmill belonging to Logan Livesay.

So by 1879 the name Beaucoup belonged to two places: the old timber settlement on Beaucoup Creek, where the Whittenburgs, Whites, Livesays, Lyons, Henrys, Carters, Rev. James Walker and others had made it the strongest settlement in the county by numbers, and a village nine years old. A post office named Beaucoup is said to have been open from 1815 to 1957, which is odd for a village platted in 1870, but the office clearly long outlived the plat. Its postmaster in 1879 was probably E. A. Patterson, railroad express agent, postmaster and merchant at Beaucoup, who with his wife was counted among the old settlers, and who would be the E. Patterson of the store.

The sawmill is the surprise. Robert Livesay’s sons, as the family remembered them, were William Edmund, Lorenzo Mastin, Jackson Monroe, David Pinkney and others, and there was no Logan among them. Lorenzo Dow Livesay died in 1876 and so cannot have been the miller of 1879, and Lorenzo Mastin Livesay, who also died in 1876, was farming in Jefferson County, Illinois, in 1860 and 1870. Logan may have been a nickname or a middle name of one of these men, or of a son or nephew of the next generation, or the name may have been set down wrongly. There was no Logan among the Livesay households near Beaucoup in 1855. The family did have a Logan tie, since Robert’s daughter Unity Jane married James L. Logan, but that says nothing about the miller.

Whose son the miller was is not known, and no Logan Livesay is known in the county in 1870 or 1880. But a Livesay was running a mill at Beaucoup in 1879, and the Walker farm and the camp ground lay in the same timber, so the families that had arrived in the 1820s were still at Beaucoup, in business as well as on the church rolls, a generation after the first settlers.
quotes: It contains at the present (1879) a Post Office, one store, by E. Patterson, and a saw-mill, by Logan Livesay. (History of Washington County, 1879)

stories.title: Anderson in the gas boom: Vine Street and a strawboard mill
stories.hook: In 1893 James T. McCormack lived on Vine Street in Anderson, Indiana, a town built in a few years on natural gas, with a strawboard mill on First Street and neighbors who worked in it.
body: In 1893 James T. McCormack was a teamster for the “A S P Co,” living at the corner of Vine and First, and around him a boom town was rising. That year Anderson’s directory makers counted 8,114 names, reduced them to 6,166 after firms and duplicates, and multiplied by three to put Anderson at 18,498 people, counting Park Place and North Anderson. It was a publisher’s estimate, not a census, but it gives the size of the town where Sadah was born in August 1893.

Natural gas had made the town. The Anderson Natural Gas and Oil Company and the Citizens’ Gas Company were both incorporated in 1887, with capital of $20,000 and $50,000. A Columbia Encaustic Tile Company followed in 1889 and the Anderson Paper Company in 1892 with $200,000. There were also the Anderson Land and Gas Company, the Hazlewood Gas Company, the North Anderson Gas Company, the East Lynne Gas Company, a Gas Belt Supply Company and a maker of gas regulators, along with a long run of gas fitters. Gas companies, glass and tile works and mills sat side by side.

His employer is a small mystery. No firm of those initials is known in town. But Vine Street was a mill street. The American Straw Board Company, general manager M. R. Williams and superintendent F. Millspaugh, made straw board on the north side of First Street, west of Milton, and its workers lived close by. H. H. Coburn, an engineer for the company, lived at 84 North Vine, and Clemens Herricks, who worked there, lived on the south side of First Street, three doors east of Vine. A teamster who lived at Vine and First, at the end of the street, could well have hauled straw and board for that mill. The initials do not obviously stand for the American Straw Board Company, so this is only a possibility, and “A S P” may have been some other firm.

What the directory does show is how McCormack’s world looked in 1893. His house stood in a street of workers, his likely employer one of several firms burning cheap gas, and the town was growing fast in the year Sadah was born. By the June 1900 census the family was farming in Stony Creek Township, and by April 1910 it was in Brazoria County, Texas, so the Anderson years were brief.
quotes: McCormack James T, teamster, ASP Co, h. cor Vine and 1st (Anderson directory, 1893–4)

stories.title: Eagle, Bok Tuklo and Towson: the Choctaw counties in the family’s papers
stories.hook: The Merry and Durant papers name three counties of the old Choctaw Nation, and the towns where later generations registered and were buried, Valliant and Millerton, lay in the same country.

subject.name: Choctaw Nation counties
subject.rel: Merry, Durant, Clay and Box families

body: Before 1907 the Choctaw Nation was divided into three districts and many counties, each with a judge, a sheriff and a clerk, and every Dawes card gave a person’s county. Louis Merry and Bessie were on the 1896 Choctaw roll in Eagle County, as numbers 14822 and 8644. Bessie’s parents, Peter and Ellen Durant, were of Bok Tuklo County, and so was her grandmother Wilsey Clay, while Wilsey’s own parents, Joe and Patsey Cahn, were of Eagle County. Ben Durant, Bessie’s brother, was on the 1896 roll twice, once in Blue County and once in Bok Tuklo.

The wedding was in Bok Tuklo County: the clerk who issued Louis’s license was clerk of that county until 1 October 1896. Eagle County lay along the Arkansas line, with Eagletown as its seat, and bordered Bok Tuklo on the east; Bok Tuklo was named for Lukfata Creek and Yasho Creek, and its seat was a meeting ground called Oak Hill. Both lay in the Apukshunnubbee District. So the two counties in the Merrys’ papers were neighbors, which fits a couple married at Lukfata but enrolled in Eagle County.

Nashoba County lay to the north of both, and an old puzzle may touch it. In 1900 a witness said Peter Durant left “that part of the country” in 1877 or 1878, and his county was taken down as “Matoon County,” a name that matches no known Choctaw county. Nashoba was a neighbor of the two counties, but nothing says the witness meant it, and no Durant or Clay of the family is known in Nashoba County, so the question stays open.

The later family’s towns sit on the same ground. Valliant was founded on 2 June 1902 for the Arkansas and Choctaw Railway and then lay in Towson County, the next county west of Bok Tuklo; Tyro Box and his brothers registered there in 1942. Tyro’s home was at Millerton, near Wheelock, and Wheelock Academy is three miles east of it. Violet Whitfield was killed in 1962 on the Oak Hill road near Golden; the old county seat of Bok Tuklo was a place named Oak Hill, but whether the road took its name from it is not known. After statehood in 1907 the counties disappeared, and the Bok Tuklo country now lies within McCurtain County.

stories.title: Esther Sandridge and Steele’s Creek, 1909
stories.hook: On a May afternoon in 1909 Clinton Sandridge’s first wife drowned in Steele’s Creek near Prescott, trying to save a five-year-old boy.
body: Clinton Sandridge’s first wife, Esther Margaret Bolls, died in 1909 and was buried at Midway Cemetery near Prescott, in Nevada County, Arkansas. On the afternoon of Monday, 10 May 1909, “Mrs. Clint Sandridge” drowned in Steele’s Creek, about three miles west of Prescott near the Washington road, while trying to save a five-year-old boy, August Dierks Jr.

The Nevada County Picayune of 13 May gives the fullest account. Mrs. Sandridge and Mrs. W. H. Siders had taken about eight small children to the creek to fish and had split into two groups. The Dierks boy fell into the water near Mrs. Sandridge, and she waded in after him. Instead of turning back the way she had come, she tried to cross the stream and was soon over her head. Mrs. Siders heard the screams and ran to them with a fishing pole, but could not pull them out, and both went down. One of the older boys ran to the mill to raise the alarm, and a crowd recovered the bodies and carried them home.

Both Prescott papers place the two families at the Ozan Lumber Company. The Picayune calls Clint a carpenter for the company. The Prescott Daily News of 11 May says he worked in the mill’s carpenter gang, that the boy’s father, August Dierks, was its foreman, and that both families lived in the western suburbs of Prescott. The accounts differ on the hour: the Daily News first says about one o’clock and later about four, while the Picayune and a Prescott dispatch printed in the Washington Telegraph and the Mena Weekly Star say four. The water was six to eight feet deep.

The Picayune added the detail that matters most for the family: “Mrs. Sandridge was a daughter of the late lamented H. C. Bolls,” and she left a husband and three children. The Daily News said one of the three was an infant. She was buried at Midway on Tuesday evening, and the boy at DeAnn Cemetery. None of the notices printed her given name, but the husband, the Midway burial, the year, the three young children and the Bolls name all fit Esther Margaret Bolls Sandridge. Her father had died before May 1909; nothing more is known of H. C. Bolls.

The death was remembered beyond the family. A week later the Picayune’s correspondent at Artesian wrote that it had been a sad day in the community when Mrs. Clint Sandridge and little August Derks were “called away so suddenly.” On 13 December 1909 the Prescott Daily News reported that the Carnegie Hero Fund Commission was making inquiries about the drowning of Mrs. Sandridge, “who gave her life in an effort to save” the boy. Whether the commission made an award is not known.
Her three children were Clinton Everett, called Chat, then about seven; Nobie, about five; and Mildred, the infant. Thirteen months after the drowning, on 19 June 1910, Clinton married Maggie.

stories.title: Everett, Nobie and Mildred in Prescott, 1915–1916
stories.hook: Six years after their mother drowned, Clinton Sandridge’s older children were on the Prescott school honor rolls, and at Christmas 1916 they wrote to Santa Claus.
body: After Esther Sandridge drowned in May 1909, Clinton married Maggie in June 1910, and Lemuel was born in December 1911, at Prescott, it is said. The family stayed in Prescott for several more years, and Esther’s children did well at school.

In January 1915 Everette Sandridge was among the first-honor pupils of the first grade at the grammar school, and Nobie Sandridge among the first-honor pupils of the second grade. In March both were on the honor rolls again, Everett now on the second-honor list, and Everett was there again in April and in December 1915.

At Christmas 1916 the Daily News printed children’s letters to Santa Claus. Mildred Sandridge asked for “a tablet and a doll and an apple that is good.” Everett Sandridge asked for ten packages of firecrackers, ten Roman candles, a bicycle, a freight train, a jumping jack, an air gun, a football and a Christmas book. The letters ran on 12, 14 and 16 December.

Everett, Nobie and Mildred were the names of Clinton and Esther’s three children, and in 1909 Mrs. Clint Sandridge had left three children, one an infant. No other Sandridge children are known in Prescott in those years, so these were probably Clinton’s children, though no parent is named. Lemuel, Maggie’s son, was too young to appear. By February 1918 Clinton was working at a lumber mill in Malvern, and in 1919 he moved to McCurtain County. What became of Nobie is not known, nor even whether Nobie was a son or a daughter.
