stories.title: Lon and Clint Sandridge, from Prescott to the Moline mill
stories.hook: Through the 1910s Clinton Sandridge and Lon Sandridge, very probably his brother, lived and worked side by side, first in Prescott and then at the Moline mill in Malvern.
body: When Clinton Sandridge died in 1961 he left a brother, Lon, of Little Rock. A Lon P. Sandridge (1889–1974) is remembered among the sons of William D. and Mary E. Sandridge of Beirne, Clark County, with Clinton, Joseph Burton and Lawrence Lafayette. And in the same years as Clint, a Lon Sandridge, and a Burton Sandridge, were living in Prescott.

In February 1908 the Prescott Daily News printed the results of a school examination, and Burton Sandridge scored 92 in the seventh grade. That September the Daily Picayune reported, under the heading “Soldier Arrested,” that Lon Sandridge had been arrested for wearing government clothes. When he was taken before J. B’Shers for trial, First Sergeant Garland Leverett dropped the case once Sandridge turned over all the government property he had. On 27 March 1912 the Daily News announced that Lon P. Sandridge and Miss Willie Denson had been married on the Saturday afternoon before, at the home of the bride’s parents, Mr. and Mrs. Jim Denson, by Squire B’Shers.

By 1917 Lon was in Malvern, the seat of Hot Spring County. On 14 June 1917 the Malvern Times-Journal printed the names of the men registering for the draft in the county, and “Sandridge, Lon P.” is under Ward Four of Malvern, a few names after “Denson, Thomas Monroe.” In January 1918 the paper listed Lon P. Sandridge of Malvern, number 756, among the registrants to whom the local exemption board was mailing questionnaires.

Clint was in Malvern too. On 16 February 1918 the Malvern Daily Record listed the Christmas Red Cross members from the town’s industrial plants. Under the Moline Lumber Company it gives “Lon Sandridge $1; C. L. Sandridge $1,” with Monroe Denson and J. M. Denson among the D’s. On 28 February the Times-Journal printed the Moline employees who had given to the Salvation Army fund: L. P. Sandridge, Monroe Denson and J. M. Denson near the top, and “Clint Sandridge 50c” further down. In 1909 Clint had been a carpenter at the Ozan mill in Prescott; in 1918 he and Lon were on the same mill’s lists.

No one in those years called Lon and Clint brothers or named their parents. But they shared a working life: the same two towns in the same years, the same mill, and the Denson family moving with them. So Lon was very probably the brother Clinton’s family remembered. In 1961 there was also a brother “L. P.” in California, and since the Malvern lists use both “Lon” and “L. P.” for what looks like one Moline worker, which initials belonged to which brother is uncertain. That William D. and Molly Cole Sandridge were the brothers’ parents is still unproved.

stories.title: William A. Nelson’s first family, Little River County, 1900
stories.hook: Sixteen years before he married Julia Myers, William A. Nelson was farming just across the line in Arkansas with a wife named Francis and two small daughters.
body: William A. Nelson married Julia Myers at Idabel in 1916, when he was forty-six, and his 1920 household held children who were not Julia’s. He is remembered with an older daughter, Rosa Isabel Nelson Flowers, born in 1894. Sixteen years before that marriage, in 1900, he was farming in Lick Creek Township, Little River County, Arkansas.

William A. Nelson was the head of the household, a white man of 29, born in May 1871 in Arkansas and married seven years. He farmed on rented land and could read and write. He gave his father’s birthplace as Texas and his mother’s as Mississippi. His wife, written “Francis E.,” was 29, born in April 1871 in Mississippi to parents from South Carolina. She had borne three children, two of them living: Rosa B., born in August 1894 in Texas, and Minnie M., born in December 1897 in Texas.

A fifth person, Harriet McLaren, about 70, born in Maryland, may also have lived with them as William’s mother-in-law. But her Maryland birthplace does not agree with the South Carolina birthplace given for Francis’s mother, so whether Francis was born a McLaren is doubtful.

This was probably the William of Redland. The name and initial, the birth month, the Arkansas birthplace and a daughter Rosa born in 1894 all fit, and Little River County has McCurtain County, Oklahoma, on its western side and Bowie County, Texas, on its southern. Two details differ. In 1900 his birth was given as 1871, where his stone has 1870, and Rosa’s middle initial as B., where she is remembered as Rosa Isabel.

The household explains part of the later story. Married about 1893, William and Francis had their first children in Texas and were in Arkansas by 1900. What became of Francis is not known. Homer E. Nelson, born in 1902 and remembered among Julia’s children in 1956, was probably born after 1900, but who his mother was is not known. For Audrey, born in 1917, Rosa and Minnie were half-sisters more than twenty years older. William said his father was born in Texas, which may or may not fit the Aaron Burr Nelson (1815–1888) he is said to have been the son of.

stories.title: Julia Stevens and Charley Ratcliff, neighbors in 1950
stories.hook: Four months before they married, the census taker found Julia Stevens and Charley Ratcliff living a few doors apart in Broken Bow.
body: Julia went by the surnames Myers, Nelson, Stevens and at last Ratcliff. On 19 August 1950, in Arkansas, Julia Ann Stevens, 76, married Charles M. Ratcliff, both of Broken Bow, and she died in 1956 as Mrs. C. M. Ratcliff. That April, four months before the wedding, the census taker found the two living a few doors apart.

On 4 April 1950 the census taker in Broken Bow found Charley M. Ratcliff, 68, white, widowed, born in Missouri, living alone. Three doors further on lived Julia A. Stevens, 76, white, widowed, born in Texas, also alone. Neither was working that week. Her surname has sometimes been read as “Stevend,” but it was Stevens.

That spring adds two small facts to Julia’s life. Her age, 76 in April, fits her birth on 17 November 1873 and her age at the August wedding, and so weighs against the 72 printed at her death. And she was described as widowed, where in 1930 she had been divorced. Whether a former husband had died in the meantime, or whether this was simply how Julia chose to describe herself, is not known.

Charley Ratcliff was born in Missouri about 1881 or 1882 and was already a widower by 1950; his first wife is not known. Julia was his neighbor that spring and his wife by August, and she died in 1956 as Mrs. C. M. Ratcliff. Her daughter Audrey was living elsewhere in Broken Bow with Lemuel and their sons.

stories.title: Three sets of Arkansas parents, still unproved
stories.hook: Clinton Sandridge’s parents, Maggie Sandridge’s and William Nelson’s father are all remembered by name, but none of them can yet be placed in Arkansas when the children were small.

subject.name: Clinton Sandridge, Maggie Sandridge and William Nelson

body: Three of the family’s Arkansas parents are known only from memory. Clinton Sandridge’s parents are said to have been William D. Sandridge and Mary E. “Molly” Cole, Maggie Sandridge’s James L. Cash and Maxie Ann McClure Cash, and William Nelson’s father Aaron Burr Nelson. None of them is yet proved, and none can yet be placed in an Arkansas household of 1880 or 1900.

No W. D. or William D. Sandridge is known at the head of an Arkansas household in 1880 or 1900. Molly Sandridge died in 1897, it is said, and by 1900 Clinton was about eighteen, so the family may have been split up, living in another household, written under a misspelled surname, or out of the state. That does not disprove the family tradition; it only leaves it unconfirmed.

In 1900 there was a James L. Cash in Arkansas, but he does not fit. He was 41, born in November 1858 in Arkansas, and lived in Caddo Township, Clark County, with his wife Martha J. and children Christina, a daughter whose name looks like Rita, Maggie L., born in January 1893, and three sons. Maggie Sandridge’s gravestone gives 2 May 1891 and the initial A., and her mother is remembered as Maxie Ann. No J. L. Cash fits either. Curiously, this household was in Clark County, where Clinton was born, but nothing ties it to him. Whether Maggie was born a Cash is still unknown, and her birthplace was Texas in 1930 and Arkansas in 1950.

No Aaron Nelson is known at the head of an Arkansas household with young children in 1880. William would have been ten that June, and in 1900 he said his father was born in Texas. Either the family was outside Arkansas in 1880, or William was living in someone else’s household. Whether Aaron Burr Nelson was his father is still unknown.

The answers may lie in Clark County, where Beirne lies, or among the Nelsons of Texas. Even Clinton and Maggie’s wedding in June 1910 passed without a word in the Prescott Daily News that week, between the 18th and the 22nd.

stories.title: Three doors, one family: Flannigan, Dolson and the widow White, 1850
stories.hook: On 8 August 1850 the Jefferson County census taker went from Thomas and Patsy Flannigan’s door to Allen Dolson’s and then to a house where Sarah White, 74, lived with the elder Dolsons. Patsy and Mrs. Dolson were, it seems, a Methodist preacher’s daughters, and Sarah was probably his widow. In Patsy’s house were also her two motherless Copple granddaughters and Tabitha J., a probable daughter.

subject.name: Martha “Patsy” White Flannigan and her family

body: On 8 August 1850 the census taker Robert Wingate came to Thomas A. and Patsy Flannigan’s house in Jefferson County, Illinois, where Thomas, 54, born in North Carolina, lived with Patsy, 48, born in Georgia, and with Tabitha J., 20, James R., 18, and Maria, 16, all three born in Illinois. After them came two small girls with a different surname, Amanda Copple, 4, and Martha L. Copple, one month old; who they were is told below. Next door was Allan Dalson, 45, a farmer born in New York, with Mary L., 40, born in Georgia, and eight children, among them Sarah, 20, Robert W., 19, Elizabeth, 16, Melville, 14, Mary J., 12, Christina, 10, William, 5, and Issac H., 3. Next to them lived Sarah White, 74, born in North Carolina, with Peter Dalson, 75, and Rachel, 73, both born in New York. Three doors before the Flannigans he had counted James C. Baldridge, 38, with Tabitha, 39, born in Illinois, and ten children under the surnames Casey and Baldridge.

The families’ own histories put names on these households. James C. Baldridge married Mrs. Tabitha Casey, widow of Isaac Casey and daughter of Robert White, on 8 January 1846; Robert White was born in South Carolina and came to Madison County, Illinois, in 1810; Tabitha was born on 10 July 1811 in Chambers’ Fort; and her mother, Sarah Holt, was a native of North Carolina who was “married in Georgia,” as Baldridge’s sketch in the 1883 History of Jefferson County tells it. In 1909 the sketch of the Baldridges’ son George Pliney Baldridge, in Brinkerhoff’s History of Marion County, named the children of Rev. Robert White, a Methodist Episcopal minister with a large circuit: Robert, who was drowned in Madison County; Martha White, who married Thomas Flannigan and had a daughter Martha, who became the wife of Eli Copple; Louisa White, who married Allen Dolson and had a daughter Sarah, who became Eli Copple’s second wife; and Tabitha White, who married Isaac Casey and then James Clark Baldridge.

Everything agrees. A North Carolina widow of 74, born about 1776, fits Sarah Holt, and she lived next door to Louisa, two doors from Patsy. Patsy, born in Georgia, and Mary L. Dalson, also born in Georgia, fit daughters of a mother who was married in Georgia, and Tabitha, born in Illinois in 1811, a year after the family’s arrival, fits too. Eli Copple remembered Allen Dolson in 1909 as a native of New York, a son of Peter and Rachael (Quinby) Dolson, both New Yorkers, with a wife born in Georgia, exactly the birthplaces of 1850. His list of Dolson children (Sarah, Robert, Elizabeth, Melville, Mary, Christina, William and Harvey) overlaps the children of 1850, and Harvey may be the Issac H., 3, of 1850. Sarah Dalson, 20, fits the Sarah Dolson whose Gilead stone gives 8 December 1829. Ten years earlier, in 1840, Thos. A. Flanagan, J. C. Baldridge, Peter Dolson and Allen Dolson were already neighbors.

Most of them lie together at Gilead. Tabitha Baldridge (10 July 1811 to 13 April 1899) and James C. Baldridge (10 December 1811 to 16 May 1897) are there, with dates that match both sketches; so is a “White, Rev. R.,” who died on 14 May 1828 aged about 55; Thos. H. Flannigan, who died on 28 January 1853, and Martha Flennigen, “w/o Thomas,” who died on 9 July 1862; Martha Copple, who died on 1 June 1850; and Mary A. Casey Noleman (6 June 1836 to 8 February 1911), who fits the Mary A. Casey, 14, in Tabitha’s household in 1850. The Whites, Baldridges, Copples and Flannigans share one burial ground in Grand Prairie Township.

A few things are still uncertain. The stone of Rev. R. White is his only by the initial, the title and the township. The two family accounts of his earlier life differ, the one of 1883 placing him in South Carolina and Madison County, the one of 1909 early in Indiana before Marion County. In 1909 Thomas Flannigan is given no initial and Martha is never called “Patsy,” and no one in 1850 wrote down how the neighbors were related, so Sarah White, 74, is known only by her name, age, birthplace and neighbors. What became of Sarah is not known, and no grave for her is known at Gilead. The Georgia births come earlier than the Indiana years of Rev. Robert’s “early life” in the 1909 sketch, but the two need not conflict. And since no one names Martha and Louisa’s mother, only Tabitha can be called Sarah’s daughter with confidence.

The two small Copple girls were Thomas and Patsy’s motherless granddaughters. Eli Copple, son of David Copple of Marion County, was born on 8 June 1820 in Washington County, Indiana, and in 1840 married “Miss Martha Flanagan.” They had two daughters who grew up, Arminda, later Mrs. William Dolson, and Loretta, later Mrs. A. J. Hartley, and three more children who died in infancy, as their son Elmer’s family remembered in 1909. Martha, of Jefferson County, Illinois, died in 1850 and lies at Gilead as “Copple, Martha, 6-1-1850, w/o E,” beside Eli (8 June 1820 to 14 August 1905) and his second wife, Sarah Dolson (8 December 1829 to 24 October 1915). A baby counted at one month old on 8 August 1850 would have been born in early July, after her mother’s death on 1 June, so the dates do not quite fit; the girls are matched by place, age and the loss of their mother, not by name, Amanda being probably Arminda and Martha L. probably Loretta, left in their grandparents’ house.

So the household of 1850 had an identity. Its head was the Thomas Flannigan whose wife Martha was a daughter of Rev. Robert White, and whose daughter Martha, Eli Copple’s wife, died on 1 June 1850. Tabitha J. was in the household but is never mentioned in the families’ histories. She was twenty, born in Illinois, the right age to be another daughter, and the stone of Tabitha J., wife of David P. Livesay, who died on 14 February 1856 aged 27, stands among the Flannigan stones. With her maiden name said to have been Flannigen, that makes her a probable daughter of Thomas and Martha. Whether she was Floyd Livesay’s mother is still unknown. Thomas’s middle initial was A in 1850 and is H on his stone.

Grand Prairie Township had no town and no railroad in 1883; its first church society was organized at the Widow Gaston’s by Rev. Samuel Walker, a pioneer Methodist minister, and the Gilead Methodist Episcopal church on section 5 was the only church building. That Walker is not known to be related to the Walkers of Beaucoup.

stories.note: Probable. The census page, the two county sketches and the Gilead stones agree on names, birthplaces, ages and neighbors, and nothing contradicts them, but no single record says that the census’s Patsy Flannigan and Sarah White were the daughter and widow of Rev. Robert White. The sketches are compiled county biographies written decades after the events. Rev. Robert White, Sarah Holt, Tabitha, James C. Baldridge, Louisa, Allen Dolson and Sarah Dolson Copple are added with the links the sources support. Probable. Four independent printed accounts and the cemetery list agree that Eli Copple’s first wife was Martha Flannigan of Jefferson County, who died in 1850, and the Brinkerhoff sketch gives her parents; the Copple girls in the 1850 household are matched by place, age and the 1 June 1850 death, not by name (Amanda and Martha L. against Arminda and Loretta). Patsy’s father, Rev. Robert White, rests on one sketch and the cemetery’s “Rev. R. White.” Tabitha J.’s link to Thomas and Martha rests on the household, the shared cemetery and the age; no record names her parents. Eli’s birth is given differently by the 1909 Elmer Copple sketch. Thomas’s middle initial is A in the census and H on the stone. The tree does not link Tabitha to Floyd Livesay.

stories.title: Was Tabitha a Flannigan? A namesake aunt three doors away
stories.hook: In 1850 Tabitha J. was living in Thomas and Patsy Flannigan’s house, with an aunt named Tabitha three doors away, and she lies among the family at Gilead; she was probably their daughter.
body: Tabitha J. Livesay lies at Gilead as the “wife of David P. Livesay.” Her maiden name is said to have been Flannigen or Flannigan, and a Thomas H. Flannigan and a Martha Flennigen, “w/o Thomas,” lie near her. She died on 14 February 1856 aged 27 years, 2 months and 4 days, which puts her birth about 10 December 1828. On 8 August 1850 the census taker Robert Wingate listed household 443 in Jefferson County: Thomas A. Flannigan, 54, a farmer born in North Carolina; Patsy, 48, born in Georgia; Tabitha J., 20; James R., 18, a farmer; and Maria, 16, all three born in Illinois. Two Copple children, Amanda, 4, and Martha L., one month old, were also in the house, and two of the households just before it were Baldridges, a family well represented among the Gilead stones. Four things bear on whether Tabitha was their daughter.

The first is how well the household fits the stones. A woman born in December 1828 would have been 21 in August 1850, a year more than she was given. Thomas H. Flannigan died on 28 January 1853 at 58 years and 11 days, so he was born in January 1795, within a year of his age of 54. Patsy was the usual nickname for Martha, and Martha Flennigen, “wife of Thomas,” died on 9 July 1862. Only Thomas’s middle initial, A in 1850 and H on the stone, does not agree, perhaps a misreading of one or the other. A Thos. Flanagan had headed a Jefferson County household in 1830, and a Thos. A. Flanagan in 1840.

The second is the family of 1840. Thos. A. Flanagan’s household then held seven people: males, one under 5, one 5 to 10 and one 40 to 50; females, one 5 to 10, two 10 to 15 and one 30 to 40. Thomas, 54 in 1850, and Patsy, 48, would have been the man of 40 to 50 and the woman of 30 to 40. James R., 18, would have been 8, and Maria, 16, would have been 6. A girl of 20 in 1850 would have been about 10 in 1840, one of the two girls aged 10 to 15. There were also a boy under 5 and a second girl of 10 to 15 who were gone by 1850. No names were written down, so this shows only that the household of 1850 was the same family ten years on, and that a girl of Tabitha’s age was in it.

The third is a name. Patsy’s sister Tabitha White, born on 10 July 1811, was Mrs. James C. Baldridge, and in 1850 she lived three doors from the Flannigans. A girl named for her aunt is an ordinary pattern. It is not proof, but it is one more point of agreement, and nothing contradicts it. The fourth is the grave. Tabitha J. Livesay lies at Gilead among the Whites, Baldridges and Flannigans, in Jefferson County, and not with the Livesays of Beaucoup in Washington County, where David P. is buried.

Taken together, a Tabitha J. of the right age in the household, a girl of her age there in 1840, a namesake aunt next door and a grave among the family make Thomas and Martha Flannigan her probable parents. No one in 1850 wrote down how a household was related, so nothing says outright that Tabitha J. was Thomas and Patsy’s daughter, or that she bore any surname but theirs. Some gaps remain. Where and when she married David P. Livesay is not known; the Jefferson County marriages known to 1850, an incomplete list, do not include them. If she was their Tabitha, she married David P. Livesay between August 1850 and 1855, when a woman aged 20 to 30 was keeping house with D. P. Livesay in Washington County. She died in February 1856, and was buried among her own family at Gilead rather than with the Livesays at Beaucoup.

None of this reaches Floyd Livesay. Floyd’s headstone gives 5 February 1856, nine days before Tabitha’s death, and at his death in Texas his birth was given as 5 February 1857 with both parents unknown, so nothing calls Tabitha his mother. If the stone is right he was a newborn when she died, which fits the possibility but proves nothing, and Floyd’s parents are still unknown. Whether she was Floyd’s mother, and so whether Thomas and Patsy were Floyd’s grandparents, is still unknown.

stories.title: Eli Copple and two cousins: a widower’s second marriage at Grand Prairie
stories.hook: Eli Copple’s first wife was Patsy Flannigan’s daughter Martha, and his second was Martha’s cousin Sarah Dolson; he lived until 1905, a prosperous farmer who once brought Norman horses home from France.
body: Eli Copple was born in Washington County, Indiana, on 8 June 1820, as his stone at Gilead has it, though one account of his life gives 8 January. He was the son of the German-born David Copple and Lavina Huckleberry, and he was twelve when the family came to Marion County, Illinois, and settled on Seven Mile Prairie. His father gave him a quarter section of land when he started out. By 1909 he was remembered as thrifty and successful, at one time the owner of as much as two thousand acres, and as a man who in 1874 went to France and brought back a large number of Norman horses.

Eli Copple married Martha Flanagan on 5 December 1839, or in 1840 as his family remembered it: “Martha Flannagan, a native of Jefferson county, Illinois, who died in 1850.” She lies at Gilead as Martha Copple, “w/o E.,” with the date 1 June 1850. She was the daughter of Thomas Flannigan and Martha White, a daughter of Rev. Robert White, as the family of her cousin George Pliney Baldridge, son of Patsy Flannigan’s sister Tabitha, recalled in 1909. Two daughters grew up: Arminda, who married William Dolson, and Loretta, who married A. J. Hartley of Irvington.

On 8 August 1850 two Copple children were living in Thomas and Patsy Flannigan’s house: Amanda, 4, and Martha L., aged “1/12,” one month. The names are close enough to Arminda and Loretta to suggest the same girls. The dates do not quite fit. If Martha died on 1 June, a baby of one month on 8 August would have been born in early July, after her death. Either the day on the stone, the baby’s age or the birth date was set down wrongly, or the baby was a little older than the census taker wrote. The simplest reading is that Martha died in childbirth or soon after, and the girls’ grandparents took them in.

In February 1851 Eli married Sarah Dolson, the daughter of Allen and Mary Louisa (White) Dolson, and the cousin of his first wife, so the two wives were first cousins through the sisters Patsy and Louisa White. In 1850 Sarah, 20, had lived next door to the Flannigans, so Eli’s girls and his future wife were neighbors that summer. The couple had seven children: Charles, Mary, Julia, Willis, Elmer, Robert and Ada. Two of the daughters married Baldridges, which kept the Copples tied to the family on the other side of the White sisters. Eli died on 14 August 1905. His widow was living in Centralia Township in 1909, and a Sarah Copple, 8 December 1829 to 24 October 1915, lies beside him at Gilead.

stories.title: Lorenzo M. Livesay: a Webber Township sketch and two stones
stories.hook: Lorenzo M. Livesay came to Jefferson County in the fall of 1856, lost his wife Margaret in 1868, married again, and died in June 1876, remembered as “a faithful Methodist, and a useful, honest man.”
body: Lorenzo M. Livesay was born in Tennessee on 9 October 1825, came to Jefferson County in the fall of 1856 and died there on 6 June 1876. He was twice married, first to Margaret J. Thompson on 22 October 1845, by whom he had twelve children, of whom four were living in 1883: Mary C., Ephraim J., Elizabeth P. and Lafayette S. Margaret died on 28 October 1868, and on 16 May 1869 he married Sarah S. Lane, daughter of the late Henry Lane. She was born in Caldwell County, Kentucky, and came with her parents to Clinton County, Illinois, in 1840. In 1883 Webber Township remembered him in the county’s history as “a faithful Methodist, and a useful, honest man.”

Everything fits. He married Margaret Jane Thompson in Washington County on 22 October 1845. His arrival in the fall of 1856 fits his being in Jefferson County by June 1860, and his signing his father’s heirs’ release in Washington County in 1856. His second wife was the Sarah S., 36, born in Kentucky, of 1870. Mary C. and Elizabeth P. were at home in 1860 and 1870, Lafayette S. by 1870, and Ephraim J., 11 in 1860, was the eldest. Two 1870 children, Wilburn W. and Elva M., were not among the four living in 1883, so they probably died between those years. Margaret died in October 1868, and Lorenzo remarried seven months later. Ephraim’s Illinois birth about 1849 fits a start in Washington County, where Lorenzo married in 1845, before the move across the county line in 1856, and a birth in 1825 fits Lorenzo Mastin’s being about five when the family came to Illinois in 1830.

Lorenzo and Margaret lie in Black Oak Ridge Cemetery, Webber Township, section 28: “Livesay, Lorenzo M.” 3-9-1823 to 6-11-1876, and “Livesay, Margaret” 6-20-1828 to 10-28-1868. Margaret’s death date agrees exactly, and her birth year fits her age of 32 in 1860. Lorenzo’s dates do not. As read, they give a birth in 1823, in March or September depending on how the figures are taken, and a death on the 11th of June rather than the 6th. His ages of 34 in 1860 and 44 in 1870 and the family’s memory all point to 1825 or 1826, so 1823 is the odd one out. Why the death dates differ by five days is not known; both say June 1876.

Several Lanes lie in the same cemetery, among them Spencer Lane (1799 to 13 September 1888) and William M. Lane (8 January 1836 to 22 August 1898). In 1860 a William M. Lane, 24, a farmer born in Tennessee, with Mary A., 23, born in North Carolina, and a daughter, lived next door to Lorenzo. How these Lanes were related to Sarah Lane, whose family settled in Clinton County, is not known, and his Tennessee birth does not match her Kentucky one. Another Livesay couple lies at East Hickory Hill Cemetery in the same county, William G. (1827 to 1887, “Co. E 80 IL Inf.”) and Margaret (1829 to 1876), but they are not known to be related to Lorenzo. Of the twelve children, only those already named are known.

Two Livesay men named Lorenzo died in 1876, Lorenzo M. in Jefferson County in June and Lorenzo Dow in Kansas, and they were different men. An estate for an “L. M.” Livesay passed through the Washington County court, though when, and whose it was, is not known. Lorenzo M.’s own parents were not named in 1883.

stories.title: Lorenzo Dow Livesay of Virginia, told by his son Evan
stories.hook: An 1894 biography of a Washington County farmer named Evan Carter Livesay names his father, Lorenzo Dow, and his grandfather, John Livesay, and gives the birth year and the death place that the veterans’ list got wrong.
body: Lorenzo Dow Livesay was remembered among Washington County’s veterans as a son of John C. and Rebecca (Carter) Livesay, a Black Hawk War private, born about 1815 and died in 1876, though a birth about 1815 is hard to square with a land patent of 1831 and his household of 1855. His own son’s life story settles the date. In 1894 Evan Carter Livesay, of section 24, Ashley Township, Washington County, born near Nashville, Illinois, on 4 March 1830, the fourth child of Lorenzo Dow and Delilah (Mayse) Livesay, had his family’s story set down in the Portrait and Biographical Record of Clinton, Washington, Marion and Jefferson Counties.

His father, Evan said, was a native of Virginia who at twelve moved to Tennessee with his own father, John Livesay, and John’s father, Thomas, had come from England in 1748 and settled in Virginia. Lorenzo D. spent some years in Tennessee, came to Illinois in 1827 and settled near Nashville; later he went to Kansas, where he died in 1876. He was born in 1806, so he was about seventy when he died, and his wife died two years earlier. A birth in 1806 puts him at 25 at the 1831 patent and 26 in the Black Hawk War company of 1832. It makes him 48 or 49 in 1855, when L. D. Livesay’s household held one man aged 50 to 60 and a woman of 40 to 50, a year or two off. The woman fits Delilah.

Evan Carter Livesay farmed 115 acres, was a Methodist and a Populist, held school offices, and in 1849 married Martha D., daughter of John and Sarah (Coten) Carter, who came from South Carolina by way of Georgia and Tennessee to Illinois. They had nine children, two of whom had died by 1894. His middle name and his wife’s surname both recall the Carter families of the district, but nothing in the sketch ties Martha’s Carters to Livesay Carter.

The family’s story of its descent does not fit everything else. The Livesay Historical Society’s family file begins with a Thomas Livesay, born in Lancashire in 1730, married in 1749, with children born in England through 1757 and a first American record, a Pennsylvania deed of 1760. Evan’s Thomas arrived in 1748 and settled in Virginia. If he was the same Thomas, the year and the colony are off; if not, Evan’s Thomas is otherwise unknown. Evan, John’s grandson, and the veterans both name Lorenzo Dow’s father as John and place the family in Virginia and Tennessee, and a John Livesay and a Rebecca Carter did marry in Virginia and go to Tennessee, so Lorenzo Dow was probably John’s son. Evan named no grandmother, so whether Rebecca was Lorenzo’s mother is uncertain, and whether John was also Robert Livesay’s father is unproved.

Evan Carter Livesay farmed on section 24 of Ashley Township in Washington County. He was born near Nashville, Illinois, on 4 March 1830, the fourth child of Lorenzo Dow and Delilah (Mayse) Livesay. His father, a native of Virginia, left it at twelve to settle in Tennessee with his own father, John Livesay, and John’s father, Thomas by name, had come from England in 1748 and settled in Virginia. The England date was family tradition, as Evan had heard it, and nothing else bears it out.

Lorenzo Dow spent some years in Tennessee, moved to Illinois in 1827 and settled near Nashville, and later went to Kansas, where he died in 1876. He was born in 1806, so he was about seventy, and his wife died two years before him. Among the county’s veterans he was remembered as a Black Hawk War private, the son of John C. and Rebecca (Carter) Livesay, who died in 1876, though there his birth was guessed at about 1815. A birth in 1806 makes him twenty-six in the Black Hawk War of 1832, when a Lorenzo D. Livesay was among the privates of Captain James Burns’s company, and about forty-nine in 1855. A birth about 1815 was hard to square with the federal patent issued to Lorenzo D. Livesay in 1831. In 1855 L. D. Livesay’s house held six people, among them one man aged 50 to 60 and one woman aged 40 to 50; a man born in 1806 would have been a year or so short of that bracket, which is no worse than the fit with 1815.

Evan and the veterans agree on the man’s name, on Nashville and Washington County as his home, on a father named John and on a death in 1876, so they speak of one man, and Lorenzo Dow now has a wife and a son. In 1849 Evan married Martha D. Carter, daughter of John and Sarah (Coten) Carter, who had come from South Carolina to Georgia, then Tennessee, and finally Illinois. They had nine children, two of them dead by 1894, among them a son Lorenzo D. of Ashley, who had married first Alice McEnalley and then Alice Cundiff, and daughters in Pennsylvania and Chicago. Evan held 115 acres, voted with the Populists and served as a school officer, and his wife belonged to the Christian Church.

So Lorenzo was probably a son of John Livesay. John’s wife was named only by the veterans, as Rebecca Carter, so she is less certain. Nothing says that this John was the father of Robert Livesay of Beaucoup. John and Rebecca are remembered as moving from Virginia to Maury County, Tennessee, some time after 1809, and a Virginia departure about 1818 would fit, but a date that fits does not make two Johns one man. John’s place as Robert’s father is unproved.

Two cautions. Evan’s middle name Carter is tempting, because the Livesay and Carter families are said to have named sons for one another. But his wife was a Carter from a different line, nothing ties his mother, Delilah Mayse, to the Carters of Nashville, and a given name alone proves nothing. And Lorenzo Dow, who died in Kansas in 1876, must not be confused with Lorenzo M. Livesay, Robert’s son, who died in Jefferson County in the same year.

stories.title: Jackson L. Livesay: Robert’s grandson, Company C, and a Centralia store
stories.hook: Jackson L. Livesay, who enlisted at Richview on 20 March 1864, the same day as William P. Walker, was the eldest son of William E. and Emily (Goodner) Livesay, and so a grandson of Robert Livesay.
body: Jackson L. Livesay was born in “Washington, Illinois,” on 28 September 1845, the son of W. E. and Emily (Goodner) Livesay. William E. was a native of Tennessee who came to Illinois at seven with his parents, settled on a farm in Washington County and married Emily Goodner, of an Illinois family. In 1871 the family moved to Kansas to farm and keep a store; William E. died there in 1872 and Emily in 1874, and the family came back to Illinois in 1881. They raised eight children, five boys and three girls, and Jackson was the eldest. So Jackson remembered it in 1909, in his sixty-third year and a well-known figure in Centralia. William Edmund was born about 1823 in Maury County, Tennessee, and was about seven at the move in 1830; he married Emily Goodner on a license of 1 August 1844, and a first child in September 1845 fits. The Goodners were a large Washington County family, and who Emily’s parents were is not known.

Jackson went to the Beaucoup school, an old log school-house, and left at sixteen. On 20 March 1864 “Livesay, Jackson L.,” of Richview, enlisted in Company C of the 60th Illinois, together with “Walker, William P.,” also of Richview; both were mustered on 17 April 1864 and “Mustered out July 31, 1865.” Jackson was a farmer, 5 feet 6 inches tall with light hair and blue eyes, mustered in at Centralia and out at Louisville, Kentucky. He joined, he recalled, at Centralia in the spring of 1864, under Colonel William Anderson of Mount Vernon and “Capt. Simeon Walker, now at Carbondale, Illinois, in active service.” Simeon Walker, Etheldra Jane Walker’s husband and probably William P. Walker’s brother-in-law, was the company’s captain from December 1862 to March 1865. Jackson followed Sherman to the sea, was mustered out at Louisville and came home in August 1865 with the First Brigade, Second Division, Fourteenth Army Corps. A John W. Livesay of Washington County had enlisted in the same company on 29 August 1862 and was discharged for disability on 16 February 1865; whether he was kin to Jackson is not known.

Jackson’s words about his old captain bear on a puzzle. Simeon Walker is said to have died on 11 October 1909, or on 29 April 1905. If he was still “in active service” when Jackson spoke in 1909, the later date is likelier, though a present tense in print can be stale, and the question stays open.

After the war Jackson took up a claim in Kansas in 1866 for a short time, returned to Washington County for two years, clerked at Richview for J. V. Holcomb & Co. for a year, and with his uncle William Shanks bought the firm out and moved the stock to Montana and Kansas, where they stayed eight years. They then farmed for three years, came back to Richview and, after three months, settled at Centralia. There he worked for several firms for twenty years and then eleven years for himself, at a store at 103 South Locust Street, eighty feet by twenty-four. He married Emma Ingram, daughter of H. P. Ingram and Millie Tyler of Richview, on 12 June 1871, and they had nine children, six boys and three girls. One daughter, Ruby, married William Severns, written Servens, on 5 July 1900. He belonged to the Modern Woodmen and the Grand Army of the Republic, voted Republican and belonged to the Methodist Episcopal church. Whether William Shanks was his father’s brother or his mother’s is not said. A Jackson Livesay (1842–1917) and a Mary A. Livesay (1847–1930) lie at Richview, but those dates do not fit this Jackson’s 1845 birth, and whether the two men were related is not known.

Some points disagree or are open. Jackson said he was born at “Washington, Illinois,” which most likely means Washington County, though elsewhere he was said to have been born about 1846 in Jefferson County. His own dates, a Kansas claim in 1866, the family’s move to Kansas in 1871, the year of his marriage, and the family’s return to Illinois in 1881, do not sit easily with eight years in Montana and Kansas with his uncle. In 1850 a William C. Livesay, 26, with a Jackson L., 4, was living beside the Walkers; the C may be a misreading of E. Who his uncle William Shanks was is not known. Abigail Walker, William P. Walker’s wife, is sometimes called Shank or Schanck, and Jackson served beside William P. at Richview, but nothing yet ties that family to William Shanks. A Jackson Lafayette Livesay died at Centralia on 25 August 1930; he would have been 84, and he was probably this Jackson, though only his name and town fit.

stories.title: Alfred and Hannah Livesay’s thirteen children
stories.hook: Alfred and Hannah Livesay had thirteen children in all, though even their own family could not agree on just which thirteen.
body: Alfred and Hannah Livesay had thirteen children, as their family remembered them in 1909: William T., a druggist at Stanley, Iowa, married to Eliza Seward; Elizabeth R., single and caring for her mother; Isaac B., married to Leticia Rock, in Kansas; Pearl, married to Joseph Larimer; Hester A., married to Perry Davidson; Ransom P., married to Louisa Suter; Marshall A., married to Rachael Walton, with nine children; Liddie, deceased, married to Robert Quale; Harvey R., married to Mollie Chick; Allen H., who stayed single and died at forty-four; Daniel R., married to Laura Cruse; Etta, married to James Smith; and Clinton O., married to Elvira McHaney. Their son Harvey R. listed them “in order of birth” a little differently: William, Lizzie, Berry, Hester, Ransom, Marshall, Lydia, Harvey R., Allen, Daniel, Clinton, Etta, and Eddie, who died young. Alfred himself was remembered that year as a Mexican War private and Methodist preacher of Patoka Township, with thirteen children and their spouses, who had died on 22 April 1883.

Their weddings bear part of this out. William T. Livesay married Eliza A. Seward on 16 November 1871; Perry G. Davidson married Hester A. Livesay on 2 November 1876; Marshall A. Livesay married Rachel C. Walton on 20 January 1880, a date also given as 20 January 1881; and Daniel R. Livesay married Laura O. Cruse on 7 August 1889. Rachel’s brother Orville T. Walton remembered her as the wife of Marshall Livesay of Foley, Missouri, and a daughter of Iradell and Louisa (Foster) Walton. J. R. Quayle, a teacher and township officeholder, married Lyda E. Livesay, “the accomplished daughter” of Alfred and Hannah, on 8 January 1889; two of their four children had died by 1909, and she herself died in June 1906.

The two lists conflict in places. One has Isaac B. in Kansas and Pearl married to a Larimer and no Eddie; Harvey’s has Berry, a merchant near Odin, Illinois, and Eddie and no Pearl. Berry may be Isaac B., but Kansas and Odin are different places, and a Pearl with a husband and two children cannot be a child who died young. Both say thirteen. A James R. Livesay married Louisa M. Souter on 5 October 1880, where the family remembered Ransom P. and Louisa Suter, and Lydia’s husband was Robert Quale to her father’s and brother’s families but J. R. Quayle in his own account. Harvey also named a Lizzie and a Lydia where his father’s family had Elizabeth R. and Liddie, and put Marshall at “Foley, Missouri.” The differences look like the ordinary drift of two family memories.

On 16 March 1867 Alfred Livesay bought two tracts in Marion County, SESW-24-04N-01E and NWSE-06-03N-02E, 40 acres each. He bought six hundred acres in Patoka Township in all, mostly unimproved government land, by Harvey’s account, and left six hundred acres of improved land, by his own family’s, so the two tracts were only a small part of it. Harvey said Alfred went to Missouri in 1866 before coming to Marion County, where Alfred himself was said to have arrived about 1866. Alfred died on 22 April 1883, and Hannah, then in her late seventies, farmed 134 acres on the old place in 1909. A Hannah Livesay died at Patoka on 28 August 1924, an Elizabeth R. Livesay at Patoka on 16 March 1934 and a Daniel R. Livesay at Centralia on 28 March 1946; they fit Hannah, Lizzie and Daniel, though only by name and place.

Harvey R., born on 10 May 1861 in Washington County, stayed at home until he was twenty-two, married Mollie Chick of Foster Township in February 1883, and lost her in 1895; she left five children. By 1909 he farmed in Foster and Patoka townships, with his home in section 29, voted Democratic like his father and was Supervisor of Foster Township. He is the one child whose own life story survives, and he named something his father’s family left out, his mother’s father. Hannah Logan was the daughter of James R. Logan, born in South Carolina, who lived in Tennessee and then came to Washington County, Illinois, where he had a well-improved farm until his death in 1860. He was a Methodist and a local exhorter. A Jas. R. Logan left an estate in Washington County, and in 1855 a James R. Logan household of seven was counted next to Henderson Darter’s. That man would have been young to father a daughter about 1830, so the household may have been a son’s or another man’s of the name. How James R. Logan was related to James L. Logan, who married Unity J. Livesay in 1849, is not known. Of the thirteen children, six can be followed beyond the family’s memory: William T., Elizabeth R., Marshall A., Lydia E., Harvey R. and Daniel R.

stories.title: Hannah Logan’s father: James R. Logan, local exhorter, died 1860
stories.hook: Hannah Logan’s father, James R. Logan, came from South Carolina by way of Tennessee to a Washington County farm, served the Methodists as a local exhorter and died in 1860.
body: James R. Logan, Hannah’s father, was born in South Carolina and lived in Tennessee until he came to Washington County, Illinois, where he had a well improved farm and lived on it until his death, which occurred in 1860. He was a member of the Methodist church and a local exhorter, as his grandson Harvey R. Livesay remembered. Hannah was born in Washington County on 30 September 1830, the year the Livesays and many of their Tennessee neighbors arrived, and the Logans were remembered, with the Whittenburgs, Lowes, Phillipses, Thompsons and Darters, among the families that founded the first Methodist church at Richview in 1842.

A few other traces may be his. A man long in the church at Richview remembered that in 1832 there was a society of Methodists at Alexander Anderson’s house, whose principal members were Alex. Anderson, “Roberson Logan,” John Darter and John Livesay. That may have been another Logan, or a form of Robertson or of a James R.; no one can say. A Jas. R. Logan left an estate in the county, in keeping with a death in 1860. And in 1855 a James R. Logan had seven people in his household and property of $775, next to Henderson Darter’s; the old columns make it hard to tell the men from the women, so no ages can be drawn from them.

The marriages show how the families crossed. Alfred Livesay and Nancy A. Darter took out a license on 6 December 1842, Alfred Livesay and Hannah Logan married on 26 February 1846, and James L. Logan and Unity J. Livesay married on 16 November 1849, when Unity Jane was sixteen. If James L. was Hannah’s brother, her brother married the daughter of the family into which Hannah married, and Alfred and Unity would be cousins if Alfred was Robert’s nephew, as seems possible. But nothing says that James L. was James R.’s son. A second Logan household of 1855, perhaps a “James L.(?)” with three people and property of $35, next to Enoch Tate’s, fits a young couple with a child, but the name is uncertain.

What became of Unity Jane is a mystery. She was born on 3 November 1833, by family tradition, and was named with “James I. Logan” in the heirs’ release of 1856, and nothing is known of the couple afterward. James R. Logan’s estate may yet tell what became of them.

The censuses fill in his household. In 1850 James R. Logan, fifty-three and South Carolina born, was farming in Washington County with his wife Rachael, forty-eight, and six children still at home, from Lewis A., fourteen, down to Thomas W. J., two. He was still alive on 1 August 1860, when the census taker found him at sixty-three with land worth $4,000, Rachel, fifty-eight and born in Tennessee, and the three youngest. A John P. Logan, thirty-nine, lived next door with a little daughter named Rachel C., and four doors on were Alfred and Hannah Livesay, whose small son was named James R. Rachel was probably Hannah's mother, though no record says so. John P. may be the John P. Logan who went to war in Company F of the 49th Illinois; the company's Captain John A. Logan and Sergeant James M. Logan were probably the sons of a Richview master carpenter, also named James Logan, a man of forty-two.

stories.title: Dr. T. N. Livesay of Patoka: a physician, a drugstore and a newspaper
stories.hook: Dr. T. N. Livesay, a cousin of Alfred Livesay, practiced medicine at Patoka in the 1880s, kept a drugstore and helped start a newspaper; he may have been Robert and Lydia’s son Thomas Newton, born in 1836.
body: Alfred Livesay was remembered in 1909 as a cousin of “Dr. Thomas Livesay, one of the leading physicians of Marion county.” By 1881 Dr. T. N. Livesay was at Patoka, one of seven physicians in the village, among them J. B. Lewis, and the two kept a drug business, Livesay & Lewis: “They also publish a newspaper.” The paper was the Patoka Enterprise, whose first number was issued on 5 August 1881, “edited and published as an auxiliary by Dr. J. B. Lewis and T. N. Livesay,” a six-column folio “independent on all subjects.” Dr. T. N. Livesay was also first among the elders of the Patoka congregation of the Cumberland Presbyterian church, and a Mrs. D. O. Livesay (the initials are uncertain) was a Patoka milliner, of whom nothing more is known.

His partner, Dr. J. B. Lewis, graduated from the Eclectic Medical Institute at Cincinnati in 1878 and began to practice at Patoka, gave up medicine in 1884 when he was elected clerk of the circuit court, and, for five years, “was engaged in the drug business in Patoka in company with Dr. T. N. Livesay,” as he recalled in 1894. On 27 October 1886 Thomas N. Livesay married Mrs. Annie M. Watts. Her brother, the real-estate man George B. Simcox, remembered her in 1909 as “Anna M., the widow of Dr. T. N. Livesay,” living near Patoka, one of the children of W. K. Simcox, a Pennsylvania-born merchant who came to Patoka in 1866.

The question is whether he was kin to Floyd’s Livesays. Robert and Lydia had a son Thomas Newton Livesay, born on 22 February 1836, by family tradition, and the doctor was Alfred’s cousin, which would fit a son of Robert if Alfred’s father John Wesley was Robert’s brother. The release that Robert’s older children signed in 1856 names eight heirs and not Thomas Newton, who would have been 20, perhaps because he had died, had been paid, or had been left off the copy. A young man away studying medicine in 1856 would fit the last, but proves nothing. Against it, other Thomas Livesays lived in Washington County, among them the Thomas W. Livesay who married Elizabeth Thompson on 22 February 1841, and “cousin” need not mean a son of Robert.

His age and birthplace, his schooling and his death would settle it, and so might Robert’s own estate, which may list his heirs. Until then the doctor is one more Livesay whose place in the family is unknown.

He died at Patoka on Tuesday, 10 January 1905. The Salem Republican gave him two lines on its front page that Thursday, calling him one of the town's leading citizens, and the St. Louis Globe-Democrat ran his name the morning before in its column of deaths from the country towns. Neither paper gave his age or the place he was born, so the question of whose son he was is still open.

stories.title: George T. Hoke, the stepson who drove the oxen
stories.hook: Livesay Carter’s wife brought a son from her first marriage to Nashville, Illinois. He drove the oxen that hauled the logs for his stepfather’s sawmill, opened a store at Nashville in 1844, and was raised in the Nashville Masonic lodge in its first chartered year, with his stepfather and a Carter son.
body: George T. Hoke, of Richview Township, told his family’s story for the county history of 1879. His father, John Hoke, was a native of Kentucky and his grandfather, George Hoke, of Pennsylvania; his mother’s father, Thomas L. Moore, was “a revolutionary soldier” whose people came from Maryland. George was born in Harrison County, Indiana, on 1 October 1819. His father died at Baton Rouge in 1821 on a trip to New Orleans, and his mother went back to Jefferson County, Kentucky, and came with her people in 1822 to Washington County, where she settled about two miles east of old Covington and met Livesay Carter. They married in July 1823, lived two miles east of Nashville for over fifty years, and Mr. Carter followed her in about two years.

In 1830 Livesay Carter built a tread saw mill two miles east of the site of Nashville, which sawed the lumber for the first buildings in the town, and George T. Hoke, then a small boy, drove the oxen that hauled the logs. Hoke farmed and went to school in winters, peddled merchandise, and in 1844 opened a store at Nashville with five hundred dollars, which at the time had the whole trade of the place. He married Rebecca Fulton on 4 October 1844. In 1851 he sold the store to Dr. Lucas, joined Judge Watts and Sheriff Jack in buying the press of the Nashville Era, the county’s first paper, and sold his share after four months to David Logan. After leasing the mill in 1852 he moved in 1853 to Richview, clerked for Dr. Lucas, opened his own store near the depot in 1856 and kept it until 1874. He was elected Justice of the Peace in 1856, and by 1879 had been re-elected five times, was appointed notary public by Governor Yates and three times reappointed, and was elected county commissioner in 1876. He was a Republican, a Methodist and a Mason.

The family stood together in the Nashville lodge. Washington Lodge No. 55 began as Hardin Lodge under a dispensation of 21 July 1847 and received its charter on 4 October 1848. It raised seventeen members in its first year under the charter, among them George T. Hoke, S. M. Carter and Livesay Carter. By 1879 most of the early members had died, but a few “old land marks” remained: George T. Hoke, S. M. Carter, Lewis N. Farmer and J. J. Swanwick. Livesay Carter, born in 1799 by the cemetery’s list, was about forty-nine when he joined. The same men had once ridden out together. About 1840 a company armed with guns and pistols went from Nashville to the “Little Muddy” settlement, later Richview, to protect the House and Carter families against old settlers who had threatened to burn Hansel House’s new house. Among them were G. T. Hoke, Robert P. Carter and Livesay Carter. They camped half a mile south of the later town, and the threat collapsed when the old squatters learned of them.

S. M. Carter was the doctor’s brother. About 1858 Dr. William D. Carter began his medical study in the office of his brother, S. M. Carter, of Pinckneyville. An S. M. Carter was among the five trustees chosen on 26 March 1857 when Pinckneyville incorporated, and an S. M. Carter was among the early members of the Nashville lodge. The initials, the town and the lodge make these one man, probably, though his given name is never stated. A Samuel M. Carter was living in Perry County in 1850, and an S. M. Carter, with Malissa and four children, in 1860. So S. M. Carter was probably a son of Livesay Carter and Mary, and George T. Hoke was Mary Moore Hoke Carter’s son by her first marriage.

stories.title: Livesay Carter’s first land: Lake Township, Clinton County, 1818
stories.hook: On 26 February 1818 Livesay Carter was among the first men to enter land in what became Lake Township, Clinton County, a year after a Methodist minister named Robert Carter had settled the next section and five years before his own joint patent with Robert Carter.

subject.name: Livesay Carter
subject.rel: Livesay Carter (kin to the Livesays, unconfirmed)

body: Livesay Carter went to Tennessee in 1807, came to Illinois in 1818 and lived four years in what is now Clinton County, as his son’s family remembered in 1879, and on 10 December 1823 he and Robert Carter received a federal patent for 160 acres at Edwardsville. His first land was in Lake Township, which until 1875 was part of Crooked Creek Township, in the southeast of Clinton County on the Washington County line. On “Feb. 26th, 1818, Livesay Carter entered S. E. ¼ Sec. 7,” among the first lands entered there, and it is the earliest date known for him in Illinois.

His neighbors were the first families of the township. William Morrison and Pierre Menard entered in September 1816, John Wakefield in January 1817, Robert C. McEver in April 1817, John Bradford on 29 January 1818, Seborn Wadsworth on 9 March 1818 and Wingate Maddux on 21 May 1818. B. Stephenson entered land for the Bank of Edwardsville and James Mitchell took 277 acres in 1818, and the last of the first entries was John D. Patton’s, in 1819. The township was first settled in 1817. Robert C. McEver, whose name is also printed McKever, came from Georgia, and Dempsey Kennedy, also a Georgian, settled on section 6 the same year and stayed about two years before moving to what is now Washington County. The first death, in 1818, was that of a man named Hull, killed felling trees and buried in what became the Wadsworth burial ground; and the township “settled very slowly” and was almost empty by 1830. Livesay Carter’s four years there, from 1818 to about 1822, fit that account.

A man of his own surname had come a year ahead of him. “Robert Carter, a Methodist minister and a pioneer from Tennessee, came to this township in 1817, and located on section 6, and afterwards removed to Washington county in company with Mr. Kennedy,” the county remembered in its History of Marion and Clinton Counties of 1881. He was the pioneer preacher of that part of the country, and his tomb could be shown in a little private burying-ground in Lake Township. He came in 1817 and “afterward settled elsewhere,” and he was remembered among the local preachers as “Robert Carter, who settled in Central Prairie in 1817.” His section 6 lay beside Livesay Carter’s section 7.

The Carters went to Illinois first, the family of Jackson Monroe Livesay remembered, and Rebecca (Carter) Livesay’s brother was a Robert Carter. The Methodist minister of 1817, with the Kennedys who later moved to Washington County, fits that family story well, but a fit is not a proof. Nothing shows that the minister was Rebecca’s brother, or that the Robert of the 1823 patent was the minister. Dempsey Kennedy matters for a second reason: in 1848 Demsy Kennedy and William E. Livesay took a joint federal patent, so a Kennedy and a Livesay were neighbors a generation later.

The entry raises a question his stone at Nashville had already raised. Livesay Carter’s birth is given as 15 November 1799, which would make him eighteen on the day of the entry, young for a man to enter a quarter section in his own name. The family tradition, which makes him the first son of a marriage of the 1780s, implies a birth a decade or more earlier, and a man born in 1799 could not have been that son. Either the entry was made for the family, or the year on his stone is late, or the Livesay Carter of 1818 was an older man, or he was not the man buried at Nashville. Only the quarter section and section are known, so the tract cannot be placed exactly.

George T. Hoke remembered that his mother, a widow, came with her people in 1822 to a place two miles east of old Covington, where she “became acquainted with Livesay Carter,” and that after their marriage in July 1823 they settled two miles east of Nashville. Dr. Carter remembered his father living four years in Clinton County and then going to Nashville. The dates fit together: an entry in February 1818, about four years in Clinton County, a meeting in 1822 or 1823 and a move to Nashville after the wedding. The entry of 1818 is the earliest date known for him, five years before the marriage and the joint patent.

stories.title: The regiment Company H joined: Collins’s Second Illinois, 1847–1848
stories.hook: Alfred Livesay’s company of the Second Illinois sailed to Vera Cruz in 1847, saw little fighting, and lost about one man in four before it came home.
body: The Second Regiment, enlisted “during the war,” was organized out of the overflow of companies raised for the Fifth Regiment, after Lieutenant Colonel Hicks and others asked the Secretary of War for leave to raise another. It was organized at Alton on 3 August 1847, with James Collins elected colonel, and sent by steamer to New Orleans, where it was divided in two. Companies A, D, E, F and H went under Collins to Vera Cruz, arriving on 31 August 1847. They were soon in a skirmish with guerrillas but saw no further actual service beyond camp and garrison duty. The other five companies, under Hicks, were sent to Tampico. Both battalions lost heavily to sickness, and the regiment was mustered out at Alton between 20 and 25 July 1848.

Company H was the Washington County company. Its officers were Captain James Burns, First Lieutenant Malachi Jenkins and four second lieutenants, all enrolled at Nashville, Illinois, on 10 July 1847, and it was discharged at Alton on 22 July 1848. It had about 97 men: 6 officers; 9 sergeants, corporals and the musician; 38 privates who served without remark; 23 sergeants and privates who died; 2 deserters; 18 men discharged for disability; and 1 man transferred. Two officers died too, Second Lieutenant James R. Lynch at Vera Cruz on 12 September 1847 and First Lieutenant Jenkins on the Gulf of Mexico on 26 June 1848, on the way home. That makes 25 deaths, about one man in four. Only one was killed in action, Private John Field at San Juan on 18 September 1847. Deaths began before the company left Illinois, with one man dead at Alton on 3 August 1847, and two more died on the Gulf of Mexico on 28 and 29 August, before the landing at Vera Cruz. The transferred man, Private Stephen G. Hicks, was elected lieutenant colonel of the regiment on 3 August 1847, so Company H supplied its second-in-command.

Three Livesays served in it. Alfred Livesay, a private enrolled on 10 July 1847, served without remark: he was not among the dead, the discharged, the deserters or the transferred, and he stayed with the company until the discharge at Alton. That fits his family’s memory of about thirteen months of service and of a sickness he never shook off; by the company’s own dates it was twelve and a half months. Carter H. Livesay, whom the roll prints as Carter A., was discharged, probably for disability at Jalapa, Mexico, on 4 February 1848, though the cramped ditto marks beside his name make that uncertain. John C. Livesay died at Jalapa, Mexico, in May 1848, on the 11th or the 14th.

Other names in the company echo the family’s neighborhood. Nicholas H. Darter, a private, shared a surname with Alfred’s first wife, Nancy A. Darter, and with the man who married Mariah Livesay in 1841. Richard P. Carter, a corporal, and Emanuel C. Carter, a private, were Carters; James B. Logan, a corporal, was a Logan. Ezekiah Walker, a private, died at Vera Cruz on 10 September 1847, and two privates named John Walker served, one who stayed and one who was discharged. Whether any of these men was kin to the Livesays or the Walkers of Beaucoup is not known; only their surnames were in the same company.

No cause of death was given except for the one man killed in action, and no residence beyond the place of enlistment. Of Alfred’s service nothing more is known, except that in 1909 his widow Hannah drew a pension of twelve dollars a month.

stories.title: Dr. William D. Carter of Nashville, surgeon in the 44th Illinois
stories.hook: Livesay Carter’s seventh child was commissioned in the 44th Illinois a week before Perryville and stayed until the regiment was mustered out in Texas in September 1865.

subject.name: Dr. William D. Carter, 44th Illinois Infantry

body: William D. Carter, of Nashville, was commissioned second assistant surgeon of the 44th Illinois Infantry on 1 October 1862, his rank and muster both dating from that day, and was “Promoted” first assistant surgeon from 25 May 1863. He was mustered out on 25 September 1865. Nashville was his home, and there he practiced after the war. Another William D. Carter, of Oxville, a private in a different regiment, was a different man.

William was born in Washington County on 12 January 1838, the seventh of eight children, five boys and three girls, of Livesay Carter and Mrs. Mary Hoke. He read medicine in the office of his brother, S. M. Carter, at Pinckneyville, and then at Rush Medical College in Chicago, graduating, as he remembered in 1879, on 4 February 1862. He volunteered, was appointed assistant surgeon of the 44th Illinois, served more than three years, spent most of the time on detached service and for part of it was on the Division Operating Staff in the Atlanta campaign. He is said also to have taken a second Chicago degree, from Chicago Medical College, on 10 March 1866, though the account of it muddles its dates. In December 1869 he married Laura A. Lecompte of Nashville; by 1879 they had had three children, two of them living, none named.

The regiment’s own history tells where he was. The 44th was organized at Camp Ellsworth, Chicago, in August 1861 and mustered in on 13 September. It fought at Pea Ridge in March 1862. In September it was at Cincinnati and Covington and then at Louisville, and it was in the battle of Perryville on 8 October, a week after Carter’s commission began. It entered Nashville in November. At Stones River, at the turn of the year, it lost more than half its number in killed and wounded, in the history’s words. In 1863 it was at Hoover’s Gap and Tullahoma, marched back to the field in time for Chickamauga on 19 and 20 September, and was foremost in the charge up Missionary Ridge on 25 November. In 1864 it passed through nearly all the battles and skirmishes of the Atlanta campaign, fell back before Hood to Franklin and took part in the battle of Nashville on 15 and 16 December. After service in Alabama and East Tennessee it went to New Orleans in June 1865, then to Texas, landing at Port Lavaca on 23 July. It was mustered out on 25 September 1865, the same day as Carter, and reached Springfield on 15 October for final payment.

The regiment’s surgeons go unnamed in its history, so what Carter himself did in those battles is not known. But the Nashville physician’s war was the long one, from the Kentucky campaign to the last garrison in Texas. His father, Livesay Carter, had come to Illinois from Virginia by way of Tennessee, and the county’s Mexican War and Civil War companies carried other Livesay and Carter names.

stories.title: Two chaplains and a captain: the preaching Walkers of Richview
stories.hook: Rev. Simeon Walker rode Illinois circuits in Peter Cartwright’s day and went to war as a cavalry chaplain at sixty-one, while one son served as an infantry chaplain and another, very probably, as a captain.

subject.name: Rev. Simeon Walker and his son Levi
subject.rel: Probable father and brother of Captain Simeon Walker

body: Simeon Walker was born in Jackson County, Georgia, on 13 April 1802, and was taken west as a boy; the family went to Kentucky in 1810, by one account. He grew up to be a Methodist preacher who rode circuit in Peter Cartwright’s day, and he was received into the conference in 1830. With his wife, Elizabeth Sharpe, he had six children by 1834, when failing health and money made him take a location and settle. Their son Levi Sharpe Walker was born in Clinton County, Illinois, on 14 September 1829.

Simeon’s own story began with a father he barely knew. Abram Walker took his wife, Rhoda Beauchamp, and their small son to the Illinois Territory in 1809, to a place on Silver Creek southeast of Lebanon. Indian troubles sent the family to Kentucky, and there, in January 1812, Abram died. Rhoda brought the boy back to Illinois in 1813 and settled on Turkey Hill, east of Belleville, within reach of her father, William Beauchamp, whose house was both a lodging for travelling Methodist preachers and a place of worship. In 1815 she married Henry Sharp. The Sharp name came into the family twice, for Simeon’s wife, Elizabeth Sharp, bore it as well, and whether the two Sharps were related nothing seen says.

Settled or not, he went on preaching in the Washington County settlements. About 1833 he visited the first Methodist class at Nashville as its pastor, and he was among the ministers who served the church at Richview. In 1855–56, when the appointed pastor at Nashville died, he filled out the year, and in 1856 he went back to riding circuits. That same year, on 30 August, Levi was licensed to preach at Richview.

The boy grew into the man the conference remembers. At a camp meeting at Old Shiloh, in St. Clair County, on the morning of 30 August 1819, he was converted. He was an exhorter by 1820 and a licensed local preacher by 1826, and in the fall of 1830 the Illinois Conference took him on probation and sent him to the Grand Prairie Mission. Bishop Roberts ordained him deacon at Indianapolis on 9 October 1831, and Bishop Soule made him an elder at Union Grove, in St. Clair County, on 3 October 1833. A year later he located, and he rode circuits again from 1856.

By then the household had changed. Simeon seems to have married again: a Simeon Walker and Sally Whittenburg were married on 11 August 1846. In 1850, in District 20, lived Simeon Walker, 48, a farmer with real estate worth $2,000, with Sally, 54, Simeon, 19, John, 17, Thomas, 10, and Eliza, 7, and two more whose names can no longer be read with confidence. His birthplace seems to have been given as Kentucky, where he grew up, rather than Georgia; Sally’s as South Carolina; and the children’s as Illinois. The age fits the preacher born in 1802, a wife of 54 with children of 10 and 7 fits a second marriage, and the nineteen-year-old Simeon was just the age of the future Captain Simeon Walker, born on 3 March 1831.

Levi had married Martha Henrietta Barnes at Mascoutah on 29 December 1849. The younger Simeon married Etheldra Jane Walker on 15 September 1852, and at his wedding he was written down as Simeon Walker Jr.

When the Civil War came, Levi and the younger Simeon went in together. Levi was commissioned chaplain of the 60th Illinois from 12 February 1862 and mustered on 17 February, giving his home as Richview, and he served the regiment as chaplain for three years. Simeon joined the same regiment that February as a sergeant and rose to captain of Company C, where William P. Walker served under him. Both men left the regiment on the same day, 14 March 1865, two days before Averysboro.

Their father went too. At sixty-one the old circuit rider “entered the army as chaplain of the Fifteenth Illinois Cavalry,” as the Methodist historian James Leaton put it. He held the rank from 5 June 1863, was mustered on 23 July 1863 and was mustered out on 25 August 1864.

After the war Levi was chaplain of the Southern Penitentiary at Chester for three years, and his daughter Flora married a merchant of Okawville. In 1879 the elder Simeon was still living at Richview, in the home of a son, spending the evening of his life in quiet. The son is not named; it was probably not Levi, who was then at Chester, so it may have been another. The old preacher died at his son’s residence at Carbondale on 22 February 1880.

Levi’s wife, Martha, died on 2 April 1886, and on 29 September 1887 he married Mrs. Emma P. McCracken of Richview. He died on 6 April 1921, almost ninety-two, and was buried at Richview after a funeral there. Grown children survived him.

In 1894, living at Carbondale, the captain told his family’s story for a county biographical review. He was born in Clinton County on 3 March 1831, he said, the son of Simeon Walker, who had been brought from Georgia by his mother in 1811, who rode circuit in Peter Cartwright’s day, and who was appointed chaplain of the 15th Illinois Cavalry by Governor Richard Yates. His mother was Elizabeth Sharp. Of the twelve children, five sons became preachers and six went to war: William H., a captain in the 111th Illinois; Samuel, a lieutenant in the same regiment; Levi S., chaplain of the 60th; Thomas C., a private in the 111th; the captain himself; and John B., whom he remembered as a captain of the 40th Illinois killed at Shiloh. Thirty years may have blurred the rank and the regiment: the roll of Company F, 49th Illinois, raised around Richview, carries a Private John B. Walker of Richview, mustered on 31 December 1861 and killed at Shiloh on 6 April 1862, and he was very probably the brother. Four were still living in 1894: Rev. Samuel of Carlyle, Rev. William H. of Kansas, Rev. Levi S. of Chester, and the captain, who drew a pension of $24 a month.

Taken together, the 1850 household, the “Jr.” at his wedding, the preacher’s long years near Richview, the brothers’ discharge on the same day and the captain’s own account make it very likely that Captain Simeon was the old preacher’s son. If so, Company C of the 60th Illinois was commanded by a chaplain’s brother and a cavalry chaplain’s son, with William P. Walker in its ranks.

Simeon Walker at Richview. Captain Simeon Walker’s own 1894 sketch names his parents as Simeon Walker, chaplain of the 15th Illinois Cavalry, and Elizabeth Sharp, and lists his brothers and sisters; it is the one record that states the father-son link, though it is a family account and not a contemporary record, and its transcription contains slips. The 1850 census birthplace (Kentucky) conflicts with Leaton’s (Georgia), and Leaton’s Carbondale death sits oddly beside the 1879 statement that he lived at Richview. Abram Walker and Rhoda Beauchamp, and the Henry Sharp marriage, rest only on Levi’s notes of about 1905 and are leads; they differ by a year or two from Leaton’s account of the move to Kentucky. John B. Walker’s identity with the Private of Company F, 49th Illinois, killed at Shiloh is a lead; no roll seen has a Captain Walker in the 40th Illinois. The 1850 names of two household members cannot be read with confidence.

stories.title: Where the 7th Alabama Cavalry rode, 1863–1865
stories.hook: Dudley Logan’s regiment was formed in July 1863, spent a year near Pollard, rode in Hood’s Tennessee campaign and ended with a surrender at Gainesville in May 1865. Two accounts of its origin disagree.

subject.name: Dudley Timothy Logan, Company B, 7th Alabama Cavalry

body: Dudley Logan’s regiment, the 7th Alabama Cavalry, was formed at Newborn, Alabama, in July 1863, with companies raised in Randolph, Shelby, Greene, Pickens and Montgomery counties. For a year it served in the Pollard area in General Clanton’s brigade. In July 1864 it counted 451 men but was not serving as one command: two companies were with General Page and eight rode with Colonel I. W. Patton. It was later attached to the brigades of B. M. Thomas, W. W. Allen and Bell, took part in the raid on Johnsonville, and fought as Hood moved toward Nashville. In April 1865 it had fewer than 300 effectives, and about half of them surrendered at Gainesville, Alabama, in May. Its field officers were Colonel Joseph Hodgson and Lieutenant Colonels Turner Clanton Jr., Henry J. Livingston and F. C. Randolph.

Greene County was one of the five, and its company was Company B, the “Broadfoots of Greene County,” under Captain D. P. Scarbrough, with several lieutenants and sergeants and a long list of privates, among them Dudley Logan, L. Logan and Zach M. Logan. When they enlisted, and how old they were, is not known. One Greene County boy’s story gives a human scale. John Henderson Gandy, born in Greene County on 12 November 1846, is said to have enlisted on 20 June 1863 for the war under Captain D. P. Scarborough of Company B, and to have been discharged on 31 October 1863 for being a minor who had enlisted without his parents’ permission. If so, the company was filling in June 1863 and boys of sixteen were being taken. Dudley, born on 8 January 1846, was seventeen that summer.

Not every account of the 7th agrees. One history of its Company K, from Morgan County, says the company began in 1862 as part of the 14th Cavalry Battalion, Partisan Rangers, commanded throughout by Colonel James C. Malone Jr.; that on 15 April 1863 the battalion was combined with the 19th Cavalry Battalion and redesignated the 7th Cavalry; that on 15 September 1864 it became the 9th Alabama Cavalry; and that it surrendered with Johnston’s army at Durham Station, North Carolina, on 26 April 1865. That is a different history from the Newborn, Pollard and Gainesville regiment, and a Greene County man could not have been at both Gainesville and Durham Station. Either two units bore the number 7 in different accounts, or one account has confused them. The Greene County company most likely belonged to the Newborn regiment, which counted Greene among its counties and whose Company B had its own captain, but that is a reading and not a proof.

This is the kind of service a Greene County cavalryman of 1863 would have seen: a year of picketing near Pollard, then the campaigns of late 1864, and a surrender in Alabama in the spring of 1865, far from Mount Pleasant, Texas, where he later lived. Whether Dudley served the whole time, was at Johnsonville or Nashville, or was among those who surrendered is not known; his service file and his widow’s Texas pension may one day say.

Johnsonville was a Union supply base on the east bank of the Tennessee River in Humphreys County. There the railroad from Nashville met the steamboats, and stores were piled on the landing for Sherman’s armies. On 4 November 1864 Forrest’s cavalry and guns lined the west bank across from it. Brig. Gen. James R. Chalmers posted Colonel Rucker, with Morton’s battery and the Seventh Alabama Cavalry, just below the town and opposite it.

The Confederate guns drove off the gunboats. Before night the garrison, fearing capture, fired its own boats, and the gunboats, transports, barges, the warehouse and most of the stores on shore burned. Forrest counted four gunboats, fourteen transports and twenty barges, and put the loss at $6.7 million; a Union officer thought $2.2 million nearer the mark. Forrest reported two men killed and nine wounded. Chalmers wrote of “the gallant conduct of the Seventh Alabama Cavalry in this their first engagement.”
If Dudley Logan was with Company B that autumn, he was on that riverbank, eighteen years old, watching the fires across the water. No muster roll yet puts him there by name.

stories.title: A Lieutenant Henry Clay in the First Choctaw Mounted Rifles, 1862
stories.hook: Abner Clay’s father, Henry Clay, is little more than a name, but a Choctaw Lieutenant Henry Clay served the Confederacy in 1862, and he may have been the same man.

subject.name: Henry Clay, 1st Choctaw Mounted Rifles (identity unproven)
subject.rel: Possible father of Abner H. Clay

body: Henry Clay is known only as Abner H. Clay’s father, dead by 1899, of Bok Tuklo County, and the husband of Wilsey Clay. The Choctaw Nation fought for the Confederacy, and among its soldiers was a Henry Clay.

He was a lieutenant of “Co. F, 1 Choctaw Mounted Rifles,” a regiment “Also known as Cavalry.” For the six months ending 23 November 1862 he was paid for commutation of clothing as a first lieutenant in Capt. Oklabi’s company, his name appearing only as a signature to a certificate. On 21 June 1862, at Fort McCulloch, he signed with other officers of the Indian regiments in Confederate service a petition to the Secretary of War asking that Colonel Sampson Folsom of the 1st Choctaw Regiment be appointed a brigadier general in the Provisional Army of the Confederate States. Nothing records his age, residence or county.

The regiment was Folsom’s. The First Choctaw Regiment was organized in early 1862 under Colonel Sampson Folsom, with David F. Harkins as lieutenant colonel and Sylvester Durant as major; it fought in many skirmishes and at the first battle of Newtonia, and 31 officers and 686 soldiers served until June 1865. It is sometimes confused with the First Choctaw and Chickasaw Mounted Rifles, Douglas Cooper’s regiment formed at Skullyville in 1861. A Silvester Durant served too, but nothing ties him to Peter Durant.

Whether the lieutenant was Abner’s father is not known. Henry Clay was a common name, and there were several Clays in the Choctaw ranks, among them a Joseph Clay and an Esaias Clay in 1862 and a Simon Clay in 1863, and nothing places the lieutenant in Bok Tuklo County or with Wilsey. A man who was a lieutenant in 1862 could have been the father of a child born about 1872, as Abner’s age implies, but that is only possible. His county in the 1860s to 1880s, a Dawes witness who remembered his war, or the county from which Captain Oklabi’s company was raised might one day tell.
