stories.title: Livesays, Carters and Walkers in the county’s Civil War companies
stories.hook: Some fifteen Livesays, Carters and Walkers served in Washington County’s Union companies, among them an Alexander Walker of Richview who was probably the Alex Walker living near William P. Walker in 1860.

subject.name: Washington County’s Union companies, 1861–1865
subject.rel: Livesay, Carter and Walker kin (relationships unproven)

body: In 1879 Washington County remembered, regiment by regiment, the men it had sent to the Union armies, and among them were a Carter and several Livesays and Walkers. In the 44th Illinois was First Assistant Surgeon William D. Carter. In the 49th Illinois, Company F, were privates Andrew Livesly, Francis M. Carter and John B. Walker and recruits William J. Livesey and George Walker; in Company I, James M. Livesay as first lieutenant, where the state roll has him a second lieutenant, and again as a private. In the 60th were Simon and William P. Walker, Jackson L. Livesay and John W. Livesay in Company C, a George W. Livesay in Company G, and Levi S. Walker as chaplain. And under the 62nd Infantry were, in Company G, First Sergeant Alexander Walker and Corporal Nelson Livesay. The spellings are the printer’s.

James M. Livesay was a private of Company I, 49th Illinois, from Nashville, enrolled on 1 November 1861 and mustered on 31 December, and was “Pro. 1st Serg’t and 2d Lt.” Nashville was the town of the Carter family and of Livesay Carter’s son the surgeon. How James M. stood to the Livesays of Beaucoup or to the Carters is not known.

The state and the county differ over Alexander Walker’s regiment. By the state’s reckoning his company was Company G of the Thirteenth (Consolidated) Illinois Cavalry, the same men, down to the captain and the sergeants, whom the county remembered under the 62nd Infantry. First Sergeant Alexander Walker, of Richview, was enrolled on 21 December 1863 and mustered on 20 January 1864; he was commissioned second lieutenant on 11 July 1865 but not mustered in that rank, and was mustered out on 31 August 1865 as a sergeant. Corporal Nelson J. Livesay, of Ashley, enrolled with him and was mustered out the same day. The regiment was in Arkansas through the Camden expedition of April 1864 and then on scouts and picket at Pine Bluff, where one of the company’s sergeants died in July 1864.

Alexander Walker of Richview bears on an old question. In July 1860, near William P. Walker at Richview, lived an Alex Walker, 24, a farmer, with a Sarah A., 21, a Wm H., 3, and an infant, Edwin F., whose place among the Walkers was unknown. His name, his age and his Richview home fit the sergeant, who would have been about twenty-seven in 1863, so he was probably the same man. Two Walker men of Richview, William P. in the 60th Illinois and Alexander in the cavalry, were then in the Union ranks at the same time, though whether they were brothers or cousins is not known.

Nothing in these rolls proves kinship. Surnames this common in the county could belong to unrelated families, and the rolls give no parents. Where James M., Andrew and Nelson Livesay grew up, and where the soldiers were later buried, may one day tell more.

One of those names has a known end. John B. Walker of Richview, a private of Company F, 49th Illinois, mustered on 31 December 1861, was killed at Shiloh on 6 April 1862. A brother remembered a John B. Walker in 1894 as a captain killed there, and the two were probably the same man.

stories.title: Township 6 South, Range 23 East: the family on the Dawes allotment map
stories.hook: A hand-colored plat made by the Dawes Commission puts Louis Merry, Bessie, Ida May and the baby Isaam Gibbs on named blocks of land in Section 4, and Lizzie Durant in Section 10.

subject.name: Louis, Bessie and Ida May Merry

body: On 30 September 1904 Louis Merry wrote that Hopper Watkins had filed on his farm on 5 April 1904, and that the farm lay in Section 4, Township 6 South, Range 23 East. The Dawes Commission kept a sheet for that township among its “Allotment Maps,” printed plats of single townships on which clerks colored each parcel and lettered the allottee’s name and enrollment number as selections were recorded, showing allotments, townsites and railway rights of way between about 1896 and about 1906. At the foot of this sheet is the imprint of the Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes at Muskogee.

Section 4 is on the sheet, and the family is in it. An irregular, L-shaped block is lettered “Louis Merry” with the number 1363, which is his roll number as an intermarried white citizen on card 5754. Two blocks hem it in, marked only A-1002 and A-1003. Lower in the same section, one block reads “Ida May Merry A. 15527,” her roll number, and the large block beside it reads “Isaam Gibbs A 14616,” the number of the baby Lizzie Gibbs bore on 30 August 1902 and whose birth affidavits Louis took as notary. Two small tracts on the section’s north edge carry only the numbers A 14616 and A 15526, Isaam’s and Bessie’s. Bessie’s name is spelled out on a larger block in the northwest corner of Section 2, “Bessie Merry A. 15526.” The neighbors lettered in Section 4 include Fannie Carn and Andrew Battiest.

Further along, in Section 10, a block reads “Lizzie Durant A2580,” Lizzie’s roll number, so the girl enrolled at Wheelock Seminary in 1899 had her land in the same township as her cousin Bessie. Next to it, toward Section 11, is “Jane Durant A2844.” A Jane Durrant, 10, full blood, had roll 2844 in the household of Alfred Nakishi, and “Selina Nakashi A2842” is lettered nearby. Thomas Durant had a second daughter named Jane, whom Wilsey Clay named in 1906, but nothing ties her to Alfred Nakishi’s household. The two Janes may have been one girl, though that is only a possibility.

The map tells where, and little else. Which block was a homestead and which was surplus land is not said, the letters P and C stamped on the parcels are unexplained, and what improvements stood on the land is not known. Louis’s number could be written only after the Secretary of the Interior approved his enrollment on 14 March 1905, so his block was probably lettered after that date, a year after Hopper Watkins’s filing; what became of that claim is not known. The township lies just north of the one where Muriel Wright placed the old Lukfata mission, so the family’s land lay in the same stretch of country as Lukfata, where Louis and Bessie were married in 1896.

stories.title: How the land was chosen: the Choctaw Land Office and an allotting party
stories.hook: The Choctaw Land Office opened at Atoka in April 1903. A clerk who later rode through the Lukfata country with a field party left his own account of how the land was placed.
body: The land the family received came from a chain of agreements. L. P. Bobo, a young clerk at the Choctaw Land Office, wrote in the Chronicles of Oklahoma in 1945 that the Choctaw Land Office at Atoka and the Chickasaw office at Tishomingo opened in April 1903 so that about thirty-five thousand citizens and freedmen could choose a homestead and surplus land. Each Indian citizen was entitled to 320 acres of average land under the Atoka Agreement (signed 23 April 1897 and carried into the Curtis Act of 28 June 1898) and the Supplemental Agreement ratified 1 July 1902, which Choctaw and Chickasaw voters approved on 25 September 1902. If a citizen had not chosen within twelve months after the offices opened, and twelve months after the Secretary approved his enrollment, the Commission could choose for him.

The family’s own lives show that machinery at work. Louis’s report that Hopper Watkins had filed on his farm on 5 April 1904 came a year after the Atoka office opened. In January 1903 the Commission wrote to Abner Clay quoting the act that let “the father or mother, if members” select for minor children. Wilsey Clay’s granddaughter Lizzie Durant swore in 1906 that her allotment was already selected. When any particular parcel was chosen is not known; the map of Township 6 South, Range 23 East is the first to put the family’s names on the ground.

A neighbor’s family shows what the Atoka office asked of an allottee. On 22 May 1903, at the Choctaw Land Office, Atoka, Ozie T. Hodges, of the Hodges family of Atoka, applied for an allotment, “the name of said applicant appearing as No. 12061 on approved schedule of Choctaws by blood.” The clerks checked him against the approved roll, and when his family’s card was found to have entered Ozie as a daughter, the young man testified that he was a son, and the Commission wrote on 1 June 1903 that the card now read “No. 3 is a male.” John M. Hodges, Ozie’s father, was very probably the witness who testified about Peter Durant in Louis Merry’s case.

Allottees who did not come in were handled differently. Bobo says that more than a year and a half after the offices opened, the Commission sent out field parties to find the stragglers, locate their improvements and place their allotments. His party left on a Thanksgiving morning with a surveyor and two interpreters, worked the Boggy River and Antlers country, then Hochatown and Mountain Fork, and later rode through Lukfata and Eagletown. He gives no year, but his account follows a mild winter of 1903–04 with a cold, snowy one, which puts the Lukfata weeks in early 1905. The party also gathered proofs of death for people on the old rolls, carrying the 1893 Leased District payment roll, whose per capita share was the same $103 that Bessie’s warrant carried, the 1896 census roll and the Commission’s 1898–99 enrollment. Some Choctaws, he adds, refused to take land “between the rocks,” that is, within surveyed lines.

Bobo names none of the Merrys, Durants or Clays, and whether his party ever met them is not known. But his account comes closest to the weeks and the country in which Louis’s enrollment was approved (14 March 1905) and his farm was claimed by another man, and it shows that the allotment of a family like Bessie’s was not one event but a long, uneven process that ran from the Atoka office to horseback visits in winter.

stories.title: Two wedding witnesses and the Lukfata post office
stories.hook: The men who stood up at Louis and Bessie’s wedding in 1896 were, one after the other, the postmasters at Lukfata.

subject.name: Lukfata and its postmasters
subject.rel: Place and neighbors of Louis and Bessie Merry

body: The two witnesses at Louis Merry and Bessie Durant’s wedding at Lukfata on 7 September 1896 were J. W. Costelow and Chas. J. Gaffney, and both later signed affidavits there as notaries, in 1899 and 1902. They were also Lukfata’s postmasters. In 1895, and again on 1 July 1899, “Lukfata, Choctaw N., C. J. Gaffney” was postmaster, paid $60.32 that year, and he was still there on 1 July 1901 at $55.42. By 1 July 1903 the postmaster was James W. Castilow, at $72.52, and in 1907 it was “Lukfata, Dist 24: Spencer, John A, PM $144.” So Gaffney, the notary before whom Mattie Clay swore to her son Abner Henry’s birth on 1 May 1899, was postmaster that July, and Costelow, the notary of October 1902, held the office soon after.

His name was spelled three ways: Costelow in 1896 and 1902, Castilow in 1903, and “Jim Costilow at Lukfata” in L. P. Bobo’s memory of an allotting party’s winter ride through McCurtain County, among the well-furnished homes where the party stopped. Those are one surname by sound and place, and the first names match as far as they go: J. W., James W., Jim.

The office itself was older than either man. A post office spelled Luk-fah-tah opened in the Choctaw Nation on 14 February 1853 with Emilius G. Corder as postmaster and was discontinued effective 9 July 1866, and Lukfata was reestablished on 21 January 1873 with John N. Hodges, as George H. Shirk recorded. In December 1849 the Nation’s annuity payments were announced for “Lukfoata,” halfway between present Idabel and Broken Bow. Lukfata was a post and meeting place for decades before the Merry wedding, which fits a neighborhood where a postmaster could also take sworn statements for the Dawes Commission.

Some things are still unknown. Whether Gaffney held the office on the wedding day itself is not certain, though he held it in 1895 and in 1899. And the minister, Rev. J. H. Sleeper, is otherwise a stranger: nothing more is known of him than his name on the certificate and his later work as a notary. Gaffney and Costelow were neighbors, not kin.

stories.title: John M. Hodges of Atoka: the man who remembered Peter Durant
stories.hook: The witness who told the Commission in 1900 that Peter Durant “had two little kids” was very probably John M. Hodges of Atoka, a Choctaw with a wife, two sons and an enrollment of his own.

subject.name: John M. Hodges
subject.rel: Witness in the Merry enrollment case

body: On 7 December 1900, at Atoka, the Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes took the testimony of a John M. Hodges on behalf of Louis Merry. He said he was fifty, a Choctaw citizen by blood, born and raised in the Nation, that he had known Peter Durant, that Peter “had two little kids” when he left “that part of the country” in 1877 or 1878, and that Peter was the son of Wilsey Clay. His words are what tie Bessie’s father to Wilsey, so it matters who he was.

He was very probably the John M. Hodges of Atoka whose family applied in August 1899 on Choctaw card 4310: John M., 50, one-eighth Choctaw; his wife Martha, 38; and sons Ozie T., 18, and Joseph M., 15. John and Martha had been on the 1896 Choctaw roll in Atoka County, both Choctaws by blood whose mothers were Choctaw, and on the final rolls John M. Hodges, then 53, one-eighth, was roll 12060, with his sons as 12061 and 12062. The age, the Choctaw blood and the Atoka home, where the hearing was held, all fit the witness, though nothing says outright that they were the same man.

Martha died, and notice of her death was approved on 22 November 1902. Ozie applied for his allotment at the Choctaw Land Office on 22 May 1903. In September 1905 John wrote to the Commission enclosing a copy of the certificate of his marriage to Mary Hunter on 6 April 1905 and asking that she be enrolled as an intermarried citizen. The Acting Commissioner answered on 14 September that under the act of 1 July 1902 no application could be received for a person who married a citizen by blood after 25 September 1902. It was the same cutoff the Commission pressed on Louis and Bessie Merry and on Abner and Mattie Clay, applied now to a witness in the Merry case himself.

There is one more thread, and it is only a possibility. The Lukfata post office was reestablished on 21 January 1873 with “John N. Hodges” as postmaster. A man who was about fifty in 1900 would have been about twenty-three then; he said he was born and raised in the Nation, and that he left “that part of the country” in 1877 or 1878. But the initial differs, M and N, perhaps a misread letter, and nothing ties the two together. The surname was at Lukfata later too: a Melissa Hodges, 17, three-quarters Choctaw, had Lukfata as her post office about 1899 to 1902, but no link to John M. is known.

What this adds to Bessie’s line is modest but real. The one man who spoke for Peter Durant’s family before the Commission was a Choctaw of the Atoka country with his own enrollment at stake, not a stranger, and his memory reached back to the 1870s, when Peter’s children were small. Which county he meant by “Matoon County” is still unknown.

stories.title: The law behind the wedding: what Choctaw statute asked of a white man
stories.hook: The 1894 laws of the Choctaw Nation set out the license, the ten Choctaw signers, the oath and the penalty that Louis Merry went through in 1896 and that his case later turned on.
body: In 1894 the General Council of the Choctaw Nation published its Constitution and Laws, compiled by A. R. Durant, with Davis Homer and Ben Watkins as assistant compilers. Under “Citizenship,” section I, “Inter-marriage,” any white man or foreign citizen who wished to marry a Choctaw woman had to get a license from a circuit clerk or a judge of a court of record, and satisfy that officer that he had no living wife from whom he was not lawfully divorced. He had to present a certificate of good moral character signed by at least ten respectable Choctaw citizens by blood who had known him for twelve months. He had to pay twenty-five dollars and take an oath to honor, defend and submit to the Nation’s constitution and laws, and not to seek protection or redress from the United States government that was incompatible with them. Marriages had to be solemnized under Choctaw law or were void, anyone who solemnized a marriage outside these rules was to be fined fifty dollars, and the person who married had to bring the certificate, attached to the back of the license, to the circuit clerk within thirty days to be recorded.

Louis Merry’s wedding followed the law closely, with differences worth noting. R. W. Thomas, clerk of Bok Tuklo County, swore in 1904 that Louis applied to him in September 1896 with a petition signed by ten Choctaws by blood, took the oath of allegiance and paid the “regular fee” of one hundred dollars, and was licensed to marry Bessie Durant; Rev. J. H. Sleeper then married them on 7 September 1896. The ten signers and the oath were the law’s certificate and oath. The fee was not: the law of 1894 says twenty-five dollars, and why Louis paid more is not known, though the fee may have been raised to one hundred dollars by an act of council in 1887. The office also differed, since the law named circuit clerks and judges and Thomas was a county clerk.

The statute also explains the quarrel over recording. It told the licensed man to hand the marriage certificate to the circuit clerk within thirty days and told the clerk to record it. Thomas swore that it was not the custom in Bok Tuklo County to record such licenses at that time. His successor Joe A. James first said he had recorded Louis’s papers and returned them, and later was uncertain. The Commission accepted the marriage anyway, but the law shows why both clerks were asked about it. Sections 5 and 6 also mattered to anyone who married in this way: an intermarried widow or widower kept citizenship unless he or she married a white person without Choctaw blood, and a spouse who abandoned the marriage forfeited the rights and could be removed as an intruder. Louis and Bessie’s separation of June to July 1902, told in his testimony, was the kind of event those words made important.

By 1905 the question was no longer the Nation’s statute alone. The Department of the Interior’s published decisions show how it read the old Choctaw law. In May 1904 the Acting Secretary approved the enrollment of Thornton D. Pearce, a white man married under Choctaw law in 1883 to a Choctaw citizen who died in 1895, though he had since married a white woman. The decision relied on article 38 of the 1866 treaty, which made a white person who married a Choctaw and lived in the Nation a member of it “in all respects as though he was a native,” and on the council act that the Choctaw digest prints at page 226. An Assistant Attorney-General’s opinion approved on 28 January 1905, on which the Secretary rejected Emma McMenamin a few days later, held that citizenship by intermarriage cannot be gained by marrying another white person who had himself become a citizen that way. Louis, married to a Choctaw woman by blood, fit the first rule and not the second, and the Commission ruled for him on 10 January 1905. The Nation’s attorneys, Mansfield, McMurray and Cornish, who protested his claim, are the same firm named in these published cases.

Nothing in Louis’s path was improvised. Each paper the Commission asked for in 1900 and 1904, the petition, the oath, the license, the certificate and the clerk’s record, matched a step the Nation’s own law required in 1896, and the license that burned in December 1897 was the paper at the center of his case.

stories.title: How the Merrys were enrolled: a card, a folder, sworn words and numbers
stories.hook: For the Merry, Clay and Durant families, enrollment meant a card for each household, a folder of sworn papers behind it, hearings taken down word for word, and a string of numbers that in the end became land.

subject.name: The Dawes records of the Merry, Clay and Durant families

body: The Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes, called the Dawes Commission after its chairman, was authorized by Congress on 3 March 1893 to negotiate agreements with the Five Civilized Tribes that would permit land to be allotted to individual tribal members. In 1896 Congress let it add names to the tribal rolls, and more than 7,500 people applied that year, but the Curtis Act of 28 June 1898 declared those “1896 applications” void and told the Commission to enroll people without tribal consent. Applications were then taken from 1898 through 1907. The “1896 roll” on which Louis and Bessie Merry already stood, as numbers 14822 and 8644, was a different list, the Choctaw Nation’s own census of that year, which L. P. Bobo called the “Census Roll.” Whether the Merrys, the Clays or the Durants also applied to the Commission in 1896 is not known.

Each family was entered on a census card, a one-page summary of the household. The Merrys’ card, 5754, dated 26 April 1899, lists Louis, Bessie and their daughter Ida May with ages, blood, the parents’ names and counties, earlier roll numbers and a column of stamps. It was filed among the Choctaws by blood, with Louis on the same card as an intermarried white citizen. The numbers on it meant different things: 5754 was the card, 1363 Louis’s roll number as an intermarried white citizen, 15526 and 15527 Bessie’s and Ida May’s roll numbers, and 14822 and 8644 their numbers of 1896. The final roll gave each approved person one roll number, and land was later allotted by that number, not by the card.

Behind each card grew a folder of papers, an enrollment application or “testimonial packet.” The Merrys’ ran to forty pages: a typed title, “Record in the matter of the application for the enrollment as a citizen by intermarriage of the Choctaw Nation of Louis Merry,” the mother’s and midwife’s affidavits, letters from the Commission, the hearing transcripts, the clerks’ affidavits, the copy of the marriage certificate and the decision. Its cover is marked “Trans from Choc #D128.” Denied or doubtful cases were marked D, and that is probably what the Merrys’ first number meant, though it is never said. The card moved to 5754 on 21 March 1904, before the decision of 10 January 1905, so the move was not simply the result of the ruling.

The hearings were taken down word for word. John M. Hodges’s answers of 7 December 1900 were typed under the caption “Choctaw D 128, Louis Merry vs Choctaw Nation,” with a line noting that no testimony was offered by the Nation. He was sworn by the acting chairman, Tams Bixby; the Choctaw commissioner, Judge Lewis, asked the follow-up questions about Abner Clay; and the next day the stenographer, Anna Bell, swore that the pages were a true copy of her notes. Every Dawes transcript carried such an oath, which is why a witness’s own words, like “he had two little kids,” survive as they were said.

Then came the land. Each allottee’s parcel and its improvements were described under his roll number, and township maps were lettered with each allottee’s name and roll number; on the map of Township 6 South, Range 23 East the Merrys’ numbers became land. Card, folder, sworn words and map together are what let a roll number such as 15526 be followed to a person, a parent and a parcel.

stories.title: Six mail towns in the family’s papers, and when each one opened
stories.hook: Garvin, Shawneetown, Wheelock, Valliant, Millerton and Idabel were the mail towns of the Merry, Clay, Durant and Box families, and each had its own beginning.

subject.name: Garvin, Shawneetown, Wheelock, Valliant, Millerton and Idabel

body: In 1948 George H. Shirk set down the first post offices within the boundaries of Oklahoma, each with the nation it served, the date its first postmaster was appointed and its changes of name and closings. Six of the Choctaw Nation’s offices were the family’s own mail towns, besides Glover and Lukfata.

Garvin opened on 19 February 1894 with James W. Kirk as postmaster. In 1895 Kirk earned $34.70, and in 1903 J. W. Kirk earned $311.50, a sign of how fast the little place grew. It was the post office of William A. Durant and Laura Clay, who lived in Red River County; Louis Merry gave his second testimony at Garvin on 28 November 1902; Mattie Clay was back there by March 1904; and G. A. Spaulding, the U.S. Commissioner before whom the Bok Tuklo clerks swore their affidavits in August 1904, sat at Garvin. L. P. Bobo’s allotting party left its mule team at a livery stable in Garvin over Christmas.

Shawneetown was first called Kulli Inla; the office was opened under the new name on 16 August 1892 with Robert M. Love as postmaster, and he was still postmaster in 1901. It is where W. F. Nichols took Mattie Clay’s affidavit for her daughter Myrtle on 24 October 1902 and where her brother Claude Denson lived when he wrote about the children’s allotments in January 1903.

Wheelock is the oldest. Its post office opened on 21 March 1845 with Henry K. Copeland, lapsed for a few weeks in 1866 and for months in 1872, and was discontinued effective 3 May 1895, with mail sent to Garvin. Lizzie Durant was at Wheelock Seminary in April 1899, and a later generation of the family knew it too: Alfreda Whitfield was born at Wheelock in 1939.

Three offices belong to the years of the Dawes enrollment. Valliant opened on 23 June 1902 with Hosea L. Fowler as postmaster, “formerly Fowlerville,” an office established on 28 August 1894. Parsons, named for W. S. Parsons, was first ordered on 17 May 1902, rescinded in September and actually opened after a new appointment ordered on 15 December 1902; its name was changed to Millerton on 5 March 1908. Bokhoma was established on 15 December 1902 with Daniel Strawn and renamed Idabel on 3 February 1904. Claude Joel Box and Archie Box registered for the draft at Valliant in 1942, Tyro Box gave Millerton, and Alfreda Whitfield Sandridge later worked in Idabel, so the Box and Whitfield families knew towns whose present names are younger than the Dawes enrollment.

stories.title: Wheelock Seminary, where Lizzie Durant was enrolled in 1899
stories.hook: The Choctaw boarding school that held Lizzie Durant on 27 April 1899 had been founded by the Nation’s General Council in 1842, and its church yard holds the missionary who began the work.

subject.name: Wheelock Female Seminary
subject.rel: School where Lizzie Durant was enrolled

body: Lizzie Durant was enrolled at Wheelock Seminary on 27 April 1899, and she said under oath in 1906 that she had been a student there that April. Wheelock Female Seminary was established in 1842 by the Choctaw General Council, as Ora Eddleman Reed told in her history of the Robe family of missionaries in the Chronicles of Oklahoma. The Rev. Alfred Wright of the American Board had begun mission work at Wheelock in 1832 and stayed until his death on 31 March 1853, and he is buried in the old Wheelock church yard near Millerton.

In the fall of 1884, when the Presbyterian board closed Old Spencer Academy, its girls were moved to Wheelock under the Robe family, and Reed describes a rebuilt stone church attended by Choctaws and by white and Black neighbors. The post office there, opened in 1845, was discontinued in 1895 and its mail sent to Garvin. The boarding schools were supported three-fourths by the Choctaw Nation and one-fourth by the mission board, with missionaries as superintendents. Lizzie, about thirteen and full Choctaw, belonged to the generation the Nation was educating in those boarding academies at the very moment the Dawes Commission was recording its children.

In 1899 Wheelock Orphan Academy was among the Choctaw Nation’s boarding schools, and in the year ended June 1900 its superintendent was W. W. Appleton. That year the Nation had 120 neighborhood schools, held back, the U.S. Indian Inspector said, by bad weather, long distances, uncomfortable buildings and the indifference of patrons, while the boarding schools were “poorly equipped.” Which neighborhood schools stood nearest Lukfata and Glover is not known.

No school or church at Glover is known, and the only Lukfata school and church known are the mission school of 1835 and a “Lukfata Chito (Big Lick) Church,” of which nothing more is known. Wheelock, by contrast, is well remembered, and Lizzie was there, a granddaughter of Wilsey Clay within its walls.

stories.title: Gilbert G. Merry’s 1916 sketch: a Calvin Merry and a brother at Golden
stories.hook: Gilbert G. Merry, a Valliant pharmacist and county commissioner, was a son of Calvin Merry and Eliza McGregory and had a brother J. L., a merchant at Golden, very probably Louis Merry himself.
body: Gilbert G. Merry’s family story begins with the old Military Highway through Eagletown, Valliant, Bismark and Glover. His father, Calvin Merry, “who died about twenty years ago, at Goodland, Oklahoma,” was reared in Arkansas near the old highway and went along with some of the pathfinders who laid it out. By 1916 Gilbert, of Valliant, was a McCurtain County commissioner, and his life was told in Thoburn’s Standard History of Oklahoma. Gilbert was born in 1879 at Chapel Hill, Arkansas, seven miles from the Indian Territory line, to Calvin and Eliza McGregory, whose parents were early settlers of the border. He entered the Territory at thirteen, living first at Eagletown and later at Lukfata, and in 1903 he watched the first net proceeds payment, a time of drinking, shooting and lawlessness. He then lived at Garvin, where he managed a store, and from 1906 was a pharmacist at Valliant. His father was a poor man, and Gilbert first read in a second reader at seventeen. He married Annie Oaks of Grant, one-fourth Choctaw, on 4 April 1906. She died in April 1915.

Gilbert had four brothers: F. L., who farmed in Cherokee County, Oklahoma; B. F., a landowner and county commissioner of Hemphill County, Texas; J. L., a general merchant at Golden, Oklahoma; and the Rev. Robert, a Baptist minister at Garvin. When Louis Merry was enrolled on 26 April 1899, his parents were given as Calvin Merry and Elizabeth Merry, both dead and both “non-citiz,” not citizens of the Choctaw Nation. They are also remembered more fully as John Calvin Merry and Eliza Jane McGregor, with Louis’s birthplace as Sevier County, Arkansas, and the 1880 census of Monroe Township, Sevier County, bears this out: it lists Calvin Merry, 48, and Eliza J., 43, with sons Festus Lee, Benjamin F., Joshua L., eight, John H. and George G. Elizabeth and Eliza Jane were very probably the same woman. Gilbert’s parents, Calvin and Eliza McGregory, fit both, and so does the Arkansas border country.

Place and time fit too. Louis Merry said in December 1900 that he had lived in the Choctaw Nation about eight years, which brings his arrival to about 1892, when he was about twenty by his gravestone’s birth year, the year Gilbert, at thirteen, reached Eagletown. Louis married Bessie Durant at Lukfata in September 1896, and Gilbert lived at Lukfata. The Commission wrote to Louis as “J. L. Merry,” and Gilbert’s brother was J. L. Merry at Golden, the town where Louis is said to have died in 1932 and where his daughter Ida later kept the post office; and Glover’s first postmaster was Joshua L. Merry. The parents’ names, the border country, the year of arrival, the Lukfata years and the initials and town of J. L. make it probable that Louis Merry was Gilbert’s brother and that Calvin and Eliza McGregory were his parents.

There is one snag. Gilbert is said to have helped educate “his younger brother,” and four are named; if all four were younger than Gilbert, born in 1879, a J. L. born after that could not have married in 1896 and given his age as 28 in 1900. Louis’s gravestone gives 10 April 1872. The sentence is loosely written, and may mean only that some of the four were younger, the 1880 census settles the ages, with Joshua L. eight then and so seven years older than Gilbert. Which county Chapel Hill lay in is not said, though Calvin’s farm lay in Sevier County in 1880. Calvin’s death “about twenty years” before 1916 fits Louis’s parents both being dead by April 1899.

So Calvin, Eliza and Gilbert were a family, and Louis very probably belonged to it, though no record yet names him beside Gilbert. Gilbert’s or Louis’s obituary, or Calvin’s estate or death, may one day settle it.

stories.title: A James C. Logan, 1773 to 1840, in the Wedgeworth Cemetery
stories.hook: A James C. Logan, 1773 to 1840, lies among the Wedgworths in a cemetery near Cook’s Store, Greene County, Alabama; he died too early to be Dudley Logan’s father, but he may have been his grandfather.
body: Near Cook’s Store, in Greene County, Alabama, lies the Wedgeworth Cemetery, with graves of the Anderson, Hanna, Wynn, Watkins, Garland and Gewin families, of several Wedgworths and of one Logan. John Wedgworth died on 11 September 1824 at 35, “the first person interred here after organization of his church.” Esther Wedgworth is remembered with the date 11 September 1832. James Wedgworth was born in Pennsylvania on 31 October 1771 and died in September 1843. Middleton Wedgworth lived from 8 September 1828 to 11 September 1889, under a title now worn away. And there is “James C. Logan, 1773 to 1840,” as Mrs. S. M. Marshall recorded the stones in 1960, in her Greene County, Alabama records printed at Tuscaloosa.

The Logan matters because of Dudley Timothy Logan. Dudley was born in Greene County on 8 January 1846, and his parents are said to have been James Clement Logan and Martha Calhoun, though that is unproved. A James C. Logan who died in 1840 cannot have fathered a child in 1846. But in 1850 Martha Logan, 71, born in South Carolina, headed a household two doors from the Wedgeworths, with Leroy Logan, 49, Willis Logan, 44, and Clement Logan, 33, all born in South Carolina, in the neighboring houses, and a Dudley, 3, in Clement’s. A widow of 71 born about 1779 would fit the wife of a man born in 1773, and her sons would be Leroy, Willis and Clement. If so, Dudley’s grandparents were James C. and Martha Logan, and the family memory has moved them down a generation. That is only a possibility.

In 1830 the heads of Greene County households included Logans named Clement, Isaac, John, Willis, Michael and Zachariah, and Wedgworths named James, James Jr., William, Joseph and Matheas. A Clement Logan heading a household in 1830 cannot be the Clement who was 33 in 1850, who would then have been thirteen. Either the head of 1830 was the older man, James Clement Logan, going by his second name, or the age of 1850 is wrong.

The Wedgworths gain something too. Middleton Wedgworth, born in 1828, is the right age for the Middleton, 22, in Elizabeth Wedgworth’s household in 1850, next door to Larkin’s, so the Wedgworth households of 1850 belonged to this burial ground. James Wedgworth, born in Pennsylvania in 1771, and the elder John Wedgworth, who died in 1824, may have been of the generation before Larkin and Stephen, who were born in South and North Carolina, but nothing says so. Which Wedgworth girl was Annie is still unknown.
The old stones were copied long ago, and their dates may have slipped in the copying. Dudley and Annie cannot yet be tied to any of these people.

The family history that calls James C. Logan a son of John Logan Sr. and Rachel Flood gives him a brother Col. John Logan Jr., a brother Andrew Logan II, and sisters Sarah, Rachel and Margaret. That family was real. In the Long Cane country of old Abbeville District, now Greenwood County, John Logan, a son of the pioneer Andrew Logan, raised sons Col. John Logan Jr., who lived from 1761 to 1820, and Andrew Logan II, a Revolutionary soldier who lived from 1763 to 1856, and a daughter Rachel, born in 1767, who in 1787 became the second wife of Dr. Zachary Meriwether. Andrew II married the doctor's daughter, Nancy Meriwether.

The Alabama end fits that family. The family history says James went west with the children of his brother Andrew, and Greene County's planters at New Prospect in 1855 included a Zachary M. Logan and an Andrew Logan, the names a grandson of Dr. Zachary Meriwether and a son of Andrew II would carry, while the Meriwethers themselves had settled near Springfield in 1818 and gave their name to a landing on the Black Warrior a few miles west of the Logan land. Long Cane was also the country of the Calhouns, which would suit a wife named Martha Calhoun. Still, no record yet found names James among John Logan's children, and no Rachel Flood has turned up at all, so James's place in the Long Cane family is a strong lead and nothing more.

stories.title: Who the old county books remembered, and who they left out
stories.hook: The Livesays, Walkers and Carters of southern Illinois filled the county histories, while the McCormacks, Whitfields, Boxes, Logans and Wedgworths were left almost entirely out.
body: The county histories and compendiums of the 1870s to the 1920s remembered some of the family’s branches generously and others hardly at all, and what they left out tells something too.

The Illinois families were well remembered. The History of Washington County of 1879, the History of Marion and Clinton Counties of 1881, the History of Jefferson County of 1883, the Portrait and Biographical Record of Clinton, Washington, Marion and Jefferson Counties of 1894, Brinkerhoff’s History of Marion County and the Biographical and Reminiscent History of Richland, Clay and Marion Counties, both of 1909, all have something to say of Evan Carter Livesay, Jackson L. Livesay, Lorenzo M. Livesay, Alfred’s children, the Flannigans and Whites, and the Carters of Lake Township. Wall’s History of Jefferson County of 1909 and the Combined History of Randolph, Monroe and Perry Counties of 1883 have no Livesay, Hoke or Flannigan of interest. The 1894 volume has only passing Walkers: a Charles Walker who married a Thompson daughter in Richview Township, and a James Walker among the husbands of a Sanders daughter.

The McCormacks of Madison County, Indiana, were never written up. Neither John L. Forkner’s History of Madison County of 1914, in both volumes, nor the Historical Sketches and Reminiscences of 1897, nor Hardesty’s history of 1874 has a McCormack or McCormick family sketch. The only McCormack in the 1914 volumes is McCormack and Sweeney, the Columbus, Indiana, contractors for the courthouse. James T. McCormack’s people are still unknown.

Nor were the Arkansas and Texas families. Goodspeed’s Biographical and Historical Memoirs of Western Arkansas (1891) and of Southern Arkansas (1890) have no sketch for Sevier County and no Whitfield or Box of this family, only a Whitfield County in Georgia, a lodge and a Corbell family with a Box mother, and a 1910 railway booklet on Sevier and Little River counties names no one. In Texas, Box burials are remembered in the Graveyards of Van Zandt County, but no Alonzo or Emma, and the History of Titus County of 1961 has a W. M. Logan in a Confederate company of 1862, but no Dudley Logan, Wedgworth or Box.

In Alabama, Brewer’s Alabama (1872) and Owen’s History of Alabama and Dictionary of Alabama Biography (1921, four volumes) have no sketch for the Greene, Hale or Tuscaloosa Logans or Wedgworths, whose name survives there mainly in place names. Snedecor’s Greene County directory for 1855 and 1856 lists planters Isaac, Willis, Zachary M., Andrew and A. L. Logan and Stephen, Larkin and John M. Wedgworth at New Prospect, and the Wedgeworth Cemetery has its own small record.

In the Choctaw Nation the great books of the day, Gideon’s Indian Territory (1901), O’Beirne’s Leaders and Leading Men of the Indian Territory (1891), Flickinger’s The Choctaw Freedmen (1914), the Standard History of Oklahoma (1916) and Thoburn and Wright’s Oklahoma: A History of the State and Its People (1929), remember one Merry, Gilbert G. Merry, but no Clays of Bok Tuklo and no Fred Gibbs. Their Durants are the large Durant family of the Atoka and Bennington country, including a W. A. Durant born in 1866, a son of Sylvester Durant, who was not the William A. Durant born about 1870 to Allington and Mary Durant. A Joseph L. Gibbs of Claremore was from Ohio and is not known to be related. And in 1914 an A. J. Whitfield was among the Valliant dealers who helped keep the Oak Hill school on a cash basis, a McCurtain County Whitfield whose tie to Oliver Clinton Whitfield, if any, is unknown.

stories.title: Two Walkers on the Mount Vernon Circuit, 1832 and 1833
stories.hook: In 1832 Simeon Walker rode the Mount Vernon Circuit and in 1833 James Walker followed him, but whether that James was the Rev. James Walker of Beaucoup is still unknown.
body: A James Walker was sent to the Mount Vernon Circuit in 1831, as James B. Leaton wrote in his History of Methodism in Illinois in 1883. That same year Jefferson County remembered its Methodist preachers at Mount Vernon from 1825 to 1854, by conference years beginning in autumn, a little differently: 1830–31, John H. Benson; 1832, Simeon Walker; 1833, James Walker; 1834, Warren L. Jenkins.

Simeon Walker was “a name that is a household word in southern Illinois,” as Marion and Clinton counties remembered him in 1881. He was sent to the Grand Prairie Mission, which took in Salem, in 1830 and 1831, and a Simeon Walker, “who recently deceased,” was preacher in charge on the Carlyle Circuit in 1833 and among the early Methodist preachers of Lake Township. That fits Simeon Walker Sr., born in Georgia in 1802, who was probably the father of Captain Simeon Walker of Beaucoup. It leaves the James Walker of Mount Vernon in 1833, two years after Leaton’s date.

Nothing joins James Walker of the circuit to James Walker of Beaucoup, who was at Beaucoup in the 1820s and 1840s and whose birthplace in 1850 was Tennessee, not Georgia. The Mount Vernon Circuit’s James Walker is remembered in 1831 and in 1833, two years apart, and nothing about either preacher tells of a home, a wife or a death. Whether they were one man is still unknown.

The church's own printed Minutes put the two Walkers in order. At the conference that met at Indianapolis in October 1831, James Walker, newly received on trial, was sent to Mount Vernon in the Kaskaskia District under the presiding elder S. H. Thompson, while Simeon Walker went back to the Grand Prairie mission; the same page calls the next conference for Jacksonville, Morgan County, on 25 September 1832. At Jacksonville the two men changed places in the list: Simeon Walker took Mount Vernon, and James Walker went south to the Brownsville mission in Jackson County, with John S. Barger now presiding elder. A year later Mount Vernon passed to Thomas C. Collins, and James was again at Brownsville.

So James rode the Mount Vernon Circuit in 1831-32 and Simeon in 1832-33, just as Leaton had it. The Jefferson County history of 1883 had Simeon's year right but set James down for 1833, the year that in fact belonged to Collins, and left out James's real year, 1831; that is why its list seemed to put him at Mount Vernon two years after Leaton. Where James went after Brownsville, and what that says about whether he was Rev. James Walker of Beaucoup, is told in "Was Rev. James Walker a circuit rider?"

stories.title: Floyd Livesay in Lydia’s household, 1860
stories.hook: In 1860 four-year-old Floyd Livesay was living with Lydia Livesay, a widow of fifty-two, and her five youngest children; in 1870, at fourteen, he was with her son David, but whose son he was is still not certain.

subject.name: Floyd Hale Livesay as a child

body: Floyd Hale Livesay is best known as a man in Brazoria County, Texas, but as a child he lived within the family of Robert and Lydia Livesay in Washington County, Illinois. In June 1860, in Township 2 South, Range 2 West, Lydia Livesay, 52, born in Tennessee, headed a household with David, 28, Thomas, 24, “Palina,” 20, Daniel, 17 and “Trumbull,” 15, all born in Illinois, and Floyd H., 4, born in Illinois. Robert Livesay died in 1855, and the 1856 release that named his heirs called Nancy P., Daniel M. and Elbert T. minors. The names of 1860 are those three: Nancy Paulina and Elbert Trumbell.

Ten years later, in 1870, Floyd H. Livesay, 14, was living with David Livesay, 40, born in Illinois, David’s wife Elisabeth, 24, and three small children. David’s wife was too young to be Floyd’s mother, and no one wrote down how they were related, so Floyd belonged to the family without its being said whose son he was. Lydia was born in 1807 and would have been 48 or 49 when Floyd was born, so he was almost certainly her grandson, a son of one of her sons, but which one is not known.

Floyd’s own later years add a clue. In 1880, at 24, farming in Ashley precinct of Washington County with his wife Alice, he gave both parents as born in Tennessee. In 1900 and 1920 his father’s birthplace was given as Tennessee, and in 1910 as Illinois; his mother’s was “unknown” in 1900 and “United States” in 1910 and 1920. A Tennessee-born father would point to one of Robert and Lydia’s older sons, William E., Lorenzo M. or Jackson M., all born in Tennessee before the move to Illinois, and not to David, who was born in Illinois. The single Illinois of 1910 could favor David. None of the older three was in the 1860 household with Floyd, so the question is open.

One fact is worth keeping in view. Tabitha J., wife of David P. Livesay, died on 14 February 1856, nine days after Floyd’s 5 February birthday. If David and Tabitha were his parents, a motherless baby raised in his grandmother’s house and then in his father’s would explain where he was in 1860 and 1870. The Tennessee birthplaces of 1880 and 1900 make that only one of several possibilities.

His ages tell something about the year of his birth too. Four in June 1860 and fourteen in June 1870 both fit a birth in early 1856, not February 1857, the year given at his death, which would make him 3 and 13. In 1900 his birth was also given as February 1856. Only his death gives the day, but the years point to 1856.

Not proven: no census states a relationship, and no record seen names Floyd’s father or mother. David P. is one candidate for his father; William E., Lorenzo M. or Jackson M. are others, if the Tennessee birthplace Floyd gave in 1880, 1900 and 1920 is right. Floyd is left unlinked in the tree, as the site’s tests require, until a record names a parent.

stories.title: Golden’s postmasters: a father, a daughter and a granddaughter
stories.hook: Golden, Oklahoma, had Joshua L. Merry as its postmaster from 1916, his daughter Ida from 1945 and her daughter Ouida from 1968.
body: Golden’s post office in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, opened on 13 March 1911, with James M. Golden as the first postmaster and General M. Robertson appointed on 20 March 1912. The third postmaster, appointed on 29 February 1916, was Joshua L. Merry.

Ida’s father had been Glover’s first postmaster from 26 June 1901, and when he left that office is not known, but at Golden he served again. He was postmaster from 29 February 1916, replaced by Cicero M. Medcalf on 30 August 1920, back as acting postmaster on 16 January 1922 and postmaster from 25 March 1924, until Mrs. Dosha L. Shane was named acting postmaster on 2 April 1928. In all he ran the office for a little under eleven years, in two stretches. Nothing at Golden says outright that this Joshua L. Merry was Ida’s father, but the full name is the one of Glover, he is said to have died at Golden in 1932, and no other Merry ever kept the Golden office, so he very probably was.

Ida’s turn came four years after her husband’s death. Mrs. Ida M. Whitfield was acting postmaster on 31 March 1945 and postmaster from 24 September 1945. That fits her family’s memory that she worked first as assistant postmaster and then as postmaster, and the widowed postmistress of Golden in 1950.

Ouida followed her. Mrs. Catherine O. Carroll was acting postmaster on 30 June 1968 and postmaster from 8 January 1969, until an officer-in-charge took over on 28 November 1990. In May 2007 the Choctaw Nation’s Biskinik remembered her as a retired postmaster who served 22 years at the post office in Golden and retired in 1990. From 30 June 1968 to 28 November 1990 is twenty-two years and five months, so her twenty-two years were her years in charge of the office, not time first spent as a clerk.

The same dates unsettle another number. Ida is said to have retired at 72. Born on 12 June 1898, Ida turned 70 on 12 June 1968, eighteen days before her daughter’s acting appointment. Ida may have left a little earlier, since only the date each postmaster was appointed is known, not the date the one before left, but there is no room for two more years in charge. Either the age at her retirement is off, or Ida stayed on in some other post after giving up the office. Which is not known.

Added up, a Merry or a Whitfield was in charge of the Golden post office for roughly 56 of its first 79 years: Joshua for about eleven, Ida for about twenty-three and Ouida for about twenty-two. The long stretch between Joshua and Ida, from 1928 to 1945, belonged to Mrs. Shane.

stories.title: John Frank Kernell, Bessie’s widower
stories.hook: Bessie Durant Merry died as Bessie Kernell, and the man behind the name was probably John Frank Kernell, a Tennessee-born farmer who got his mail at Glover and was a widower three weeks after she died.
body: Bessie Durant Merry’s flat marker in the Denison Cemetery at Idabel reads “Wife, Bessie E. Kernell, Nov. 11, 1879, Mar. 22, 1950,” with the line “Mother waits for us in Heaven” cut below. It does not name her husband. He is said to have been John Frank Kernell, married to her in 1907, though neither the name nor the year is proved, and a John Frank Kernell of the right place and age did live near her.

In April 1942, in the draft registration for older men born between 28 April 1877 and 16 February 1897, John Frank Kernell registered on 27 April 1942 with McCurtain County Local Board No. 2 at the City Hall in Broken Bow. He gave his residence as Wright City, McCurtain County, and his mailing address as Glover. He was 59, born on 9 March 1883 at “Overton, Tenn.,” whether a town or a county is not said. He had no telephone, and the person who would always know his address was Porter Kernell of Durant. His work was “farming, self,” at Wright City. He signed with a mark, an X written between his first and last names, and the registrar described a white man of about six feet and 160 pounds with brown eyes.

On 11 April 1950, in Sulphur Township, the census taker found J. F. Kernell, head, white, male, 67, widowed, born in Tennessee, living alone. Sixty-seven in April 1950 fits a man born on 9 March 1883, and the birthplace matches. The same district held the Whitfield store near Golden, where Bessie is said to have died, and the census taker came twenty days after the date on her stone.

So there was one man, a Tennessee-born farmer whose mail came to Glover in 1942 and who was a widower in the Golden district in 1950. That he was Bessie’s husband rests on less: the surname on her stone, his widowhood so soon after her death, and the neighborhood where the Merry family had lived. It is probable, not proven. When they married is not known.

A John F. Kernell died on 4 October 1966 in McCurtain County, the only man of that name to die in Oklahoma, at 83 if he was the farmer of 1942. Nothing then named his parents or his wife. A Porter A. Kernell died on 27 June 1951 in Bryan County, where Durant stands; he was probably the Porter Kernell of Durant whom John named in 1942, though how they were related is not known.

The order of Bessie’s marriages is a mystery. She married Louis Merry at Lukfata in 1896, and the two were enrolled together on Dawes card 5754 in 1904 and 1905. Louis died in 1932, eighteen years before she did, and a Joshua L. Merry of Glover took out a license to marry a Mrs. Mattie Erwin. When and how the Merry marriage ended, and when Bessie became Mrs. Kernell, are still unknown, and her daughter Ida remembered her as Bessie Durant Merry. Porter of Durant is the only other Kernell known in John’s life.

Probable that he was Bessie’s husband: the evidence is her stone’s surname, his widowed status three weeks after her death and the shared neighborhood; no record states the marriage. The Find a Grave claim of a 1907 marriage is unverified. The registrar’s name and the hair color on the card are not recorded here because the handwriting is hard to read. Porter Kernell’s relationship is unknown. The 1966 death is an index entry (name, date, county only); that it belongs to this man is probable, as he is the only John F. Kernell in the index.

stories.title: When the Whitfields, Boxes and Merrys died
stories.hook: Oklahoma’s own register of deaths agrees with nearly all the family’s death dates, differs by a day for Clint Whitfield, and has no word of Louis Merry.

subject.name: The Whitfield, Box and Merry families

body: Oklahoma has registered its deaths since 1908, and for each the state kept a name, a date of death, a county and a sex, and nothing else: no parents, no age, no town. Its index “does contain errors,” the state itself warns, from misread handwriting and mistaken forms. Still, it is the state’s own word, to set beside the dates the family carved on stones and printed in notices.

Most of the family’s dates hold. In McCurtain County, Ida M. Whitfield died on 28 January 1993, Lewis O. Whitfield on 9 August 2004, Violet Whitfield on 30 July 1962, Catherine Ouida Carroll on 16 March 2007 and Elma Mae Severn on 31 October 2011, each on the date of a stone or an obituary, and Elma, whose obituary named no county, died in McCurtain County. Annie F. Box (28 December 1959) and Tyro S. Box (5 October 1967) died in Choctaw County, which fits the Hugo hospital where they died. Flossie James, Tyro’s sister Birdie, died on 14 November 1979, and an “R B James” on 5 January 1928, the date on Rafe James’s stone. Bessie E. Kernell died on 22 March 1950 in McCurtain County, the date on her gravestone and the date her granddaughter gave for Bessie Merry in 1997, so two separate accounts agree on the day and the county, which helps tie the Kernell on the stone to the Bessie of Dawes card 5754.

Two dates do not behave. The state dates the death of Oliver C. “Clint” Whitfield to 22 March 1941 in McCurtain County, one day after the 21 March on his gravestone. A one-day difference could be the stonecutter’s or the clerk’s, and which is right is not known. And Louis Merry’s death on 1 July 1932, the date on his Glover stone, has no state record at all; in the years around it only two Merrys died in Oklahoma, both on 9 August 1930. He may have been registered under another spelling or county.

The state’s register also remembers relatives whose deaths were unknown. An Archie W. Box died on 28 April 1970 in McCurtain County, the only man of that name, and he was probably Tyro’s brother Archie of Kirk Township, the “Arch Box” who survived Tyro in 1967. A Claude J. Box died on 19 November 1961 in Oklahoma County, far from Valliant, where Claude Joel Box registered for the draft in 1942; the initial and the age fit, but nothing else ties the two, so he was only probably Tyro’s brother. Walter, the eldest Box brother, is not among Oklahoma’s dead; the one Walter Box died in 2021.

Two deaths bear on Clint Whitfield’s parents. A William F. Whitfield died on 21 July 1944 in McCurtain County. A William Franklin Whitfield, 1867 to 1944, is said to have been Clint’s father, and the W. F. Whitfield of Sevier County, Arkansas, in 1900 was born in January 1868. The year and county agree, but no family is named, so he was possibly Clint’s father and no more. An Emma Whitfield died on 30 June 1955, but in Cimarron County in the Panhandle, and an Emma Whitfield there in 1950 was 76, widowed and born in Illinois, whereas the Emma of 1900 was born in Arkansas. They were probably two different women.

stories.note: The index is a transcription made over many years and gives only name, date and county, so every identification here rests on name and place. Probable: the Box brothers (Archie fits the 1950 census and the 1967 obituary; Claude’s county does not fit). Lead only: William F. Whitfield and any link to Clint. The date conflict for Clint Whitfield (22 March in the index, 21 March on the stone) is not resolved. No index entry was found for Louis Merry, Walter Box, Erma Box, Alonzo Box, Emma Box, Raphael James by full name or Eugene Carroll; a missing entry is not evidence of anything. Persons who may be living are not searched or named.

stories.title: Where Ida’s children were born
stories.hook: Four of Ida Whitfield’s children and Violet Box were registered at birth in Oklahoma, and two of the births fall in counties far from Golden.

subject.name: Ida Whitfield’s children and Violet Box

body: Oklahoma began registering births in 1908, though most were not filed on time until about 1950, so some early ones were registered late, and for each the state kept only a name, a date, a county and a sex. Four of Clint and Ida Whitfield’s children were registered, each under a name and exact date that fit, though two of the entries raise questions, and the state warns that its index contains errors.

Lewis O. Whitfield was born on 24 August 1916 in LeFlore County, by the state’s register. The date is the one on his stone and plaque, but the family’s other births were in McCurtain County, and nothing else places the family in LeFlore County in 1916. Elma M. Whitfield was born on 12 January 1918 in McCurtain County, the date in her obituary, which gave Glover as the place. Ouida was registered as “Cathrine Oudla” Whitfield, born 15 January 1924 in McCurtain County, the date in her obituary, under a third spelling of her name: Ouida in her own obituary, “Oulda” in her sister’s, and “Oudla” by the clerk.

Omagene’s birth is the puzzle. He was registered with the middle initial C and a birth date of 1 January 1922, as the family remembered, but in Beaver County, in the Oklahoma Panhandle, hundreds of miles from McCurtain County. He is said to have been born at Golden, and his brother and sisters were registered in McCurtain County in 1918 and 1924. Either the county was set down wrongly, or the family was in the Panhandle for a time. Which is not known.

Violet Box was born on 22 September 1920 in McCurtain County, by the state’s register; her gravestone gives 22 September and her 1962 obituary 21 September, so the stone was right. A Tyro Box was also born in McCurtain County, on 26 February 1909. That cannot be Violet’s father, who was born in 1888 in Texas, but Tyro and Annie Box had come to the county by 1906 or 1907, and a first son named for his father is plausible. No parents were named, and nothing else is known of the child, not even his death, so he may have been Violet’s brother, but that is only a possibility.

Five other Whitfield children were born in McCurtain County between 1915 and 1925. At least three were children of John Whitfield and Ida Austin Whitfield of Valliant, a different family, as a Bishinik obituary of January 2009 shows. They were not Clint and Ida’s children, and the remaining one goes unnamed because he could be living.

stories.note: Each indexed birth is matched to a person by name, middle initial and the exact date already in the tree, which is probable and not proof of parentage, since the index names no parents. The LeFlore County (Lewis) and Beaver County (Omagene) entries conflict with or add to the tree and are unexplained; either could be an indexing error. The 1909 Tyro Box is a lead only. The other Whitfield births in the index belong, at least in part, to the John Whitfield family of Valliant; the one not matched by an obituary is not named.

stories.title: The Livesay Store at the Pearland crossroads
stories.hook: Floyd and Alice Livesay’s grocery was, by Pearland’s own memory, a two-story building at the corner where the town’s two highways cross.
body: Floyd Livesay was a groceryman in 1914 and still called one at his death in 1932, and Pearland remembers more of the business. When Wayne Livesay died on 18 April 2013 at Cushing, Texas, the Pearland Historical Society’s July newsletter called the Livesays one of Pearland’s pioneer families. Mr. and Mrs. Floyd Livesay came in the early 1900s, it said, “opening up a livery stable and the historic Livesay Store in 1906,” though the Houston Chronicle in 1932 had Floyd arriving in the mid-1890s, so 1906 is better read as the year the business began; and they are buried in the Old Settlers Cemetery. The issue printed a photograph captioned “Livesay Store approx. 1906 at corner of Main and Broadway.” It called Floyd and Alice Wayne’s grandparents, but they were his great-grandparents: Wayne’s father was Lester Jr., Lester Jr.’s father was Lester Sr., and Lester Sr. was Floyd and Alice’s son, so “grandparents” was a slip of one generation.

The Society’s August 2022 issue says where the building stood. In a piece on the Pearland Drugstore it names Floyd Hale Livesay and his wife, Alice Walker Livesay, as the owners of the Livesay General Grocery Store, “believed to have been built about 1906,” on the southeast corner of State Highway 35 (Main Street) and FM 518 (Broadway). A service station stood on the corner until it was demolished in June 2021, and a coffee shop is there now. The April 2022 and April 2026 issues name the same corner. A reminiscence of Pearland in 1940, written by the Society’s president and printed in January 2017, describes the town center at those crossroads: the drugstore on one corner, a café and beer joint on another and, on a third, a two-story building “which had been the ‘Livesay’ store.” By the author’s memory of 1940, eight years after Floyd’s death, it was no longer the store.

The upper floor had other tenants. The August 2022 issue says the second floor was also a boarding house, and the April 2022 and August 2022 issues say the town physician, Dr. William E. Long, began his practice upstairs. The Society’s own dates for him disagree. The August 2022 and April 2026 issues have him coming to Pearland in 1911, and the April 2022 issue in 1921, which the August issue calls a typo. He died in 1941 in the April 2022 issue and in 1944 in April 2026. The July 2008 issue reprints an early teacher’s memoir saying that when the county school closed, the lessons were divided between the school building and the “Livesay Store building.” The passage gives no date and the teacher is not named in the part read. On these accounts the building served in turn as store, boarding house, doctor’s office and, at least once, schoolroom.

So Floyd was more than a retail grocer: he kept the store on the best corner in town, in a building he owned, with a livery stable in the family’s early years. That is Pearland’s memory rather than a deed or an advertisement, and the 1906 date is a belief, not a certainty. Pearland remembers the next generation too. Wayne graduated from Pearland High School in 1958, which fits his birth in 1940, and a Carolyn Livesay was in the class of 1955 and in a varsity volleyball photograph. A Carolyn Livesay was in the seventh grade in 1950, which fits the class of 1955, and she was probably Wayne’s sister Carylon, who died in 2014.

stories.note: Probable. The newsletters are local history written decades later and cite no sources; their claims about 1906, the livery stable and the ownership of the building are unverified, and the 1914 directory (earlier story) is the only contemporary record of Floyd’s grocery. The Society’s dates for Dr. Long conflict between issues (arrival 1911 or 1921, death 1941 or 1944) and are not reconciled. The July 2013 notice calls Floyd and Alice Wayne’s grandparents; they were his great-grandparents in this tree. The 1906 photograph printed in the July 2013 issue is not reproduced, because its rights are not cleared. Which Livesay boy or girl lived above or beside the store is not stated anywhere.

stories.title: Melvin T. Livesay: Floyd and Alice’s son, and the Pearland carpenter of 1950
stories.hook: Melvin was twelve in 1900, the third son in Floyd and Alice Livesay’s Brazoria County house. Fifty years later an Illinois-born carpenter of the same name, sixty years old, was building in Pearland.

subject.name: Melvin T. Livesay
subject.rel: Son of maternal ancestors Floyd and Alice Livesay

body: Melvin T. Livesay grew up between two states. Born in Illinois about 1888, he was a boy of six or seven when his parents, Floyd and Alice, left Washington County for the new fruit-growing town of Pearland, and in June 1900 he was the twelve-year-old son between Call, seventeen, and Lester, six. By 1910, when his parents’ house held only Lester, Ruth and the little Texas-born Earl, he had gone out on his own.

Melvin Livesay registered for the draft in 1917 or 1918, born at Beaucoup on 15 October 1891, single, working in the Texas oil fields. The age is three years short of the boy of 1900, but ages ran loose in this family: Lester Sr. was born in 1894 by his stone and 1895 by his draft card, and the same Beaucoup birthplace and Texas home make the two Melvins very likely one man.

In April 1950 the census taker came to a house in Brazoria County not far from Lester Jr.’s farm: Melvin T. Livesay, head, sixty, born in Illinois, a carpenter working for himself, who had put in twenty-four hours the week before. His wife Daisy E., forty-seven and born in Mississippi, was the only other person in the house. Sixty puts his birth about 1889 or 1890, close to the boy of 1900 and to the oil-field hand of 1918, and a carpenter in Pearland in 1950 is just where an oil-field hand and farm boy might have ended up, living near his nephew Lester Jr.

That the boy of 1900 and the carpenter of 1950 were the same man rests on the first name, the middle initial, the age and the Illinois birthplace, and it is probable rather than proved. When he and Daisy died is not known.

stories.title: Another Ida Whitfield: John and Ida Austin Whitfield of Valliant
stories.hook: The Ida Whitfield of Valliant who stood behind John Grover Whitfield in 1942 was probably Ida Austin, a Choctaw original enrollee and John’s wife, not Ida Merry Whitfield of Golden.

subject.name: John and Ida Austin Whitfield
subject.rel: A different Whitfield family in McCurtain County

body: John Grover Whitfield registered for the draft in 1942 at Valliant, aged 53, born on 6 July 1888 in “Sever Co.,” Arkansas, which is Sevier County; he farmed for himself at Valliant, and for the person who would always know his address he wrote Ida Whitfield, Valliant. In a county where Ida Merry Whitfield lived, that Ida could easily be taken for Clint’s widow. She was not.

Her daughter’s death tells who she was. When Dell Marie Whitfield Bates died on 25 November 2008 at Oak Ridge Manor in Durant, the Choctaw Nation’s Bishinik remembered her in January 2009 as born on 11 September 1919 near Valliant, “daughter of Choctaw original enrollee Ida Austin and John Whitfield.” She attended Wheelock Academy and the Valliant schools, worked for a utility company in California and came home to Oklahoma in the 1980s. Among the relatives who died before her were two brothers, Sam and Guy Whitfield, and three sisters, one of them Betty Whitfield Vedder. Her other survivors go unnamed.

The state’s own registers agree. Dell Marie Bates died on 25 November 2008 in Bryan County, where Durant stands. Whitfield children were born in McCurtain County on 23 May 1915 (Betty F.), 11 September 1919 (Dell Marie), 28 September 1921 (Guy), 27 February 1922 (a boy named Grover McKinley) and 13 March 1925 (Samuel). Dell Marie’s birthday matches exactly, and three of the other first names match the brother and sister remembered at her death. These were the five Whitfield children born in the county between 1915 and 1925 who were not Ida Merry’s, and at least three belonged to this family.

So the Ida Whitfield of Valliant was probably Ida Austin, John’s wife, though that rests on the name, the place and the date, since nothing names John Grover’s Ida and Dell Marie’s mother as one woman in a single line. Ida Merry’s children were not the Whitfield children born around Valliant, and the Ida of 1942 does not belong in her story. Whether John Grover Whitfield, born in Sevier County in 1888, was a brother or cousin of Clint, born in Sevier County in 1893, is not known. He was too old to be the son of W. F. and Emma, who married about four years later, but an earlier marriage of W. F. or a shared grandparent is possible, and nothing names either. No Clint or Ida Merry was mentioned at Dell Marie’s death.

stories.title: Clinton, Clam O. and Oliver C.: one Whitfield in four censuses
stories.hook: A boy called Clinton in 1900, “Clam O.” in 1910 and Oliver C. in 1920 and 1930 turns up with the same birthplace, the same age and, in 1910 and 1930, the same parents’ birthplaces.
body: In 1900 a Clinton Whitfield, 6, born in July 1893 in Arkansas, was living in Sevier County with a W. F. Whitfield, born in Mississippi, and Emma, born in Arkansas. No second name was given, so nothing tied him to the Oliver Clinton Whitfield who later lived at Glover and Golden in McCurtain County, Oklahoma. Three later censuses close most of that gap.

In 1910 William F. Whitfield, 42, born in Mississippi, and his wife Emma, 35, born in Arkansas, were living in Township 6 of McCurtain County, Oklahoma, with a son whose name was written something like “Clam O.,” 16, born in Arkansas. The other children were William G., 15, Rhoda W., 13, Fannie J., 10, Lula B., 9, Ben L., 6, Jeff Davis, 4 and Ola M., 2, all born in Arkansas. The names match the children of 1900 in part: Willie G., Robbie W. and Fannie I. had been 5, 3 and 2. The ages and the sex of one child differ, which is not unusual for census takers, and William F.’s own parents were said to have been both born in Mississippi.

In 1920 Oliver C. Whitfield, 26, born in Arkansas, headed a household in McCurtain County with his wife Ida M., 21, born in Oklahoma, a son, Oliver L., 3 years and 4 months, and a daughter, Elma, 2. The ages fit Ida May Merry, born in June 1898, and the children later known as Lewis and Elma. In 1930, at Sulphur, O. C. Whitfield, 36, born in Arkansas, headed a household with Ida, 32, and four children whose names and ages fit Lewis, Elma, Omagene and Ouida. This time his father was said to have been born in Mississippi and his mother in Arkansas, the same birthplaces as William F. and Emma in 1910. In 1920 both parents had simply been born in the “United States.”

Taken together, the censuses join a Clinton born in July 1893 in Arkansas to the Oliver C. who married Ida Merry, and give him the same parents’ birthplaces as W. F. and Emma in 1910. Nothing yet names his parents in words, at his death or at his marriage, and W. F. was written W. H. in 1900 and William F. in 1910. So W. F. and Emma were probably, but not certainly, his parents.

stories.title: Emma Box and Emily Wilkerson: two Texas births and two Mississippi marriages
stories.hook: Emma Box was probably born Emily Wilkerson: two of her children were born in Texas to “Emily Wilkerson,” and an A. F. Box married an Emily Wilkerson in Mississippi in the 1870s.
body: Emma Box, the mother of Tyro Box, was long said to have been born a Wilkerson, “Emillie (Wilkerson)” in a family note, though nothing from her own time said so, and in 1900 she was simply Emma, 40, born in Mississippi, wife of Alonzo Box in Van Zandt County, Texas. Two of her children’s births now give the name.

Claude Joel Box was born on 26 August 1891 at Rockwall, Texas, to Alonza Box and Emily Wilkerson, and Flossie Bell Box was born on 4 August 1894 at Rockwall to Lonzo Box and the same mother. They were the Claudy J. and Flossie B. of 1900. Both their ages in 1900 run a year ahead of these dates (9 and 6 in June 1900, where the births would make them 8 and 5), while Walter’s, Tyro’s and Archie’s fit their dates, so the dates do not line up perfectly. But the names, the shared parents and the county, where Tyro too was born, make them the same children.

An A. F. Box married an Emily Wilkerson in Benton County, Mississippi, on 1 January 1876 or 3 January 1877; the two dates may be a license and a return of one marriage. Alonzo and Emma had been married 23 years in 1900, which points to 1877. No ages or parents were given, and the groom was A. F., not Alonzo. Emma’s birth in Mississippi fits a marriage there, and Alonzo’s Arkansas birth does not rule one out. Some have joined this man to a different Alonzo F. Box, born in 1853 in Tennessee, who cannot be the Alonzo born in December 1850 in Arkansas, so the two men may have been confused.

She was Emma Box to the census and to her family. Her maiden name was probably Wilkerson, with Emily as the fuller form, but her parents are still unknown. Alonzo, who died in Texas as “Bud Box,” and Emma may yet have their parents named at their deaths.

stories.title: Carl and Beulah Phillips, from Nacogdoches to Houston
stories.hook: Carl Phillips, a Mississippi-born man, married Beulah Turner of Nacogdoches in 1918 and raised Barbara and her brothers in Montgomery County and then in Houston.
body: Barbara Phillips Livesay’s parents were Carl C. and Beulah Turner Phillips. Carl, whose full name was Carl Cherry Phillips, was born on 17 December 1895 in Mississippi, perhaps at Jacksonville. Beulah was born at Nacogdoches, Texas, on 5 February 1900, the daughter of Tom N. Turner and Emma Stacy; when she applied for Social Security in November 1942 she gave their names as Tom N. Turner and Emory A. Stacy. Her parents have a story of their own.

Carl was living in Nacogdoches County when he registered for the draft in the First World War, and it was there, it seems, that he married Beulah, on 15 February 1918. Barbara was born in Nacogdoches on 7 April 1918.

By 1920 the young family had moved to Justice Precinct 8 of Montgomery County, Texas: Carl, 24, born in Mississippi; his wife, 19, born in Texas; and Barbara, aged one year and eight months. The wife’s name was taken down as “Eula,” probably a slip for Beulah, whose age and birthplace fit.

Later the family lived in Houston. There a son, Randell, was born on 24 September 1932; he died on 13 March 1935, aged two, the son of C. C. Phillips and Beulah Turner. Barbara’s family remembered him, as Randall, among the brothers who died before her. In 1950 Carl C. and Beulah B. Phillips were still in Houston, with sons R. Jay and Ralph at home; R. Jay, too, was one of Barbara’s brothers.

Carl died in Houston on 28 April 1960 and was laid to rest, it seems, in Woodlawn Cemetery. Beulah outlived him by almost thirty-three years. She died in Houston on 26 February 1993 and probably lies in the same cemetery.

Carl’s own beginnings are still hazy. When he died, his parents were named as John Phillips and Blanche, with no surname for her, and little more is known of them. John is said to have died in 1897, when Carl was a baby, but nothing yet ties that John and his Blanche to Carl, and Blanche’s own family and marriages remain a tangle. Where Carl spent his boyhood, in 1900 or 1910, is still unknown.

Carl Phillips, a veteran of the First World War, spent his last years in the veterans' hospital at Houston and died there in April 1960. Beulah gave the facts for his certificate from their home on Capitol Street, and he was buried at Woodlawn Garden of Memories.

stories.title: Thomas Turner and Emma Stacy of Nacogdoches
stories.hook: Thomas Turner and Emma Stacy married in Nacogdoches County in 1893, and by 1910 they had a houseful of seven children in the town, Beulah among them.

subject.name: Thomas N. Turner and Emma Stacy Turner

body: Thomas N. Turner and Emma Stacy were married in Nacogdoches County, Texas, on 17 September 1893. Half a century later their daughter Beulah Turner Phillips gave her parents’ names as Tom N. Turner and Emory A. Stacy when she applied for Social Security, in November 1942.

By 1900 they were living in Justice Precinct 1 of Nacogdoches County, the part east of the railroad outside the town. Thomas, written down that year as Thos W. Turner, was 49, born in October 1851 in Tennessee, and seven years married. Emma A. was 28 and born in Louisiana. They had three children: a daughter of four, a son of two whose name was taken down as something like Doytre, and a baby daughter, Beaulah B. When the household was counted on 1 June 1900 the baby was said to be no days old, though by her own later account Beulah had been born on 5 February, four months before; one of the two dates is wrong.

By 1910 the family had moved into the town of Nacogdoches itself, and there were seven children: Verra, 13; Datro, 12; Beulah, 10; Thelma, 8; Opal, 5; Harval, 3; and Ivey, an infant. The father, now T. M. Turner, was 55 and said to have been born in Pennsylvania; Emma was 34 and, as before, a native of Louisiana.

Thomas is hard to pin down. His middle initial was written W, M and N; his birthplace was Tennessee in 1900 and Pennsylvania in 1910; and Emma’s age shifted enough to put her birth near 1872 at one count and 1876 at the next. Through it all, Emma’s Louisiana birth, the children’s names and the Nacogdoches home held steady.

Where Thomas was born, and who his parents were, is unknown; he is said to have died in 1916, but nothing confirms it. Emma was a daughter of James Willis Stacy and Mary Jane Edwards, a Stacy family of Nacogdoches told in “James Willis Stacy: a Louisiana conscript’s road to Nacogdoches.” Emory Ann, as they called her, was born in Louisiana on 10 June 1871 and lived to 1964, and her death certificate, made out at Jacinto City on 20 March 1964, names her parents as James Stacey and Mary Edwards. The father’s full name was Thomas Newton Turner, as a son’s death in 1972 attests.
