stories.title: Alexander Franklin Stacy: three wives, a family Bible and a last ride west
stories.hook: Alexander Franklin Stacy buried a wife and two little girls in a single Tennessee summer, started again in Louisiana, married twice more, and in 1865, at sixty-seven, rode toward Texas to find a place to settle.
body: Alexander Franklin Stacy was born on 14 January 1798 in Sussex County, Virginia, one of two sons of Edmund Stacy and Rebecca Harrison. The brothers seem to have grown up without their father: only one other child, Willis, born in 1802, is ever named, which suggests Edmund died while they were small. Rebecca outlived him by nearly half a century, and when she died on 22 March 1850, at about seventy-five, her son's family Bible wrote her down as Rebecca Halloway, probably a second husband's name.

By 1821 Alexander was in Madison County, Alabama, and on 15 August of that year he married Rebecca Hathcock, who would turn sixteen two months later. They had three daughters in the next eight years, Elizabeth Jayne in September 1824, Mary Esther in March 1827 and Sarah Catherine in March 1829, and somewhere in those years they crossed into West Tennessee. In 1830 Alexander was farming in Hardeman County, and his brother Willis, who had married Mary Ann Knight in 1827, was living next door.

That summer took nearly everything. Sarah Catherine, “my dear little Sarah Catherine” in the Bible, died on 23 May. Mary Esther died on 20 July, and Rebecca died two days after her, on 22 July. Alexander was thirty-two, with a five-year-old daughter left and a new grave beside two small ones.

He did not stay. By 1832 he was in Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana, and about then he married Marinda Stanley, born 11 January 1817 and, like Rebecca, only fifteen. They settled around Marthaville, and the Bible fills again: Edmund in November 1833, Nancy in December 1836, William Harrison in February 1839. Marinda died at Marthaville on 22 January 1844, aged twenty-seven. By 1850 the parish held Alfred Hathcock, who bore his first wife’s family name, and Joseph Gardner, a son-in-law, in the same part of the parish as Alexander.

Seven months after Marinda’s death, on 1 September 1844, Alexander, forty-six, married Eliza Ann Wagley, who was eighteen. Their first child, Margaret, lived four months and was “the first child of Elizer Ann Stacy” in the Bible. Then came James Willis in September 1847, the boy who would carry the name to Nacogdoches, and Alexander Franklin Jr. in December 1849 and Louisiana Virginia in July 1852. Thomas Jefferson was born on 10 December 1854 and died on 8 December 1855, two days short of his first birthday. Laura Jane followed in 1858.

In 1865 the war was over and Alexander was sixty-seven. The family says he rode out to Texas to find a place to settle, went as far as the Concho country, caught pneumonia and died there on 16 August, and was buried at Eden. The grave is the puzzle. Concho County was not organized until 1879 and Eden was founded in 1882; in 1865 the Concho valley was open range with a few cattle camps, and Comanches still raided along the river. Wherever he fell ill, the stone at Eden must have come later, or the story has lost a few miles and a few years on the way down. His son James Willis, seventeen, had been paroled at Natchitoches only eight weeks before, and by the next March he would be in Nacogdoches, married.

stories.note: Evidence: probable. The dates all come from one compiled book that quotes a family Bible transcript; no primary record was opened (Madison Co. AL marriage, 1830 Hardeman census, Natchitoches censuses, any Texas record of his death). Conflicts to settle before publishing: (1) The Louisiana group sheet gives his second wife as Marinda Stanley married 26 Aug 1832 in Alabama and has no Hathcock marriage; Farrell has Hathcock 1821 and Stanley about 1832. (2) Farrell's prose calls the first child Martha Anne (married Joseph William Gardner) but the Bible list names Elizabeth Jayne; the daughters' names need sorting out, so the Gardner son-in-law sentence is hedged. (3) Edmund H. died 14 Dec 1846 in Farrell's Bible list but 1848 on the group sheet; left out of the prose. (4) Margaret (27 Sep 1845) and James Willis (27 Sep 1847) share a birthday in the Bible list; may be a copying slip. (5) 'Rebecca Halloway' as his mother's later name is Farrell's transcription; the second-husband explanation is a guess, kept hedged. (6) The Eden grave is anachronistic for 1865 (Eden founded 1882); the prose says so rather than resolve it. Existing site entries (MAT_ALEXANDER_FRANKLIN_STACY and the Wagley and Stanley wives) currently carry the wives as leads; this story would upgrade Hathcock, Stanley and the 1844 Wagley marriage to probable. Marinda Stanley and Rebecca Hathcock could be added to the tree as MAT_ people (gen 8, side N, probable). The 'eight weeks' count runs from 21 June 1865 (James Willis's parole, in the existing story) to 16 Aug 1865.

stories.title: James Willis Stacy: a Louisiana conscript's road to Nacogdoches
stories.hook: Drafted into the Louisiana Reserve Corps at seventeen, James Willis Stacy was paroled at Natchitoches in June 1865, married in Nacogdoches the next spring, and raised a family that kept crossing the Texas-Louisiana line.
body: James Willis Stacy was born on 27 September 1847 in Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana, and grew up near Marthaville. His father, Alexander Franklin Stacy, was already 49 and had been married more than once; his mother, Eliza Ann Wagley, was the third wife. By 1850 he was a boy of three in their household, and in 1860 a boy of fourteen, written down as Willice.

In 1864, at seventeen, he was drafted into Company B of Maddox's Regiment, Louisiana Reserve Corps. The Reserves had been created that February to hold the boys too young and the men too old for the regular army, and to keep them inside their own state. His company was surrendered at New Orleans on 26 May 1865, and on 21 June he was paroled at Natchitoches, back in his home parish.

His father had already gone west. In 1865 Alexander Franklin Stacy went to Texas looking for a place to settle, and he died there that year, buried, the family says, in Texas soil. The family has wondered whether James went along with him, but nothing says so.

The next March James was in Nacogdoches. On 22 March 1866 he married Mary Jane Edwards, born in Arkansas on 16 March 1847, the daughter of John Edwards and Mahulda, who would one day live in James's household. They settled in Nacogdoches, where their first son, John Alexander, was born in 1868 or 1869.

Then the family began crossing the line. Emory Ann, the daughter the family called Emma, was born in Louisiana on 10 June 1871, and so was Susie in 1875. Henry Coleman was born in 1874 in Madison County, Texas, where they were living in 1880, and James Elam in 1878 in Atascosa County, far to the southwest. Ruben Paschal was born in Nacogdoches in 1880 and Mary Elizabeth in 1886, in Texas or Louisiana depending on whom you ask. Mahulda, 77 in 1880, lived in James and Mary Jane's house by then, and she was still with them in 1900, when the family was back in Nacogdoches County.

Emma grew up to marry Thomas N. Turner at Nacogdoches in 1893. She lived to 1964, and her daughter Beulah Turner Phillips is our line. Mary Jane died in Nacogdoches on 6 March 1918, and James Willis on 3 March 1925 at Lufkin, aged 77. They lie side by side in Christian Cemetery in Nacogdoches.

stories.note: Evidence: probable. Almost everything here is from one family-history blog (Beyond the Tree) quoting censuses and a Stacy group sheet; the censuses were not opened by the drafter. Emma as James Willis's daughter is probable (given name Emory, Louisiana birth, Nacogdoches, Turner marriage), not proven; no record seen names her husband inside the Stacy family. Two blog dates disagree: John Alexander's birth (1868 vs 1869) and James's death place (Lufkin vs Angelina Co., which agree, Lufkin being in Angelina Co.). The blog's 'surrendered at New Orleans 26 May 1865' is its own statement; the Natchitoches roll index confirms Company B men paroled there in June 1865. The explanation of the Reserve Corps (created Feb 1864, under 18 and over 45, state service) is general background from search results, not from a source about this company; confirm before publishing or soften. 'Perhaps James went with his father' is the blog's speculation and is kept as a wondering only. Mahulda is also in tree.json as MAT_MAHULDA_EDWARDS (Mary Jane's mother, 1880/1900 households). Alexander Franklin's parents (Edmond Stacy and Rebecca Harrison) are a lead only and left out of the prose.

stories.title: Mrs. Elizabeth Walker, ninety, of Beaucoup
stories.hook: At Christmas 1919 Elizabeth Walker, widow of Beaucoup’s Mexican War lieutenant, was ninety and in the best of health, and her son came from East St. Louis to see her.

subject.name: Elizabeth Walker
subject.rel: Beaucoup neighbor of the Walkers (kinship unproven)

body: Just before Christmas 1919, J. E. Walker, a desk clerk at police headquarters in East St. Louis, went home for a two-day visit with his mother, Mrs. Elizabeth Walker, of Beaucoup, Illinois. Mrs. Walker, the East St. Louis Daily Journal reported in its “Local Brevities” on 26 December, “observed her 90th birthday several months ago” and was in the best of health despite her age.

She was Rev. G. W. Walker’s widow. At Beaucoup lie Rev. G. W. Walker, 1826 to 20 October 1902, and Elizabeth, “wife of Rev. G. W.,” 1829 to 1920; a ninetieth birthday in 1919 points to 1829. Elizabeth Walker died in Beaucoup Township on 11 February 1920, less than seven weeks after her son’s visit. When Rev. George Walker died in 1902, the Nashville Journal named three surviving children: Mrs. A. B. Stephens, D. A. Walker and J. E. Walker. And when Mrs. Cora A. Stephens died in April 1919, the same East St. Louis paper listed among her survivors “an aged mother, Mrs. Betsy Walker,” a sister, Miss Dora, of Beaucoup, and a brother, “James E. Walker of East St. Louis.” Betsy was a common nickname for Elizabeth, and Cora’s husband was A. B. Stephens, so the two notices name one family: J. E. was James E., and Mrs. Elizabeth Walker of 1919 was George’s widow. A James E. Walker, 1862 to 1946, lies at Beaucoup, probably the same man.

Cora herself had died that spring. On Monday, 7 April 1919, Mrs. Cora A. Stephens, the wife of A. B. Stephens, entered into eternal rest at the Deaconess Hospital in East St. Louis after a week's illness. She left a married daughter at St. Louis, two children at East St. Louis and a son with the 124th Field Artillery in France, five months after the Armistice, and her funeral left her home for Mt. Hope Cemetery on the Wednesday afternoon.

Dora bears on the children of 1902. She still lived at Beaucoup, and in 1902 a “D. A. Walker” was named without saying whether a man or a woman. Dora A. would fit, and then the three children of 1902 were Cora, Dora and James E., all still living in 1919. But Dora’s middle name is not known, and a brother D. A. who died before 1919 would fit just as well, so that is only a possibility.

Their marriage date is clear. George W. Walker and Elizabeth Walker married on 21 December 1848, not on 23 October 1849, a date that belongs to another couple, Ernst H. A. F. Walker and Justine W. H. Grefe. A December 1848 wedding agrees with the month given in 1902 (its printed year, 1828, is a slip for 1848) and puts their daughter Frances’s birth, on 19 September 1849, nine months later. Whether Walker was Elizabeth’s maiden name or her married one is not known.

Two of their daughters lie at Beaucoup. Frances C. E. Walker, 19 September 1849 to 18 February 1874, “dau of Rev. G. W. & E.” and “wife of Chas. M. Livesay,” was how a Beaucoup Walker came to marry a Livesay; a second daughter, Eudora B. A., lived from 7 July 1852 to 24 November 1854. Their neighbor William P. Walker died in Beaucoup Township on 20 May 1919 by the state’s register, a day after the 19 May usually given, perhaps the day his death was registered, and Abigail Walker died at Richview on 28 January 1923.

How George W. Walker was related to Rev. James Walker, to Simeon, or to William P. Walker, who lived a few doors away in 1860, is not known. George, Elizabeth, Frances, Cora, Dora and James E. were neighbors and in-laws of the Beaucoup Walkers and Livesays, not links in Sloan’s line. Cora's death shows how far the Beaucoup household had spread by 1919: a daughter married in East St. Louis, a son working there, and a daughter at Beaucoup, where their mother still lived.

stories.title: Seven Livesay brothers at East St. Louis, July 1916
stories.hook: A front-page notice in July 1916 gathers seven Livesay brothers “formerly of Washington county, Illinois,” and the first one named may be a man the Beaucoup stones already know.

subject.name: Charles M. Livesay
subject.rel: Possible Livesay kin of the Beaucoup Walkers

body: On 31 July 1916 the Daily Journal of East St. Louis, Illinois, printed on its front page a notice headed “Livesay Family Annual Reunion.” It describes the reunion of “the Livesay brothers, formerly of Washington county, Illinois,” and their families, held through the week beginning Sunday, 23 July, at the home of Mr. and Mrs. L. C. Livesay on North Forty-fifth Street. The brothers named are C. M. Livesay of Purdy, Missouri; L. C. Livesay of East St. Louis; P. B. Livesay of Kansas City, Missouri; A. R. Livesay of Evansville, Indiana; R. C. Livesay of Moline, Illinois; F. G. Livesay of Milwaukee; and L. G. Livesay of Louisville, Kentucky.

The paper says the seven “had not previously all been together for a period of ten years,” and spent most of the week on boyhood memories. It lists the brothers’ daughters and in-laws as well. C. M. Livesay is given daughters at Iuka, Carbondale, Richview and Purdy, and the Richview daughter shows that the family still had ties to Washington County. Between them the seven lived in seven different places, from Moline and Milwaukee to Louisville, so by 1916 the sons of one county had scattered across five states.

Who their father and mother were, and in which township they grew up, is not said. The first of them may have been a man Beaucoup already knew. Frances C. E. Walker, who died on 18 February 1874, lies at Beaucoup as the wife of Chas. M. Livesay, and Charles M. Livesay married Theresa E. Tate on 17 May 1877. A Charles M. Livesay of Washington County was a widower in 1874 and married again by 1877, and he could have been the C. M. of 1916, though nothing says so. Charles P. Livesay of Jefferson County (1865 to 1915) was a different man, with another middle initial, who died the year before the reunion.

Floyd Hale Livesay, born in Illinois in 1856 or 1857 and dead at Houston in 1932, was not among the seven: by his initials he would be F. H., and the Milwaukee brother was F. G. Nothing ties him to this family either way, and his father is still unproven. An obituary of one of the brothers, or the household of 1880 that held them as boys, would show which Washington County Livesay family they belonged to.

stories.title: Livesay Carter and the christening of New Nashville
stories.hook: The county seat of Washington County, Illinois, got its name from two Tennesseeans on its board of commissioners, and one of them was the Livesay Carter whose given name has puzzled the Livesay story.

subject.name: Livesay Carter
subject.rel: Carter kinsman of the Livesays (link unproven)

body: Nashville was laid out on 8 June 1830 by its proprietors, Robert Middleton and G. Brown, who filed the plat with the county commissioners, and “David White, Joseph Whittenberg and Livesay Carter were the commissioners.” Carter and Whittenberg, being Tennesseeans, “reverenced everything relating to that state,” and so, with the proprietors’ permission, “christened the town ‘New Nashville.’” The “New” was soon dropped. In March 1831 the commissioners declared the town the permanent seat of justice. So Washington County remembered it in 1879.

Livesay Carter had been elected to the county’s eighth board in 1828, with David White and Joseph Whittenburg, re-elected that year. In 1830 he built a tread sawmill two miles east of where Nashville now stands, and the mill sawed the lumber for the first buildings in the town. He was among the first settlers of Nashville precinct, who settled “from 1818 to 1833,” along with an L. D. Livesay, possibly Lorenzo Dow Livesay, and he was among the seventeen men raised in the first year of Washington Lodge.

Charles Baldwin of Nashville told the story again, with more of its troubles, in his column “Looking Back” for the Centralia (Illinois) Sentinel. The county seat had moved from Covington to a short-lived Georgetown, Beaucoup objected, and a compromise in 1827 put the seat where Nashville now stands. The new site was government land, and where was “the hundred dollars” to buy it to come from? The commissioners, David White, Livesay Carter and Joseph Whittenberg, “spent three years” on the question and raised nothing, until two promoters from St. Clair County put up the cash in 1830. Because Carter and Whittenberg “came from near Nashville, Tennessee,” they voted for the name New Nashville.

Baldwin follows the older history in outline, including March 1831 and the Tennessee reason for the name, and when he wrote is not known, so his telling is a retelling rather than a second witness. What he adds is the slow business of raising the money. What is certain is Livesay Carter’s place on the board from 1828, his hand in naming the town, and his mill. His son Dr. William D. Carter later practiced in Nashville. His given name, and the family memory that he and Carter Livesay were cousins named for each other’s families, are why the Carters stand beside the Livesays, though nothing yet ties him to the Livesay line.

The column’s sources are not given.

stories.title: Livesay or Lewsey? Company F of the 44th Illinois, June 1862
stories.hook: Francis M. Lewsey of Richview, printed once as F. M. Livesay, served in Company F of the 44th Illinois, Dr. William D. Carter’s regiment, and died of wounds received at Murfreesboro in February 1863.

subject.name: Francis M. Lewsey (Livesay?)
subject.rel: Washington County soldier; kinship to the Livesays unproven

body: In the summer of 1862 the 44th Illinois called its absentees back. A notice headed “A Call on Absentees,” dated at the regiment’s headquarters at Camp Rienzi, Mississippi, on 26 June 1862 and printed in the Chicago Daily Tribune on 19 July under “Col. Knobelsdorff’s Regiment,” warned the men named that they must send in certificates from an army medical officer of their inability to rejoin the regiment within thirty days, or be “reported and treated as deserters.” Under “Company F, Ashley, Ill.” were Sergt. Waldo Gilbert, Chas. T. Laur, F. M. Livesay, James Langsford, John Emert, Geo. W. McCovan, Lewis Peters, John H. Morris and Jas. H. Pugh. Why any man was absent is not said.

The same men served in Company F as privates Emert, John; Laur, Charles T; Lennington, Isaac; Langford, James; Lacy, Theopholis; “Lewsey, Francis M.”; McCowen, George; Morris, John H; and Peters, Lewis, as the state recorded them, with the spellings shifted (Langsford and Langford, McCovan and McCowen). So the F. M. Livesay of the newspaper was Francis M. Lewsey, with the same initials, company and place, and Livesay was a variant of his name.

Francis M. Lewsey was a married farmer from Richview, born about 1827 in Illinois, who enlisted at Ashley on 10 July 1861, was mustered in at Chicago on 13 September 1861 and died on 18 February 1863 of wounds received at Murfreesboro. He lies at Stones River National Battlefield, though there he is remembered with the 42nd Illinois, not the 44th, and which is right is not known. His absence in June 1862 was no mark against him; six months later he was with his company.

The regiment matters for the Carters. Dr. William D. Carter, son of Livesay Carter, graduated from Rush Medical College on 4 February 1862 and “was appointed assistant surgeon of the 44th Regiment, Illinois Vols.,” serving more than three years; he was of Nashville. Whether he and Lewsey ever met is not known. Other Washington County Livesays served in other companies, Jackson L. and John W. in the 60th Illinois and James M. and William J. in the 49th, but no F. M. Livesay, which is why this man is known as Lewsey. His wife, parents and brothers and sisters are not known, so whether he belonged to one of the Livesay families of Richview is an open question.

stories.title: Robert, Gilbert, Ben and Lewis: the Merry brothers of Sevier County
stories.hook: A county newspaper in Sevier County, Arkansas, mentions Lewis Merry’s brothers by name, and a Hortense column of 1903 puts Lewis in the Indian Territory with a brother recovering from illness.

subject.name: The Merry brothers
subject.rel: Probable brothers of Lewis (Louis) Merry of Glover

body: Sevier County’s weekly paper, the De Queen Bee, followed a family of Merrys in its neighborhood columns, “Hortense,” “Milford Dots” and the like, from 1897 to 1906. The first notice is a wedding. On 31 December 1897 it reported “a double wedding” at Kings Chapel in the Red Colony on Sunday, 26 December: Ben Merry married Miss Addie Harrison, and Luther Revels married Miss Jennie Harrison, with Rev. A. D. Jenkins officiating. A year later, on 23 December 1898, the Bee said Ben Merry, “formerly a citizen of this county,” had lived for the past year in the Chickasaw Nation and would make his home near De Queen.

In 1903 the columns turn to Robert, “Bob.” On 15 May the Bee’s Hortense column had Robert Merry of Milford visiting; on 24 July Bob Merry had gone to Hortense to work for the summer; and on 4 September the Milford Dots said that Robt. Merry and friends from Hortense “visited his brother, B. F. Merry,” a second name for Ben. On 18 September Robert left “to visit his brother, who is very ill, in the Indian Territory,” and on 30 October the Hortense column said that Robert Merry “returned from Indian Territory last week; his brother Lewis accompanied him and report their brother Gilbert convalescing.” Later items follow Robert to Provo for timber work and school in 1904, and on 18 May 1906 two neighborhood columns said Robert Merry “of Garvin, I. T.,” was visiting friends.

Lewis Merry (Louis, J. L.) of Glover told the Dawes Commission in 1900 that he had lived in the Choctaw Nation about eight years, and he was the postmaster at Glover from June 1901. A brother Lewis who “accompanied” Robert out of the Indian Territory in October 1903 fits him, and so does the place: Robert himself was “of Garvin, I. T.” by 1906. The Bee never gives Lewis a home, and Merry is not a rare name, so he was probably, not certainly, the same man. No parent is named in the paper, and when Louis was enrolled his parents, Calvin and Elizabeth Merry, were named without his brothers, but the 1880 census of Monroe Township, Sevier County, names a Benjamin F. and a Joshua L. among the sons of Calvin and Eliza J. Merry, which joins the paper’s Ben (B. F.) and Lewis as brothers.

What the notices do give is a home neighborhood and a way of life. The brothers were Sevier County young men who went to the Chickasaw and Choctaw nations to work, as Ben did in 1897 and Gilbert and Lewis by 1903, and who kept coming back to Hortense and Milford. That fits the memory that Lewis was born in Sevier County, though it does not prove it, and his own birthplace is still unknown.

stories.title: Frank Whitfield’s homestead at De Queen, 1902 to 1907
stories.hook: A land-office notice that ran for nine weeks in the De Queen Bee in 1907 gives W. F. Whitfield’s first name, a homestead entry in Sevier County, and a witness named Ward.

subject.name: William F. “Frank” Whitfield
subject.rel: Probable father of Oliver Clinton Whitfield (link unproven)

body: On 12 February 1907 the land office at Camden, Arkansas, gave notice that William F. Whitfield, of De Queen, Arkansas, intended to make final proof on his claim: Homestead Entry No. 25306, made 17 January 1902, for the W½ NE¼ of section 28, township 8 south, range 32 west, fifth principal meridian. He would make his proof before the Clerk of the Circuit Court of Sevier County at De Queen on 6 April 1907, and four witnesses would vouch for his “continuous residence upon, and cultivation of, the land”: Phillip A. Ward, William Miller, Benjamin F. Whitfield and W. Steel White, all of De Queen. The notice ran in the De Queen Bee every Friday from 22 February through 19 April 1907.

So the W. F. Whitfield of Monroe Township, Sevier County, who with his wife Emma had a son named Clinton, born in July 1893, was very probably William F. Whitfield, who entered a homestead in January 1902, two years after the census. That rests on the initials, the county and the date, and no other W. F. Whitfield is known there, so it is probable and not proven. A Frank Whitfield, written “jr.,” was among the grand jurors for the court term opening on 29 January 1907, and Oliver’s father is remembered as William Franklin “Frank” Whitfield. The “jr.” suggests an older Frank Whitfield in the county, though who he was is not known.

Two of the witnesses are worth a second look. A boarder surnamed Ward, born in August 1871 in Arkansas, his given name hard to read, had lived with the Whitfields in 1900, and Emma is said to have been born a Ward. A Phillip A. Ward who vouched for the Whitfield homestead could have been that boarder, or Emma’s brother, or only a neighbor; nothing of kin is said. Benjamin F. Whitfield was another Whitfield of De Queen. A B. F. Whitfield of Chapel Hill gave a daughter in marriage in November 1906, and a B. F. Whitfield was among the men questioned as jurors in a trial in November 1910, but whether he was W. F.’s father, brother or neither is not known.

No wife or child is named, so nothing here shows whether Clinton was Oliver Clinton Whitfield, born on 27 July 1893 and died in 1941, and W. F. and Emma are still only probably his parents. But the family held land in Sevier County until at least April 1907, and William F.’s own testimony at his final proof, if it survives, may yet tell of his household and his home.

stories.title: Whitfields of Chapel Hill, and a sawmill that moved to Valliant
stories.hook: The same Sevier County paper that printed Frank Whitfield’s homestead notice follows other Whitfields from Chapel Hill to a sawmill at Valliant, Indian Territory, where John Grover Whitfield farmed in 1942.
body: Clint Whitfield is said to have been born at Chapel Hill, Sevier County, and a second Whitfield household lived beside W. F.’s in Monroe Township in 1900. The De Queen Bee shows a larger family still. On 9 July 1897 Miss Tennie Whitfield of Chapel Hill was helping to post the books of Ogden & Whitfield, a firm at Cerro Gordo in which Luther B. Whitfield was a partner by 18 February 1898. On 25 November 1898 Joe Whitfield married Miss Maggie Roberts “of Chapel Hill.” On 23 November 1906 Miss Amanda Whitfield of Chapel Hill married Clement Banks at the home of her parents, Mr. and Mrs. B. F. Whitfield.

One member of the family went south and west. On 5 May 1905 Mrs. A. J. Whitfield returned to Texarkana after a visit to relatives “here and at Chapel Hill,” and on 26 January 1906 A. J. Whitfield, up from Texarkana, had bought a sawmill at McNab, Arkansas. By 5 April 1907 the Bee gives Mr. and Mrs. A. J. Whitfield as “of Valliant, I. T.”, and on 21 August 1908 it says A. J. Whitfield, “formerly of De Queen,” had formed a partnership with Jess Braden at Valliant to make lumber and had installed a large plant. On 3 September 1909 it reports that he lost his sawmill and stock by fire, with a loss of about $10,000 and no insurance. His wife went on visiting “relatives at Chapel Hill and De Queen” from Valliant in 1908, 1909 and October 1910.

Valliant is in McCurtain County, where John Grover Whitfield, born on 6 July 1888 in Sevier County, was farming in 1942. The neighbors of 1900 in Monroe Township, headed by a man whose initials look like R. H., had a John born in July 1888. The month, the year and the county agree. If they were the same, it was the R. H. Whitfield household, not W. F.’s, that sent a son to Valliant, but that is only a possibility. A Mrs. Ollie Harmon of Garvin, Oklahoma, visited Whitfield relatives in March 1909, and the household of 1900 had an Ollie, born in April 1883, but the printed line is garbled and nothing can be built on it.

None of this says that Clint Whitfield was kin to A. J., B. F., Luther B. or Joe Whitfield. The notices do show where the Whitfield name was thick on the ground: Chapel Hill, Cerro Gordo and De Queen before 1905, and Valliant after 1907, in the same Oklahoma county as Glover and Golden, where Clint Whitfield later lived. Nothing yet names a brother Frank or W. F. among them.

stories.title: Joe Denson of Fowlerville, ex-clerk of Sevier County
stories.hook: Mattie Denson went to Lockesburg, Arkansas, after leaving Abner Clay, and a Sevier County paper explains why: a Joe Denson, a former county court clerk there, had moved to Fowlerville in the Choctaw Nation by 1897.

subject.name: Joe Denson of Fowlerville
subject.rel: Possible kin of Mattie Denson Clay (unproven)

body: Mattie Denson married Abner H. Clay in the Choctaw Nation on 20 May 1897; her parents were Joseph H. and Mattie E. Denson, both non-citizens. When she and Abner separated in 1902 she went to Lockesburg, Arkansas, a town in Sevier County. In 1903 the Commission wrote to Claude Denson of Shawneetown, Indian Territory, who called himself her brother. The De Queen Bee, in the same county as Lockesburg, tells of a Denson family on the Indian Territory side.

On 5 November 1897 the Bee passed on news from Fowlerville, Indian Territory: a baby boy had been born to Mr. and Mrs. Joe Denson of Fowlerville, and the writer hoped the child would comfort them in their later years. On 18 February 1898 it said Joe Denson of Fowlerville, I. T., “ex-Clerk of the county court of Sevier county,” was in De Queen the Thursday before. How long ago he had held the office, or when he left Arkansas, is not said.

A Joe Denson who had been Sevier County’s court clerk and then lived at Fowlerville, a Choctaw Nation town counted in 1900 with Lukfata, Eagletown and Shawneetown, fits a family that had moved across the line from Sevier County. It does not prove that he was Joseph H. Denson, Mattie’s father. Other Densons lived at Hortense, in Sevier County, in 1903 and 1904, J. J. Denson with sons Joe L. and J. S., and none is known at Fowlerville. “Joe” may have been Joseph H., a brother, or an unrelated man.

If Joe Denson was her father, Mattie’s retreat to Lockesburg in 1902 was a return to her family’s old county. Sevier County’s own books, or its household of 1880, may one day show whether Joseph H. Denson was that clerk, and whether Mattie and her brother Claude grew up in his house.

Sevier County kept a roll of its officers, and when it was printed in 1890 it answered the Bee's riddle. After the war the county clerks ran W. J. Denson, 1860 to 1868; H. H. Clay, 1868 to 1872; and J. H. Denson, 1872 to 1884, when Alex Luther took the office he still held in 1890. So the ex-clerk who rode into De Queen in February 1898 had kept the county court's books for twelve years, and he carried the very initials of Mattie's father, Joseph H. Denson. That makes Joe Denson of Fowlerville very probably Joseph H. himself. The county seat in all those years was Lockesburg, laid out on the Locke family's land in 1868, so the courthouse where he kept the records stood in the very town Mattie went back to in October 1902.

The roll leaves two smaller threads. William J. Denson had held the same clerk's office through the war years, so the Densons were a courthouse family in Sevier County a generation before Mattie was born; whether William J. was Joseph's father, brother or only a namesake is not known. And the clerk between the two Densons was an H. H. Clay. Mattie's husband Abner H. Clay was a Choctaw of the Lukfata country, and nothing ties him to the Arkansas clerk, so the shared surname may be chance.

stories.title: Deer tags and a five-year pin: Junior in the Hugo papers, 1961–62
stories.hook: One November he lined up with the rest of Hugo for a deer tag. The next spring he got a pin from the glove factory.
body: Deer season in Oklahoma opened on a Wednesday in late November 1961, and Hugo took it seriously. On Tuesday, 21 November, The Hugo Daily News ran “Local Sportsmen Purchase Deer Tags” across the top of its front page. Tags were on sale at D. C. Patterson Hardware, Leard Hardware and Askew Service Station, and one seller, Mrs. Tom Baskin, had sold all 25 of hers by Monday. Many hunters had already moved into the woods to set up camp. The paper then printed the name and town of everyone who had bought a tag, a list that ran down several columns, from a 12-year-old to a 78-year-old. Partway down the second column is “William Thompson Jr., Hugo.”

Four months later, on 2 April 1962, a front-page photograph showed a crowd of employees of the Wells Lamont glove factory in Hugo receiving five-year service pins, standing with the assistant manager, Robert Bowen. The caption lists them by name, and among them is “Junior Thompson.” A five-year pin in April 1962 would mean he had been on the factory's payroll since about 1957, the year after his marriage license with Mary Ellen Hulsey was announced.
Neither item says much, but together they fill in an ordinary working life that the censuses skip: a young husband in Hugo with a factory job and a deer tag.

stories.title: Wildcat whisky: three and a half pints in Hugo, 1957
stories.hook: The sheriff counted it out to the half-pint. And yes, he drank it.
body: On the morning of Thursday, 30 May 1957, The Hugo Daily News reported that Johnny Moffitt, 31, of Hugo had pleaded guilty to a disorderly-house charge before Justice of the Peace Bert Bush. He had been arrested the night before by Sheriff Ed Thornton and Constable Lonnie Wright, who said they found one quart and three half-pints of “wildcat whisky” at his home.

“Wildcat” was the old word for liquor made without a license, and it has never sounded like anything you would want to drink. He drank it anyway. The sheriff, to his credit, counted precisely: one quart plus three half-pints comes to three and a half pints, so nobody could later argue about the arithmetic. That makes the half-pints sound less like a stockpile and more like a supply.

The law was the point. Oklahoma had been officially dry since statehood in 1907 and did not repeal statewide prohibition until 1959, so in May 1957 a cupboard with the wrong bottles in it was a matter for the sheriff and the justice of the peace. Four years later a much more serious whisky case followed. This one stayed small.

stories.title: Henry and Hannah's other children: a section hand, a plainsman and three sisters
stories.hook: Grady was the youngest. His brother Tom farmed next door to him in Oklahoma, and his brother Jesse went all the way to the Texas plains.
body: Henry and Hannah Moffitt started their family in Randolph County, Arkansas. In 1880 at Janes Creek Township they had Josephine, 3, and Jesse, 1. Hannah later said she had borne seven children and that six were living, so one died young and left no record. By 1900 the family was in Franklin Township, Stone County, with Jesse; a daughter “Gimsa,” born in August 1883; Bertha, born in March 1886; Tom; and the youngest, Woodford Grady. Josephine, who would have been about 23, was no longer at home.

Thomas Berry “Tom” Moffitt, born at St. James in Stone County on 17 February 1889, was the first of the children known to be born in Stone County. After his father died in 1901 he stayed with his widowed mother, and in 1910 he was working as a railroad section hand. By 1920 he had followed, or led, his brother across the Red River and was farming next door to Grady in Wilson Township, Choctaw County, Oklahoma. His wife Vesta died at Holdenville, Oklahoma, in October 1930, aged 38. Tom ended up at Paris, Texas, where he died on 21 March 1953; his grave marker is carved for service in both world wars.

Jesse Gee Moffitt (1879–1957) went the farthest, out onto the Texas plains. He is buried at Tahoka in Lynn County, and family notes place his death at Amarillo. Of the sisters, less is known. A Bertha May Moffitt Barham (1888–1930) is buried at Herpel Cemetery near her mother and may be the Bertha of 1900, but that is not proved.

stories.title: Ten children of a preacher, from Hot Springs to Wright City
stories.hook: Oscar was the fourth of ten. Here is what the records say about the other nine, and where they go quiet.
body: George Washington Hulsey and Sarah Rebecca Graves married on 22 December 1901 and had ten children over twenty-one years. The first three were boys: William Roy in 1904, John Wesley in 1906 and Noah in 1908. In April 1910 the young family was in Mountain Township, Garland County, Arkansas, with “William R.,” “John W.” and Noah at home. Their father farmed, and the family remembers him as a preacher. Oscar arrived that October at Hot Springs.

Then the family started moving. Fred came in 1913 and Ruby Ellen in 1915, the first daughter after five sons. Grady was born in 1918, the year his father, whose home was at Story in Montgomery County, registered for the draft while working on the Camp Pike construction job near Little Rock. By 1920 the household had crossed into Oklahoma and was tenant-farming in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, with six children at home. Louis Daniel was born at Bethel that May. Grace Irene followed in 1923, when her mother was about 39, and George Paul, the last, in 1925, when his father was nearly fifty. In 1930 they were a renting household of ten near Wright City, deep in the sawmill country.

Their father died on 5 August 1935 and was buried at Breashears Cemetery near Story. The eldest, William Roy, was about 31; the youngest, George Paul, was nine or ten. Their mother later went west and died at Bandon, Oregon, in 1972. When Oscar died in 1982, four brothers and two sisters were still living. Ruby, who married a Stipe, and Grace, who married a Dunagan, are the only daughters in the family list, so they were evidently those two sisters. Three of the ten had died by then, Louis Daniel among them.

After 1935 most of the siblings are hard to follow. A John Hulsey (1929), a Noah Hulsey (1930) and a Roy Hulsey (1931) married in McCurtain County, and a Roy Hulsey, 34, married in Montgomery County, Arkansas, in 1938. Any of them may be Oscar’s brothers, but nothing names their parents.

stories.title: Kentucky, Minnesota and back: John C.'s brothers and sister
stories.hook: Their father took the family to Minnesota and brought it home again, and one brother married his brother's wife's cousin.

subject.name: John C. Satterfield's brothers and sister

body: James H. Satterfield's 1885 biography names six children of his first marriage, to Malissa Gibson: “Henry W., John C., Sidney R., James D., Martha A. and Mary C.” It also says that “in 1867 he removed to Dakota County, Minn., and in 1875 he returned to Kentucky.” Malissa died in 1877, soon after the move back, and James remarried in 1878.

Sidney Rufus, born 2 September 1865 and the third son named in the sketch, stayed in Kentucky and kept the family close. He married Eliza “Ancie” Johnson, a daughter of James P. Johnson and Martha J. Clark. Martha was the older sister of Melvina (Clark) Johnson, the mother of Samantha, who married Sidney's brother John C. in 1892. So two Satterfield brothers married first cousins from the same Clark-Johnson family. Sidney died at Richardsville, Warren County, on 19 November 1949, and Ancie in 1951; both are buried at Satterfield Cemetery near Jetson.

James Doiser was born in February 1867 in Allen County, the year the family left for Minnesota. He married in 1889, had five children, and went south to Arkansas; he died at Hickoria, Clay County, on 10 July 1929 and is buried at Redenbo Cemetery. The only child known to have been born in Minnesota was a daughter, A. M., on 23 July 1870. She married Calvin H. Coots in 1891 and died on 25 May 1892, only 21. Her Minnesota birth bears out the family's Minnesota years.

stories.title: Pearl's brothers and sister: two soldiers, a Riddle wedding and a death at seventeen
stories.hook: John C. and Samantha Satterfield's children followed them from Kentucky to Texas to the Oklahoma side of the Red River, and most came home to be buried near their mother.
body: Wavey Lincoln Satterfield was the oldest surviving child. His World War I and World War II draft cards both give his birth as 28 December 1895 at Morgantown, Butler County, Kentucky; his headstone at Soper Cemetery says 9 January 1896, so the stone is probably the mistake. The stone is marked “TEXAS PVT. U.S. ARMY World War I,” which fits the family's move to Franklin County, Texas, about 1907. In 1925 he married Jewel Dale Weems, and they settled in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, near his mother. He died at Soper on 24 March 1952, aged 56, and lies in plot E4, the same plot as Samantha.

James Bethel was born on 12 May 1901 in Butler County and was about six when the family went to Texas. He married Alice Elizabeth Riddle, and they had seven children between 1922 and 1940; one, Charlie, died in 1940 at about ten. James died at Paris, Texas, on 7 December 1964 and was buried at Soper, near his mother.

Stella B., “little Stella” in the Hagansport household of April 1910, was born on 6 October 1907, one of the two children born after the move to Texas. She married Clifford Calvin Riddle. Whether her husband and her brother James's wife Alice were brother and sister is not known. Stella died on 25 January 1925, only 17, and was buried at Chillicothe Cemetery in Hardeman County, Texas, far from the rest of the family. No cause of death is given.

Ira L. was born in 1905 in Kentucky, was five at Hagansport in 1910, served in World War II (his stone reads “AMRY WWII”), died in 1977 and is buried in plot B2 at Grant Cemetery, where Pearl and Charles Oscar Smith also lie. Jewel Thompson Satterfield, the last child, was born at Talco, Titus County, Texas, on 3 May 1912. He married Marie Nabors in 1929, when he was 17, had five children, and died at Hugo on 13 January 1995. He is buried at Mount Olivet Cemetery in Hugo.

stories.title: From Gadsden to Apache and California: Mamie's brothers and sisters
stories.hook: John Morgan and Lizzie Shackleford raised a big family that scattered from Alabama to the Pacific, and two obituaries twenty years apart count them off.

subject.name: Mary Tinsley Shackleford's brothers and sisters

body: In June 1900 at Gilbert, Etowah County, John Shackleford, 37, and his wife Elizabeth, 28, married ten years, had five children, all living: “Balous,” 8; Myrtle, 6; May, 5, who was Mary Tinsley; Robert, 3; and Eddie, 8 months. More were born after the family moved to Texas, among them Hazel, born in 1908 at Rattan in Delta County.

Balis Anthony, the eldest, was born on 5 February 1892 in Alabama and went west. He married Bertha Mae Fox, and he died in Los Angeles County on 9 January 1982, nearly ninety, and is buried at Green Hills Memorial Park, Rancho Palos Verdes. Robert Yates, born at Gadsden on 25 October 1897, also ended up in California. When he died at Oroville in June 1961, aged 63, he was called a World War I veteran (his stone carries a World War II marker) and named his survivors: brothers “Bayles of Los Angeles and Ed and John of Oklahoma,” and six sisters, among them “Mamie Moffett” of Oklahoma.

Hazel stayed closest to the Red River. She married John Wesley King, who died in 1968, and she died at Paris, Texas, on 22 December 1980. Her parents were named as John Morgan Shackleford and Kathryn Elizabeth Newton and listed her surviving sisters, Mrs. Joe Haskell, Mrs. Beula Hutchings and Mrs. Helen Josey, all of Apache, Oklahoma, and Mrs. Eular Tillman of Lawton, and her brothers Balis of California and John S. and Edward of Apache. Three of her six pallbearers were Moffitts. Two of them, Donald and Odis, were very likely Mamie's sons and so Hazel's nephews, though no relationships are given.

Apache in Caddo County was where much of the family landed: Lizzie moved there from Dawson County, Texas, in 1933 and is buried at Fairview Cemetery. Two of the 1900 children, Myrtle and Eddie, do not appear in either obituary; they may have died young or be known by other names. Josephine, Eulah and Beulah are known only by their married names, so their birth years and places are still open.

stories.title: Noah Smith: Kentucky farmer, Franklin County justice of the peace, Confederate pensioner
stories.hook: John B. Smith's father farmed around Mount Pleasant and Hagansport, with his son beside him through 1880.
body: In the summer of 1870 Noah Smith, 40, born in Kentucky, farmed near Mount Pleasant in Titus County, Texas, with land worth $1,200 and $200 in personal property. In the house were Mary, 16; John B., 11; and a girl, Annie L. No relationships were given in 1870, but ten years later they were.

In 1875 the southern part of Titus County became Franklin County, and in June 1880 Noah Smith, 51, was in its Precinct 2, listed as a farmer and a justice of the peace. His wife was Mary E., 25. The household was spelled out this time: John B. Smith, 20, son; Anna L., 11, and Eliza A., 8, daughters; Mary B., 5; George R., 2; and a baby boy a month old. Noah gave his father's birthplace as Maryland and his mother's as Virginia. Twenty years later John B. Smith, the 2nd great-grandfather of this family, was farming his own land in the same Precinct 2 of Franklin County.

On 5 July 1899, at about seventy, Noah applied to the State of Texas for a Confederate veteran's pension from Franklin County. In 1900 he was still on his own farm in Justice Precinct 2, now a widower, with two young daughters, Flora, 17, and Oma, 15. He died on 28 January 1906 and is buried at Smith Cemetery in Franklin County; his memorial gives his birth as 6 June 1831 in Greenup County, Kentucky.

Who John B.'s mother was is still open. Noah's wife in 1880, Mary E., was only 25, and when their daughter Flora died her mother was named as Mary Keith. Born about 1855, Mary Keith cannot be the mother of a son born in the late 1850s. John B.'s mother was evidently an earlier wife, and no record names her.

A veteran’s notice written when he died gives the soldier behind that pension: Noah Smith of Mount Vernon, born in Greenup County, Kentucky, who went to Texas “quite a youth,” settled first at Rusk, and served in Company I of the 19th Texas Infantry in Walker’s Division. The pieces fit this Noah—the Greenup County birth on his memorial, the Methodist church, the Franklin County home—but the notice names no wife or child, and its 23 February 1906 death date is a month after the 28 January on his memorial.

Noah told the county judge that July that he had come to Texas in 1856, that he had served more than three years in Company I of the 19th Texas Infantry, and that the measles he caught in the army camps in Arkansas had left him with a cough he never lost. He was seventy, farming 160 poor acres with two ponies, a cow and calf, a wagon and fourteen sheep, and he had sold nothing in two years but a crop that did not pay his expenses. Austin turned him down that September. Two years later a neighbor from Sulphur Bluff wrote to the capital on his behalf: Noah had volunteered early in the war in Captain W. C. Loving's company of Waterhouse's regiment, he was now seventy-two and feeble, his wife had died some years before, and his children were nearly all grown and married. In September 1901 the state reversed itself and put him on the pension roll.

stories.title: Two Moffitt sisters, two Cox grooms
stories.hook: William Moffitt's daughters Catherine and Hannah married Nathan and Jacob Cox, probably brothers, at Holly Spring and Cane Creek in 1789 and 1791.
body: On 16 April 1789, at Holly Spring Meeting on the waters of Deep River, Nathan Cox, twenty-six, took as his wife Catherine Moffitt, who had turned twenty-four eleven days earlier, the daughter of William and Mary Moffitt. Two years and eight months later, on 22 December 1791, Jacob Cox, about twenty-four, married her sister Hannah at Cane Creek Meeting. The two grooms are listed together in the Cox family under Harmon and Jane Cox, so they were probably brothers, from a family that had been on Deep River so long the neighborhood was called the Cox Settlement.

Nathan and Catherine raised a family there: Jane (born 23 August 1790), Mahlon (2 March 1792), Jonathan (27 January 1795), William (22 November 1797), Mary (15 April 1800), Nathan (2 February 1809), Margaret (25 March 1812), and others between. One account prints a death for Catherine on 9 March 1792, a week after Mahlon's birth, and that cannot stand: children kept arriving through 1812, and when Catherine's mother, Mary Moffitt, made her will in 1820 she still left "Catharine Cox" the dresser and cupboard. Nathan died on 10 October 1842. A misprint of 1842 for 1792 would make the dates fit, but nothing shows it.

Hannah and Jacob had at least three children: Harmon, Mary, and a daughter Hannah (1798 to 21 January 1844), who married Charles Cox on 23 March 1820. The family's printed birth date for Hannah Moffitt, 22 December 1771, is the day and month of her wedding twenty years later and looks like a wedding date copied into the birth field; her birth itself is not recorded. Between them the two Moffitt sisters carried the family into the Cox households of Randolph County, where Moffitts and Coxes were marrying each other for three generations.

The 1792 death date for Catherine is the outline's; 1842 is a guess from the children and the 1820 will. Hannah's printed birth, 22 December 1771, equals her wedding date and is unsupported.

stories.title: Which Hugh? Charles Moffitt, Mary Cox and fourteen cousins
stories.hook: The 1928 Moffitt family book gives William's probable brother Charles a Cox wife and fourteen children, which raises a puzzle about two men named Hugh.
body: The family tradition counts Charles Moffitt among the brothers who came from Donegal to Philadelphia and on to Randolph County, North Carolina. His wife, in the 1928 Moffitt genealogy, was Mary Cox, and together they had nine sons and five daughters: Hugh, Margaret, Charles, Robert (born 1778), Solomon, John, Samuel, Catharine, Ruth, Isaac, Jonathan, Mary, Silas (1794) and Rebecca (1797). Even the family knew little about Mary: the tradition was that her people had come from Holland and that she had been born on shipboard on the way over. Those children were first cousins of our Robert Moffitt, and the Robert born in 1778 shares his birth year, which makes the two men easy to confuse.

The next generation can be followed in Quaker records. Hugh Moffitt, son of Charles and Mary (Cox) Moffitt, married Hannah Cox on 15 March 1798. Elizabeth Cox, born 6 July 1784, married a Charles Moffitt at Cane Creek on 14 March 1805. Margery Cox, born in 1794, married Jeremiah Moffitt, "bro. of Charles," at Whitewater, Indiana, in February 1824. And Silas, the youngest son, married Hannah Wilkinson, a granddaughter of William Moffitt, in Randolph County on 4 May 1820; the two of them took their children to Hamilton County, Indiana, and are the people the 1928 book was written for.

The puzzle is Hugh. The 1928 book says William married Mary Davis and Hugh married Hannah Davis, both daughters of Charles Davis, which makes Hugh William's brother, and the family has long said he built the mill on Richland Creek that gave the community of Moffitt its name. The Cox outline, though, has a Hugh who is Charles's son marrying Hannah Cox in 1798. They can be two men, an uncle and a nephew, both Hugh Moffitt, which would also explain why "Hugh Moffitt and Charles Moffitt" witnessed William's will in 1796. No one knows which Hugh signed.
src: Frank Moffitt, Moffitt Genealogy: A Genealogical Record of Silas Moffitt and Hannah Wilkinson Moffitt (1928), pp. 3-4, Internet Archive moffittgenealogy00moff (https://archive.org/details/moffittgenealogy00moff)

stories.title: Holly Spring and the Cox Settlement
stories.hook: The Quaker meeting on Deep River where William Moffitt's daughter married was so full of Coxes that it was first called the Cox Settlement.
body: Friends living on the waters of Deep River asked Cane Creek Meeting in the second month of 1758 for leave to hold a meeting every First-day, and the request was granted. The old stone graveyard on Cox land holds some two hundred pioneers, the first of them, tradition says, two Indians, and a Cane Creek minute of 1765 mentions a Meeting of Indulgence on Mill Creek in Cox's settlement. The name Holly Spring first appears in the minutes of the eighth month of 1769, when Christopher Hussey and Joseph Comer were appointed overseers. In 1787 Richard Caswell deeded fifty acres to Benjamin Cox for the use of the Quakers at a place named for the holly trees over a nearby spring. The first meetinghouse was of logs; a frame house went up about 1830 and a new one in 1890.

The oldest certificate of membership was brought down from Pennsylvania by William Cox in 1752 and had to wait at Cane Creek until Holly Spring was established. The community was first known as the Cox Settlement because of the abundance of Cox families, and the other early names were Moffitt, Barker, Hadley, Comer, Hinshaw, Kemp, Davis and Allen. William Moffitt's daughter Catherine married Nathan Cox there in 1789. A Preparative Meeting was set up in 1790, and an independent Monthly Meeting in 1818 with Robert Moffitt as clerk; the history does not say which Robert, and one candidate is the Robert born in 1778 to Charles Moffitt and Mary Cox, who would have grown up in this very settlement.

The meeting policed its members closely: committees labored with Friends who had slipped in dress and conduct, and disowned those who would not change. By 1832 the great western migration had set in, and Holly Spring never again was the stronghold it had been. The Civil War hurt it worse, since men unwilling to bear arms were severely punished and Friends in the North sent help. That is the world Nathan Moffitt left in the 1840s.

stories.title: The brother who stayed: Amos Alexander of Cecil County
stories.hook: While his brother Hezekiah carried the family south to Sugaw Creek, Amos Alexander stayed on the Maryland tract where they were born: cooper, mill owner, church elder, justice, legislator and wagon colonel, dead of wounds in 1780.
body: Amos Alexander was born in 1729 in Cecil County, Maryland, on the New Munster tract at the head of the Chesapeake, where the Scots-Irish Alexanders had farmed and worshipped for a generation. His father was James Alexander, a yeoman, and his mother Margaret McKnitt, and he grew up in a crowded house of brothers: Theophilus, Hezekiah, Josiah, Ezekiel and John McKnitt, with four sisters.

The brothers split in two. John McKnitt went to North Carolina in 1754, and Hezekiah too made his way to the Carolina backcountry, where he became a blacksmith, a planter and a member of the state's Council of Safety. Amos stayed. He worked as a cooper, owned a mill, and married Sarah Sharp, a name that belonged to the neighborhood's Presbyterian families. They raised four sons, Walter, James, Amos and Mark, and six daughters, one of them Mary, who married John Evans. Like his brother Theophilus he became an elder of the Rock Church, the congregation that families from Head of Christiana had founded in 1720 to have a church nearer home.

As the Revolution came on, the quiet cooper became a public man. He was commissioned a justice of the peace for Cecil County in 1774, and again in 1777 and 1778. Men came to him at Elkton to swear their oaths of allegiance to the new State of Maryland, among them David Barr and John Waggoner. In 1777 and 1778 he sat in the Lower House of the Maryland legislature for Cecil County. By 1779 he was called Esquire.

The war reached him through wagons. Amos held a colonel's rank in the Continental service in John Patterson's Brigade of Wagons, and from 29 November 1779 he was deputy quartermaster general for Delaware, the man responsible for moving the army's supplies through that state, and still at it in February 1780. Sometime between 16 February and 1 May of that year he died of wounds he had received in the war. His own father had died in 1779, only the year before. His eldest son Walter, a captain in the Maryland militia, died at about the same time, and the two are remembered together among the patriots of the Head of Christiana cemetery, where Amos was buried.

Amos was a man of property, and part of that property was people. His personal estate was valued at £1,735 2s., counting books, mills and five enslaved people whose names have not been found. On his brother Hezekiah's Sugaw Creek plantation at least seventeen enslaved people are known by name from the Alexander wills and the 1801 inventory, and the 1790 census counted thirteen there at one time. The two brothers both sat as justices of the peace, one in Maryland and one in North Carolina, in the years of the Revolution, and both lived on the labor of people they held in bondage.
Hezekiah outlived Amos by twenty-one years. In Maryland the widow Sarah was charged with 247 acres on the 1783 tax assessment.

The Archives of Maryland entry (a published reference) names Amos's parents, his brothers including Hezekiah, his offices, rank, estate and death; Johnston's 1881 Cecil County history and Johns's Rock Church history independently call Amos and Theophilus brothers, elders and burials at Head of Christiana. Son Walter's death in 1780 and burial at Head of Christiana come from a cemetery volunteer list, not a gravestone seen. The story says 'five enslaved' from the entry; ages and names unknown. Hezekiah's year of leaving Maryland is not documented here (John McKnitt's 1754 date is from Johnston). The Maryland legislature entry gives his son Walter's death as by 1779; a cemetery list puts it in 1780, so the story says only that he died at about the same time.

stories.title: Silver City, 1880: the boom B. F. Hulsey walked into
stories.hook: The summer B. F. Hulsey gave his work as miner, a crossroads on Gap Creek held more than a thousand people hunting silver, and within two years it was nearly empty.
body: For a few years around 1880 the crossroads called Silver City, in the eastern end of Montgomery County, was the most crowded place in the Ouachita hills. Men had been picking at lead and silver near Gap Creek since before 1840, but it took the news of the mid-1870s to bring the crowd. Miners pushed out of the Colorado and California camps drifted in, the crossroads got its name in 1876, and after 1878 they came faster. By 1880 Silver City was said to hold more than a thousand people, with hundreds of claims and prospects scattered within a few miles of it.

Some of those claims belonged to men with far deeper pockets than a Georgia-born miner. Joseph “Diamond Jo” Reynolds, the riverboat magnate who built the Hot Springs Railroad, owned the Minnesota mine. A Joplin smelter owner, Elliott R. Moffet, who had been Joplin’s first mayor, worked the Walnut. About three dozen mines actually shipped ore and made the newspapers. The rest were holes in a hillside and a hope.

In June 1880 B. F. Hulsey, 32, was a miner in Center Township, whose center sits about six-tenths of a mile from Silver. His wife Sarah G., 30, born in Arkansas, was keeping house, and with them were Margaret, six, George W., four, and Charles F., five months old. Two other men on the same page also called themselves miners. Whether Hulsey held a claim of his own, dug for wages or hauled ore is not known, and nothing names a mine. But a man who wrote “miner” in that township that summer was working in the boom, at the busiest moment it ever had.

It did not last. By the end of 1882 every mine had closed. A gold rush at Bear City, in Garland County, gave Silver City a brief second wind in 1888, until the Bear hills turned out to be barren and the rush was blamed on crooked assayers. Silver City settled back to the size it had been before the boom and stayed that way into the 1900s.

George was not yet seven when the mines closed. A Benjamin F. Hulsey of about the right age turns up in Garland County, with a marriage license in 1893 and households there in 1900 and 1910, which is the county where the next boom had been, but no record ties that man to this household, and the boom itself ties nothing. All the 1880 page can honestly say is that the family’s earliest known home in the Ouachitas sat next to a silver camp, in the one season when the camp was full.

stories.title: Benajah Nordyke and Captain Dunn’s company
stories.hook: A Quaker boy in the Georgia backcountry went off with the rebels, and seventy years later, at 87, he asked for a pension because he thought a man ought to work while he could.
body: Abraham and Mary Nordyke took their Burlington County Quaker household south in the 1770s, and the family’s own history says they spent eight years in Georgia. It remembers two things from those years: little Micajah, four, hiding all night in the woods when an Indian invasion was feared, and Aden, the oldest, being shot in the arm in an Indian attack. It says nothing at all about the war. The war was there anyway.

The Quaker settlement of Wrightsborough in Wilkes County, founded in 1768 by Joseph Maddock, was no place to sit out a rebellion. Its leaders leaned toward the Crown, and its young men leaned the other way. Twenty members of the meeting were dealt with for military activity during the Revolution and fifteen were disowned. One of them, Josiah Dunn, had been put out of the meeting in 1775 and went on to lead rebel partisans, recruiting young men from among the Wrightsborough Friends he had left.

Benajah Nordyke was apparently one of those boys. In November 1852, at 87, he stood before a magistrate in Rockcastle County, Kentucky, and swore that he had been a volunteer soldier in Wilkes County, Georgia, from 1779 to 1782, about eighteen months in all. He named Captain Dunn among his officers, and Colonel Few’s regiment; he had been at Kettle Creek, and at the siege of Augusta in 1781, when the British commander Colonel Brown was shut up in the town, and he had served as drum major. Captain Josiah Dunn, he said, was killed at Kettle Creek. Eighty-seven in 1852 makes him about fourteen in 1779.

He had waited a long time to ask. He said he had never applied because he thought every man ought to work for his living while he could, and that freedom had been pay enough; now he was old, and had begun to lose his memory, and could find no living comrade to vouch for him. A minister who had known him fifty years, and two others, signed for his good name. The file number suggests the claim was not allowed.

Benajah was born on New Year's Day 1766, the third son of Abraham and Mary Nordyke, and he was carried as a baby on the certificate that brought the family back from Chesterfield to Burlington Meeting that March. He was three when his mother took him and his brothers Aaron and Israel south to Bush River in South Carolina, and nine when the family settled among the Friends at Wrightsborough. At fifteen he took up a musket in the Wilkes County militia, and yet in October 1783 the meeting still wrote his name, with his seven brothers and sisters, on the certificate that sent the family on to Deep River in North Carolina. He spent his middle years in Washington County, Virginia, came to Kentucky in 1837, and at eighty-seven, nearly blind and living on his neighbors' kindness, asked the government for the pension he had never claimed; Georgia's burned records could not find him, and it was refused.

quotes.t: Freedom was sufficient pay for him while he could work

stories.title: Stephen Henry Nordyke and the Czar’s mill
stories.hook: A family story sends the first Nordyke to Holland to teach Peter the Great to grind grain. The New Jersey papers find a young man named Henry in debt and in love in 1731.
body: The Nordykes tell a good one. When Marmon Motor Car Company’s history was printed in an Indianapolis trade paper in 1927, it opened with the family: the Nordykes, it said, were descended from Stephen Henry Nordyke, who in 1697 taught Peter the Great the art of grinding grist when the Czar traveled to Holland to learn Western ways. His three sons, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, then went to Pennsylvania. The family’s 1960 genealogy has a fuller version, printed earlier in an 1895 Indiana biographical encyclopedia: Peter fell in love with a Dutch girl, a morganatic marriage followed, and the son was Stephen Henry, who took the girl’s name. Nordyke, it adds, would be “north dike.”

It is exactly the sort of story a family of mill builders would keep. The Nordyke and Marmon works in Indianapolis made flour-mill machinery before it made the Wasp that won the first Indianapolis 500, and the first Nordyke at the Czar’s mill gave the whole business a pedigree.

The papers are plainer. Peter was in the Dutch Republic from mid-August 1697 to January 1698, and a man who could teach a monarch his trade that autumn was no boy; he would have been far past fifty when Rebecca Perkins married a Henry Nordike at Willingboro, New Jersey, in 1731/2. The New Jersey wills have a Henry Nordike in Burlington County owing and being owed in his father-in-law’s estate, and signing as a witness to Rebecca’s brother’s will, which is a young householder’s paper trail, not a courtier’s. The family trees that call him Stephen Henry took the first name from the legend; none of the New Jersey papers has it.

What the legend does carry correctly are the sons’ names. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are the names the family trees give to Henry and Rebecca’s sons, and Abraham’s birth about 1736 and his 1761 marriage to Mary Rogers are what make him our ancestor. The sons did not start in Holland. The family appears to have kept the right children and put them in a more romantic doorway.

Where Henry came from is not known. There were Dutch families with similar names around the Raritan, in Piscataway, whose Van Nortwick name could easily shorten, and a Burlington County widow’s will of 1766 leaves five shillings to “Hannah Nordike,” so the name was in use there. That is a guess, not a link.

stories.title: A full-blood woman's land and the long road to Washington, 1914–1915
stories.hook: Two Austin women from Choctaw County each asked Washington to lift the restrictions on their allotments: Molsey in July 1914, Lizzie in July 1915. Both were answered within days of reaching the capital, but each waited months for the paperwork to get there.

subject.name: Lizzie and Molsey Pisachubbi: two applications at the Indian Office, 1914-1915

body: A full-blood Choctaw's allotment was not hers to sell. Congress had settled that in 1908: land of Indians with less than half Choctaw blood came free of restrictions, land of those with half to three-quarters blood lost its restriction except for the homestead, and everyone else, full-bloods above all, stayed under the Secretary of the Interior's eye until he chose to lift it, wholly or in part. The Assistant Commissioner of Indian Affairs told a House committee in 1916 that about 26,800 of the 101,500 citizens of the Five Civilized Tribes were full-bloods, and that some 33,000 people were still restricted. For a woman like Lizzie Pisachubbee, the way out of those restrictions began with a written application and ended at a desk in Washington.

Lizzie was a full-blood, enrolled at Fowlerville at seven in 1899 as the daughter of Legion and Molsey Austin, and by 1915 she was about 23, married to Robert Pisachubbe, and living on a farm near Speer. On 17 July 1915 her application was made out. It went first to the Superintendent for the Five Civilized Tribes at Muskogee, who sat on it for eleven weeks before forwarding it on 2 October. It reached the Indian Office on 5 October, was acted on on 8 October, and went back to the superintendent on 9 October: four days in Washington after eleven weeks at Muskogee. The printed list of cases does not say whether the answer was yes or no, and nothing else turned up says what it was.

The same list has the older woman's case a year earlier. "Molsey Pisachubbi, née Austin" applied on 22 July 1914; the superintendent forwarded the papers on 14 January 1915, the Indian Office received them on 18 January and decided on 23 January, and they went back on 25 January. The name is probably Lizzie's mother, who had been Molsey Austin in 1899 and appears with the Pisachubbi name in this one line. The "née Austin" is a puzzle, since Austin was her husband Legion's name and not her own; the clerk may simply have written what he found on the card. She died in 1924. If she did marry a Pisachubbi after Legion's death, the papers have not yet turned up.

What did a lifted restriction mean for a household like this one? It meant that the land could be sold, mortgaged or lost for taxes, and the same Assistant Commissioner told the committee that an estimated nine out of ten Choctaws, Chickasaws, Creeks, Cherokees and Seminoles freed by Congress were by then landless. Some families wanted the freedom, to settle debts, to buy equipment, or to leave a farm too poor to live on. The land that these women owned stayed in the family in the end. In 1920 Lizzie and Robert were farming their own place in Jeter Township, and when Robert's mother Eunice died in 1927 her 159 acres still needed a county judge's approval before they could be sold.

quotes.t: It is estimated that 90 per cent of the enrolled members of the Five Civilized Tribes who had their restrictions removed by legislation are to-day without any lands whatever.

stories.title: The year Doaksville's store moved to the railroad, 1903
stories.hook: When the railroad came through in 1903, the first store of the new town of Fort Towson was stocked by the Doaksville Trading Company, and the older village that the Tims family had known for seventy years began to empty.

subject.name: The Doaksville Trading Company and the move to Fort Towson

body: For the Tims and Thompson families, Doaksville was where you bought what you could not raise. Joel Thompson remembered that his people did "all of our trading" there, and the same crossroads had been V. B. Tims's stand in the 1830s and 1840s, in front of the old rock jail. The name outlived the stand by a long time. It was still the family's post office on their enrollment papers of 1899.

In 1903 a railroad was being built through that part of the Choctaw Nation, and a new town was laid out beside the line, not far from the ruins of the old fort that gave Fort Towson its name. A history of Oklahoma printed in 1916 says the new town "was established in 1903," and that the first store in it was built and stocked by the Doaksville Trading Company, which had grown into a substantial business at Doaksville. Other merchants followed from the older place, "the result being that within a comparatively short time Doaksville became little more than a memory." The post office followed the stores: on 12 June 1903 the Doaksville office took back the name Fort Towson, and the Thompsons, who had been writing Doaksville on their papers for years, found themselves at Fort Towson on a pencil note of 1905 and, by 1915, at Corinne over the mountain.

The man who bought the old company's stock was William Ward Wilson, called Billy, a cattleman who had herded on the very ground where the new town went up, with his brother. By 1915 the Wilsons and a partner controlled the First National Bank of Fort Towson, and Billy Wilson, not yet sixty in 1916, could remember deer in herds of forty or fifty within a few hundred yards of the abandoned army post. That is how recent the old frontier was. Joseph Thompson's boyhood, Betsy Tims's school days and the old trader's grandchildren had all come out of it, and by 1916 a banker could talk about them as the people who had known the country when it was wild.

Judge Edward Tims, the old trader's son, had been Doaksville's postmaster from 1887, and the log house that may have been his father's stand was still known as the family's in 1940, when a newspaper suggested making it a museum. Doaksville itself dwindled to a cemetery on a hill.

quotes.t: The Town of Fort Towson is new and vital. It was established in 1903, at the time when a line of railroad was in process of construction through this section.

stories.title: Land from Lord Granville: the Moffitt grants on Richland Creek
stories.hook: In 1760 and 1761 the Earl of Granville's land office gave William Moffitt 130 acres on Tibbs Run and Hugh Moffitt 330 acres near Tick Creek, and William bought 225 more from a neighbor on Deep River.
body: North Carolina's best Piedmont land in the 1750s was not the king's to give. It belonged to the Earl of Granville, the one Lord Proprietor who had refused to sell his eighth share, and his land office in Orange County issued grants, collected the rents and kept the books. William Churton, who had laid out the county seat at Hillsborough, was the county's first register and its surveyor, and when a Granville grant was entered at the county court it was Churton who proved it.

On 1 August 1760 the Earl granted William Moffitt 130 acres on Tibbs Run, a branch of Richland Creek, next to a rise called Crow Hill. It is the same Richland Creek where the Moffitt family would later keep the mill that gave the neighborhood its name, and it is the same Tibbs Run where William's will of 1796 left land to his youngest son, David. It was a small farm, not a plantation, and it was probably where the family began.

A little over a year later, on 2 October 1761, the Earl granted Hugh Moffitt 330 acres on a drain of Tick Creek, next to a branch of Brush Creek. Hugh was probably William's brother, the one who would marry Mary Davies's sister Hannah and later write his will in Chatham County before leaving for the Northwest Territory. The Moffitts were taking up land two at a time, side by side.

William also bought. Peter Youngblood, who had his own Granville grant on the east side of Deep River, and his wife Magdaline sold William Moffitt 225 acres, a deed acknowledged in the county court around 1761. That is the figure that turns up again in 1796, when William left his son William 'the 225-acre plantation' where he lived.

From then on William was a man other men brought to court. Between 1765 and 1767 his name appears again and again as the witness who swore to a neighbor's deed in open court: Thomas Cox to Jacob Grigg, 179 acres; David Jenkins to Jacob Grigg, 349 acres; Solomon Cox to Nicholas Barker, 235 acres; Frederick Sypart to Thomas Davis, 205 acres on both sides of Deep River beside Peter Youngblood and Harmon Cox. These were the Deep River neighbors who would soon sign the Regulators' petitions with him. A man who is asked to swear to other men's deeds is a man whose word the county takes: by 1768 William Moffitt was first on the Regulators' list.

The abstractor matched each deed to the Granville grant at the NC State Archives, but the grant papers were not seen here. The match of the Tibbs Run grantee to our William rests on the same creek and the 1796 will's Tibs Run land for David, and on William's 225 acres; a second William Moffitt on Richland Creek is not impossible. The Youngblood deed is entered without a date in the abstract and is placed near 1761 by the entries around it. Hugh the grantee of 1761 is the elder Hugh; Charles's son Hugh was born about 1774 and is a different man.

stories.title: Adam Moffit, a road jury and two witnessed deeds
stories.hook: Adam, the brother the family Bible says died in North Carolina, appears in the Orange County court books in 1764 laying out a road beside Harmon Cox.
body: The family Bible lists Adam among the six brothers who left Ireland and says he died in North Carolina. For years he was only a name in that list. The court books give him a little more.

In August 1764 the Orange County court named a committee to lay out a road from the line between Rowan and Orange, across Sandy Creek about two miles above Guess's Mill, and on into the best road to Cape Fear. Sixteen men were ordered to mark it, among them Harmon Cox, Thomas Aldred, Semore and Henry York, Edward Welbourne and Adam Moffit. Harmon Cox was the head of the Cox Settlement on Deep River, where Adam's brother William would marry a daughter into the neighborhood's Quaker families and where William's daughters would marry Coxes.

Adam proved deeds in the same court, as his brother William did. He swore to David Jenkins's sale of 300 acres to Christian Hussey, a tract on Mill Creek of Deep River, and to William Cox's sale of 240 acres to Phebe Allen. Both Hussey and Allen belonged to the Holly Spring neighborhood. Twenty-one years later, on 17 August 1785, an Adam Moffitt was one of three witnesses to the will of Thomas Matthews of Chatham County, whose daughters included Sarah Morgan, Hannah Griffith and Margaret McDade.

It is not much. But a road jury was made up of neighbors who knew the country, and a man called to witness a will or a deed was a man the family trusted. Adam was in the same few square miles as William and Hugh before the Regulators and was still there, probably, after the Revolution.
