stories.title: Noah Smith in Walker’s Texas Division
stories.hook: A Kentucky boy who turned up in a few-hundred-person East Texas county seat went to war in the 19th Texas Infantry, and forty years later a comrade wrote his death notice for the Confederate Veteran.
body: Noah Smith grew up in Greenup County, Kentucky, a river county on the Ohio that had been cut from Mason County in 1803 and held about 5,850 people when he was a baby. He told his comrades later that he went to Texas “quite a youth,” and that he first settled at Rusk. In the years a young man from Kentucky could have arrived, Rusk was hardly a town. The legislature had made Cherokee County in 1846 and named its seat for Thomas Jefferson Rusk; the county bought a hundred acres in 1847, laid them out around a courthouse square, and held court in a log cabin until a two-room frame building went up. About 355 people lived there in 1850.

When the war came he joined Company I of the 19th Texas Infantry. Richard Waterhouse, a Jefferson merchant, had raised that regiment in the first months of 1862 from the counties of northeast Texas; its 886 men elected their officers on 13 May and camped at Camp Waterhouse. In June they marched to Arkansas, where disease and exposure killed many before they reached Little Rock in the fall. By the end of 1862 the regiment belonged to Walker’s Texas Division, the biggest all-Texas command of the war, in its Third Brigade, and it stayed there until the end. Where and when Noah put his name down, and how old he was, is not known; he would have been about thirty-two.

The Texans never crossed the Mississippi. Their war was fought in the swamps and cane brakes of Louisiana and the hills of Arkansas, and it began in earnest at Milliken’s Bend, above Vicksburg, on 7 June 1863. Waterhouse’s regiment went forward with the rest of the brigade, drove the Federals from behind a levee and charged on through their camp to the water’s edge, where the gunboats forced a withdrawal; the regiment lost two killed, eleven wounded and six missing. The next spring the division was in the Red River campaign. On 8 April 1864 at Mansfield it helped break the Union left, and the next day at Pleasant Hill the 19th lost two killed, five wounded and twenty-one captured. At Jenkins’ Ferry, in the Arkansas mud on 30 April, the division lost roughly a quarter of its Texans in its last great battle. Which of those fights Noah saw is not known; his company rolls would say.

The division melted away in May 1865 as men went home without waiting for the surrender. By 1870 Noah was farming near Mount Pleasant in Titus County, and by 1880 he was a farmer and justice of the peace in Franklin County’s Precinct 2, with young John B. beside him. In July 1899 he applied for the Confederate pension that Texas paid its old soldiers. He belonged to the Ben McCulloch Camp of the United Confederate Veterans at Mount Vernon, and was a Methodist.

When he died, his old comrade P. A. Blakey of Mount Vernon wrote him up for the Confederate Veteran: a pioneer citizen of Texas, long a resident of the community around Mount Vernon, “a good citizen,” an exemplary member of the Methodist church and a loving husband and father. The notice gives 23 February 1906 as the day; his memorial at Smith Cemetery says 28 January. One of them is a month off.
His own pension papers put his coming to Texas in 1856, when he was about twenty-five, so the "youth" of his comrade's notice was perhaps a kindly rounding.

stories.title: Oakland, before it was Oakland: the township Parses Watt farmed
stories.hook: When Archibald and Parses O’Neal brought a baby to Gibson County in 1839 there was no Oakland; by the time Parses was twice widowed there was a town with a steam mill, two railroads and a brick school.
body: In 1839 Archibald O’Neal carried his wife Parses and their baby, Daniel Waters, from Tennessee to Columbia Township in Gibson County, Indiana. The land was hilly and heavily timbered, drained by creeks that all rose within a mile or two of one another, and bears had been so thick along one of them that it was called Bear Creek. There was no Oakland yet. There were farms, and on the high ground a few settlers who had been there since the 1820s.

One of them, Jesse Houchins, sold his place in 1827 to James W. Cockrum. Cockrum sold out again in 1833 and went down the rivers as a steamboat man, then came back in 1835 and bought a farm on the hill from his brother-in-law Richard Barrett. Part of that farm became the town. Archibald did not live to see it. He died in April 1841, and Parses, a widow with a two-year-old, later married Hugh Watt, an Irishman from County Down.

For fifteen years the neighborhood’s door to the world was Dongola, a canal town two and a half miles north, where the Wabash and Erie Canal and the state road crossed the Patoka River. The proprietors laid Dongola out in March 1851 with broad streets and a public square, and for a few years it packed pork. In 1855 Cockrum and Jacob Hargrove opened the first store on the hill and shipped flatboat loads of pork, corn and flour out the Patoka and Wabash to New Orleans. That year a stock company built a steam grist mill with four run of burrs, which cost $8,000 and lost money, the county not being yet developed enough to feed so large a mill. A railroad was supposed to cross the hill and was started; in 1856 its promoters ran into trouble and the work stopped.

The town came anyway. Cockrum and Warrick Hargrove filed the plat on 15 January 1856 and named it Oakland for the grove of oaks on the site. The first blacksmith opened that year, a wagon shop and a cooper shop in 1857, and a harness shop and a shoe shop. William Cockrum put up a tobacco compress and shipped two hundred hogsheads down the canal. The Baptists held their first meeting on 15 July 1858 and built a church in 1859, beside the cemetery Cockrum had laid out in 1855, where the first stone marked a child’s grave. The first school opened in the winter of 1860–61. Daniel O’Neal, who was seventeen when the plat was filed, enlisted in Company F of the 42nd Indiana that October.

The railroads came later: the Air Line from Louisville and Evansville to St. Louis, and the Straight Line from Indianapolis to Evansville, which cross at Oakland. A subscription brick school, the Oakland Institute, went up in 1868–69 for about $8,000 and was sold to the township in 1877. A newspaper began in 1871, the same year Hugh Watt died. Through all of that Parses stayed on the old home farm. When the county history was compiled in 1884, “Mrs. Parsis Watt” was still farming in Section 32, with Oakland City on her mail, and her two husbands’ names under hers.

The history’s OCR gives Cockrum’s dates as 1833 (sold, went south) and 1835 (returned, bought the farm), and 1827 for the Houchins sale; the Oakland Institute years read “1863’’69” in the OCR and are given here as 1868–69 from the surrounding text and should be checked on the scan page (p. 214). stories.title: Mountain Valley, where the water was named for a crossroads
stories.hook: A farm family in Mountain Valley Township in 1900 lived beside the spring that sold its water coast to coast under the name of their own little community.
body: North of Hot Springs, about twelve miles from the bathhouses, a small farming community called Mountain Valley lent its name to one of the best-known bottled waters in America. The spring itself had belonged to Benjamin Lockett and his son Enoch, who had noticed how clear it ran, and the neighbors called it Lockett’s Spring Water. In 1871 two brothers from Arkadelphia, the druggist Peter E. Greene and John Greene, began selling it. They bought the land, built a two-story hotel, opened a distribution office on Central Avenue in Hot Springs, and renamed the water for the community nearby.

By 1900 the spring had been through several owners. A St. Louis insurance man bought the business in the summer of 1879, and in 1883 a company was formed with Zeb Ward and three other investors, with Greene staying on as manager. The first hotel burned in the late 1880s and a larger three-story hotel took its place. Ward bought out his partners in December 1892 and talked of a railroad from Hot Springs to Mountain Valley, which was never built. In 1894 a distribution center opened in Philadelphia. The valley around the spring was still mostly farms.

In June 1900 “Benjaman F Hulsey,” fifty-nine, headed a household in the Mountain Valley and Union township area of Garland County with a wife, Lucy L., and six children. Charles F., Martin S., Mary J. B. and Francis M. were probably from an earlier marriage; Lillian and Thomas M. were Lucy’s. Whether he is the Benjamin of the Silver City household of 1880 is the question the family has not been able to settle, and his age, which the census puts about seven years older than that household’s, does not help. But two of the names in the house repay a second look. The 1880 household had a baby named Charles F., who would have been twenty in 1900, and family accounts name a son of Benjamin’s as Martin Salathiel, which Martin S. could stand for. Neither is proof. The 1900 page, read with the children’s ages and birthplaces, may settle it.

The spring went on without them. August Schlafly of St. Louis and his family became its sole owners in 1902, and by 1908 the company had franchise offices in Chicago and New York. The big hotel burned in 1934 with the singer Kate Smith as a guest, and it was never rebuilt.

The two name coincidences (Charles F. and Martin S.) are new observations, not documents: the 1880 Silver City baby is Charles F. and a family account names a son Martin Salatheil (see salathiel). The 1900 ages are in the census image and have not been read; the ages in benjaminh (59 in 1900, 68 in 1910) are seven to ten years older than the 1847 or 1880 ages. The 1883 company is from the Encyclopedia of Arkansas; the Mountain Valley railroad that was never built is Ward's plan after 1892. stories.title: Company F: the Richview boys at Donelson, Shiloh and Pleasant Hill
stories.hook: Company F of the 49th Illinois was a Richview company, and between February 1862 and April 1864 it buried a startling share of its men: John B. Walker at Shiloh, a first sergeant at Pleasant Hill, and neighbors whose names the Livesays, Carters and Thompsons would have known by heart.

subject.name: John B. Walker and the men of Company F

body: The 49th Illinois was put together at Camp Butler, near Springfield, and mustered in on the last day of 1861. Company F came from Richview. Of the roughly 140 men on its roster, about seventy gave Richview as home, and the families around the Beaucoup settlement were among them. The captain was Benjamin W. Jones of Richview; the first lieutenant, Ransom C. Hagerman; the first sergeant, James A. Reed; and a sergeant named John A. Logan, who would be a captain by autumn. In the ranks were Andrew Livesly and Francis M. Carter, two names the county would later list among its own, and a private named John B. Walker.

They went south at once. The regiment was ordered to Cairo on 3 February 1862, and on the 8th it moved to Fort Henry and joined the Third Brigade of McClernand's division. On the 11th it marched for Fort Donelson, and on the 13th it was in the fight, losing fourteen killed and thirty-seven wounded; Colonel William R. Morrison, commanding the brigade, was among the wounded. Company F's first death was Private Robert Ford of Richview, killed on 13 February. A corporal, Joseph J. Newcomb, died of wounds on 5 March. They had been soldiers for six weeks.

On 6 March the regiment embarked for Pittsburg Landing. The camp the 49th made there is marked today by a National Park Service tablet: the regiment belonged to Raith's Third Brigade of McClernand's First Division, and on the morning of Sunday, 6 April 1862, its first line of battle was formed on the color line of that camp. The day cost the regiment seventeen killed and ninety-nine wounded, among them Lieutenant Colonel Phineas Pease, who commanded it, and Major Bishop. Company F lost John B. Walker, a private, killed on the 6th. It lost Matthew B. Pray, killed; Robert Stirling, who died of his wounds at Savannah, Tennessee, the same day; and two Richview recruits, Richard Alcorn and Robert Bundy, who died at Shiloh that April. Parker G. Dillinger died at Corinth on the 9th, a prisoner. Corporal Lucius Graham was captured, exchanged, and died at Washington that October.

John Walker's family remembered him a little differently. In 1894 his brother Captain Simeon Walker, speaking for a family of five preaching sons and six soldiers, called John B. a captain killed at Shiloh. The muster roll has him a private, and it is the roll the family ought to trust on his rank. The rest of the brother's memory, the place and the day, agrees with it and if John B. was the preacher Simeon Walker's son, as the name and the town suggest, then the Walkers of Beaucoup lost a brother at Shiloh before Simeon had put on a uniform.

The spring and summer after Shiloh took more than the battle had. Between early May and November 1862 seven more men of the company died of sickness or old wounds: Francis M. Driver, Lieutenant Hagerman, Michael Trout, Jackson Reeves, Corporal James E. Reed, Sergeant Samuel M. Casey and Samuel Craig. Three of them died at home in Richview or in Illinois hospitals; two died in camp at Bethel, Tennessee. Captain Jones resigned in June. Sergeant John A. Logan became first lieutenant in May and captain by September, and he was still captain when the regiment mustered out.

New men came in September 1862. Five recruits from Richview were mustered on the 12th, and one of them was Thomas B. Thompson, the son of Lydia Jane Livesay and William Thompson, who by his family's account was then twenty. With him went William J. Livesey, who would come home a sergeant, and James M. Logan, another sergeant by the end. Thomas came home a corporal on 1 July 1865. Another Walker, George W., was a recruit too, but he was discharged at Bethel before he had seen much of the war.

Then came the long middle of the war: Helena, the capture of Little Rock in November 1863, Memphis, and in January 1864 a reenlistment of three-fourths of the regiment as veterans. Thomas M. Brown, Francis Carter and William Stonecipher of Richview signed again on 16 January. In March the veterans went up the Red River, took Fort DeRussy on the 14th and fought at Pleasant Hill on 9 April. Company F's first sergeant, Patrick Nixon of Richview, was killed there, and so was Sergeant Willis Nazworthy.

Those who had not reenlisted stayed behind in Memphis, and some of them, like Andrew Livesly, would muster out in January 1865. The rest went home on furlough in June 1864 and gathered at Centralia before going back to the front. By September 1865, when the regiment was mustered out at Paducah, Kentucky, the roster of Company F carried the notation of death beside more than forty names.

stories.note: Evidence: events and roster entries are proven from the Adjutant General's transcribed report; the family links are probable or lead. John B. Walker (private, Richview, killed at Shiloh 6 Apr 1862) is tied to Rev. Simeon Walker's family only by the 1894 sketch (brother John B., captain, killed at Shiloh) and the name; the sketch's 'captain' conflicts with the roster's 'private', and his regiment (the sketch says 40th; the roster says 49th) conflicts too. Thomas B. Thompson as Lydia Jane Livesay's son rests on the Thompson family account already on the site. My counts of 'about seventy' Richview men and 'more than forty' deaths are a hand tally of the online transcription (139 entries, some men listed twice, residence field often missing for recruits) and should be rechecked against the Illinois Civil War Muster and Descriptive Rolls database, which was unreachable when this was written; 'more than forty names' is my hand count of death notations (about 40 in the 139 entries parsed) and is the figure most likely to need adjusting. The 'seven more men' are Driver, Hagerman, Trout, Reeves, J. E. Reed, Casey, Craig; Driver's place of death is not given. A search-result summary attributed to a Shiloh marker the text 'formed here about 8:30 a.m. ... attacked upon the left flank and fell back, fighting, to the Cross Roads', and an Illinois state marker (HMDB 42969) gives regimental loss as 2 officers and 17 men killed, 4 officers and 79 men wounded, 8 missing, total 110, against the Adjutant General's 17 killed and 99 wounded; I left both out of the prose until the tablets are read in person. The Adjutant General's history names a Captain John A. Logan as commander of the non-veteran detachment at Tupelo, 14-15 July 1864; he is probably Company F's Richview captain but nothing says so, and he must not be confused with General John A. Logan, who commanded the division the regiment joined at Bethel. The sentence about Simeon's later company is cautious but could be cut.

stories.title: Pearland in the Santa Fe's pamphlet, October 1899
stories.hook: In the autumn of 1899 the Santa Fe Railway told prospective settlers across the Midwest that Pearland was a thriving village of 300 with schools, churches and one of the finest young pear orchards on the coast. Floyd and Alice Livesay, with their small children, were somewhere among those 300.
body: In October 1899 the passenger department of the Santa Fe Route printed the twentieth thousand copy of a booklet called Texas Coast Country, the second in its Seekers' Series. It was written for people who lived where the winters were long, the soil was tired and a farm could grow only one main crop a year. Page after page of it described the towns along the Gulf, Colorado and Santa Fe line, and on page 50 it came to Pearland.

The town of Pearland, it said, lay fifteen miles south of Houston, at the center of a splendid country. The townsite had been laid out on a modern plan, with boulevards and broad streets and places kept back for churches and parks, and the railroad expected to build there a model community. Ten thousand acres around it had been cut into ten-, twenty- and forty-acre tracts, to be sold at fifteen to twenty-five dollars an acre, a third down and the rest in one and two years, each tract fronting a broad, graded road. Pearland was, the pamphlet said, a thriving village of 300 inhabitants, with schools and churches, and for its age it could show one of the finest pear orchards along the coast.

Further on, the booklet let settlers speak for themselves, and two of them lived at Pearland. Eli Landreth, a quarter of a mile from the station, had come down from Iowa two years before and farmed 269 acres, ninety of them in oats, cotton, corn and sweet potatoes, and said he had never had a crop fail in whole or in part. Another Iowa man, a Mr. Martin who lived four miles out, said that with a family of seven he had not needed a doctor in four years and had never regretted leaving the snow banks of the North. Both said the climate was healthy, and Landreth added that a man of small means could make a home there if he was willing to hustle.

Somewhere among those three hundred people were Floyd and Alice Livesay. Floyd had come from Illinois about 1895, as the Houston paper said when he died, within a year or so of the platting of the townsite; Lester was born in Illinois in November 1894, and Ruth about 1898 in Texas. Floyd is not named in the booklet, and nothing says that a Santa Fe pamphlet, rather than a neighbor's letter, a land agent or a railroad ticket, brought him south. But the Livesays were the sort of family the booklet was written for: northern people, with children, on a few acres in a town that had been laid out on paper only five years before.

The booklet is honest about what it did not promise. Mr. Landreth warned that new settlers should come with money enough to last, and a settler at Alta Loma along the same line wrote that a slight freeze had cut down his cauliflower the November before and that his young orchard had not yet begun to bear. The orchard that was called the finest on the coast was still a young one; the grocery and the livery stable that made the Livesays' name in Pearland, with the store at the corner of Main and Broadway dated by the family to about 1906, were still several years away.

stories.title: Centralia, 1864: where two regiments came home and went back
stories.hook: In the spring and summer of 1864 two Illinois regiments with Washington County men in them came home on furlough and met again at Centralia, and on 17 April William P. Walker and Jackson L. Livesay were mustered into the 60th there, the day before it left for Atlanta.

subject.name: William P. Walker and Jackson L. Livesay

body: Centralia was a railroad town, and in 1864 the railroad was how southern Illinois went to war and came home from it. The Illinois Central ran through it, and so did the soldiers.

The first regiment to come was the 60th. In February 1864 it was in winter quarters at Rossville, Georgia, and three-fourths of its men reenlisted as veterans on the 22nd. Four days later it took part in the reconnoissance toward Dalton that became the fight at Buzzard Roost, where it lost forty-two killed and wounded. On 6 March it was ordered to Illinois on veteran furlough, and the men were furloughed from Centralia on 15 March 1864.

The furlough was a month long, and the regiment filled its thinned ranks at the same station. On 20 March a farmer of Richview named William P. Walker, thirty-three years old, and an eighteen-year-old named Jackson L. Livesay, who had left the Beaucoup school at sixteen, enlisted in Company C, the company of Captain Simeon Walker, who may have been William's brother-in-law. Both were mustered into the service at Centralia on 17 April. The next day, 18 April, the regiment left, by way of Louisville, Nashville and Chattanooga, for Rossville, and by 2 May the Atlanta campaign had begun. For William and Jackson the road from Centralia led to Ringgold, Dalton, Resaca, Kennesaw Mountain, Peach Tree Creek and Jonesboro, where on 1 September the division and corps commanders complimented the regiment for its gallantry. They mustered out at Louisville on 31 July 1865.

The second regiment to come was the 49th. In January three-fourths of it had reenlisted, and after the Red River campaign it was ordered to Illinois on veteran furlough on 24 June. When the furlough was over the men rendezvoused again at Centralia and went by way of Cairo and Memphis to Holly Springs, which they reached in time for the Oxford expedition of 12 August. The men who had not reenlisted had stayed behind at Memphis under Captain John A. Logan and fought at Tupelo on 14 and 15 July.

Centralia gave soldiers as well as sending them off. The Company F roster of the 49th lists a handful of recruits from Centralia that spring and summer: Thomas C. Drake and John C. Holt, mustered on 22 February; Arthur C. Leonard, John W. Shelton and Jesse West, on 25 April; and William V. Shelton on 5 July. Drake died at Memphis on 29 March, five weeks after he enlisted. Leonard died on 9 January 1865. The others came home in September.
For two regiments, then, Centralia was both the last stop on the way out and the first on the way back.
src: Report of the Adjutant General of the State of Illinois, 60th Infantry regimental history (organized Camp Dubois, Anna, 17 Feb 1862; reenlisted 22 Feb 1864; furloughed from Centralia 15 Mar 1864; left 18 Apr 1864 for Rossville; Atlanta campaign, Jonesboro 1 Sept 1864), transcribed by the Illinois Civil War Project: https://civilwar.whalen-family.org/history/060.html (read 4 Nov 2026)

The regimental dates (furlough from Centralia 15 Mar 1864, departure 18 Apr 1864; 49th rendezvous at Centralia after the June 1864 furlough) are the Adjutant General's; Jackson and William's enlistment and muster dates are the site's existing roll readings; the roster does not say whether the 17 April muster at Centralia was at the regiment's furlough camp, so 'the day before it left' is an inference from two dates and is hedged by wording only. The story's first paragraph and its last paragraph are interpretive and can be cut. William P. Walker's age (thirty-three) is from b. 15 Mar 1831 per the tree. 'Captain Simeon Walker, who may have been William's brother-in-law' is already a hedged claim on 'Etheldra J. and Captain Simeon'. 'A Richview family that remembered its soldiers in 1864 remembered them at that depot' is invented sentiment and should be removed. The Sanborn sheet is an index-map sheet; check that it shows the depot area before using, or choose a later sheet. The Adjutant General's phrase for Tupelo is 'commanded by Captain John A. Logan' (see note on the Company F story). Thomas B. Thompson is in 'people' only as a possible cross-link to the Company F story.

stories.title: Rhoda Beauchamp's people: the Eastern Shore, Georgia and Turkey Hill
stories.hook: Two family genealogies printed thirty years apart carry Simeon Walker's mother back to the Maryland marshes, and through the Georgia where Simeon was born.
body: Rhoda Beauchamp was born on 18 July 1781, a daughter of William Beauchamp and Nancy Parker, on the lower Eastern Shore of Maryland, where Somerset and Worcester counties run down to the Pocomoke. Her father had been born there in 1760, one of six children of Fountain Beauchamp and Rhoda Adams, who married in 1746 and whose children's births went into the registers of Coventry Parish. Her mother, born about 1761, was the fifth child and eldest daughter of Jacob Parker, born in Somerset County in 1724, and his wife Mary Smith. William and Nancy married about 1780, and Rhoda, born the next year, was the eldest of their daughters in one account and is listed last of seven children in the other.

In 1790 Jacob Parker sold up. He deeded his wife's family land, Bacon's Quarter, back to her father, gave his son Elisha a farm called Forest Hill, and late that year sailed from Baltimore for Savannah with his family, the Turner brothers and sisters and enough neighbors to fill a ship. The voyage was remembered as a stormy one: the water ran out, and a young mother on board, the wife of Zadoc Turner Jr., died. From Savannah they went up the country to the part of Greene County that in 1793 became Hancock County, Georgia. Jacob died in 1791, and Nancy Parker Beauchamp died in Hancock County in 1796, when Rhoda was fifteen.

The Georgia years explain a puzzle in Simeon Walker's story. Rhoda married Abram Walker, who was also from Worcester County, and their son Simeon was born in Jackson County, Georgia, on 13 April 1802. Simeon's own son, the captain, remembered in 1894 that his father had been brought from Georgia by his mother, and Levi Walker's notes take the young family to Illinois in 1809 and back to Kentucky, where Abram died in January 1812. Rhoda then came to Turkey Hill, east of Belleville, near her father's house, which the Methodist preachers used as an inn and a church. She married Henry Sharp at Belleville in 1815, a son, Andrew Jackson Sharp, was born there the next year, and she died on 31 March 1846.

The descent rests on compiled genealogies, not on original records, and the later of the two may have borrowed from the earlier. Neither says when William Beauchamp left Georgia or how he reached Illinois. What makes it probable is agreement: a Maryland-born Rhoda Beauchamp who married Abram Walker and then Henry Sharp at Belleville, a Georgia-born son, and a father named William Beauchamp, told three times by three branches of the family.
src: Daughters of the American Revolution Magazine, vol. 68, no. 12 (December 1934), Parker family genealogy in the genealogical pages, about pp. 727-730 (Jacob Parker, born Somerset Co., Md., 1724, married 1748 Mary Smith; removal from Baltimore to Savannah and Hancock Co., Ga., 1790; Jacob died 1791; children including Nancy, married 1780 William Beauchamp, died Hancock Co., Ga., 1796; her eldest daughter Rhoda married first Abram Walker of Worcester Co., Md., and second Henry Sharp at Belleville, Ill.; son Andrew Jackson Sharp born Belleville 1816), Internet Archive sim_american-spirit_1934-12_68_12, full text read 5 Nov 2026: https://archive.org/details/sim_american-spirit_1934-12_68_12

stories.note: PROBABLE: William Beauchamp (b. 1760) and Nancy Parker as Rhoda's parents (two compiled genealogies plus Levi's notes, which name her father William). PROBABLE: Rhoda's dates 18 Jul 1781 - 31 Mar 1846 (Perry only; DAR says she died at Belleville in 184-, last digit unreadable in the OCR). LEAD: the grandparents Fountain Beauchamp and Rhoda Adams (Perry, citing Coventry Parish) and Jacob Parker and Mary Smith (DAR only). The DAR article's Georgia details (ship from Baltimore, Hancock County) are family tradition as printed. Not claimed: when William Beauchamp came to Illinois; that Henry Sharp was kin to Elizabeth Sharpe. Both sources are compiled works; quote nothing from Perry (1963). Check 'Hancock' against 'Greene' (the DAR says Jacob died in Green County, 'made from Hancock', which is backwards: Hancock was made from Greene and Washington in 1793). No image offered.

stories.title: Before Doaksville: the Tims family of Lunenburg and Chester
stories.hook: A family Bible, a backcountry land petition and two wartime claims carry Vincent Tims's family back from Chester to Virginia and, by its own account, to Northamptonshire.
body: The Tims family remembered its beginnings in England. By the account kept in one branch's family Bible, the elder Amos Tims was born in Northamptonshire in March 1684, and his son Amos was born in Virginia and married a wife named Frances, born on 30 August 1718. The old man was still the senior Amos Tims of Lunenburg County, Virginia, in 1760, when he helped value a neighbor's estate, and he died on 3 August 1766.

The younger Amos and Frances had a son Joseph, born on 2 December in the 1740s or 1750s, and Joseph married Mary Glover. By 1770 the family was in the South Carolina backcountry. Joseph Tims was among the men whose petitions for land came before the colony's council on 6 November 1770, Amos Tims had a grant of 400 acres in 1774 in what became Union District, and Joseph and Mary's children were born there: Amos on 31 August 1771 and Sarah on 13 October 1776.

The war came through that country, and the family fed it. In April 1785 the state issued indents, its paper for wartime debts, to Joseph Tims for provisions supplied for the use of the militia in 1781, and to Amos Tims for provisions and forage for the Continental troops that same year. Joseph's claim came to two pounds, twelve shillings and a penny. These were small farmers' sales of corn, beef and fodder, the kind of account thousands of Carolina families settled after the Revolution.

Joseph died on 16 August 1801, and Mary lived until November 1825. Sarah married William Estes and spent her life in Chester County, where she died in 1849 and was buried in a family graveyard. Her name is the link to Doaksville. The Chester will that the family calls Joseph's first names a daughter Sarah Estes, with sons Amos, John and Joseph and daughters Mary Carter, Frances Boyd and Elizabeth Tims. So that will was the older Joseph's, the husband of Mary Glover, and the son Joseph it names was very probably the Joseph Tims whose will of 1844 left land and a woman named Mary to 'my son Vincent Brown Tims.' If that is right, Vincent's grandparents were Joseph and Mary (Glover) Tims, and Amos and Frances were his great-grandparents.

Three things are unsettled. Later accounts called V. B. Tims a man of Irish descent, while the Bible puts the family's origin in Northamptonshire. The family dates survive only in a typed copy of the Bible made from a photostat, and several of the year digits are lost. The Amos Timms who died in Chester in 1831, leaving his plantation to a sister Johannah, cannot be Joseph's son Amos, who married Mary Cabeen, went west to Alabama and lived until 1867; who he was is not yet known.

The older Joseph Tims made his will on 26 July 1801, 'weak in body but of sound and perfect mind', and was dead within weeks; it was proved on 4 September 1801. He divided the people he held among his children: Jesse to Amos, Nathaniel to John, Jeremiah to Joseph, Hannah to Sarah Estes, Dinah to Mary Carter, Lucey to Frances Boyd, and Ned and Jude to Elizabeth, the youngest. To his son Joseph he left all the land he owned. Everything else went to his 'beloved wife Mary' for her lifetime, and he made Mary and Amos his executors. After signing, he had John Pratt add a note giving Elizabeth twenty pounds more, since she was only twelve or thirteen.

Mary outlived him by twenty-four years. When she died in November 1825, Amos was still the executor, and his brother-in-law William Estes, Sarah's husband, came into court as his attorney to have what she had held appraised and sold. Settling up was not peaceful. In June 1827 the neighbors were called to the Court of Ordinary to testify. Eli Cornwell told how the old lady's accounts were shown to 'Jos Tims after the death of his mother Mary Tims', and how Joseph agreed that they were just. Amos Tims gave his account too. Mrs. Roda Cornwell remembered what Mary had told her a few days before she died: that she had already paid her daughter Elizabeth, now Mrs. Brown, the twenty pounds in clothing and schooling; that Brown had written her a very insulting letter and then a friendly one taking it back; that someone had broken open her chest and taken papers; and that she expected Vincent Brown to make a fuss about the money once she was gone.

Those few pages do what the Bible could not. They prove that Joseph and Mary Tims of Chester had a son Joseph who was still living near his mother in the 1820s, and they bring onto the record the uncle whose name Joseph's son Vincent Brown Tims carried west.
